title: Introducing Beautiful Bleep
text: Beautiful Bleep is a digital modular synthesizer. Instead of one fixed instrument you get small sound building blocks (oscillators, filters, envelopes, effects) and connect them with virtual cables to build your own sounds. If you would rather not patch, you can play one of the ready-made instruments and effects and never touch a cable. It is free, open source, and very new. This post is a tour of what is in it today, with links to everything you can try. One engine, three places The same engine, the same modules and the same project files run in three places. A project you start in one place opens in the others, and the three can exchange audio, MIDI and tempo. Ways to use Beautiful Bleep explains how they fit together. In your browser Bleep Play needs no install and no account. Open the board, pick an instrument or start from an empty canvas, and you are making sound within seconds. When the board needs a module it has not seen yet, it fetches the module from the Bleep Library, checks it and runs it, so a visitor needs nothing installed. That makes the browser the easiest way to try Beautiful Bleep and to share a project: send a link and the other person hears what you hear. It does not have every module yet, and the board page lists what is missing. If you are curious, play now or browse the instruments and effects that open directly in it. In Ableton Live The Bleep plugins are VST3 plugins for Ableton Live. Put Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track or Bleep FX on an audio track, pick a preset and play. All the modules of a set live on one canvas, the board, and small plugins called ports connect the board to your tracks. This is where Beautiful Bleep is meant to feel like part of your music rather than a separate tool: a modular system that sits inside your project, saved with your set. The install guide walks through the steps, and Your first sound gets you to a note without any patching. You can get the plugins on the download page. As a standalone app The Bleep App is the board without a DAW. It is for playing, sound design and live use, and it can sit next to Live and trade MIDI, audio and tempo with the plugins. It also acts as the hub between the three places, so that a plugin in Live can send its audio through Bleep Play in your browser. If you prefer to keep the DAW out of the way while you patch, or you want a fixed instrument on stage, this is the place. The standalone app covers setup, and Connecting plugin, app and Bleep Play has the recipes and the latency numbers. Playing it with a MIDI controller A MIDI keyboard or a box of knobs works in all three places. In the standalone app and in the browser you add a MIDI Device node, choose your controller, and cable its notes into a synth; its eight controller outputs turn your knobs into modulation. In the browser this needs Chrome or Edge, which ask once for permission to use your MIDI devices. In Live, the controller plays a Bleep plugin like any other instrument. Play with a MIDI controller has the steps for each. More than patch cables A modular synthesizer is wonderful to build and awkward to play. Beautiful Bleep adds three things on top of the cables to fix that. Custom UIs with panels A patch with forty modules is hard to read and harder to play. Select some modules, press ⌘G , and they become a cell that hides the wiring behind a few jacks. Cells can be saved as presets, so a patch you build once becomes a module you reuse everywhere. Then give the cell a panel : a front panel with just the dials, faders, buttons, keyboard, XY pad and meters that matter. A panel has an Interface view for playing and a Wiring view for building, and a control can load another panel, which is how large instruments are split into tabs. Cells and panels are what turn a tangle of cables into something that plays like an instrument; see Cells and panels, and Voice Cells for polyphonic synths. Bleep Script Bleep Script lets you write parts of a patch as code. A Code node on the board has an editor and a Compile button. Write a class with a sample() method and the node becomes a new module with its own jacks, dials and meters; write a patch script and it builds a whole cell of modules and cables for you, for example a hundred oscillators from a loop. In Bleep Play, Bleep Script needs no installation: no toolchain, no setup. The compiler runs in your browser and compiles all the code right there, in about a second, so you can open the board, write a script and hear it. Scripts can also route messages: handlers for notes and control edges run at their exact sample, so timing stays tight. Modules are written in AssemblyScript, a TypeScript-like language that compiles to WebAssembly,. Start with the overview or the quickstart, and follow the tutorials from a sine oscillator up to a step sequencer. Bleep Assistant The Bleep Assistant is a chat window in the board where an AI agent helps with your patch. It answers questions from the documentation, finds out why there is no sound, adds and wires modules, builds panels, programs sequencers and designs a sound from scratch ("build an acid synthesizer") step by step, using tools instead of just replying. You stay in control. Every change is a visible changeset that the board applies as one undo step, you can approve it first, and the model never writes raw patch data: it calls typed operations that are checked against the module catalog before anything reaches the board. The assistant is measured with a benchmark. How the assistant works describes the design, and the benchmark page shows how it is tested. Modules and the Bleep Library Beautiful Bleep ships with over a hundred modules in categories from oscillators, envelopes and filters to sequencers, drum machines, logic and metering. Each one has a manual, with demo patches and presets that show what it does, and the manuals are the same pages the board shows behind each module's ? button. Modules, plugins and presets live in the Bleep Library, where anyone can browse and download without logging in. Modules are WebAssembly packages that run in a sandbox, so the library is also how third parties can add modules. Sharing a preset needs a free account. How the library works explains packages and releases, and Write a module shows how to contribute one. Under the hood: Bleep Bus The cables between the Bleep plugins run on Bleep Bus, an open, MIT-licensed protocol with a small C SDK. It sends per-sample control signals between audio plugins through named shared memory, which is what lets a modulation signal from one plugin reach another in your DAW. It works between any plugins in any DAW and does not need Beautiful Bleep at all. The protocol has a public specification, a conformance suite to prove an implementation correct, and an RFC process for changes, so anyone can build on it. Try the quickstart, read the specification or look at the overview. Where to go next If you are a musician, play in your browser, then follow Your first sound and Your first patch. The musician documentation covers the rest. If you are a developer, start from the developer overview. The code is on GitHub; this is a young project, so feedback is very welcome, through the contact form or an issue on GitHub.

title: What is planned for Beautiful Bleep
text: Beautiful Bleep is new, and most of what it will become is not built yet. The introduction described what you can use today. This post is the other half: what we plan to build, roughly in the order we think about it, and what is still open. Nothing here is a promise or a date. These are plans, and they change when we learn what people need. If one of them matters to you, tell us through the contact form or on GitHub. That is the best way to move something up the list. Plugins for other DAWs Today the Bleep plugins are VST3 plugins, and Ableton Live is the host we build and test against. The plan is to make Beautiful Bleep a good citizen in more DAWs: More formats. VST3 covers many hosts, but not all of them. Logic and GarageBand on the Mac need an Audio Unit, and some people would like CLAP. The plugins are built on JUCE, which makes the extra formats a packaging job rather than a rewrite. Testing in more hosts. A plugin that loads is not the same as a plugin that behaves. Hosts differ in how they save state, how they treat several instances of one plugin, and how they schedule audio. We want to test the Instrument, FX, Board and port plugins in the other major DAWs, and write down what works and what does not, the way the install guide does for Live. Windows and Linux. The apps and the Bleep Bus reference implementation already build for Windows, and the standalone app has audio capture for Windows and Linux. The plugins for those systems need more testing before we call them supported. The part we are most curious about is Bleep Bus, the protocol that lets one plugin send control signals to another. It does not depend on Ableton Live, so the cables between plugins should work in any DAW that can host two plugins at once. Whether a given host allows that is one of the things the testing will tell us. A closer bridge to Ableton Live Right now Live and Beautiful Bleep meet at the plugin: Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track, Bleep FX on an audio track, and ports that carry signals between the board and your tracks. Tempo and transport follow Live. We would like the two to know more about each other. The ideas on the table are: Live's parameters on the board. Automate a Bleep dial from a Live clip, or send a Bleep signal back as something Live can map to. Sessions that stay in sync. Open a Live set and have its Bleep board, presets and ports come back as you left them, without a manual step in the standalone app. Less setup. Today the app has to be running for some connections, and the cables between several plugins need the Bleep Board plugin in the set. A bridge should make the common case work with fewer steps. How this is built is still open. It could be a Max for Live device, it could grow out of the existing plugins, or it could be a mix. We would rather hear how you use Live with Bleep before we choose, so this is the item where your feedback counts most. Instruments and effects in the app and the browser In Live, you can pick an instrument or an effect preset and never see a cable. In the Bleep App and in Bleep Play you currently start from the full board. The table of ways to play lists the Instrument and Effect modes there as planned. The goal is that you can open Bleep Play, pick Slate Stabs or Dub Ping-Pong , and play it with a panel in front of you, the same as in Live, and press Open Board when you want to look inside. Bleep Play catches up The browser version runs the same projects as the plugins, but a few things are not ported yet: Voice Cells, the Harmony bus, Ableton Link, Macros, audio input, MIDI out to a host, and the media folder that sample-based modules use. Some of these need a browser feature that does not exist everywhere, and some are just work. Bringing them across is what lets you start a project in the browser and finish it in Live without losing anything. Safari is on the list too. Bleep Play works best in Chrome and Edge today, and a browser that handles audio and MIDI differently needs its own testing. Playing together across computers Everything is on one machine for now. The plugin, the app and Bleep Play can talk to each other, but only on the same computer. A shared session, such as a web board on your phone or a friend playing your synth, needs a server between the computers. Sending notes over the internet is easy. Sending audio live is limited by the delay of the network, and no setting hides that. So the first version will focus on what works well at a distance: shared boards, shared presets, notes and control signals. Live audio between two rooms is a different problem, and we will be honest about its limits. Getting sound out as a file Rendering a Bleep sound into an audio file is easy in a DAW, which can bounce or freeze a track. It is harder from the browser, where there is no DAW. We plan to add an export and freeze path so that something you make in Bleep Play can end up as a file, or as a clip in your project, without a recording workaround. Modules, the library and the assistant A synthesizer is only as good as what you can patch with, so a large part of the plan is to grow the Bleep Library: More modules , from us and from other developers, with a manual, demo patches and presets for each one. Easier sharing. Sandboxed modules already let third parties publish safely. We want to make it simpler to take a patch from your board, turn it into a module and share it, with a picture, a description and its source. A better Bleep Assistant. The assistant is measured with a benchmark, and the benchmark is how we decide what to improve: harder tasks, more kinds of sounds, and fewer wrong turns. Other models and ways to run it, including offline, are things we want to try. More of Bleep Script. More built-in helpers, more tutorials, and better error messages. Smaller rough edges Some items are small, but they are the ones that make a tool pleasant to live with: Signed and notarized builds, so the system stops warning you about an unknown developer when you install. A more helpful first run, with clearer messages when a plugin cannot find the app or a module is missing. More documentation: more recipes for connecting the plugin, the app and the browser, and more walkthroughs for the modules. What is not on the list We do not plan to turn Beautiful Bleep into a DAW. It is meant to sit inside the music software you already use, or next to it, and to be a modular instrument that you can play. Anything that makes it a better instrument is welcome. Anything that makes it a worse DAW is not. Help decide This list is short on purpose, and the order is not fixed. If you want Bleep in a particular DAW, a particular kind of bridge to Live, or a module we do not have, write to us or open an issue on GitHub. If you would rather build it yourself, the code is open, the developer documentation has the way in, and the Bleep Bus quickstart is a good place to start.

title: API reference
text: Bleep Bus API reference (spec v0.1) The complete reference for plugin developers using the SDK: concepts, lifecycle, every function, type and error code, the C++ and JUCE helpers, host notes, pitfalls and the conformance checklist. The source of truth is the commented header bus/include/bleep bus.h ; CI checks that every function in it is documented here. Language: plain C99 API, usable from C, C++, Rust, Zig, Swift … Linking: one static library ( bleep bus ), no dependencies. License: MIT. Link it into closed-source plugins freely. Thread markers used below: [RT] real-time safe: no locks, no allocation, no system calls. Call it from the audio thread. [non-RT] may lock or allocate. Never call it from the audio thread.

title: Concepts
text: Concepts Term Meaning Bus One shared-memory segment per namespace ( default unless set). Open one handle per plugin instance, or share one per process. Endpoint One registered plugin instance, with a stable 64-bit UID that you save in the plugin state. Output A named signal an endpoint publishes every block. Input A named destination. It sums all cables into it. Cable (source UID, output name, amount) , stored with the receiving input. Block One audio callback (≤ 4096 samples), framed by bb begin block / bb end block . Signal conventions Type Range Notes BB SIGNAL CONTROL −1..+1 (bipolar) or 0..1 (unipolar) declare polarity per output BB SIGNAL GATE high ≥ 0.5 BB SIGNAL TRIGGER single sample of 1.0 take the max when decimating BB SIGNAL PITCH 1.0 per octave, 0 = C4 (MIDI 60) Latency A reader gets each source's block for the reader's previous block: exactly one block late, whatever order the host runs the tracks in. That keeps renders deterministic, including offline export. Don't use the bus for phase-critical audio. Applying modulation Apply an input as an offset in the parameter's normalised range, inside your DSP. Never move the host parameter. float base = knob normalised; / what the user set / uint32 t n sources = bb read input(cutoff in, mod, n); for (uint32 t i = 0; i 1.f ? 1.f : v; cutoff hz[i] = 20.f powf(1000.f, v); / exponential mapping = octaves / }

title: Lifecycle
text: Lifecycle constructor bb bus open → bb register instance → bb add output / bb add input restore state bb set instance uid(saved uid) → bb load connections(saved text) audio callback bb begin block → bb read input … bb write output → bb end block save state bb endpoint uid → bb save connections UI / timer bb list outputs (source menus), bb connect / bb disconnect, bb endpoint patch version (mark the set dirty) destructor bb unregister instance → bb bus close Rules: Register in the constructor with UID 0 (a fresh UID), so the instance is on the bus before the host restores its state. When the host restores state, call bb set instance uid with the saved UID. If it returns BB ERR UID IN USE , the user duplicated the device: keep the fresh UID, and still load the saved cables. Add all inputs before bb load connections . Save bb endpoint uid (not the UID you asked for) and the bb save connections text in your plugin state. Poll bb endpoint patch version on the message thread a few times per second. When it changes, tell the host your state changed. In JUCE: updateHostDisplay(ChangeDetails().withNonParameterStateChanged(true)) . Unregister before closing the bus.

title: Bus functions
text: Bus functions bb bus open bb bus bb bus open(uint32 t spec version, const char bus namespace, bb error err); Opens the bus segment, creating it if needed. [non-RT] spec version : pass BB SPEC VERSION . bus namespace : NULL for the environment variable BLEEP BUS NAMESPACE , else "default" . Otherwise 1–16 characters from [a-z0-9 -] . err : optional. Returns a handle, or NULL . Errors: BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH (you or the existing segment speak another version), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR SHARED MEMORY , BB ERR CORRUPT , BB ERR TIMEOUT . bb error err; bb bus bus = bb bus open(BB SPEC VERSION, NULL, &err); if (!bus) log("bus offline: %s", bb error string(err)); / keep working without it / bb bus close void bb bus close(bb bus bus); Unmaps the bus. Unregister all endpoints opened through it first. NULL is ignored. [non-RT] bb bus unlink bb error bb bus unlink(const char bus namespace); Removes the named segment from the operating system. For tools and tests only. Processes that still map it keep using the old segment. On Windows this is a no-op; the mapping disappears with its last handle. [non-RT] bb generate uid uint64 t bb generate uid(void); Returns a random, non-zero 64-bit UID. [non-RT] bb error string const char bb error string(bb error err); Static English text for an error code. [RT]

title: Endpoint functions
text: Endpoint functions bb register instance bb endpoint bb register instance(bb bus bus, const bb instance info info, bb error err); Registers a plugin instance. [non-RT] bb instance info info = BB INSTANCE INFO INIT; / sets struct size / info.uid = 0; / 0 = generate / info.display name = "Function"; / user-facing; may be NULL / info.track name = NULL; / if known / info.vendor = "Brilliant Bleep"; info.product = "Function"; bb endpoint ep = bb register instance(bus, &info, &err); If info.uid is already live, a fresh UID is used. The endpoint is still returned, and err is BB ERR UID IN USE . Endpoints of crashed processes are reclaimed here. Names are truncated at a UTF-8 boundary. Errors: BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR FULL (64 endpoints), BB ERR TIMEOUT . bb unregister instance void bb unregister instance(bb endpoint ep); Removes the instance, its ports and the cables into its inputs. Cables from its outputs stay with their receivers and read silence until the UID returns. Frees ep . [non-RT] Removing ports is not safe while audio runs. bb unregister instance MUST NOT overlap bb begin block , bb write output , bb read input or bb end block on the same endpoint; stop audio processing first. (Adding ports is safe, see Ports.) bb endpoint uid uint64 t bb endpoint uid(const bb endpoint ep); The current UID. Save this one. [RT] bb endpoint bus bb bus bb endpoint bus(const bb endpoint ep); The bus the endpoint belongs to. [RT] bb set instance uid bb error bb set instance uid(bb endpoint ep, uint64 t uid); Switches to a saved UID after state restore. [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR UID IN USE (another live endpoint owns it; nothing changes), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT (0), BB ERR NOT FOUND . bb set instance name bb error bb set instance name(bb endpoint ep, const char display name); Sets the user-facing name shown in other plugins' source menus. [non-RT] bb set track name bb error bb set track name(bb endpoint ep, const char track name); Sets the host track name if your plugin learns it (JUCE: updateTrackProperties ). That callback may come on any thread, so store the name and apply it from your message thread. [non-RT] bb endpoint patch version uint32 t bb endpoint patch version(const bb endpoint ep); Increases whenever any process changes a cable into this endpoint. Poll it and mark your state as changed when it moves. [RT]

title: Port functions
text: Port functions bb add output bb output bb add output(bb endpoint ep, const char name, bb signal type type, bb polarity polarity, bb error err); Adds an output. [non-RT] name : 1–31 bytes UTF-8, no control characters, no / , unique among this endpoint's outputs. Keep it short and stable ( "A" , "EOC" , "Env" ), because cables refer to it by name. type : BB SIGNAL CONTROL , GATE , TRIGGER or PITCH . AUDIO is reserved. Errors: BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT , BB ERR ALREADY EXISTS , BB ERR FULL . Outputs live until the endpoint is unregistered. Adding a port while audio runs is safe: the port is published to the audio thread with release/acquire ordering. Removing ports is not (see bb unregister instance ). bb add input bb input bb add input(bb endpoint ep, const char name, bb signal type type, bb error err); Adds an input, with the same naming rules. Name a parameter's modulation input after the parameter ( "Cutoff" ). [non-RT]

title: Audio-thread functions
text: Audio-thread functions typedef struct bb block info { uint32 t struct size; / BB BLOCK INFO INIT / uint32 t num samples; / 1..4096 / int64 t transport sample pos; / host position of the first sample / double sample rate; uint32 t flags; / BB BLOCK PLAYING / uint64 t host time ns; / 0 = library clock / } bb block info; bb begin block void bb begin block(bb endpoint ep, const bb block info info); Starts a block. [RT] Split host blocks larger than BB MAX BLOCK SAMPLES into sub-blocks and advance transport sample pos for each. Set BB BLOCK PLAYING whenever the transport runs, offline export included. The deterministic timing rule depends on it. bb write output void bb write output(bb output out, const float samples, uint32 t num samples); Publishes this block's samples. [RT] A shorter write holds its last sample to the end of the block. A second call in the same block overwrites. Outputs you don't write publish zeros. bb read input uint32 t bb read input(bb input in, float dest, uint32 t num samples); Fills dest with Σ (source × amount) over all cables. [RT] Returns the number of cables whose source is present. Use it to tell "unpatched" from "patched but zero". Each source arrives one block late (see Concepts). If the source has no suitable block, its last value is held. bb end block void bb end block(bb endpoint ep); Ends the block. [RT] bb block info b = BB BLOCK INFO INIT; b.num samples = n; b.sample rate = sr; b.transport sample pos = pos; b.flags = playing ? BB BLOCK PLAYING : 0; bb begin block(ep, &b); bb read input(rate in, rate mod, n); render lfo(lfo, rate mod, n); bb write output(lfo out, lfo, n); bb end block(ep);

title: Connection functions
text: Connection functions Cables are stored with the receiving input in shared memory, so any process can edit them. The receiver saves them with its state. bb connect bb error bb connect(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name, uint64 t src uid, const char output name, float amount); Adds a cable, or updates the amount if the cable already exists. [non-RT] The destination must be registered. The source doesn't need to be: the cable reads silence until it appears. The amount is clamped to ±1000. Errors: BB ERR NOT FOUND (no such destination input), BB ERR FULL (8 cables per input), BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT . bb connect(bus, filter uid, "Cutoff", lfo uid, "A", -0.3f); bb disconnect bb error bb disconnect(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name, uint64 t src uid, const char output name); Removes one cable. [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR NOT FOUND . bb disconnect all bb error bb disconnect all(bb bus bus, uint64 t dst uid, const char input name); Removes every cable into an input. [non-RT]

title: Discovery functions
text: Discovery functions Each list function copies up to capacity records and returns the total available. Call it with capacity = 0 to size a buffer. Records are ordered by table slot, which is stable while the bus runs. All are [non-RT] . bb list endpoints uint32 t bb list endpoints(bb bus bus, bb endpoint info dest, uint32 t capacity); bb endpoint info : uid , pid , num outputs , num inputs , display name , track name , vendor , product . bb list outputs uint32 t bb list outputs(bb bus bus, bb output info dest, uint32 t capacity); Every output on the bus with its owner's names. This is what a source menu shows. bb output info : endpoint uid , type , polarity , name , endpoint name , track name . bb list inputs uint32 t bb list inputs(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, bb input info dest, uint32 t capacity); The inputs of one endpoint, with num connections . bb list connections uint32 t bb list connections(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, const char input name, bb connection info dest, uint32 t capacity); The cables into one input. bb connection info : source uid , amount , output name , source present (0 for a ghost source). bb registry generation uint32 t bb registry generation(const bb bus bus); Changes whenever an endpoint or port appears, disappears or is renamed. Cache your lists and refresh them when it changes. [RT] bb connection generation uint32 t bb connection generation(const bb bus bus); Changes whenever any cable on the bus changes. [RT] bb peek output uint32 t bb peek output(bb bus bus, uint64 t endpoint uid, const char output name, float dest, uint32 t capacity); Copies the newest completed block of any output, e.g. for a scope. Returns the number of samples copied (0 if the output doesn't exist).

title: State functions
text: State functions bb save connections size t bb save connections(bb endpoint ep, void buf, size t cap); Writes all cables into this endpoint's inputs as NUL-terminated UTF-8 text. Returns the bytes needed, including the NUL. If that exceeds cap , nothing is written. [non-RT] size t n = bb save connections(ep, NULL, 0); char text = malloc(n); bb save connections(ep, text, n); / store text next to your parameters / Format (tab-separated, locale-independent): bleep-bus-connections 1 Cutoff 0123456789abcdef A -0.300000 bb load connections bb error bb load connections(bb endpoint ep, const void buf, size t len); Replaces all cables into this endpoint's inputs with the saved ones. Add your inputs first. Lines for unknown inputs are skipped. Loading does not change bb endpoint patch version . [non-RT] Errors: BB ERR PARSE .

title: Types, constants and errors
text: Types, constants and errors Constants Name Value Meaning BB SPEC VERSION BB MAKE SPEC VERSION(0, 1) pass to bb bus open BB MAX ENDPOINTS 64 per bus BB MAX OUTPUTS 256 per bus BB MAX INPUTS 512 per bus BB MAX CONNECTIONS PER INPUT 8 BB MAX PORTS PER ENDPOINT 64 outputs, and inputs, each BB MAX BLOCK SAMPLES 4096 split larger blocks BB NAME BYTES 64 endpoint/track name field, incl. NUL BB PORT NAME BYTES 32 port name field, incl. NUL BB BLOCK PLAYING 1 bb block info.flags Errors Code Value When BB OK 0 BB ERR INVALID ARGUMENT 1 NULL, bad name or namespace, NaN amount BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH 2 incompatible spec version (yours or the segment's) BB ERR SHARED MEMORY 3 the OS refused the segment (sandbox?) BB ERR CORRUPT 4 the segment is not a Bleep Bus segment BB ERR FULL 5 a table is full BB ERR NOT FOUND 6 no such endpoint, input or cable BB ERR ALREADY EXISTS 7 port name taken BB ERR UID IN USE 8 UID owned by another live endpoint BB ERR TIMEOUT 9 registry lock or initialisation took > 2 s BB ERR PARSE 10 saved cable text is malformed A plugin MUST keep working (passing audio, using its knobs) when the bus is unavailable.

title: C++ and JUCE helpers
text: C++ and JUCE helpers bus/wrappers/cpp/bleep bus.hpp is a header-only C++17 RAII wrapper. Each method maps to one C function and has the same thread rules. #include "bleep bus.hpp" bleep::Bus bus; // bb bus open bleep::Endpoint ep(bus, "Bass Wobble", "Function", "Me"); // bb register instance bleep::Output a = ep.addOutput("A", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, BB POLARITY UNIPOLAR); bleep::Input rate = ep.addInput("Rate"); for (const bb output info& o : bus.outputs()) { / source menu / } bus.connect(ep.uid(), "Rate", otherUid, "Out", 0.5f); std::string saved = ep.saveConnections(); bus/wrappers/juce/bleep bus juce.h fills bb block info from JUCE's play head and splits large blocks: #include #include "bleep bus juce.h" void processBlock(juce::AudioBuffer & buffer, juce::MidiBuffer&) override { auto t = bleep::juce helpers::readTransport(getPlayHead(), fallbackPos); fallbackPos += buffer.getNumSamples(); bleep::juce helpers::forEachBusBlock(t, getSampleRate(), buffer.getNumSamples(), & { endpoint.beginBlock(info); rate.read(rateMod.data(), info.num samples); renderLfo(lfo.data(), rateMod.data(), info.num samples); a.write(lfo.data(), info.num samples); endpoint.endBlock(); }); } CMake: add subdirectory(path/to/bleep/bus) and link bleep bus cpp . That target brings in the C library and both wrapper folders.

title: Host notes and pitfalls
text: Host notes Ableton Live hosts plugins in one process and runs tracks on parallel threads. Each track keeps its own transport stamps, so the position rule applies. MIDI generated by a plugin is only routable from VST3 instruments: use the "MIDI From" routing of a second MIDI track. Bitwig can sandbox plugins in separate processes. The bus is shared memory, so this works. All processes must use the same namespace. Logic / AUv3 sandbox: sandboxed app extensions may not open POSIX shared memory. bb bus open then fails with BB ERR SHARED MEMORY ; keep working without the bus. Offline export runs faster than real time. Report BB BLOCK PLAYING and the true transport position, and timing stays exact. Pitfalls Calling [non-RT] functions on the audio thread. bb connect , the list functions and registration take a cross-process lock. Saving the requested UID instead of bb endpoint uid . After a device duplication they differ. Loading cables before adding inputs. Unknown inputs are skipped. Moving host parameters to show modulation. Apply modulation inside the DSP and draw it in your UI instead. Assuming zero latency. Feedback through the bus adds one block per pass. Renaming outputs between versions breaks users' cables. Treat port names as API. Forgetting BB BLOCK PLAYING . Without it, timing falls back to the wall-clock rule, which isn't deterministic during export.

title: Conformance checklist
text: Conformance checklist Before you call your plugin "Bleep Bus compatible": [ ] Opens the bus with BB SPEC VERSION and keeps working when it is unavailable. [ ] Registers one endpoint per instance and saves bb endpoint uid in its state. [ ] Restores the saved UID with bb set instance uid and handles BB ERR UID IN USE . [ ] Saves and restores cables with bb save connections / bb load connections . [ ] Frames every audio block with begin/end, ≤ 4096 samples, true transport position and BB BLOCK PLAYING . [ ] Calls only [RT] functions on the audio thread. [ ] Applies modulation as a normalised offset without moving host parameters. [ ] Watches bb endpoint patch version and marks its state as changed. [ ] Unregisters in its destructor. [ ] Uses stable, short port names; parameter inputs are named after the parameter. [ ] bb conformance run passes against the library build you ship. See Conformance for running the suite and the validator.

title: Standalone app
text: Standalone app The Bleep App is the same engine, board and modules as the plugins, without a DAW. Besides the board it adds projects, a preset browser, an audio device, system audio, its own MIDI ports, Ableton Link and the servers that connect it to Live and to the browser. Prerequisites CMake 3.22 or newer, a C++ compiler (Xcode command line tools on macOS, Visual Studio on Windows), optionally Ninja, and JUCE 8.0.9 (downloaded on the first build, or --juce / BLEEP JUCE DIR ). The first build also fetches Ableton Link 4.1. Build and run ./bleep run app # Release build, then start with console output here ./bleep run app my-project.bleepboard # open a project ./bleep run app --no-build # start the last build ./bleep run app --smoke # no audio inputs or Link; print a report and quit ./bleep run app --ui-dev # read the board UI from patch/; ⌘R after an edit Without the script: cmake -S patch -B build/patch -DCMAKE BUILD TYPE=Release -DBLEEP JUCE DIR=… , then cmake --build build/patch --target BleepApp . The result is build/patch/BleepApp artefacts/Release/Bleep App.app (macOS) or an executable in the same folder on Windows. CMake option Default Effect BLEEP BUILD APP ON Build the standalone app BLEEP LINK ON Include Ableton Link. This makes the app binary GPL. Turn it off for a build that must stay MIT BLEEP UI DEV OFF Development only: the UI comes from the source tree. Never ship BLEEP LINK DIR unset Use a local Link checkout instead of downloading it What the app adds Projects and presets: .bleepboard projects; a preset browser with five demo boards for every advanced module and your own boards. Audio and MIDI: channel pairs of the audio device become In 1/2 , Out 1/2 … ports. The app creates its own MIDI ports ( Bleep App 1…n ), which Live can use as MIDI From and MIDI To . System audio: what the computer plays, as a System node. Core Audio tap on macOS 14.2+, WASAPI loopback on Windows, PulseAudio or PipeWire monitor on Linux (needs libpulse at build time). Ableton Link: the Link node puts tempo, beat, bar, clock and start/stop on the board. Bleep Audio Bridge: each bridge plugin in Live is a node with Send and Return ; while bridges are connected, Live's audio blocks drive the app. Settings: File → Settings (⌘,) has Audio, MIDI and sync, Web, Library and Security; plugins and Bleep Play have their own tabs (design: doc/specs/settings.md in the repository; for musicians: Settings). The module update check at start is updateCheck in the library's settings.json , shared with the plugins. Web connection: off by default. File → Settings → Web listens on 127.0.0.1:47100 for Bleep Play pages and for plugins whose Board is Bleep Play . BLEEP WEB PORT= turns it on for one run; BLEEP WEB ROOT= makes the app serve Bleep Play from a folder scripts/build/build-web.sh wrote. Checks before you hand out a build ./bleep build plugins # plugins and tests; the app is built from the same tree ./bleep run app --smoke On macOS, start the smoke run with --system-audio through LaunchServices ( open -W … --args --smoke --system-audio ), or the audio permission is not the app's and the capture stays silent. Licences and signing Link is GPLv2-or-later , so app binaries built with it are distributed under the GPL with their source. A closed-source build needs a licence from Ableton, or -DBLEEP LINK=OFF (the app then uses an internal clock). JUCE is AGPLv3 or commercial. No script here signs or notarises the app. A downloaded unsigned macOS build is blocked by Gatekeeper until it is signed with a Developer ID and notarised; users of unsigned builds follow Installing unsigned builds. The app is released to the Bleep Library like the plugins. Modules in the app The app loads modules from the Bleep Library as .wasm files, through an embedded WebAssembly runtime. See the Module ABI and the Bleep Library.

title: How a turn works
text: How a turn works A turn is one user message and everything the assistant does about it. The code is agent/src/bleep agent/runner.py ( run chat ). A request with messages and a board snapshot is routed to a skill by keywords. The skill sets the prompt and the tools. The agent loop builds instructions, calls the model, and the model either answers in text or calls read, write or live tools. Read and write tool results go back to the model; live tools pause the run. Events stream to the board. 1. The request POST /api/agent/chat carries the conversation as plain text, a snapshot (the board as JSON, the selected module ids, optional environment), the mode ( ask or auto ) and an optional skill hint. Everything the run needs is in it; nothing is stored between requests. 2. Route skills.route picks a skill from the last message. An explicit skill hint wins; otherwise keyword patterns decide, in this order: a "why is there no sound" pattern selects diagnose ; a question about Bleep (how, what, which...) selects docs , unless it says "for me" or "please"; then panel , compose , design and patch by their words; anything else is docs . Routing is plain code, not a model call, so it costs nothing and is easy to test. 3. The skill The skill fixes two things: the prompt (the shared base.md plus the skill's own file in prompts/ ) and the tools offered . Only the tools a skill uses are sent, because every tool definition is sent on every model call. See Skills and tools. 4. The agent loop The loop is Pydantic AI's. Each step: Build the instructions. Stable text comes first (base prompt, skill prompt, the mode, the module index and jacks-and-knobs sheet), volatile text last (the board right now , including changes made earlier in this run, and a step warning). The model API caches the longest unchanged prefix of a request, so this order makes every step after the first cheaper. Call the model with the tools of the skill. Read the response. If it has tool calls, run them and loop. If it is plain text, that is the answer and the run ends. The three kinds of tool behave differently: Kind Runs Result Read ( describe module , search docs , trace signal ...) In Python, against the run's working copy of the patch, the catalog and the indexes A value for the model, no round trip Write ( propose changes , set pattern , propose panel ...) In Python: the operation is applied to the working copy and validated A changeset event for the board, and a short result for the model. If validation fails the model gets the error and may retry Live ( get environment , probe signals , play , highlight , ask user ) In the browser The run pauses (below) Because writes are applied to the working copy first, the model sees the effect of its own edits within a run, and a changeset that does not validate is never sent. Lookups that were already answered A lookup repeated in the same run (the same describe module , the same read doc ) is not answered again: the tool returns a one-line note telling the model to use the earlier result, which keeps the large result out of the history a second time. The prompt also asks for independent lookups to be made together, several tool calls in one step. The step budget is a rule, not a request A run has at most agent max steps model calls (20 on the site). Telling the model to hurry is unreliable, so the tool list enforces it: in the last four steps only tools that change something remain (lookups disappear), and on the very last step no tools are offered at all, so the model can only answer in text and says what it did and what is still open. A run that nevertheless reaches the hard limit ends with the limit event. 5. Pause and resume for live tools Some answers exist only in the browser: whether signals move, which MIDI devices are connected, what the user picks from a question. The server does not hold a connection open for that. The model calls a live tool. The run ends with a live event per call and a pause event carrying a token . The token is an HMAC-signed, compressed copy of the run's message history and working copy, valid for 15 minutes. The browser executes the tool ( probe signals listens to engine state for up to two seconds, optionally with a test note) and sends a new request with resume: {token, results} and a fresh snapshot, which is the truth after anything the user did meanwhile. The server verifies the token, restores the history, hands the results to the model as the tool's output and the loop continues. ask user waits for a person for up to ten minutes; the other live tools are time-boxed to five seconds in the browser. 6. Events The turn is a stream of Server-Sent Events: Event Meaning run The run id, to fetch its log later activity A short status line for the chat ("Checking signal levels") text A piece of the answer changeset A proposed change: summary, operations, readable diff lines, whether it is destructive and whether it needs confirmation live , pause The browser must run tools and resume usage Tokens so far in this run and today error budget , rate , model , invalid or internal done final , pause , budget , error or limit A changeset needs confirmation when it is destructive, and for every changeset in ask mode. In auto mode the board applies the others as they arrive, as one undo step each, and the chat shows "Applied: ... (Undo)". run chat never raises: a failure becomes an error event followed by done , so the stream always ends cleanly. Prompt-injection Retrieved documents, presets, module names and patches are data . The base prompt says so: text inside them is never to be followed as an instruction. The tools the assistant has are the limit of what a hostile patch could make it do, which is why changes always pass through a changeset the user can see and undo.

title: Assistant architecture
text: Assistant architecture The chat panel in the board posts the message history and a snapshot of the board to the website API. The API checks sign-in, rate and the daily token budget, calls the bleep-agent library, and streams events back. The library holds the agent loop, the skills and tools, the patch model and the documentation search. It calls an LLM provider and reads built data files. The pieces The board (browser). The chat panel ( agent-chat.js ) sends the conversation and a snapshot of the board with every request, shows the streamed answer, and applies changesets to the real board as one undo step. It also runs the live tools , the few things only the browser can do: measure signals, play notes, highlight a jack, ask the user a question. The website API. A thin FastAPI router ( routers/agent.py ) mounted only when the assistant is enabled. It requires a signed-in user (the website's session cookie, or the library token of the standalone app and the Bleep Board plugin), applies a per-user rate limit and a daily token budget for the whole site, turns the library's events into a Server-Sent Events stream, and writes the run log. It holds no conversation state. The bleep-agent library. Everything that makes it an assistant, with no web code: the agent loop, the skills and tools, the patch model, the catalog, the documentation search. It is given a model by its caller and never imports a provider itself, so the site, the command line and the benchmark can use different models. The model provider. Gemini first, OpenAI for comparison. The library talks to it through Pydantic AI, wrapped in a metering layer that counts tokens after each call and refuses the call when the budget is gone. Built data. Three git-ignored files in website/api/agent data/ , produced by ./bleep build agent-data : File Holds Built from catalog.json Every module type: knobs with ranges and units, jacks with signal types, roles, typical wiring, pitfalls The engine's module registry ( demo-types.json ), each module's module.json , the signal compatibility rules presets.jsonl Example patches the assistant can study The factory presets docs.sqlite The documentation, chunked, with a keyword index and optional embeddings website/content/ and the module manuals; see Documentation search Design decisions One agent with skills, not several agents. Nearly every request works on one patch and builds on the previous turn, so a single conversation with shared context fits. A skill is a prompt plus a subset of tools; see Skills and tools. Stateless backend. The client sends the history and a snapshot with every request, so the API needs no session storage and any worker can serve any request. The price is a larger request (limits: 40 messages, 200 kB, a board of at most 150 kB; embedded sample audio is stripped from the snapshot). Pause and resume instead of a connection. When the model needs something only the browser can do, the run ends with a pause and a signed token; the browser answers in a new request. The server never waits on a browser. See How a turn works. Validate in Python, not in the prompt. The catalog is generated from the engine, so a jack that does not exist is refused immediately with a message that names the real ones. See Edits and changesets. Pydantic AI as the framework. The backend already uses Pydantic v2; the framework adds typed tools, validation with retries, streaming, external (deferred) tools and a test model, and supports the providers directly. Backend settings Settings use the BLEEP prefix and live in website/api/app/config.py . Setting Default Meaning agent enabled false Mounts the router. When off, GET /api/agent/status still answers {"enabled": false, "reason": "disabled"} ; the board keeps the Assistant button and its panel says the assistant is not available yet agent daily tokens 1,000,000 The site-wide daily budget; a run is refused with 429 when it is used up and reset at is the next UTC midnight agent model a Gemini flash model The model the site uses agent embed model gemini-embedding-2 Must equal the model in docs.sqlite , otherwise documentation search falls back to keywords only agent user per minute 6 Per-user rate limit agent max steps 20 The most model calls one run may make agent state secret random per process HMAC key for resume tokens; set it when running more than one worker Provider keys are the providers' own variables, GOOGLE API KEY and OPENAI API KEY . The run log Every run is logged so it can be debugged: the prompt, the board snapshot, every model call with the full messages sent and the usage, every tool call with its arguments and result, and every event. The log is a database table kept to the newest BLEEP AGENT LOG MESSAGES rows (0 turns it off). The board's Copy chat button exports the transcript plus the server's log for the runs in it as one JSON document ( format: bleep-assistant-chat ), and the benchmark writes the same shape for every case it runs. The log holds users' prompts and patches, so the privacy notice must say so. Further reading Formats and protocol, as built: doc/specs/agent.md Goals, reasoning and evaluation design: doc/agent-concept.md In the standalone app and the Bleep Board plugin The assistant is the same panel ( agent-chat.js ) everywhere. Bleep Play is a page of the website and calls /api/agent/… with the session cookie. The app and the plugin serve their page themselves, so the page cannot call the website: it goes through the native account calls ( patch/library/Account.cpp ) to the library address from the settings, with the personal token from the OS keychain. The answer is a stream, which the page pulls piece by piece ( streamStart , streamRead , streamCancel ); agent-chat.js wraps it in a standard Response , so the rest of the panel does not know which transport it uses. Signing in is the library login (device flow): the first time the panel opens without a login, a dialog shows a code to confirm on the website. Settings > Library has the same sign in and sign out; one login serves the app and every plugin. Instrument and FX plugin windows show only a cell's panel and have no assistant.

title: Benchmark and results
text: Benchmark and results Prompts and tools change how the assistant behaves in ways that are hard to predict, so every change is measured. The benchmark runs a fixed set of requests against the real agent loop and scores each result by code. The numbers on this page come from the report that bleep-agent eval compare writes to agent/evals/runs/compare.md . That file is generated and git-ignored; the results below are a snapshot of it from 2026-10-18 (five versions) and are not updated by a build. Cases run through a harness that calls the real agent loop with a simulated browser, with every model call going through a replay cache. Checks in code and an optional judge model score each run. Results and full logs go to a run folder. The lab notebook lists versions of the assistant with their run folders, and the compare command writes compare.md. What is measured A case is one user request on a known board, with checks that define success. There are 187 cases in six groups, one per skill, kept as YAML in agent/evals/cases/ / : Skill Cases How the cases are made Example of what must hold docs 32 Hand-written from the documentation, including 8 whose answer is not in it The right page is cited and the key fact stated; for the unanswerable ones the assistant says it does not know diagnose 45 Generated: a working preset is damaged on purpose (cable removed, module muted, knob closed, transport stopped) and kept only if the graph model confirms the damage silenced it The assistant names the cause and its changes make the patch audible again, with few unrelated changes patch 40 Generated from templates over the presets: insert effects, wire an LFO to the cutoff, add a MIDI keyboard, change a value The cables exist, the effects are in the requested order before the output, the patch is valid panel 25 Generated: build a panel, or organise a scrambled one Every wired knob is on a panel, and the panel is valid compose 25 Generated: melodies, bass lines, drum patterns with requested length, range and feel A pattern of the right length, pitch span and gate count, with a repeating motif and ties where asked design 20 Generated: build a sound from an empty board A connected chain from a source through a filter and a VCA to the output Each case also has a difficulty (58 easy, 99 medium, 30 hard) and tags. A run, and what counts as success The harness ( evals/harness.py ) runs a case the way a user would, with the browser simulated : Load the board, apply the damage if any, send the request. Run the real agent loop. Every changeset is applied to a copy of the board, as if the user approved it. When the model calls a live tool, the simulated client answers it from the graph model: probe signals reports from the simulation, get environment reports a running audio engine, ask user picks the first choice. The run is resumed, up to six times. Run the checks on the final board, the changesets, the tool calls and the answer text. A run is a success only if every check passes and there was no error. The checks are code, not opinion: audible , fixes fault , unrelated changes , cable , has path , fx before output , param range , layout , module added , valid patch , no state change (a question must not change the patch), text contains , cites , says unknown , tool used , panel valid , panel covers , pattern . An optional judge ( --judge ) scores the answer 1 to 5 against a rubric in evals/rubrics/ for what code cannot decide, such as musical quality or faithfulness to the docs. The judge is a pinned model with a fixed rubric and a structured verdict, and it sees the ground truth as context. The results below were run without a judge, so they measure what code can check. Reproducible and cheap to repeat Every model, judge and embedding call goes through a content-addressed cache ( .eval-cache/ , modes use , refresh , replay-only , off ). The key is the model, the repeat index, the messages, the tool definitions and the settings. An unchanged rerun costs nothing and reproduces its numbers; a changed prompt re-runs only the calls that depend on it. A replayed call keeps its recorded latency , so speed figures stay meaningful. Cost figures use a price table ( evals/prices.yaml ) and count provider-cached input tokens at their lower price. Every run is also logged in full under /logs/ / / .r .json and .md : the transcript, every model call with the messages sent, every tool call with arguments and result, and timestamps. It is the same shape as the chat's Copy chat export, and logs/index.md lists them. Reading the log of a failed case is how most fixes started. Running it .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval generate # regenerate evals/cases/ /generated.yaml .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval run --models gpt-6-luna --repeats 1 .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval report agent/evals/runs/ .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval retrieval --embed gemini-embedding-2 # documentation search on its own A full run calls a paid model API for every uncached case: 187 cases at one repeat is about 600 model calls. Use --skills docs or --limit 5 for a smoke test first, and --cache replay-only in CI, where a missing call fails instead of spending money. Versions and the lab notebook agent/evals/lab-notebook.json lists every version of the assistant that was benchmarked, oldest first: a name, the run folder of its benchmark and what changed since the previous version. The first entry is the baseline. Add an entry whenever you benchmark a new version. .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval compare # all versions in the notebook .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval compare --versions 1,3 # some of them .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent eval compare "Before=agent/evals/runs/ " "After=agent/evals/runs/ " The report is compared on the cases every run contains , so a version is not flattered by cases the others never saw ( --all-cases includes the rest). A version whose folder has no results yet is skipped. Results All runs so far used one model, gpt-6-luna , one repeat, no judge, on the same 187 cases. Five versions have been benchmarked. # Version Success Δ Check score Cost / request Tokens in / out per request Model calls / request Latency p50 / p95 1 First implementation 74% (68%-80%) 0.91 $0.0015 21,513 / 827 3.7 11.5s / 46.1s 2 Quick Wins 90% (85%-93%) +16 pp 0.96 $0.0015 21,007 / 760 3.6 11.8s / 35.4s 3 Motif tiling & lean lookups 91% (87%-95%) +17 pp 0.97 $0.0016 21,232 / 811 3.4 11.8s / 39.8s 4 Lean tools & citations 93% (88%-96%) +19 pp 0.97 $0.0015 19,195 / 828 3.4 10.3s / 39.0s 5 Flow layout 94% (89%-96%) +19 pp 0.97 $0.0015 19,236 / 770 3.2 9.5s / 30.5s The ranges are 95% confidence intervals (Wilson). With 187 runs they are about ±4 points, so only the jump from version 1 to 2 is clearly real. From version 2 onwards the steps are 1 to 3 points and the intervals overlap: the later versions are better than version 1, but the benchmark cannot rank them against each other. Cost. Every run is now priced with the provider's prompt cache accounted for (about half of the input tokens are cache hits), so the costs of all five versions are comparable. Cost per request is flat at about $0.0015; cost per success fell from $0.0021 to $0.0016 only because more requests succeed. One whole benchmark costs about $0.28 without any cache (a fresh run of version 5 cost $0.2757). Model time fell from 54 minutes to 42; at concurrency 4 a fresh run takes about 10 minutes of wall time. Tokens and speed. Input tokens fell 11% at version 4, when each skill was offered only its own tool definitions and the schemas were slimmed, and have stayed there. Calls per request fell from 3.7 to 3.2, p50 latency from 11.5 s to 9.5 s and p95 from 46 s to 30.5 s. Input is still about 19,000 tokens per request because each of the 3 to 4 calls repeats the instructions (prompt, module index, the board); that is why prompt caching matters more than shorter prompts. By skill Success rate, 187 runs per version. Skill Cases 1 2 3 4 5 Δ 1 to 5 compose 25 68% 68% 84% 96% 88% +20 pp design 20 80% 100% 100% 100% 100% +20 pp diagnose 45 84% 96% 98% 98% 96% +11 pp docs 32 62% 78% 81% 78% 81% +19 pp panel 25 56% 92% 92% 84% 96% +40 pp patch 40 85% 100% 92% 100% 100% +15 pp By difficulty Difficulty Cases 1 2 3 4 5 Δ 1 to 5 easy 58 93% 95% 93% 97% 95% +2 pp medium 99 68% 91% 90% 90% 95% +27 pp hard 30 60% 77% 93% 97% 87% +27 pp The gains are in the medium and hard cases; the easy ones were already solved. What each version changed Version 1 to 2 (+16 pp). Most of the gain came from fixing the assistant and the benchmark where they disagreed with reality, not from a better model: an unmute operation, so five muted-module diagnose cases pass ( set node data refuses muted ), embedded sample audio left out of the board snapshot (boards with a sample were refused as too large), the board in the instructions and no get patch calls, panels are rearranged and never trimmed (11 panel covers failures became 2), "Minor", "Aeolian" and "Ionian" understood as the scale they mean, unanswerable docs questions now say so ( says unknown : 8 failures became 2). Version 2 to 3 (+1 pp). set pattern tiles a short motif and accepts variations, which fixed seven compose cases (no repeating motif, no ties). It cost six: compose-07 , -09 and -17 missed the requested pitch span or length, and patch-insert-fx-02 , -14 and -16 no longer put the requested effects in order before the output. Net 9 improved, 6 regressed, 172 unchanged. Version 3 to 4 (+2 pp). Each skill is offered only its own tools, tool schemas are slimmed (25-58% smaller per skill), the docs tools return ready-made cite as links, set pattern requires a length so a motif is always tiled, and build panel completes an envelope section with all four stages. Two checks were also relaxed ( fx before output accepts the effects anywhere on a signal path into the output, docs-24 accepts the publishing page), so the effect-insertion and docs-24 cases are not strictly comparable with versions 1 to 3. Net 13 improved, 10 regressed, 164 unchanged: the citation, compose and effect-insertion cases came back, while three unanswerable docs questions and three panel cases failed. Version 4 to 5 (+1 pp). New modules are placed by code ( layout.py ) from their cables: flow runs left to right on the preset grid, voices are stacked as rows, nothing is placed on top of another module, and a prompt section gives layout guidelines. A new check, layout (no overlaps, at least 90% of the cables touching new modules run left to right), applies to 20 design and 34 patch cases; only run 5 was scored with it, and design and patch both stayed at 100%. Net 9 improved, 8 regressed, 170 unchanged. How much of the movement is noise Between versions 4 and 5, 17 cases changed outcome while the total moved by one. Several of the flips cannot be caused by a layout change: compose-01 , -07 and -21 flipped to a pattern-length or pitch-span failure, and docs-17 and docs-22 lost a fact in their text. With one repeat, a case near its pass boundary flips from run to run, so differences of a few points between versions, and the per-skill figures (n of 20 to 45), should be read as likely noise until a change is confirmed with --repeats 3 or more. The effects that repeat across versions are the real ones: the panel and muted-module fixes, and the docs says unknown and citation fixes. Failing in every run Two cases fail in every version. Case Why (latest run) docs-05 The page about voice cells is not cited and the fact "CV to Notes" is missing docs-unanswerable-05 Answers instead of admitting the documentation has no answer Whether a failure is the assistant's or the check's is decided from the case's log. Several early failures turned out to be the check (curly apostrophes, a waveform-specific jack name), and fixing a check is recorded in the notebook so the versions stay honest. Reading the compare report compare.md has these sections, in this order: Section Answers Versions and what changed The notebook entries, so the numbers sit next to their causes Runs Date, models, repeats, cost without cache, cost of that run, model time Summary The change from the baseline to the last version, per model Overall Success with its confidence interval, check score, tokens, provider cache hit rate, cost per request and per success, latency, calls, retried tool calls, errors By skill, By difficulty Where the change landed Tokens and speed by skill What each skill costs Failed checks by kind Which kind of check fails (for example compose: pattern ) Cases: A to B Every case that improved or regressed between consecutive versions, with why it fails now Case outcomes across all runs One grid of the cases that differ Failing in every run The list above Cost per success (cost divided by the share of requests that succeeded) is the number to watch when comparing models: a cheap model that fails often is not cheap. Limits of these results One model, one repeat. Models answer differently each time; use --repeats 3 or more before concluding that a small change helped, and read the confidence intervals. Code-checked, not heard. The checks prove that a patch is valid, audible and wired as asked, not that it sounds good. The graph model is an approximation by module role, not DSP. A real render of the patch is planned to replace it. Generated cases are close to the presets they come from. They test the assistant on known boards, not on the strange boards users build. The benchmark was tuned against. Fixes were made by reading failed cases of these 187, so the later versions are partly fitted to them. Add new cases when you fix a bug a user reports.

title: Documentation search
text: Documentation search The documentation is about 250,000 tokens: the musicians' and developers' pages in website/content and the manual of every module. That is too much to put into every prompt, in cost, in latency and against the daily token budget, so a documentation question runs a retrieval step : find the relevant chunks, hand only those to the model, and have it answer from them with links. Code: agent/src/bleep agent/docs index.py , embeddings.py ; the tools are search docs and read doc . At build time pages are split by heading into chunks of at most 450 tokens, each indexed for keywords and embedded, and stored in one SQLite file. At question time a keyword search and a vector search run, the rankings are merged by reciprocal rank fusion, and the top six chunks go to the model. Why two kinds of search The text is full of exact terms (module, jack and knob names, file names), where keyword search is strong. Musicians ask in everyday words ("why does my sound crunch?" for a page about aliasing and Drive), where embeddings are strong. So the search is hybrid , and the benchmark measures each method on its own ( bleep-agent eval retrieval ). Build time python -m bleep agent.docs build (run by ./bleep build agent-data ) writes one SQLite file: Chunks. Each page is split by heading. A chunk is at most 450 tokens; very long sections are split at paragraph boundaries, sections under 50 tokens merge into their neighbour. The chunk's text starts with its heading path ("Modules > Multi Filter > Drive"), because the path carries most of the meaning of a short section. Each chunk has an id # , the audience ( musicians , developers , module ) and the URL with anchor. Keyword index. SQLite FTS5 over the title, heading path and text. Embeddings (optional). One vector per chunk from the configured model, stored as a BLOB in the same file. The API loads them into one in-memory matrix at start and does a brute-force cosine search, which takes milliseconds for a few thousand chunks. No vector database is needed. A cache. Each embedding is keyed by the model and a hash of the chunk text, so after a docs edit only the changed chunks are embedded, and a rebuild without changes makes no API calls. The file records the docs version, the chunking version and the embedding model in a meta table. Question time The query runs a keyword search (FTS5 bm25 , top 20) and, if embeddings exist, a vector search (the query is embedded as a retrieval query, top 20 by cosine). The two rankings are merged with reciprocal rank fusion : a chunk scores the sum of 1 / (60 + rank) over the lists it appears in, so a chunk both searches like beats a chunk only one search loves, and the scores of the two methods never need to be comparable. Chunks whose audience matches the question (musicians or developers) get a boost of 25%. The top six are returned with title, path, URL and a short excerpt. The model reads a full page with read doc when an excerpt is not enough. The docs skill also gets a table of contents of the pages in its instructions, so it can ask for a page by id directly. The embedding model must match Vectors from different models cannot be compared. If BLEEP AGENT EMBED MODEL differs from the model recorded in docs.sqlite , the search logs it and falls back to keywords only, instead of returning nonsense. Rebuild the index with the new model to switch. Answers The docs prompt tells the assistant to answer from what it retrieved, link the pages it used as markdown links, and say clearly when the documentation does not cover the question. Musicians get plain musical language, developers get technical detail. "Says when the documentation has no answer" is a benchmark check of its own; see Benchmark and results. These pages are part of the index: the assistant can answer questions about itself from them.

title: Edits and changesets
text: Edits and changesets The assistant never writes patch JSON. It sends operations ; the library turns them into a changeset the board applies. Code: agent/src/bleep agent/ops.py , patch.py , catalog.py , sim.py . The patch and the catalog The patch is exactly the board's own JSON ( nodes , cables , panels ; the format board::parse reads), so a snapshot, a changeset, a benchmark fixture and an example preset are the same data. Knob values in it are normalised to 0..1; the library converts to and from real units (Hz, seconds, choice names) with the catalog. The catalog describes every module type: knobs with range, mapping and choices, jacks with a signal type ( audio , control , pitch , gate , trigger , notes ), and a small hand-written agent block per module (roles such as filter , typical connections, pitfalls) so "chorus and reverb" resolves to module types without guessing. It is generated from the engine's module registry, with a check ( python -m bleep agent.catalog check ) that fails when the file is out of date. Operations propose changes takes a list of operations (a Pydantic discriminated union on op ): op Does add module Adds a module with knob values in real units; ref gives it a local handle, usable as $ref by later ops of the same call remove module Removes a module and its cables (destructive) connect , disconnect Cables; the target may be an input jack or a knob id, which modulates it with amount as depth set param , set cable amount Values; a clamped value is reported insert on cable Breaks a cable and puts a module in it; stereo pairs ( l / r ) are handled together rename module , move module , set node data , set muted , set tempo The rest Adding and wiring happen in one call , so a module never arrives without its cables. Validation apply ops is transactional: either every operation is valid and the patch changes, or an error names the failing operation ( op 3: ... ) and nothing changes. It checks that: the module type and every jack and knob exist (the error lists the real ones), cables run from an output to an input and the signal types are compatible, there is no duplicate cable, values are in range, or are a valid choice name. The error goes back to the model as a retryable tool error, and the model corrects itself, usually in one more step. This is why a typo in a jack id is cheap while a hallucinated module would be fatal to a design that writes JSON directly. From operations to a changeset Valid operations are compiled to primitive operations that the client applies in order: add node, remove node, add cable, remove cable, set param, set cable amount, set data, set muted, rename node, move node, set tempo, set panel, remove panel A changeset is {id, summary, ops, lines, destructive} : the primitives, readable diff lines for the chat ("+ Chorus, + Reverb, 2 cables rewired") and a destructive flag. The board applies it as one undo step , so the board's own Cmd/Ctrl+Z is the safety net in both modes. Ids generated by the library follow the board's style and never collide with the snapshot. A changeset id is a hash of its operations, which makes a replayed conversation (the benchmark's cache) identical. Mode A changeset is ask Shown as a diff with Apply and Reject auto Applied as it streams in; destructive ones still ask The client prefixes a note about applied, rejected or undone changesets to the next user message, so the model knows what became of its proposals. Why is there no sound: diagnosis without audio check audibility answers from a graph model ( sim.py ), not from DSP. It propagates "does this output carry a signal, and does it move" through the cables by module role , with a held note and the transport running as stimulus, and returns structured findings, each with a code, a severity, the module and jack, and a ready fix. The checks include: no Audio Out, or Audio Out not connected, or no path from any source to it, a source with no trigger path (a VCA driven by an envelope whose gate has no cable), a VCA or mixer gain at zero, a filter cutoff closed with no modulation, a muted module, a wrong signal type on a cable, a disconnected required jack. It is an approximation, so the diagnose skill uses it first and, when it is not conclusive, measures with the live tool probe signals and walks the path backwards from the output to the first silent point. The same graph model is the benchmark's stand-in for the browser, and what makes a fault-injected diagnose case have a ground truth; see Benchmark and results. Panels and sequencers Panels are JSON with sections and controls on a grid. For build panel the model chooses what goes on the panel and how to group it; the library places the controls. propose panel is stricter than the model: it refuses to drop a knob that is wired to a control. Sequencer tools validate the step shape (length 1..64, gate, integer pitch, velocity 1..127) and tile a short motif to the requested length with ties for held notes.

title: Bleep Assistant
text: Bleep Assistant Not in the first release. The assistant calls a paid AI model, so the first public release ships with it switched off ( BLEEP AGENT ENABLED=false ). The board shows the Assistant button with a note that it is not available yet. It will come in a later version. The Bleep Assistant is a chat window in the board in which an AI agent helps with a patch. It answers questions about Bleep, finds out why there is no sound, adds and wires modules, programs sequencers, builds panels and designs a sound from scratch. It is agentic : it does not just reply, it looks things up and acts through tools, step by step, until the request is done. Two rules shape everything else: The user stays in control. Every change to the patch is a visible changeset that the board applies as one undo step. In ask mode the user approves it first; in auto mode it is applied at once, and destructive changes (removing a module, replacing a panel) still ask. The model never writes raw patch JSON. It calls typed operations ("add this module, connect these jacks"). The library checks each one against the module catalog before anything reaches the board, and a mistake comes back to the model as a message it can retry on. What it does Skill Handles Example docs Questions about using or extending Bleep, answered from the documentation with links "What does Drive do in the Multi Filter?" diagnose Finds out why something is silent, by reading the patch and measuring signals, then fixes it "Why do I not hear sound?" patch Small precise edits: insert effects on a cable, add a MIDI device, change a value "Add chorus and reverb between the synth and the output" panel Builds or tidies a front panel "Build a panel for this patch" compose Programs a sequencer "Program an acid line in the step sequencer" design Builds a whole sound or instrument "Build an acid synthesizer" The assistant is off by default. It is switched on in the website with BLEEP AGENT ENABLED=true and a provider key; see Configuration and website/.env.example . Where the code is Piece Path The library bleep-agent (Python 3.12, Pydantic AI) agent/src/bleep agent/ Backend integration (auth, rate limit, budget, streaming, run log) website/api/app/routers/agent.py , agent quota.py , agent log.py The chat panel in the board patch/board/ui/agent-chat.js , agent-chat.css The benchmark agent/evals/ and agent/src/bleep agent/evals/ Generated data (git-ignored) website/api/agent data/ : catalog.json , presets.jsonl , docs.sqlite Formats and protocol, normative doc/specs/agent.md Goals and reasoning doc/agent-concept.md The library has no FastAPI dependency, so it also runs from a command line, which is how the benchmark and local experiments use it: .venv-agent/bin/bleep-agent chat "add chorus and reverb between the synth and the output" --preset additive-osc-tilt-sweep --model gemini-3.8-flash The pages Page What it explains Architecture The pieces, how they talk, and what is kept where How a turn works One request from routing to events, with pause and resume for live tools Skills and tools Which tools each skill sees, and how the prompts are built to stay cheap Edits and changesets The typed operations, validation, diagnosis without audio, and undo Documentation search How a docs question finds the right pages Benchmark and results The 187-case benchmark, how a run is scored, and the results so far Working on the assistant Set up the library and build its data once: python3 -m venv .venv-agent && .venv-agent/bin/pip install -e "agent[dev]" PYTHON=.venv-agent/bin/python ./bleep build agent-data .venv-agent/bin/pytest agent/tests Every change to a prompt, a tool or the catalog can change how the assistant behaves, so measure it: run the benchmark before and after, and record the new version in the lab notebook.

title: Skills and tools
text: Skills and tools A skill is a prompt section plus a subset of tools. One agent serves all six; the skill changes what it is told and what it can call. Skills are defined in agent/src/bleep agent/skills.py , tools in tools.py , prompts in prompts/ . Which skill sees which tools Skill Read and lookup tools Write tools Live tools docs describe module , search docs , read doc none none diagnose describe module , trace signal , check audibility propose changes get environment , probe signals , highlight , ask user patch describe module , list module types , trace signal , search presets , get preset propose changes get environment , highlight , ask user panel describe module , get panel build panel , propose panel highlight compose describe module , get sequencer , search presets , get preset propose changes , set pattern , set drum pattern play , ask user design describe module , list module types , search presets , get preset , get sequencer , get panel , check audibility propose changes , set pattern , set drum pattern , build panel , propose panel get environment , probe signals , play , highlight , ask user The table is not arbitrary. Every tool definition is sent on every model call, so a tool a skill never uses is pure cost; the split came from counting which tools were used in the benchmark's runs. The documentation tools belong to docs only, list module types to the skills that look for modules, trace signal to those that follow cables. The tools Lookups run against the catalog, the patch and the indexes: Tool Does list module types(query, role, category) Finds module types, for example by role ( reverb , filter ) describe module(type) Jacks with signal types, and each knob on one line with range, unit and choices trace signal(from, to) Lists the cable paths between two modules check audibility() Static and simulated diagnosis with structured findings and ready fixes; see Edits and changesets search presets , get preset Finds and reads example patches to learn from get panel , get sequencer Reads a panel or a sequencer's steps search docs , read doc Searches the documentation and reads a page; see Documentation search Writes produce a changeset or an error text: Tool Does propose changes(ops, summary) A list of typed operations: add, remove, connect, set a knob, insert on a cable and so on set pattern , set drum pattern Writes a step sequencer or drum grid; a short motif is tiled to the requested length build panel(plan) The model picks which knobs go on a panel and how to group them; the library does the layout propose panel Replaces a panel; refuses to drop a knob that is wired, so panels are rearranged, never trimmed Live tools run in the browser (see How a turn works): Tool Does get environment Audio state, MIDI devices, transport, keyboard modules probe signals Listens at jacks, optionally while the browser plays a test note; returns whether a signal is present and moving play Plays notes, so the user hears a pattern highlight Points at modules, jacks or cables on the board ask user One short question with choices How the prompts are built The shared base.md teaches how Bleep works: patches, signal types, that every knob is also a modulation input, the typical subtractive voice, what ports and cells are, and the working rules (look things up, add and wire in one call, make the smallest change, say plainly what changed, never claim a change you did not make). Each skill adds a short task section, for example the diagnose steps "run check audibility , then measure, then walk the path backwards from the output". Several choices keep the cost per request down, and each one was measured in the benchmark: The board is in the instructions. There is no get patch tool; the current board, with the user's selection marked, is part of the instructions of every step, so the model never spends a call reading it and always sees its own changes. A jacks-and-knobs sheet for the twelve most used modules sits in the prompt, because looking those up was most of the describe module calls. Slim tool schemas. The JSON schema of each tool is stripped of what the model does not need (titles, default: null , nullable wrappers). propose changes alone is about 1,700 tokens, sent on every call. Stable prefix first , so provider prompt caches hit; for OpenAI each skill also gets its own prompt cache key so requests of one skill are routed together. A bad value is a retryable tool error , not the end of the run: a scale called "Minor" is read as the scale it means, an unknown knob returns the real ones. Adding a tool or a skill Write the tool as a function in tools.py and add it to the right list ( READ , WRITE , SEQ ...). Keep its description short: it is paid for on every call. Offer it in skills.py only to the skills that need it. Add an ACTIVITY line in runner.py so the chat shows something while it runs. Add benchmark cases that need it, run the benchmark and record the version in the lab notebook.

title: Architecture overview
