text: Architecture overview Audio plugins in a DAW are isolated from each other: each one has its own audio thread, and the host decides in which order the tracks run. Bleep Bus gives them a way to exchange per-sample control signals anyway, for example an LFO in one plugin that moves the filter cutoff of another plugin on a different track. It does this without a server and without any help from the host, using one block of named shared memory that every plugin opens. This page explains the bus in three steps. The first picture shows who takes part and where the state lives. The second follows one signal from the sender's output to a parameter of the receiver. The third explains the one rule that makes the result identical on every run, even though the host runs the tracks in no fixed order: the receiver always reads the block the sender produced for the receiver's previous block. If you only want to use the bus, the Quickstart is faster. If you want to implement it yourself, the specification has the exact rules behind each picture, and each section below links to the relevant chapters. Architecture Plugin instances in different tracks, processes or threads each register an endpoint in one shared-memory segment. The segment holds a header and tables of endpoints, inputs and outputs. There is no server process. The whole bus is one block of operating-system shared memory, called the segment . Its name is built from the major version of the protocol and a namespace : by default /bleepbus-v0-default on macOS and Linux, and Local\bleepbus-v0-default on Windows. Every plugin that uses the same namespace opens the same segment. The first plugin to open it creates and initialises it, later ones just map it. Nobody removes the segment while plugins come and go, so a plugin that is loaded later finds everything its predecessors left. Users and test setups can run separate buses side by side, for example two DAWs at once, by setting the BLEEP BUS NAMESPACE environment variable. Inside the segment there are four parts, shown at the bottom of the picture: The header holds the protocol version, the sizes of the tables and a few counters. The counters are generations that change whenever the registry or a cable changes, so a plugin can cheaply notice that something happened. The endpoint table has room for 64 endpoints. An endpoint is one plugin instance. It has a stable 64-bit UID, a display name and the process it belongs to. The UID is what other plugins use to refer to it, and it survives saving and loading a project. The input table has room for 512 inputs. An input has a name that is unique within its endpoint, and it holds up to 8 cables. The output table has room for 256 outputs. An output has a name and a type, and it keeps four slots with the most recent blocks of samples. Each plugin instance registers one endpoint and then adds the outputs and inputs it wants to offer. Names are short and stable ( "LFO" , "Env" , "Cutoff" ), because a cable refers to its source by endpoint UID and output name, and saved projects store cables in that form. There is no server, no socket and no thread that has to stay alive. Everything a plugin needs to know is in the segment, and the audio threads only read and write memory. Changes to the structure, such as registering an endpoint or adding a cable, are done under a lock inside the segment and never on the audio thread. That is also how the third box in the picture works: a patchbay in one plugin window, or a tool such as bb conformance inspect , can list every endpoint and edit the cables into any input, and the plugin that owns the input notices through the counters in the header and tells its host that its state has changed. The segment is created with permissions for the current user only, so the peers on a bus are processes of the same user. They are not necessarily trustworthy: a plugin can have bugs. The library therefore validates everything it reads from the segment and a writer re-checks that it still owns its output before every write. The remaining known limits are listed under Hostile peers. Related: Naming, Layout, Registry. What is not part of the bus The wasm modules are not part of this architecture. Bleep Bus is a separate protocol: it works between any plugins in any DAW and does not need Beautiful Bleep. The Bleep plugins, the Bleep App and Bleep Play each run their own engine and board, and the cables on the board connect modules inside that one engine. Those cables never touch the shared-memory segment. A plugin takes part in the bus only if it calls the Bleep Bus SDK (or implements the specification itself), whatever it is made of inside. See the developer overview for how the two fit side by side. Signal flow A sender writes a block into an output slot. Cables multiply it by an amount and sum them into an input. The receiver reads it one block later and applies the sum to a parameter. The picture follows one control signal from a sender to a parameter of a receiver, for example an LFO that modulates a filter cutoff. The sender writes a block. Once per processing block, the sender calls bb begin block to announce the block (its length, the transport position, whether the transport is playing and a timestamp). Then it writes the samples of each of its outputs with bb write output and finishes with bb end block . The samples go into one of the four slots of the output, together with the stamps of the block. A slot is written under a sequence counter (a seqlock), so a reader can tell whether it saw a complete block. An output that was not written during a block publishes silence at the end of that block. Cables select the sources. A cable belongs to the receiving input. It stores the UID of the source endpoint, the name of the source output and an amount . An input holds up to 8 cables, and any process can add, change or remove one. A source that does not exist, for example because that plugin is not loaded, simply reads as silence until it comes back. The input sums the cables. When the receiver calls bb read input , the bus takes the block of each connected output (see the next section for which block), multiplies it by the cable's amount and adds the results. Samples and amounts that are not finite numbers count as 0, and amounts are limited to the range of ±1000. The receiver applies the sum. Signals are 32-bit floats, one per sample, in virtual volts : a control signal is nominally between -1 and +1, a gate is high from 0.5, and a pitch signal has 1.0 per octave. A receiving plugin should apply the sum as an offset in the normalised 0..1 range of the parameter, inside its own DSP: effective = clamp(knob + Σ source × amount, 0, 1) . It must not move the host-visible parameter, so the modulation causes no automation writes and no undo entries, and a parameter with an exponential mapping such as a cutoff is modulated in octaves. Types and ranges are advisory: any output can be connected to any input, and values outside the nominal range are allowed, for example when several cables add up. Receivers clamp where it matters. Related: Signals, Connections and state, API reference. Why one block of latency, and how a block is chosen Each output keeps four block slots. A reader considers the three newest finished blocks and picks one by the position rule, then the time rule, otherwise it holds its last sample. Hosts such as Ableton Live process tracks on parallel threads, and nothing guarantees the order. If a reader took whatever the sender wrote last, the result would depend on which thread happened to run first: sometimes the modulation would arrive in the same block and sometimes one block late, and two renders of the same set would differ. That is unacceptable for an offline export, and it makes a live set hard to reproduce. The bus therefore fixes the latency at exactly one block . A reader always takes the block that the sender produced for the reader's previous block, no matter which side ran first. At 256 samples and 48 kHz that is 5.3 ms, which is inaudible for modulation but too much for phase-critical audio. Keep in mind that Live's delay compensation does not know about the bus, and that an endpoint that is patched into itself works but also has one block of latency. To make this possible each output keeps the last four blocks in its four slots, as shown at the top of the picture. The block that is currently being written is never read. The reader considers the three finished blocks before it, newest first, and applies three rules in order: Position rule. If the reader's previous and current block were both playing, it takes the newest candidate whose transport position is the same as the position of its own previous block. This is exact: it also works when a loop repeats positions and when an export runs faster than real time. Time rule. Otherwise, or if the first rule finds nothing, it takes the newest candidate that was written at least half a block earlier than the start of the current block, judged by a monotonic system clock. This covers a stopped transport and peers that have only just appeared. Hold. If neither rule finds a block, the reader repeats the last sample it read from that cable, or 0 if there is none yet. A candidate only counts if its sequence counter reads consistently and its block number matches, so a half-written block is never used. The audio thread never waits or spins for a block: it skips a candidate that is not ready and uses another one, or holds. If the chosen block is shorter than the reader's block, the rest of the block holds the last sample of the chosen one. Related: Timing, Memory ordering, Host notes.

title: Conformance
text: Conformance suite bb conformance is the open test host and validator. cmake -S bus -B build/bus && cmake --build build/bus ./build/bus/bb conformance run # all checks, TAP output, private namespace ./build/bus/bb conformance inspect # print + validate the live "default" bus ./build/bus/bb conformance peer-send # interop peer run checks: Area What Layout struct sizes and offsets match the spec; a fresh segment's header Versioning wrong requested version, foreign segment versions, corrupt magic Registry ports, names, listings, generations, UID collisions, dead-process reclamation, lock recovery Timing one block of latency in random thread order, offline export, loops, stopped transport, real threads Signals summing and amounts, ghost sources, unwritten/short/oversized blocks State save/load round trip, locale-independent amounts, malformed input IPC a second process publishes, this one reads To test another implementation of the C API, build the sources in bus/conformance/ ( bb conformance.c and the files it lists in bus/CMakeLists.txt ) against it instead of bleep bus . To test interop between your implementation and the reference, run peer-send from one and a reader from the other. "Bleep Bus compatible" Plugins that pass the suite and the checklist may use the "Bleep Bus compatible" badge. The protocol is free to use; the names and logo are trademarks of Brilliant Bleep.

title: Bleep Bus
text: Bleep Bus Bleep Bus is an open protocol (MIT) and a small C SDK for sending per-sample control signals between audio plugins through named shared memory. It works between any plugins in any DAW; it does not need Beautiful Bleep. It is separate from the cables on the Bleep board, which connect modules inside one engine. The pages Step Page See how it fits together Architecture overview Send and receive a signal in 15 minutes Quickstart Every function, type and error API reference Implement the protocol without the SDK Specification v0.1 Prove your implementation is correct Conformance Propose a change to the protocol RFC process What is in the repository The code is in bus/ : the C API ( include/bleep bus.h ), the shared-memory layout for reimplementations, a reference implementation for POSIX and Windows, a header-only C++17 wrapper, JUCE helpers, examples and the conformance test host. bus/README.md lists every folder and the build command. The sidebar of this section holds three groups: the guides (this group), the API reference and the specification.

title: Bleep Bus quickstart
text: Bleep Bus quickstart A minimal sender and receiver in 15 minutes. This page is complete on its own; paste it into a coding assistant together with your plugin source. 1. Build the SDK git clone https://github.com/brilliantbleep/bleep.git cmake -S bleep/bus -B build/bus cmake --build build/bus ctest --test-dir build/bus # conformance suite 2. See it work (two terminals) ./build/bus/minimal sender # publishes a 0.5 Hz sine on output "LFO" ./build/bus/minimal receiver # patches LFO → In and prints it ./build/bus/bb conformance inspect # shows endpoints, ports and cables 3. Add it to your plugin CMake: add subdirectory(path/to/bleep/bus bleep bus) target link libraries(MyPlugin PRIVATE bleep bus cpp) # C only: bleep bus Sender (any plugin, C API): #include "bleep bus.h" / constructor / bb bus bus = bb bus open(BB SPEC VERSION, NULL, NULL); bb instance info info = BB INSTANCE INFO INIT; info.display name = "My LFO"; info.product = "My LFO"; info.vendor = "Me"; bb endpoint ep = bb register instance(bus, &info, NULL); bb output out = bb add output(ep, "LFO", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, BB POLARITY BIPOLAR, NULL); / audio callback / bb block info b = BB BLOCK INFO INIT; b.num samples = n; b.sample rate = sr; b.transport sample pos = transport pos; b.flags = playing ? BB BLOCK PLAYING : 0; bb begin block(ep, &b); bb write output(out, lfo samples, n); bb end block(ep); / destructor / bb unregister instance(ep); bb bus close(bus); Receiver: the same setup with an input, plus a cable. bb input cutoff in = bb add input(ep, "Cutoff", BB SIGNAL CONTROL, NULL); / message thread: patch the first output named "LFO" into Cutoff / bb output info outs[BB MAX OUTPUTS]; uint32 t count = bb list outputs(bus, outs, BB MAX OUTPUTS); for (uint32 t i = 0; i 1.f ? 1.f : v); set cutoff normalised(i, v); / never move the host parameter / } 4. Save the cables / getState / uint64 t uid = bb endpoint uid(ep); / save this / size t len = bb save connections(ep, NULL, 0); / + this text / / setState / bb set instance uid(ep, saved uid); / BB ERR UID IN USE: device was duplicated, fine / bb load connections(ep, saved text, saved len); 5. Load it in Live Build your plugin twice (or load two instances), put one on each of two tracks, and press play. Modulation arrives one block late, independent of track order. Next: the API reference for every function, host notes and pitfalls; the specification if you implement the bus without the SDK.

title: RFC process
text: Changing the standard: RFCs Bleep Bus is maintained by Brilliant Bleep in public. Anyone can propose a change. Issue. Open a GitHub issue labelled rfc describing the problem, not the solution. Design doc. If maintainers agree it is worth solving, open a pull request adding website/content/rfcs/NNNN-title.md : motivation, design, layout changes, compatibility, alternatives. Discussion. At least two weeks in the open. Decision. Maintainers accept, postpone or reject, and record the reasoning in the RFC. Implementation. Spec text, SDK, conformance checks and docs change in the same pull request. Version rules: 0.x minors may break the layout; after 1.0, minor versions only add fields in reserved space and new majors use a new segment name.

title: Programming with AI
text: Programming with AI A coding assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, a coding agent in your editor) does not know Bleep Script: it is new, it is a strict subset of AssemblyScript, and its rules are different from ordinary audio code. This page has one prompt that teaches it. It holds the language, the module format, the rules of real-time code, the whole library, a checklist and two complete examples. How to use it Copy the prompt below with the button in its top right corner, or download it as a Markdown file (and attach it to a chat, or put it in a project's instructions). Paste it into a new chat , then say what you want in the next message, in your own words: "Implement a phaser with 4 to 12 stages, rate, depth, feedback and a mix knob." "A tape-style delay with wow and flutter." "A monophonic synth: two detuned band-limited saws, a sub oscillator and a filter envelope." "A sidechain compressor with a lookahead-free peak detector and a gain-reduction meter." "A router that splits notes by velocity and sends a gate out for every note-on." Paste the answer into a Code node and press Compile. If the compiler reports a problem, paste the message back into the chat: every message names the line and what to do. A request can be short. The prompt tells the assistant to choose sensible knobs and ranges itself and to say what it chose, so you can tweak them afterwards. What to expect If you ask for a custom look (a drawn curve, your own meters), it writes the UI tab too: a second code block of JavaScript that you paste into the Code node's UI tab, next to the module in the Script tab. Without such a request it leaves the standard controls alone, or arranges them with a layout. The assistant writes a module script (one module: a class with sample() and knobs), because that is what nearly every request needs. If you ask for a patch built from existing modules, say so, and it writes a patch script instead. It can only use what the Bleep Script library offers. The library covers oscillators, filters, delays, noise, envelopes and LFOs, dynamics, effects, an FFT and helpers; anything else (a vocoder, convolution, granular) it writes inside the module, which takes more code and may need a round of fixes. That is normal and takes a few lines. The first answer often compiles. When it does not, or when it sounds wrong, say what you hear ("it clicks when I turn the rate knob", "the feedback blows up at the top") and let it fix that. It cannot hear. Check the result by ear, and with the meters ( @probe ) it adds when you ask for them. The prompt describes the library as it is when this page was built. A newer library may have more in it; the Library page is the full list. The prompt ~~~~markdown Bleep Script: write audio modules You write code in Bleep Script , the scripting language of the Bleep modular synthesizer. A Bleep Script module script is one file that becomes one module on the board: it has jacks (inputs and outputs), knobs, meters and buttons, and DSP code that runs in real time. The user will ask for something to build (an effect, an oscillator, a filter, an envelope, a modulator, a sequencer, a utility, a note router, ...). Your job is to write that module, as code that compiles on the first try and sounds right. Everything you need is in this document. Follow it exactly. Do not use APIs, decorators, options or functions that are not described here: this language is not TypeScript with an npm ecosystem, and anything you invent will fail to compile. 1. What you deliver One complete module script in a single code block. Never partial code, never "the rest stays the same". Then a short note (a few lines, not an essay) listing the knobs and jacks you chose and anything the user may want to change. If the request left something open (ranges, number of stages, mono or stereo), decide it yourself with a sensible default and say so. Ask a question only if the request cannot be built at all without the answer. No imports except ./bleep/dsp , ./bleep/notes and ./bleep/env . No other files, no build setup. Default to a module script (section 2). Write a patch script (section 12) only if the user asks to wire up existing Bleep modules rather than write DSP. Add a doc comment ( / ... / ) on the class and on any knob whose purpose is not obvious from its name; it shows up as help text. 2. The shape of a module script A module script is AssemblyScript (a strict, statically typed subset of TypeScript that compiles to WebAssembly) with decorators that describe the module's interface. One class marked @module is one module. import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Gain", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Gain { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: -60, max: 6, init: 0, unit: "dB", decimals: 1 }) level: f32 = 0; private g: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.g = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } block(): void { this.g.target = dbToLin(this.level); } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.g.next(); } } The compiler generates all the glue to the audio engine. You never touch buffers. You read @input and @param fields, you write @output and @probe fields. Member Runs Use it for constructor(sampleRate: f64) once, when the module is created allocating buffers and objects, constants that depend on the sample rate. The only place that may allocate. Always write it, even if empty: constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} block(): void once per block of 32 samples everything derived from knobs: dB to gain, filter coefficients, increments, smoother targets sample(): void once per sample the signal path itself reset(): void when the engine resets the module clear state (filter memories, delay contents, phases) @on(...) methods once per event, at the exact sample note events and control edges (section 7) @transport method once per block, before block() tempo and position (section 8) @button methods when the user presses the button one-off actions such as "Reset" All are optional. A module with only sample() is an effect or an oscillator; one with only @on handlers is a router. The order in a block for every block of 32 samples: @transport method (tempo, position) @param fields are filled (in their own units) block() (slow work, once) for every sample 0..31: @input fields hold this sample @on handlers for events at this sample sample() (fast work) @output fields are read Which rate for what (this matters more than anything else) Put every calculation in the slowest place that is still correct : constructor : allocation, tables, 1 / sampleRate . block() : anything that depends only on knobs. A knob changes at most once per block anyway, so computing Math.pow , Math.exp , Math.sin , Math.tan , pitchToHz , dbToLin or filter coefficients per sample is wasted work and counts against the cost limit. sample() : only the signal: oscillators, filters, delays, envelopes, waveshapers, mixing. @on : things that happen at a moment (a note, a gate rising), sample accurate. A value set in block() is constant for 32 samples; if it jumps, that is a step, and a step in a gain is a click. So never feed a knob straight into the signal path : set a Smoother target in block() and read the smoothed value in sample() (section 9). 3. No closures, no arrow functions as values, no classes as expressions, no exceptions ( try , throw ), no regular expressions, no any , no undefined , no union types, no optional parameters left unassigned , no destructuring of objects, and no for...of . Private fields: private phase: f64 = 0; . Methods are plain methods. 5. What the compiler refuses in the audio code The checker walks block() , sample() , reset() , the @on handlers and everything they call. It refuses, with a message naming the line: recursion, closures, exceptions, regular expressions; anything that allocates or copies at run time: new anywhere outside the constructor, push , map , filter , concat , slice , split , string building, Array growth, Map and Set ; calls to anything except your own functions, Math , the built-ins above and the bleep/ libraries; declare , and these names, anywhere, even as your own variable or parameter : load , store , memory , changetype , unchecked , unreachable , abort , trace , seed , unsafe , call indirect , and any name starting with ; imports from anywhere but ./bleep/dsp , ./bleep/notes and ./bleep/env ; loops without a bound the checker can see, and loops longer than 4096 iterations. Events: notes and edges An @on method runs at the exact sample of the event, in order with sample() . import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Out", type: "notes" }) out!: NoteStream; @on("notes") handle(n: NoteEvent): void { // the string names the INPUT FIELD if (n.isOn) { / n.pitch, n.note, n.value (velocity) / } else if (n.isOff) { / ... / } this.out.push(n); // forwards it at the same sample } @input({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @on("gate", { rising: 0.5 }) open(): void { / the sample the signal crosses 0.5 upwards / } @on("gate", { falling: 0.5 }) close(): void { / ... downwards / } Give exactly one of rising and falling . For a monophonic instrument, keep the current pitch and a gate flag in fields and set them in the handler; for polyphony , keep a fixed number of voice objects in a StaticArray allocated in the constructor and assign notes to free voices (steal the oldest when none is free). A voice is a small undecorated class with its own phase, envelope and filter state. 7b. The UI tab (only when asked) By default a module shows one control per @param , a meter per @probe and a button per @button . Change that only if the user asks for a particular look, in one of two ways. Do nothing here for an ordinary request. A layout (no code, safe, enough for most requests): a layout list in @module , arranging the standard widgets. Any item may have label and title . A container with repeat (a number or a setting's name) makes one copy per channel; {n} in ids and titles becomes the copy number from 1. At most 400 widgets. A self-made UI : the Code node has a Script tab (the module, everything above) and a UI tab. The UI tab holds plain JavaScript (not AssemblyScript, no types, no decorators) that draws on a canvas and talks to the module through a global bleep object. It is a second file: when the user wants a custom UI, deliver the module script in one block and the UI in a separate block, and say which goes in which tab. The ids you use in the UI must match the module's @param and @probe field names. const level = bleep.canvas(60); // as wide as the node, 60 px high bleep.onFrame(() => { // every animation frame const { g, width, height } = level; // g is a 2D canvas context g.clearRect(0, 0, width, height); g.fillStyle = bleep.theme.accent; g.fillRect(0, 0, width bleep.probe("level"), height); }); Member What it does bleep.params / bleep.param(id) All params / one param (throws on an unknown id).
