Use them so the UI fits the board. Rules: a UI sets at most 240 values per second (so a drag may call param.set freely, but not in a tight loop); it runs in a sandboxed worker, with no network, storage, DOM or access outside bleep (no document or window : everything is drawn on bleep.canvas ), and it runs without asking; an error in the UI code stops the UI and is shown with its line; a loop that never ends gets the UI stopped, it does not freeze the page. To let the user drag a point or curve, read the pointer on canvas.el ( pointerdown , pointermove ) and call bleep.param(id).setNormalised(x) . Redraw in onFrame or onValues , never keep a second copy of the state: the params are the state. 8. Tempo sync @transport tempo(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void { ... } At most one per module. Called once per block before block() : the tempo, the position at the start of the block in quarter notes, and whether the transport plays. Between blocks, advance the position yourself per sample ( this.beat += bpm / (60 sampleRate) ) and take ppq again when playing . Use it for tempo-synced LFOs, delays and sequencers; derive musical divisions from beats (a sixteenth note is 0.25 beats). The tempo does not exist without it: a module has no clock. 9. Making it sound right These are the things that separate a module that works from one that clicks, rings or blows up. Apply them without being asked. Smoothing. Any knob that changes a gain, a mute, a mix, a cutoff, a delay time or a pan goes through a Smoother : target in block() , next() in sample() . 5 to 20 ms for gains and mixes, 10 to 30 ms for cutoffs, 50 to 200 ms for delay times (a fast change in delay time bends the pitch). Smooth the linear gain, not the dB value. Toggles ( bool ) and choices are knobs too: smooth a mute with a 0/1 target; crossfade between two shapes or filter types. Filters. Recompute coefficients in block() from the smoothed frequency, not per sample. Clamp frequency to a safe range ( min(max(f, 10), 0.45 sampleRate) ) and Q to something finite. Use f64 for filter state and coefficients. A filter or any feedback path should start from a defined state and clear it in reset() . Feedback. Keep loop gain strictly below 1 (limit the feedback knob to, say, 0.95 or 0.98, or soft-clip inside the loop). Put a DcBlocker in a feedback loop that contains a nonlinearity. Never divide by something that can be 0. Aliasing. A naive saw or square ( 2 phase - 1 ) and any hard nonlinearity (clipping, folding, rectifying, bit-crushing, ring modulation by a square) create harmonics above Nyquist that fold back as inharmonic noise. For oscillators use sawBlep , squareBlep , triangle , Wavetable or Supersaw from ./bleep/osc ; for tanh soft clipping use AdaaTanh ; for other non-linear steps (clipping, folding) run them between up and down of Oversampler2x from ./bleep/dynamics . Oversampling costs CPU, so say so when you use it. Level. Audio is nominally within -1..1. Keep gain staging sane: normalise the sum of mixed voices, compensate drive with make-up gain, and never let an effect add large gain at its default settings. Give gains in dB with unit: "dB" , and a bottom of "-inf" through minText when the lowest value should mean silence ( this.level allocated in the constructor at the longest delay plus 2 samples, a write index that wraps, a fractional read with linear interpolation ( read = write - delay , add size if negative, interpolate between buffer[i] and the next index, wrapping). Delays shorter than one sample do not work in a feedback loop; keep a minimum of 1 or 2 samples. Modulation. An LFO is a Phasor (or an f64 phase) at rate Hz with a shape function of the phase. A modulated delay or filter needs the modulator at audio rate: compute it in sample() . A rate knob is converted to a phase increment in block() . When a module should take an external modulation signal, add a control input and read it in sample() . Stereo. Two inputs, two outputs, one state object per channel. Decorrelate stereo modulation by offsetting the right LFO's phase (for example by a quarter or half cycle). Meters. Add @probe fields for anything worth watching (input and output level with PeakHold , gain reduction, an LFO, an envelope) when it helps; they cost almost nothing. Defaults. Choose defaults that give a useful sound at once: effects at about 50 % mix or a clearly audible setting, a filter open enough to hear the input, an oscillator at a moderate level. 10. Two complete examples A modulated delay effect built from library parts ( Lfo , DelayLine , Smoother , DcBlocker ), with a meter and a block-rate/audio-rate split: import { Smoother, DcBlocker } from "./bleep/dsp"; import { Lfo } from "./bleep/env"; import { DelayLine } from "./bleep/delay"; / A flanger: a short delay swept by an LFO, mixed back with the dry signal. / @module({ name: "Flanger", category: "Effects/Script", colour: "#38bdf8" }) export class Flanger { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Rate", min: 0.05, max: 10, init: 0.4, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 2 }) rate: f32 = 0.4; @param({ name: "Depth", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.6 }) depth: f32 = 0.6; @param({ name: "Delay", min: 0.1, max: 8, init: 2, unit: "ms", decimals: 2 }) delayMs: f32 = 2; @param({ name: "Feedback", min: -0.95, max: 0.95, init: 0.5 }) feedback: f32 = 0.5; @param({ name: "Mix", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) mix: f32 = 0.5; @probe lfo: f32 = 0; private lfoOsc: Lfo; private line: DelayLine; private center: Smoother; // the base delay in samples private sweep: Smoother; // how far the LFO moves it, in samples private fb: Smoother; private wet: Smoother; private dc: DcBlocker; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.lfoOsc = new Lfo(sampleRate); // a sine, -1..1 this.line = new DelayLine( (sampleRate 0.02)); // 20 ms of room this.center = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.05); this.sweep = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.05); this.fb = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.02); this.wet = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.02); this.dc = new DcBlocker(sampleRate, 20); this.center.target = (sampleRate 0.002); this.center.snap(); } reset(): void { this.lfoOsc.reset(); this.line.reset(); this.dc.reset(); } block(): void { const base = this.delayMs 0.001 this.sampleRate; this.center.target = base; this.sweep.target = (base 0.9 this.depth); // never reaches 0 or below the minimum this.fb.target = this.feedback; this.wet.target = this.mix; } sample(): void { this.lfoOsc.next( this.rate); const m = this.lfoOsc.uni; // 0..1 this.lfo = m; const d = max( 1.0, this.center.next() - this.sweep.next() (1 - m)); // delay in samples, at least 1 const delayed = this.line.readCubic(d); // read before writing: the line holds the past const input = this.x; this.line.write(this.dc.next(input + delayed this.fb.next())); this.out = input + (delayed - input) this.wet.next(); } } A note-driven monophonic synth with a band-limited saw ( sawBlep ), an ADSR, a state-variable filter and a note handler: import { Phasor, Smoother, pitchToHz, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; import { sawBlep } from "./bleep/osc"; import { Svf } from "./bleep/filters"; import { Adsr } from "./bleep/env"; @module({ name: "Mono Saw", category: "Sources/Script", colour: "#f59e0b" }) export class MonoSaw { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Cutoff", min: 40, max: 16000, init: 2500, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 0 }) cutoff: f32 = 2500; @param({ name: "Resonance", min: 0.5, max: 8, init: 0.9, map: "exp" }) resonance: f32 = 0.9; @param({ name: "Attack", min: 0.001, max: 2, init: 0.01, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) attack: f32 = 0.01; @param({ name: "Decay", min: 0.005, max: 4, init: 0.2, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) decay: f32 = 0.2; @param({ name: "Sustain", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.8 }) sustain: f32 = 0.8; @param({ name: "Release", min: 0.005, max: 4, init: 0.3, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) release: f32 = 0.3; @param({ name: "Level", min: -40, max: 0, init: -9, unit: "dB", decimals: 1 }) level: f32 = -9; @probe env: f32 = 0; private osc: Phasor; private filter: Svf; private adsr: Adsr; private cut: Smoother; private gain: Smoother; private step: f64 = 0; private velocity: f32 = 0; private gate: f32 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.osc = new Phasor(sampleRate); this.filter = new Svf(); this.adsr = new Adsr(sampleRate); this.cut = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.02); this.gain = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); this.cut.target = 2500; this.cut.snap(); } reset(): void { this.filter.reset(); this.adsr.reset(); this.gate = 0; } @on("notes") handle(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.isOn && n.value > 0) { this.osc.frequency = pitchToHz( n.pitch); // pow per note, not per sample: fine this.step = this.osc.frequency / this.sampleRate; this.velocity = n.value; this.gate = 1; } else if (n.isOff (n.isOn && n.value == 0)) { this.gate = 0; } } block(): void { this.cut.target = this.cutoff; this.gain.target = dbToLin(this.level); this.adsr.set( this.attack, this.decay, this.sustain, this.release); this.filter.set(this.sampleRate, this.cut.value, this.resonance); // clamped below Nyquist by the library } sample(): void { this.cut.next(); const e = this.adsr.next(this.gate); this.filter.tick(sawBlep( this.osc.next(), this.step)); this.out = this.filter.low e this.velocity this.gain.next(); this.env = e; } } 11. Recipes for what the library lacks Look in section 6 first : the library has random numbers and noise ( Xorshift , WhiteNoise , PinkNoise ), state-variable, ladder, one-pole and all-pass filters, delay lines, envelopes, followers, wavetables, band-limited oscillators and wave shapers. Use these recipes only for what no library class does, or for a deliberately different shape. Write them inside the module file (as top-level functions or small undecorated classes). Random numbers : a linear congruential generator, u32 state, no Math.random : class Noise { private state: u32; constructor(initial: u32) { this.state = initial; } /// White noise, -1..1. next(): f32 { this.state = this.state 1664525 + 1013904223; return ( this.state) / 2147483648.0; } } A state-variable filter (low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch from one structure; stable under fast modulation; the right choice for resonant filters that move): class Svf { private ic1: f64 = 0; private ic2: f64 = 0; private a1: f64 = 0; private a2: f64 = 0; private a3: f64 = 0; private k: f64 = 1; low: f32 = 0; band: f32 = 0; high: f32 = 0; /// Call from block(). q is about 0.5 to 10. set(sampleRate: f64, frequency: f64, q: f64): void { const g = Math.tan(Math.PI min(frequency, 0.45 sampleRate) / sampleRate); this.k = 1.0 / max(q, 0.1); this.a1 = 1.0 / (1.0 + g (g + this.k)); this.a2 = g this.a1; this.a3 = g this.a2; } /// Call per sample; read low, band and high afterwards (notch = low + high). next(x: f32): void { const v0 = x; const v3 = v0 - this.ic2; const v1 = this.a1 this.ic1 + this.a2 v3; const v2 = this.ic2 + this.a2 this.ic1 + this.a3 v3; this.ic1 = 2.0 v1 - this.ic1; this.ic2 = 2.0 v2 - this.ic2; this.low = v2; this.band = v1; this.high = (v0 - this.k v1 - v2); } reset(): void { this.ic1 = 0; this.ic2 = 0; } } A first-order allpass stage (the building block of phasers; the coefficient a follows the frequency, a = (tan(pi f / sr) - 1) / (tan(pi f / sr) + 1) ; compute it in block() or per sample when swept by an LFO): class Allpass1 { private z: f64 = 0; /// y = a x + z; z = x - a y next(x: f32, a: f64): f32 { const y = a x + this.z; this.z = x - a y; return y; } reset(): void { this.z = 0; } } A simple envelope (prefer Adsr , Ar or Ad from ./bleep/env ; hand-roll only for a special shape; attack and release as rates, as in the example above): a stage or a level, moved towards a target by a fixed step or by a fraction of the distance. A one-pole follower level += (target - level) coefficient with coefficient = 1 - exp(-1 / (seconds sampleRate)) computed in block() gives exponential segments. Retrigger on NOTE ON ; do not restart from 0, continue from the current level to avoid a click. An envelope follower or compressor detector : PeakHold for the level, or abs(x) smoothed by two coefficients (attack when rising, release when falling). Convert to dB with linToDb in sample() only when needed (it calls log10 ); a compressor often does the comparison in the linear domain, or in dB at block rate for a slow control signal. A waveshaper : AdaaTanh for tanh . Others (hard clip max(-1, min(1, x)) , a foldback, an asymmetric curve) are one line each; put a DcBlocker after an asymmetric curve and make up the gain. Wavetable or sine lookup : a StaticArray filled in the constructor (a loop of at most 4096 iterations, so tables up to 4096 entries), read with a fractional index and lerp . Band-limited square, triangle and pulse : PolyBLEP corrections at each edge ( square = (t { c.input("pitch", "Pitch", "pitch"); c.stereoOut(); const filter = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 2000 }); for (let i = 0; i and are cast back with ; typed locals ( let s: f32 = 0; ). Every @param has min and max (numbers) or choices ; init equals the field's initial value; both are inside the range; exp has min > 0 . Expensive calls ( pow , exp , tan , sin for coefficients, pitchToHz , dbToLin , setLowpass ...) are in block() , not sample() (unless they must follow an audio-rate modulator). Every knob that reaches the signal path through a gain, mix, mute, frequency or delay time goes through a Smoother . Nothing can blow up: feedback below 1, no division by zero, frequencies clamped below Nyquist, state cleared in reset() , no NaN from log(0) or sqrt of a negative. Time-based values come from sampleRate , not from a fixed number of samples. Sensible defaults: it makes a useful sound the moment it is added. The reply is the complete file in one code block (plus one block for the UI tab only if a self-made UI was asked for), followed by a short note on the knobs and the choices you made. The request The user's request for the module follows in their next message. ~~~~

title: Using other modules
text: Using other modules A module script can use any module of the library that follows the module ABI: you import it, make one, and hand it audio. The compiler links your script and the module into one .wasm file that imports nothing, so everything on Limits and safety still holds. This is the first slice of the feature. It works in the compiler (node, a page, a Worker) and is tested with the Gains module. The Code node in the board does not pass library modules to the compiler yet, so a script cannot use it there until that is wired. The script import { Gains } from "./bleep/module-gains"; @module({ name: "Wrap", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Wrap { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Volume", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.909 }) vol: f32 = 0.909; private fx: Gains; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.fx = new Gains(sampleRate); } chunk(n: i32, ins: StaticArray , outs: StaticArray ): void { this.fx.set(Gains.PARAM VOL, this.vol); this.fx.feed(Gains.INPUT X, ins, 0); this.fx.process(n); this.fx.fetch(Gains.OUTPUT OUT, outs, 0); } } ./bleep/module- is the library id of the module, and the class is named after the module. The compiler writes the class from the module's node type description; you do not write it. Whole chunks, not single samples A module of the library processes a chunk of up to 32 samples at a time. So the class does not have a per-sample call. It has four steps, and you do them in a new method, chunk : Call What it does set(Class.PARAM X, v) Sets a parameter. v is the normalised value from 0 to 1, the same as the knob. feed(Class.INPUT X, rows, row) Copies row row of rows into an input jack. process(n) Runs the module for n samples (1 to 32). fetch(Class.OUTPUT X, rows, row) Copies an output jack into row row of rows . chunk(n, inputs, outputs) runs once per chunk, after sample() . It gets the chunk's input and output rows, jack by jack, 32 floats per row (row 0 is your first jack). Rows you write in chunk replace what sample() wrote to the same output. It follows the same real-time rules as sample() and its cost is counted. Signals that run through a child module are not available sample by sample in sample() . If you need to mix its output with something you compute per sample, write that into a row first, then chunk can add the two. What the compiler needs compile(source, { children: { gains: { wasm, spec, typeIndex } } }) Field What it is wasm The bytes of the module's .wasm file. A host gets them from the library by id and version and checks it as it does for any module , before it passes them in. spec The node type description of the type to use: its params, inputs and outputs. typeIndex Which node type of the file it is (default 0). A script that imports no library module needs none of this and is compiled as before. How it is linked The script compiles to a .wasm that imports the child's functions from a module named bleep-module: . Binaryen's wasm-merge merges it with the child's file and a 127-byte glue file. Calls into the child become plain calls inside one file. The compiler removes the child's and the glue's exports, so the result exports exactly what your script exports, with one memory , and checks that no import is left except the few the module ABI allows. The child keeps its own memory . A script cannot address a second memory, so the glue copies rows between the two with memory.copy : one copy per feed and per fetch , 128 bytes each. wasm-merge is an Emscripten tool for node. Bleep runs it inside a Worker on a stand-in node ( compiler/wasm-merge.mjs : a process , a require and an in-memory fs ) and loads it only when a script imports a module: it is a separate file, bleep-script-merge.js , about 12 MB. Limits The child's own work is not in the cost estimate. The checker counts your script. A child is a library module and is trusted as such. The host must run files with more than one memory. Browsers do (Chrome 120, Firefox 125, Safari 18.4) and so does the engine's Wasmtime. wasm3 does not. Modules built with JUCE bring the WASI imports and exception handling of the module ABI into your file. They are allowed to stay, so a linked file can need a host that supports them. Not tried yet: no module of that kind was available to test with. Parameters are normalised , not in units. A setter in units is the next step. Transport and note jacks are not passed to the child yet.

title: The Code node
text: The Code node The Code node (Add menu: Utility › Script ) holds one script. Click the node to open its view. The view Part What it does Compile Compiles the script. Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter does the same while the cursor is in the editor Convert to module Turns this node into the module itself: it keeps its cables and knob values, appears in the Add menu and shows its own UI. The same button on the module's window says Convert to code and turns it back. See Convert to module Share… Publishes the module in the Bleep Library, after asking for the metadata and the help text. See Share Settings A number field per setting the script declares, such as Channels . Changing one compiles again. See Settings Editor CodeMirror with TypeScript highlighting, line numbers, bracket matching, folding, undo within the editor, and completion for the decorators and library (type @ or press Ctrl+Space ) Status line Fold: compiled · about 3,000 ops per block (1 % of the limit) , or the number of errors Problems One line per error or warning with line and column; click one to jump to it. The first 30 are shown. Errors are also underlined in the editor Help tab The module's help page in Markdown ( Write and Preview ). The ? button of the node's window shows it, and a module saved from the node keeps it. Without one, the ? shows a page made from the module's description: its text, knobs with their ranges, jacks and meters. Headings, lists, tables, bold, code and links work; images are left out Meters One bar per @probe the module declares Knobs The module's own knobs and buttons, built from its @param and @button declarations Typing in the editor never triggers the board's shortcuts or plays notes on the computer keyboard. Compiling Compiling a module script takes about a second (the first time after loading the page, a few seconds while the compiler loads, about 3 MB over the network). On success , the new module replaces the running one, the node's jacks and knobs are rebuilt, and the source is saved on the node. Cables stay where the jack still exists, and knob values stay where the parameter id still exists. Undo restores the previous source, jacks and module together. On failure , nothing changes. The previous version keeps running, the problems are listed, and the status line says 1 error; the previous version keeps running . Running a patch script builds a cell next to the node. See Patch scripts. Saving and loading The source, the jacks and knobs it declares, and the settings are saved in the patch , on the node. A saved patch shows its Code nodes with their jacks, cables and knob values at once, before anything is compiled. When a patch with a module script is loaded, the page compiles the source in the background and starts the module when it is ready (a few seconds); until then the node is silent. Patch scripts are not compiled on load: the cell they built is ordinary patch content and is already there. Convert to module A script you want to keep using does not have to live in a Code node. Convert to module (once the script has compiled) compiles it for good, keeps it on this computer and turns the node into the module: the same node, with the same cables and knob values, now an ordinary module of the category its @module names (for example Effects › Distortion ), with its own UI and help page. It also appears in the Add menu, so you can place more of it. The button on the module's window says Convert to code . It turns that node back into a Code node with the module's source, UI, help page and metadata, so you can change it and convert it again: the two modes are two views of the same thing, to try either. The module is stored in the browser (IndexedDB) and is yours alone: it is your own code and runs in the same sandbox as every module. Its type id is / (see the Metadata tab; mine until you have a library name). Converting again replaces the stored module with the Code node's current source. Other nodes of it get the new version after a reload. A module is not part of a patch file: someone who opens your patch needs the module too, so share it (see Share). Modules written in Bleep Script and released in the library (the vintage modules, in Add › Effects ) carry their source, so Convert to code opens them too. The converted copy is yours (publisher mine ); the original stays as it is. Metadata The Metadata tab holds what the module says about itself: the publisher (your library name, filled in when you are logged in, otherwise mine ), the module name (from @module({ name }) ), the version , a summary of up to 280 characters, the category , the licence , whether to share the source code (on by default), tags , a web page , release notes and the picture for the library (a screenshot you choose, made smaller to fit: it goes on the module's tile in the library). It is saved with the node and with the module. Share Share… publishes the module in the Bleep Library as a community module, for everyone to install. It asks for the summary, category, licence, version and the help page, builds the package in the browser and uploads it under your library name ( / ); you must be logged in to the library. The library checks it. Each share needs a higher version than the last. With Share the source code on (the default, in the Metadata tab and in the dialog) the script goes with it too, under the same licence: anyone who installs the module can press Convert to code on it, read it, change it and make their own. Turn it off to share only the compiled module. The module's own UI goes with it (as view.sandbox.js ) and runs only in the same sandbox as in your Code node, so a module from the library can show its picture, and its help page, like one you made. Panels A Code node's knobs can be put on a panel like any module's: right-click a knob in the view and choose Add to panel . Where it is available Host Compile Run Bleep Play (the browser) Yes Yes Dev server ( scripts/run/ui-server.py ) Yes No audio (the demo engine) Standalone app and plugins Not yet: the compiler is not shipped with them The engine runs a Code node's module once the UI has registered it, and keeps the node's cables, knob values and source The compiler is a separate file, bleep-script-compiler.js (about 15 MB, 3 MB compressed), and the editor another, bleep-script-editor.js (about 470 KB). Without the compiler the Code node says so and keeps working as far as already compiled scripts go; without the editor it falls back to a plain text box. Building the bundles cd patch/script npm install npm run bundle # dist/bleep-script-compiler.js and dist/bleep-script-editor.js cd ../.. scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules # copies them next to the board scripts/run/ui-server.py serves them straight from patch/script/dist , and a native build with BLEEP UI DEV ROOT does too. The website image builds them as part of its web stage. The playground patch/script/playground/ is the same editor and compile flow as a stand-alone page, with a test signal and live audio, handy for working on the compiler or a library module. Start the script-spike server from .claude/launch.json and open /script/playground/ . Known limits No state-keeping hot reload. A recompile starts the module fresh: smoothers and filters begin from zero. There is no crossfade between versions. The same source and settings compile once. Pressing Compile again without a change answers at once. Instances. Each Code node has its own source and its own interface. Two nodes with the same script compile once but are separate modules. Browser support. The compiler runs in a module Worker and uses WebAssembly, so it needs a current browser.

title: Custom UIs and widgets
text: Custom UIs and widgets By default a Code node shows one control for every @param , a meter for every @probe and a button for every @button . You can replace that in two ways: a layout in the @module decorator, which arranges the standard widgets: no code, safe, and enough for most modules; a self-made UI in JavaScript, which draws whatever it likes on a canvas. The Code node's editor has a Script tab and a UI tab for this. Resizing and fullscreen Drag the lower right corner of the Code window to make it larger or smaller: the editors and the UI area grow with it. The fullscreen button in the title bar (or F11, or a double click on the title bar) fills the board; Esc or the same button brings the window back to its size. Layout @module({ name: "Mixer", settings: [{ id: "CHANNELS", name: "Channels", min: 1, max: 16, init: 4 }], layout: [ { row: [ { repeat: CHANNELS, title: "Ch {n}", column: [ { fader: "level{n}", meter: "peak{n}" }, "pan{n}", "mute{n}", ] }, { title: "Master", column: [{ fader: "master", meter: "peakMaster" }] }, ] }, ], }) A layout is a list. Each item is one of: Item Shows "id" The widget that suits the id: a knob for a number, a toggle for a boolean, a select for a choice, a meter for a probe, a button for a @button . { knob: "id" } A round knob for a number param. { fader: "id" } A vertical fader. Add meter: "probeId" to put a level meter beside it. { toggle: "id" } An on/off switch for a boolean param. { select: "id" } A drop-down for a choice param. { meter: "id" } A meter for a @probe . { value: "id" } The value of a param as text, read only. { button: "id" } A button for a @button method. { label: "text" } A line of text. { spacer: true } Empty space. { row: [...] } , { column: [...] } Groups items side by side or one above the other. Any item can have label (replaces the name) and title . A container with repeat makes one copy per channel: repeat is a number or the name of a setting, and {n} in ids and titles becomes the copy number from 1. Repeats can be nested. The transform checks the layout when you compile: every id must be a param, probe or button of the module, a toggle needs a boolean, a select needs a choice, and a layout holds at most 400 widgets. Errors name the id and the line. A self-made UI Open the UI tab, write JavaScript, and use the bleep object. Here is a small meter: const level = bleep.canvas(60); bleep.onFrame(() => { const { g, width, height } = level; g.clearRect(0, 0, width, height); g.fillStyle = bleep.theme.accent; g.fillRect(0, 0, width bleep.probe("level"), height); }); The playground example Fold (own UI) draws a transfer curve and lets you drag it to set Drive and Mix. The bleep object Member What it does bleep.params Every param of the module. bleep.param(id) One param; throws with the known ids when there is none. bleep.probe(id) The latest value of a @probe , 0 until the module reports one. bleep.button(id) Presses a @button method. bleep.onFrame(fn) Calls fn(dt) every animation frame, dt in seconds. bleep.onValues(fn) Calls fn() when a param or probe has changed. bleep.size(h) Asks for a height in pixels, 40 to 800. The width is the node's. bleep.canvas(h) Makes a canvas as wide as the view and h high, scaled for the screen: { el, g, width, height } . bleep.canvas("fill") makes it as high as the view too, so it follows the window when it is resized or fullscreen. bleep.theme The board's colours: bg , panel , line , text , muted , accent , warn . A param has id , name , kind , unit , min , max , steps , choices , a value in its own units, a normalised position from 0 to 1, and set(units) and setNormalised(x) to change it. A UI can set at most 240 values per second. An error in your code stops the UI and is shown in the editor with its line. What a UI can use A UI draws on canvases and listens to the pointer. It runs in a worker, so there is no DOM : no document , no window , no buttons or inputs (draw them on the canvas, as the vintage modules' UIs do). The element canvas.el is a small stand-in with what a picture needs: On canvas.el addEventListener(type, fn) pointerdown , pointermove , pointerup , pointercancel , pointerenter , pointerleave , wheel , click , dblclick . The event has clientX , clientY , pointerId , pointerType , button , buttons , the modifier keys and deltaX , deltaY . A press captures the pointer, so a drag keeps working outside the picture getBoundingClientRect() Where the canvas is, for turning clientX and clientY into picture coordinates style.cursor pointer , crosshair , grab , move , ns-resize , ew-resize and the other common cursors canvas.g is an ordinary 2D context (the browser's OffscreenCanvas ): paths, gradients, shadows, roundRect , text with system fonts. Math , Date , typed arrays and the rest of JavaScript's own library are there. The sandbox A self-made UI is code written by whoever made the script, so it runs where the browser keeps it apart from the board, and it runs without asking : it runs in a worker inside a sandboxed frame with no network, storage, cookies or access to the board, your patches or the native app: it can compute, draw and talk to its module through bleep , nothing else; the frame hands each finished picture to the board and watches the worker. A UI that stops answering for a moment (an endless loop in a frame callback) or never gets started (an endless loop at the top of the code) is stopped , the UI shows the error, and the board carries on. It cannot freeze the page; a UI cannot use more than the messages bleep has: it sets at most 240 values per second, and a flood of messages stops it. What a UI can still do is use your processor until the watchdog stops it, and draw whatever it likes inside its own box. Neither reaches your patches or your data. The UI is stored with the script, so it is shared and versioned with it. See Limits and safety.

title: Events and routing
text: Events and routing Some things happen at a moment, not continuously: a key goes down, a gate rises. A module script handles them with @on methods. The engine runs them at the sample where the event happened , in order with sample() , so timing is exact. Notes A notes jack carries a stream of note events. Declare it with type: "notes" and the NoteStream type, imported from the library: import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @module({ name: "Router", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Router { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Low", type: "notes" }) low!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "High", type: "notes" }) high!: NoteStream; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @on("notes") route(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.pitch < 0) { this.low.push(n); } else { n.transpose(12); this.high.push(n); } } } @on("notes") names the input field . The method is called once per event arriving on that jack, with the event. Whatever you push goes out of that output jack at the same sample. A notes jack cannot have a count . NoteEvent Field Meaning type 0 note on, 1 note off, 2 pressure, 3 control change, 4 program change, 5 pitch bend, 6 channel pressure, 7 realtime message. Constants: NOTE ON , NOTE OFF , … channel MIDI channel, 0 to 15 offset The sample inside the block where it happens note The MIDI note number (for types 3 to 7, the controller or program number, 0, 0 or the status byte) pitch Pitch in volts: 1.0 is one octave, 0 is C4 value Velocity or pressure from 0 to 1; for a control change the data divided by 127; for a bend −1 to +1 Helpers: isOn , isOff , isCc , and transpose(semitones) , which shifts note and pitch together. Handle the types you know and ignore the rest: if (n.isOn) { … } . NoteStream Member Meaning length Events waiting on this jack (at most 64 per block) read(i, into) Copies event i into a NoteEvent you own push(e) Sends an event; dropped silently when 64 are already queued clear() Forgets the queued events (an output starts every block empty) You rarely need more than push : the handler already gets each incoming event. Control edges Handlers also fire when a control, gate or trigger signal crosses a level: @input({ name: "CC", type: "control" }) cc1: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @on("cc1", { rising: 0.5 }) open(): void { this.gate = 1; } @on("cc1", { falling: 0.5 }) close(): void { this.gate = 0; } A rising edge fires on the sample where the signal goes from below the level to at or above it; a falling edge the other way round. Give exactly one of rising and falling . The first block never fires an edge: the previous value is taken from the first sample. Order within a sample Before the samples of a block, the @transport method runs, then block() . For each sample, in this order: inputs are set, note events at this sample are handled, edge handlers run, then sample() runs, then outputs are read. block() runs once before the first sample (see Rates and timing), and sees each input at its first sample of the block. Cost Handlers count in the cost estimate at their worst case: a note handler is assumed to run for 64 events per block, an edge handler for every sample. A router Put the two handlers together and you have a router: notes below middle C go out Low , the others go out High an octave up, and a control above 0.5 opens a gate. Cable a Keyboard's Notes into it and press keys.

title: The board and the engine
text: The board and the engine The Code node Piece Path The node, its view, Compile, settings, saving patch/board/ui/board-code.js , board-code-view.html The Worker that loads the compiler patch/board/ui/board-code-worker.js The standard widgets and the sandboxed custom UI patch/board/ui/board-code-widgets.js The Worker keeps the compiler off the page: the first compile takes seconds of CPU, and the board seals the page's built-ins, while the compiler needs a plain JavaScript environment. The page and the Worker talk with three messages: init -> the example scripts compile { source, typeId, constants } -> { wasm, specs, problems } patch { source, settings, types } -> { ok, nodes, cables, interface } board-code.js caches compiled results by a hash of the source and the settings, so the same source is compiled once, however many nodes use it. What is saved A compile result is saved with the node as three things: the source , the settings and the interface (the node type description). The .wasm is not saved in the patch. That is why a shared patch is text, and why opening one means compiling it yourself. In the browser patch/web/js/module-host.js instantiates the .wasm in the AudioWorklet, through the same code path as every other module. Compiling happens in the Worker, and the compiled module is handed to the engine with BleepWeb.registerCode , so the audio thread never compiles. In the app and the plugins patch/engine/wasm/CodeNodes.cpp registers the Code entry in the engine's module registry. A Code node's real type id is code: : , so the same source and settings are the same module, and a changed source is a new type. registerCodeModule(...) takes the compiled bytes, loads them as a package ( WasmPackage::load checks the ABI and refuses any import the ABI does not allow), gives the module that type id and registers it. When a patch is loaded and the module is not registered yet, resolve(...) builds a spec from the saved interface . The node is silent, but it has its jacks and knobs, so cables and knob values survive loading. The engine runs the file in Wasmtime ( WasmRuntime.cpp ), the same sandbox as the other WebAssembly modules. Today the compiler is not shipped with the app and the plugins; see The Code node.

title: The compiler
text: The compiler A module script goes through four steps. All of the code is in patch/script/ . The module pipeline: the source is parsed, the Bleep transform checks it and adds the entry file, asc and Binaryen compile it to module.wasm. The node description and the problems come out on the side. 1. asc, in memory compiler/compile.mjs exports compileScript(asc, source, { lib, typeId, constants }) . It calls the AssemblyScript compiler, asc.main , with in-memory readFile and writeFile hooks: the script and the library sources are strings in a map, and the output .wasm is captured as bytes. There is no file system. The same function runs in node (tests, the build), in a page (the playground) and in a worker (the board). It resolves to { wasm, specs, generated, problems, ms } . wasm is null when there is an error. The flags are fixed, and each has a reason: Flag Why --runtime stub No garbage collector. Nothing is allocated while audio runs. --use abort= Removes the env.abort import, so the file imports nothing. --exportStart initialize The module ABI's initialize runs the global initialisers. --optimizeLevel 3 --shrinkLevel 1 --noAssert Speed and size. --use NAME=value One constant per settings entry of the module. If the module declares settings , the compiler runs twice . A quick first pass stops right after parsing and only reads the settings, because their values are compile-time constants ( --use ) and must be known before the real compile. 2. The Bleep transform transform/bleep.mjs is an AssemblyScript transform : a plugin the compiler calls between parsing and compiling. In afterParse it: reads the decorators ( @module , @input , @output , @param , @probe , @button , @on , @transport ) with a small literal parser. Decorator arguments are never evaluated; an identifier or a call in a decorator is an error; builds the node type description : the JSON the rest of Bleep uses to draw the node, its jacks, knobs and meters; generates an entry source file with the bleep exports of the module ABI and a glue class that copies the ABI's buffers into the module's fields (params once per chunk, inputs per sample, outputs read back after sample() ); adds that entry file to the compilation with parser.parseFile , so the compiler type-checks it like your own code and errors read as source lines. The transform only reads syntax trees, with no file system and no eval , so it runs unchanged in node and in a page, and the output is byte-identical in both. 3. The subset checker transform/subset.mjs runs inside the transform, on the syntax tree, before the compiler sees the code. It does two jobs: The whole file: nothing that adds a host import or reaches memory directly ( declare function , @external , load , store , changetype , unchecked , imports other than bleep/ ). Real-time code ( block() , sample() , reset() , @on handlers, and everything they call): no loop without a constant bound, no recursion, no allocation, no exceptions, no call to something unknown. It also estimates the cost of one 32-sample chunk in abstract operations: loops are multiplied by their bound and calls by the callee. A module over the budget is a warning, and far over it is an error. See Limits and safety. The library sources in src/bleep/ are trusted: they are read for their cost but not held to these rules. 4. The module file The result is one .wasm file with no imports. It exports memory , initialize and the bleep functions, which is the same module ABI every other Bleep module uses. A typical module is under 20 KB. The library patch/script/src/bleep/ .ts is the standard library (see Library). It is plain AssemblyScript, compiled into your module together with your script: import { Svf } from "./bleep/filters" pulls the source in, and unused code is dropped. The library sources are also embedded in the compiler bundle as strings, which is how an in-memory compile finds ./bleep/... . The bundle npm run bundle ( bundle.mjs , using esbuild) produces two files in patch/script/dist/ : File Content bleep-script-compiler.js asc , Binaryen, the transform, the library sources, the example scripts and the patch runner, in one file. Exports compile , patch and examples . bleep-script-editor.js The CodeMirror 6 editor, with completion for the decorators and the library. The board loads them only when a Code node is opened for the first time, so a patch without scripts pays nothing. Binaryen embeds its own .wasm ; bundle.mjs replaces its fetch("data:...") of it, which a content-security policy without data: in connect-src would block.

title: The lifecycle of a script
text: The lifecycle of a script A script has three lives that overlap: the source you edit and save, the compiled module the board keeps, and the instance the engine runs. From the editor to sound: edit, compile in the Worker, register with the engine, run. The result is saved with the patch as source, settings and interface, and opening the patch compiles it again. 1. Edit The source is text in a CodeMirror editor. Nothing is compiled while you type, and typing never triggers the board's shortcuts. The node keeps the last compiled version running. 2. Compile Compile (the button, or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) sends the source to the Worker. board-code.js hashes the source and the settings. If that hash was compiled before, the cached result is used and nothing else happens. If the script is a patch script , it runs in the QuickJS sandbox and the board builds the cell (Patch script runner). The rest of this list is for module scripts. If the module declares settings , a first pass reads them. The Bleep transform reads the decorators, the subset checker looks at the real-time code, and asc compiles (The compiler). On failure , nothing changes. The problems are listed and marked in the editor, and the previous version keeps running. On success , the result is the .wasm file and the node description, and it is kept in the cache. 3. Register The board gives the compiled module to the engine under the type id code: : . The hash is in the id on purpose: the same source and settings are the same type, so the engine keeps the running instance; a changed source is a new type, so the engine builds a new instance and replaces the old one. The jacks and knobs are rebuilt, and cables and knob values stay wherever the jack or parameter id still exists. The browser engine takes the module at once. The native engine checks it first: it compiles the file, verifies the ABI, and refuses any import the ABI does not allow. 4. Run: the life of an instance This is the module ABI's life of a module instance, as the generated code sees it. Step What happens Instantiate The host compiles and instantiates the file, once per node. initialize The module's global initialisers run. bleep spec json , bleep chunk The host reads the node description and checks that the chunk is 32 samples. bleep create(type, sampleRate) The generated glue constructs your class, passing the sample rate to the constructor. Everything you allocate, such as a delay buffer, is allocated here. Knobs The host sets every knob once, so the module sees the saved state. Every chunk of 32 samples The glue copies the params in, calls block() once, then calls sample() for each sample (copying inputs in and outputs out), and runs @on handlers at the sample where their event happened. bleep reset A transport jump or a cleared tail calls your reset() . bleep destroy The node was removed or its source changed. With the stub runtime nothing is freed, so bleep destroy frees nothing. The host drops the whole instance with its memory (capped at 64 MiB), so nothing leaks across nodes. This is why allocation is allowed in the constructor and refused in real-time code. 5. Save The patch stores, on the Code node: the source , the settings and the interface (the node description). It does not store the .wasm . Because the interface is saved, a patch shows its Code nodes with their jacks, cables and knob values at once, before anything is compiled. 6. Open When a patch is opened, the board calls sync for every Code node that has a source: The node is claimed with its hash, so a second board message does not start another compile. The source is compiled in the Worker (nodes with the same source and settings share one compile), and the result goes through step 3. If the source does not compile, or the compiler cannot be loaded, the node stays silent and a message goes to the console. Its jacks and knobs are still there from the saved interface. Patch scripts are not compiled on open. The cell they built is ordinary patch content and is already in the file. In the standalone app and the plugins the compiler is not shipped yet, so a Code node opened there keeps its saved interface and is silent unless the module was registered by a UI that has the compiler.

title: Limits and safety
text: Limits and safety A script is code that runs while you play, so Bleep Script is strict about what it accepts. Module scripts: the checker Before a module script compiles, a checker walks the code that runs on the audio thread ( block() , sample() , reset() , @on handlers and everything they call). It refuses: recursion, closures, class expressions, exceptions and regular expressions; anything that may allocate or copy at run time: push , map , concat , slice , split , string building and similar. Allocate in the constructor; calls to anything but your own functions, Math and the bleep/ libraries; declare (host imports), load , store , memory , changetype , unchecked , unreachable , abort and names starting with ; imports from anywhere but bleep/ ; loops with no bound the checker can see, and loops longer than 4096 iterations. Each message names the line and says what to do instead. Cost bound The checker also adds up the work of one chunk of audio (32 samples): every operation, with each loop counted at its bound. It is a bound, not a time, and one op is about a nanosecond. Over 60,000 ops: a warning. Over 400,000 ops: the module is refused. A module that is too costly would make the audio glitch, so refusing it at compile time is the safe choice. Patch scripts A patch script runs in a QuickJS sandbox inside a worker, with no access to the page, the network or storage. Its only output is the patch it returns. It is held to: Limit Value Time 3 seconds, then it is stopped Memory 64 MB Source 200,000 characters Result 4 MB The result is checked against the module types on your board before anything is created: unknown knobs, jacks or modules are errors with the line. Custom UIs A self-made UI (see Custom UIs and widgets) is JavaScript from the script's author. It runs in a worker inside a sandboxed frame with no network, storage, cookies or access to the page, so it needs no approval. The frame watches the worker: a UI that stops answering for 1.5 seconds, does not start within 3 seconds or floods the board with messages is terminated and shows an error, and the board keeps running. The UI can still use your processor until then, and draw anything inside its own box. Scripts from other people Read a script before you run it, as with any code. The sandboxes keep a script away from your files, other patches and accounts, and the checker keeps a module script from using more time than its budget. They do not make a script good, only contained.

title: Implementation
text: Implementation Bleep Script is not one program. It is a compiler pipeline that runs in your browser, a sandboxed interpreter for patch scripts, a node in the board's UI, and a place in the engine where the result is loaded. This section is for people who work on the language itself. If you only write scripts, you do not need it. The big picture The Code node sends the source to a Worker that holds the compiler bundle. A module script becomes a wasm file and a node description; a patch script becomes nodes and cables. The wasm file runs in the browser and in the app and plugins through the same module ABI. Everything except the last row runs on your machine, in the page. Nothing is sent to a server to be compiled. Two kinds of script, two pipelines Module script Patch script Recognised by @module on a class export default cell(...) Language AssemblyScript (a strict subset) TypeScript or JavaScript Runs Every sample or block, on the audio thread, as WebAssembly Once, when you press Compile Produces A .wasm file and a node type description A list of modules and cables Code patch/script/transform/ , compiler/ , src/bleep/ patch/script/patch/ Where the code is Piece Path Compiler, transform, library, patch runner, playground, tests patch/script/ (see its README.md ) The editor patch/script/editor/ The Code node in the board, and its Worker patch/board/ui/board-code.js , board-code-worker.js The browser module host patch/web/js/module-host.js Native engine support patch/engine/wasm/CodeNodes.cpp Concept and design, with what differs from it doc/specs/bleep-script.md Where to start reading If you want to change... Start here A decorator, or what a module's node looks like transform/bleep.mjs What the compiler refuses, or the cost estimate transform/subset.mjs The compile flags, or how errors are reported compiler/compile.mjs A library function src/bleep/ .ts , and its page in Library What a patch script can build patch/prelude.mjs , patch/materialize.mjs The editor editor/editor-entry.mjs The Code node's behaviour in the board patch/board/ui/board-code.js How the engine loads a Code node patch/engine/wasm/CodeNodes.cpp The pages in this section Page Content The compiler asc in memory, the Bleep transform, the subset checker, the library and the bundle Patch script runner The QuickJS sandbox and how a description becomes nodes and cables The board and the engine The Code node, its Worker, and how the result is loaded in the browser and in the app The lifecycle of a script From typing to sound, and from opening a patch to sound, step by step Limits and safety What is refused, the cost estimate, and the sandboxes Running the tests Every test suite, the commands, and what each one covers

title: Patch script runner
text: Patch script runner A patch script never touches the audio thread. It runs once, and what it returns is a description that the board checks and builds. The code is in patch/script/patch/ . File Role run.mjs Strips the TypeScript types (with Sucrase, keeping line numbers) and runs the script in QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly : no network, no files, no clock, no DOM, a 64 MiB memory limit and a 3 second time limit. The only thing that leaves the sandbox is the data the script returns. prelude.mjs The code that runs inside the sandbox before yours. It defines cell() and the builder, and records what you ask for as plain data. materialize.mjs Back in the host: checks the description against the board's module types and turns it into nodes and cables. materialize.mjs checks that every module exists and can be added, that the knobs exist and the values fit, and that the jacks exist and the signal types match. Units are converted to the knob's 0 to 1 range with the same rules as the engine's ParamSpec::toNormalised , and the checks are those of the factory preset kit ( patch/presets/kit.mjs ), which builds the factory cells the same way. A mistake in a patch script can only produce a description that materialize.mjs then refuses. See Limits and safety for the sandbox limits.

title: Running the tests
text: Running the tests All Bleep Script tests are in patch/script/test/ and run with node. They need no browser and no audio device. Setup You need node 22 or later. cd patch/script npm install Run everything npm test This is what CI runs. It takes about a minute and a half, and ends with all library tests passed . It runs these steps in order, and stops at the first one that fails: Step What it covers node build.mjs Compiles the two example modules ( src/gains.dsp.ts , src/synth-voice.dsp.ts ) and the script modules of patch/modules/ ( language: bleep-script ) to build/ . A compile error here fails the run. test/transform.test.mjs The transform: the generated description against a hand-written one, errors with file and line, int, choice, bool and float params, two modules in one file, the subset checker and the cost estimate test/patch.test.mjs Patch scripts: the sandbox and its limits, materialize against the module types, unit conversion test/docs.test.mjs The documentation: every block fenced as compile in website/content/developers/bleep-script/ compiles, and the tutorials' modules do what the text says test/spike.mjs The Gains module in the browser module host (V8): behaviour against a reference model, knob changes, speed test/dsp/all.mjs The library, one process per file (see below) Run one file node test/transform.test.mjs node test/dsp/filters.test.mjs node test/dsp/all.mjs # all library tests Each prints one ok or FAIL line per check and exits non-zero if any failed. The library tests test/dsp/ has one test file per library file ( osc , filters , delay , random , env , dynamics , fx , util ), each with a .harness.ts : an AssemblyScript wrapper that exposes the functions to node. They check shapes, aliasing, filter responses, timing, and that processing allocates nothing. File What it covers module.test.mjs The library inside a module script, with the subset checker: calling library code breaks no real-time rule, and a cost is estimated docs.test.mjs Every export of the library is listed in library.md , and the page's examples compile ( test/doc-examples.mjs wraps each one into a whole module) If you add a library function, docs.test.mjs fails until the function has an entry and an example in Library. Checks that need more Check How Needs The engine's Wasmtime host runs the same module test/wasmtime-check.sh The Wasmtime C API that scripts/experiments/wasm-spike.sh downloads to build/wasm-spike/wasmtime , and clang++ A module's own UI in the real sandbox (a worker in a sandboxed frame), driven by a real mouse, with screenshots node test/browser/ui-chrome.mjs Chrome ( CHROME=… if it is not in the usual place) and node build.mjs first The sandbox of the UI frame: escape attempts, endless loops test/browser/run-custom-ui.sh Chrome The compiler runs in a page Start the script-spike server from .claude/launch.json (it serves patch/ on port 8767) and open /script/test/browser/index.html A browser The custom UI frame test/browser/custom-ui.html , served the same way A browser The board's side CI also runs three tests for the browser part of the Code node, from the repository root: node patch/web/test/board-code-test.mjs node patch/web/test/library-client-test.mjs node patch/web/test/user-modules-test.mjs node patch/web/test/web-settings-test.mjs board-code-test.mjs checks the Code node without a compiler: its type description, when its view is rebuilt, and that a board with Code nodes is handed to the compiler once. When you change something You changed Run A library file node test/dsp/ .test.mjs , then node test/dsp/docs.test.mjs The transform or the checker node test/transform.test.mjs , then npm test A page in website/content/developers/bleep-script/ that has code node test/docs.test.mjs The patch runner node test/patch.test.mjs board-code.js node patch/web/test/board-code-test.mjs user-modules.js , or how library-client.js lists the saved modules node patch/web/test/user-modules-test.mjs

title: Library
text: Library Module scripts can import only from bleep/ . These libraries are plain AssemblyScript that is inlined into your module, so using them costs nothing extra. For how to use the pieces together, see the tutorials and the synth voice tutorial. Three rules hold for all of them: Allocate in the constructor, never in block() or sample() . Every class that needs memory (a delay line, a table, a reverb) takes its size in its constructor and allocates then. Nothing in the library allocates afterwards. set and update methods may call sin , tan , exp or pow . Call them in block() , and only when a setting changed, not in sample() . The next() methods are made for sample() . Audio is f32 , Math takes f64 . Phases and frequencies are f64 where precision matters (a phase accumulator in f32 goes wrong after a few seconds); audio samples and levels are f32 . Frequencies are in Hz, times in seconds, levels in dB when a name says so ( thresholdDb ) and linear otherwise. Each library section ends with Examples : one for every function and class. An example shows the members of a module class, the part you would write inside export class ... { } . They assume the class has the audio input x , the audio output out and the field sampleRate (set in the constructor), as in the module at the top of this page; any other jack they need is declared in the example. Every example is compiled by the documentation test. Import What is in it ./bleep/osc Band-limited saw, pulse and triangle, fast sine, wavetables, supersaw, FM operator ./bleep/filters One-pole, state-variable and ladder filters, resonator, formants, all-passes, comb ./bleep/delay Delay line, table interpolation, tape delay, plucked string ./bleep/random Seeded random numbers, white, pink and brown noise, sample and hold, random LFO ./bleep/env ADSR and friends, followers, slew, LFO, ramps, triggers, tempo clock ./bleep/dynamics Compressor, limiter, gate, wave shapers, bitcrusher, oversampling ./bleep/fx Reverb, phaser, chorus, pitch shifter ./bleep/fft A fixed-size FFT ./bleep/util Ranges, pitch conversion, fast math, pan and mid/side, RMS ./bleep/dsp Smoothing, meters, biquad filter, dB conversion ./bleep/notes Note events A short example, a saw voice with a filter that follows an envelope (see also the synth voice tutorial): import { sawBlep } from "./bleep/osc"; import { Svf } from "./bleep/filters"; import { Adsr } from "./bleep/env"; @module({ name: "Pluck", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Pluck { @input({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Pitch", min: 40, max: 2000, init: 110, unit: "Hz" }) pitch: f32 = 110; private phase: f64 = 0; private filter: Svf = new Svf(); private env: Adsr; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.env = new Adsr(sampleRate); this.env.set(0.002, 0.25, 0.0, 0.2); } sample(): void { const e = this.env.next(this.gate); const dt = this.pitch / this.sampleRate; this.phase += dt; if (this.phase >= 1.0) this.phase -= 1.0; this.filter.set(this.sampleRate, 200.0 + 4000.0 e, 2.0); this.filter.tick(sawBlep(this.phase, dt)); this.out = this.filter.low e; } } The set call inside sample() there costs a tan per sample: fine for a single voice, but when the sweep does not need sample accuracy set the filter from block() (once per 32 samples), as the synth voice does. bleep/osc import { sawBlep, squareBlep, triangle, Wavetable, Supersaw } from "./bleep/osc"; Phases run from 0 to 1 over one cycle and dt is the phase step of one sample ( frequency / sampleRate ). A naive saw or square aliases: harmonics above half the sample rate fold back as inharmonic whistles. The Blep and triangle functions remove most of that by correcting the waveform near its jumps and corners (polyBLEP and polyBLAMP). Keep phase accumulators in f64 . Name What it does polyBlep(t, dt) The polyBLEP residual of a unit step at phase 0. Add height polyBlep(phase, dt) to a naive waveform at each jump to make your own band-limited shape. polyBlamp(t, dt) The same for a corner (a change of slope). It is already multiplied by dt ; multiply by the slope change per unit of phase. sawBlep(phase, dt) A band-limited sawtooth rising from -1 to 1. squareBlep(phase, dt, width) A band-limited pulse wave, +1 for the first width (0 to 1) of the cycle and -1 for the rest. width 0.5 is a square. triangle(phase, dt) A band-limited triangle, starting at 0 and rising. Stateless (polyBLAMP on the naive triangle), so it has no drift or leak. fastSin(phase) A sine from a polynomial, error below 4e-6. phase in cycles, any value. SineTable(size = 4096) A sine from a lookup table with linear interpolation. read(phase) . Wavetable(size = 2048, levels = 10) A mip-mapped wavetable: each level has half the harmonics of the one before, and read(phase, dt) picks the level that does not alias at the pitch it is played. Fill it in the constructor with setSaw() , setSquare() , setTriangle() or setHarmonics(amps, count) (the amplitude of harmonic k + 1 is amps[k] ): building takes size times the number of harmonics operations. Supersaw(sampleRate, voices = 7, detuneCents = 20) A stack of detuned band-limited saws. setDetune(cents) is the total spread; next(frequency) per sample. The mix is scaled by 1 / sqrt(voices). The start phases are fixed, so it sounds the same on every run. FmOp(sampleRate) One FM / phase-modulation operator. next(frequency, modulation, feedback) : modulation is in cycles (another operator's output times an index), feedback times the operator's own last output is added to the phase. reset() . Examples polyBlep example import { polyBlep } from "./bleep/osc"; private phase: f64 = 0; sample(): void { const dt = 220.0 / this.sampleRate; this.phase += dt; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); // a naive saw, minus the smoothed step where it wraps this.out = (2.0 this.phase - 1.0 - polyBlep(this.phase, dt)); } polyBlamp example import { polyBlamp } from "./bleep/osc"; private phase: f64 = 0; sample(): void { const dt = 220.0 / this.sampleRate; this.phase += dt; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); // a naive triangle with the corner at the valley smoothed (the library's triangle() does both corners) let q = this.phase + 0.25; if (q >= 1.0) q -= 1.0; this.out = (1.0 - abs(4.0 q - 2.0) + 8.0 polyBlamp(q, dt)); } sawBlep example import { sawBlep } from "./bleep/osc"; private phase: f64 = 0; sample(): void { const dt = 110.0 / this.sampleRate; Frequencies are clamped below Nyquist, so a modulated cutoff cannot make a filter unstable. All filters have reset() . For a plain low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, all-pass or shelf at a fixed setting, Biquad is the cheapest. Name What it does OnePole A 6 dB per octave filter. setLowpass(sr, f) or setHighpass(sr, f) (exactly -3 dB at f ), then next(x) . Svf A state-variable filter (Cytomic / Simper), stable under fast cutoff modulation. set(sr, f, q) ( q from 0.5; 0.7071 is flat), then tick(x) and read low , high , band (peak gain q ), bandUnity (peak gain 1), notch , peak or all . LadderFilter A Moog-style 24 dB per octave low-pass with tanh saturation in each stage. set(sr, f, resonance, drive = 1) , next(x) . Resonance 0 to 1 (it self-oscillates near 1); the passband level drops as it rises, like the real thing. Resonz A resonator with peak gain 1 (SuperCollider's Resonz). set(sr, f, bandwidthHz) , next(x) . Formant Three resonators tuned to the formants of a vowel. setVowel(sr, position, shift = 1) morphs through a, e, i, o, u (0 to 4); shift scales the formants (1.15 is a smaller voice). Feed it a saw or noise. Allpass1 A first-order all-pass (unit gain, phase turns a quarter cycle at f ). set(sr, f) , next(x) . Chain a few for a phaser. Allpass2 A second-order all-pass (phase turns half a cycle at f ). set(sr, f, q) , next(x) . CombFilter(maxDelay) y = x + feedforward x[n - D] + feedback y[n - D] . Set the public feedforward and feedback , setDelay(samples) (fractions allowed), next(x) . Feedforward only is a notch comb (flanger); feedback only rings at multiples of sampleRate / D. Name What it does DelayLine(maxSamples) A delay line. write(x) once per sample, then read: read(d) (linear), readCubic(d) (Catmull-Rom, better highs, d from 1), readAllpass(d) (flat response, best for a steady d , one tap, d from 1.5); Ad(sampleRate) A one-shot attack-decay envelope started by a trigger (a rising edge): it plays out whatever the trigger does. set(attack, decay) , next(trigger) . Slew(sampleRate) A slew limiter (portamento, click-free controls). rise and fall are the fastest the output may move, in units per second. next(x) , snap(x) . Lfo(sampleRate, seed) A low-frequency oscillator from -1 to 1. Line(sampleRate) A straight line between two values. set(from, to, seconds) , next() ; done says it arrived. Ramp(sampleRate) A 0 to 1 ramp started by a trigger. setTime(seconds) , next(trigger) , start() . Trigger next(x) is 1 for the one sample in which x rises through threshold (0.5), else 0. Limiter(sampleRate, lookahead = 0.002, release = 0.08) A look-ahead brick-wall limiter: nothing leaves above ceiling . The output is latency samples late. next(x) , gainReductionDb . Gate(sampleRate, attack, release) A noise gate with hysteresis: opens above openDb , closes below closeDb after holdSeconds , down to rangeDb . next(x) , nextKeyed(x, key) , isOpen . softClip(x) Soft saturation (a tanh). hardClip(x, limit = 1) Clips at +-limit. foldback(x, threshold = 1) Folds the signal back from +-threshold (a wavefolder). asymSat(x, amount) Asymmetric saturation: adds even harmonics, no DC, small-signal gain 1. amount 0 to 1. chebyshev(x, order) The Chebyshev polynomial of that order: a sine of amplitude 1 comes out at order times the frequency. Decimate Sample-rate reduction: ratio 1 passes the signal, 0.25 keeps every fourth sample. next(x) . Oversampler2x , Oversampler4x Oversampling around a non-linear step, with half-band filters (flat to 0.375 of the sample rate). up(x) sets a , b (and c , d for 4x); shape each; down(a, b) ( down(a, b, c, d) ) returns the sample. latency is the delay in samples. HalfBandUp , HalfBandDown The two filters inside the oversamplers, for a different ratio or a custom chain. The shapers have hard corners that alias when the input is loud or bright. // look-ahead, release this.limiter.ceiling = 0.9; } sample(): void { this.out = this.limiter.next(this.x); } // arrives limiter.latency samples late Gate example import { Gate } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private gate: Gate; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.gate = new Gate(sampleRate, 0.001, 0.1); this.gate.openDb = -40.0; this.gate.closeDb = -46.0; this.gate.holdSeconds = 0.05; } sample(): void { this.out = this.gate.next(this.x); } softClip example import { softClip } from "./bleep/dynamics"; sample(): void { this.out = softClip(this.x 3.0) 0.5; } hardClip example import { hardClip } from "./bleep/dynamics"; sample(): void { this.out = hardClip(this.x 3.0, 0.5); } // clips at +-0.5 foldback example import { foldback } from "./bleep/dynamics"; sample(): void { this.out = foldback(this.x 4.0, 1.0); } // the peaks fold back instead of clipping asymSat example import { asymSat } from "./bleep/dynamics"; sample(): void { this.out = asymSat(this.x, 0.6); } // even harmonics, like a tube chebyshev example import { chebyshev } from "./bleep/dynamics"; sample(): void { // an exciter: the signal plus its second and third harmonics this.out = this.x 0.7 + chebyshev(this.x, 2) 0.2 + chebyshev(this.x, 3) 0.1; } Bitcrush example import { Bitcrush } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private crush: Bitcrush = new Bitcrush(8.0); block(): void { this.crush.setBits(6.5); } // fractions are fine sample(): void { this.out = this.crush.next(this.x); } Decimate example import { Decimate } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private decimate: Decimate = new Decimate(); block(): void { this.decimate.ratio = 0.25; } // keeps every fourth sample sample(): void { this.out = this.decimate.next(this.x); } HalfBandUp and HalfBandDown example import { HalfBandUp, HalfBandDown, hardClip } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private up: HalfBandUp = new HalfBandUp(); private down: HalfBandDown = new HalfBandDown(); sample(): void { this.up.up(this.x); // one sample in, two out: a and b const a = hardClip(this.up.a 4.0); const b = hardClip(this.up.b 4.0); this.out = this.down.down(a, b) 0.5; // two samples in, one out } Oversampler2x example import { Oversampler2x, hardClip } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private os: Oversampler2x = new Oversampler2x(); sample(): void { this.os.up(this.x); const y = this.os.down(hardClip(this.os.a 4.0), hardClip(this.os.b 4.0)); this.out = y 0.5; // this.os.latency says how many samples late it is } Oversampler4x example import { Oversampler4x, foldback } from "./bleep/dynamics"; private os: Oversampler4x = new Oversampler4x(); sample(): void { this.os.up(this.x); const y = this.os.down( foldback(this.os.a 3.0), foldback(this.os.b 3.0), foldback(this.os.c 3.0), foldback(this.os.d 3.0)); this.out = y 0.5; } bleep/fx import { Reverb, Phaser, Chorus, PitchShift } from "./bleep/fx"; Name What it does Reverb(sampleRate) A Freeverb reverb: mono in, stereo out. Set roomSize , damping , width and call update() ; next(x) sets left and right . The output is the reverb only: mix it with the dry signal. It allocates about 1 MB. Phaser(sampleRate, stages = 4) A phaser with 2 to 12 all-pass stages swept between minHz and maxHz at rate . feedback , mix , centre (the sweep position when rate is 0). next(x) . Chorus(sampleRate, voices = 2) Up to 4 modulated delay voices spread across left and right. rate , delayMs , depthMs , mix . next(x) sets left and right and returns their mean. PitchShift(sampleRate, windowSeconds = 0.06) A two-tap delay-line pitch shifter. ratio is the frequency ratio (2 is an octave up). Good on single notes, grainy on chords. Examples Reverb example import { Reverb } from "./bleep/fx"; @output({ name: "Out R", type: "audio" }) outR: f32 = 0; private verb: Reverb; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.verb = new Reverb(sampleRate); this.verb.roomSize = 0.8; this.verb.damping = 0.4; this.verb.width = 1.0; this.verb.update(); // after changing the settings } sample(): void { this.verb.next(this.x); // mono in, left and right out: the reverb only this.out = this.x 0.7 + this.verb.left 0.3; this.outR = this.x 0.7 + this.verb.right 0.3; } Phaser example import { Phaser } from "./bleep/fx"; private phaser: Phaser; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.phaser = new Phaser(sampleRate, 6); // six all-pass stages this.phaser.rate = 0.3; this.phaser.minHz = 400.0; this.phaser.maxHz = 3500.0; this.phaser.feedback = 0.5; this.phaser.mix = 0.5; } sample(): void { this.out = this.phaser.next(this.x); } Chorus example import { Chorus } from "./bleep/fx"; @output({ name: "Out R", type: "audio" }) outR: f32 = 0; private chorus: Chorus; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.chorus = new Chorus(sampleRate, 3); this.chorus.rate = 0.6; this.chorus.delayMs = 18.0; this.chorus.depthMs = 4.0; this.chorus.mix = 0.5; } sample(): void { this.chorus.next(this.x); this.out = this.chorus.left; this.outR = this.chorus.right; } PitchShift example import { PitchShift } from "./bleep/fx"; import { semitones } from "./bleep/util"; private shifter: PitchShift; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.shifter = new PitchShift(sampleRate, 0.06); this.shifter.ratio = semitones(7.0); // a fifth up } sample(): void { this.out = this.shifter.next(this.x); } bleep/fft import { Fft } from "./bleep/fft"; Name What it does Fft(size) A complex FFT of size points (a power of two) in place on the public arrays re and im . forward() , inverse() (divides by size ), clearImag() , applyHann() , magnitude(k) , phase(k) . A transform costs about 5 size log2(size) operations: do it once per hop in block() , not per sample. Bin k is at k sampleRate / size Hz. Examples Fft example import { Fft } from "./bleep/fft"; @probe peakHz: f32 = 0; private fft: Fft; private filled: i32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.fft = new Fft(256); } sample(): void { if (this.filled peak) { peak = m; best = k; } } this.peakHz = ( best this.sampleRate / 256.0); // bin k is at k sampleRate / size this.filled = 0; } Fft.inverse example import { Fft } from "./bleep/fft"; private fft: Fft; private filled: i32 = 0; private at: i32 = 0; private frame: StaticArray = new StaticArray (256); constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.fft = new Fft(256); } sample(): void { if (this.filled = 256 ? 0 : this.at + 1; } block(): void { if (this.filled midiToHz(69.0); } // 440 hzToMidi example import { hzToMidi } from "./bleep/util"; @probe note: f32 = 0; block(): void { this.note = hzToMidi(261.63); } // about 60 hzToPitch example import { hzToPitch } from "./bleep/util"; @probe volts: f32 = 0; block(): void { this.volts = hzToPitch(523.25); } // about 1.0: an octave above C4 semitones example import { semitones } from "./bleep/util"; private ratio: f64 = 1.0; block(): void { this.ratio = semitones(-5.0); } // a fourth down: about 0.749 clamp example import { clamp } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = clamp(this.x 2.0, -0.8, 0.8); } wrap example import { wrap } from "./bleep/util"; private phase: f64 = 0.9; sample(): void { this.phase = wrap(this.phase + 0.001, 0.0, 1.0); // like a phase: 1.0 comes back as 0 this.out = this.phase; } fold example import { fold } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = fold( this.x 3.0, -1.0, 1.0); } // mirrors back and forth between the limits mix example import { mix } from "./bleep/util"; @input({ name: "B", type: "audio" }) b: f32 = 0; sample(): void { this.out = mix(this.x, this.b, 0.3); } // 30 % of B mapRange example import { mapRange } from "./bleep/util"; @probe cents: f32 = 0; sample(): void { this.cents = mapRange( this.x, -1.0, 1.0, -50.0, 50.0); } expMap example import { expMap } from "./bleep/util"; @param({ name: "Freq", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) freq: f32 = 0.5; @probe hz: f32 = 0; block(): void { this.hz = expMap( this.freq, 20.0, 20000.0); } // the middle of the knob is 632 Hz fastTanh example import { fastTanh } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = fastTanh(this.x 3.0) 0.5; } fastExp2 example import { fastExp2 } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = this.x fastExp2(-0.5); } // 2 to the power of -0.5, without Math.pow fastLog2 example import { fastLog2 } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = fastLog2(1.0 + abs(this.x)); } fastPow2 example import { fastPow2 } from "./bleep/util"; sample(): void { this.out = this.x fastPow2(10.0, -0.1); } // 10 to the power of -0.1: -2 dB Pan example import { Pan } from "./bleep/util"; @output({ name: "Right", type: "audio" }) right: f32 = 0; private pan: Pan = new Pan(); block(): void { this.pan.equalPower(-0.4); } // -1 left to 1 right; linear() is the other law sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.pan.left; this.right = this.x this.pan.right; } Crossfade example import { Crossfade } from "./bleep/util"; @input({ name: "B", type: "audio" }) b: f32 = 0; private fade: Crossfade = new Crossfade(); block(): void { this.fade.equalPower(0.5); } // 0 is all A, 1 all B; linear() is the other law sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.fade.a + this.b this.fade.b; } MidSide example import { MidSide } from "./bleep/util"; @input({ name: "Right", type: "audio" }) inRight: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Right out", type: "audio" }) right: f32 = 0; private ms: MidSide = new MidSide(); sample(): void { this.ms.encode(this.x, this.inRight); this.ms.decode(this.ms.mid, this.ms.side 1.5); // widen the stereo image this.out = this.ms.left; this.right = this.ms.right; } Rms example import { Rms } from "./bleep/util"; @probe level: f32 = 0; private rms: Rms; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.rms = new Rms(sampleRate, 0.3); // averaged over about 300 ms } sample(): void { this.level = this.rms.next(this.x); this.out = this.x; } bleep/dsp import { dbToLin, linToDb, lerp, pitchToHz, Smoother, PeakHold, Biquad, AdaaTanh, DcBlocker, Phasor } from "./bleep/dsp"; Functions Name What it does dbToLin(db) Decibels to a linear gain. linToDb(gain) A linear gain to decibels, −144 for silence. lerp(a, b, t) a at 0 and b at 1, linearly in between. pitchToHz(volts) A pitch in volts (1.0 is an octave, 0 is C4) to a frequency in Hz. Uses pow : call it per block when you can. Classes Class Constructor Use Smoother (sampleRate, seconds) One-pole smoothing towards target . Set target in block() , call next() once per sample. value is the current value, snap() jumps to the target (after a reset, or the first block). See smoothing. PeakHold (sampleRate, seconds) A peak meter: rises at once, falls with seconds as time constant. next(x) per sample, value for the probe or an output, reset() . Biquad none A second-order filter section (RBJ cookbook), transposed direct form II. Set it up with setLowShelf(sr, f, gainDb) , setHighShelf(sr, f, gainDb) , setPeaking(sr, f, q, gainDb) , setLowpass(sr, f, q) , setHighpass(sr, f, q) , setBandpass(sr, f, q) (0 dB at the peak), setNotch(sr, f, q) or setAllpass(sr, f, q) , then call next(x) per sample. reset() clears it. Each set call takes a few trigonometric calls, so call it in block() and only when a setting changed. AdaaTanh none tanh as a soft clipper with first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing. next(x) per sample, reset() . See drive. DcBlocker (sampleRate, hz) A one-pole high-pass that removes a constant offset, 20 Hz is a good value. next(x) per sample, reset() . Phasor (sampleRate) A phase from 0 to 1 that wraps. Set frequency in Hz (in block() ), next() per sample returns the phase before this sample's step. reset() . The core of an oscillator or an LFO. Examples dbToLin example import { dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; private gain: f32 = 1; block(): void { this.gain = dbToLin(-6.0); } // about 0.5 sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.gain; } linToDb example import { linToDb } from "./bleep/dsp"; @probe db: f32 = 0; sample(): void { this.db = linToDb(abs(this.x)); } // -144 for silence lerp example import { lerp } from "./bleep/dsp"; sample(): void { this.out = lerp(this.x, -this.x, 0.25); } // a quarter of the way from x to -x pitchToHz example import { pitchToHz } from "./bleep/dsp";
