@input({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; private hz: f64 = 261.63; block(): void { this.hz = pitchToHz( this.pitch); } // 0 volts is C4, 1.0 volts one octave up Smoother example import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; @param({ name: "Level", min: -60, max: 6, init: 0, unit: "dB" }) level: f32 = 0; private gain: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.gain = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); // a 10 ms glide this.gain.target = 1.0; this.gain.snap(); // start there, no fade-in } block(): void { this.gain.target = dbToLin( this.level); } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.gain.next(); } PeakHold example import { PeakHold } from "./bleep/dsp"; @probe peak: f32 = 0; private meter: PeakHold; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.meter = new PeakHold(sampleRate, 0.5); // falls with a time constant of half a second } sample(): void { this.peak = this.meter.next(this.x); this.out = this.x; } Biquad example import { Biquad } from "./bleep/dsp"; private lowpass: Biquad = new Biquad(); private bell: Biquad = new Biquad(); block(): void { this.lowpass.setLowpass(this.sampleRate, 5000.0, 0.7071); // also setHighpass, setBandpass, setNotch, setAllpass this.bell.setPeaking(this.sampleRate, 1000.0, 1.0, 6.0); // +6 dB around 1 kHz; also setLowShelf, setHighShelf } sample(): void { this.out = this.bell.next(this.lowpass.next(this.x)); } AdaaTanh example import { AdaaTanh } from "./bleep/dsp"; private shaper: AdaaTanh = new AdaaTanh(); reset(): void { this.shaper.reset(); } sample(): void { this.out = this.shaper.next(this.x 5.0) 0.5; } // soft clipping with much less aliasing than Math.tanh DcBlocker example import { DcBlocker } from "./bleep/dsp"; private dc: DcBlocker; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.dc = new DcBlocker(sampleRate, 20.0); } sample(): void { this.out = this.dc.next(this.x + 0.2); } // the 0.2 offset is removed Phasor example import { Phasor } from "./bleep/dsp"; private osc: Phasor; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.osc = new Phasor(sampleRate); } block(): void { this.osc.frequency = 220.0; } sample(): void { const phase = this.osc.next(); // 0 to 1, then wraps this.out = (2.0 phase - 1.0) 0.5; // a naive saw } bleep/notes import { NoteEvent, NoteStream, NOTE ON, NOTE OFF } from "./bleep/notes"; NoteEvent has type , channel , offset (the sample inside the block), note (MIDI number), pitch (virtual volts, 1.0 is one octave, 0 is C4) and value (velocity, pressure, a control change divided by 127, or a bend from −1 to 1). It also has isOn , isOff , isCc and transpose(semitones) . NoteStream is the events of a notes input for this block, or the events a notes output sends: length , offsetAt(i) , read(i, into) , push(event) , clear() . At most 64 events fit in a block; further ones are dropped. The event types are the constants NOTE ON , NOTE OFF , NOTE PRESSURE , NOTE CC , NOTE PROGRAM , NOTE BEND , NOTE CHANNEL PRESSURE and NOTE SYSTEM . See Events and routing for how to use them in @on handlers. Examples NoteEvent example import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Out", type: "notes" }) played!: NoteStream; @on("notes") onNote(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.isOn && n.value > 0.5) { // only hard hits n.transpose(12); // up an octave this.played.push(n); } } NoteStream example import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Out", type: "notes" }) played!: NoteStream; @probe waiting: f32 = 0; @on("notes") onNote(n: NoteEvent): void { this.waiting = this.notes.length; // events on the jack in this block this.played.push(n); // forwarded at the same sample } NOTE ON, NOTE OFF and the other event types example import { NoteEvent, NoteStream, NOTE CC, NOTE BEND } from "./bleep/notes"; @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @probe cc1: f32 = 0; @probe bend: f32 = 0; @on("notes") onNote(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.type == NOTE CC && n.note == 1) this.cc1 = n.value; // the mod wheel, 0 to 1 if (n.type == NOTE BEND) this.bend = n.value; // -1 to 1 } What is not exported bleep/abi (the glue between the engine's buffers and your fields) and bleep/format (number text for knob values) are used by the generated code. A script has no reason to import them. From AssemblyScript These come with the language and the checker allows them in real-time code: Math: Math.sin , cos , tan , tanh , exp , log , log10 , pow , sqrt , floor , ceil , abs , min , max , PI , SQRT2 , LN2 and the rest of Math . Mind that Math takes f64 : convert with x and back with y . Built-in functions: abs , min , max , sqrt , floor , ceil , trunc , nearest , copysign , isNaN , isFinite , clz , ctz , popcnt , rotl , rotr . Arrays: StaticArray allocated in the constructor. Growing Array s, strings built at run time, Map and Set allocate and are refused in real-time code. See Limits. Not available at all: the wall clock, files and the network. What the library does not have (yet) minBLEP and BLIT oscillators. The saw, pulse and triangle use polyBLEP / polyBLAMP, which is good below a few kHz and loses ground near Nyquist. A minBLEP table for hard sync and the highest notes is not there; use Wavetable or Oversampler2x if that matters. Convolution (impulse responses, cabinets) and a vocoder . Granular engines, time stretching, and an FFT-based phase vocoder pitch shifter ( PitchShift is a delay-line shifter; Fft gives you the building block). A feedback delay network reverb. Reverb is Freeverb; for denser, less metallic tails build an FDN from DelayLine and Allpass1 . Sample buffers. A module has no access to audio files; Wavetable , DelayLine and plain StaticArray s are the memory it can have. Oversampled filters. The ladder and the state-variable filter are not oversampled; for heavy resonance with drive, wrap them in an Oversampler2x . Multiband and lookahead-compressor variants. Compressor is feed-forward with a peak detector; Limiter has look-ahead. A transport and tempo map. Clock follows a bpm you give it or a beat position you pass to setBeat() ; reading the host transport depends on the module's inputs.

title: Module scripts
text: Module scripts You write a module script when the board has no module that does what you want. It is how you make your own oscillator, filter, distortion or any other effect, and also modules that handle notes and control signals instead of audio, such as a router or a note splitter. Compile the script and the Code node turns into a module of its own, with the jacks, knobs and meters you declared. You can patch it like any other module and it is saved with the patch. A module script describes one module as a class. The class says what goes in and what comes out, which settings the player can turn, and what to compute for each sample of audio or for each incoming event. This page explains all of that; the Reference lists every built-in with its signature and a complete example. If you have not written one yet, start with the Quickstart. A module script is an AssemblyScript file with one or more classes marked @module . AssemblyScript is a strict subset of TypeScript that compiles to WebAssembly, so ordinary TypeScript syntax works, with these differences that matter here: numbers are typed ( f32 , f64 , i32 , bool ), there are no closures or exceptions in real-time code, and Math.sin takes an f64 . import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; // the library, see Library @module({ name: "Gain", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Gain { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: -60, max: 6, init: 0, unit: "dB", decimals: 1 }) level: f32 = 0; private g: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.g = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } block(): void { this.g.target = dbToLin(this.level); } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.g.next(); } } The class Member Runs Use constructor(sampleRate: f64) Once, when the module is created Allocate objects, set up state. The only place that may allocate block(): void Once per 32 samples Slow work: read dials, set smoother targets, compute coefficients sample(): void Once per sample Per-sample DSP reset(): void When the engine resets the module Clear state @on(...) methods Once per event Events and routing @transport method Once per block, before block() The tempo and position, see Transport @button methods When a button is pressed See below The constructor is required ( constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} when it has nothing to do); the rest are optional. A module with only @on handlers is a router; one with only sample() is an effect. When each part runs, and what to put where, is the subject of Rates and timing. Several @module classes in one file make several modules (the Code node shows the first). How fields are filled The compiler generates the glue between the engine's buffers and your fields, so you never touch buffers: Field Holds Set @param The value in its own units (dB, an integer, a choice index, a boolean) Once per block, before block() @input The signal In block() , its first sample of the block; in sample() , the current sample @output What you wrote Read back after each sample() (and after block() for a block-rate output such as a flag) @probe A value for the meter Polled by the view about ten times a second @module @module({ name: "Mixer", type: "mixer", category: "Utility/Script", colour: "#60a5fa", description: "…", settings: [{ id: "CHANNELS", name: "Channels", min: 1, max: 16, init: 4 }] }) Option Meaning Default name Name in the Add menu and on the node The class name type The module's type id The name, in kebab case category Group in the Add menu, "Group/Subgroup" "Utility/Script" colour The module's accent colour "#94a3b8" description The text under the knobs The class's / / comment settings See Settings none @module("Name") is short for @module({ name: "Name" }) . Signal types Type Meaning Field type audio An audio signal f32 control A control signal f32 pitch Pitch in volts: 1.0 is one octave, 0 is C4 f32 gate High (0.5 or more) while a key is held f32 trigger A short pulse f32 notes A stream of note events NoteStream (see Events) Cables follow the board's rules: anything connects to anything except notes , which connects only to notes . @input and @output @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; Option Meaning Default name Jack label The field name, in words type A signal type from the table "audio" bipolar Whether the signal goes below zero (for meters) true , except gate , trigger and notes count Make numbered jacks, see below one jack names Labels for numbered jacks: ["Kick", "Snare"] "In 1" , "In 2" … description Help text The field's / / comment The jack's id is the field name, and it is what cables are saved against. Rename a field and its cables are lost. @param A knob (or a toggle or a dropdown). It is modulatable by cables unless you say otherwise. @param({ name: "Time", min: 0.01, max: 4, init: 0.5, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 2 }) time: f32 = 0.5; @param({ name: "Mute" }) mute: bool = false; @param({ name: "Shape", choices: ["Sine", "Triangle"] }) shape: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Steps", min: 1, max: 8 }) steps: i32 = 4; Field type Kind Needs f32 A continuous knob min , max i32 with min and max A stepped integer knob min , max i32 with choices A dropdown; the field holds the index choices (two or more names) bool A toggle nothing Option Meaning Default name Knob label The field name, in words min , max The range in units ( max above min ) required for numbers init The default value in units The field's initial value, or min unit A suffix shown with the value, such as "dB" or "Hz" none decimals Digits shown 2 map "linear" , "exp" or "skew" : how the knob's travel maps to the range "linear" centre For "skew" : the value in the middle of the knob (between min and max ) required with skew minText Text shown at min , such as "-inf" none group A card the knob sits in, such as "Ch {n}" none modulatable Whether cables can drive it true for numbers, false for toggles and choices count , names , description As for jacks exp needs min above zero and suits frequencies and times; skew puts a chosen value in the middle of the knob. They follow the engine's own mappings, so a script's knob feels like a built-in module's. Defaults. init and the field's initial value are the same thing; if you give both and they differ, the compiler reports an error. A value outside the range is an error too. @probe @probe level: f32 = 0; A value the view polls and shows as a meter. It does not appear as a jack. name , count and description work as above. Your code writes the field as often as it likes; the view reads it about ten times a second. @button @button({ name: "Reset" }) reset(): void { this.count = 0; } A button in the view. Its method runs when the button is pressed, between blocks. The method name is the button's id and must be a plain identifier. @transport @transport tempo(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void { this.bpm = bpm; if (playing) this.beat = ppq; } One method can be the transport handler. The engine calls it once per block, before block() , with the tempo in beats per minute, the position at the start of the block in quarter notes ( ppq ) and whether the transport is playing. Use it for anything that follows the tempo: a tempo-synced LFO or delay, a step sequencer. It is block rate (see Rates and timing): advance the position yourself per sample and take the host's value again at the next block, as the step sequencer does. When playing goes from false to true the transport has started. The method takes exactly these three arguments. Settings and counted jacks A setting is a whole number the user chooses, such as the number of channels. It is a constant of the module: changing it recompiles, and it can decide how many jacks, knobs and meters there are. @module({ name: "Mixer", settings: [{ id: "CHANNELS", name: "Channels", min: 1, max: 16, init: 4 }], }) export class Mixer { @input({ name: "Ch", type: "audio", count: CHANNELS }) ch!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Gain", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1, count: CHANNELS, group: "Ch {n}" }) gain!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Mute", count: CHANNELS, group: "Ch {n}" }) mute!: StaticArray ; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @probe({ name: "Level", count: CHANNELS }) level!: StaticArray ; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { let sum: f32 = 0; for (let i = 0; i 0 : this.ch[i] this.gain[i]; this.level[i] = abs(y); sum += y; } this.out = sum; } } A setting has an id in capitals, min , max , init (whole numbers) and a name . In your code, the id is a constant: CHANNELS . count (a number or a setting) makes numbered jacks, params or probes: ch1 , ch2 … with labels Ch 1 , Ch 2 …. The field is a StaticArray of the element type, which the compiler allocates for you (use ! so TypeScript does not ask for an initialiser). group: "Ch {n}" puts the numbered knobs of one channel in one card. The count is at most 64. A setting's value is held to its range. The Code node shows a number field per setting; the choice is saved with the patch. The Mixer (configurable) example adds a three-band EQ, low-pass, fader, mute and solo per channel using these features. Doc comments A / … / comment right before a class, field or button becomes its description in the module's interface (and so in tooltips and the API reference). Joined lines become one paragraph; blank lines separate paragraphs. Several modules in one file, and errors Every error carries the file, line and column. Declaration mistakes (a field of the wrong type, a missing min , an unknown option, two decorators on one field) are reported by the Bleep transform, and type errors by the compiler, in the same problem list.

title: Bleep Script
text: Bleep Script Bleep Script lets you write parts of a patch as code. A Code node on the board has an editor and a Compile button. Depending on what you write, it becomes a new module with its own jacks, knobs and meters, or it builds a whole cell of modules and cables for you. A Code node in Bleep Play holding the Tremolo example: the Compile button and status line on top, the script in the editor, and below it the module's meter and knobs. This is a small tremolo script. Compile it and the node gets an In jack, an Out jack, the Rate and Depth dials, a Shape menu and a meter for the LFO. Nothing else is needed: the decorators on top declare all of that, and sample() at the bottom is the sound. What it is for Bleep Script does three jobs. Custom modules. When the board has no module that does what you want, you write one. A module is a class with a sample() method that does the DSP for each audio sample, and decorators such as @input , @output and @param declare its jacks and knobs. This is how you make your own oscillator, effect or distortion. See Module scripts. Message routing and scripting. Some jobs are about logic rather than sound: splitting notes between voices, reacting to a gate going high, building a router. For these you write @on handlers for notes and control edges. A handler runs at the exact sample the event happens, so timing stays precise. Handlers live in a module script, so they use the same language and compiler as a custom module. See Events and routing. Complex patches. Some patches are too big or too repetitive to place by hand. A patch script does not process audio. It runs once and describes which modules and cables to create, so a loop can build 100 oscillators and wire them up, and the shape of the result can depend on parameters. See Patch scripts. How it works Two kinds of script. A module script (it has @module ) is AssemblyScript, a TypeScript-like language that compiles to WebAssembly. A patch script (it ends in export default cell(...) ) is TypeScript or JavaScript that runs once and describes modules and cables. You pick the rate by the method you write. block() runs once per 32 samples, sample() once per sample, @on handlers once per event. No installation on the web. In Bleep Play there is nothing to install: the compiler runs in your browser and all the code is compiled there, on your machine. Compiling takes about a second and produces one .wasm file that follows the module ABI, the same format as every other module. The engine runs it in the same sandbox. Real-time code is restricted. The compiler rejects what an audio thread must not do, and estimates the cost of a block. See Limits and safety. Share source, not binaries. A script is text saved in the patch. Whoever opens the patch compiles it themselves, in a sandbox. Where things stand Where State Bleep Play in the browser Works: compile, edit, run, save with the patch The standalone app and the plugins The engine can run Code nodes and keeps their cables and knob values; the compiler is not shipped with these builds yet, so you cannot compile there. See The Code node These pages Page Content Quickstart Your first script, in five minutes Rates and timing When each part of a script runs, and what to put where Tutorials A step sequencer, drive, smoothing, sample and hold, inputs, the DSP toolbox The Code node The editor, compiling, settings, saving, and what is available where Module scripts Reference: decorators, signal types, parameters, probes, buttons, settings Events and routing Notes and edge handlers, with a router Patch scripts Reference: building cells from code Custom UIs and widgets Layouts of knobs, faders and meters, or a self-made canvas UI Library bleep/osc , filters , delay , random , env , dynamics , fx , fft , util , dsp , notes : oscillators, filters, delays, envelopes, dynamics, reverb, notes Programming with AI One prompt that teaches a coding AI Bleep Script, to copy or download Reference Every built-in one by one, with its API and a complete example: lifecycle methods, decorators, @transport , note types, the patch builder and the UI object Implementation How the language is built in the repo: the compiler, the lifecycle of a script, limits and safety, and how to run the tests Where it lives Piece Path Compiler, transform, library, patch runner, playground, tests patch/script/ (see its README.md ) The Code node in the board patch/board/ui/board-code.js Native engine support patch/engine/wasm/CodeNodes.cpp Concept and design, with what differs from it doc/specs/bleep-script.md

title: Patch scripts
text: Patch scripts A patch script builds a cell of modules and cables. It runs once, when you press Compile, and the result is ordinary patch content: you can open the cell, change it by hand, cable to it, and save it. Where a module script describes one module that runs in real time, a patch script describes a patch , so loops and arithmetic are free. import { cell } from "bleep/patch"; export default cell("Stack", { description: "Three oscillators into a filter." }, (c) => { c.input("pitch", "Pitch", "pitch"); c.stereoOut(); const filter = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 2000 }); for (let i = 0; i { … }) . The builder c Call What it does c.input(id, name, type) A shared input jack on the cell. Type: control (default), audio , pitch , gate , trigger or notes c.output(id, name, type) A shared output jack. Type defaults to audio c.stereoIn() , c.stereoOut() The jacks l and r (In L, In R / Out L, Out R) c.add(type, values, opts) Adds a module and returns a handle c.cable(from, fromJack, to, toJack, amount) A cable from an output to an input jack or to a modulatable knob. Amount −1 to +1, default 1 c.stereo(from, to, jacks) Both channels: from.l to to.l and from.r to to.r . jacks : { from: ["l","r"], to: ["l","r"], amount } c.place(handle, x, y) Puts a module at a pixel position inside the cell c.cin , c.cout The cell's own input and output sides, to cable from and to c.add(type, values, opts) type is the module's type id, the one used in the Add menu's search and in saved patches: "oscillator" , "filter" , "vca" , "adsr" , "lfo" . values is an object of knob values in their own units : { cutoff: 4000, resonance: 0.2 } , { fine: -12 } . Choices take the choice's name ( { mode: "LP" } ) or its index; toggles take true or false . A value outside the knob's range, of the wrong kind, or for a knob that does not exist is an error. opts : name (the module's name), id , at: [column, row] (a grid of 300 by 220 pixels), x and y in pixels, data (a module's node data). Without a position, modules are laid out in a grid between Cell In and Cell Out . Cables c.cable(osc, "saw", filter, "l", 0.5) reads: from the oscillator's output saw to the filter's input l , at half strength. A cable can also end at a knob that cables can drive: c.cable(lfo, "out", filter, "cutoff", 0.3) . Several cables into one input add up, which is how a hundred oscillators mix into one filter. Notes connect only to notes; everything else connects freely. A cable to a jack or knob that does not exist is an error that names the module and the jack. What compiling does The script runs in a sandbox and returns a description. The description is checked against the board's module types. If it is valid, the cell is built next to the Code node in one undoable step. The cell and everything in it are marked as generated by that node. Pressing Compile again replaces what was generated before. The cell keeps its position and any name you gave it. Cables you drew from outside to the cell's own jacks are kept as long as those jacks are still declared; cables you drew to modules inside the cell are lost, because the modules are rebuilt. If the script has errors, nothing changes: the cell stays as it was and the problems are listed with their lines. A patch script's own Code node has no jacks or knobs: the jacks are on the cell it built. Limits Limit Modules added 1000 Cables added 5000 Source size 200,000 characters Memory 64 MB Run time 3 seconds Result size 4 MB A script that goes over a limit is stopped and the problem says which. TypeScript or JavaScript Write either: type annotations, interfaces and as casts are removed before the script runs. Error lines refer to your source. Example: a chain of delays export default cell("Echo chain", { settings: [{ id: "TAPS", name: "Taps", min: 1, max: 8, init: 4 }] }, (c, s) => { c.stereoIn(); c.stereoOut(); let previous = c.cin; for (let i = 0; i < s.TAPS; i++) { const tap = c.add("delay", { time: 0.12 (i + 1) }, { name: "Tap " + (i + 1) }); c.stereo(previous, tap); previous = tap; } c.stereo(previous, c.cout); }); Look up the exact module and knob ids in the module reference or by adding the module on the board; a mistake is reported with the knobs that do exist.

title: Quickstart
text: Quickstart You need Bleep Play in a browser with the Bleep Script compiler (see The Code node for what is available where). Start audio first: browsers only allow sound after a click. A module in five steps Add a Code node. Press Tab on the board, type code , press Enter. A node called Code appears with no jacks yet. Open it. Click the node. The editor opens with a Wave folder example loaded. Compile. Press Compile (or Ctrl+Enter , Cmd+Enter on a Mac). A second later the status line reads Fold: compiled , the node has an In and an Out jack, and the view shows two dials, Drive and Mix , and a Level meter. Patch it in. Cable an oscillator into In and Out into the next module or the speakers. Turn Drive while a note plays. Change the code. Edit the source, compile again. The running module is swapped, your cables stay as long as the jacks still exist, and Undo brings the previous source back. If something is wrong, the problems list under the editor shows the line and column; click a problem to jump to it. A failed compile leaves the previous version running. What you just compiled import { Smoother, PeakHold } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Fold", category: "Utility/Script", colour: "#f6c35b", description: "A wave folder: pushes the signal into a sine fold and mixes it back." }) export class Fold { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Drive", min: 0, max: 20, init: 2, decimals: 1 }) drive: f32 = 2; @param({ name: "Mix", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1, decimals: 2 }) mix: f32 = 1; / The output level, for the meter. / @probe level: f32 = 0; private k: Smoother; private meter: PeakHold; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.k = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); this.meter = new PeakHold(sampleRate, 0.3); } block(): void { this.k.target = this.drive; } // once per 32 samples sample(): void { // once per sample const folded = Math.sin( (this.x this.k.next())); this.out = this.x + (folded - this.x) this.mix; this.level = this.meter.next(this.out); } } The decorators declare the interface. The compiler turns them into the node's jacks, dials and meter. Fields hold the values: x is the current input sample, drive is the dial's value in its own units, out is what you write. block() is for slow work, such as setting a smoother's target. sample() is for per-sample work. Smoother and PeakHold come from the library. More in Module scripts. A patch script The same Code node can build patches. Paste this into a Code node and press Compile: import { cell } from "bleep/patch"; export default cell("SuperSaw", { description: "Many detuned saw oscillators into one filter.", settings: [ { id: "VOICES", name: "Oscillators", min: 1, max: 200, init: 100 }, { id: "SPREAD", name: "Spread (cents)", min: 0, max: 100, init: 30 }, ], }, (c, s) => { c.input("pitch", "Pitch", "pitch"); c.stereoOut(); const filter = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 4000, resonance: 0.2 }); for (let i = 0; i 1 ? (i / (s.VOICES - 1) - 0.5) 2 s.SPREAD : 0; const osc = c.add("oscillator", { fine: detune }, { name: "Saw " + (i + 1) }); c.cable(c.cin, "pitch", osc, "pitch"); c.cable(osc, "saw", filter, "l", 1 / Math.sqrt(s.VOICES)); } c.stereo(filter, c.cout); }); A cell called SuperSaw appears next to the Code node, with a Pitch input and Out L and Out R outputs, holding 100 oscillators and a filter. Two number fields, Oscillators and Spread , appear above the editor: change one and the cell is rebuilt. More in Patch scripts. Next The Code node: settings, saving, panels, what to do when the compiler is missing Events and routing: notes and control edges Limits and safety: what the compiler refuses and why

title: Rates and timing
text: Rates and timing A module script does not have one clock. Different parts of it run at different rates, and choosing the right place for each calculation is most of what makes a script fast, click-free and sample-accurate. Bleep Script makes the choice by which method you write the code in . The rates Rate Where you write it How often At 48 kHz Once constructor(sampleRate) When the module is created once Audio rate sample() Every sample 48,000 per second Block rate (control rate) block() Once per block of 32 samples 1,500 per second Event rate @on(...) handlers Once per event, at the sample it happens as often as events come Transport rate @transport method Once per block, before block() 1,500 per second Button rate @button methods When the button is pressed, between blocks rarely View rate @probe fields The view reads them about ten times a second 10 per second The engine processes audio in blocks of 32 samples . A block is about 0.67 ms at 48 kHz. Everything is organised around it: for every block of 32 samples @transport method the tempo and position are told knobs are read @param fields are filled, in their own units block() slow work: once per block for every sample 0 … 31 inputs are read @input fields hold this sample @on handlers run notes and edges at this sample sample() fast work: per sample outputs are written outputs of block() are written (flags) What arrives at which rate Thing Rate @param Block rate. One value per block, in its own units. A knob that is modulated by a cable still changes only once per block @input Sample rate in sample() (the current sample), but block rate in block() (its first sample of the block) @output Whatever you write in sample() is sent at audio rate; whatever you write in block() holds for the whole block Note events Event rate, with the exact sample in offset Edges ( rising , falling ) Event rate: the handler runs on the sample where the signal crosses the level Transport ( bpm , ppq , playing ) Block rate @probe You write it at any rate; the view samples it at view rate Choosing the rate Put each calculation at the slowest rate that is still correct . Once (constructor): allocations, tables, constants that depend on the sample rate ( 1 / sampleRate ). Block rate ( block() ): anything derived from a knob. Converting a gain from dB, computing filter coefficients, choosing a lookup. A knob only changes once per block, so doing this per sample is wasted work. This is the main reason block() exists. It also decides cost: the cost estimate counts block() once and sample() 32 times per block. Audio rate ( sample() ): the signal itself: filters, oscillators, waveshapers, envelopes. It is the most expensive place, so keep trig, pow and exp calls out of it when a block-rate value will do. Event rate ( @on ): things that happen at a moment: a note, a gate rising. This is sample-accurate : the handler sees the event at the exact sample, so timing is not rounded to a block (about 0.67 ms). Rounding to the block Block rate is also a limit. A value set in block() is constant for 32 samples, so if it jumps, it jumps in a step, and a step in a gain is a click. Smooth it per sample: Preventing pops and clicks. Because only the block's first sample of an input is visible in block() , a fast control signal read there is sampled at 1,500 Hz and anything faster is lost (and can alias). Read it in sample() instead when its details matter. Examples A tremolo: the rate of the LFO is a knob, so its increment is computed once per block; the LFO itself runs per sample. compile @module({ name: "Tremolo", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Tremolo { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Rate", min: 0.1, max: 20, init: 4, unit: "Hz" }) rate: f32 = 4; @param({ name: "Depth", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) depth: f32 = 0.5; private phase: f64 = 0; private increment: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } // once block(): void { this.increment = this.rate / this.sampleRate; } // per block: one division sample(): void { // per sample: the cheap part this.phase += this.increment; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); const lfo = (0.5 + 0.5 Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI this.phase)); this.out = this.x (1 - this.depth (1 - lfo)); } } A gate that must start on the exact sample is an event, not a block-rate value: @on("gate", { rising: 0.5 }) start(): void { this.env = 0; this.stage = 1; } // at the sample the gate rises What there is not No oversampling or sub-block rates are built in: you can run your own faster loop inside sample() (a bounded for , see Limits), as the drive tutorial discusses. The sample rate is given to the constructor and does not change while the module lives (a different rate creates a new module). It is typically 44.1 or 48 kHz: use it, never assume it. Time is always samples and transport : a module has no clock of its own, so a script cannot read the wall time.

title: Reference
text: Reference This page lists every built-in a module script has: the methods the engine calls, the decorators that declare jacks and knobs, the transport handler and the note types. Each entry has the same three parts: What it does , in a few sentences. API , the exact signature and options. Example , a complete module you can paste into a Code node and compile. Every example on this page is compiled by the documentation test. For the story behind them, see Module scripts, Events and routing and Rates and timing. The bleep/ functions (oscillators, filters, delays) are on the Library page, and the calls of patch scripts and custom UIs are at the end of this page. Contents Methods the engine calls: constructor , block , sample , reset Decorators: @module , @input , @output , @param , @probe , @button , @on for notes, @on for edges, @transport Note types: NoteEvent , NoteStream The patch builder: cell , c.input and c.output , c.add , c.cable , c.stereo , c.place , c.cin and c.cout The bleep UI object: param and params , probe , button , onFrame and onValues , size and canvas , theme Methods the engine calls constructor What it does. Runs once when the module is created. It is the only place that may allocate: create filters, delay lines, tables and smoothers here and keep them in fields. It receives the sample rate, which you need for any frequency or time. The constructor is required, with exactly this argument, even when it does nothing: constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} . API. constructor(sampleRate: f64) Example. compile import { Smoother } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Ref constructor", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefConstructor { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1 }) level: f32 = 1; private smooth: Smoother; // allocated once, in the constructor constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.smooth = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.02); // a 20 ms glide } block(): void { this.smooth.target = this.level; } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.smooth.next(); } } block What it does. Runs once per block of 32 samples, before the samples of that block. Use it for slow work: read the knobs, set smoother targets, compute filter coefficients. Knobs are filled before it runs, and an input holds its first sample of the block. An output you set here (a flag, say) is read back after the block. API. block(): void Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref block", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefBlock { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Gain", min: -60, max: 12, init: 0, unit: "dB" }) gain: f32 = 0; private lin: f32 = 1; // 10^(dB/20) is costly: once per block, not once per sample constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} block(): void { this.lin = Math.pow(10.0, this.gain / 20.0); } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.lin; } } sample What it does. Runs once per sample, with the inputs set to the current sample. Write the outputs here. This is where the DSP goes; keep it small, because it runs 48,000 times a second or more. The compiler estimates its cost and rejects what is too much (see Limits and safety). API. sample(): void Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref sample", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefSample { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Drive", min: 1, max: 20, init: 4 }) drive: f32 = 4; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { const y = this.x this.drive; this.out = y / (1 + abs(y)); // a soft clipper, per sample } } reset What it does. Runs when the engine resets the module (for example when playback restarts). Clear everything that holds a history: delay lines, filter states, phases, counters. Do not allocate here. API. reset(): void Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref reset", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefReset { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; private z: f32 = 0; // one-pole low-pass state constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} reset(): void { this.z = 0; } sample(): void { this.z += 0.05 (this.x - this.z); this.out = this.z; } } Decorators @module What it does. Marks a class as a module and says how it appears in the Add menu: its name, group, colour and description. It also declares the module's settings and its layout. Without it a class is an ordinary class. @module("Name") is short for @module({ name: "Name" }) . API. @module({ name?: string, // default: the class name type?: string, // the type id; default: the name in kebab case category?: string, // "Group/Subgroup"; default "Utility/Script" colour?: string, // "#rrggbb"; default "#94a3b8" description?: string, // default: the class's / / comment settings?: { id: string, name: string, min: number, max: number, init: number }[], layout?: LayoutItem[], // see Custom UIs and widgets }) Example. compile / Doubles the signal. The description is taken from this comment. / @module({ name: "Ref module", category: "Effects/Script", colour: "#f59e0b" }) export class RefModule { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.out = this.x 2; } } @input What it does. Declares an input jack. The field holds the signal: its first sample of the block in block() , the current sample in sample() . The jack's id is the field name, and cables are saved against it, so renaming a field drops its cables. With count it makes numbered jacks and the field is a StaticArray . API. @input({ name?: string, // jack label; default: the field name in words type?: "audio" "control" "pitch" "gate" "trigger" "notes", // default "audio" bipolar?: boolean, // goes below zero (for meters); default true, except gate, trigger, notes count?: number, // a number or a setting: numbered jacks names?: string[], // labels for numbered jacks description?: string, }) field: f32 // f32; StaticArray with count; NoteStream for notes Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref input", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefInput { @input({ name: "Audio", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "CV", type: "control", description: "Scales the audio, 0 to 1" }) cv: f32 = 1; @input({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.out = this.gate >= 0.5 ? this.x this.cv : 0; // a gate is high at 0.5 or more } } @output What it does. Declares an output jack. Whatever the field holds after sample() is sent out (after block() too, for a block-rate output). A notes output is a NoteStream : you push events into it. API. @output({ name?: string, type?: "audio" "control" "pitch" "gate" "trigger" "notes", // default "audio" bipolar?: boolean, count?: number, names?: string[], description?: string, }) field: f32 // f32; StaticArray with count; NoteStream for notes Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref output", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefOutput { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Level", type: "control", bipolar: false }) level: f32 = 0; // a second output, from the same input constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.out = this.x; this.level = abs(this.x); } } @param What it does. Declares a knob, a toggle or a dropdown, depending on the field's type. The field always holds the value in its own units (dB, Hz, an integer, a choice index, a boolean), filled once per block before block() . Cables can modulate a numeric knob unless you set modulatable: false . API. @param({ name?: string, min?: number, max?: number, // required for f32 and for a stepped i32 init?: number, // default: the field's initial value, or min unit?: string, // "dB", "Hz", "s" ... decimals?: number, // digits shown; default 2 map?: "linear" "exp" "skew", // default "linear"; exp needs min > 0 centre?: number, // for skew: the value in the middle of the knob minText?: string, // text at min, such as "-inf" choices?: string[], // i32 only: a dropdown; the field holds the index group?: string, // a card: "Ch {n}" modulatable?: boolean, count?: number, names?: string[], description?: string, }) field: f32 i32 bool Field type You get f32 with min , max A continuous knob i32 with min , max A stepped integer knob i32 with choices A dropdown; the field is the chosen index bool A toggle Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref param", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefParam { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Cutoff", min: 20, max: 20000, init: 1000, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 0 }) cutoff: f32 = 1000; @param({ name: "Mode", choices: ["Low", "High"] }) mode: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Steps", min: 1, max: 8 }) steps: i32 = 4; @param({ name: "Bypass" }) bypass: bool = false; private z: f32 = 0; private a: f32 = 0.1; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} block(): void { this.a = (1.0 - Math.exp(-6.283185307 this.cutoff / 48000.0)); } sample(): void { this.z += this.a (this.x - this.z); const y = this.mode == 0 ? this.z : this.x - this.z; this.out = this.bypass ? this.x : y; } } @probe What it does. Declares a value the view shows as a meter. It is not a jack: nothing can be cabled to it. Write the field as often as you like; the view reads it about ten times a second. Use it to show a level, a gain reduction, a phase, or a step counter. API. @probe({ name?: string, count?: number, description?: string }) field: f32 @probe field: f32 // without options Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref probe", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefProbe { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @probe({ name: "Peak" }) peak: f32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.out = this.x; const a = abs(this.x); this.peak = a > this.peak ? a : this.peak 0.9999; // a peak meter that falls slowly } } @button What it does. Declares a button in the module's view. The method runs when the button is pressed, between blocks. The method name is the button's id and must be a plain identifier. API. @button({ name?: string, description?: string }) methodName(): void Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref button", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefButton { @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @probe({ name: "Pressed" }) pressed: f32 = 0; private count: i32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @button({ name: "Count" }) bump(): void { this.count++; this.pressed = this.count; } @button({ name: "Clear" }) clear(): void { this.count = 0; this.pressed = 0; } } @on for notes What it does. Runs a method once for every note event that arrives on a notes input, at the sample where it happens. Whatever you push to a notes output leaves at the same sample. The decorator names the input field . API. @on("inputField") handler(e: NoteEvent): void Example. compile import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @module({ name: "Ref note handler", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefNoteHandler { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) out!: NoteStream; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} // every note on and off goes out a fifth higher; other events pass unchanged @on("notes") fifth(e: NoteEvent): void { if (e.isOn e.isOff) e.transpose(7); this.out.push(e); } } @on for edges What it does. Runs a method at the sample where a control , gate or trigger input crosses a level. rising fires when the signal goes from below the level to at or above it; falling the other way round. Give exactly one of them. The first block never fires an edge. API. @on("inputField", { rising: level }) handler(): void @on("inputField", { falling: level }) handler(): void Example. compile @module({ name: "Ref edge", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefEdge { @input({ name: "Trig", type: "trigger" }) trig: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @probe({ name: "Count" }) count: f32 = 0; private n: i32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @on("trig", { rising: 0.5 }) hit(): void { this.n++; this.count = this.n; } } @transport What it does. Tells the module where the host's transport is: the tempo, the position and whether it is playing. The engine calls the method once per block, before block() . Use it for anything that follows the tempo: an LFO or delay synced to the beat, an arpeggiator, a step sequencer. One method per module can have it, and it takes exactly these three arguments. Because it is block rate, take the host's value at the start of each block and advance the position yourself per sample in between, as the example does. When playing turns from false to true, the transport has started. A module that never uses the transport simply leaves the method out. API. @transport name(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void Argument Meaning bpm The tempo in quarter notes per minute ppq The position at the start of the block, in quarter notes (beats) from the start of the song. 4.0 is the start of the second bar in 4/4 playing true while the transport runs, false when it is stopped The Clock class in bleep/env does the position bookkeeping for you. Example. A tremolo that runs once per beat, locked to the song position while it plays and free-running when it is stopped: compile @module({ name: "Ref transport", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefTransport { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Cycles per beat", min: 0.25, max: 8, init: 1, map: "exp" }) rate: f32 = 1; @param({ name: "Depth", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.7 }) depth: f32 = 0.7; private bpm: f64 = 120; private beat: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } @transport tempo(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void { this.bpm = bpm; if (playing) this.beat = ppq; // take the song position; when stopped, free-run } sample(): void { this.beat += this.bpm / 60.0 / this.sampleRate; // beats per sample const p = this.beat this.rate; const lfo = (0.5 + 0.5 Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI (p - Math.floor(p)))); this.out = this.x (1 - this.depth (1 - lfo)); } } Note types NoteEvent What it does. One note, control or pitch-bend event. The handler of an @on method receives one, and you push one to send. Handle the types you know and ignore the rest. API. class NoteEvent { type: u8 // NOTE ON 0, NOTE OFF 1, NOTE PRESSURE 2, NOTE CC 3, NOTE PROGRAM 4, NOTE BEND 5, NOTE CHANNEL PRESSURE 6, NOTE SYSTEM 7 channel: u8 // MIDI channel, 0 to 15 offset: i16 // the sample inside the block note: i32 // MIDI note number; for types 3 to 7 the controller or program number pitch: f32 // pitch in volts: 1.0 is one octave, 0 is C4 value: f32 // velocity or pressure 0 to 1; a control change's data / 127; a bend -1 to +1 get isOn(): bool get isOff(): bool get isCc(): bool transpose(semitones: i32): void // shifts note and pitch together } Example. Turn a note-on velocity into a control signal, and drop the pitch by an octave: compile import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @module({ name: "Ref note event", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefNoteEvent { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) out!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Velocity", type: "control", bipolar: false }) velocity: f32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @on("notes") handle(e: NoteEvent): void { if (e.isOn) { this.velocity = e.value; e.transpose(-12); } this.out.push(e); } } NoteStream What it does. The events of a notes input for this block, or the events a notes output will send. An output starts every block empty. A handler gets each incoming event already, so you need read only to look at all the events of the block at once. API. class NoteStream { get length(): i32 // events waiting (0 to 64) offsetAt(i: i32): i32 // the sample offset of event i read(i: i32, into: NoteEvent): void // copies event i into a NoteEvent you own push(e: NoteEvent): void // sends an event; dropped silently when 64 are queued clear(): void // forgets the queued events } Example. Pass notes through, but only the first four of each block: compile import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @module({ name: "Ref note stream", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class RefNoteStream { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) out!: NoteStream; private e: NoteEvent; // allocated once, in the constructor constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.e = new NoteEvent(); } block(): void { for (let i = 0; i = this.notes.length) break; this.notes.read(i, this.e); this.out.push(this.e); } } } The patch builder A patch script builds a cell from TypeScript or JavaScript. It runs once, when you compile. These are all its calls. cell(name, options, build) What it does. The one thing a patch script exports: export default cell(...) . It names the cell and gives the function that builds it. options can be left out. API. cell(name: string, options: { description?: string, settings?: Setting[] }, build: (c: Builder, s: Settings) => void) cell(name: string, build: (c: Builder, s: Settings) => void) Example. patch export default cell("Two oscillators", { description: "A saw and a pulse, mixed." }, (c) => { c.stereoOut(); const a = c.add("oscillator", { coarse: 0 }); const b = c.add("oscillator", { coarse: 7 }); c.cable(a, "saw", c.cout, "l"); c.cable(b, "saw", c.cout, "r"); }); c.input and c.output What it does. Adds a jack to the cell, shared by everything inside. c.stereoIn() and c.stereoOut() add the pair l and r . API. c.input(id: string, name: string, type?: "control" "audio" "pitch" "gate" "trigger" "notes") // default "control" c.output(id: string, name: string, type?: ...) // default "audio" c.stereoIn(): void c.stereoOut(): void Example. patch export default cell("Gated voice", (c) => { c.input("pitch", "Pitch", "pitch"); c.input("gate", "Gate", "gate"); c.stereoOut(); const osc = c.add("oscillator"); const amp = c.add("vca"); c.cable(c.cin, "pitch", osc, "pitch"); c.cable(c.cin, "gate", amp, "gain"); c.cable(osc, "saw", amp, "l"); c.stereo(amp, c.cout); }); c.add What it does. Adds a module and returns a handle to cable from and to. values sets knobs in their own units; a value outside the range, of the wrong kind or for a knob that does not exist is an error that lists the real knobs. API. c.add(type: string, values?: Record , opts?: { name?: string, id?: string, at?: [column: number, row: number], // a grid of 300 by 220 pixels x?: number, y?: number, // pixels data?: unknown, // the module's node data }): Handle Example. patch export default cell("Filtered saw", (c) => { c.stereoOut(); const osc = c.add("oscillator", { fine: -12 }, { name: "Saw", at: [0, 0] }); const lp = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 800, mode: "LP" }, { at: [1, 0] }); c.cable(osc, "saw", lp, "l"); c.stereo(lp, c.cout); }); c.cable What it does. Draws a cable from an output jack to an input jack, or to a knob that cables can drive. The amount runs from −1 to +1 (default 1). Several cables into one input add up. API. c.cable(from: Handle, fromJack: string, to: Handle, toJack: string, amount?: number): void Example. patch export default cell("Wobble", (c) => { c.stereoOut(); const osc = c.add("oscillator"); const lfo = c.add("lfo", { rate: 4 }); const lp = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 1200 }); c.cable(osc, "saw", lp, "l"); c.cable(lfo, "out", lp, "cutoff", 0.4); // an LFO into a knob c.stereo(lp, c.cout); }); c.stereo What it does. Cables both channels at once: from.l to to.l and from.r to to.r . API. c.stereo(from: Handle, to: Handle, jacks?: { from?: [string, string], to?: [string, string], amount?: number }): void Example. patch export default cell("Pass through a filter", (c) => { c.stereoIn(); c.stereoOut(); const lp = c.add("filter", { cutoff: 3000 }); c.stereo(c.cin, lp); c.stereo(lp, c.cout); }); c.place What it does. Puts a module at a pixel position inside the cell. Without a position, modules are laid out in a grid between Cell In and Cell Out . API. c.place(handle: Handle, x: number, y: number): void Example. patch export default cell("Placed", (c) => { c.stereoOut(); const osc = c.add("oscillator"); c.place(osc, 40, 40); c.cable(osc, "saw", c.cout, "l"); }); c.cin and c.cout What it does. The cell's own input and output sides, as handles. Cable from c.cin to feed things inside from the cell's inputs, and to c.cout to send things to the cell's outputs. API. c.cin: Handle c.cout: Handle Example. See c.input and c.output above. The bleep UI object A self-made UI is JavaScript in the UI tab. It runs in a worker and talks to its module only through bleep . These are all its members. bleep.param(id) and bleep.params What it does. bleep.param(id) returns one param of the module and throws with the known ids when there is none; bleep.params has all of them. A param has id , name , kind , unit , min , max , steps , choices , value in its own units and normalised from 0 to 1, plus set(units) and setNormalised(x) . A UI can set at most 240 values per second. API. bleep.param(id: string): Param bleep.params: Record param.set(units: number): void param.setNormalised(x: number): void Example. const drive = bleep.param("drive"); const c = bleep.canvas(40); c.el.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => drive.setNormalised(e.clientX / c.width)); bleep.probe(id) What it does. The latest value of a @probe , 0 until the module reports one. API. bleep.probe(id: string): number Example. const m = bleep.canvas(20); bleep.onFrame(() => { m.g.clearRect(0, 0, m.width, m.height); m.g.fillStyle = bleep.theme.accent; m.g.fillRect(0, 0, m.width bleep.probe("peak"), m.height); }); bleep.button(id) What it does. Presses a @button method of the module, as if the user had clicked it. API. bleep.button(id: string): void Example. const c = bleep.canvas(30); c.el.addEventListener("click", () => bleep.button("clear")); bleep.onFrame(fn) and bleep.onValues(fn) What it does. onFrame calls your function every animation frame with the time since the last one, in seconds: draw animation here. onValues calls it only when a param or probe has changed: redraw here if the picture does not move on its own. API. bleep.onFrame(fn: (dt: number) => void): void bleep.onValues(fn: () => void): void Example. let phase = 0; const c = bleep.canvas(60); bleep.onFrame((dt) => { phase += dt bleep.param("rate").value; // a dot that moves at the LFO's rate c.g.clearRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); c.g.fillStyle = bleep.theme.accent; c.g.fillRect((phase % 1) c.width, 20, 8, 8); }); bleep.size(h) and bleep.canvas(h) What it does. bleep.size(h) asks for a height in pixels, 40 to 800; the width is the node's. bleep.canvas(h) makes a canvas as wide as the view and h high, scaled for the screen, and returns { el, g, width, height } . bleep.canvas("fill") is as high as the view too, so it follows the window when it is resized. API. bleep.size(h: number): void bleep.canvas(h: number "fill"): { el, g: CanvasRenderingContext2D, width: number, height: number } Example. const c = bleep.canvas("fill"); bleep.onFrame(() => { c.g.fillStyle = bleep.theme.panel; c.g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); }); bleep.theme What it does. The board's colours, so a UI looks at home in both themes. API. bleep.theme: { bg: string, panel: string, line: string, text: string, muted: string, accent: string, warn: string } Example. const c = bleep.canvas(40); c.g.strokeStyle = bleep.theme.line; c.g.strokeRect(0.5, 0.5, c.width - 1, c.height - 1);

title: An advanced oscillator
text: An advanced oscillator The sine oscillator had one waveform and a pitch. This one has what a real synth oscillator has: four waveforms: sine, triangle, saw and a square with pulse width; anti-aliasing on the saw and the square (PolyBLEP); an FM input , per sample, for frequency modulation; a sync input : a rising edge restarts the oscillator (hard sync); a sync output that pulses at the start of each cycle, so that one oscillator can sync another. Read Rates and timing and the drive tutorial first; this page uses the block-rate / sample-rate split and the idea of aliasing. The module compile import { Smoother, pitchToHz } from "./bleep/dsp"; /// The PolyBLEP residual: a small curve that, added around a jump, replaces the jump by a band-limited step. It is nonzero only within one /// phase step dt of the jump. t is the phase relative to the jump (0 to 1). function polyBlep(t: f64, dt: f64): f64 { if (t 1.0 - dt) { const x = (t - 1.0) / dt; return x x + x + x + 1.0; } return 0.0; } @module({ name: "Oscillator", category: "Sources/Script", description: "Sine, triangle, saw and pulse with PolyBLEP, audio-rate FM and hard sync.", }) export class Oscillator { @input({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "FM", type: "audio" }) fm: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "Sync", type: "trigger" }) sync: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Sync out", type: "trigger" }) syncOut: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Waveform", choices: ["Sine", "Triangle", "Saw", "Square"] }) waveform: i32 = 2; @param({ name: "Octave", min: -3, max: 3, init: 0 }) octave: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Semitones", min: -12, max: 12, init: 0 }) semitones: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Fine", min: -100, max: 100, init: 0, unit: "cents", decimals: 0 }) fine: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Pulse width", min: 0.05, max: 0.95, init: 0.5 }) width: f32 = 0.5; @param({ name: "FM amount", min: 0, max: 5000, init: 0, map: "skew", centre: 300, unit: "Hz", decimals: 0 }) fmAmount: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) level: f32 = 0.5; private phase: f64 = 0; private base: f64 = 0; // the frequency of the pitch and tuning, in Hz private inverse: f64; // 1 / sampleRate private gain: Smoother; private pulseWidth: Smoother; private pulse: i32 = 0; // samples left of the sync output pulse constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.inverse = 1.0 / sampleRate; this.gain = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); this.pulseWidth = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); this.pulseWidth.target = 0.5; this.pulseWidth.snap(); } reset(): void { this.phase = 0; this.pulse = 0; } /// Hard sync: a rising edge on the Sync input restarts the cycle, at the sample where the edge happens. @on("sync", { rising: 0.5 }) restart(): void { this.phase = 0; } block(): void { const volts = this.pitch + this.octave + this.semitones / 12.0 + this.fine / 1200.0; this.base = pitchToHz(volts); // the expensive part, once per block this.gain.target = this.level; this.pulseWidth.target = this.width; } sample(): void { // frequency modulation: the FM input adds Hz to the frequency, every sample. It can go negative: the oscillator then runs backwards. const step = (this.base + this.fm this.fmAmount) this.inverse; // phase per sample const dt = abs(step); // how far the phase moves, whichever direction const direction: f64 = step this.pulseWidth.next(); let v: f64; if (this.waveform == 0) { v = Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI t); } else if (this.waveform == 1) { v = 1.0 - 4.0 abs(t - 0.5); // -1 at the start, +1 half way } else if (this.waveform == 2) { v = 2.0 t - 1.0 - direction polyBlep(t, dt); // a saw, with its jump at the wrap smoothed } else { v = t v this.gain.next(); // advance, and tell the world when the cycle starts again this.phase += step; if (this.phase >= 1.0 this.phase 0 ? 1 : 0; if (this.pulse > 0) this.pulse--; } } How it works The phase and the three waveform families The phase runs from 0 to 1 as before. The waveforms are all functions of it: Waveform Function of the phase t Aliasing Sine sin(2π t) none: it has no harmonics Triangle a ramp up and down, 1 − 4· t − 0.5 very little: its harmonics fall off as 1/n² Saw 2t − 1 strong: a jump at the wrap, harmonics fall off as 1/n Square +1 below the pulse width, −1 above strong: two jumps The sine and the triangle need nothing more. The saw and the square have jumps , and a jump is an infinite number of harmonics: sampled naively, those above Nyquist fold back and make the inharmonic grit described in the drive tutorial. PolyBLEP PolyBLEP ("polynomial band-limited step") is the cheap fix. A band-limited jump is smooth: it is a step run through a low-pass filter. PolyBLEP approximates what that filter would do to the two samples around the jump with a small parabola and adds the difference to the naive waveform. Away from the jump polyBlep returns 0, so it costs a comparison; near the jump it is a few multiplications. t 1 − dt : the sample just before it. For the saw, the jump is at the wrap, so the correction is subtracted at the phase's start and end. For the square there are two jumps: the rising edge at the wrap and the falling edge at the pulse width. The second one calls polyBlep with the phase relative to the pulse width , which is t − w , brought back into 0 to 1. The documentation test measures it: a saw at about 3.3 kHz carries roughly 16 dB less folded (non-harmonic) energy with PolyBLEP than the naive saw. The test also checks the other parts: all four waveforms at the right pitch, a pulse width of 0.25 being high a quarter of the time, FM with a modulation index of 2 giving exactly the sideband amplitudes theory predicts (0.22 at the carrier, 0.58 at each first sideband), and a synced slave repeating with the master's period. The triangle has no jump but a corner, whose harmonics fall off fast; correcting it is possible (PolyBLAMP) and unnecessary for most uses. FM: audio-rate frequency modulation The FM input is an audio signal that is added to the frequency, in hertz, every sample : step = (base + fm · amount) / sampleRate . With a sine on FM and a sine on the carrier you get the classic bell and electric-piano sounds. Two things matter for FM: It must be read per sample . If the pitch were read per block (as base is), the modulation would be sampled 1,500 times a second and anything above about 750 Hz would alias. This is why the pitch is block rate and FM is sample rate: the pitch moves slowly, the modulator does not. The frequency can go below zero . The phase then runs backwards ( through-zero FM ), which is musically interesting. For that reason the step is signed, the wrap code handles both directions, and the PolyBLEP corrections use abs(step) for their width and the sign for their direction: a saw running backwards has its jump with the opposite sign. The FM amount is a skew knob: most of its travel is below 300 Hz, where the useful settings are, with the rest reaching 5 kHz. Hard sync @on("sync", { rising: 0.5 }) runs at the sample where the Sync input rises through 0.5 and restarts the phase at 0. Feeding it the sync output of another oscillator (the master ) makes the slave restart with the master's period, while the slave's own pitch sets how much of its waveform fits in that period. Sweeping the slave's pitch with the master fixed gives the classic sync sweep. The Sync out output is a short trigger pulse (8 samples) each time the phase wraps, so a master is just another copy of this module with its Sync out cabled to the slave's Sync . Because the restart is a jump, hard sync has the same aliasing problem as a saw. This version does not correct it: the first sample after the restart is a discontinuity. A better one adds a PolyBLEP-style correction of the size of the jump at the restart; that is a good extension. The pulse width The pulse width knob is smoothed ( pulseWidth.next() once per sample): a stepped width is a click, and an automated width (PWM) from a slow control signal sounds smoother. Its value is only used by the square. Try it Compile it, cable Pitch from a Keyboard and Out to the speakers. Change the Waveform . Put a second Oscillator (this module, added twice) as the modulator, cable its Out into the first one's FM , and raise FM amount . For sync, cable the master's Sync out into the slave's Sync , set the master to a low note and sweep the slave's Semitones . Ideas to extend it Detune and unison: several phases at slightly different frequencies, summed. A StaticArray of phases and a loop with a constant bound. A PolyBLAMP triangle , or a wavetable read at the phase, with the table switched by frequency to avoid aliasing. Corrected sync , as described above. A phase modulation input (add the input to the phase instead of the frequency), as in DX-style synths; it is the same line in sample() .

title: Drive with anti-aliasing
text: Drive with anti-aliasing A drive (a soft clipper, a saturator) pushes the signal through a curve such as tanh . It is the simplest nonlinear effect, and the simplest way to meet aliasing . The naive version compile import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Drive Naive", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class DriveNaive { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Drive", min: 0, max: 40, init: 12, unit: "dB", decimals: 1 }) drive: f32 = 12; private g: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.g = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } block(): void { this.g.target = dbToLin(this.drive); } sample(): void { this.out = Math.tanh( (this.x this.g.next())); } } It does what it says, and it sounds harsh on a bright sine. The reason is not the curve but the sampling. What aliasing is A clipper adds harmonics : a sine at 5 kHz becomes 5, 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on. A digital signal at 48 kHz can only hold frequencies up to 24 kHz (the Nyquist frequency). Harmonics above it do not disappear, they fold back below it: 35 kHz comes out as 48 − 35 = 13 kHz, which is not a harmonic of 5 kHz at all. These folded partials are aliasing , they sound inharmonic and dirty, and the harder you drive, the more of them there are. You can avoid aliasing by making the nonlinearity less sharp, by raising the sampling rate (oversampling), or by computing what a band-limited waveshaper would output. Anti-derivative anti-aliasing (ADAA) The cheapest good fix is ADAA , and it is short enough to write yourself. Here is the idea in four steps. 1. The problem is the point sample. The naive shaper evaluates tanh at one instant. A real, continuous signal that passes through tanh has harmonics far above Nyquist, and sampling the result folds them back. If the shaper's input had been band-limited after the curve, the folded partials would not exist. 2. Use the average instead of the point. Between two samples the input moves from x₁ to x . Instead of tanh(x) , output the average of tanh over that interval : y = 1/(x − x₁) · ∫ tanh(u) du from x₁ to x Averaging over the interval is a gentle low-pass on the shaped signal, which is just what removes the folding. 3. The integral has a closed form. If F is an antiderivative of tanh , the integral is F(x) − F(x₁) , so y = (F(x) − F(x₁)) / (x − x₁) and for tanh the antiderivative is F(x) = ln(cosh x) . You only need to remember the previous input and the previous F . 4. Two numerical details. cosh overflows for a large x , so use the identity ln cosh x = x + ln(1 + e^(−2 x )) − ln 2 , which never overflows. And when x and x₁ are almost equal the quotient is 0/0; in the limit it is just tanh at the midpoint, so use that when the difference is tiny. Put together, the shaper is a function and two fields: compile import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; /// ln(cosh(x)): the antiderivative of tanh, written so that it cannot overflow. function lnCosh(x: f64): f64 { const a = abs(x); return a + Math.log(1.0 + Math.exp(-2.0 a)) - Math.LN2; } @module({ name: "Drive", category: "Effects/Script", description: "A soft clipper with anti-derivative anti-aliasing." }) export class Drive { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Drive", min: 0, max: 40, init: 12, unit: "dB", decimals: 1 }) drive: f32 = 12; @param({ name: "Mix", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1 }) mix: f32 = 1; @probe level: f32 = 0; private gain: Smoother; private wet: Smoother; private makeup: f32 = 1; private previousX: f64 = 0; // the input one sample ago private previousF: f64 = 0; // ln(cosh) of it constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.gain = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); this.wet = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } block(): void { this.gain.target = dbToLin(this.drive); this.wet.target = this.mix; // keep the loudness roughly constant as the drive rises this.makeup = (1.0 / Math.sqrt( dbToLin(this.drive))); } reset(): void { this.previousX = 0; this.previousF = 0; } sample(): void { const dry = this.x; const driven = (dry this.gain.next()); // ADAA: the average of tanh between the previous and the current sample const f = lnCosh(driven); const dx = driven - this.previousX; const shaped = abs(dx) shaped this.makeup - dry) w; this.level = max(abs(this.out), this.level 0.9995); } } Compared with the naive module, only the middle of sample() changed: Math.tanh(driven) became the three lines of ADAA and the two fields that remember the previous sample. Because the shaper now has state , reset() clears it. The smoothing of drive and mix is the same as in the smoothing tutorial. You do not have to write this every time: bleep/dsp has the same shaper ready-made as AdaaTanh , with a next(x) method. Does it work? The documentation test of this page measures it: a 5 kHz sine at 48 kHz with 30 dB of drive, through the naive shaper and through the ADAA module above, and looks at everything that is not a harmonic of the tone (the folded partials). In total they carry about 7 dB less energy with ADAA, and in the band below the fundamental , where folded partials stand out most because nothing masks them, about 27 dB less. It is a large improvement for a few operations; it is not perfect, and a hard-driven bright tone still has some aliasing: that is where oversampling comes in. Try it on your own patch: sweep the input frequency upward while listening to a hard-driven tone. Aliased partials move down while the input goes up, which no real harmonic does. Oversampling ADAA suits a smooth curve like tanh . For another curve, repeat the recipe: find its antiderivative F and use (F(x) − F(x₁)) / (x − x₁) . For a hard clipper the antiderivative is piecewise quadratic. And for very high drive the traditional method is oversampling : run the shaper at 2x or 4x the sample rate, low-pass before downsampling, and keep only what is in the audible band. Bleep Script does not have a built-in oversampler: a module is called once per sample. You can write one yourself with sample() computing two shaper steps for each input sample (an interpolated one in between), followed by a half-band filter, but note that: the cost doubles per step, and the cost estimate will say so; a linear-phase filter adds latency, an IIR one does not but disturbs phase; for most drives, ADAA alone is audibly clean up to the moderate settings. Try ADAA first, and add oversampling only when you can hear a problem. Check the output A drive makes output you did not have: a DC offset (when the shaper is asymmetric) and a louder signal. Put DcBlocker after an asymmetric curve, and mind the level: import { DcBlocker } from "./bleep/dsp"; private dc: DcBlocker; // in the constructor: new DcBlocker(sampleRate, 20) this.out = this.dc.next(shaped);

title: The DSP toolbox
text: The DSP toolbox The usual pieces of audio code, each as a small complete module. Copy one into a Code node and compile it. Most use something from bleep/dsp for the parts that are easy to get wrong. Common rules, from Rates and timing: derive things from knobs in block() , run the signal in sample() , allocate only in the constructor, and smooth anything a knob can step. Oscillators and phase Every oscillator is a phase that runs from 0 to 1 and a function of it. Phasor is the phase. A naive saw ( 2 phase - 1 ) aliases (see the drive tutorial); PolyBLEP corrects the jump where the saw wraps, which removes most of it. The sine oscillator and the advanced oscillator tutorials go further; this is the short version: compile import { Phasor, pitchToHz } from "./bleep/dsp"; /// The PolyBLEP correction: nonzero only within one phase step of the wrap. function polyBlep(t: f64, dt: f64): f64 { if (t 1.0 - dt) { const x = (t - 1.0) / dt; return x x + x + x + 1.0; } return 0.0; } @module({ name: "Saw Osc", category: "Sources/Script", description: "A band-limited saw (PolyBLEP) and a sine." }) export class SawOsc { @input({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Saw", type: "audio" }) saw: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Sine", type: "audio" }) sine: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Octave", min: -3, max: 3, init: 0 }) octave: i32 = 0; private osc: Phasor; private step: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.osc = new Phasor(sampleRate); } block(): void { this.osc.frequency = pitchToHz( this.pitch + this.octave); // the pitch at the start of the block this.step = this.osc.frequency / this.sampleRate; } sample(): void { const t = this.osc.next(); this.saw = (2.0 t - 1.0 - polyBlep(t, this.step)); this.sine = Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI t); } } The pitch is read at block rate here, which is fine for a held note. For vibrato or a fast pitch envelope, read this.pitch in sample() and set this.osc.frequency there (it costs a pow per sample, so keep that to oscillators that need it). Noise A white noise source is a pseudo-random number generator. A linear congruential generator is a few integer operations and has no state but one number: compile @module({ name: "Noise", category: "Sources/Script" }) export class Noise { @output({ name: "White", type: "audio" }) white: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Pink", type: "audio" }) pink: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) level: f32 = 0.5; private state: u32 = 22222; private b0: f32 = 0; private b1: f32 = 0; private b2: f32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.state = this.state 1664525 + 1013904223; const w = ( this.state) / 2147483648.0; // -1 to 1 this.white = w this.level; // a cheap pink noise: three one-pole filters of white noise, added up with the white this.b0 = 0.99765 this.b0 + w 0.0990460; this.b1 = 0.96300 this.b1 + w 0.2965164; this.b2 = 0.57000 this.b2 + w 1.0526913; this.pink = (this.b0 + this.b1 + this.b2 + w 0.1848) 0.25 this.level; } } There is no Math.random() here: it is not available in real-time code, and a fixed seed makes the module repeatable. Delay lines A delay is a buffer written at one position and read at another. Allocate it in the constructor (the only place that may) at the size of the longest delay: compile import { Smoother } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Echo", category: "Effects/Script" }) export class Echo { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Time", min: 0.01, max: 1, init: 0.3, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) time: f32 = 0.3; @param({ name: "Feedback", min: 0, max: 0.95, init: 0.4 }) feedback: f32 = 0.4; @param({ name: "Mix", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.4 }) mix: f32 = 0.4; private buffer: StaticArray ; private size: i32; private write: i32 = 0; private filled: i32 = 0; // how much of the buffer has been written since the last reset private delay: Smoother; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { const size = sampleRate + 2; // one second, and two samples for the interpolation this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.size = size; this.buffer = new StaticArray (size); this.delay = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.1); // a slow glide: a fast change in delay time bends the pitch this.delay.target = (sampleRate 0.3); this.delay.snap(); } reset(): void { this.filled = 0; this.write = 0; } // forget the old contents without clearing a whole second block(): void { this.delay.target = (this.sampleRate this.time); } sample(): void { const d = this.delay.next(); // the delay in samples, fractional let delayed: f32 = 0; if ( d this.write - d; if (read this.size; const i = read; const frac = read - i; const a = this.buffer[i], b = this.buffer[i + 1 >= this.size ? 0 : i + 1]; delayed = a + (b - a) frac; // linear interpolation between two samples } this.buffer[this.write] = this.x + delayed this.feedback; this.write = this.write + 1 >= this.size ? 0 : this.write + 1; if (this.filled p 0.5 Math.PI; this.left = this.x Math.cos(angle); // equal power: left² + right² = 1 this.right = this.x Math.sin(angle); } } Counting triggers A clock divider counts triggers and passes every n-th. It is an edge handler and a counter, with nothing per sample: compile @module({ name: "Divider", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Divider { @input({ name: "Clock", type: "trigger" }) clock: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "Reset", type: "trigger" }) restart: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "trigger" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Divide by", min: 1, max: 32, init: 2 }) divide: i32 = 2; @probe count: f32 = 0; private counter: i32 = 0; private pulse: i32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @on("clock", { rising: 0.5 }) tick(): void { if (this.counter == 0) this.pulse = 64; // the pulse lasts 64 samples this.counter = (this.counter + 1) % this.divide; this.count = this.counter; } @on("restart", { rising: 0.5 }) rewind(): void { this.counter = 0; } sample(): void { this.out = this.pulse > 0 ? 1 : 0; if (this.pulse > 0) this.pulse--; } } Tempo sync A module learns the tempo and position through a @transport method, called once per block before block() .
