This LFO runs in musical time : one cycle every Beats quarter notes, locked to the host's position, so it stays in step when the tempo changes or the transport jumps. compile @module({ name: "Beat LFO", category: "Modulation/Script" }) export class BeatLfo { @output({ name: "Out", type: "control" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Beats", min: 0.25, max: 16, init: 1, map: "exp", unit: "beats", decimals: 2 }) beats: f32 = 1; private beat: f64 = 0; private perSample: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } @transport tempo(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void { this.perSample = bpm / (60.0 this.sampleRate); // quarter notes per sample if (playing) this.beat = ppq; // the position at the start of this block } sample(): void { this.beat += this.perSample; const phase = this.beat / this.beats; this.out = Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI (phase - Math.floor(phase))); } } bpm is the tempo, ppq the position at the start of the block in quarter notes, playing whether the transport runs. Between blocks the module advances the position itself, per sample, and takes the host's value again at the next block: this keeps it exact even when the tempo is automated. When the transport is stopped, ppq holds still; the module keeps its own running position or stops, as you decide. The step sequencer tutorial uses this and a clock input together. Other things you will want A list of the usual building blocks and where each is in or how to make it: Thing How Gain in dB, linear to dB dbToLin , linToDb Interpolation lerp , or a fractional read as in the delay above Smoothing a value Smoother ; or a one-pole with your own coefficient (S&H tutorial) Peak meter, level follower PeakHold Shelving, bell, low-pass filters Biquad (high-pass and band-pass are the same cookbook formulas with other coefficients: write them in a set method like the library's) Soft clipping AdaaTanh ; Math.tanh is fine for gentle drive, see drive DC offset removal DcBlocker Phase, LFO Phasor A lookup table A StaticArray filled in the constructor, read with lerp A one-sample delay (feedback in a filter) A f32 field Random per trigger The LCG above, advanced in the handler Notes Events and routing Oversampling Not built in, see drive FFT, convolution, long buffers Not a good fit: the cost bound is per block (see Limits)

title: Processing different inputs
text: Processing different inputs Every jack has a type , and the type tells you how to read it. The first five ( audio , control , pitch , gate , trigger ) are all just an f32 that holds the signal's value at the current sample. What differs is what the values mean , and which tool fits: read the value directly, watch it for an edge , or treat it as a pitch . The sixth, notes , is not a signal at all but a list of events. Type What the value is Read it with audio A waveform, usually −1 to 1 The field in sample() control A slowly moving value (an LFO, an envelope, a knob) The field in sample() or block() pitch A pitch in volts: 1.0 is an octave, 0 is C4 The field, converted with pitchToHz gate High (0.5 or more) while something is held @on(..., { rising }) and { falling } , or the level trigger A short pulse @on(..., { rising }) notes Note events with an exact sample @on("jack") with a NoteEvent Remember the rates: in sample() an input field holds this sample ; in block() it holds the first sample of the block . Audio: an envelope follower Audio is processed per sample. This module turns audio into a control signal that follows its level, using a peak meter with a release time: compile import { PeakHold } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Follower", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Follower { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Level", type: "control", bipolar: false }) level: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Release", min: 0.005, max: 2, init: 0.15, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) release: f32 = 0.15; @param({ name: "Gain", min: 0, max: 10, init: 1 }) gain: f32 = 1; private peak: PeakHold; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.peak = new PeakHold(sampleRate, 0.15); } sample(): void { this.level = this.peak.next(this.x) this.gain; } } The PeakHold rises at once and falls with the time you gave it. (Its time is fixed when it is made. To make Release a knob, compute a decay from the knob once per block, as the sample and hold does for its glide.) Pitch: transpose and convert A pitch signal is in volts per octave : adding 1.0 goes up an octave, adding 1/12 goes up a semitone, and 0 is C4 (261.63 Hz). That makes transposing a plain addition: compile import { Smoother, pitchToHz } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Transpose", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Transpose { @input({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) out: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Hz", type: "control", bipolar: false }) hz: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Semitones", min: -24, max: 24, init: 0 }) semitones: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Fine", min: -100, max: 100, init: 0, unit: "cents", decimals: 0 }) fine: f32 = 0; private shift: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.shift = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.005); } block(): void { this.shift.target = ( this.semitones / 12.0 + this.fine / 1200.0); } sample(): void { const v = this.pitch + this.shift.next(); this.out = v; this.hz = pitchToHz( v); } } Two things: the offset is smoothed so a knob change does not step the pitch (a stepped pitch is a click on the oscillator after it), and pitchToHz is the conversion for anything that needs a frequency. It uses pow , so call it per block when you can, per sample only when the pitch itself is modulated. Gate and trigger: edges A gate is high while a key is held; a trigger is a short pulse. Both are edges you react to . Do not compare the level in sample() every sample and remember the previous value yourself: declare @on handlers and the engine does it for you, at the exact sample. compile @module({ name: "Gate Envelope", category: "Utility/Script", description: "Rises while a gate is high and falls when it ends. A trigger restarts it." }) export class GateEnvelope { @input({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "Retrigger", type: "trigger" }) retrigger: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Env", type: "control", bipolar: false }) env: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Eoc", type: "trigger" }) eoc: f32 = 0; // a pulse when the release ends @param({ name: "Attack", min: 0.001, max: 2, init: 0.01, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) attack: f32 = 0.01; @param({ name: "Release", min: 0.001, max: 4, init: 0.3, map: "exp", unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) release: f32 = 0.3; private level: f32 = 0; private up: f32 = 0; // the step per sample while the gate is high private down: f32 = 0; private high: bool = false; private pulse: i32 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } @on("gate", { rising: 0.5 }) open(): void { this.high = true; } @on("gate", { falling: 0.5 }) close(): void { this.high = false; } @on("retrigger", { rising: 0.5 }) again(): void { this.level = 0; } block(): void { this.up = (1.0 / (this.sampleRate this.attack)); this.down = (1.0 / (this.sampleRate this.release)); } sample(): void { if (this.high) this.level = min(1, this.level + this.up); else if (this.level > 0) { this.level = max(0, this.level - this.down); if (this.level == 0) this.pulse = 48; // end of cycle: a short pulse } this.eoc = this.pulse > 0 ? 1 : 0; if (this.pulse > 0) this.pulse--; this.env = this.level; } } A rising edge happens on the sample where the signal goes from below the level to at or above it, so a gate and a retrigger that arrive together are both seen at the right sample. A cable that is not connected reads 0, and the first block never fires an edge. Use 0.5 as the level for gates and triggers: it is the board's own threshold (a gate is high at 0.5 or more). Notes: events with a sample position A notes input is a list of events, not a stream of values. Each event arrives in its @on handler, at the sample where it belongs. This module turns notes into a monophonic pitch, gate and velocity , last note wins: compile import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; @module({ name: "Mono Note", category: "Utility/Script", description: "Notes to pitch, gate and velocity." }) export class MonoNote { @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @output({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Gate", type: "gate" }) gate: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Velocity", type: "control", bipolar: false }) velocity: f32 = 0; private held: StaticArray = new StaticArray (16); // the notes that are down, in the order they were pressed private count: i32 = 0; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} @on("notes") handle(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.isOn && n.value > 0) { this.remove(n.note); // a repeated note goes to the top if (this.count (this.held[this.count - 1] - 60) / 12.0; // back to the key still down } } private remove(note: i32): void { let to = 0; for (let i = 0; i = this.count) break; if (this.held[i] != note) { this.held[to] = this.held[i]; to++; } } this.count = to; } } n.pitch is already in volts, n.note is the MIDI number, n.value the velocity from 0 to 1. Notes to other notes (a transposer, a router, an arpeggiator) push events instead: see Events and routing. The fixed-size StaticArray and the bounded loop are the usual way to keep a list in real-time code: there is no growing array in sample() or a handler. Several inputs of one kind count makes numbered jacks, and the field is a StaticArray . Read them in a loop with a constant bound. See Module scripts and the Mixer example. Summary audio , control , pitch : read the field. gate , trigger : add an edge handler. notes : a note handler. Do derived work (coefficients, conversions) in block() , and per-sample work in sample() . Smooth anything that steps (smoothing).

title: Tutorials
text: Tutorials Each tutorial builds a complete module that you can paste into a Code node and compile. They go from a bigger project to small techniques; if you are new to this, start with the sine oscillator; read Rates and timing first, since every one of them depends on it. Tutorial You build You learn A simple sine oscillator A sine from a phase accumulator, with a pitch input, tuning and a lookup-table version Phase, f64 , volts per octave, block rate against sample rate An advanced oscillator Four waveforms with PolyBLEP, pulse width, FM and hard sync Anti-aliasing a jump, per-sample FM, edge-triggered sync An 8-step, 4-lane step sequencer Four gate lanes that follow the tempo or a clock input @transport , edge handlers, counted outputs, a layout Preventing pops and clicks A gain, a mute and a low-pass that never click Smoothing, block rate against sample rate Drive with anti-aliasing A soft clipper that aliases much less Aliasing, ADAA, oversampling Sample and hold A sample and hold, with the generated UI and with a self-made UI Triggers, a layout, a custom canvas UI Processing different inputs An envelope follower, a transposer, a gate envelope and a note converter Audio, pitch, gate, trigger and notes inputs A synth voice A supersaw voice with a ladder filter, an ADSR, notes and a chorus The bleep/osc , filters , env and fx libraries, block-rate modulation The DSP toolbox An oscillator, noise, a delay, a pan, a clock divider and a tempo LFO The usual building blocks Every code block marked as a module compiles as shown. The documentation tests compile them and, for the larger ones, run them: the step sequencer's timing, the drive's aliasing, and the others' behaviour are checked, so what you read is what the module does.

title: Sample and hold
text: Sample and hold A sample and hold takes a snapshot of a signal at the moment a trigger arrives and holds it until the next one. Feed it noise and it makes random steps; feed it a slow LFO and it makes a staircase. It is also a small tour of a trigger input, an edge handler and a smoothed output. The module compile @module({ name: "Sample and Hold", category: "Utility/Script", description: "Holds the signal at each trigger." }) export class SampleHold { @input({ name: "Signal", type: "control" }) signal: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "Trigger", type: "trigger" }) trig: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "control" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Glide", min: 0, max: 0.5, init: 0, unit: "s", decimals: 3 }) glide: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Mode", choices: ["Sample", "Track"] }) mode: i32 = 0; @probe held: f32 = 0; private value: f32 = 0; // what the last trigger took private smooth: f32 = 0; // the output, gliding towards it private coefficient: f32 = 1; // 1 means no glide private tracking: bool = false; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } @on("trig", { rising: 0.5 }) take(): void { this.value = this.signal; // the signal at exactly this sample this.tracking = this.mode == 1; } @on("trig", { falling: 0.5 }) release(): void { this.tracking = false; } block(): void { // the glide time becomes a per-sample coefficient once per block: one exp() here, none in sample() this.coefficient = this.glide 1 : (1.0 - Math.exp(-1.0 / (this.sampleRate this.glide))); this.held = this.value; } sample(): void { if (this.tracking) this.value = this.signal; // Track mode follows the signal while the trigger is high this.smooth += (this.value - this.smooth) this.coefficient; this.out = this.smooth; } } What each part does @on("trig", { rising: 0.5 }) runs at the exact sample where the trigger crosses 0.5. At that sample this.signal already holds the signal's value, so the snapshot is sample-accurate, not rounded to the block (Rates and timing). Mode chooses between Sample (snapshot at the rising edge) and Track (follow the signal while the trigger is high, hold when it falls). The held value is a probe , which the view shows as a meter. Glide slews the stepped output so it can be made smooth. It is a one-pole whose coefficient is computed from the knob once per block , so the exp is not paid per sample. With Glide at 0 the coefficient is 1 and the output follows the held value exactly. The prebuilt UI The Code node generates a control for every @param , a meter for every @probe and a button for every @button , with no further work: after compiling you get the Glide knob, the Mode dropdown and a meter for held . To arrange them, add a layout to @module : @module({ name: "Sample and Hold", layout: [ { row: [{ knob: "glide" }, { select: "mode" }, { meter: "held" }] }, ], }) A layout only places the standard widgets; it needs no code and cannot go wrong at run time. See Custom UIs and widgets for every widget. A custom UI When the standard widgets are not enough, the UI tab holds JavaScript that draws the module's own panel. This one draws a scope of the held value : a trace that steps whenever a new sample is taken. const view = bleep.canvas(120); const history = new Array(240).fill(0); // the last 240 frames of the held value let tick = 0; bleep.onFrame(() => { if (++tick % 2) return; // a column every second frame history.push(bleep.probe("held")); history.shift(); const { g, width, height } = view; g.clearRect(0, 0, width, height); g.strokeStyle = bleep.theme.line; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(0, height / 2); g.lineTo(width, height / 2); g.stroke(); // the zero line g.strokeStyle = bleep.theme.accent; g.lineWidth = 2; g.beginPath(); history.forEach((v, i) => { const x = (i / (history.length - 1)) width; const y = height / 2 - v (height / 2 - 6); if (i === 0) g.moveTo(x, y); else g.lineTo(x, y); }); g.stroke(); }); view.el.addEventListener("pointerdown", () => bleep.param("glide").set(0.1)); // a click sets the glide What to take from it: bleep.probe("held") is how the UI reads a module's @probe . The view receives it up to 30 times a second. bleep.canvas(h) gives a canvas as wide as the node, scaled for the screen. bleep.param("glide").set(v) writes a knob in its own units (seconds here). Everything runs in a sandbox: no network, no storage, and it only talks to its module. It runs in a worker that the board stops if it hangs, so a UI that came with a patch needs no approval. See Limits and safety. The vintage modules (Add › Effects) have larger UIs, each with a picture you can drag. Add one, open its window and press Convert to code to read how it is written. Using it Cable a Noise or an LFO into Signal , a clock or a gate sequencer lane into Trigger , and Out into a pitch or a filter cutoff: the classic random stepped voltage. A slower trigger gives longer steps.

title: A simple sine oscillator
text: A simple sine oscillator Every oscillator, from a sine to a supersaw, is built on one idea: a number called the phase that goes from 0 up to 1 over and over, and a function that turns the phase into a sample. This tutorial writes the simplest one, a sine, in three steps. The advanced oscillator builds on it. The idea: a phase accumulator A sine at 440 Hz completes 440 cycles per second. At 48,000 samples per second that is 440 / 48000 of a cycle per sample. So: keep a phase between 0 and 1; for every sample, output sin(2π · phase) ; then add frequency / sampleRate to the phase, and wrap it back below 1. The wrap is phase -= floor(phase) : it subtracts the whole part and keeps the fraction. Step 1: a fixed frequency compile @module({ name: "Sine", category: "Sources/Script", description: "The simplest oscillator." }) export class Sine { @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Frequency", min: 20, max: 2000, init: 440, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 1 }) frequency: f32 = 440; private phase: f64 = 0; private increment: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } block(): void { this.increment = this.frequency / this.sampleRate; } // cycles per sample sample(): void { this.out = Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI this.phase); this.phase += this.increment; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); // wrap into 0 to 1 } } Compile it, cable Out into a Speakers node and you hear a sine. Notes on the choices: The increment is computed in block() . The knob only changes once per block, so the division is paid once per block, not per sample (Rates and timing). sample() only adds, wraps and calls sin . The phase is an f64 . An f32 has about seven digits. A phase near 1.0 with a tiny increment, added a million times, would drift and wobble in pitch. Keep phases and phase increments in f64 , and convert to f32 only for the output. The phase stays in 0 to 1 , not in radians. The wrap is simple, it never grows large, and every waveform you add later (a saw, a triangle) is a function of the same number. The knob is exp , because pitch is logarithmic: the same turn of the knob should give the same musical interval, not the same number of hertz (Module scripts). Step 2: a pitch input, tuning and a level A real oscillator is played from a keyboard or a sequencer, so it takes a pitch input. Pitch signals are in volts per octave : 0 is C4 (261.63 Hz) and each 1.0 is one octave up, so a frequency is 261.63 · 2^volts . pitchToHz in bleep/dsp does this conversion. compile import { Smoother, pitchToHz } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Sine Osc", category: "Sources/Script", description: "A sine with a pitch input, tuning and level." }) export class SineOsc { @input({ name: "Pitch", type: "pitch" }) pitch: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Octave", min: -3, max: 3, init: 0 }) octave: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Semitones", min: -12, max: 12, init: 0 }) semitones: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Fine", min: -100, max: 100, init: 0, unit: "cents", decimals: 0 }) fine: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 0.5 }) level: f32 = 0.5; private phase: f64 = 0; private increment: f64 = 0; private gain: Smoother; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.gain = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } reset(): void { this.phase = 0; } block(): void { // octaves, semitones and cents are all just offsets in volts const volts = this.pitch + this.octave + this.semitones / 12.0 + this.fine / 1200.0; this.increment = pitchToHz(volts) / this.sampleRate; this.gain.target = this.level; } sample(): void { this.out = Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI this.phase) this.gain.next(); this.phase += this.increment; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); } } What changed: All tuning is addition in volts. An octave is +1 , a semitone +1/12 , a cent +1/1200 . Convert to hertz once, at the end. The pitch is read in block() , so it is sampled 1,500 times a second (once per 32 samples). That is plenty for a held note, a slow glide or a vibrato; a pitch that moves faster than that, such as audio-rate FM, belongs on its own input, read per sample. The advanced oscillator does exactly that. The level is smoothed , so turning it does not click (Preventing pops and clicks). reset() restarts the phase. Every note then starts the sine at the same point, which makes an attack repeatable. Without it the oscillator is "free running" and each note starts wherever the phase happens to be. Try a pitch from a Keyboard into Pitch , an ADSR into a VCA after it, and you have a voice. Step 3: a table instead of sin Math.sin is accurate and, in WebAssembly, not free. If thousands of sines are running, a lookup table with interpolation is cheaper: the table is filled once in the constructor (the only place that may allocate) and each sample reads two entries and blends them. compile import { lerp } from "./bleep/dsp"; const TABLE SIZE: i32 = 2048; @module({ name: "Sine Table", category: "Sources/Script", description: "A sine from a lookup table." }) export class SineTable { @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Frequency", min: 20, max: 2000, init: 440, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 1 }) frequency: f32 = 440; private table: StaticArray = new StaticArray (TABLE SIZE + 1); // one extra entry: the end equals the start private phase: f64 = 0; private increment: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; for (let i = 0; i Math.sin(2.0 Math.PI i / TABLE SIZE); } block(): void { this.increment = this.frequency / this.sampleRate; } sample(): void { const position = this.phase TABLE SIZE; const i = position; // the entry below const fraction = (position - i); this.out = lerp(this.table[i], this.table[i + 1], fraction); // blend the two neighbours this.phase += this.increment; this.phase -= Math.floor(this.phase); } } The for loop in the constructor has a constant bound (2048), which the checker accepts. With 2048 entries and linear interpolation the error is below 0.00001, about −100 dB: inaudible. The cost per sample is a multiply, a floor and a lerp instead of a trigonometric call. For a single oscillator Math.sin is the simpler and better choice; use a table when you need many. Where to go from here Other waveforms are other functions of the same phase: 2 phase - 1 is a saw, abs(...) a triangle. They alias, so they need extra work: the advanced oscillator. A second phase at another rate gives unison and detune; a phase offset gives a stereo pair. A sync input , FM and several waveforms: the advanced oscillator.

title: Preventing pops and clicks
text: Preventing pops and clicks A knob arrives once per block of 32 samples (Rates and timing). If you multiply a signal by it directly, the gain changes in a step every time the knob moves. A step in a signal is a click, and a fast sweep of a knob sounds like a buzz ("zipper noise"). The fix is always the same: do not use the knob's value directly, glide to it. The problem compile @module({ name: "Gain Naive", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class GainNaive { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1 }) level: f32 = 1; constructor(sampleRate: f64) {} sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.level; } } Play a steady tone through it and drag the knob: every block the multiplier jumps, and you hear it. The fix: a smoother Smoother from bleep/dsp moves a value towards a target by a fixed fraction of the remaining distance each sample (a one-pole filter). You set the target once per block and read the smoothed value once per sample : compile import { Smoother } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Gain", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Gain { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: 0, max: 1, init: 1 }) level: f32 = 1; private g: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.g = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } // a 10 ms glide block(): void { this.g.target = this.level; } sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.g.next(); } } Three things to notice: The smoother is made in the constructor. Objects are allocated once; block() and sample() never allocate. The time is the time constant. After 10 ms the value is about 63 % of the way, after 50 ms about 99 %. 5 to 20 ms suits gains and mutes. Longer glides sound like a lag; shorter ones can still click on a big jump. The target is set in block() : it only changes once per block, so there is no reason to set it per sample. Gains in decibels Smooth the linear gain, not the dB value: the ear hears dB, but the multiplication is linear, and a glide in linear gain has no overshoot or sign problem near silence. compile import { Smoother, dbToLin } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Gain dB", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class GainDb { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Level", min: -60, max: 6, init: 0, unit: "dB", decimals: 1, minText: "-inf" }) level: f32 = 0; private g: Smoother; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.g = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.01); } block(): void { this.g.target = this.level <= -59.9 ? 0 : dbToLin(this.level); } // the bottom of the knob is silence sample(): void { this.out = this.x this.g.next(); } } Mutes, bypasses and switches A toggle is the worst click: it jumps from 1 to 0. Smooth it the same way, by giving the smoother a target of 0 or 1: @param({ name: "Mute" }) mute: bool = false; block(): void { this.g.target = this.mute ? 0 : 1; } The same goes for any switch that changes what you hear: a bypass, a solo, a filter type. Crossfade between the two signals with a smoothed 0 to 1 value (see the toolbox). Starting up and resetting A smoother starts at 0. If a module is created with a knob already at 1, the first few milliseconds fade in, which is usually what you want for a new module. After reset() (a transport jump, the engine clearing the module) you may want the value to jump , since there is no signal to protect. snap() does that: reset(): void { this.g.snap(); } Call snap() in block() on the first block, or in the constructor after setting target , when the module must be audible at once. Smoothing other things What changes What to do A gain, pan, send level A Smoother per value, as above A filter's cutoff or Q Smooth the frequency , not the coefficients, and recompute the coefficients each block (see below) A delay time Smooth it with a longer time constant (50 to 200 ms), or the pitch jumps. A fast change on purpose is a different effect A choice (wave shape, filter type) Crossfade the two outputs A control signal arriving as an input Already per sample. Smooth it only to round its corners A filter whose coefficients change in a block-sized step is a classic source of zipper noise on a cutoff sweep. Smooth the cutoff in Hz at block rate and update the filter from it once per block: compile import { Smoother, Biquad } from "./bleep/dsp"; @module({ name: "Low-pass", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class LowPass { @input({ name: "In", type: "audio" }) x: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Cutoff", min: 40, max: 16000, init: 1000, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 0 }) cutoff: f32 = 1000; @param({ name: "Q", min: 0.3, max: 10, init: 0.7, map: "exp" }) q: f32 = 0.7; private freq: Smoother; private filter: Biquad = new Biquad(); private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.freq = new Smoother(sampleRate, 0.02); this.freq.target = 1000; this.freq.snap(); // start at the knob's default, not at 0 Hz } block(): void { this.freq.target = this.cutoff; // the coefficients follow the smoothed frequency, once per block: a step of 0.67 ms in the filter is inaudible this.filter.setLowpass(this.sampleRate, this.freq.value, this.q); } sample(): void { this.freq.next(); // the glide itself runs per sample, so its time (20 ms) is exact this.out = this.filter.next(this.x); } } The glide runs per sample (cheap), and the expensive part, the trigonometry in setLowpass , runs once per block. That split, a smoothed value at audio rate and the costly derivation at block rate, is the usual shape of a module with a filter. Summary Never feed a knob straight into the signal path. Set a target in block() , read a smoothed value in sample() . Smooth the quantity the ear hears as a smooth thing (linear gain, frequency), and recompute derived values from it. Toggles and choices are knobs too. snap() when there is nothing to protect.

title: An 8-step, 4-lane step sequencer
text: An 8-step, 4-lane step sequencer This tutorial builds a step sequencer with four lanes of eight steps. Each lane has its own gate output, so one pattern can play a kick, a snare, a hat and an accent. It can run from the host tempo or from a clock input , and a reset input starts the pattern again. It uses most of what the other pages teach: rates, a @transport method, edge handlers, counted outputs and a widget layout. The design Inputs: Clock and Reset , both triggers. Outputs: four gates, one per lane. Knobs: Source (tempo or clock in), Division (how long a step is when following the tempo), Steps (the pattern length, 1 to 8), Pulses per step (how many clock pulses make one step), Gate length (a fraction of the step). Pattern: 32 toggles, eight per lane. Two questions drive the code: when does a new step begin , and when does its gate end . When a step begins Source A step begins when Tempo the position in beats, times the steps per beat, passes a whole number. The module counts the position itself, per sample, and takes the host's value ( ppq ) at the start of each block Clock in a rising edge arrives on Clock (and pulses of them have gone by) In both cases the module calls the same method, begin(n) , which opens the gates of the lanes that have step n switched on. When a gate ends A gate should be high for a fraction of the step , so the module needs to know how long a step lasts, in samples. Following the tempo, that is sampleRate 60 / (bpm stepsPerBeat) . Following a clock, it is measured : the time between two pulses, times the pulses per step. The gate closes when the time since the step began passes stepSamples gateLength . The module compile @module({ name: "Step Sequencer 4x8", category: "Sequencing/Script", description: "Eight steps, four lanes, one gate out per lane. Runs from the tempo or from a clock input.", layout: [ { row: [{ select: "source" }, { select: "division" }, { knob: "steps" }, { knob: "pulses" }, { knob: "gateLength" }] }, { title: "Lane 1", row: [{ repeat: 8, column: ["a{n}"] }] }, { title: "Lane 2", row: [{ repeat: 8, column: ["b{n}"] }] }, { title: "Lane 3", row: [{ repeat: 8, column: ["c{n}"] }] }, { title: "Lane 4", row: [{ repeat: 8, column: ["d{n}"] }] }, { meter: "position" }, ], }) export class StepSequencer { @input({ name: "Clock", type: "trigger" }) clock: f32 = 0; @input({ name: "Reset", type: "trigger" }) restart: f32 = 0; @output({ name: "Gate", type: "gate", count: 4 }) gate!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Source", choices: ["Tempo", "Clock in"] }) source: i32 = 0; @param({ name: "Division", choices: ["1/4", "1/8", "1/16", "1/32"] }) division: i32 = 2; @param({ name: "Steps", min: 1, max: 8, init: 8 }) steps: i32 = 8; @param({ name: "Pulses per step", min: 1, max: 24, init: 1 }) pulses: i32 = 1; @param({ name: "Gate length", min: 0.05, max: 1, init: 0.5, unit: "of a step", decimals: 2 }) gateLength: f32 = 0.5; @param({ name: "Step", count: 8, group: "Lane 1" }) a!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Step", count: 8, group: "Lane 2" }) b!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Step", count: 8, group: "Lane 3" }) c!: StaticArray ; @param({ name: "Step", count: 8, group: "Lane 4" }) d!: StaticArray ; @probe position: f32 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; private bpm: f64 = 120; private beat: f64 = 0; // the position in quarter notes, advanced per sample private playing: bool = false; private step: i32 = -1; // the step that is sounding; -1 before the first private pulse: i32 = 0; // clock pulses since the step began private stepSamples: f64 = 0; // how long a step lasts, to time the gates private sinceStep: f64 = 0; private sinceClock: f64 = 0; private open: bool = false; private fresh: bool = false; // a reset happened on this sample constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; this.stepSamples = sampleRate / 8.0; } @transport tempo(bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: bool): void { this.bpm = bpm; if (this.source == 0) { if (playing && !this.playing) this.step = -1; // the transport started: begin again if (playing) this.beat = ppq; // follow the host's position exactly once per block if (!playing) this.closeAll(); } this.playing = playing; } reset(): void { this.step = -1; this.pulse = 0; this.closeAll(); } private stepsPerBeat(): f64 { return this.division == 0 ? 1.0 : this.division == 1 ? 2.0 : this.division == 2 ? 4.0 : 8.0; } private closeAll(): void { for (let i = 0; i (n + 1) / this.steps; } @on("restart", { rising: 0.5 }) rewind(): void { this.pulse = 0; this.fresh = true; this.begin(0); } @on("clock", { rising: 0.5 }) tick(): void { if (this.source != 1) return; if (this.sinceClock this.pulses; // a step lasts as long as the clock says this.sinceClock = 0; if (this.fresh) return; // a reset on the same sample wins: the clock does not move on if (this.step >= 0 && this.pulse + 1 Math.floor(this.beat this.stepsPerBeat()) % this.steps; if (n != this.step) this.begin(n); this.beat += this.bpm / (60.0 this.sampleRate); // after the check: the first sample of a block is exactly at ppq } if (this.open && this.sinceStep >= this.stepSamples this.gateLength) this.closeAll(); } } How it works The layout. The layout in @module arranges the knobs at the top and one row of eight toggles per lane, with a meter showing the position. repeat: 8 makes one column per step, and "a{n}" becomes a1 to a8 , the ids of the first lane's toggles. See Custom UIs and widgets. Counted outputs and params. count: 4 on the gate gives gate1 to gate4 . Each lane is a field of eight toggles ( a , b , c , d ), count: 8 , in a group of its own. @transport tempo(bpm, ppq, playing) . The engine calls it once per block, before block() . The module stores the tempo, and, when it is following the tempo, takes the host's position. This is what makes it follow tempo changes and transport jumps : a loop that wraps, or a click on a different bar in the host, moves ppq , and the next block sets the sequencer to that position. When the transport starts ( playing goes from false to true) the step is cleared so the pattern begins at the right step, and when it stops, the gates close. sample() . In tempo mode it checks whether the step number has changed at the current position, then advances the position by bpm / (60 sampleRate) quarter notes. This costs a floor and a few multiplications per sample, and it gives the step change sample accuracy : not a block (about 0.67 ms) late. In both modes it closes the gate when the time is up. @on("clock", { rising: 0.5 }) tick() . On each pulse the module measures the time since the last one, so a tempo change on the clock is followed automatically, and advances a step every pulses pulses. The first pulse starts the pattern at step 1. @on("restart", { rising: 0.5 }) . A rising edge on Reset jumps to step 1 at that sample. If a clock pulse arrives on the very same sample, the reset wins (that is what the fresh flag is for): the pattern starts on step 1 instead of moving on to step 2. Try it Add a Code node, choose this module (copy the source above into the editor) and press Compile . Add a Clock or let the transport run, and put some toggles on. Cable Gate 1 into a drum module's gate input, Gate 2 into another one. Switch Source to Clock in , cable a clock into the Clock jack and set Pulses per step : with a clock that sends 24 pulses per quarter note, 6 pulses give 16th notes. A trigger on Reset every bar keeps a shorter pattern aligned: set Steps to 7 or 5 for a polyrhythm, and reset on the bar. Ideas to extend it Swing: delay every second step by a fraction of stepSamples before calling begin . Probability or ratchets: a per-step count that opens the gate several times inside a step. The pieces are there: a counter and stepSamples . Pitch lanes: replace the toggles with count: 8 knobs and send the value of the current step to a control output. More lanes: make the lane count a setting ( settings: [{ id: "LANES", ... }] ) so the user chooses it; the loops over the lanes use the constant. See Module scripts. Several patterns: a notes output whose events are pushed in begin instead of gates. See Events and routing.

title: "Tutorial: a synth voice"
text: Tutorial: a synth voice This tutorial builds the Synth voice example (in the Code node's example list, and as patch/script/src/synth-voice.dsp.ts ) one piece at a time. Each step is a complete module you can paste into the Code node and compile. You need the quickstart first. Everything used here is in the library. 1. An oscillator The simplest sound is a saw wave. A naive saw ( 2 phase - 1 ) aliases audibly above a few hundred Hz, so use sawBlep , which corrects the waveform at its jump: import { sawBlep } from "./bleep/osc"; @module({ name: "Saw", category: "Utility/Script" }) export class Saw { @output({ name: "Out", type: "audio" }) out: f32 = 0; @param({ name: "Pitch", min: 30, max: 2000, init: 110, map: "exp", unit: "Hz", decimals: 1 }) pitch: f32 = 110; private phase: f64 = 0; private sampleRate: f64; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.sampleRate = sampleRate; } sample(): void { const dt = this.pitch / this.sampleRate; // phase step of one sample this.phase += dt; if (this.phase >= 1.0) this.phase -= 1.0; this.out = sawBlep(this.phase, dt) 0.3; } } Two habits to notice: the phase is an f64 (an f32 phase loses precision within seconds), and dt is passed to sawBlep because the correction depends on how far the phase moves per sample. 2. Seven oscillators Supersaw is a stack of detuned band-limited saws. Create it in the constructor, set the detune in block() (it computes a pow per voice), and call next(frequency) per sample: import { Supersaw } from "./bleep/osc"; // in the class: private saw: Supersaw; constructor(sampleRate: f64) { this.saw = new Supersaw(sampleRate, 7, 20.0); } block(): void { this.saw.setDetune( this.detune); } sample(): void { this.out = this.saw.next( this.pitch) 0.6; } 3. A filter A ladder low-pass makes it warm. set computes an exp , so set the filter from block() : import { LadderFilter } from "./bleep/filters"; private filter: LadderFilter = new LadderFilter(); block(): void { this.filter.set(this.sampleRate, this.cutoff, this.resonance); } sample(): void { this.out = this.filter.next(this.saw.next( this.pitch)) 0.6; } 4. An envelope An Adsr turns a gate into a level. Give it its times in block() and feed it the gate every sample: import { Adsr } from "./bleep/env"; private env: Adsr; // new Adsr(sampleRate) in the constructor block(): void { this.env.set( this.attack, this.decay, this.sustain, this.release); } sample(): void { const e = this.env.next(this.gate); / ... e / } To make the filter follow the envelope, read the envelope's last value in block() and open the cutoff by up to five octaves ( fastExp2 is 2 to the power of its argument): const cutoff = this.cutoff fastExp2(this.envAmount 5.0 this.env.value); this.filter.set(this.sampleRate, cutoff, this.resonance); The filter then moves in steps of one chunk (32 samples, under a millisecond), which sounds smooth, and the exp runs once per chunk instead of once per sample. This is the usual way to put a slow modulation on a filter. 5. Notes A notes input delivers events to an @on handler (see Events and routing). The handler sets the pitch and the gate; midiToHz converts the note number. A Smoother on the pitch gives a short glide between notes: import { NoteEvent, NoteStream } from "./bleep/notes"; import { midiToHz } from "./bleep/util"; import { Smoother } from "./bleep/dsp"; @input({ name: "Notes", type: "notes" }) notes!: NoteStream; @on("notes") play(n: NoteEvent): void { if (n.isOn) { this.note = n.note; this.pitch.target = midiToHz( n.note); this.gate = 1.0; } else if (n.isOff && n.note == this.note) this.gate = 0.0; // only the last note can release it } 6. Chorus, and the whole thing Chorus thickens the sum. Its mix is set in block() , next(x) in sample() . Put together, sample() is four lines: sample(): void { const e = this.env.next(this.gate); const tone = this.saw.next( this.pitch.next()); const filtered = this.filter.next(tone); this.out = this.fx.next(filtered e 0.6); } The full source is the Synth voice example. Compile it, cable a keyboard or a sequencer into Notes , and turn the knobs. Where to go from here Swap Supersaw for FmOp (two operators make a bell), a Wavetable , or KarplusStrong for a plucked string. Put a Reverb or TapeDelay after the chorus; mix the effect with the dry signal yourself. Put an Oversampler2x around a softClip for a driven sound that does not alias. Drive a Clock and Lfo for a tempo-synced filter wobble.

title: Architecture overview
text: Architecture overview Beautiful Bleep is a modular board: oscillators, filters, sequencers and effects are modules , you connect them with cables, and the result runs as audio. The same board runs in three places: as plugins inside Ableton Live, as a standalone app, and in a web browser. This page explains how that works underneath: what a module is, how the engine runs it, where modules come from and how they are distributed, how a script becomes a module, and what differs between the three places. If you only want to use Bleep, the musicians' documentation is the place to start. If you want to connect your own plugin to other plugins, that is a different system, the Bleep Bus. This page is about the board itself. The big picture The Bleep plugins in Live, the Bleep App and Bleep Play each run a board UI, an engine and a module host. All three load the same standalone wasm module files. Bridges connect the plugins to the app by shared memory and the app to the browser by WebSocket. Every host is built from the same three layers: The board UI is the window you patch in: the cables, the module panels, the preset browser and the library view. It is written in HTML and JavaScript, and it is the same code in the plugins, in the app and in the browser. It edits a copy of the board document and sends the result to the engine. The engine owns the board. It sanitises the document, compiles it into a program (cells are flattened, cables are sorted into an order that respects what feeds what, and a cycle gets a 32-sample feedback delay), keeps the undo history and runs the program for every block of audio. The native hosts share one C++ engine. The browser has a JavaScript port of it that runs in an AudioWorklet and follows the same rules, so a board sounds the same everywhere. The module host loads module files and makes one instance per node on the board. The native hosts embed the Wasmtime WebAssembly runtime for this. The browser uses its own WebAssembly support. Under all of it are the modules : one standalone .wasm file for each module, with no per-platform code. This is the central design decision. A module is compiled once and the same file runs in a plugin on a Mac, in the app on Windows and in a browser tab. Because a WebAssembly module can only compute (it has no files, no clock and no network), it is also safe to run modules that other people wrote. The three hosts are connected by bridges : the plugins and the app share audio, MIDI and sync through shared memory, and the app talks to Bleep Play through a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1 . The bridges are described in Bleep plugins, the standalone app and Web. What a module is A module is a folder in patch/modules/ / with a module.json (name, category, colour, documentation), the DSP source, optionally a custom view in JavaScript, and its documentation. Building the folder produces one module.wasm that provides one or more node types . Most modules provide one; the drum modules provide several. The file follows the Module ABI, a small C interface that every module exports. The important parts: Standalone. One exported memory, no JavaScript glue and nothing shared with other modules. The only imports allowed are a few stubs, so a module that asks for anything else is refused. Described by the file itself. bleep spec json returns the node types as JSON: their jacks, knobs, ranges, meters and defaults. The board UI builds a module's panel from that description, so adding a module touches no shared file. Deterministic. There is no clock and no randomness from the host, so the same input and knob values give the same output on every host. Single-threaded instances. An instance is entered by one thread at a time. Knob changes, buttons and other messages are queued by the host and applied between chunks, and nothing on the audio thread waits. Modules are written in C++ (about a third of them use juce core for node data, and the build links that in for the browser), or in Bleep Script. The browser build compiles the C++ ones with Emscripten and adds a small shim that turns the module into the exported C interface. How the engine runs a module The engine splits a host block into 32-sample chunks. For every chunk it calls bleep process of each node in cable order, one module instance per node. When a node of a given type is first needed, the module host compiles the file once, and then creates one instance per node . The engine reads the pointers to the instance's parameter, input and output buffers once, because they stay fixed for the life of the instance. Audio runs in chunks of 32 samples , whatever the host block size is. A host block of 256 samples is eight chunks. For each chunk the engine goes through the nodes in the order the compiled program gives, writes each node's input buffers, knob values and the transport position, calls bleep process , and reads the output buffers. The next node then reads what the previous one wrote. Slow work, such as reading dials or computing filter coefficients, is done once per chunk; per-sample work is done inside bleep process . A module can allocate when it is created or prepared, but never while processing: the audio thread must not allocate, lock or do I/O. Where modules come from Modules reach the module host from the Bleep Library, from local files, or from a Code node compiled in the browser. All three pass the same checks before loading, then the host compiles a module when its node type is first used and runs one instance per node. The apps and plugins can be built without modules (that is the default when the Wasmtime host is built in): every module, first-party or not, is then installed from one place and goes through one set of rules. A build option, BLEEP BUNDLE MODULES , compiles the modules into the host instead, which skips everything below. There are three ways for a module to arrive. The Bleep Library The Bleep Library is the central place for plugins, modules and presets. Everything that installs, updates or loads one of them talks to the library and nothing else. A module is published as a .bleepmod package: a zip with module.json , module.wasm , optional custom views, and its documentation and screenshot. Published versions are immutable: a fix is a new version, and files are stored under their hash so a cache never goes stale. The library's index.json lists the packages; each carries what it needs ( requires.engineAbi , other modules). Nothing is signed; modules run in a sandbox. A module that someone shares through their account is checked by the library (its files, its imports and exports, its node types and its licence) before it is published, and every host checks the file list, the imports and the ABI version before it loads anything. See Publishing a module for the author's side. Modules reach people in three ways: On demand. The Library section of the app, or of the plugin window, installs and updates modules one by one. In the browser, the page fetches a module the first time a board contains one of its node types, and checks it before running it. In bundles. The first-run setup offers a default modules bundle (every first-party module, about 25 MB of wasm) and a default plugins bundle, so a new user does not install eighty modules by hand. An offline installer carries both. By hand , as described next. A plugin in Live never downloads anything by itself. A download inside an audio host would be risky, so the plugin uses the set of modules installed on the machine. A board that uses a module that is not installed shows a placeholder node until the module is installed from the Library section. Local files Modules can also be copied into a folder. Modules installed from the library live in /modules/registry/ / / , which the Library section manages. Your own modules go in /modules/local/ , as a .bleepmod , or as a .wasm with a .json (the module.json ) next to it. The folder is read at start and again when it changes. is ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep on macOS, %APPDATA%\Bleep on Windows and ~/.local/share/Bleep on Linux. Local files go through the same checks as a download. When several copies provide the same node type, the engine picks the highest compatible version, then the manual folder over the library. Bleep Script modules Bleep Script is a third way to get a module. A Code node on the board has an editor and a Compile button. A module script is an AssemblyScript class, with decorators such as @input , @output and @param that declare the jacks and knobs, and a sample() or block() method that does the DSP. The compiler turns it into a .wasm file that follows the same Module ABI as every other module, so the engine cannot tell the difference. Where this runs today: In Bleep Play the compiler runs in the browser, in a Worker, and everything is compiled on your own machine. There is nothing to install. In the app and the plugins the engine can already run Code nodes and keeps their cables and knob values, but the compiler is not shipped with those builds yet. A patch saved in Bleep Play with Code nodes in it therefore plays there, but you cannot edit the script. The node's source is saved with the patch as text and the compiled module travels with the node. The engine registers a node type for that node alone (named from the node and a hash of its source), and it applies the same checks as for an installed module: it must be a conforming module with exactly one node type and may import nothing the ABI does not allow. Its own limits for memory and time per call still apply. The first-party script modules in patch/modules/ (they have "language": "bleep-script" in their module.json ) are built and packaged like the C++ ones, so for a user they are ordinary library modules. A patch script is different: it does not process audio, it runs once and describes which modules and cables to create. See Patch scripts. The three hosts Bleep plugins in Live Bleep App Bleep Play What it is VST3 plugins in Ableton Live A standalone program The board in a browser tab, served at /play/ Engine C++. The first Bleep plugin loaded creates one engine per Live set; the others find it and use it through IEngine C++, the same engine code JavaScript port, running in an AudioWorklet Module host Wasmtime Wasmtime WebAssembly in the AudioWorklet Who owns the audio Live. Ports (MIDI In/Out, Audio In/Out, Instrument, FX) connect a track to the board The app's own audio device, and System audio from the computer; while a Live bridge is connected, Live's blocks drive the app The browser's AudioContext MIDI Live's tracks, through the ports The app's own MIDI ports ( Bleep App 1…n ) Web MIDI and the computer keyboard Modules arrive from The set installed on the machine by the app or the plugin window; never downloaded inside Live The Library section, local files, bundles Fetched from the site's library on first use, checked in the browser Code nodes Run; compiler not shipped yet Run; compiler not shipped yet Compile and run Sync Live's transport Ableton Link, and Live's transport while bridged The app's tempo and beat, when connected Latency between ports With Bleep Board in the set, its own track has no latency and each crossing to or from another track takes exactly one block, whatever order Live runs the tracks in (input port to output port: two) Not applicable Not applicable A few differences deserve more explanation. One engine per Live set. Each Bleep plugin is its own compiled file, yet a set has only one board. The first plugin loaded creates the engine and publishes it in the process, and it pins itself so it is never unloaded. The other plugins call it through IEngine . Two builds can share an engine only when their major ABI versions match; a different minor version is fine. See the Engine ABI. For each host block the first plugin to run claims the block and runs the compiled board, and plugins exchange their audio with the engine through small tagged rings. The app is the hub. Browsers cannot open shared memory or talk to a plugin, and a plugin that hosted a socket server would make every Live set run a server. So the app, which runs once per machine anyway, is the hub: Live reaches the app through shared memory that is locked to the sample clock, and Bleep Play reaches the app through a WebSocket on localhost, where audio is buffered with a jitter buffer instead. A plugin whose Board menu says Bleep Play goes through the app as well. Both bridges work on one computer only, and the web connection is off until you turn it on in Settings → Web . See doc/specs/bridges.md in the repository for the protocols. The browser has no plugin and no installation. Bleep Play needs no server for audio: it is static files plus the library the page installs its modules from. The price is that some things are not ported yet: Voice Cells, the Harmony bus, Link, Macros, audio input, host MIDI out and the media folder. Not the Bleep Bus The Bleep Bus is a different thing with a similar name. It lets any plugins, with or without Bleep, exchange per-sample control signals through shared memory, and it does not know about the board, the engine or any module. The cables on the board stay inside one engine. The two systems share only an idea, signals between things, and are described in separate places: the Bus in its architecture overview, and the board and modules here. Where to read next I want to… Read Write a module in C++ Writing a module, Module ABI Write a module as a script Bleep Script, Module scripts Publish a module Publishing, Library Change how plugins share an engine Engine ABI, Bleep plugins Change the app or the browser version Standalone app, Web

title: Engine ABI
text: The engine ABI: how Bleep plugins share one engine Every Bleep plugin is its own compiled file, but a set has one engine ( specs.md §5.3). The first plugin loaded creates it and publishes it in the process; the others find it and call it through IEngine ( patch/engine/EngineApi.h ). ABI (application binary interface) is the contract about how two compiled pieces talk: the order of the methods in the interface (a plugin calls "the 14th method", not a name), the layout of the data they pass in memory ( BlockIO , PortFrame , NoteEvent ) and the types used (plain integers, pointers and char arrays: no std::string or JUCE class crosses a binary). If both sides agree, any two builds can share an engine. If not, the result is wrong sound or a crash. Versions Changes when Builds that differ Major ( kAbiTag , bleep-engine-abi-N , plus the sizes of BlockIO , MidiEvent , Transport and a pointer) A method is inserted or removed, a shared struct changes, a type changes Refuse to share. The plugin shows "Another version of Bleep Board is loaded." Minor ( kAbiMinor , IEngine::abiMinor() ) A method is added at the end of IEngine Share. Old plugin on a new engine: fine. New plugin on an old engine: it asks engine.supports(minor) before it calls the new method, and does without it. The minor is the first method of IEngine and never moves, so a plugin can always read it. A minor starts at 0 with every major. Minors so far (of bleep-engine-abi-8 ): 1 setBridged(handle, bool) : a plugin whose Board is the app or Bleep Play (doc/specs/bridges.md) tells the engine that its node is a ghost on this set's board. A plugin checks supports(1) before calling it; without it the node stays live and receives nothing. 3 liveParams(float values32) : the values of the board's Live Params nodes (0..1 per row, 32 rows, plus the mask of the rows a node drives), which Bleep Board sends to the Bleep Live Link devices in Live. A plugin checks supports(3) before calling it; without it nothing is sent. 4 setLiveRowInfo(channel, row, json) : a Bleep Live Link device says what one of its rows is mapped to (name, continuous or discrete, range, choices), and the engine keeps it for the Live Params node's view and moves the node's row knob to the parameter's position. A plugin checks supports(4) before calling it; without it the board shows nothing about the rows. Rules for changing IEngine Add a method: put it below the destructor, after a public: , with [minor N] in its comment; raise kAbiMinor to N ; guard every call in the plugins with supports(N) ; add it to MismatchEngine . Anything else (insert, remove, reorder, change a signature, change a shared struct): raise the major ( kAbiTag ). Reset kAbiMinor to 0 and drop the guards of the old major. A change in what an existing method does (not its shape) is not an ABI change, but if a plugin relies on the new behaviour it needs a minor that says so. Where the engine lives The engine's code is in the first Bleep plugin loaded in the process; it pins itself so it stays until Live quits. So the engine is as old as that plugin: with a mix of builds, the oldest plugin loaded first decides what the engine can do, which is why plugins check supports rather than assume. After updating plugins, restart Live. Two contracts, two numbers A plugin talks to the engine through IEngine; the engine talks to a module through the module ABI. A plugin never talks to a module directly. A plugin never talks to a module. It talks to the engine, and the engine runs the modules. So there are two contracts, each with its own version: Contract Between Form Version Engine ABI (this document) Bleep plugins and the one engine in the process C++ virtual interface, in-process kAbiTag (major) and kAbiMinor Module ABI ( module-abi.md ) The engine and a .bleepmod (WebAssembly) C functions exported by the .wasm file engineAbi , one integer in the module's requires First-party modules compiled into the plugins are not a cross-binary case: the engine creates them from the registry of its own binary, so the engine and the module are always the same build. Library modules (wasm) are where the module ABI matters: the engine checks requires.engineAbi against the range it supports, and refuses a module outside it with a message that says which. The module host that does this is part of the engine, so it is as new as the plugin that created the engine. The two numbers move independently. A new IEngine method (engine minor) says nothing about modules; a changed module export (module ABI) does not touch the plugins' interface. The module ABI could take the same major and minor scheme (compatible additions keep the number, today they are listed as "stay version 1"); that is for module-abi.md to decide, not this document. Not the Bleep Bus The Bleep Bus is a protocol between external plugins (Grit, Cinch …) and the board, with its own version. The engine ABI is the contract among the Bleep plugins themselves; the two are numbered separately.

title: Development
text: Development These pages are for working on Beautiful Bleep itself and the things that run on its board. To connect your own plugin to others, use Bleep Bus. To write code that runs on the board, see Bleep Script. To install tools and build, see Developer setup. I want to… Read See how board, engine, modules and hosts fit together Architecture overview Add a sound, effect or utility to the board Modules, Writing a module Publish a module in the library Publishing, Library Know what a .wasm module must export Module ABI Change the Bleep plugins in Live Plugins, Bleep plugins Change the standalone app Standalone app Change Bleep Play, the board in the browser Web Know what the plugins and the engine promise each other Engine ABI One engine, four hosts The same engine and board run in every host. A module is one .wasm file that all of them load, so modules need no per-platform code. The plugins share one engine per Live set, the app runs it without a DAW, and Bleep Play runs it in the browser. The sidebar of this section has one group per host, plus modules and the engine ABI.

title: Bleep Library
text: Bleep Library and release system Plugins, modules and presets are managed in one place, the Bleep Library . Everything that installs, updates or loads one of them (the standalone app, Bleep Play, the release pipeline) talks to the library and nothing else. Kind What it is Who loads it Form Plugin Something you load in Ableton: Bleep Board, the ports, later Bus receivers Live, the app's Library section installs it Installer per platform and format (VST3, AU, CLAP) Module A node type on the board: its DSP, view and docs The engine in the plugins, the app and the browser .bleepmod package Preset A patch (a whole board) or a cell (a subgraph, with its panel) The board .bleeppreset file (JSON) Naming: the library was first called the registry, and its technical names keep that word: the URL path /registry/v1/ , BLEEP REGISTRY URL , /api/registry , the bleep-registry bucket. In prose it is the Bleep Library, "the library" after the first mention. Plugins and modules are code , immutable once published. Plugins and first-party modules are released by a developer with a release token; a module anyone shares through their account is checked by the library on upload (a community module). Presets are data : published by anyone with an account. Nothing in the library is signed: what protects the user is the sandbox the modules run in and the checks the library makes on upload. What a module is to the engine is in module-abi.md . Decisions Modules are WebAssembly everywhere (web and native), hosted by an embedded wasm runtime in the engine. See 4.2. The library is part of the website stack (Caddy, the FastAPI website/api and its Postgres), hosted locally for now and moved with the stack later. No separate infrastructure. Modules are sandboxed, and nothing is signed. A module is WebAssembly that can only do what the host's imports allow, so the sandbox is the defence, not knowing the author. A release is authorised by the API token that uploads it (bound to a publisher, the namespace of its ids); a community module by the account that uploads it, after the library has checked the package (files, the .wasm 's imports and exports, node types, licence). Closed-source community modules are allowed. The apps load every module that passes the same checks on their side (file list, imports, ABI version), with no setting to switch. A community module's id is / . Modules and plugins reach the user three ways: from the library on demand, through two bundles the setup offers ( default modules , default plugins ), or by copying files into a folder (section 5a). Everything is free. There is no licence-key or entitlement logic anywhere. Downloading needs no login : browsing, installing plugins, modules and presets, and update checks are anonymous. Sharing a preset needs an account (the existing website/api accounts). 1. Where this stands today Modules are folders in patch/modules/ / with a module.json ; native builds compile them into the plugins through BLEEP REGISTER MODULE (static). The browser build already produces one standalone .wasm per module and a manifest.json ( patch/web/build modules.py ), loaded on demand. But website/Dockerfile runs it (emscripten, a JUCE clone) on every site build. Presets are presets/ .bleepboard plus patch/board/ui/factory-presets.json , built into the UI. The wasm-per-module work is the seed of the system: the module package is that file plus its metadata. 2. Common to every artifact Every entry in the library has the same envelope: { "kind": "module", // plugin module preset "id": "dual-filter", // slug; presets: " / " "version": "1.2.0", // semver, immutable once published "channel": "stable", // stable beta "title": "Dual Filter", "author": "brilliant-bleep", "license": "MIT", "requires": { "engineAbi": 3, "bus": ">=0.1", "modules": { "lfo": ">=1.0" } }, "files": [ { "path": "dual-filter.bleepmod", "sha256": "…", "bytes": 48213, "platform": "any" } ], "published": "2026-10-09T10:00:00Z" } Immutable and content-addressed. A published id@version never changes; a fix is a new version. Files are named by sha256 in storage, so caches never go stale. engineAbi is an integer bumped when the module ABI (specified in module-abi.md ; the C interface in patch/web/src/WebShim.cpp ) changes incompatibly. Hosts refuse modules they cannot run and the Library section explains why. Download check. Every file of an entry has a sha256 , the checksum of the download; hosts compare it after fetching. There are no signatures, certificates or revocation list: taking a release down removes it from index.json . 3. The library It lives in the website stack. Published files are objects in a SeaweedFS bucket ( storage service, data on the registry-data volume; S3 API, so moving to AWS S3, R2 or similar later is a change of endpoint; MinIO was considered but no longer publishes images). The bucket is public-read and Caddy proxies /registry/ to it, so downloads are cacheable and run no app code; the API owns what is dynamic. S3 bucket bleep-registry (SeaweedFS) → Caddy proxies it read-only at /registry/v1/… /registry/v1/ ├── index.json plugins and modules per channel ├── plugins/ / / installers + entry.json ├── modules/ / / .bleepmod + entry.json (+ doc, screenshot) └── presets/ / / .bleeppreset /api/… (FastAPI + Postgres, existing accounts and sessions) ├── GET /api/presets?q=&type=&tag=&sort= search (anonymous) ├── GET /api/presets/ / metadata, versions, download counts (anonymous) ├── GET /api/presets/ / /used-in listed presets that name this one in their credits (anonymous) ├── POST /api/presets publish a version (login) ├── DELETE/PATCH /api/presets/ own presets (login); admin may unlist any ├── POST /api/presets/ /report report (anonymous or login) ├── GET/POST/DELETE /api/tokens personal access tokens of the user (cookie login) ├── POST /api/auth/device app starts a sign-in: device code (secret), user code, interval ├── POST /api/auth/device/token app polls; the personal token comes once, when approved ├── GET /api/auth/device/ , POST /api/auth/device/approve the site's /device/ page (cookie login) ├── GET /api/presets/ / /file the .bleeppreset (anonymous, counts the download) ├── GET/POST /api/social/ / /comments list (public), comment (login); slug of a preset is author/slug ├── GET/PUT/DELETE /api/social/ / /rating average and count (public); 1-5 stars, one per user (login) ├── DELETE /api/social/comments/ the author or an admin; POST …/ /report reports it └── GET /api/admin/reports, POST …/ /resolve reports of presets and comments (admin) Who may do what. Reading (browsing, downloading, comments, ratings) is anonymous. Sharing, commenting and rating need a login: the website's session cookie, or Authorization: Bearer blu … , the personal token of the app. Such a token works only on these library endpoints, never on the account, profile or admin endpoints. A cookie-authenticated write whose Origin is another site is refused ( BLEEP ALLOWED ORIGINS lists extra hosts for a dev server). Comments and ratings belong to the entry (plugin, module or preset), not to one version; nobody rates their own preset; a comment is up to 2000 characters, at most 5 a minute per user. Part Where Written by Plugins and modules (files, index.json ) S3 bucket Only the release pipeline: scripts/release/release.py uploads over the S3 API (port 8333, bound to localhost; credentials S3 ACCESS KEY / S3 SECRET KEY in website/.env ) Preset files Same bucket under presets/ The API after validation Preset metadata (title, tags, author, versions, downloads, reports, state) Postgres, new Alembic migration The API What a tile shows. Every plugin, module and preset has a title, a summary (up to 280 characters), a category and an optional screenshot, as metadata of its release: entry.json carries summary , category and image (the file name next to it, image.png , .jpg or .webp ). release.py takes them from the module package (its module.json and doc/ .png ) and, for plugins, from PLUGIN TILES and doc/library/ .png , and uploads the image with PUT /api/registry/ / /releases/ /image (PNG, JPEG or WebP up to 1 MB; display data, replaceable by the token that made the release). Without a screenshot the library draws a placeholder in the colour of the kind. GET /api/library returns them with image url and the categories of the matching entries, and filters by category . GET /registry/v1/index.json is the one call a client needs at start. It lists, per id, the newest version per channel, so an update check is one small request with an ETag . The API only ever sees preset search and publishing, so a stopped API doesn't stop installs of plugins and modules. Login in the app. The app has no browser cookie. Sign in opens the website's login page for a one-time device code (like gh auth login ): the app shows a code, the user types it on the site (the page never takes the code from the address, so a link someone sends cannot fill it in) and sees the name the app gave itself, which is not verified, and the address and program that started the sign-in before choosing Refuse or Allow , and the app stores a personal access token in the OS keychain. The token only allows publishing and managing the user's own presets. Not signed in, the app works fully except Share… . How it is built. patch/library/Account.{h,cpp} does the device flow and the authenticated calls on a worker thread; the page reaches it through the native function account ( patch/board/ui/account.js , used by the Library section's Account tab, Share… on the Presets tab and in the patch browser). The token is kept per library address: macOS Keychain (service Bleep Library ), Windows Credential Manager, elsewhere a file in the data folder readable by the user only ( account.json ); with BLEEP DATA DIR set (tests, development) always that file, so a test never touches the real login. The app and the plugins share it, so one sign-in covers both; macOS asks once when a DAW first reads an item the app created ( Always Allow ). The page can only call /api/… of the configured library. A token the site revoked (account page) is dropped at the next check, and Sign out revokes it at the library ( DELETE /api/tokens/self ; GET /api/tokens/self says whose it is). Bleep Play has no token: it is a page of the site and uses the session cookie, so it only asks /api/auth/me and sends people to /login/ . scripts/check/account-live.py runs the real HTTP stack against a local API. Moving later. Everything is addressed by one base URL ( registry in the app's settings and the site's config), so moving the stack into the Brilliant Bleep Compose stack or behind a CDN changes configuration, not code. 4. Modules 4.1 Package A .bleepmod is a zip: module.json existing fields (name, slug, tagline, colour, category, doc) + version, requires, types[] module.wasm the DSP, standalone, C ABI (no JUCE, no JS glue) ui/ .js the module's custom view (optional) doc/ .md, .png user documentation and screenshot summary (one or two sentences, from the module's tagline , else its first node type's description) and category ("Sources", "Modulation", …, from the module's node types) are filled in by the package step. The library shows them, with the screenshot, on the module's tile. types[] replaces the generated manifest.json "types → module" map: one package can provide several node types (the drum modules do). The source layout in patch/modules/ / does not change; a package step ( scripts/package-module.py , built on build modules.py ) turns a folder into a package. Adding a module still touches no shared file. 4.2 Native modules: wasm everywhere (decided) Modules are statically linked into the plugins today. For the app to install, update and uninstall modules, the plugins need to load them at run time. Options: Native shared library per OS/arch WebAssembly everywhere Keep static, ship everything with the plugin One artifact for web, macOS, Windows, Linux no (6 builds each, code signing and notarisation per file) yes n/a Speed best AOT-compiled wasm: close to native; interpreted: too slow best Sandbox: safe to run modules from other people no yes (no syscalls, own memory) n/a Updating a module without updating the plugin yes yes no Decision: wasm everywhere. The engine gets a WasmModuleHost (embedded WAMR or wasmtime, AOT-compiled at install time and cached per machine) that implements the same Module interface the static modules do. The apps and plugins ship without modules (decided): every module, first-party or not, is installed from the library, so there is one path and one set of rules. Offline, the installer carries the default module bundle. The native sources stay in the repository: the tests run them as the reference the wasm builds are compared with, and a module that turns out too heavy as wasm may later get a native package for its platform. Gate, first answer (Verb, Apple M-series, Live 12; patch/wasm-host/ ). Wasmtime (Cranelift JIT) costs about 1.2× the native module in a standalone benchmark and 1.5 to 1.7× through the plugin, copies around each 32-sample chunk included (3.2 % of a core against 1.9 %), and loads in 44 ms; the output matches the native build to about 1e-6. The wasm3 interpreter costs ten times Wasmtime (32.5 % of a core), so it is only a fallback for very light modules. Both run in Live, which allows the executable memory Wasmtime needs. Consequences: Wasmtime is the runtime ; wasm3 stays an option for trusted, cheap modules; a host without executable memory runs only what wasm3 can carry (cheap modules; the rest show as unavailable: open , section 12) (a plugin cannot "try and fall back": Wasmtime is killed, not refused, so the runtime is chosen from the host's entitlements or a setting before any code is compiled). Still to run: the heaviest modules (Grains, Delay Network, Modal Voice). If one costs more than about 2× native, it stays static-only and is also offered as a native package (the platform field in files already allows per-platform files). Not yet tested: other DAWs, Windows, Linux. 4.3 Resolution on the board A board file lists the node types it uses. On load, a host resolves each type: bundled → installed → library (browser: fetch; app: offer to install; plugin in Live: use the installed set and show a placeholder node for a missing type, never download inside an audio host). 5. Plugins Plugins are installed from the Library section of the app, not hot-loaded: Artifacts: an installer per OS ( .pkg , .msi , .zip for Linux) containing all formats of one plugin, or the whole bundle. Install paths are the system's ( /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 , …). Live must not be running while a loaded plugin is replaced (the README warns of crashes); the app checks for Live and asks the user to quit it first. The library entry says which formats and OS versions each file supports. Third-party Bus receiver plugins can be listed with a download link (not hosted by us) so the Library section is one place for everything that works with the Bus. A plugin states the module engineAbi range it can host, so the app can warn when a module needs a newer plugin. 5a. Bundles, first run, and manual installs Bundles. A bundle is an entry of kind: "bundle" : no files, a list of members with their versions. Two exist, both published by bleep : Bundle Members Why default-modules Every first-party module (80 today, about 25 MB of wasm) What the board offers out of the box, one tick instead of 80 installs default-plugins Every Bleep VST3: Bleep Board, the port plugins (MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In, Audio Out), Bleep Instrument and Audio Insert The plugins Live needs; they must all be the same version, because they share one engine Installing a bundle installs its members, each on its own. A bundle update is a new bundle version; the Library section shows "Update all" and installs only the members that changed. First run. When the app is installed (the installer's last page, or the first launch for a download without an installer), a setup assistant asks, with sizes and both pre-ticked: Download the default module bundle (the modules from the library, into the library folder below). Install the default plugin bundle (all VST3 bridges into the system plugin folder). If Live is running it asks to quit it first, as in section 5. Declining either is fine: the app works, a missing module is a placeholder node with an Install button, and the Library section keeps a "Default modules are not installed" banner until it is done. Offline: an offline installer carries both bundles. The apps ship without modules (4.2), so until the module bundle is installed a board shows placeholder nodes. A plugin in Live never downloads anything on its own: modules are installed from the Library section of the app or of the plugin window, on a non-audio thread. Manual installs. Everything can also be copied by hand: What Folder Notes Modules from the library /modules/registry/ / / Written by the Library section; do not edit Modules by hand /modules/local/ A .bleepmod , or .wasm with a .json (the module.json ) beside it. Read at start and when the folder changes. Plugins The system VST3 folders Copied by hand as usual; the Library section lists them with their status is ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep (macOS), %APPDATA%\Bleep (Windows), ~/.local/share/Bleep (Linux); the settings can point at another folder. Every file in these folders goes through the same check as a download (file list, imports, ABI version); there is no setting to allow anything. When several copies provide the same node type, the choice is: highest compatible version, then the manual folder over the library. Build options and the library configuration. config/library.json is the one place that says where the library is ( libraryUrl , the website's address; the library lives under /registry/v1/ ).
