The apps' and plugins' build bakes it in ( BLEEP LIBRARY CONFIG names another file, BLEEP LIBRARY URL overrides it for one build) and scripts/release/release.py uses libraryUrl when no --registry or $BLEEP REGISTRY URL is given; the user can still change the address in settings.json . With -DBLEEP WASMTIME DIR= the apps and plugins are built without modules ( BLEEP BUNDLE MODULES=ON puts them back). BLEEP DATA DIR moves the data folder (tests, development). The first-run assistant answers once ( firstRunDone in settings.json ). The plugin download: the app reads the plugin entries of the index, takes the build for its platform ( macos-arm64 , ...), checks the sha256 and unpacks the .vst3 bundles into the user's VST3 folder, with Live closed; an offline installer's Plugins folder (macOS: Contents/Resources/Plugins in the app) is copied instead. The pretend Library for working on the UI is the board dev server with ?library in the address. 6. Presets Two kinds, one file format ( .bleeppreset , JSON, same schema as board persistence plus the envelope in section 2): preset.type Contains Loaded as patch A whole board: nodes, cables, panels, settings. In the apps it is a project shared in the Library Opens as a project, or merges into the current board cell One cell: its inner graph, jack names, its panel Dropped onto the board as a cell Dependencies. A preset, cell or patch, may carry needs : the modules it requires, by module slug, each with an optional inclusive min and max version: "needs": { "lfo": { "min": "1.2.0" }, "reverb": { "min": "2.0.0", "max": "2.9.9" } } Saving a preset from the board writes needs for every module its node types come from, with min set to the version installed at that moment; an author adds max by hand. Before a preset or project is loaded or placed (the project browser, Add → Cell ), the board checks needs and, without a version, every module that provides one of its node types. If something is missing or too old, a dialog lists it and offers Download n from the Bleep Library , then loads; Load anyway keeps placeholder nodes, Cancel loads nothing. Versions the library cannot supply are listed with the reason and cannot be fixed by the dialog: a max below the installed version (the library's index offers only the newest version of a module; older ones are fetched by number, see Versions on the board below), a local copy of a module, or a module the library does not have can only be loaded anyway. Factory presets carry no needs (the default module bundle covers them). The check runs in the app and in plugin windows (installing happens off the audio thread); Bleep Play installs the types a board uses by itself (section 8). Placing a preset works offline and without a library. An app built without the module library (modules compiled in; the native side's init has no library ) does not check at all. With a library, the check looks only at the modules installed here and at the library index if it is already loaded: it never waits for the network, and if the local status does not answer within 5 seconds the preset is placed anyway, with a notice. The index is cached on disk ( /cache/index.json , with the library address, the channel and the time it was fetched): every successful fetch saves it, the first look at the library reads it, and when the library cannot be reached the saved copy is used and the Library section says so. A copy saved for another address or channel is ignored. Versions on the board. A node does not state its module's version, but a copy of it can say which version it was made with, and a node can be pinned to one. What says which version. needs. .version is the version the nodes were made with: written by Save as preset , Save to Library , Share… and by ⌘C (the clipboard carries needs too, from the app's library or from the web board's loaded modules). A node may carry version ( "version": "0.1.2" ): it is pinned , and runs exactly that version of its module, next to the newest. A node without version runs the newest installed. The question. When a preset, project or paste comes with a version that is not the one installed (newer or older, also when the modules are all there), the dialog asks: Use the latest versions (the nodes are not pinned; the settings may sound or look different if the module changed) or Use the versions it was made with (the nodes get version ; each missing version is fetched from the library by number). A module whose version matches asks nothing. The app compares versions in board/ui/library.js ( ensureNeeds ); the same question runs when a project is opened and its pinned nodes are missing or its modules differ. In the engine. Registry::find(type, version) finds a version; the newest of a type is what find(type) returns, older ones are registered with addOlder and listed by describeTypes as {type, version, older: true} (the board page keys them type@version ). A pinned node whose version is not installed is a placeholder with everything it was saved with, and an Install button for that version. An older version has no custom view: it gets the plain knob view, because the view script that is loaded belongs to the newest version. On this machine. The library keeps every version it published ( modules/ / /entry.json , section 3); its index lists only the newest. Client::installVersion(slug, version) fetches one by number, checks it like any install and puts it next to the newest ( /modules/registry/ / / ). Old versions are not kept for their own sake: installing a newer version removes the older ones (the board asks again when a pinned node needs one). The native function libraryInstallVersion(slug, version) starts it; libraryStatus lists these as versions and says pinning: true . Bleep Play has no dialog: it runs the version a project, cell or paste names (the nodes are pinned on the way in, BoardEdit.pinToMade ) and loads that module by number ( BleepLibrary.fetchModule(slug, version) ), so a project opens the way it was made. Publishing: from the board, Share… (needs an account; browsing and downloading never do), a title, tags, optional audio preview. Every preset is CC BY 4.0 : there is no licence choice and no remix switch (a preset shared as CC0 before this keeps that licence, also in its new versions). The API validates the schema, checks all referenced types exist in the library, enforces a size limit and per-user rate limit, and rejects anything that is not pure data. Presets are copied, never referenced. A downloaded or placed preset is a full copy; a preset built from another holds its own copy of it, so an author editing or deleting the original breaks nothing, and nothing asks to update. A copy keeps a list of credits (the presets it was made from, see doc/specs/preset-system-plan.md ); the user can edit it. On publish the API cleans the list (at most 50 {name, author, address?, license} ; address is author/slug and only a key to find the preset again, never fetched) and indexes the entries that have an address, so the source's author sees Used in N presets (only listed ones; the rows of the newest version, replaced on each publish; a deleted or unlisted preset drops out). Deleting a preset ( DELETE /api/presets/ ) removes it from the library only. Audio in presets. A node stores only a media id ( .wav , engine/Media.h ); the WAV lives in the computer's media folder. A preset takes the audio its modules use along, as an optional media map { " .wav": { name, data: } } next to nodes : Save as preset , Save to Library and Share… attach the files their nodes use (every string in a node's data that is a media id), and loading or placing a preset imports the files it does not have yet (importing a file again stores it once, as the id is the hash of the audio). The audio is inline, not a shared store: ids are a 64-bit FNV hash, not collision-resistant, so a store shared by all authors would let one file stand in for another. A shared preset may carry up to 8 files and 5 MB of audio together, WAV only; the API checks the header, answers 422 or 413, and the 512 KB limit is for the patch alone ( POST /api/presets bodies may be 8 MiB). A file that cannot be read when saving, or imported when loading, is left out and the node shows as missing, as for any board whose media folder lacks a file. Not yet: Bleep Play (no media folder in the browser), and the Instrument and FX plugins' cell presets, which are loaded natively. Credits for samples are not part of this; the licence of a preset, CC BY 4.0, covers its audio, and the terms say that publishers must have the right to share it. Versions: re-publishing creates a new version, kept as the author's history; the newest is the one served by default and older ones stay downloadable by number. An installed copy is not tied to it. Moderation: report button, takedown by an admin (the existing admin role) sets the preset's state to unlisted; the file stays but is no longer served in search. The factory presets move out of factory-presets.json into the library's bleep author, so the app, the website and the plugins all show the same library. A small set stays bundled for offline. My projects on the website. The board in the browser has no folder to keep a user's own projects in, so they live in the account: GET /api/projects (the user's list: id, name, description, tags), GET /api/projects/{id} (the project, the same JSON as a Library preset ), POST /api/projects ( {name, preset} , a project of that name is replaced) and DELETE /api/projects/{id} . They are private to the account (a login by cookie or token), limited to 200 per user and 2 MB each; publishing one for others is Share… (a patch preset). The apps keep them as .bleepboard files in /Projects/ . 7. Release process Single source: the repository. CI builds and publishes; nobody uploads by hand. Version. Every plugin and module has its own version, counted by the library: scripts/release/release.py --level x 1.x 1.1.x major minor patch takes the newest published version and counts up at that level (built for plugins; see doc/release.md ). A module's module.json carries the version once modules are released. Detect what changed. Hash the module's folder plus the patch/common/dsp/ headers it includes (and engine/ ABI). If the hash differs from the last release, the module needs a new version, and CI fails if its version was not bumped. Build and test (existing CI): the DSP tests, the module harness, the wasm build, then the harness against the wasm. Plugins: the macOS/Windows/Linux matrix and notarisation. Package ( scripts/package-module.py , scripts/package-plugin.sh ): produce the artifacts and the entry.json files. Stage. Upload to …/staging/ / . A smoke job loads every staged module in the node host test and in a headless browser. Publish. Copy staged files into the immutable paths, then write index.json last, in one atomic replace. A release is visible only when the index changes; rollback is putting the previous index back. Channels. beta index first for testers; promoting to stable is a new index, not a rebuild. scripts/release/release.py is built for plugins (steps 4 to 6 in a simpler form: a draft release, size- and hash-checked uploads, publish, index regenerated). It authenticates with an admin-created release token ( python -m app.cli token-create ), not with the storage credentials, so the machine that releases never holds S3 keys. Built since: adding the build of another platform to a published release ( --add-platform ), and publishers : the library binds a token to a publisher (the namespace of its ids) and records who uploaded. Not built yet: change detection, staging. 8. Website Docker no longer builds wasm. The web stage of website/Dockerfile is removed. The site image contains only the Next.js static export and the board UI. Modules load from the registry. bleep-web.js fetches index.json (cached) and then modules/ / / .bleepmod on demand, from the CDN, exactly as it loads .wasm today. Pinned for reproducibility. The site build commits a web-lock.json (module id → version → sha256) so a given site release always runs the module set it was tested with; updating it is a normal commit ( scripts/release/release.py --update-web-lock ). A newer module reaches the website when the lock is bumped, never silently. The board UI and patch/web/js/ (graph runner, worklet) are versioned with the site and declare the engineAbi they implement. The site's module catalog and docs pages read the library entries at build time instead of patch/modules/ /module.json from the repo, with the repo as a fallback in development. Preset browser on the site: read-only listing from presets/index.json , Open in Bleep Play and Open in the app ( bleep://preset/ / ). 9. The two sections: Library and Board The board is always on screen. The Library, Settings and Help topics open as dialogs over it, from the File and Help menus of the top bar (the File menu offers Open Library… and Upload Project to Library… ): Section For What is in it Board Creating patches The board (nodes, cables, cells, panels, module views, undo), loading and saving projects and presets, the transport. What the app and the plugin show today Library Managing what is on this machine Modules , Plugins and Presets tabs: installed, available and updates; Install, Update, Remove; the two default bundles; the release channel; disk use. In the app also Devices (audio device, MIDI ports, Link, connected plugins), and the account for sharing presets and the library URL (for self-hosting) A missing module on the board is a placeholder node with an Install button that opens the Library section at that module. In a plugin window , the Library installs modules and presets (outside the audio thread); Plugins only lists what is installed and what is newer, and says "close Live, then update with the Bleep App", because replacing a plugin Live has loaded can crash it. Bleep Play has no Library section: it installs the modules a board needs by itself, checks them, and keeps them in the browser's cache. It has no plugins to manage and presets come from the site. Docs: module manuals are read from the installed packages (each carries its docs) and open from a module's node or from its card in the Library. Not planned: a built-in shop, a patch library with payments. Local state in ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep/ (and equivalents), read by the app and by every plugin: settings.json (channel, library URL), installed.json (id, version, sha256, channel, source), modules/ / / / , presets/ , a cache of index.json . Remove deletes the version folder; the board's nodes of a removed type show as missing, a board is never changed by it. 10. Repository layout registry/ ├── schema/ JSON Schemas: entry, index, module.json, preset └── README.md scripts/ ├── package-module.py folder → .bleepmod ├── package-plugin.sh built plugin → installer ├── release.py detect, package, stage, publish (dry run by default) └── registry-client.py fetch, used by the website build and tests patch/engine/WasmModuleHost. native host for .bleepmod patch/app/SoftwareCenter. the installer logic (UI is board-style web UI like the rest) check-repo.py gets rules: registry/ depends on nothing else; the schemas are the contract the others validate against. 11. Order of work Schemas and package format. module.json gets version , requires , types . package-module.py produces .bleepmod from the existing wasm output. Validate all current modules. Library v0. The SeaweedFS service and the Caddy route (done in the compose file); release.py publishes into the bucket. The website reads from it; remove the web stage from the Dockerfile; add web-lock.json . Wasm host in the engine and the CPU gate from 4.2. Decide per module: static-only or installable. The Library section in the app and the plugin window, with Modules, Plugins and Presets; the update check at start (13 has the steps). Plugin release pipeline : notarisation, installers. Presets : the schema with needs , local Library, then the /api/presets endpoints, the Postgres migration, device-code login and Share… . 12. Open questions Hosts that forbid executable memory (4.2, 13): with every module a wasm package, such a DAW can only run what wasm3 carries. Options: accept it (a message that names the DAW and the missing entitlement), keep a native build of the cheap-to-port modules as packages for that platform, or ship a second plugin build with the modules compiled in. Needs a decision before M6. Release credentials. release.py uses a release token (revocable, expiring, listed with last use), so S3 credentials stay on the server. Third-party modules. Any account can publish modules under its own handle ( acme/fuzz ); modules are sandboxed, plugins are reviewed before a token gets the plugin scope. Open: whether third-party modules sit in a separate community channel or in one list with the publisher shown. Naming: the product name, package extensions and the bleep:// scheme are placeholders like the rest of the project's names. 13. Moving the apps and plugins to library modules: work plan Done: the module packages ( package-module.py ), their release, the library reading each module's node types, and the Bleep Play , which installs its modules from the library ( patch/web/js/library-client.js , tested against the Python tools). Left: the standalone app and the plugins, which today compile the modules in. What is known about the 80 modules, from their sources and the browser build: all 80 build to standalone wasm and pass the ABI check. 26 use juce core and wasm exceptions (Wasmtime only; wasm3 cannot run them). 4 read the harmony bus (chord-quantizer, harmony-master, quantizer-suite, step-sequencer), 6 use the per-voice index (beat-oscillator, chart-recorder, macro-osc, pulse-generator, test-oscillator, wave-analyzer), 4 load sample files (grains, sampler, splice, wavetable-osc). Those 14 need an ABI addition before they can leave the apps ( module-abi.md , section 9). Cells, Voice Cells and the port nodes stay in the engine: only the DSP nodes become wasm. Step What Done when M1 The gate A WasmModuleHost (Wasmtime) in the engine, used first by bleep module harness : every module runs natively and as wasm on the same inputs and knob changes. ABI additions for harmony bus, voice index and media Per module: maximum difference within rounding and CPU relative to native. All 80 pass, or the list of those that do not and why. The heaviest (Grains, Delay Network, Modal Voice; a 16-voice Voice Cell) are within about 2× native M2 Library client in C++ HTTP with juce::URL and SHA-256, the same checks as library-client.js , the install folders and installed.json , the shared settings.json The packages in patch/tests/library-fixtures give the same verdicts in C++ and JavaScript; an install from a library on another port works end to end M3 Dynamic registry Registry becomes append-only and thread-safe (modules keep references to their specs, so a spec never moves or goes away); the type list the UI shows refreshes after an install; installed modules load at start Installing a module while a board is open adds its node type without a restart M4 Library and Board The two sections in the board UI, shared by the app and the plugins, with native functions for install, update, remove, progress and the Security settings Section 9 works in the app and in a plugin window in Live M5 First run The setup assistant with the two default bundles, the installers, the plugin bundle install (app only, Live closed) A clean machine reaches a working board with one click per bundle M6 Remove the modules from the apps The CMake option that compiles modules in is off for shipped builds; the plugins lose the module code; the tests keep it as the reference The plugins are small, load no module code, and the same boards sound the same Risks, in the order they bite: a wasm instance per voice (a 16-voice cell with five modules is 80 instances of 1 to 2 MB each); hosts that forbid executable memory (Wasmtime would be killed; the choice of runtime must be made before any code is compiled); the 26 exception-using modules cannot fall back to wasm3; start-up time (compile lazily on first use, cache compiled code per machine, keyed by the package hash); first run offline . M1 decides most of these, which is why nothing is removed from the apps before it passes.

title: Licensing
text: Licensing The short version: Bleep itself is free software under the GPL (version 3 only). Your module is yours. Write it against the module API and you can license it as you like: open source, free, closed source or paid. Forks of Bleep stay free. If you change Bleep itself and give it to others, your version stays under the GPL. This page is a plain-language summary, not legal advice. The licence texts decide: LICENSE and LICENSE-EXCEPTION.md . Which part has which licence Part Licence Why The engine, board, apps and hub ( patch/ ) GPL-3.0-only with the Bleep Module Exception Keeps Bleep and everything built from it free, while letting modules be anything The built-in modules ( patch/modules/ ) GPL-3.0-only , unless a module's module.json says otherwise (the three ported ones keep their original licence) Free to copy as a starting point for your own, under the GPL Bleep Bus ( bus/ ) MIT An open protocol: anyone can implement it in any product Scripts and the website ( scripts/ , website/ ) MIT Tools, not the product Factory presets ( patch/presets/ ) MIT Shared patches Presets shared in the Library CC BY 4.0 See the library Every source file has an SPDX-License-Identifier line that states its licence, and CI checks it. The module exception The GPL says that a program combined with GPL code must be GPL too. A module runs inside Bleep, so without a special rule every module would have to be open source. The Bleep Module Exception removes that for modules. You may license your module however you like (open, closed, free or paid) when it meets two conditions: It talks to Bleep only through the module API : the Module ABI, the contract of the .wasm file, and the module SDK: Module.h , Spec.h , Registry.h , DrumModule.h and Media.h in patch/engine/ , and the headers in patch/common/dsp/ . It does not copy or derive from any other GPL-licensed part of Bleep. Code that is under another licence, like the MIT-licensed Bleep Bus, can be reused under that licence. Examples You do this Result Write a module with the SDK headers and ship it as a closed-source .wasm Fine. You need not publish the source Sell that module, on your own site or elsewhere Fine. The exception says nothing about price Start from a built-in module (MIT) and keep your changes private Fine. Keep the MIT notice of the original code Port an open-source plugin under the MIT licence Fine. Keep its notice, see ported code Port a GPL plugin or firmware Your module must then be GPL too. That comes from the original code, not from Bleep Paste code from the engine or board into your module The module becomes a derivative of Bleep and must be GPL Change the engine, then give the modified Bleep to others That version is GPL. Share its source under the same terms Fork Bleep and remove the exception Allowed (the exception says so). Your fork is then plain GPL Things the exception does not do It does not cover changes to Bleep itself , only modules that plug in. It does not give you the name or logo . You may say your module is "for Beautiful Bleep", but not use the name or logo as your own. It does not make a module safe . To run in the apps, a module must still pass the library's checks and meet the ABI. Selling a module Nothing in the licence stops you from charging for a module, and you pick the terms your buyers get (a licence key, a EULA, a subscription). The Bleep Library is free today : there is no payment or licence-key support in it yet, so paid modules are distributed by you for now. Paid listings in the library are planned; this page will say when they are available. If your module is GPL (for instance because it is a port of GPL code), a buyer may pass it on under the GPL. That is how the GPL works for everyone. Binaries and other licences The source licence is not the only one that affects a build: Binaries built with JUCE also fall under JUCE's licence (AGPLv3 or a commercial JUCE licence). Check that before you distribute a build. App builds with Ableton Link are distributed under the GPL with their source. Because Bleep is now GPL, this no longer affects how Bleep itself is licensed; closed-source builds still need a Link licence from Ableton. Contributing to Bleep To contribute code to Bleep, read the contributing guide. You agree to a contributor licence agreement once. You keep your copyright. The agreement lets the project change the licence or its exceptions later, always staying open source. Questions Ask before you ship if you are unsure whether your module is covered. Write to beautifulbleep@gmail.com.

title: Module ABI
text: Module ABI (version 1) The contract between a host (the engine in the plugins and the app, the browser's worklet, the tests) and a module , a standalone WebAssembly file. It is what engineAbi in the library's requires (see library.md ) counts. This document describes the interface that exists today in patch/web/src/WebShim.cpp , which every one of the 80 module files in the browser build already implements, plus what a host must do around it. Items marked proposed are not in the code yet. Hosts that exist: the browser ( patch/web/js/module-host.js ). A native host for the plugins and the app is the next step. A spike that ran modules inside the plugins with Wasmtime and wasm3 (commit 70c3314 ) was removed again; its measurements are in patch/wasm-host/README.md . The conformance test in section 10 is for every host. 1. Versioning engineAbi is one integer. ABI 1 is everything in this document. A change is compatible if a host that knows version N still runs every module of version N: new optional exports, new fields in the spec JSON that hosts may ignore. It is incompatible otherwise: a changed signature or layout, a changed meaning, a removed export. Incompatible changes bump the integer; compatible ones do not, and get a note under "History" below. A module states the version it was built for in module.json ( requires.engineAbi ). Proposed: the file also exports bleep abi version() → i32 , so a host can check the file itself and a file cannot lie about its package. A module without that export is ABI 1. A host supports a range and refuses modules outside it with a message that says which (never a crash). The Library section explains it ("this module needs Bleep App 1.3"). 2. The file One module.wasm holds the node types of one module folder (usually one, the drum modules have several). It is standalone : no JS glue, no JUCE, no shared memory with other modules, no table shared with the host. Requirement Detail Memory One exported linear memory named memory , growable (1 to 2 MB at start, 64 to 256 KB of stack). A host should cap it (64 MB is a sensible limit; the largest module today starts at 2 MB) and must re-read the memory base after every call, because growing moves it. Imports Only these, and the host provides them as stubs (see section 8): env.emscripten notify memory growth(i32) , bleep media info and bleep media read (section 5a; only modules that load sample files import them), bleep record open , bleep record take , bleep record write , bleep record status , bleep record text , bleep record free and bleep record close (section 5b; only modules that record audio import them), and, for modules using juce core , seven WASI preview 1 functions: fd close , fd read , fd seek , fd write , environ get , environ sizes get , clock time get . Across the 80 current files these are all the imports that occur. A module importing anything else is refused. Start Exports initialize (runs C++ static constructors); the host calls it once, first. No start , no start section that does I/O. Features Whatever the pinned Emscripten (4.0.10) emits by default: no SIMD and no threads are requested, but the files do not record their feature set (the target features section is stripped), so the exact list is to be confirmed by the package step. The modules built with juce core (26 of the 80, the same 26 that import WASI) use wasm exception handling in its standardised form ( try table : -fwasm-exceptions -sWASM LEGACY EXCEPTIONS=0 ). Emscripten's older default ( try / catch ) is not accepted : Wasmtime refuses to compile it, which a first version of the host found out. Browsers have the standard form since 2025 (Chrome 137, Firefox 131, Safari 18.4). wasm3 does not support exception handling at all , so as a fallback it only runs the modules without. Proposed: the package step reads the used features out of each file and writes them to module.json ( features ), and the host checks them at load, so a missing feature is a clear message. Determinism No clock, no randomness from the host: clock time get returns 0. Any random stream is seeded by the module. The same input and knob values produce the same output on every host (the spike matched the native build to about 1e-6 on a peak of 0.4; wasm does not fuse multiply-adds the way a native build may). 3. Life of a module instance compile + instantiate the file (once per process may be shared; one instance per node) initialize() once per instance bleep spec json() the node types the file provides (JSON) bleep chunk() must equal 32, otherwise refuse h = bleep create(typeIndex, sampleRate) 0: failed, the reason is in bleep error() ptrs = bleep params ptr(h), bleep inputs ptr(h), bleep outputs ptr(h), bleep in connected ptr(h) … once repeat: knobs, data, connections … then, per 32-sample chunk: write buffers, bleep set transport, bleep process bleep destroy(h) Threads. An instance is single-threaded : a wasm runtime's store must not be entered by two threads at once, and native modules' atomics (knobs, command queues, live values) do not exist across the boundary. bleep process and the buffer writes around it run on the audio thread. Every other call ( create , destroy , set data , perform , command , live , param text , take data , sanitise data ) must not overlap with bleep process of the same instance, and must never make the audio thread wait. The host therefore marshals them onto the audio thread through queues (knobs: the host keeps the latest value and calls bleep set knob between chunks; buttons and gestures: a queue drained before the chunk; live , take data : answered from a snapshot the audio thread refreshes), or it runs them only while the audio thread is not using the instance (creation, destruction, reconfiguration). The spike did the knob and button part this way. bleep spec json , bleep type count , bleep chunk and bleep note event size touch no instance and are safe at any time after initialize . Real time. bleep process must not allocate, lock, or do I/O. Modules that allocate on create , prepare or set data do it outside the audio thread, as in native. 4. Exports h is the instance handle (an i32 address; 0 means failure). All sizes and addresses are i32 ; f32 and f64 as named. Export Signature Meaning bleep error () → ptr NUL-terminated message of the last call that failed (empty: none). bleep spec json / bleep spec json length () → ptr / () → i32 The node types as a UTF-8 JSON array (section 7). The pointer stays valid for the life of the file. bleep type count () → i32 Number of node types. bleep chunk () → i32 The chunk size, 32. Buffers are sized by it. bleep create (typeIndex: i32, sampleRate: f64) → h A new instance; runs the module's prepare and reset . bleep destroy (h) bleep reset (h) Clears state (a transport jump, a cleared tail). bleep params ptr , bleep inputs ptr , bleep outputs ptr (h) → ptr The three float buffers, fixed for the life of the instance (section 5). bleep in connected ptr , bleep out connected ptr (h) → ptr One byte per input / output jack ( ni + 1 , no + 1 bytes): 1 when patched. An output nobody reads may be skipped but must still hold valid numbers. bleep set knob (h, index: i32, normalised: f32) The value a module reads with setting() : the knob without modulation. Call it when the knob changes, and once for every knob after create , so the module sees the saved state. bleep set transport (h, bpm: f64, ppq: f64, playing: i32, samplePos: i64) Before each chunk. ppq is the position at the chunk start in quarter notes. The module is told the transport started when playing goes from 0 to 1 between two calls (a host that restarts the transport without stopping it calls once with 0 first). bleep set voice (h, voice: i32) Optional. Inside a Voice Cell: the voice this instance plays ( ProcessContext::voice ); −1 outside. Call after create and when it changes. bleep harmony ptr , bleep harmony size (h) → ptr , () → i32 Optional. The board-wide harmony buses (section 5). bleep host ptr , bleep host size (h) → ptr , () → i32 Optional. The mailbox of a module that asks the host to change the transport (section 5). bleep process (h, numSamples: i32) → i32 Runs numSamples (1 to 32) samples. Returns 0, or non-zero when the call was refused or failed (the outputs are then unspecified and the host should bypass). bleep notes in ptr , bleep notes out ptr (h, jack: i32) → ptr The note buffer of a notes jack (section 5). bleep note event size () → i32 16. The host checks it. bleep scratch (h, size: i32) → ptr A buffer of size bytes in the module's memory for strings going in. Valid until the next bleep scratch call; any call that reads it says so. bleep text , bleep text length (h) → ptr , (h) → i32 The last string the module handed out (UTF-8, not terminated), valid until the next call that produces one. bleep set data (h, length) Node data (the board document's data , JSON) from the scratch buffer. bleep sanitise data (h, typeIndex, length) → i32 Makes node data valid, with defaults, from the scratch buffer; the result is in bleep text (its length is returned), −1: the type has no node data. Any instance of the file will do as h . bleep perform (h, argOffset: i32, numArgs: i32) A performance gesture from the module's view (a key, a pad): the action name (NUL-terminated) in the scratch buffer, then numArgs doubles at argOffset (8-byte aligned). No undo, not saved. bleep command (h, value: f32) A view button: its id (NUL-terminated) in the scratch buffer. bleep live (h) → i32 {"values":{name:number},"arrays":{name:[number]}} for the view, in bleep text ; its length is returned. Polled about ten times a second. bleep param text (h, index, normalised: f32) → i32 How the board shows a knob at that value ("2.5 s"), in bleep text . bleep output display (h, index) → f32 The value of an output's meter. bleep take data (h) → i32 Node data the module changed itself (a captured loop): its JSON in bleep text , −1 if none. Polled. A call that throws inside a module (only the modules built with exceptions) is caught inside the file: bleep create returns 0 or the call returns its failure value, and bleep error has the message. An exception never crosses the boundary. 5. Buffers Chunks. The host cuts every block into chunks of at most 32 samples and calls bleep process once per chunk. A block of 128 samples is four calls. (Native modules see whole blocks; modules must not depend on the block size, and the harness checks this.) Layout. Jack-major, float32 , little endian, one row of 32 per jack: params : [paramIndex × 32] the effective normalised value (0 … 1) at every sample, knob plus modulation inputs : [inputJack × 32] the summed signal; a notes jack's row is unused outputs : [outputJack × 32] written by the module Rows have 32 floats even for the last, shorter chunk; the first numSamples are valid. A buffer for zero jacks still has one row. The pointers do not change for the life of the instance, so the host fetches them once; the base of the memory may change, so it adds them to the current base every call. Normalised values. A param is always 0 … 1 on the boundary. Its units (Hz, seconds, choices) come from the spec JSON and the module's own mapping ( ParamSpec ). bleep set knob and params use the same scale. Signal types (the type of a jack): audio , control , pitch (virtual volts, 1.0 = one octave, 0 = C4), gate , trigger (≥ 0.5 is high), notes . All but notes are floats in the rows above. Notes. A notes jack is a NoteBuffer in the module's memory: 64 events of 16 bytes, then an i32 count (1028 bytes). Per event: u8 type (0 on, 1 off, 2 pressure, 3 control change, 4 program change, 5 pitch bend, 6 channel pressure, 7 system realtime), u8 channel (0 to 15), i16 offset (sample inside the chunk), i32 note (MIDI number, identifies the note; for types 3 to 7 the controller number, the program number, 0, 0, or the status byte of the realtime message), f32 pitch , f32 value (velocity or pressure, 0 … 1; for a control change data ÷ 127, for a bend −1 … +1). A module handles the types it knows and ignores every other type : older modules never see types 3 to 7 do anything, because they test for 0, 1 and 2 by name. The host keeps the last 16 slots of a buffer for notes: control changes and the other new types are dropped first when a chunk is crowded. The host writes the events of an input jack and the count before each chunk; it reads an output jack's events and count after it. More than 64 per chunk are dropped. Harmony buses (modules whose spec says "harmony": "writer" or "reader" ). bleep harmony ptr(h) is the address of dsp::kHarmonyBuses (4) HarmonyState records in the module's memory, bleep harmony size() their total size ( HarmonyState is plain data, 16 bytes: valid , key , chordRoot , bass , scale , chord , quality , degree , serial , laid out as the C++ struct). The host copies the board's buses in before every chunk and, for a writer , copies them back out after it; every writer runs before every reader on the board, as natively. Host mailbox (the Transport module). A module cannot change the transport: it reads it. A module that must ask for a change (a new tempo, play and stop, Ableton Link on or off) writes the request into a record in its own memory, and bleep host ptr(h) is the address of that record, bleep host size() its size (40 bytes, little endian, no padding): Offset Type Field Direction Meaning 0 f64 tempo module → host A requested tempo in BPM; 0 = no request. 8 i32 play module → host 0 stop, 1 start from the beginning, 2 continue; −1 = no request. 12 i32 link module → host 1 Link on, 0 off; −1 = no request. 16 i32 startStopSync module → host 1 Link start/stop sync on, 0 off; −1 = no request. 20 i32 hosted host → module 1 when the host acts on requests (the standalone app); 0 in plugins and the browser. 24 i32 linkAvailable host → module 1 when the host has Ableton Link. 28 i32 linkEnabled host → module 1 when Link is on. 32 i32 linkPeers host → module The number of Link peers. A host that answers requests writes the four status fields before each block and, after the block, takes the requests and sets them back to "no request" (0 and −1). A host that does not know the export, or does not act on requests, leaves the record alone and the module still runs: its requests go nowhere. A request that is not yet taken is replaced by a newer one. Strings are UTF-8. Numbers crossing through the scratch buffer are little endian and aligned as stated. 5a. Media Four modules (Grains, Sampler, Splice, Wavetable Osc) read audio files from the computer's media folder by id ( .wav ). A module file has no disk, so the host answers through two imports of the module, env : Import Signature Meaning bleep media info (id: ptr, idLength: i32, sampleRate: ptr→f64, channels: ptr→i32) → i64 Length of the clip in frames, its sample rate and channels written to the two pointers; 0 if the clip is not available . bleep media read (id: ptr, idLength: i32, channel: i32, dst: ptr, frames: i64) → i32 Copies frames samples of one channel to dst (float32); 1 on success. The host must not block to answer: these calls come from inside bleep set data on the audio thread. A clip that is not in memory is "not available"; the host reads it on another thread and, when it is there, sends the module's last node data again ( bleep set data ), which makes the module ask again and succeed. A host with no media folder answers 0 to everything. The browser build keeps the files in IndexedDB and gives the worklet the decoded clips a board uses ( patch/web/js/web-media.js ). 5b. Recording The Audio Console records its channels to files. A module file has no disk, no paths and no threads, so the host answers through eight imports of the module, env . They hand audio to the host's recorder service and read back nothing but its status: there is no way to name a path, read a file or reach anything else through them. What the service does with the audio (the Recordings folder, file names, formats, limits) is described in recorder-service.md . Import Signature Meaning bleep record open (spec: ptr, specLength: i32, sampleRate: f64, format: i32) → i32 Opens a session. spec is UTF-8 JSON, {"name": "Audio Console", "folder": "/full/path", "tracks": [{"name": "Kick", "channels": 1}, …]} : one to 40 tracks of one or two channels. folder is optional: a full path this module records to instead of the folder from Settings (the host refuses the session, with a reason, when it cannot write there). format : 0 = WAV 16-bit, 1 = WAV 24-bit, 2 = WAV 32-bit float. Returns a handle (≥ 1), or 0 if this host has no recorder (a host that only runs modules for tests, say), or −1 for a spec the service refuses; bleep record text(0, 1, …) then gives the reason. bleep record take (handle: i32, begin: i32) → i32 Marks the start ( begin = 1) or the end (0) of a take on every track at once. 1 if accepted. bleep record write (handle: i32, track: i32, left: ptr, right: ptr, frames: i32) → i32 Appends frames float32 samples to a track: left , and right for a two-channel track (a mono track ignores it). Every track must get the same number of frames between the two take marks. 1 if accepted; 0 if the host fell behind and dropped the session (see bleep record status ). bleep record status (handle: i32, frames: ptr→i64, take: ptr→i32) → i32 The frames written to the current take and its number, and flags: bit 0 a take is open, bit 1 the session failed (disk full, too slow, file too big). bleep record text (handle: i32, what: i32, dst: ptr, capacity: i32) → i32 Writes UTF-8 text to dst and returns its length (cut to capacity , no terminator). what : 0 = where the files go (handle 0 is allowed), 1 = the message of the last failure or refusal, 2 = this session's folder (empty until the first take begins). bleep record free () → f64 Bytes the recorder can still take (free disk space minus a reserve; in the browser what is left of its memory budget), 0 if there is none. The module divides it by its data rate to show how long it can record. bleep record room (folder: ptr, length: i32) → f64 Like bleep record free , for a module that records to a folder of its own (a full path, UTF-8, at most 1024 bytes): the bytes left on that folder's disk. 0 if there is none; in the browser it is the same as bleep record free . bleep record close (handle: i32) → void Ends the session. The host finishes every file on another thread; the call returns at once. The host must not block to answer. A module runs on one thread, so all of these, including the ones a button causes, are called on the audio thread: open does only the quick part (it allocates the buffers and starts the writer; files are made later, on the writer's thread), write copies into a ring buffer, and close hands the session on. A host with no recorder answers 0 to open and bleep record free and does nothing else. A module that is destroyed with a session open has it finished by the host. A session belongs to the instance that opened it: handles are not shared between instances. 6. Transport and time bleep set transport(bpm, ppq, playing, samplePos) is called before every chunk; the module derives its tempo-synced timing from it ( ppq and bpm give the position at every sample of the chunk). sampleRate is fixed at create ; a different rate needs a new instance. The module sees no wall clock. 7. The spec JSON bleep spec json() is the same description the board UI gets from the engine for native modules ( describeTypes() ), and complete: a host rebuilds a node type's whole ModuleSpec from it, so the engine cannot tell it from a compiled-in one. Per node type: type , name , category , colour , description , port , creatable , standaloneOnly , params[] ( id , name , kind float int bool choice, default in 0 … 1, def in units, min , max , map exp skew and centre , format , decimals , label , steps , modulatable , choices , groups , group , conditional display showIf , namesBy and names ), inputs[] and outputs[] ( id , name , type , bipolar , normal , conditional display, names), buttons[] , memoryHeavy , groupColumns and, for the harmony bus, harmony . The parity test compares it with the native description of every module. Unknown fields are ignored by hosts, so adding one is compatible. The order of params , inputs and outputs is the index order of every call above and of the buffers. 8. What a host must do Provide the imports as stubs. The seven bleep record imports (section 5b) answer "no recorder" ( bleep record open returns 0, the others do nothing) unless the host has a recorder service. emscripten notify memory growth does nothing; the WASI functions give no files, no environment, no clock: fd write accepts and drops its bytes, fd read , fd seek and fd close fail, environ report none, clock time get returns 0, and proc exit is not imported by any current file; a host that is asked for it traps the instance. This makes the sandbox complete: a module can compute and nothing else. Own the memory. Instantiate with the file's own memory, cap it (64 MB suggested), and never share it between instances. Bound time. A bleep process that runs longer than a few blocks of audio is stopped (Wasmtime: epoch interruption or fuel) and the instance is bypassed (silence out, an error in the log, a mark on the node), never allowed to stall the audio thread. wasm3 has no such interruption, so it is only for trusted (first-party, signed) modules. Proposed ; the spike does not do it yet. Check the file before running it. Its file list, the imports, bleep chunk() == 32 , bleep note event size() == 16 , the ABI version. Choose the runtime deliberately. Wasmtime needs executable memory. A host that forbids it (macOS hardened runtime without allow-unsigned-executable-memory , which Ableton Live 12 has) kills the process when it is asked for, so a plugin can't try and fall back: the choice is made from what the host process is entitled to, or by a setting, before any code is compiled. Measured for the Verb on an Apple M-series: about 1.2× the native cost in the standalone benchmark and 1.5 to 1.7× through the plugin (the copies around each 32-sample chunk included, Live 12: 3.2 % of a core against 1.9 % native); wasm3 ten times Wasmtime (32.5 %). See patch/wasm-host/README.md . Compile once. One compiled module per file per process, one store and instance per node. Ahead-of-time compiled code may be cached per machine, keyed by the file's hash and the runtime version; the cache is never trusted over the file. 9. Not in ABI 1 What a native module can do today and a wasm module cannot, yet: the port nodes (audio and MIDI in and out; they are not DSP modules and stay in the engine) and the Link tempo (a module can read the tempo, and ask for changes through the host mailbox). The harmony buses, the per-voice index, the transport-start event, sample files and the host mailbox were missing from the first version of the shim and are now optional exports and imports (sections 4, 5 and 5a), added as compatible changes. 10. Conformance A host passes when, for the same inputs and knob values, a module's output equals the native build's within rounding. The spike showed how: it ran the Verb as native, in Wasmtime and in wasm3 on the same noise with random knob changes mid-run and compared the outputs; the largest difference was 7e-7 on a peak of 0.43, and the tolerance was 1e-3 relative to the peak. Every module that ships as wasm gets the same check in the module harness (the native engine's tests keep the native modules for exactly this: the reference). A new host implementation runs the same cases against the browser host ( patch/web/test/ ). History 1, recorder imports: the seven bleep record imports (section 5b) for modules that write audio to files. A compatible addition, like the media imports: a module that does not import them is unaffected, and a host that does not know them refuses a module that does, with the usual message about imports. 1 (this document): the interface of the 80 browser files, written down. Proposed additions that keep it version 1: bleep abi version , a features list in module.json , per-block time limits in hosts.

title: Module developers
text: Module developers A module is a node on the board: a folder in patch/modules/ / with a module.json , a C++ node that declares its knobs and jacks and processes audio in process() , DSP without JUCE, an optional custom view in JavaScript, tests, and a user manual. The same source is built for every host. The result is one standalone .wasm file that the engine in the plugins, the Bleep App and the browser all run, so a module you write works everywhere without per-platform code. The path Write it. Writing a module: the folder layout, BLEEP REGISTER MODULE , shared DSP in patch/common/dsp/ , engine features (stepped knobs, groups, buttons, node data, media, voices, custom views). Test it. DSP tests per module, plus bleep module harness , which runs every module with every input fed at several sample rates and checks that outputs stay finite and bounded. Document it. A manual in doc/ .md with a screenshot. The board shows it behind the view's ? button and this website shows it under Modules. Package it. Publishing a module: a .bleepmod package. Release it. To the Bleep Library, where users and the apps install it. What a module must satisfy Module ABI: the exports, memory limits, determinism rules and versioning a host expects of the .wasm file. Recorder service: how a module writes audio to files without a disk: sessions, takes, the Recordings folder and the imports that reach it. Licensing: modules may be open source, closed source or paid; the module exception explains what that needs. Licences of ported code: a module ported from other code keeps the original's licence and says so in module.json ; copyleft ports ship only through the library, never inside the apps. Writing a module has the rules. Modules and the Bleep Bus Modules talk to each other with cables on the board. They do not use Bleep Bus, which connects separate plugins in a DAW.

title: Publishing a module
text: Publishing a module Modules run in a sandbox, so the apps load every module that passes their checks: nothing is signed. The library's layout is in Bleep Library; this page is the practical path. There are two: Share with the community Release as a developer For Any module you made, closed source included Plugins, Bleep's own modules, modules with their own JavaScript Needs An account on the library's site A release token from the admin Who authorises it Your account The token, bound to your publisher name Section Share a module with the community 1 to 4 Share a module with the community You upload the module; the library checks it and publishes it as / . Your name is the handle of your account (the one in the address of your presets, set when you first publish). From a Code node, the Share… button does steps 2 and 3 for you in the browser while you are logged in to the library: it asks for the metadata and help text, builds the package and uploads it (see The Code node). The rest of this section is the same thing from the command line. 1. Make a token. Log in to the library's site, open Account > Apps ( /account/apps/ ) and create an access token. Save it in a file only you can read, for example ~/.bleep-token . It is shown once. 2. Prepare the package. A folder (or a .bleepmod ) with: File module.json Required. types : the node types it provides, all starting with / ; requires.engineAbi : 1 ; optionally title , summary , category , license (SPDX, default MIT) and origin for ported code module.wasm Required. Imports only what the Module ABI allows and exports the whole ABI spec.json Required. The node types' descriptions view.sandbox.js Optional. The module's own picture, written as a Code node's UI: it runs only in the sandboxed worker frame (no network, no storage, no DOM, stopped if it hangs), never in the page source.dsp.ts Optional. The module's Bleep Script source, so that everyone can open it in a Code node ( Convert to code ) and change it. The module's licence applies to it image.png , image.jpg or image.webp Optional. The picture on the module's tile in the library, up to 1 MB: a screenshot of the module LICENSE , doc/ .md , doc/ .png Optional Nothing else is allowed. In particular there is no ui/ .js : a module's page scripts run in the page, which only first-party modules may do. Its picture is view.sandbox.js instead, which is safe because it never runs in the page. Limits: 12 MB per package, 8 MB for the .wasm , 24 files. 3. Check and publish. scripts/release/community-publish.py my-module/ --name wobble --version 1.0.0 --check scripts/release/community-publish.py my-module/ --name wobble --version 1.0.0 \ --registry https:// --token-file ~/.bleep-token --check runs the library's own checks locally and sends nothing. The id of this module is /wobble . Each upload needs a higher version than the one before, and a version you withdrew stays used. You can publish up to 100 modules and 10 uploads an hour. 4. After publishing. The module appears in the library marked community . Users need no setting to run it; it runs in the same sandbox as every module. To withdraw a release, call POST /api/registry/community/modules/ . / /takedown while logged in (or ask the admin); it leaves the index, so nobody can install it any more (copies already installed stay until removed). If the library refuses your upload, the message names the rule and the file. Release as a developer The steps 1 to 4 below are for publishers with a release token. Sharing a module with the community does not need them. 1. Build the .wasm files scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker --modules-only This compiles every module with Emscripten (in Docker, so no local SDK is needed). Later builds recompile only the modules whose files changed. BLEEP WEB ONLY=oscillator,filter builds just those. 2. Package scripts/release/package-module.py One reproducible .bleepmod per module, in build/library/modules . The packager checks each .wasm against the Module ABI and adds your licence and provenance information. 3. Get a token A publisher needs a release token for their publisher name from the library's admin. Module ids outside the library's own team carry your publisher namespace. Keep the token private; it is never a command-line argument. 4. Release scripts/release/release.py --modules --level patch \ --registry https:// \ --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token --modules releases only the modules whose package content changed since their newest published version. --dry-run checks everything without publishing. Versions are immutable: a fix is a new version. Compatibility Your package states the module ABI it was built for ( requires.engineAbi in module.json ). A host that does not support it refuses the module with a message instead of crashing, and the library tells the user which app version is needed.

title: Recorder service
text: Recorder service A module is sandboxed: it has no disk, no paths and no threads, and that is what makes it safe to run code that somebody else wrote. A module that records audio (the Audio Console writes every armed channel to its own file) therefore cannot write the files itself. It hands the audio to the recorder service , which belongs to the host and does the writing. Three rules shape it: The module never sees a path. It names tracks; the host decides where files go, what they are called on disk and whether it can write at all. The audio thread never waits. Writing a block is a copy into a ring buffer, and a failure is a flag, not a stall. Files, folders and flushing happen on the service's own thread. The service says how much room is left , so a module can show how long it can record instead of guessing. Sessions, tracks and takes Term What it is Session What a module opens when it starts recording: a list of tracks, fixed until the session ends. Track One file. One or two channels (mono or stereo); at most 40 per session. Take The audio between a start and a stop. A session has any number of takes, recorded one after the other into new files. A module opens a session on its message side, pushes blocks of samples from its audio code, and marks where each take begins and ends: open(name, tracks, sampleRate, format) → session once, when recording is armed beginTake() at a start write(track, left, right, frames) → ok every block, for every track endTake() at a stop close() the session ends; every file is finished Every track must receive the same number of frames between beginTake() and endTake() . A take boundary is stored as an exact frame position per track, so a take ends where the audio thread ended it, however far behind the writer is, and stopping and starting again within a few milliseconds does not mix two takes. In C++ ( patch/engine/Recording.h , header only) it looks like this: #include "Recording.h" using namespace bleep::engine; recording::Service svc = recording::service(); // null: this host cannot record if (!svc) return; std::string why; auto session = svc->open("My module", {{"Left", 1}, {"Room", 2}}, sampleRate, recording::Format::Pcm24, &why); // audio thread, every block session->beginTake(); const float room[2] = {roomL, roomR}; session->write(0, &left, frames); // mono track: one channel session->write(1, room, frames); // stereo track: two session->endTake(); session.reset(); // finishes the files write() returns false when the host fell behind and dropped the session. The module should stop writing and show session->status().message . The formats WAV, as 16-bit or 24-bit integer or 32-bit float. Other formats (MP3, FLAC) are not offered: an MP3 encoder (LAME, LGPL) would be a dependency a release has to bring and a licence it has to carry, and the WAV files are easy to convert afterwards. What the apps and the plugins do They install a disk service ( patch/engine/Recording.cpp ). It writes to the Recordings folder , next to the media folder: System Default folder macOS, Linux ~/Music/Beautiful Bleep/Recordings Windows %USERPROFILE%\Music\Beautiful Bleep\Recordings /2026-10-24 14.32.07 Audio Console/Kick.wav Kick (take 2).wav Aux 1.wav Master.wav Each session gets its own folder, named after the time it started and the module. The folder and the files are made when the first take begins, so a session that waits for the transport leaves nothing behind. Track names are made safe (no separators or reserved characters, at most 60 characters) and made unique within the session ("Kick", "Kick 2"). The files are classic WAV with a 44-byte header. The header is written empty and patched when the take ends, so a file left by a crash is still readable by editors that go by the file length. A file stops at 4 GB, the limit of a WAV file: the take ends and the service says so. Time left. freeBytes() is the free space of the volume minus a reserve of 1 GB. Divide it by tracks × channels × sample rate × bytes per sample. A full disk, a missing permission or a writer that falls behind ends the take and sets a message. What was written stays valid. The default folder is chosen in Settings → Recordings (the app and the plugins): a full path that Bleep can write to, or the default. recording::saveFolder(path, &error) checks it (by making the folder and writing a file) and keeps it in recordings.json in the data folder the library's settings use, which the app and every plugin share ( BLEEP DATA DIR moves it); recording::setFolder changes it for one run only. A module can pass a folder of its own when it opens a session (the Audio Console's folder field); it is checked the same way, and an empty one means the folder from Settings. A session keeps the folder it started in. Reaching the service from a wasm module Shipped modules are WebAssembly files and cannot call the C++ service. In a wasm build the same recording::service() is a small client whose calls become eight imports the host provides ( bleep record open , bleep record take , bleep record write , bleep record status , bleep record text , bleep record free , bleep record room , bleep record close ). They are specified in the Module ABI, section 5b. They only hand audio to the host and read its status back: there is no way to name a path or read a file through them, so the sandbox is as tight as before. A module runs on one thread, so even the calls a button causes arrive on the audio thread. The imports never block: open allocates the buffers and starts the writer (about a millisecond for a typical session), close hands the session to a background thread to finish, and write is a copy. A host without a recorder answers 0 to open , and the module says that recording is not available there. The browser Bleep Play has no disk and no Recordings folder. Its recorder is the simplest one that cannot take a tab down. It is built ( patch/web/js/web-recorder.js in the audio worklet, web-recordings.js on the page) and tested under node with the real Audio Console; it has not been run in a browser yet: In memory, then download. A memory service answers the same imports and keeps the samples in chunks. When the session ends, the takes are handed to the page without copying, and the Audio Console's view lists them with Download .zip and Discard . The zip holds a WAV file for every track of every take, built from the recorded chunks themselves, so the memory is not doubled. What the page still holds counts against the budget until you discard it. A budget, not "all free memory". A browser cannot say how much memory is free. The service uses a fixed budget (about a quarter of navigator.deviceMemory where that exists, between 256 MB and 1 GB, 256 MB where it does not) and reports what is left of it through freeBytes() , so the Audio Console shows the time left exactly as it does with a disk: at 1 GB, 16 bit and 48 kHz, about three hours for one track, 23 minutes for eight and under six for 32. It stops before it fails. The take ends when the budget is used up, keeps what it has and says why; a warning comes at 90 %. Memory is allocated in small blocks inside a try/catch, so an allocation the browser refuses ends the take and not the tab. Planned next: recording into the browser's Origin Private File System from a worker (no budget; a take survives a reload), streaming downloads through a service worker, and MP3 conversion after the take. Tests patch/tests/recording test.cpp is pure C++: files per track in every format with the right header and the samples that were written, safe and unique names, numbered takes, five takes within moments with their exact lengths, a session closed in the middle of a take, a writer that falls behind, and refused sessions. patch/tests/audio console record test.cpp drives the real Audio Console against it with the audio on its own thread. The full specification is doc/specs/recorder-service.md .

title: Writing a module
text: Writing a module A module is a folder in patch/modules/ with a module.json . The build finds it on its own and the module registers itself, so adding one touches no shared file: patch/modules/ / ├── module.json name, slug (= type id), tagline, colour, formats, doc ├── Module.cpp the node: spec (params, jacks, buttons) and process() ├── dsp/ Dsp.h the DSP, no JUCE (namespace bleep::patch) ├── doc/ .md the user documentation (the view's ? button and the website) ├── doc/ .png screenshot of the module view, shown at the top of the doc ├── ui/ .js optional custom displays for the module view └── tests/test .cpp DSP tests: each file is its own executable and ctest End Module.cpp with the registration function ( static , it is only used here) and BLEEP REGISTER MODULE(registerFooModule); The design lives in doc/specs/modules/ .md (in the repository); the module follows it, and the spec is updated where the implementation had to differ. Advanced modules also get five demo patches ( patch/presets/demos/ .mjs , whole boards for the app's preset browser, see patch/presets/demos/README.md ) and a Demo patches section in their doc. A module written in Bleep Script A module can also be written in Bleep Script instead of C++. It lives in the same place, and the build, the packager and the library treat it like any other module; only the compiler differs (node, not Emscripten). Its module.json says "language": "bleep-script" : patch/modules/ / ├── module.json as above, plus "language": "bleep-script" and "category" ├── .dsp.ts the module: a Bleep Script class (see Module scripts) ├── .view.js optional: its own UI, as a Code node's UI tab (runs only in the sandboxed worker frame) ├── LICENSE └── doc/ .md, .png the manual and its picture, as for every module scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only compiles it ( patch/web/build modules.py calls patch/script/build-module.mjs ; run npm install in patch/script once), with the module's slug as its node type id. The package gets two extra files: view.sandbox.js (the UI) and source.dsp.ts (the source, so that anyone can open the module in a Code node with Convert to code ). CMake skips these folders. The DSP tests are .mjs files in patch/script/test/modules/ ( node test/modules/ .test.mjs ), see Running the tests. The vintage modules (Preamp, Valve Stage, Channel Strip, Tone EQ, Opto Compressor, Mic Colour, Tape Machine, Vinyl, Cheap Speaker) are written this way. Ported code and licences A module that is ported from, or adapted from, someone else's code (an open-source plugin, firmware, a library) must say so, and keeps the original's licence terms. scripts/check/check-repo.py enforces all of it in CI. module.json gets two fields: { "license": "MIT", "origin": { "name": "PitchShifter (DaisySP)", "author": "Electrosmith, LLC", "url": "https://github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP", "license": "MIT", "copyright": "Copyright (c) 2020 Electrosmith, Corp", "changes": "Rewritten for block processing; interpolation and crossfade changed" } } license is the module's SPDX id; leave it out for MIT (the built-in modules are GPL-3.0-only). Every source file of the module ( .cpp , .h , .js , tests) starts with // SPDX-License-Identifier: . origin is present exactly when code was taken from somewhere: name , author , url , license (SPDX id of the original) and copyright (its notice, verbatim) are required; changes says what we altered. Permissive originals (MIT, BSD, ISC, Apache-2.0, Zlib, ...) may be ported into an MIT module. The original copyright notice and licence text stay. Copyleft originals (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL) make the module keep that licence: license must equal origin.license . Such a module is never compiled into the apps and plugins (CMake leaves it out of them; tests and tools still build it): it ships only as an optional .wasm module from the Bleep Library, under its own licence, with its source. The library shows the licence on the module's detail view. A module with an origin , or any licence other than MIT, has a LICENSE file in its folder with the full licence text and the original copyright notice. The package carries it. The library's detail view shows the module's license and, for a port, its origin . The module's doc has an ## Origin section that names the source, links it and gives the licence. The package's library summary gets "Based on by ( )." added by the packager. Code under no clear licence, or "all rights reserved", is not ported. Algorithms described in papers or books may be reimplemented freely; say so in the Origin section, and leave out origin if none of the source's code was used. Building and testing cmake -S patch -B build/light -G Ninja -DBLEEP LIGHT TESTS=ON # juce core only, no plugins cmake --build build/light && ctest --test-dir build/light build/light/bleep module harness artefacts/Release/bleep module harness # one module, with CPU use bleep module harness runs every module type on a compiled board with every input fed (noise, control, gates, triggers, pitch, notes), knobs at defaults, at 0, at 1 and random, at three sample rates, with the transport starting, stopping and jumping. Outputs must stay finite and within ±64. After changing params or jacks, regenerate the board UI's type list ( bleep dump types --write patch/board/ui/demo-types.json ). The website reads each module's category from it. A module whose type list entry doesn't exist yet needs "category" in its module.json . Every doc starts with its screenshot ( Name in the module view under the title). With scripts/run/ui-server.py running, scripts/docs/module-screenshots.py [type ...] retakes them after a view changes. The website shows them; the plugins only embed the .md files. When it works, publishing shows how to share it: any account can publish a module to the community without a key. Shared code Before writing DSP, look in patch/common/dsp/ (namespace bleep::dsp ): Header What OscCore.h , Wavetable.h , Partials.h , Formant.h , Folder.h oscillators, tables, additive, formant bursts, wavefolding ModalBank.h , Waveguide.h , Exciter.h , Room.h , Vactrol.h physical models, small rooms, low-pass-gate cells Delay.h , Hilbert.h , Fdn.h , Grains.h , Lofi.h delays, frequency shifting, reverb, granular, degradation Chords.h , Harmony.h , Scales.h , SeqClock.h , SeqNotes.h , Tempo.h chords and voicing, the harmony bus, scales, sequencer timing and note output Waves.h , Shapes.h , Slope.h , Chaos.h , Random.h , Noise.h LFO waves, shape library, slope generators, chaos/neurons, seeded randomness Svf.h , Smoothing.h , Oversampler.h , Clip.h , Gain.h , Drums.h filters, smoothing and edges, oversampling, limiting, faders, drum parts Randomness is always seeded and counter-based ( Random.h ), so offline renders repeat. Transport-synced timing derives positions from ctx.ppqAt(i) so a module stays on the grid after loop jumps. Engine features All in patch/engine/Spec.h and Module.h . Stepped knobs. ParamSpec::stepped(id, name, choices, def) and ParamSpec::steppedInt(id, name, min, max, def) are choices and integers that can be modulated: the view shows a knob that snaps, a cable moves it through the steps. value(c, i, s) returns the rounded value. Groups. ParamSpec::percent(...).inGroup("Envelope") puts knobs under a heading in the module view. Use groups on modules with many knobs. Shown in some modes. .when("mode", 2, 3) on a param or a jack shows it only while the setting mode is 2 or 3 (in its own units). Use it for jacks beyond a Count setting ( .when("count", 5, 8) on jack 5) and for knobs that only mean something in one mode. Hidden jacks keep their cables and show dimmed; the module still receives them. Names that follow a mode. .namedBy("mode", {"Tone", "Shape", "Blend"}) renames a knob or jack with the setting's value, for modules whose knobs mean different things per model. Normalled inputs. JackSpec{"b", "Trig B", Signal::Trigger}.normalledTo("a") : while unpatched, Trig B reads Trig A 's signal. ctx.inputConnected[b] stays false, so the module can tell. Unread outputs. ctx.isOutputConnected(k) is false when nothing reads output k . Skip expensive work for it (a filter bank's band outputs), but leave the buffer finite (the node's scope shows it). Buttons and commands. s.buttons = {{"ping", "Ping", true}, {"clear", "Clear"}} adds buttons to the view (true = momentary: press sends 1, release 0). They arrive on the audio thread through the command queue: void process(const ProcessContext& c) override { pollCommands(& { if (cmd.index == Ping) ping = cmd.value > 0.5f; }); ... } Override Module::command(id, value) for commands a custom view sends with view.api.command(id, value) . Node data. s.sanitiseData (JSON in, valid JSON out) and Module::setData(json) for state beyond knobs: steps, patterns, drawn shapes, media ids. Parse on the message thread and hand the result over with RtHandoff ( Handoff.h ): publish(shared ptr) on the message thread, get() on the audio thread. Media. Audio files live in one media folder and are referenced by id ( Media.h ). A custom view makes a drop target with BleepView.mediaDrop(element, view.api, (r) => view.api.setData({...data, sample: r.id})) ; setData then calls media::load(id) and publishes the clip with RtHandoff . Modules that record override exportMedia(slot) ; the view saves with view.api.exportMedia(slot) and stores the returned id in its data. Memory. Set s.memoryHeavy = true on modules with large buffers; the board warns when one goes into a Voice Cell. Harmony bus. s.harmony = HarmonyRole::Writer (Harmony Master) or Reader (anything that follows it). Writers run before readers; the state is in ctx.harmony ( dsp/Harmony.h , kHarmonyBuses buses). Voices. Inside a Voice Cell, ctx.voice is the voice's index (−1 outside): use it as a random stream so voices vary but renders repeat. Data the module changes itself. Override takeData(json) (message thread, polled ten times a second) to store node data the module produced, e.g. a captured loop; the engine saves it in the board and calls setData . Custom views. view.api.isPatched(input) tells whether an input has a cable; hideParams: [ids] in the view hooks hides knobs the custom section edits itself. Live values for views. liveValues() for numbers (a playhead), liveArrays() for arrays (a spectrum, register bits). They arrive in the view's onState(st) as st. and st.arrays. .

title: Developer documentation
text: Build with Beautiful Bleep Bleep is GPL-3.0-only with a module exception, so your modules can be closed source or paid; Bleep Bus is MIT. See Licensing. The documentation has five parts, each with its own overview page and its own menu in the sidebar. Section What it is for Start here Bleep Bus Make plugins talk to each other in any DAW: the open protocol, SDK, specification and conformance Bleep Bus overview Bleep Assistant The AI assistant in the board: how it works, how to extend it, how it is measured Assistant overview Development Work on Bleep itself: the plugins in Live, the standalone app, Bleep Play in the browser, and modules Development overview Bleep Script Write modules, message routing and generated patches in code (AssemblyScript and TypeScript) Bleep Script overview Setup and release Install the tools, build everything, cut a release, configure the website Setup overview I want to… I want to… Read Send or receive a per-sample signal from my own plugin Bleep Bus quickstart Add a sound, effect or utility to the board Modules Check an exact contract (module ABI, library) Module ABI, Library Write a module or a patch in code, in the browser Bleep Script Change the Bleep plugins in Live Plugins Change the standalone app Standalone app Change Bleep Play, the board in the browser Web Work on the Bleep Assistant, or measure it Bleep Assistant Set up my computer, build or release Developer setup, Build and release Set an environment variable or option Configuration How the pieces fit Bleep plugins in Live, the Bleep App and Bleep Play in the browser each run an engine and board. They load modules, one .wasm file each, installed from the Bleep Library. The Bleep Bus is a separate open protocol between any plugins. The Architecture overview explains all of this in more depth. Modules are the nodes on the board (oscillators, filters, sequencers). Each is a standalone WebAssembly file, so the same module runs in the plugins, the app and the browser. They are installed from the Bleep Library. Bleep Script is a way to write them in code. Plugins are the VST3s you add in Live. A set has one engine; the first plugin loaded creates it and the others share it. Ports connect a track to the board. The app and the web build run the same board without a DAW. The three can exchange audio, MIDI and sync through bridges. The Bleep Assistant is a chat in the board in which an AI agent helps with a patch. Bleep Bus is separate from all of this: an open protocol for per-sample control signals between any audio plugins.

title: Bleep plugins
text: Bleep plugins The Bleep plugins are VST3s for Ableton Live. Modules are not plugins: they are nodes on the board. In Live you add only: Plugin Live device On the board Bleep Board instrument (MIDI in, audio out) required once per set; stores and opens the board; 16 macros Bleep MIDI In instrument notes, pitch, gate, velocity and CCs from a MIDI track Bleep MIDI Out instrument (VST3 MIDI out) notes, gate/pitch, CCs and bend to another track Bleep Audio In audio effect the track's audio Bleep Audio Out instrument board audio on its own track Bleep Instrument instrument one instrument preset with its panel: MIDI in, its cell, audio out Bleep FX audio effect one effect preset with its panel: the track's audio through its cell, dry/wet Bleep Audio Bridge audio effect connects Live to the standalone Bleep App MIDI In/Out and Audio In/Out have a Board menu ( This set , Bleep App , Bleep Play ): the plugin then talks to that board instead of this set's. How they fit together One engine per process. Every plugin binary contains the engine code. The first Bleep plugin loaded creates the engine and publishes it in the process; the others use it. That binary pins itself so it is never unloaded. The rules, and how the interface may change, are in the Engine ABI: plugins share an engine when their major versions match, and a different minor is fine. Ticks. For each host block, the first plugin to run claims the block number. Bleep Board runs the compiled board in its own process() , with its own track's audio and MIDI of that block: no latency. Plugins on other tracks exchange their block with the engine through small tagged rings: a signal from them reaches the board one block later, and the board's output reaches an Audio Out on another track one block later, whatever order Live runs the tracks in. Bleep Board and the output ports report that latency to Live; the setting 0 host latency for inputs keeps the input's block inside the board instead. Without Bleep Board the first plugin of a block runs the board and every crossing takes two blocks. The board is a JSON document owned by the engine and saved in Bleep Board's state. The page edits a copy and commits it; the engine sanitises it, compiles it (cells are flattened, cycles get a 32-sample feedback delay) and keeps the undo stack. Ports appear on the board on their own and cannot be deleted there. They turn into ghosts, with their cables kept, when their plugin is gone. Build ./bleep build plugins --juce /path/to/JUCE # or BLEEP JUCE DIR; otherwise JUCE 8.0.9 is downloaded ./bleep build plugins # builds, then copies the VST3s to your plugin folder (not while Live is running) ./bleep build plugins --no-install # only build them; --install copies even while Live is running The script builds into build/patch/ and runs the DSP, engine and headless-host tests. VST3 and Live only for now.
