Without the script: cmake -S patch -B build/patch -DBLEEP JUCE DIR=… -DBLEEP FORMATS=VST3 , then cmake --build , with --target BleepMidiIn VST3 and so on to build only some plugins. Build them all when the engine major has changed. Developing in Live Live keeps a plugin's code loaded until it quits, and overwriting a loaded plugin can crash it. So: UI changes (HTML, CSS, JS): build once with --install --ui-dev . These builds read the board UI from patch/ instead of the embedded copy; press ⌘R in the board window after an edit. Never ship --ui-dev builds. DSP, bus or C++ changes: save your test set and run ./bleep run live . It builds first and quits Live only if the build succeeded. It never force-quits Live. Without Live: scripts/run/ui-server.py runs the board UI in a browser with a fake engine, and the engine tests simulate Live's parallel tracks ( ctest --test-dir build/patch ). Talking to other boards A plugin's Board setting chooses the board on its other side. The wire formats between Live, the app and the browser are described in the bridges design document in the repository ( doc/specs/bridges.md ); the app's side is in Standalone app and the browser's in Web. Release Plugins are released to the Bleep Library with scripts/release/release.py . The operating-system signing (macOS Developer ID and notarisation) is separate and not automated. Licences The source is MIT. Binaries built with JUCE are also covered by JUCE's licence (AGPLv3 or a commercial one): check that before you distribute builds.

title: Plugin developers
text: Plugin developers "Plugin" means two different things here. Your own plugin, using Bleep Bus You have a plugin (any format, any DAW) and want it to send or receive per-sample control signals to other plugins. That is Bleep Bus , an open protocol over named shared memory with a small C SDK and C++/JUCE helpers. Step Page Send and receive a signal in 15 minutes Quickstart Every function, type and error API reference Implement the protocol without the SDK Specification v0.1 Prove your implementation is correct Conformance Propose a change to the protocol RFC process The Bleep plugins in Live You want to change or extend the plugins that connect Ableton Live to the board. Bleep plugins covers how they share one engine, how to build and reload them, and how they are released. If you want to add a new sound rather than a new plugin, write a module instead: it works in the plugins, the app and the browser.

title: Build, release and upload
text: Build, release and upload The commands for the things we ship: the standalone app, the plugins, the modules and the web board, plus running the website. More detail: building the standalone app, rebuilding the Live plugins and releasing. All commands run from the repository root ( bleep-patch/ ). Install the tools first: Developer setup. "Release" and "upload" are one step: scripts/release/release.py zips the build, uploads it to the library and publishes it. Versions are immutable, so a fix is a new version. Contents One-time setup (all three) Standalone app Plugins Modules Web board Rebuild Bleep Play in the running website Website (dev and production) One-time setup (all three) A release token (shown once) from the website stack; see "Releasing plugins to the library" in release.md. Do this once: if ~/.bleep-release-token already exists, skip it (the token lasts 90 days): cd website docker compose exec api python -m app.cli token-create "my laptop" --days 90 > ~/.bleep-release-token chmod 600 ~/.bleep-release-token In every new shell , before a release, put the shared options in the environment so the commands below stay short. The export only lasts for that shell, so The token is passed with --token-file (it picks the blp … token out of the file, so the two-line output of token-create works as saved); without it release.py stops with "A release token is required": the library (website address; the API is under /api) export BLEEP REGISTRY URL=http://localhost:8080 Or skip the export and pass the options on every command: --registry http://localhost:8080 --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token . Keep the whole command on one line (or end each line but the last with \ ), otherwise the shell runs the next line as a separate command and fails with "command not found: --token-file". Always rehearse first: add --dry-run (no token needed, changes nothing). --level says what to count up: patch (1.4.2 → 1.4.3), minor (→ 1.5.0), major (→ 2.0.0). Each plugin and each module has its own counter. Standalone app ( bleep-app ) Build (needs CMake 3.22+, a C++ compiler, JUCE 8.0.9; Link 4.1 is downloaded on the first build): Release build of the app target, then starts it ./bleep run app quick check of the last build: prints a report and quits ./bleep run app --no-build --smoke Result: build/patch/BleepApp artefacts/Release/Bleep App.app . Without the script: cmake -S patch -B build/patch -DCMAKE BUILD TYPE=Release -DBLEEP JUCE DIR=/path/to/JUCE cmake --build build/patch --config Release --target BleepApp --parallel Skip the tests: ./bleep run app builds only the app target and runs no tests, so there is nothing to skip. The optional --smoke check is the only test step, so leave it out. If you build the app with ./bleep build plugins (same tree as the plugins), pass --no-test . Release and upload: scripts/release/release.py bleep-app --level patch --dry-run scripts/release/release.py bleep-app --level patch --notes "what changed" --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token The app includes Ableton Link, which makes the binary GPL ( -DBLEEP LINK=OFF for an MIT build). Never ship a BLEEP UI DEV=ON build. The zip is not signed with a Developer ID or notarized by any script. Gatekeeper blocks a downloaded unsigned app until you do that by hand. One release holds this machine's build ( macos-arm64 , …). Add another platform to a published version from the other machine: release.py bleep-app --add-platform latest . Plugins (VST3) Library ids: bleep-board , bleep-midi-in , bleep-midi-out , bleep-audio-in , bleep-audio-out , bleep-instrument , bleep-fx . Build and install only the VST3s (no tests, no standalone app; the fast path): ./bleep build plugins --juce ../bastelbox/brilliant-bleep/plugins/JUCE --plugins-only --no-app --install Give --juce (or set BLEEP JUCE DIR ) on every run. Without it the script falls back to downloading JUCE 8.0.9 into build/patch/ deps , a different path, and everything is compiled again. --install copies the VST3s to ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 (quit Live first); leave it out to only build. The full build (the plugins and the app, then the DSP, engine and bridge tests): ./bleep build plugins --juce ../bastelbox/brilliant-bleep/plugins/JUCE build the tests but do not run them ./bleep build plugins --juce ../bastelbox/brilliant-bleep/plugins/JUCE --no-test Skip the tests: --no-test only skips running them; --plugins-only does not build them either. release.py --build runs ./bleep build plugins --plugins-only (no tests, no test targets), so after a ./bleep build plugins --plugins-only run it has nothing left to compile. Run the tests separately with plain ./bleep build plugins before a release. Modules are not part of the plugins. With the wasm module host ( BLEEP WASMTIME DIR , found by default in build/wasm-spike/wasmtime ) and BLEEP BUNDLE MODULES=OFF , the plugins carry no modules. They load the .bleepmod packages installed on the machine, from the same data folder the standalone app installs into ( library::defaultDataDir() , ~/Library/Application Support/Bleep on macOS). The app and the plugins share one module installation. What compiles every module in is the test targets ( bleep module harness , bleep wasm parity , ...), which are the reference the wasm builds are checked against. --no-test only skips running them; --plugins-only does not build them either (the command at the top of this section). What the options do. --plugins-only skips the test targets, but still builds the standalone app ( BleepApp ) in the same tree; --no-app turns it off ( -DBLEEP BUILD APP=OFF ), so only the seven plugins and Bleep Audio Bridge are built. Install the app and its modules once through the app; the plugins pick the installed modules up from the data folder. The settings are kept in build/patch/CMakeCache.txt , so a later run without --no-app turns the app back on (the script passes ON again). To build a single plugin, name its CMake target ( BleepBoard VST3 , BleepMidiIn VST3 , BleepMidiOut VST3 , BleepAudioIn VST3 , BleepAudioOut VST3 , BleepInstrument VST3 , BleepFx VST3 , BleepAudioBridge VST3 ) after the first configure: cmake --build build/patch --target BleepBoard VST3 --parallel If BLEEP WASMTIME DIR is empty (no Wasmtime under build/wasm-spike ), the plugins fall back to compiling all modules in. Check with grep BLEEP WASMTIME DIR build/patch/CMakeCache.txt . Bundles end up in build/patch/ artefacts/Release/VST3/ . Plugins share one engine only when the engine major ( kAbiTag ) matches: rebuild and release all of them if it changed. Release and upload ( --list shows the ids): scripts/release/release.py bleep-board --level 1.x --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token scripts/release/release.py --all --level patch --dry-run scripts/release/release.py --all --level patch --notes "what changed" --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token runs ./bleep build plugins first scripts/release/release.py --all --build --level patch --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token The product version is project(BleepBoard VERSION …) in patch/CMakeLists.txt ; plugins and app take it from there. For a tagged release also tag plugin-vX.Y.Z (see "The manual release" in release.md). Modules Modules are WebAssembly ( .bleepmod packages). One .wasm build, one package and one release serve the web board, the standalone app and the plugins, so local and web stay in sync. The native apps load the same .wasm files through Wasmtime; build-web.sh is the only module build. Building needs emcc (the Emscripten SDK), python3 and node, or Docker. Local emsdk (recommended, fast). The SDK lives next to the repository, in ../emsdk , pinned to 4.0.10 like CI and the Docker image. One-time install: git clone https://github.com/emscripten-core/emsdk.git ../emsdk ../emsdk/emsdk install 4.0.10 && ../emsdk/emsdk activate 4.0.10 In every new shell , before building (it only puts emcc on the PATH of that shell; run the build in the same terminal): source ../emsdk/emsdk env.sh Then: build/web/modules/ .wasm + manifest.json scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only One module only (or a few): name the module folders in BLEEP WEB ONLY , comma separated (the names under patch/modules/ ). The other modules already in build/web/modules stay in the manifest. The Docker variant passes the variable through too. BLEEP WEB ONLY=reverb scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only BLEEP WEB ONLY=reverb,filter scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only Then package and release just that module (see below): package-module.py reverb , release.py --modules reverb --level patch . Modules that use juce core need the one-time JUCE build described above, which a single-module run triggers by itself. The emsdk brings its own Node and Python, which come first on the PATH in that shell. If conda's Python gets in the way, run conda deactivate first. The first build also clones JUCE into build/web/JUCE and compiles juce core once. Docker (no local install, slow on Apple Silicon). The emscripten/emsdk image is amd64 , so on an M-series Mac every compiler call runs under x86 emulation. Use it where there is no emsdk, e.g. on a machine you only release from: same build, in the Emscripten image scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker --modules-only The per-module cache is in build/web/modules/.cache . Use one method (local or Docker) consistently: the cache key includes the compiler command and paths, so switching probably rebuilds every module. Skip the tests: none of the module steps ( build-web.sh , package-module.py , release.py --modules ) run a test suite, so there is nothing to skip. Packaging does check each .wasm against the module ABI, and that check can't be turned off. Package (checks each .wasm against website/content/developers/modules/module-abi.md , writes reproducible zips to build/library/modules/ ): every module with a built .wasm scripts/release/package-module.py just these scripts/release/package-module.py reverb filter Release and upload. Each module counts its own version, and a module whose content did not change since its newest published version is skipped ( --force overrides). Both the app and the web board install modules from the library, so this one release reaches both: scripts/release/release.py --modules --package --level patch --dry-run all changed modules scripts/release/release.py --modules --package --level patch --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token one module scripts/release/release.py --modules reverb --level minor --token-file ~/.bleep-release-token --package runs package-module.py first; leave it out to release what is already in build/library/modules/ . Web board The board UI and web engine are built by build-web.sh (the modules too, unless you skip them). The board doesn't load the .wasm files from its own folder: it installs its modules from the library as packages, so a module reaches the web only through the release steps above. the whole site: UI, web engine and modules, into build/web/site scripts/build/build-web.sh only the UI and the web engine (seconds, no Emscripten or JUCE needed; what the website image does) scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules same, in the Emscripten image scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker look at the result python3 -m http.server -d build/web/site 8000 The website is deployed by rebuilding its containers (see website.md); deploying from CI is not set up yet. A change to the board UI needs a website deploy; a change to a module needs only the module release. Rebuild Bleep Play in the running website build-web.sh writes the board UI to build/web/site and nothing more: a website that is already running does not see it. Its /play/ files come from inside the website stack, so what you do depends on how the stack runs. Either way, only the board UI and the web engine ( patch/board , patch/web ) are involved. Modules are not part of the site; they come from the library. Dev stack ( docker-compose.dev.yml , see below). The one-shot play service runs build-web.sh --no-modules itself and copies the result into website/app/public/play , which next dev serves. You do not need to run build-web.sh first. With the stack up: docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml -f website/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file website/.env run --rm play Reload http://localhost:8080/play/ (hard reload if the old UI stays). Modules and UI in one go (dev stack). After changing a module as well as the board UI, one script does both: it runs build-web.sh --modules-only (which publishes the modules to website/app/public/play/local-modules ) and then the play service above. ./bleep run play modules built in the Emscripten image ./bleep run play --docker Reload Bleep Play afterwards. It takes the local modules by itself. This is for development only; users get modules through the release steps above. Production stack ( ./bleep run site ). The site container is read-only and its files are baked into the image, so copying build/web/site into it does not work (and would be lost on the next restart). The image build runs build-web.sh --no-modules itself; rebuild the image and recreate the container: ./bleep run site up Only the changed layers run again; the database and the library keep their data. Then open http://localhost:8080/play/. If you ran build-web.sh only to check the result ( python3 -m http.server -d build/web/site 8000 ), that is a separate preview and has no effect on either stack. Website (dev and production) The site is the docs and homepage ( website/app , Next.js, static export), the board UI, and the library backend: Caddy, the API (FastAPI), PostgreSQL and the library's storage (SeaweedFS). All of it runs with Docker Compose from website/ . The image has the board UI but no modules ; they come from the library (see Modules). Details, the admin user: website.md. One-time: copy the config and fill it in (database password, first admin, storage keys): cp website/.env.example website/.env Production (static export behind Caddy, built into the image; about a minute): build the images and start everything: http://localhost:8080 ./bleep run site after changing website/content, website/app, the board UI or module docs: rebuild and restart ./bleep run site up rebuild from scratch, without Docker's layer cache ./bleep run site rebuild follow the logs ./bleep run site logs stop (the database and the library keep their data; docker compose down -v in website/ deletes it) ./bleep run site down On a real server set BLEEP COOKIE SECURE=true (the site is served over HTTPS) and BLEEP SITE PORT if 8080 is taken. Deploying is rebuilding the containers on the server; deploying from CI is not set up yet. A module release needs no website deploy. Development ( next dev with hot reload behind the same Caddy routes, no image rebuild; needs Docker Compose 2.24+): docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml -f website/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file website/.env up Open http://localhost:8080. After editing website/content or a module's doc/ , regenerate the docs: docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml -f website/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file website/.env restart dev After editing the board UI ( patch/board , patch/web ), rebuild it into the site: docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml -f website/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file website/.env run --rm play Without Docker (docs and pages only, no API or library): cd website/app && npm install , then npm run dev (http://localhost:3000) or npm run build (static export to website/app/out/ ).

title: Configuration (.env)
text: Configuration ( website/.env ) The site is configured through one file, website/.env . Docker Compose reads it ( --env-file website/.env ) and hands the values to the containers. Start from the template: cp website/.env.example website/.env The file holds secrets and is git-ignored: never commit it. Lines starting with # are comments. A value that contains $ (the password hash below) goes in single quotes, otherwise Compose expands it. After changing the file, recreate the containers: docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml --env-file website/.env up -d . Production checklist POSTGRES PASSWORD and S3 SECRET KEY set to long random values. BLEEP COOKIE SECURE=true and BLEEP PUBLIC URL set to the real https:// address. BLEEP ADMIN PASSWORD removed again after the first start. Optionally BLEEP BASIC AUTH HASH set, to keep an installation private while it is online. Database and storage Variable Default Meaning POSTGRES PASSWORD none, required Password of the bleep user in PostgreSQL. Compose refuses to start without it. S3 ACCESS KEY bleep Access key of the object storage (SeaweedFS) that holds releases and preset files. S3 SECRET KEY none, required Secret key of the object storage. Also used by the release script when it uploads. BLEEP REGISTRY BUCKET bleep-registry Name of the storage bucket. It is created on start if missing. Caddy serves it read-only at /registry/ . BLEEP S3 PORT 8333 Port on 127.0.0.1 where the storage S3 API listens, for the release script. Never published to the network. Site and accounts Variable Default Meaning BLEEP SITE PORT 8080 Port on the host where the site (Caddy) listens. TLS ends in front of this port, in a load balancer or reverse proxy. BLEEP PUBLIC URL http://localhost:8080 The address people reach the site at, without a trailing slash. The links in emails (confirmation, password reset) point here. BLEEP COOKIE SECURE true Send the session cookie over HTTPS only. Must be true in production. Set false only for local http://localhost development; .env.example ships with false . BLEEP ADMIN EMAIL empty Email of the first admin. If this and the password are set and no user has the email yet, the account is created when the API starts. BLEEP ADMIN PASSWORD empty Password of that first admin. Remove it from the file after the first start. BLEEP ALLOWED ORIGINS empty Extra hosts (comma separated host[:port] ) that may send cookie-authenticated writes to the API, for example a development server on another port. Not in .env.example ; add the line when you need it. Email Registration confirmation, password reset and the contact form send email. Without BLEEP SMTP HOST nothing is sent: each message, link included, is written to the API log ( docker compose logs api ), which is how to try it locally. Variable Default Meaning BLEEP SMTP HOST empty SMTP server, for example smtp.gmail.com . Empty means log only. BLEEP SMTP PORT 587 SMTP port (STARTTLS). BLEEP SMTP USER empty SMTP login. For Gmail, turn on 2-step verification and create an app password. BLEEP SMTP PASSWORD empty SMTP password (the app password for Gmail, without spaces). BLEEP SMTP FROM the SMTP user Sender address of outgoing messages. BLEEP CONTACT TO the SMTP user Where the contact form delivers messages. BLEEP EMAIL VERIFICATION true true : registering sends a confirmation link. false : nobody is asked to confirm (password reset still works). Password for the whole site Keeps an online installation private: Caddy asks for a user name and password (HTTP basic auth) before it serves anything. It is off while the hash is empty. Variable Default Meaning BLEEP BASIC AUTH USER bleep User name the browser asks for. BLEEP BASIC AUTH HASH empty bcrypt hash of the password. Empty means no password. Make the hash and paste it in single quotes : docker run --rm caddy:2-alpine caddy hash-password --plaintext 'the-password' BLEEP BASIC AUTH USER=bleep BLEEP BASIC AUTH HASH='$2a$14$...' The password covers everything, /api and /registry included, so the Bleep App and Bleep Play cannot use a protected site. It does not replace HTTPS: basic auth sends the password with every request, so serve the site over HTTPS only. Only the production Caddyfile has it; Caddyfile.dev does not. Other variables These are not in .env.example . They are read by the API or by scripts, mostly when run outside Compose. Variable Default Meaning BLEEP DATABASE URL local PostgreSQL URL Database connection. Compose builds it from POSTGRES PASSWORD ; set it yourself only when running the API directly ( uvicorn , tests use in-memory SQLite). BLEEP RELEASE TOKEN , BLEEP REGISTRY URL unset Used by the release script to publish to a library. See build and release.

title: Developer setup
text: Developer setup What to install before you build anything in this repository. You do not need all of it: pick the goal you have and install only that row's tools. I want to… You need Jump to Write or change a module Git, Python 3, Node 22, Emscripten 4.0.10 (or Docker) Modules Change the plugins or the standalone app Git, CMake 3.22+, a C++ compiler, JUCE 8.0.9 Plugins and app Change Bleep Play (the board UI, the web engine) Git, Python 3, Node 22 Bleep Play Work on the website , the API or the library Git, Docker with Compose 2.24+ Website Release anything Python 3, the website stack Build, release and upload The commands in these pages are written for macOS and Linux and run from the repository root ( bleep-patch/ ). Everything: get the code git clone bleep cd bleep/bleep-patch Keep sibling tools next to the repository, not inside it: the instructions below put the Emscripten SDK in ../emsdk . Modules A module is a folder in patch/modules/ and compiles to one .wasm file that the plugins, the app and Bleep Play all load. The only module build is scripts/build/build-web.sh , which needs Emscripten. Python 3 and Node 22. Check with python3 --version and node --version . Node 22 is what CI and the Docker images use. The Emscripten SDK, pinned to 4.0.10 (same version as CI and the Docker image). One time: git clone https://github.com/emscripten-core/emsdk.git ../emsdk ../emsdk/emsdk install 4.0.10 && ../emsdk/emsdk activate 4.0.10 In every new shell before building, so that emcc is on the PATH of that shell: source ../emsdk/emsdk env.sh If conda's Python gets in the way, run conda deactivate first. No local SDK? Use Docker instead and add --docker to every build-web.sh call. It works anywhere but is slow on Apple Silicon, because the image is amd64 . Pick one method and stay with it: the module cache is keyed on the compiler command and paths. The first build clones JUCE 8.0.9 into build/web/JUCE and compiles juce core once; later builds are cached. To use a JUCE checkout you already have, set BLEEP JUCE DIR . Try it with one existing module: BLEEP WEB ONLY=reverb scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only The result is build/web/modules/reverb.wasm plus manifest.json . Native tests (optional but what CI runs for DSP changes): CMake 3.22+ and Ninja, then cmake -S patch -B build/light -G Ninja -DBLEEP LIGHT TESTS=ON cmake --build build/light && ctest --test-dir build/light This compiles only juce core , no plugins, so it needs no plugin SDKs. Next: Writing a module, then publishing. To see a module in a browser, rebuild Bleep Play (below) and load it from the library, or release it to a library on your local website stack. Plugins and app The Bleep plugins (VST3, for Ableton Live) and the Bleep App are one CMake project in patch/ . CMake 3.22 or newer and a C++ compiler: the Xcode command line tools on macOS ( xcode-select --install ), Visual Studio on Windows. Ninja is optional. JUCE 8.0.9. The build downloads it for you. To use your own checkout, pass --juce to the scripts or set BLEEP JUCE DIR . Internet on the first app build: Ableton Link 4.1 is fetched (set BLEEP LINK DIR for a local copy). Ableton Live to try the plugins. The app and Bleep Play need no DAW. Try it: build the app, then start it ./bleep run app build the plugins, run the DSP, engine and bridge tests, copy the VST3s to ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 ./bleep build plugins --install While you edit the board UI ( patch/board/ui , HTML/CSS/JS), ./bleep run app --ui-dev reads it from patch/ instead of the embedded copy: edit, then press Cmd-R in the board window. The Link library makes the app binary GPL. Build with -DBLEEP LINK=OFF if it has to stay MIT. Details: standalone app, plugins. Bleep Play The board UI and the web engine build in seconds and need neither Emscripten nor JUCE: scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules python3 -m http.server -d build/web/site 8000 Open http://localhost:8000. This is a plain static preview; the board installs its modules from a library, which a bare file server does not have. To see Bleep Play with modules, run it inside the website stack: Rebuild Bleep Play in the running website. More: Bleep Play. Website The website is the docs, the homepage, the board at /play/ , the accounts API and the library, all started with Docker Compose from website/ . Docker with Compose 2.24 or newer ( docker compose version ). The dev stack uses !reset , which older versions reject. Configuration. Copy the template and fill it in (database password and storage secret are required; everything is described in Configuration): cp website/.env.example website/.env For plain http://localhost also set BLEEP COOKIE SECURE=false , or the browser drops the session cookie. Start it. Production style (static export behind Caddy, about a minute to build) or the dev stack with hot reload: ./bleep run site docker compose -f website/docker-compose.yml -f website/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file website/.env up Both serve http://localhost:8080. Without Docker you can only work on docs and pages: cd website/app && npm install && npm run dev (http://localhost:3000), with no API and no library. The docs live in website/content as Markdown. After editing them in the dev stack, restart the dev service; the commands are in Build, release and upload. Check your setup If this works… …then you are set for BLEEP WEB ONLY=reverb scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only modules ./bleep run app --smoke the app and the plugins scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules Bleep Play http://localhost:8080 shows the site the website python3 scripts/check/check-repo.py the repository rules CI enforces (licence headers, module provenance, dependencies between parts) Running the tests Every part has its own unit tests (CTest, pytest, Node scripts). Which command runs which suite is in Running unit tests. Releasing Releasing needs a release token from your own website stack. The one-time steps and every release command are in Build, release and upload.

title: Running unit tests
text: Running unit tests The repository has one test suite per part. Run the ones for the part you changed; the setup for each is in Developer setup. All commands run from the repository root ( bleep-patch/ ). I changed… Run Needs DSP, a module, the engine Native tests (CTest) CMake, a C++ compiler The bus library ( bus/ ) Bus tests CMake, a C++ compiler Board UI or the web engine ( patch/web ) Bleep Play tests Node 22 Bleep Script ( patch/script ) Bleep Script tests Node 22 The website API ( website/api ) API tests Python 3 The patch assistant ( agent/ ) Agent tests Python 3 Release scripts ( scripts/release ) Release script tests Python 3 Native tests (CTest) The quick way compiles only juce core , with no plugins and no plugin SDKs: cmake -S patch -B build/light -G Ninja -DBLEEP LIGHT TESTS=ON cmake --build build/light && ctest --test-dir build/light --output-on-failure It runs the DSP, utility DSP and module tests. Run one test by name, for example patch.dsp : ctest --test-dir build/light -R patch.dsp --output-on-failure To also run the engine, bridge and plugin tests, use the full build, which compiles the plugins and runs ctest at the end: ./bleep build plugins Bus tests cmake -S bus -B build/bus -DCMAKE BUILD TYPE=Release cmake --build build/bus --config Release ctest --test-dir build/bus -C Release --output-on-failure Bleep Play tests Plain Node scripts, one per area, without a test framework. A script exits non-zero when it fails. Some of them test the built site, so build it first ( scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules ). node patch/web/test/library-client-test.mjs node patch/web/test/board-code-test.mjs node patch/web/test/graph-test.mjs build/web/site The other files in patch/web/test/ run the same way; the full list that CI runs is in .github/workflows/ci.yml . To run all of them, loop over the folder (the ones that need the built site take build/web/site as argument): for t in patch/web/test/ -test.mjs; do node "$t" build/web/site break; done Bleep Script tests cd patch/script npm ci --no-audit --no-fund npm test Website API tests pytest, with an in-memory SQLite database, so no Docker and no .env are needed: python3 -m venv .venv-api && .venv-api/bin/pip install -r website/api/requirements-dev.txt cd website/api && ../../.venv-api/bin/pytest Run one file or one test with pytest tests/test registry.py or pytest -k login . Agent tests python3 -m venv .venv-agent && .venv-agent/bin/pip install -e "agent[dev]" .venv-agent/bin/pytest agent/tests The tests do not call a model API. The evaluation workbench ( bleep-agent eval run ) does, and costs money, so it is not part of the unit tests. Release script tests cd scripts/release && python3 -m unittest test release test package module Repository rules Not unit tests, but CI enforces them and they run in seconds: python3 scripts/check/check-repo.py python3 scripts/check/check-api-docs.py

title: Bleep Bus specification v0.1
text: Bleep Bus specification, version 0.1 (experimental) Bleep Bus lets audio plugins exchange per-sample control signals through named operating-system shared memory. This document specifies the bus exactly enough to implement it without the reference SDK. If you only want to use the bus, read the Quickstart and the API reference instead. Status: 0.x is experimental. Every minor version MAY change the layout; implementations MUST refuse to share a segment with a different 0.x minor version. From 1.0 on, compatibility is guaranteed within a major version. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Model A bus is one shared-memory segment, identified by a namespace . An endpoint is one plugin instance. It has a stable 64-bit UID . An endpoint owns outputs and inputs (together: ports), each with a name unique per endpoint and direction. A connection (cable) links an input to a source (endpoint UID, output name) with an amount . Connections are stored with the input, i.e. with the receiving endpoint. Audio threads exchange blocks : an output publishes one block of samples per processing cycle; an input reads, for each connection, the block the source wrote for the reader's previous block (one block of latency). Contents Naming — segment names and namespaces Layout — every byte of the segment Memory ordering — atomics, seqlocks and the registry lock Registry — endpoints, ports, reclamation of dead processes Timing — block stamps and the block selection rules Signals — value conventions ("virtual volts") Connections and state — cables, amounts and the saved-state format Versioning and extensions

title: Naming
text: 1. Naming A namespace is 1 to 16 characters from [a-z0-9 -] . The default namespace is default . An implementation SHOULD use the value of the environment variable BLEEP BUS NAMESPACE when the plugin does not choose one; this lets users and test hosts separate buses (for example two DAWs running at once). The segment name is built from the major spec version and the namespace: Platform Name API macOS, Linux, other POSIX /bleepbus-v0- shm open , mmap Windows Local\bleepbus-v0- CreateFileMappingA on the paging file, MapViewOfFile macOS limits POSIX shared-memory names to 31 characters, which is why the namespace is limited to 16. The segment MUST be created with permissions for the current user only (POSIX mode 0600 ). It is never unlinked during normal operation: plugins come and go, the segment stays. Tools MAY unlink it when no host is running. Creating and opening Open the object with create permission ( O RDWR O CREAT ). If its size is 0, set it to the v0.1 total size (17 187 072 bytes). The operating system MAY round the size up to whole pages; a size at least the total size is valid. If two processes race, one resize fails harmlessly; re-read the size. Map the first 17 187 072 bytes read/write. Initialise: compare-and-swap header.init state from 0 to 1. The winner writes the header (section 2) and then stores 2 with release semantics. Everyone else waits (up to 2 s) until init state reads 2. If the initialiser has crashed (its process is gone, or it never recorded itself), exactly one waiter MAY take over after the timeout: it claims the initialiser field, resets the header and stores 2. A waiter MUST NOT take over from a live initialiser. Validate the header (magic, version, sizes, offsets). On a mismatch the implementation MUST NOT touch the segment and reports a version error.

title: Layout
text: 2. Layout All integers are little-endian with natural alignment and no packing. Strings are NUL-terminated UTF-8 within fixed-size fields. Reserved bytes MUST be zero when written and MUST be ignored when read. The reference header bus/include/bleep bus layout.h declares the same structures in C with static size checks. Segment Offset Size Content 0 256 header 256 64 × 256 = 16 384 endpoint table 16 640 512 × 576 = 294 912 input table 311 552 256 × 65 920 = 16 875 520 output table 17 187 072 total Header (256 bytes) Offset Type Field Value / meaning 0 u32 magic 0x53554242 ("BBUS") 4 u16 spec major 0 6 u16 spec minor 1 8 u32 header bytes 256 12 u32 init state atomic ; 0 empty, 1 initialising, 2 ready 16 u64 total bytes 17 187 072 24 u32 max endpoints 64 28 u32 max outputs 256 32 u32 max inputs 512 36 u32 max connections per input 8 40 u32 max block samples 4096 44 u32 output slots 4 48 u64 endpoints offset 256 56 u64 inputs offset 16 640 64 u64 outputs offset 311 552 72 u32 registry lock atomic ; 0 free, else PID of the holder 76 u32 registry generation atomic ; +1 on any endpoint or port change 80 u32 connection generation atomic ; +1 on any cable change 84 u32 reserved 0 88 u8[168] reserved 0 Endpoint record (256 bytes) Offset Type Field Meaning 0 u32 state atomic ; 0 free, 1 active 4 u32 pid owning process 8 u64 uid atomic ; stable instance ID, never 0 16 u32 patch version atomic ; +1 when a cable into this endpoint changes 20 u32 reserved 24 u64 last block ns atomic ; time of the last block begin 32 char[64] display name user-facing instance name 96 char[64] track name host track name, may be empty 160 char[32] vendor 192 char[32] product 224 u8[32] reserved Input record (576 bytes) Offset Type Field Meaning 0 u32 state atomic ; 0 free, 1 active 4 u32 endpoint index owner's index in the endpoint table 8 u64 name hash FNV-1a 64 of name 16 u32 seq atomic seqlock over connections (odd while changing) 20 u32 signal type see section 6 24 char[32] name 56 u8[8] reserved 64 connection[8] connections 8 × 64 bytes Connection (64 bytes): Offset Type Field Meaning 0 u32 state 0 free, 1 active (guarded by the input's seq ) 4 u32 amount bits atomic ; IEEE-754 binary32 bits of the amount 8 u64 source uid guarded by seq 16 u64 output hash FNV-1a 64 of output name , guarded by seq 24 char[32] output name 56 u8[8] reserved Output record (65 920 bytes) Offset Type Field Meaning 0 u32 state atomic ; 0 free, 1 active 4 u32 endpoint index 8 u64 endpoint uid atomic ; mirrors the owner's UID 16 u64 name hash FNV-1a 64 of name 24 u64 blocks written atomic ; number of completed blocks 32 u32 incarnation atomic ; +1 each time the record is allocated 36 u32 signal type 40 u32 polarity 0 bipolar, 1 unipolar 44 u32 reserved 48 char[32] name 80 u8[48] reserved 128 slot[4] slots 4 × 16 448 bytes Output slot (16 448 bytes): Offset Type Field Meaning 0 u32 seq atomic seqlock; odd while the writer fills the slot 4 u32 num samples 1..4096 8 u32 flags bit 0: transport playing 12 u32 reserved 16 i64 transport sample pos stamp: transport position of samples[0] 24 u64 time ns stamp: monotonic time the block began 32 u64 block index value of blocks written before this block was published 40 u8[24] reserved 64 f32[4096] samples Block k of an output is stored in slot k mod 4 . Hash name hash and output hash are 64-bit FNV-1a over the UTF-8 bytes (offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325 , prime 0x100000001b3 ). Hashes speed up lookups; equality of names is decided by the hash on the audio thread and by the full string elsewhere.

title: Memory ordering
text: 3. Memory ordering Fields marked atomic MUST be read and written with atomic operations of their full width: loads with acquire, stores with release semantics, unless stated otherwise. All other fields are plain memory protected by one of the three mechanisms below. 3.1 Registry lock (non-real-time only) Every change to the endpoint, input or output tables, and every change to a connection, happens while holding header.registry lock : Acquire: compare-and-swap 0 → own PID. While it fails, yield; after a few attempts, sleep 1 ms between attempts. If the holder's process no longer exists, a waiter MAY take the lock over with compare-and-swap holder PID → own PID. Give up after 2 s ( BB ERR TIMEOUT ). Release: store 0. The lock MUST NOT be taken on an audio thread. Readers that need consistent strings (names in listings) SHOULD take it too. 3.2 Seqlocks (audio thread readers) Output slots and the connection list of an input use sequence locks. Writer (holding the slot exclusively; for inputs, holding the registry lock): s = load relaxed(seq); store relaxed(seq, s + 1); / odd: writing / fence release(); / write the protected fields / store release(seq, s + 2); / even: consistent / Reader: s1 = load acquire(seq); if (s1 & 1) retry or skip; / copy the protected fields / fence acquire(); s2 = load relaxed(seq); if (s1 != s2) retry or skip; A reader on an audio thread MUST NOT spin on a seqlock; it skips the candidate and uses another block or its held value (section 5). 3.3 Publication order To activate a record, fill every field first, then store state = 1 with release. To change an output owner's UID, store endpoint uid (atomic) and then increment registry generation . Readers on the audio thread cache the mapping of a cable to an output index and recompute it only when registry generation or the input's seq changes. Before using a cached output they re-check state , incarnation and endpoint uid .

title: Registry
text: 4. Registry 4.1 Endpoints To register, under the registry lock: Reclaim dead endpoints (4.3). If the requested UID is 0, or already owned by an active endpoint, generate random non-zero UIDs until one is free. A plugin whose saved UID was taken (the user duplicated the device) MUST save the new UID. Take the first free endpoint record, fill it, store state = 1 . Increment registry generation . UIDs are chosen by plugins and saved in their state, so cables survive closing and reopening a set. A plugin SHOULD register immediately (with a random UID) and switch to its saved UID when the host restores its state ( bb set instance uid ); the switch fails with BB ERR UID IN USE if that UID is live elsewhere. 4.2 Ports Outputs and inputs are records in their own tables with the owner's endpoint index. Names: 1..31 bytes of UTF-8, no control characters, no / . Unique per endpoint and direction (an input and an output MAY share a name). Stable: cables refer to outputs by name. Renaming an output breaks existing cables to it. Convention: the bus input for modulating a parameter carries the parameter's display name, e.g. Cutoff . To allocate an output: set blocks written = 0 , increment incarnation , fill the remaining fields, store state = 1 , increment registry generation . An input is reset with its seqlock held odd and its connections zeroed. Limits per bus: 64 endpoints, 256 outputs, 512 inputs; per endpoint the reference SDK allows 64 outputs and 64 inputs. 4.3 Reclamation An active endpoint whose pid is not a live process (POSIX: kill(pid, 0) fails with ESRCH ; Windows: the process cannot be opened or has exited) is dead. On registration (and MAY on other occasions) implementations free it: its outputs and inputs (with their connections) are freed, the endpoint record is freed, and both generations are incremented. Unregistering frees an endpoint the same way. Cables from a removed endpoint stay stored at their receivers and read silence ("ghost source") until an endpoint with that UID and output name appears again. 4.4 Addressing Bridges (OSC, network) address ports as / / / , where each segment is the corresponding name lower-cased, with runs of characters outside [a-z0-9] replaced by - . Example: track "Bass", instance "Function 1", output "A" → /bass/function-1/a . Inside the bus, ports are addressed by (endpoint UID, port name) .

title: Timing
text: 5. Timing Hosts such as Ableton Live process tracks on parallel threads in no guaranteed order. The bus therefore has a fixed latency of one block : a reader sees what a writer produced for the reader's previous block. The result does not depend on which thread ran first, so a set renders the same way every time, including offline export. 5.1 Blocks Every block of every endpoint is framed by begin/end and carries: num samples (1..4096). Hosts with larger blocks MUST split them; peers then split the same way. transport sample pos : the host's transport position of the first sample. playing : the transport runs (also during offline export). time ns : a monotonic, system-wide clock (macOS CLOCK UPTIME RAW , Linux CLOCK MONOTONIC , Windows QueryPerformanceCounter ) or a host supplied equivalent. 5.2 Writing For each output, once per block, the writer fills slot blocks written mod 4 under its seqlock with the block's stamps and samples, sets block index = blocks written , then increments blocks written (release). Writing again within the same block rewrites the same slot. Outputs not written during a block publish zeros at block end. 5.3 Selecting the block to read Let W be blocks written of the source output and prev the reader's previous block. Candidates are blocks W−1 , W−2 , W−3 (newest first); a candidate is only valid if its seqlock reads consistently and its block index equals its number. Position rule. If the reader's previous and current blocks are both playing, choose the newest playing candidate whose transport sample pos == prev.transport sample pos . Time rule. Otherwise, or if rule 1 finds nothing, choose the newest candidate with time ns + guard <= current.time ns , where guard = 0.5 × num samples / sample rate (1 ms if the rate is unknown). This picks a block from an earlier processing cycle. Hold. If neither rule finds a block, the reader repeats the last sample it read from that connection (0 at first). Rule 1 is exact and deterministic, also when loops repeat positions and when export runs faster than real time. Rule 2 covers a stopped transport and peers that just appeared. If the chosen block is shorter than the reader's block, the remainder holds the block's last sample. 5.4 Consequences Modulation arrives one block late. At 256 samples and 48 kHz that is 5.3 ms: inaudible for modulation, unsuitable for phase-critical audio. A self-patched endpoint (output into its own input) works and also has one block of latency. Live's delay compensation does not know about the bus. These rules are what Phase 0 of the project measures in real hosts; they may be refined before 1.0.

title: Signals
text: 6. Signals All signals are 32-bit floats, one per sample, in virtual volts , chosen so that bridges to CV hardware and VCV Rack map directly. Type Value Rule Virtual volts control (0) bipolar −1..+1 or unipolar 0..1 Polarity declared per output ±1 ≈ ±5 V gate (1) high ≥ 0.5 high ≈ +5 V trigger (2) one sample of 1.0, otherwise 0.0 Readers that decimate MUST take the maximum of the span pitch (3) 1.0 per octave 0.0 = C4 = MIDI note 60 1 V/oct audio (4) reserved MUST NOT be used in v0.1 Types and polarity are advisory: any output may be connected to any input. Values outside the nominal range are allowed (a sum of cables may exceed it); receivers clamp where it matters. 6.1 Applying modulation to a parameter A receiving plugin SHOULD apply an input to a parameter as an offset in the parameter's normalised range (0..1), inside its DSP: effective = clamp(knob normalised + Σ source i × amount i, 0, 1) It MUST NOT move the host-visible parameter (no automation writes, no undo entries). Parameters with exponential mappings (cutoff, rates) are thus modulated in octaves.

title: Connections and state
text: 7. Connections and state 7.1 Cables An input holds up to 8 connections. Each is (source UID, output name, amount) . Its value is the sum over connections whose source exists of sample × amount . The amount is a finite float, clamped to ±1000. Any process MAY add, change or remove a cable into any registered input (this is how a patchbay in one plugin window edits another plugin), under the registry lock: Add : seqlock odd, fill a free connection, state = 1 , seqlock even. Change amount of an existing cable: atomic store of amount bits only; no seqlock. Remove : seqlock odd, zero the connection, seqlock even. After any of these: increment the owner's patch version and connection generation . A receiving plugin watches its patch version and tells its host that its state changed, so the set is marked as modified. 7.2 Saved state Cables belong to the receiving instance and are saved in its plugin state. The reference format is UTF-8 text, one cable per line, fields separated by a tab: bleep-bus-connections 1 The amount is written as [-]digits.digits (six fraction digits) and parsed without the C locale, so it is stable across user locales. Readers accept CRLF line ends, a missing final newline and + / - signs; lines naming inputs the endpoint does not have are ignored. Loading replaces all cables of the endpoint's inputs and increments connection generation , but not patch version (loading is not an edit).

title: Versioning and extensions
text: 8. Versioning and extensions 8.0 Hostile peers The segment is created with mode 0600 , so peers are same-user processes that may be buggy or hostile. Implementations MUST validate what they read from shared memory: Table offsets and sizes come from the layout constants, not from a second read of the header. Header values are validated once, at open. An endpoint index outside the endpoint table makes a record invalid; listings skip it. Strings are copied with a bound and always NUL-terminated. Non-finite samples and amounts are treated as 0; amounts are clamped to the documented range, and a sum that overflows to Inf is treated as 0. Before each write, a writer re-checks that the output record is still its own ( state , endpoint uid , incarnation ). Process IDs of 0 or above INT32 MAX are invalid and never probed. Known limits: Truncation. A same-user peer that shrinks the segment with ftruncate makes later accesses to the removed pages raise SIGBUS in every process that maps it. The audio thread cannot re-check the size without a system call, and POSIX named shared memory cannot be sealed. PID namespaces. Dead endpoints are reaped with kill(pid, 0) . Processes in separate PID namespaces (containers) that share one segment can look dead to each other. Run all peers of a bus in one PID namespace. The segment name carries the major version. The header carries major and minor. 0.x : implementations MUST match major and minor exactly and report BB ERR VERSION MISMATCH otherwise. From 1.0 : a minor version MAY only use reserved bytes and MUST keep every existing field's meaning; peers with the same major are compatible. A new major version uses a new segment name, so old and new plugins run side by side without seeing each other. Extensions (planned): string-identified, versioned capabilities, in the style of CLAP extensions ( "com.example.osc-bridge/1" ), declared per endpoint in a table that a future minor version adds in reserved space. Changes Version Date Changes 0.1 2026-10 First draft: layout, timing rules, cables, saved state. Open questions for 0.2 Pitch convention: keep 1 V/oct with 0 = C4, or switch to semitones? Namespace defaults per host process, to separate two running DAWs without configuration. A held "cable in hand" field for pick-up-and-drop patching across windows. Audio signals (stage 2): per-endpoint audio buffers allocated on demand.

title: Web developers
text: Web developers Bleep Play is the board running completely in the visitor's browser: no server and no plugin. The website serves it at /play/ and embeds it on /board/ . main thread AudioWorklet (real time) board UI (patch/board/ui, unchanged) worklet.js board-demo.js — the document, undo, graph.js — the graph runner presets module-host.js — one instance per node, bleep-web.js — loads module .wasm each its own .wasm on demand, keyboard, MIDI The UI is the same as in the plugins and the app. The engine is a JavaScript port of the native one ( graph.js : cell flattening, normalled jacks, topological order, feedback through the previous chunk, 32-sample chunks inside the 128-sample render quantum). Port nodes are built in; the computer keyboard and Web MIDI play MIDI In . Modules in the browser Each module folder is compiled, with a small shim, to one standalone .wasm : no JUCE glue, no Emscripten JS loader, no shared memory. module-host.js instantiates it with plain WebAssembly.Module and Instance , so the same code runs in an AudioWorklet and in Node (the tests). The file's contract is the Module ABI. build modules.py builds every folder, reads each file's node types back out, and writes manifest.json . The page loads a module the first time a board contains one of its types, from the Bleep Library of the site, and checks it in the browser before running it. Build scripts/build/build-web.sh # needs the Emscripten SDK scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules # UI and engine only scripts/build/build-web.sh --modules-only # modules only scripts/build/build-web.sh --docker # Emscripten in Docker About a third of the modules use juce core for node data; build modules.py --juce compiles it once for WebAssembly and links it into those modules (about +200 KB each). Test node patch/web/test/graph-test.mjs build/web/site The bridge tests ( bridge-protocol-test.mjs , bridge-ring-test.mjs , bridge-client-test.mjs , bridge-engine-test.mjs ) run in plain Node with no build and no network. Hosting Static files, plus the library the page installs its modules from ( /registry/v1/index.json ). manifest.base can point at another origin to ship modules separately from the site. The whole website stack runs with ./bleep run site (Caddy, the API, PostgreSQL and the object storage). Connecting to the app The page can join the Bleep App, and through it Live, over a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1 : audio and MIDI both ways, plus the app's tempo and beat. Nothing connects until the page calls BleepWeb.connectBridge() . const bridge = await BleepWeb.connectBridge({ name: "Chrome", mode: "low" }); bridge.on("channels", (list) => { / Live ports the hub announces / }); bridge.on("status", ({ state }) => { / idle connecting handshake open retrying failed denied closed / }); bridge.sendMidi("node-7", [[null, 0x90, 60, 100]], { lookaheadBeats: 0.1 }); bridge.requestTempo(128); Two paths, one API. When the page is cross-origin isolated (the app serves it with COOP and COEP), the Worker and the worklet share a SharedArrayBuffer ring: mode low , 16 ms target fill. Otherwise the client falls back to safe with MessagePort chunks and 64 ms. Browser limits. Safari blocks ws://127.0.0.1 from a secure page and Chrome may ask for local-network access. connectToApp() explains the failure and points at the app's own page, http://127.0.0.1:47100/ . Remote nodes. A board node bound to a channel carries what the hub sends and sends what is patched into it. Remote Audio and Remote MIDI nodes let two boards exchange audio and MIDI without Live. Settings The board's Settings section is answered by BleepWeb.settings ( patch/web/js/web-settings.js ), so a page that embeds the board gets the Audio, MIDI, App, Library and Data tabs without code of its own. The script loads before bleep-web.js , after library-client.js . Stored in localStorage under bleep.web.settings : output (a device id), latency ( interactive , balanced or playback , the AudioContext 's latencyHint ), midiOff (input names to ignore), and channel . Saved junk is ignored, and a browser that refuses storage keeps the choices for the visit. Applied at load: the library choices go to BleepLibrary.configure({ channel }) once, before the library is first used, so a change needs a reload. Output uses AudioContext.setSinkId where the browser has it; a saved device that has gone falls back to the default. Data → Clear removes keys by prefix: the board and presets ( bleep-demo-… ), these settings ( bleep.web.… ) and the library's caches ( bleep.library.… ). Other sites' keys are never touched. Test: node patch/web/test/web-settings-test.mjs (plain Node, no build). The design, with the tabs of the app and the plugins, is doc/specs/settings.md in the repository. For musicians: Settings. Not yet in the browser Voice Cells, the Harmony bus, Link, Macros, audio input, host MIDI out and the media folder (Splice, Grains and Wavetable Osc import find no files) are not ported yet.

title: Connecting plugin, app and web
text: Connecting plugin, app and web Bleep runs in three places: the plugins in Live, the app and a board in your browser. Each has its own board. This page is about making them work together: a synth built in the browser and played from Live, an effect in the browser on a Live track, a sequencer in the browser that plays an instrument in Live, a patch in the app whose sound lands on a Live track. The idea is one setting, the Board menu on the plugins, plus one switch in the app and one button in the browser. Live plugins connect to the app through shared memory; Bleep Play in the browser connects to the app over a WebSocket. The app is the hub in the middle. The app sits in the middle. Live and the browser both talk to it, never to each other directly. That is why the app has to be running for any of this. Everything stays on your computer: the app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. What delay to expect Audio cannot travel for free. Each hop adds a little time, and it is better to know the numbers than to be surprised. Connection Delay Good for Live ⇄ app 2 audio buffers (about 5 ms at 256 samples) Almost anything, including playing Live → browser → Live About 45 ms for the whole round trip with the page from the app ( Low latency , 256-sample buffer, measured on a laptop with a Chrome-based browser); more with a bigger buffer or the Safe mode Sound design, effects you hear, sequences Browser page from the website Safe mode: about 64 ms of buffering in each direction, on top The same, with more headroom The browser's share is its jitter buffer (16 ms in Low latency , at least 1.5 audio buffers of the app or of Live) and the browser's own audio output. The plugin that brings the sound back reports the total to Live. Two things make the delay mostly invisible in a song: Sources that follow the transport are lined up for you. When Live's own MIDI plays a browser synth, or a browser sequencer plays a Live instrument, the plugin tells Live how late the sound will be, and Live's delay compensation moves everything else to match. On the timeline it is on the beat. Sources that answer you live are not. Playing the browser synth with a keyboard, or running a live input through a browser effect, you hear the full delay. For playing, run the instrument in the app or in a plugin instead, and use the browser for sequencing, effects and sound design. Turning it on In the app: File → Settings → Web , then Let Bleep Play pages connect to this app . It is off until you do this. The port is 47100 ; change it only if something else uses it. In a plugin: open a port plugin's window (Bleep MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In or Audio Out) and choose its Board : Board The plugin talks to This set The board of this Live set, as always Bleep App The board in the running app Bleep Play Bleep Play that has joined (through the app) In the browser: open the board and press ⇄ Connect to app (next to Start audio ). The button is in the current web build only: a copy of the board built earlier does not have it. Rebuild with scripts/build/build-web.sh --no-modules . For the lowest delay, open the board from the app instead of the website: the Web section of the app's Settings shows the address ( http://127.0.0.1:47100/ ). The app serves the board page from the folder named by the BLEEP WEB ROOT environment variable (the folder build-web.sh wrote, build/web/site ), for example BLEEP WEB ROOT=build/web/site "Bleep Patch.app/Contents/MacOS/Bleep Patch" . Without it the app shows only a placeholder page at that address. That page can use a faster path between the browser and its audio engine, which is what Low latency means. The website's page works too, in Safe mode, with more delay and a little more headroom. Safari does not let a website talk to an app on your computer, so use the app's page there. The first time a page from anywhere else connects, the app asks whether to allow it. Allow only pages you opened yourself. You can forget them again in Settings → Web. Which plugins do I need? Only four of the port plugins can talk to the app or Bleep Play: Bleep MIDI In , MIDI Out , Audio In and Audio Out . They are the ones with a Board menu. Pick the plugin for what should travel, then set its Board to Bleep App (a patch in the app) or Bleep Play (the browser). You want Put this on a track Board MIDI from Live to the board (Live's notes play a synth in the app or browser) Bleep MIDI In on a MIDI track Bleep App or Bleep Play MIDI from the board to Live (a board sequencer plays an instrument in Live) Bleep MIDI Out on a MIDI track, routed to your instrument (how) Bleep App or Bleep Play Audio from a Live track to the board (an effect, a sampler or analysis) Bleep Audio In on that track Bleep App or Bleep Play Audio from the board back into Live (the sound of a synth or an effect) Bleep Audio Out on its own MIDI track Bleep App or Bleep Play Sync (tempo, beat, play and stop) Nothing extra: any one of the four plugins above carries it A few things follow from that: Audio and MIDI are separate. A browser synth played from Live needs two plugins: MIDI In for the notes and Audio Out for the sound. A browser effect needs Audio In and Audio Out. Sync has no plugin of its own. As soon as one plugin with a Board other than This set is connected, Live leads the tempo and transport, and the app and Bleep Play follow it (see Tempo and transport). The other port plugins stay in Live. Bleep Board , Bleep Instrument and Bleep FX have no Board menu: they always use the board of this set. Put Bleep Board once per set if you want macros as usual. The recipes below walk through the common combinations. What you see On the app's board , a plugin with Board = Bleep App appears as the same node it would be in Live (a MIDI In , an Audio Out …), named after its track. When you set it back, or delete the plugin, the node turns grey and its cables stay. On the browser's board , a plugin with Board = Bleep Play appears as a node named Live: track name , in the same colour as the app's remote nodes. Pressing Connect again after a break reconnects them. Nodes you add yourself from the Add menu, Remote Audio and Remote MIDI , appear on the app's board as Web: name nodes. A plugin with a Board other than This set has no node on Live's own board: Bleep App there shows it as a grey ghost until you switch it back. Recipes Play a browser synth from Live In Live, make a MIDI track with Bleep MIDI In , Board = Bleep Play . Play or draw notes on it. Make another MIDI track with Bleep Audio Out , Board = Bleep Play . This is where the sound comes back. In Bleep Play, connect to the app. Live: your MIDI track and Live: your audio track appear. Cable the MIDI node's Notes into an oscillator or a synth cell, and the synth's output into the audio node's L and R . Audio Out reports the way there and back to Live, so a clip's notes sound on their beat. If you play the MIDI track live with a keyboard, expect the delay from the table above. Put a browser effect on a Live track Put Bleep Audio In ( Board = Bleep Play ) on the track to send its audio to the browser, and Bleep Audio Out ( Board = Bleep Play ) on its own track to get the result back. Mute the original track if you want only the effect. Audio travels there and back, so the delay is twice that of the table. Live lines it up with the rest of your set when the clips play. Play an instrument in Live from a browser sequencer Put Bleep MIDI Out ( Board = Bleep Play ) on a MIDI track in Live and route that track's output to the track with your instrument (see MIDI Out routing). In Bleep Play a node Live: track name appears with a Notes input: cable your sequencer's notes into it. The sequencer follows Live's tempo and position, and sends notes a short time ahead, each with the beat it belongs to. The plugin plays every note at its place in the right buffer, so it is on the beat, not just about on the beat. When you change the tempo or jump the playhead, the sequencer drops what it had queued and starts again from the new place, so nothing plays in the wrong spot. To use the browser's MIDI in the app instead, add a Remote MIDI node from the Add menu: in the app it appears as a Web: Remote MIDI node you can patch like any other MIDI source. A patch in the app, as a sound source in Live In Live, put Bleep Audio Out with Board = Bleep App on a track: the app's board now plays on that track, with its own mixer channel. The app follows Live's tempo and position while it is connected. The delay is two buffers, and Live compensates it. Do the same with Bleep MIDI In ( Board = Bleep App ) to play the app's patch from a Live MIDI track. MIDI and audio then travel in the same way, so they stay together. While Live is connected to the app, the app's own audio interface stays silent : Live's audio buffers drive the app, and its sound goes back through Live. Disconnect the plugins, or close the set, to use the app on its own. Tempo and transport One of them leads at a time: Live , as long as one of its plugins talks to the app or Bleep Play. Ableton Link in the app, if it is on. The app's own clock. Bleep Play follows whoever leads: tempo, beat and play/stop. It can ask for a new tempo or for play, and only the leader decides. If Live leads, a request from the browser changes nothing. Export and freeze A browser works on the clock of its own sound card and cannot go faster than real time. When Live exports , freezes or flattens a track faster than real time, a Bleep plugin with Board = Bleep App waits for the app and everything is in the file. With Board = Bleep Play the browser's share is silent. To get it into a file: record the web part to an audio track in real time (a track with Audio In/Out is enough), then export. When it does not work The plugin window says what it sees: It says What to do The Bleep App is not running Start the app. Until then the plugin passes its track through untouched The app is connected to another host Only one Live at a time can drive the app The app has no free bridge slot 32 plugins at most can talk to the app. Remove some The app is another version Update the plugins and the app, then restart Live Late blocks counting up The computer is busy or the buffer is small. Raise Live's buffer size In the browser, the Connect button says why it could not connect (the app is not running, the Web setting is off, the browser blocks the connection, you declined the question). In the app, Settings → Web shows who is connected and how many channels each has, and counts MIDI that arrived late or after a tempo change. What is not there yet Another computer. Everything is on one machine. A shared session (a web board on your phone, a friend playing your synth) needs a server between the computers and is planned. Playing notes across the internet is easy; sending audio live is limited by the network's delay, which no setting hides. A browser sound in a file, automatically. See Export and freeze . The page from the website in Safari. Use the page from the app. Live without the app. The app has to be running. A plugin that can take its place is a possibility later. The formats and numbers behind all this are in the design notes for developers, doc/specs/bridges.md in the source.

title: Control Live from the board
text: Control Live from the board Cables on the board can do more than move other modules. With the Live Params node and the Bleep Live Link device, a signal on the board can move a knob of any device in Live, or of any plugin in your set. It can switch a device on and off, and it can pick a choice in a menu, such as a filter type. An LFO can sweep a Live filter, a clock can pulse a device on and off, and a stepped source can walk through the filter types, all from the board. You need Live Suite (the device is a Max for Live device), the Bleep Board plugin on a track, and the Bleep Live Link device on a track. Without Max for Live, there is a simpler way for continuous parameters. Try it in five steps Put Bleep Board on a track (once per set), and open the board. Put the Bleep Live Link device on any track. Leave its Channel at 1. On the board, choose Add → Module → Ports → Live Params . Leave its channel at 1. In the device, click Map on row 1 , then click a knob in Live, for example the Frequency of an Auto Filter. The button turns yellow, shows the knob's name and locks. On the board, cable an LFO into CV 1 of the Live Params node. The knob in Live moves. Open the node's view (double-click the node) to see what it is doing. Row 1 now shows the name of the knob and the word continuous . The two halves The two halves share a channel , from 1 to 8: The Live Params node lives on the board. It has four rows . Each row has a value that you set with the board's usual tools: a knob and a CV input, with cables at their own amounts. The Bleep Live Link device lives in Live. It also has four rows, each with a Map button. A row of the device is mapped to a parameter in Live, and the matching row of the node gives it its value. For more than four parameters, add another node on the next channel and another device on that channel. A set can use up to eight channels, so 32 parameters. A row's value A row's value is its Row knob plus what you patch into its CV input . The knob sets the centre; the cable's amount sets how far the modulation goes. You can also drag a cable straight onto the knob. When you map a row, the node's knob jumps to the parameter's position , so nothing jumps in Live. From then on the node is in charge. Continuous parameters: a slider with two handles Most knobs in Live are continuous . For these the node's view shows a slider with two handles : The circle is Min , the square is Max . The row moves the parameter through the part of its range between them. 0% to 100% is the whole range; 30% to 70% keeps the sweep in the middle. The triangle is the row's value (the knob). Drag it to move the centre. The thin line is where the row is asking the parameter to be right now, with the CV input and the cables included. Double-click a handle to reset it. Drag a handle past the other and the range turns round: a rising LFO then makes the parameter fall. Row 80% in the read-out means the row's value is 80% of the way from Min to Max. Now is the position in the parameter's whole range. Discrete parameters: switches and menus Some controls in Live have a fixed set of choices: a device's on/off, a filter type, a sync mode. The node knows when a row is mapped to one of these, and its view lists every choice with the number that picks it : # Choice Send Knob 0 Lowpass 0.00 0% 1 Highpass 0.33 33% 2 Bandpass 0.67 67% 3 Notch 1.00 100% Click a choice to set the row to it. Send is the value that picks it. With N choices, choice i is picked by i ÷ (N − 1) , and a value in between picks the nearest one. Patch a stepped source, a quantizer or a sequencer into the row's CV input and it walks through the choices. A switch is a menu with two choices ( Off , On ): below one half is the first, one half and above the second. A gate or a clock into the CV input switches it on and off. Min and Max do not apply to a discrete row. Letting go While a row drives a knob, you can't move that knob with the mouse in Live. To get it back: press × on the row in the device, or delete the Live Params node, or change its channel. The parameter goes back to where it was when you mapped it . Nothing is written to Live's automation, and nothing lands in Live's undo history. The device saves its mappings with your set, and the node is part of the board, so both come back when you open the set. What you can control Works Doesn't Continuous knobs of Live's own devices The song's Tempo , and Solo : we could not control them Switches and menus of Live's own devices Anything Live greys out Mixer knobs: volume, pan, sends Parameters of VST3 plugins, once you have added them to the plugin's list of parameters in Live (the Configure button) Values go out about a hundred times a second: smooth for modulation, but not sample-accurate and not delay-compensated. See Ableton Live goes modular for what that means next to audio latency. Ideas A filter that breathes: an LFO into CV 1 , row 1 mapped to an Auto Filter's frequency, Min 20%, Max 60%. A device that pulses: a clock divider into CV 2 , row 2 mapped to a device's on/off. A filter type that changes by itself: a stepped random source into CV 3 , row 3 mapped to the filter type of the same filter. One knob for several things: cable the same source into several rows, each with its own Min and Max. When something doesn't work What you see What to check Nothing moves The device and the node must be on the same channel . Is the node's channel the one in the device's Channel menu? Is the device's row mapped (the button shows a name)? The node says not mapped but the knob moves The board hasn't heard the device yet. The device repeats its report every two seconds, so wait a moment. If it stays, another program may be using the network port 9880 that Bleep uses to hear the device. The knob jumps between two values Two sources are writing to the same row: a second node on the same channel, or two devices on one channel. Give each node and device its own channel. The menu picks the wrong choice Look at the table in the node's view and send the number it shows for that choice, or click the choice. The Map button says not mappable Live doesn't let a device map that control (for example Solo ). Click something else. The Map button says no answer Live didn't answer when the device asked about the parameter. Press ×, and map it again. Where to go next Ableton Live goes modular: everything the board adds to Live, and what it costs in latency Ports: the plugins you add in Live Modulation: sources, cables and amounts Modulating any Live parameter without Max for Live: the MIDI loopback way

title: Modulating any Live parameter (loopback workaround)
text: Modulating any Live parameter (loopback workaround) Without Max for Live, a virtual MIDI port lets you map signals from the board to any parameter in Live. With Max for Live, Control Live from the board is simpler and also handles switches and menus: macOS: open Audio MIDI Setup → MIDI Studio → IAC Driver , tick Device is online . Windows: install loopMIDI and create a port. In Live's MIDI preferences, enable Remote for the IAC/loopMIDI input. Route the Bleep MIDI Out track's MIDI To to that port. Enter MIDI Map mode, click the target parameter, then patch a moving signal into MIDI Out's CC 1 input on the board. Live learns the mapping. Limits: 7-bit resolution, updates at Live's control rate, and the mapping overrides automation on that parameter.

title: Play with a MIDI controller
text: Play with a MIDI controller A MIDI keyboard, a pad controller or a box of knobs can play Bleep in all three places. How you connect it depends on where you play. You play in The controller is read by You add The Bleep App the app itself a MIDI Device node (or MIDI In ) Bleep Play (browser) your browser a MIDI Device node, or nothing at all Live Live the Bleep Instrument plugin on a MIDI track Connect the controller to your computer with USB before you start Bleep or open the page. Most controllers need no driver. In the Bleep App The quick way: MIDI Device Plug in the controller and start the app. Choose Add → Module → Sources → MIDI Device . Click the node and choose your controller from the list. Cable the node's Notes output into a Voice Cell, for example Slate Stabs , and the cell's Out L/R into Out 1/2 . Play a key and you hear it. The node remembers the controller in the project, so it is there again the next time you open it. You do not have to switch anything on in Settings. The other way: MIDI In If you would rather switch controllers on once for every project: Open Settings → MIDI and switch on your controller under Inputs . Choose Add → Port and add the MIDI In node of that controller. A controller that is switched off in Settings is ignored by MIDI In . A MIDI Device node works either way. In Bleep Play (the browser) Open the board in Chrome or Edge . Safari has no Web MIDI. Press ▶ Start audio . The browser asks whether the page may use your MIDI devices. Allow it. Play. With no MIDI Device node on the board, every connected controller plays the board's MIDI In. To choose one controller, add a MIDI Device node as in the app and pick it in the node. A MIDI Device node wins over the switches in Settings → MIDI , which only apply to boards without one. If you pressed Don't allow by mistake, change the page's MIDI permission in the browser's site settings (the lock icon next to the address), then reload. The browser passes on notes, controller (CC) knobs and pitch bend. Channel pressure and program changes are not passed on yet. Playing the app from the browser The other direction works too: add a Remote MIDI node from the Add menu once the board is linked to the app, and the browser's controller plays the app's patch. See Connecting plugin, app and web. In Live Live reads the controller. Put Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track, arm the track and play. To play a board that runs in the app or in Bleep Play, set the plugin's Board ; Connecting shows how. Use the knobs Every MIDI source node has eight controller outputs, CC 1–8 , plus Pitch , Gate , Velocity , Trigger , Pressure , Bend and Mod Wheel . Turn a knob on your controller and see which controller number it sends: cable Notes into a Monitor , which lists every note, controller number and program change. Set one of the CC 1–8 # fields of the node to that number. Cable the matching CC output to what it should move, for example a filter's cutoff. The defaults are 2, 4, 7, 10, 11, 71, 74 and 64. Many controllers send 1 (mod wheel), 7 (volume) and 74 (brightness) out of the box. Channel limits a node to one MIDI channel, or All . When nothing plays The controller is not in the list. Plug it in before you start the app or open the page, or reload. The node shows the controller but there is no sound. Check that Notes goes into a Voice Cell (or Pitch into an oscillator and Gate into an envelope), and that the cell's output goes to Out 1/2 . Only the wrong channel plays. Set the node's Channel to All . The browser does not offer MIDI. Use Chrome or Edge, and check that you allowed MIDI access. More about the nodes Each node has a manual behind its ? button: MIDI Device and MIDI In list every setting and output. Settings are explained in Settings.

title: Routing MIDI Out in Live
text: Routing MIDI Out in Live Create a MIDI track ("Mod MIDI") and load Bleep MIDI Out (VST3) as its instrument. Create a second MIDI track with the instrument you want to play. On the second track set MIDI From to Mod MIDI , choose Bleep MIDI Out in the second menu, and set Monitor to In . On the board, patch a gate (e.g. Function's EOC through Utility, or Random's Trig ) into MIDI Out's Gate , and a pitch (e.g. Random with Semitones on) into Pitch . Or patch a Notes output (from MIDI In) into its Notes input. CC numbers, channel and transpose are in its view. Live merges MIDI channels on internal routes, so one MIDI Out instance carries one stream. Use more instances for more streams.

title: Process what your computer plays
text: Process what your computer plays The System node puts everything your computer plays onto the board: a music player, a browser tab, a video call, a game. Patch it into a filter, a reverb or a delay network, and listen to the result. Or record it. It is a feature of the Bleep App. The plugins have your DAW for this, and Bleep Play cannot see other programs. You don't need a virtual audio driver (BlackHole, Loopback, VB-Cable). Bleep App asks your operating system for the sound directly. Turn it on Open File → Settings → Audio . Under System audio , tick Capture what this computer plays . Allow the permission if your system asks (macOS does, once). On the board, choose Add → Port → System . The node has two outputs, L and R , and a Gain dial, like the other Audio In nodes. It stays off until you tick the box: nothing is captured before that.
