The settings show what is going on: the sample rate, whether your own sound is left out, and whether sound arrives ( signal ) or not ( silent ). Recipes Hear your music player through an effect. Play something in another program, then patch System L/R → Reverb → Out 1/2 . You hear the player itself and, a moment later, the effect. Play Bleep App to headphones and the player to speakers (or mute the player's output) to hear the effect alone. A filter sweep over a song. System L/R → Filter → Out 1/2 , and an LFO on the cutoff. Record what you hear. Patch System and your synth into a mixer node and on into a recorder. Because the captured sound reaches Bleep App a moment after it leaves the other program, the effect is slightly late. See Delay below. Feedback If Bleep App plays to your speakers and System captures your speakers, a cable from System to Out 1/2 would feed back: what comes out is captured, played, captured again. Bleep App prevents this by default: Leave out Bleep App's own sound is on. The capture then holds everything except Bleep App. System Own sound left out? macOS 14.2 or later Yes Windows 10 build 20348 or later, Windows 11 Yes Older Windows No Linux No Where it can't be left out, the setting is disabled and says so. Play Bleep App to another output than the one you capture (headphones for Bleep App, speakers for everything else), or don't patch System to an output. Turn the setting off if you want to record Bleep App's own sound together with everything else. macOS You need macOS 14.2 or later . The first time you turn the capture on, macOS asks if Bleep App may record system audio. If it doesn't ask, or you said no, System stays silent. Allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording (the System Audio Recording Only list), then turn the capture off and on again. If the app is started from a terminal rather than by double-clicking it, macOS may credit the terminal instead of Bleep App, and the capture stays silent. Start the app from Finder or the Dock. Sound that is protected against copying (some streaming services) arrives as silence. That is the system's rule, not a setting. On older macOS, use a loopback driver such as BlackHole as an input device instead (File → Settings → Input). Windows Windows 10 or later. No permission prompt. With Windows 10 build 20348 or later (and Windows 11), Bleep App captures everything except itself, whichever output device you use. On older versions it captures the default output device including its own sound. If you change the default output (plug in headphones), the capture follows within a second. Linux You need PulseAudio, or PipeWire with its PulseAudio support ( pipewire-pulse , the default on most desktops), and a build of the app with libpulse (install libpulse-dev before building). Every output has a monitor , a source that carries what that output plays. The settings list them under Output to capture . Default output follows your system's default. Linux can't leave Bleep App's own sound out of a monitor: use a different output for Bleep App than for the rest, as described under Feedback . Delay The captured sound takes about 40 ms to arrive: 30 ms is a buffer that absorbs hiccups, and the system's own capture adds 10 to 20 ms. That doesn't matter for processing, mixing or recording. It does matter for playing live against the captured sound; for that, use a normal audio input (a cable or a loopback driver). Two sound cards never run at exactly the same speed. Bleep App corrects for that continuously with a tiny pitch adjustment (well below what you can hear) instead of dropping or repeating samples, so long sessions stay clean. When it doesn't work What you see What to do silent in Settings, but sound plays macOS: allow Bleep App under Privacy & Security, then turn the capture off and on. Otherwise check that the other program plays to the output that is the system default "needs macOS 14.2 or later" Update macOS, or use a loopback driver as an input device "No PulseAudio or PipeWire sound server was found" (Linux) Start your sound server; check with pactl info "This system cannot leave Bleep App out" Not an error: see Feedback The node is grey (a ghost) The capture is off or failed. Tick the box in Settings again and read the message A crackle once in a while Raise the buffer size in Settings → Audio; the capture follows it Notes for developers How it is built, the clock-drift handling and the open questions are in the specification, doc/specs/system-audio.md in the repository.

title: Cells and panels
text: Cells and panels A patch with forty modules is hard to read and harder to play. Two ideas fix that: a cell hides a part of the patch behind a few jacks, and a panel puts the dozen controls that matter on a front panel. Make a cell Select some nodes. Right-click and choose Create cell ( ⌘G ). Cables that cross the cell's border become its jacks . Double-click a cell to go inside; Esc takes you back out. Inside, Cell In and Cell Out are the cell's jacks, and you can add more. ⌘⇧G ungroups it again. For a polyphonic synth, make a Voice Cell: you patch one voice and the cell plays it up to 16 times. Save as preset (right-click the cell) keeps it under Add → Cell in every project, so a patch you build once becomes a module you reuse. Give it a panel A panel is the front of a cell: dials, faders, buttons, a keyboard, an XY pad, meters, labels and the views of modules inside. Right-click a cell: Build panel from cell makes a first panel from what is inside. New panel starts an empty one. Open panel and Edit panel open it. A panel has two views. Interface is for playing: only the controls, nothing else. Wiring is for building: every control shows what it is connected to, and you connect it to a knob, a jack, a button or a note input and set its range. Layout (adding, moving and resizing controls) happens in the Interface view, behind an unlock. To put a knob on a panel, right-click it (or its module) and choose Add to panel . A control can also load another panel, which is how large panels are split into tabs. A panel shows what you play with, not everything. The rest stays one right-click away: a control's menu has Open module view . Where this leads A cell with a panel, saved as a preset, is how Bleep Instrument and Bleep FX presets are made. You are building the same thing the factory presets are. Reference: the board, Voice Cells.

title: Your first patch
text: Your first patch This is a five-minute tour of the board in Ableton Live. You need the plugins installed (Install in Live) and a synth on a track. The board is the same in the Bleep App and in Bleep Play; only the first two steps are specific to Live. The patch (5 minutes) Put Bleep Board on a MIDI track (it is an instrument, so it can't go on the master or a return track). Every set that uses Bleep Board needs exactly one. Its window opens the board. Put Bleep FX on a synth track, after the synth. It appears on the board by itself, named after the track. The board with one node, Synth, of type Bleep FX: Return L and Return R on the left, Send L and Send R on the right. On the board, press Tab , type filter and press Enter. The search box after pressing Tab and typing filter: Multi Filter is the first result. Drag from the Insert's Send L to the Filter's In L , and from the Filter's Out L and Out R to the Insert's Return L and Return R . The Filter is cabled between the Insert's sends and returns: the audio of the track now goes through it. Press Tab again and add a Function . The search box with function typed: Function is the first result. Click the Filter to open its view, then drag Function's A onto the Cutoff knob. The yellow ring shows the cutoff the filter really uses; drag the amount chip under the knob to set how much. The Filter's view. A cable runs from Function's A output to the Cutoff knob; the knob has a yellow ring and an amount chip showing 100%. Now modulate the modulator: add a Random and drag its Out onto Function's Rise knob. Function's view with Random's Out cabled to the Rise knob, which now has a yellow ring. You have now used the three ideas the rest of Bleep is built on: modules joined by cables, a knob that is also a modulation destination, and a modulator that can itself be modulated. Good to know Ports (MIDI In, Audio Out, …) appear on the board when you add them in Live. You can't delete them on the board; when a track is deactivated or the plugin is removed, its node turns into a grey ghost and keeps its cables. The board is saved in Bleep Board. A second Bleep Board in the same set stays inactive and shows a warning. Latency. Audio that goes from Live into the board and back is two audio buffers late. The output ports report this to Live, so Live's delay compensation lines it up with the rest of the set. Undo. The board has its own undo (⌘Z in the board window). Live's undo doesn't include board edits. Next Modulation: what the rings, chips and cable colours mean. Cells and panels: keep a patch tidy and turn it into an instrument. The board: the full reference for patching.

title: Modulation
text: Modulation On the board, almost everything is a cable. A cable from a module's output to a knob modulates that knob, and every knob can be a destination . There is no special modulation matrix and no list of what you are allowed to modulate. How a modulated knob works Drag from an output and drop it on a knob in an open module view. The modulation is an offset : the knob stays where you put it, and the cable adds to it. A ring around the knob shows the value the module really uses. The amount chip under the knob sets how much the cable counts. Drag it up or down; double-click for 100 %. Several cables into one input are added up . You can also drop a cable on a node (a list of its knobs appears), or on empty space, which adds a module and connects it right away. Cable colours Colour Carries Yellow control Green (dashed) gate and trigger Blue pitch Red audio Purple notes Inputs that cannot take the signal you are dragging fade out. Notes only connect to notes. Modulating the modulator A modulator is a module like any other, so its knobs take cables too. In Your first patch a Random module drives the Rise of a Function that drives a filter's cutoff. Patches get musical when slow and fast movements meet this way. Following a signal T (trace) highlights what feeds and is fed by the selection. M (mute) silences the node's outputs, to hear what the rest does without it. Click a cable to change its amount or delete it. Drag its end at an input to move it. Next Cells and panels: group a patch, then give it a front panel. Every module and its knobs are in the module manuals.

title: Musician documentation
text: Beautiful Bleep for musicians Beautiful Bleep is a modular sound engine that runs as a plugin in Ableton Live, as a standalone app and in your browser. Play a ready-made instrument or effect, or patch your own with cables between small building blocks. Every knob is a modulation destination. Pick your starting point I want to… Read Try it right now, no install Bleep Play in your browser Use it in Ableton Live Install in Live, then Your first sound Use it without a DAW The Bleep App Understand what runs where Ways to use Bleep Learn to patch Your first patch The documentation Section What is in it Start Ways to use Bleep, Install in Live, Your first sound Learn A short path through the ideas: Your first patch, Modulation, Cells and panels Use How each part works: the board, Voice Cells, ports, the Bleep App, Settings, sharing modules Connect Moving audio, MIDI and tempo between Live, the app and Bleep Play: Connecting and three recipes Reference Glossary, Shortcuts and the module manuals Three ideas to know One engine, three places. Plugin, app and browser run the same board and modules, and a project made in one opens in the others. Cables everywhere. Drag a cable onto any knob to modulate it. See Modulation. Play first, patch later. Presets work without a cable. When you want more, open the preset as a cell and change it. See Cells and panels. Building plugins or modules yourself? That is in the developer documentation.

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Beautiful Bleep is the whole technology: the engine, the board, the modules, the plugins for your DAW, the app, the browser version, the library and the open protocol. The names below are the ones used everywhere in the docs and in the programs. Ways to run it The same board runs in three places. Patches, presets and modules work in all of them. Term What it is Bleep plugin Everything you add in your DAW (Ableton Live today): the main plugin, which stores and opens the board, and the ports. VST3. Bleep App The standalone app: the board without a DAW, with its own MIDI ports and Ableton Link. Bleep Play The board in your browser, with no install. Modules load from the Bleep Library on demand. The board and what is on it Term What it is Board The patching canvas. One per Live set, or per project in the app. It shows every node, cable and cell. Node Anything on the board that has jacks: a module, a port, a cell, an external plugin. Module A node type that processes signals: Function, Random, Filter and so on. Modules exist only on the board, never as plugins in Live. Shipped as .bleepmod packages. Cable A directed connection from an output jack to an input jack. Jack An input or output on a node. Cell A named group of nodes with its own jacks. Cells nest, can be copied and saved as cell presets. Voice Cell A cell that runs the voice you patch inside it once per note, so one voice becomes a polyphonic instrument. Panel A front panel of controls (dials, sliders, buttons, keys) for a cell or the board. Module view A module's full interface: knobs, switches, scopes. It opens as a window inside the board. Engine The shared code that runs the board. One engine runs per process, shared by every Bleep plugin loaded. Bleep plugins in Live Term What it is Bleep Board plugin The main plugin. Every Live set that uses Beautiful Bleep needs exactly one, on any track. It stores the board and opens it. Port A Bleep plugin on a track that connects that track to the board: Bleep MIDI In , MIDI Out , Audio In , Audio Out , Instrument , FX . Each port is one node on the board. Ableton bridge The ports together. Later bridges connect the board to other worlds the same way. Ghost A node whose port is not available right now (deleted, deactivated, not loaded yet). It is greyed out and keeps its cables. Bleep Audio Bridge A plugin in Live that connects a track's audio to a running Bleep App. Saving and sharing Term What it is Project A whole board with its panels: what you save, open and share. Demo projects, your own and the Library's are all projects. Preset A reusable cell (a cell preset ), which can bring a panel of its own. Whole boards are projects, not presets. Bleep Library Where plugins, modules and presets are installed from. Downloading needs no login; sharing a preset needs an account. "Patch" and "patching" stay everyday words for connecting cables. They are not names of a file or a product. For developers Term What it is Bleep Bus The open protocol and SDK that lets other plugins (Grit, Cinch, third-party) send and receive per-sample control signals through shared memory and join the board. Registry The technical name of the Bleep Library's interface ( /registry/v1/ , BLEEP REGISTRY URL ). In prose it is always the Bleep Library.

title: Shortcuts
text: Shortcuts Key Action Tab, double-click Add a module ⌘G / ⌘⇧G Create a cell from the selection / ungroup ⌘D / ⌘⇧D Duplicate / duplicate with incoming cables Delete Remove the selection (not ports) Esc Close a view, leave a cell, clear the selection F Fit the board to the window T Trace: highlight what feeds and is fed by the selection M Mute: the node's outputs fall silent ⌘Z / ⌘⇧Z Undo / redo Scroll, ⌘-scroll or pinch Pan, zoom Space-drag or Alt-drag Pan

title: Ableton Live goes modular
text: Ableton Live goes modular Live is built around tracks: each track has its own chain, and tracks talk to each other through sends, sidechains and "MIDI From". Beautiful Bleep adds something Live does not have, a patch bay for the whole set . You put a few small plugins on your tracks (ports) and every one of them shows up on one shared canvas, the board. There you connect them with cables, the way you would in a modular synthesizer. This page lists what that gives you that Live cannot do by itself, then explains what it costs in latency, especially when several plugins are connected to each other. What you can do now Modulate anything from anything, across tracks. Live has no modulation system. With the board, one source (an envelope, a random generator, a track's audio) can drive many parameters, and one parameter can take several sources. Source and target can sit on different tracks. Modulate at audio rate. Every signal except notes is calculated per sample, so a modulation cable can carry an audio-rate LFO, an oscillator or a whole audio signal. FM-style effects are a cable away. Build feedback loops. Filter into grit and back into the filter; a delay that feeds a synth. Live's routing refuses feedback. On the board, a cable that closes a loop is marked with a loop icon and delayed by a few samples (see Feedback). Use modular building blocks. Function generators, quantized random, chaos sources, comparators, clock dividers and keyframe morphing are modules, not separate devices. Because a comparator turns a signal into a trigger, a random source can fire envelopes or notes. Patch audio, MIDI and modulation in one place. Today Live keeps these in separate menus. On the board they are cable types, and the board only allows connections that make sense. Design your own synths and effects inside Live. Build an instrument or an effect out of modules, then load it as a normal plugin on a track ( Bleep Instrument or Bleep FX ) with its own front panel. Modulate other plugins. Plugins that use the Bleep Bus protocol appear on the board as nodes, so the board can modulate them too. Control Live itself from the board. With the Live Params node and the Bleep Live Link device (Max for Live), a cable on the board can move a knob of any Live device or of any plugin in your set, switch a device on and off, or pick a choice in a menu such as a filter type. The node shows what each of its four rows is mapped to, and for a menu every choice with the number that picks it. A slider with two handles keeps a sweep to the part of the range you want. Nothing is written to Live's automation, and a parameter goes back where it was when you let go. See Control Live from the board. Take the board out of Live. The Bleep App runs the same board next to Live and stays in time through Ableton Link. How the board connects to Live Everything you cable on the board happens inside one engine, and the engine runs sample-accurately . Latency only appears where audio or notes cross the border between Live and the board: Live track ──► Bleep Audio In ──┐ ┌──► Bleep Audio Out ──► Live mixer Live track ──► Bleep MIDI In ──┤ B O A R D (no delay ├──► Bleep Instrument Live track ──► Bleep FX (send) ─┘ between modules) └──► Bleep FX (return) Bleep Board runs the board on its own track, in the same audio buffer as the rest of that track. Its own MIDI In, its own Audio In and its own Audio Out cost nothing. Only a signal that really goes between plugins on other tracks adds latency, one audio buffer each way. A plugin that is only there, or an Audio Out with nothing patched into it, adds none: Into the board from another track (Bleep MIDI In, Bleep Audio In): 1 audio buffer. Out of the board to another track (Bleep Audio Out): 1 audio buffer. Cables between modules on the board cost nothing. How much is one buffer? Buffer size in Live 44.1 kHz 48 kHz 64 samples 64 samples, 1.5 ms 64 samples, 1.3 ms 128 samples 128 samples, 2.9 ms 128 samples, 2.7 ms 256 samples 256 samples, 5.8 ms 256 samples, 5.3 ms 512 samples 512 samples, 11.6 ms 512 samples, 10.7 ms Bleep Board, Bleep Audio Out, Bleep Instrument and Bleep FX report their delay to Live, so Live's delay compensation lines everything up. Your drums, your bass and the board's audio stay in time with each other. What you pay is the total latency of the set : Live delays the other tracks to match, which you feel when you play or record on a monitored track. Right after you load a set the plugins assume a larger buffer for a moment, then settle to your real buffer after the first block has played. After that the number only changes if you change the buffer size, the sample rate or the ports on the board. 0 host latency for inputs This is on by default. Bleep Board reports no latency to Live, however many Bleep MIDI In and Bleep Audio In plugins you add on other tracks. Their signals are delayed by one buffer inside the board instead: they arrive one buffer late against the rest of the set, and Live does not know. Your own track stays at zero latency, which is what you want when you play it. If you need the inputs lined up with the rest of the set, for example to blend a processed track with its dry original, open Settings → Latency in the board and turn 0 host latency for inputs off. Bleep Board then reports that buffer and Live delays everything else by it. That only works while no audio goes back to Live on another track. As soon as a Bleep Audio Out on another track plays something from the board, Live must be told about the input's buffer too, or that track would be a buffer late. The board then reports it again and says so in the setting. Several plugins connected to each other This is the part that matters when you build bigger setups. The rule is simple: you pay once for every crossing between another track and the board, not for every cable. Setup Added latency Bleep Board alone: its own MIDI In, its own Audio Out none One track, Bleep Instrument played from a keyboard, cabled to nothing else none Bleep Audio In on track A into the board's own Audio Out 1 buffer The board's own MIDI In into a Bleep Audio Out on track B 1 buffer Bleep Audio In on track A, ten modules cabled together, Bleep Audio Out on track B 2 buffers (the same as with one module) Several Bleep MIDI In and Audio In ports feeding one Audio Out , all patched on the board 2 buffers (inputs are processed together) Bleep FX cabled to other plugins 2 buffers Bleep FX on track A, then Bleep FX on the same track after it 4 buffers (two crossings, one after the other) Track A: Audio In , board, Audio Out on track B. Then track B: Audio In , board, Audio Out on track C 4 buffers at track C (two crossings) Same as above, but you cable A straight to C on the board 2 buffers Three Bleep FX in a row, each on its own track or in one chain 6 buffers Tip: keep chains on the board. If two Bleep effects follow each other, don't put a Bleep FX after a Bleep FX. Put both effects in one board patch (or one cell) and cable them there. Audio then goes into the board once and comes out once, whatever happens in between. Live compensates, but only for what it can see. Live adds the delays that the output plugins report along the signal path, so the sum of crossings is lined up with the rest of your set. Parallel tracks that do not use Bleep are delayed to match. Some paths are not compensated: Bleep MIDI Out sent to another track. Live does not reliably compensate this routing. Notes arrive one or two buffers late relative to the rest. Move the target track earlier in your timeline or nudge it with the track delay. Tracks you monitor with Reduced Latency When Monitoring on. Live skips delay compensation for them. Modulation sent to other plugins through the Bleep Bus. It arrives one buffer late, which you cannot hear for modulation. Control of Live's own parameters (Live Params). The values go out about a hundred times a second, so they are smooth for modulation but not sample-accurate and not delay-compensated. Use it to move knobs, not to time events to the beat. Feedback cables. A cable that closes a loop is delayed by one engine step (32 samples, 0.7 ms at 44.1 kHz). Feedback loops A feedback cable adds 32 samples inside the board. It does not add to the buffers above. In a tight filter-grit loop that small delay slightly changes the pitch of the ringing, which many people use on purpose. A tight feedback option that reduces the delay to one sample is planned. Tips for low latency Playing live: set Live's buffer to 128 samples or lower for the tracks you play. Play Bleep Board 's own track, or a Bleep Instrument that is cabled to nothing else: they add no latency at all. Mixing and producing: buffer size does not matter for the sound, only for how fast the controls respond. Bigger buffers are fine. Don't use the board for phase-tight parallel processing. Bleep FX delays its own dry signal to match, so its Dry/Wet is safe. A dry/wet blend you build yourself from separate Audio In and Audio Out tracks depends on Live's compensation, and can comb-filter if that compensation is off. Count crossings. Before you add another Bleep FX in a row, ask whether the new effect can live on the board with the others. Rendering: latency does not matter for exports. The board follows Live's time stamps in real time and offline alike. Where to go next Ports: every plugin you can add in Live Your first patch: build your first connection Control Live from the board: move Live's own parameters, switches and menus from the board Modulation: sources, cables and amounts Connecting plugin, app and web: latency when the board lives in the Bleep App or in the browser

title: Your first sound
text: Your first sound You do not need to patch anything to make a sound. Bleep Instrument and Bleep FX are ready-made patches with a front panel of knobs and sliders. An instrument Put Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track in Live. Pick a preset, for example Slate Stabs . Play it with MIDI. An effect Put Bleep FX on an audio track. Pick a preset, for example Dub Ping-Pong . Play audio through it. Both open on the preset's panel , not on the board. Turn the knobs; that is all there is to it. When you want more An instrument or effect preset is a small cell on the same board as everything else. Press Open Board and you see it there. You can open the cell, change what is inside, cable it to other parts and save it under your own name. Factory presets are never overwritten. Cables between several plugins need Bleep Board in the set, because the board is saved there. Your first patch walks through it. Instruments and effects are planned for the Bleep App and Bleep Play; today they are Live plugins. Ways to use Beautiful Bleep has the table.

title: Install in Live
text: Install in Live This page is for Ableton Live. Bleep also runs as a standalone app and in your browser. Beautiful Bleep makes Ableton Live feel modular. All modules live on one canvas per set, the board . You connect them with cables, and small plugins called ports connect the board to your tracks. Just want a sound? Put Bleep Instrument on a MIDI track or Bleep FX on an audio track and pick a preset. No patching needed; see Your first sound. Install Copy the .vst3 files to your plugin folder, then rescan plugins in Live (Settings → Plug-Ins, with "Use VST3 Plug-In System Folders" on). The plugins appear in Live's browser under Plug-Ins → Beautiful Bleep . VST3 folder macOS ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 Windows C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 The plugins are not signed with a paid certificate. If your system or DAW refuses to load them, see Installing unsigned builds. What next Your first sound: a preset, no cables. Your first patch: the board, a filter and a modulator, in five minutes. Ports: every plugin you can add in Live.

title: Installing unsigned builds
text: Installing unsigned builds The Bleep App and the plugins are free, and for now they are not signed with a paid developer certificate . Apple and Microsoft charge for those, so macOS and Windows warn you the first time you open a download. The files are not damaged, and the warning does not mean something is wrong: the system just doesn't know who made them. It is a one-time step per download. You can check a download against the checksum (SHA-256) shown for it in the Bleep Library before you open it. macOS The Bleep App Open the downloaded file and drag Bleep App to Applications . Open it. macOS says it cannot verify the app. Click Done . Open System Settings → Privacy & Security , scroll down to the message about Bleep App and click Open Anyway . Confirm with your password. On macOS 14 and older, right-click the app and choose Open instead; that works there too. The VST3 plugins Copy the .vst3 files to ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 as described in Install in Live. If your DAW does not list them, or says a plugin could not be loaded, macOS has quarantined the files. Remove the flag in Terminal, then rescan plugins: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/ .vst3 The same command works for the app: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Bleep\ App.app Windows The Bleep App Run the downloaded file. Windows shows Windows protected your PC . Click More info , then Run anyway . If you downloaded a zip, right-click it, choose Properties , tick Unblock and click OK before you extract it. That avoids the warning for every file inside. The VST3 plugins Copy the .vst3 files to C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 and rescan in your DAW. Plugins rarely trigger a warning. If one does not load, unblock it as above: right-click the file, Properties , Unblock . Linux No signing is involved. Make the app executable ( chmod +x ) and run it. Still stuck? The DAW does not show the plugins: rescan, and check that the files are in the VST3 folder of your system, not in a subfolder of another folder. macOS keeps blocking the app: run the xattr command above on the app, then open it again.

title: Ways to use Beautiful Bleep
text: Ways to use Beautiful Bleep Beautiful Bleep is one sound engine you can reach in three places, and in each place you can use it at three levels of effort. Three places What it is Best for Bleep plugin VST3 plugins for your DAW (Ableton Live today). See ports Making music inside a DAW project Bleep App The standalone app: the board without a DAW Playing, sound design, live use next to a DAW Bleep Play Bleep Play in your browser, no install Trying things out, sharing a project All three run the same board, the same modules and the same project files, so a project made in one place opens in the others. (Bleep Play does not have every module yet; the board page lists what is missing.) Connecting them The places work together: MIDI, audio and tempo can travel between them, and you choose where in the place you are. The plugins have a Board menu ( This set , Bleep App or Bleep Play ), the Bleep App has a Web switch in Settings, and Bleep Play has a Connect to app button. The Bleep App sits in the middle, on your computer. What works: Plugin ⇄ App App ⇄ Play Plugin ⇄ Play (through the app) MIDI Board menu on MIDI In/Out, or the app's MIDI ports Remote MIDI nodes Board menu: Bleep Play Audio Board menu on Audio In/Out, or Bleep Audio Bridge Remote Audio nodes Board menu: Bleep Play Tempo and transport Live leads; Ableton Link Bleep Play follows the app Bleep Play follows Live Audio between the plugin and the app is two buffers late; through Bleep Play it is a little more. Connecting plugin, app and Bleep Play has the numbers, the setup and some recipes. Another computer, or Bleep Play without the app, is planned, not built. Three ways to play Whichever place you are in, you choose how to start: Instrument. Pick a preset such as Slate Stabs , play it with MIDI. For when you want a sound, not a board. In Live this is Bleep Instrument . Audio effect. Pick a preset such as Dub Ping-Pong , send audio through it. In Live this is Bleep FX . Full board. Every module, every cable, your own project. In Live this is the Bleep Board plugin, with ports that connect the board to your tracks. These are not three different systems. An instrument or an effect preset is a small cell on the same board as everything else. The simple modes are a shortcut: you can try presets without ever touching a cable, and when you want more, open the board, edit the preset's cell, cable it to other parts, and save it as your own. Instrument Audio effect Full board Bleep plugin Bleep Instrument Bleep FX Bleep Board and the ports Bleep App Planned Planned Yes Bleep Play Planned Planned Yes In the plugins, Instrument and FX open on the preset's panel (knobs and sliders) rather than on the board. Open Board shows the preset as a cell on the board. Cables between several plugins need the Bleep Board plugin in the set, because the board is saved there. Next: Install in Live, Your first sound, the Bleep App, or Bleep Play in your browser.

title: The board
text: The board One canvas per Live set with every module, port and cable. Open it from any Bleep plugin's window (it opens with the window, or comes to the front). Adding things Right-click on empty space opens the Add menu: Module › one submenu per category: Sources , Modulation , Audio , Effects , Utility , Controllers , Sequencing and Drums . Each has subcategories, e.g. Sequencing › Melodic and Sequencing › Drum . Cell › New Cell , New Voice Cell , and your cell presets by category ( Synthesizers › Slate Stabs comes with Beautiful Bleep). Tab (or a double-click on empty space) opens a search at the cursor instead. See Voice Cells for polyphonic synths. Patching Drag from an output (the dots on the right of a node) to an input on the left of another node. Inputs that can't take the signal fade out. Drop on a knob in an open module view to modulate it. Every knob is a destination. The modulation is an offset: the knob stays where you put it, and a ring shows the value really used. The chip under the knob sets the cable's amount (drag up or down, double-click for 100 %). Drop on a node to pick one of its knobs from a list. Drop on empty space to add a module that is connected right away. Click a cable to set its amount or delete it. Drag a cable's end at an input to move it; drop it on empty space to remove it. Several cables into one input are added up. Cable colours: yellow control, green gate and trigger (dashed), blue pitch, red audio, purple notes. Notes only connect to notes. Module views Click a node to open its view: knobs, settings and its own displays. Views float over the board; open as many as you like, drag them by the title, pin them (📌) to keep them open when you enter or leave cells. Module presets Most modules with sound-shaping knobs (oscillators, filters, effects, envelopes, drums, …) have a preset bar at the top of their view. It looks the same in every module: ‹ › step to the previous or next preset. The name in the middle opens the list, which has two parts: Factory presets that ship with Beautiful Bleep, and User presets that you saved yourself. A dot (●) next to the name means you changed a knob after loading the preset. Save keeps the current settings as a preset of your own: type a name and press Enter. If the loaded preset is one of yours and you changed it, Save overwrites it. In the menu, × (click twice) deletes one of your presets. Factory presets can't be changed or deleted. To build on one, load it, change it and save it under a new name. Reset to defaults (at the bottom of the list) puts every knob back. A preset sets the module's own knobs and settings, never its cables. Modules that keep a pattern or other content in their view (sequencers, for example) save that content in your own presets too. Modules like the Patch Bay, meters and mixers have no presets. Your presets are shared by all your boards and live next to your cell presets (in the folder Module Presets ). Cells Add → Cell → New Cell or New Voice Cell places an empty cell. Select nodes, right-click and choose Create cell ( ⌘G ) or Create voice cell . Cables that cross the new border become the cell's jacks. Drag nodes onto a cell to move them into it; the cell lights up when it takes them. Cables to the rest of the board become cell jacks (an input that already carries the same signal is reused). Inside a cell, right-click a node → Remove from cell moves it out next to the cell; its cables are rerouted over cell jacks. Cables to Voice In and Voice Out can't be kept. Double-click a cell to enter it; Esc or the path at the top leads back out. Inside, Cell In and Cell Out are the cell's jacks: drop a cable on their new input / new output row to add one. ⌘⇧G ungroups a cell again. Right-click a cell → Save as preset to keep it in the Add menu for every set: Add → Cell → . Your own presets can be deleted there under Delete preset . Keyboard shortcuts are listed under Shortcuts.

title: Ports
text: Ports: the plugins you add in Live These are the only Bleep plugins in Live's browser. Each one (except Bleep Board) appears on the board as a node, named after its track. Settings such as MIDI channels and CC numbers are in the node's view on the board. Plugin Put it on On the board Bleep Board any track, once per set Macros : 16 outputs you can automate and MIDI-map in Live Bleep MIDI In a MIDI track Notes (polyphonic), mono Pitch , Gate , Velocity , Trigger , Pressure , Bend , Mod Wheel , 8 CCs Bleep MIDI Out a MIDI track inputs Notes , Gate + Pitch (mono), 8 CCs, Bend . See routing Bleep Audio In any track, anywhere in the chain the track's audio at that point ( L , R ); the audio passes through unchanged Bleep Audio Out its own MIDI track board audio ( L , R ) on that track, with its own mixer channel Bleep Instrument a MIDI track MIDI In and Audio Out in one plugin: a board synth on one track Bleep FX any track Send (the track's audio) and Return (back to the track), with Dry/Wet. With nothing patched into Return , the audio passes through Board: Bleep MIDI In, MIDI Out, Audio In and Audio Out have a Board menu in their window: This set (the default), Bleep App or Web board . With the app or Bleep Play, the plugin talks to that board instead of this set's, and has no node on this set's board. See Connecting plugin, app and web. Latency: audio through the board arrives two audio buffers late. Audio Out, Instrument and Audio Insert report it to Live (Live's delay compensation then lines them up). It isn't compensated for MIDI Out, or for tracks you monitor while Reduced Latency When Monitoring is on. Ghosts: when a port's plugin is deleted, deactivated or its track is frozen, its node turns grey and its outputs fall silent. The cables stay; when the plugin comes back (for example after undo in Live), it reconnects. Controlling Live itself: the Bleep Live Link Max for Live device is not one of these plugins. It pairs with the Live Params node on the board and moves parameters of other devices. See Control Live from the board.

title: Recording
text: Recording The Audio Console (Add menu → Audio → Mixing) is a mixing console with a multitrack recorder. Every channel you arm is written to its own audio file, so you can mix the stems afterwards in Live or any other editor. Record Put sounds into the console's channels and set Channels to the number you need (up to 32). Arm what you want with the red R buttons. Each channel has one; the aux buses and the master have one too. Arm all and Unarm all in the Record panel do all of them at once. Press Record . Press it again to stop. The panel shows how long you can still record and where the files go. The tracks you armed when you pressed Record are the tracks of that recording. Arm or disarm during it and the change applies to the next one. What gets recorded Armed The file holds A channel The channel as it arrives, before the filters, EQ and fader: the dry stem. Set Channel Tap to Post-fader to record it after the filters, EQ, fader and mute instead. A stereo channel makes a stereo file. An aux bus The send bus, as it leaves the console: the sum of every channel's send. The master The main output (after the master's EQ, fader and limiter). The files are WAV, 24-bit by default (16-bit and 32-bit float are in Format ). Channels are named after their strip: click the name above a channel to rename it, and the file gets that name ("Kick.wav"). Takes: manual or with the transport Start and Stop decides what a take is: Manual : one take, from Record to Stop, however often you start and stop the transport. Use it to record a Live session without caring about play and stop. Follow Transport : press Record once, then every play-to-stop is its own take, in new files. If the transport is already running, the first take starts at once. Takes after the first are numbered: "Kick.wav", "Kick (take 2).wav". Where the files go In the apps and the plugins, into the Recordings folder : System Folder macOS, Linux ~/Music/Beautiful Bleep/Recordings Windows %USERPROFILE%\Music\Beautiful Bleep\Recordings Each recording gets a folder named after the time it started, so nothing is overwritten. The Record panel shows the folder. Change it in Settings → Recordings : type a path or press Choose… . It applies to the next recording. In the browser (Bleep Play) a page cannot write into a folder, so the console records into memory. When you press Stop the recording appears in the Record panel with Download .zip , which holds a WAV file for every track of every take, and Discard , which frees the memory. Time left is what is left of a fixed memory budget (a quarter of what your browser reports as its memory, between 256 MB and 1 GB), so long recordings of many channels are short there: at the 1 GB budget a take of 8 mono tracks at 16 bit runs about 23 minutes. When the budget is used up the recording stops and keeps what it has: download it before you start another. See the recorder service. How long can I record? The panel shows Time left . It is the free space on the disk divided by how fast your armed tracks fill it: a mono track at 24 bit and 48 kHz is about 12 GB per day, so 32 tracks make about 0.4 TB per day. If the disk cannot keep up or a file reaches 4 GB (the limit of a WAV file), the take ends and the panel says why. What was recorded up to then is kept. Tips Record dry, mix later : keep Channel Tap on Input and arm every channel; the master is a convenient reference of what you heard. A quick stem pass : arm only the aux buses and the master. The Recording output is high while a take is written: use it to light something up, or to start a sequence together with the recording.

title: Settings
text: Settings File → Settings… opens the settings of the place you are in. Changes apply the moment you make them; there is no Save button. In the app the shortcut is ⌘, (Ctrl+, on Windows and Linux). Each place has its own tabs, because each place controls different things. Live runs the audio and MIDI of a plugin, and your browser runs those of Bleep Play. Bleep never offers a setting it cannot change. Tab Bleep App Plugins in Live Bleep Play Audio yes yes MIDI yes, with sync yes Web / App Web App Recordings yes yes Library yes yes yes Data yes Audio In the Bleep App Driver, Output and Input: your audio interface. Pick None to leave the output or the input unused. Sample rate and Buffer size: a smaller buffer means less delay and more chance of dropouts. The menu shows the delay of each size in milliseconds. If your interface does not offer a size with this input and output, the Settings say so and the interface keeps the size it runs at. Output channels and Input channels: shown for interfaces with more than one pair. Each pair you switch on becomes an In or Out port you can place with Add → Port . Right now: the delay, the CPU load and the number of dropouts. These numbers move while you play. System audio: captures what your computer plays. See Process what your computer plays. If no audio device runs, the tab says so: pick an output. In Bleep Play Output: the speakers or headphones to play to. Only Chrome and Edge can choose; other browsers always use the system's default output, and the tab says so. The list shows device names once your browser has been given audio or microphone permission; before that the devices are numbered. Latency: Interactive (the lowest delay, the default), Balanced or Playback (the fewest dropouts, for slower computers). The browser reads it when audio starts. If audio is already running, a Restart audio button appears: it reloads the page, your board is kept, and you press Start audio again. Right now: the sample rate and the delay your browser reports. In a plugin there is no Audio tab: Live owns the audio device, so choose it in Live's own Settings. The audio dot in the board's top bar opens Settings only in the app and in Bleep Play. MIDI In the Bleep App (MIDI and sync) Inputs: switch on the controllers the app listens to. Output: where the app's MIDI Out goes. Bleep App MIDI ports: how many virtual ports the app offers to other programs, such as Live (0 to 8, default 2). See the standalone app. Ableton Link and Tempo: share tempo and play state with other Link apps on your network. The tempo you set is used when nobody else sets it. In Bleep Play The browser asks once whether the page may use your MIDI devices. The tab shows Allow MIDI access until you decide; the question comes when you press it, not when you open Settings. Inputs: a switch for each controller. A switched-off controller is ignored. A MIDI Device node on the board picks its own controller and wins over these switches. They apply to boards without one. Safari has no Web MIDI, and the tab says so there. Web (the app) The link to Bleep Play and to Live plugins whose Board is Bleep Play . It is off until you switch it on; see Connecting for the whole path. Let Bleep Play pages connect to this app: the app then listens on this computer only. Port: 47100 unless it is taken. Connected boards: which pages are connected and in which latency mode. Pages you allowed: a page that is not served by the app asks first. Forget takes a page off the list. Recordings Where the Audio Console and other recording modules save their files. Folder: the Recordings folder. The default is Music/Beautiful Bleep/Recordings in your home folder. Type a full path, or press Choose… to pick a folder. A path that is not a full path, that cannot be made or that Bleep cannot write to is refused with a reason, and nothing changes. Show in the file manager opens the folder, and Use the default folder goes back to the default. The line below shows how much room the disk has. A change applies to the next recording; one that is running keeps writing where it started. The choice is kept in Bleep's data folder, which the app and every plugin share, so a folder chosen in one is the folder of all. Bleep Play has no folder: it keeps recordings in memory and offers them as a download. App (Bleep Play) The side of the link that lives in the browser: whether this page is connected to Bleep App, and a Connect to app button. It is the same button as in the side menu. The port is set in the app, under Settings → Web; the page uses the app's own address when the app serves it, and the standard port otherwise. Library The Library holds the modules and plugins you install. Its settings are the same in all three places, except where noted. Channel: stable or beta . Beta has newer modules that are less tested. Check for module updates at start (app only, on by default): the app asks the library what is new every time it starts. Switch it off and you check by hand with Check for updates . Library address (app, under Advanced ): only for a self-hosted or development library. It takes effect at the next start, and the app asks you to confirm before it uses another library. Check for updates and Show data folder (app and plugin). The app and the plugins share one data folder . The channel and the other library settings you set in a plugin are the app's too, and the other way round. In Bleep Play the library is the website you are on, so there is no address field. A change of channel is read when the page loads: the tab offers Reload now . In a plugin, Settings has only the Library tab. The Library window itself (where you install modules) is under File → Open Library… . Data (Bleep Play) What Bleep Play keeps in this browser: your board, your saved presets and these settings. Nothing is sent anywhere. Each row has a Clear button: Row What it removes Board Your board. The page reloads with the default one. Saved presets The presets you saved in this browser. Settings Puts the settings of this page back to their defaults. Everything All three, then the page reloads. Each asks first. To keep a board, use File → Download Project before you clear it. If your browser does not let the page store anything (a private window, or blocked site data), the tabs say so at the top: your choices last until you close the page.

title: Share a module
text: Share a module with the Bleep Library A module you wrote in a Code node can be published in the Bleep Library, where anyone can install it from the module list and use it like any other module. You do not need a key or any tools: everything happens in the browser. Before you start You have a script in a Code node that compiles (the status line under the editor says so). You are logged in to the Bleep Library in the same browser. If you are not, the Share dialog says so and links to the login page: log in in another tab, then press Share again. Your library name is the name your module is published under. If you have none yet, the library makes it when you share for the first time. Share it Open the Code node and press Compile . Fix any problems listed under the editor. Open the Metadata tab if you want to fill in details first: version, summary, category, licence, tags, a web page and release notes. You can also set them in the dialog. Press Share… . The dialog asks for: Field What to put Summary One or two sentences, up to 280 characters. The library shows it next to the module. Required Category Where the module goes in the Add menu, for example Effects Licence The terms others get: MIT, Apache-2.0, CC0-1.0, GPL-3.0-only and others Version Three numbers with dots, such as 1.0.0 Share the source code On by default. See Source code Help page Markdown, shown by the module's ? button. Headings, lists, tables, bold, code and links work; images are left out Press Share . Bleep compiles the module, packs it, uploads it and tells you the result, for example Shared as yourname/wobble 1.0.0 . The library checks the upload. It appears in the library list shortly afterwards, marked community . Your module's id is / . Whatever you typed in the dialog is kept, even if the upload fails, so you can fix the problem and press Share again. Share a new version Each share needs a higher version than the last one. The dialog suggests the next number for you. Versions cannot be replaced: a fix is a new version. Put what changed in the release notes on the Metadata tab. Share the source code With Share the source code on, the script goes with the module, under the same licence. Anyone who installs it can press Convert to code on it, read how it works, change it and make their own version. Turn it off to share only the compiled module. The module's picture If your script draws its own interface, that picture goes with the module. It runs in a locked-down frame: no network, no storage, and it is stopped if it hangs. Nobody's module can run code in the page. Install a module from the library Anyone can install a shared module from the module list in the Bleep Library, or find it in the Add menu once it is installed. It runs in the same sandbox as every other module, and no setting is needed. Limits and good to know You can publish up to 100 modules and make 10 uploads an hour . A package is at most 12 MB. A module is not part of a patch file . If you send someone a patch that uses your module, they need to install the module too, so share it first. If the library refuses your upload, the message in the dialog names the rule that failed. To withdraw a release, ask the library's admin. Apps that already have it stop loading it after their next update check. See also The Code node for the editor, Convert to module and the Metadata tab Publishing a module for the command-line route and developer releases

title: The standalone app
text: The Bleep App The board without a DAW: for playing and sound design on its own, or next to Live. It is one of three places to use Bleep (plugin, app, web). Open the app, add modules with Tab, and patch as in Live. Projects are saved as .bleepboard files (File → Save). Audio Choose your audio interface in File → Settings (all its tabs are in Settings). A new board starts with just In 1/2 and Out 1/2 . More pairs of your interface, the MIDI ports and the Link node are there when you need them: Add → Port . Delete the ones you don't use. What your computer plays The System node carries everything your computer plays: a music player, a browser, a video call. Patch it into effects, or into an Audio Out to process it. No virtual audio driver is needed. Turn it on in File → Settings → Audio → System audio → Capture what this computer plays . It is off until you do, because capturing sound needs your permission. Then add the node from Add → Port , like the other inputs. Your own sound is left out by default, so patching System to an output does not feed back. Where the system cannot do that (Linux, older Windows), play Bleep App to a different output than the one you capture. macOS 14.2 or later. The first time, macOS asks to allow Bleep App to record system audio. If System stays silent, allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording . Windows 10 or later. Leaving your own sound out needs Windows 10 build 20348 or later. Linux with PulseAudio or PipeWire. Settings lists the outputs you can capture. The capture adds about 40 ms of delay. It is meant for processing and recording, not for playing live against it. More, with the setup for each system and what to do when it stays silent: Process what your computer plays. A MIDI keyboard Add MIDI Device ( Add → Module → Sources ), click it and choose your controller. Patch its Notes into a Voice Cell — e.g. Slate Stabs — and the cell's Out L/R into Out 1/2 . MIDI Device also has mono Pitch , Gate , Velocity , Bend , Mod Wheel and CCs. It exists only in the app. MIDI to and from Live The app has its own MIDI ports, Bleep App 1 and Bleep App 2 (more in Settings). No loopback tool needed. Add their nodes from Add → Port . Play the app from Live: on a MIDI track, set MIDI To to Bleep App 1 . On the board, the Bleep App 1 MIDI In node gets the notes. Play Live from the app: patch into the Bleep App 1 MIDI Out node; on a MIDI track in Live, set MIDI From to Bleep App 1 and Monitor to In . Audio to and from Live: Bleep Audio Bridge Put Bleep Audio Bridge on any track in Live while the app runs. In the app it appears as a node named after the track: Send L/R: the track's audio, into the board. Return L/R: audio from the board, back to the track. The plugin's Monitor setting chooses what the track plays: Send (its own audio), Return (the app's audio) or Mix . With nothing patched into the return, the track's audio passes through. While bridges are connected, Live sets the pace: the app follows Live's audio, so nothing drifts. The bridge delays audio by two audio buffers and tells Live, so Live's delay compensation keeps everything in time. Exports include the app. Tempo and transport: Ableton Link Turn on Transport → Ableton Link in the app and the Link button in Live: both share tempo, beat and (with Start/Stop Sync) play and stop. The Link node puts tempo, beat, bar, clock and play state on the board.

title: Voice Cells
text: Voice Cells: polyphonic synths A Voice Cell turns one synthesizer voice into a polyphonic instrument. Inside, you patch one voice, like a mono synth. The cell plays it once per note, up to 16 voices at a time. Make one Add → Cell → New Voice Cell gives you a cell with a starter voice inside: Oscillator → VCA, with an ADSR on the VCA's gain. It makes sound right away. Add → Cell → Synthesizers → Slate Stabs is a ready-made synth: Dual Osc → Multi Filter → VCA, one ADSR for the filter and one for the VCA. Right-click an ordinary cell → Make Voice Cell turns it into one. Connect it From outside, a Voice Cell has: Jack What Notes all notes, e.g. from MIDI Device Notes Out L / Out R all voices, mixed your own inputs the same signal for every voice: an LFO, a cutoff macro, pitch bend your own outputs summed over the voices To play it from a sequencer or any pitch + gate source, put CV to Notes in between. Design the voice Double-click the cell. Inside are two fixed nodes: Voice In gives this voice its note: Pitch , Gate , Trigger , Velocity , Release , Pressure , Voice # (0, 1, 2 …) and Random (a new value per note, for a little variation between voices). Voice Out takes the voice's audio ( Out L , Out R ) and Active : patch the amp ADSR's Active here, so the voice is freed exactly when its sound has faded. A knob you turn inside changes it in every voice. Add your own shared inputs and outputs by dropping a cable on Cell In 's or Cell Out 's "new" row. Pitch bend: patch MIDI Device Bend into a shared input and, inside, into the oscillator's Pitch with amount 2/12 for ±2 semitones (that's how Basic Poly does it). Settings Click the cell to open its view: Setting What it does Voices 1–16 Allocation which free voice a new note gets: round robin, the lowest free one, or the voice that last played the same note Stealing when all voices are busy: take the oldest, quietest, lowest or highest note — or none (the new note is dropped) Mode Poly; Mono (one voice, every note restarts the envelopes); Legato (one voice, overlapping notes don't restart them) Glide time to slide from one pitch to the next; Glide Mode : always, or only when notes overlap Stereo Spread spreads the voices from left to right Output plain sum, or compensated (quieter per voice, so 8 voices don't clip) The dots on the node light up for the voices that play. Voices that don't play use no CPU. Save it Right-click → Save as preset , give it a name and a category (e.g. Synthesizers ). It then appears under Add → Cell → in every project.

title: Additive Osc
text: Additive Osc Additive Osc in the module view Introduction The Additive Osc builds its sound from up to 64 sine waves, the partials . Instead of 64 sliders it has a handful of spectral knobs: Tilt darkens or brightens, Odd/Even moves between hollow and full, Stretch and Shift bend the series into bells and metal, Comb carves moving notches and Chorus detunes the partials against each other. You can also draw your own spectrum. Partials above the top of the audio band are simply left out, so it never aliases, at any pitch. How does it work? Pitch. The fundamental is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), clamped to 1 Hz – 20 kHz and followed sample by sample. Partial n plays at the fundamental × its ratio (n, unless stretched) plus Shift . Levels. Each partial's level is the product of: Base: Saw 1/n, Square 1/n on odd partials only, Flat 1/√n (even energy per octave), or Drawn : your own bars. Tilt: dB per octave of partial number (−24 dark … +12 bright). Odd/Even: −1 odd partials only, +1 even only; the fundamental stays. Partials: how many sound; the last one fades in fractionally, so modulating it is smooth. Comb: notches every Comb Spacing partials; Comb Phase slides them along the spectrum and wraps, so an LFO sweeps them endlessly. Band limit: partials fade out between 40 % and 45 % of the sample rate and are dropped above. Levels glide over 2 ms, so all of these can be modulated without zipper noise. Normalise keeps the loudness constant (RMS 0.3) while you change the colour; off, a 64-partial saw spans about ±1. Stretch and Shift. Stretch above 0 makes upper partials go sharp (stiff strings, pianos, bells); below 0 it squeezes them together. The fundamental always stays on the note. Shift adds the same frequency (±1 × the note) to every partial: inharmonic, metallic, ring-modulated. Chorus. Each partial wanders by up to Chorus cents at about Chorus Rate , seeded, so the ensemble shimmer never repeats a pattern but every render is the same. Phases. Random starts each partial at a seeded phase (smooth, no peaky waveform); Aligned starts them all together (the sharp shape of a true saw). A Trigger restarts them. Decay. With Decay below its maximum, a Trigger strikes: every partial decays, the fundamental by 60 dB in Decay , higher partials faster by Damp (at 100 % partial 10 dies 100× faster than the fundamental). A new trigger brings the levels back up within 2 ms. At maximum (20 s) the sound sustains; without triggers it always sustains. Stereo. Width pans the odd partials left and the even partials right (up to 70 % at full width); the fundamental stays centred and the mono sum stays within 1.5 dB. How to use it? Organ / drawbars: Base Square or Drawn, Partials 8–16. Bell: Stretch +0.6, Phases Aligned, Decay 3 s, Damp 60 %, triggers from the note's gate. Pluck: Decay 0.4 s, Damp 80 %, Tilt −3 dB/oct. Moving notches: Comb 80 %, a slow LFO on Comb Phase . Ensemble pad: Chorus 20 ct, Chorus Rate 0.5 Hz, Width 70 %. Sub-bass: use the Fundamental output under the main sound. Drawing With Base on Drawn the view shows 64 bars. Drag across them to paint levels (Shift: fine, relative), double-click a bar to reset it to 1/n, or use Saw , Square , Flat , Smooth and Randomize . A drag is one undo step. The drawing is saved with the board. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Additive Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Additive Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Additive Osc: Tilt Sweep A saw-shaped stack of partials whose Tilt is swept by a slow LFO, from dark and woolly to bright and ringing, with no filter involved. Reduce Partials for a rounder tone or push Tilt up for an organ-like glare. Additive Osc: Odd Partials Reed Odd/Even is pulled to the odd side so only the 1st, 3rd, 5th partials sound: a hollow, reedy tone. Move Odd/Even through zero to bring back the even partials and watch the reed turn into a full saw. Additive Osc: Stretched Bells A flat spectrum with Stretch pushing the partials apart gives inharmonic, bell-like tones, and each trigger restarts a decay that makes the high partials die first. Change Stretch for a metallic or glassy family, or Decay for longer ringing. Additive Osc: Comb Choir A slow chord line played by a comb-notched spectrum with a wide chorus, giving a shimmering, voice-like pad. Change Comb Spacing to move the notches or raise Chorus for a bigger, more unstable cloud. Additive Osc: Odd and Even Split The odd-partial and even-partial outputs go to separate mixer channels whose pans drift in opposite directions, so the two halves of one tone circle each other. Mute one channel to hear its half alone. Presets The preset bar of the Additive Osc view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Saw A smooth, slightly darkened additive saw. Organ Drawbars Odd partials with a limited count: a hollow organ. Clarinet Mostly odd partials: hollow and woody. Even Glass Even partials only: a thin, glassy octave-like tone. Dark Sine Pad Few, quiet upper partials: a dark, near-sine pad. Bright Buzz Strong high partials: a very bright, buzzing tone. Ensemble Pad Detuned partials and stereo spread: a shimmering ensemble pad. Bell Stretched partials struck by a trigger: patch the note gate to Trigger. Pluck A short, plucked string-like tone; needs a trigger from the note. Metal Shift Shifted, inharmonic partials: ring-modulated and metallic. Comb Notches Notches carved in the spectrum: modulate Comb Phase with a slow LFO. Squeezed Choir Compressed partials: dense, vocal and choir-like. Stiff Strings A slightly stretched, piano-like struck tone. Fundamental Whisper Just the first few partials: a pure, flute-like tone. Random Phase Cloud Heavily detuned partials: a wide, cloudy texture.
