title: Beat Oscillator
text: Beat Oscillator Introduction Beat Oscillator is a heterodyne tone source, the way old laboratory signal generators worked. Two high carriers, A and B , run close together and are mixed, and what you hear is their difference. Turn Beat a little around zero and the tone sweeps from several kilohertz down to a slow pulse, then stops. The charm is in how imperfect it is. Pull couples the carriers so they try to lock. Inside the lock range the beat disappears; just outside it the tone stumbles along in uneven blips. Drift lets both carriers wander, and close to zero beat even a tiny wander is a big change. Warm-up starts the carriers flat, so the tone glides into tune like a cold valve instrument. How does it work? Two carriers. A runs at Carrier . B runs at Carrier plus Beat plus Fine . Pitch (1 V/oct) transposes both, so the beat tone moves with them. The Detune input adds hertz to B ( Detune Range per 1.0) without being scaled by Pitch, like a hand moved near a tuning capacitor. FM modulates B's frequency directly and can push it through zero: 1.0 is 1 kHz of deviation. Beat. The knob is cubic, so the middle is very fine: on Range ±2 kHz, 10 % is 2 Hz and 50 % is 250 Hz. Range sets the full swing (±20 Hz, ±200 Hz or ±2 kHz). Fine adds ±2 Hz for finding zero beat. The view shows the actual beat in hertz. Mixer and detector. The carriers are multiplied, and a steep low-pass (the detector ) keeps only the difference. Mixer picks the circuit: Ideal: a clean multiplier. The beat is a pure sine. Diode: a half-wave square-law mixer. The beat is brighter and slightly buzzy, with its own harmonics. Overdriven: both carriers clipped almost to squares first. The beat sounds like a triangle, with a little carrier leaking through. At 0 %, Detector passes beats up to about 2 kHz and nothing else. Open it and the sum of the carriers comes through as a whistle. You only hear it when the carriers are low: turn Carrier below about 11 kHz with the detector open. Pull. The carriers are coupled, so each one drags the other. The lock range grows with Pull (25 % → 3 Hz, 50 % → 25 Hz, 100 % → 200 Hz). Inside the lock range both carriers run at one frequency and the beat stops. Lock goes high. Just outside it the beat is much slower than the detuning (the square-root law: 30 Hz detuning with a 25 Hz lock range beats at 16.6 Hz). The phase difference crawls, then whips round once, so Out plays one-cycle blips between near-silences. Let Drift or a slow Detune move the pair across the edge and the blips lurch, bunch up and stop. Far outside it is a plain beat again. Coupling. AC removes DC from Out (below 5 Hz). Slow beats become swells, and a locked pair is silent. DC keeps slow beats as a usable modulation signal, and a locked pair holds a steady level. Drift and warm-up. With Drift up, each carrier wanders on its own smooth random curve, by up to ±25 cents at 100 %. At 10 kHz that is about ±145 Hz, enough to throw a 2 Hz beat all over the place, while a 2 kHz beat barely notices. While the transport plays, the wander follows the song position (a slow turn every 8 beats, small wobbles every beat). With Warm-up on, both carriers start up to 40 cents flat, by different amounts, and settle over the warm-up time. Warm-up starts when the transport starts. While stopped it starts when the board loads, or when you press Cold . Beat and Lock outputs. Beat measures the beat frequency by counting how often the phase difference slips a full turn, and puts it out as 1 V/oct (0 V = 261.6 Hz, i.e. C4). When the pair locks it falls smoothly to its floor of 0.1 Hz (−11.35 V). Lock is high while the carriers are locked. Repeatable. The drift curves come from Seed . A transport start resets the phases, the filters and the warm-up, so a render from the same start is always the same. Inside a Voice Cell each voice drifts on its own. The view Two dials show the actual frequencies of A and B, after drift, warm-up and pulling. Between them is the beat B − A in hertz (signed, in millihertz below 1 Hz) and the Lock lamp. The lamp is lit while locked. Outside lock it flashes once per slip, so a slow beat shows as a blinking lamp. Below them, the circle shows the phase difference ψ as a dot with a fading tail. Locked, the dot stands still. Near the edge it creeps, then flicks round. Far out it spins and blurs into a ring. How to use it? Theremin sweep: Range ±2 kHz, sweep Beat slowly from 0 % to 60 % with a slow LFO or by hand. Lurching pulse: Pull 50 %, Range ±200 Hz, Beat just past the lock edge (B − A around 27 Hz), Drift 30 %. Out into a VCA or filter. Lock as a gate: the same patch with Lock into an envelope. Drift pulls the pair in and out of lock at irregular times. Tape-warmup intro: Warm-up 30 s, Beat around 100 Hz: the tone slides into tune when the transport starts. Slow modulation: Coupling DC, Range ±20 Hz, Beat near zero: Out is a drifting sub-hertz wave for filters or panning. Whistle: Carrier 3 kHz, Detector 100 %: the sum tone joins the beat. Melodic beat: a sequencer into Pitch transposes the beat tone by octaves, and Beat (the output) gives back its pitch for a second oscillator. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Beat Oscillator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Beat Oscillator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Beat Oscillator: Heterodyne Drone Two high carriers beat against each other and a slow LFO sweeps Beat, so a pure tone glides down into a throbbing pulse and back. Turn Drift up for a wandering, unstable tone or move Beat by hand for a held pitch. Beat Oscillator: Played Melody The sequencer's pitch is fed to the Pitch input so the heterodyne tone plays a tune, with a gentle envelope for each note. Change Carrier to shift the character, or raise Fine to detune the whole line. Beat Oscillator: Pull and Stutter A slow LFO raises Pull so the two carriers try to lock: the tone stutters, drops into pulses and jumps into pitch as they catch each other. Move Pull and Detector by hand to hear the stutter appear and disappear. Beat Oscillator: Slow Pulse Bass A low heterodyne bass under a drum loop: each sequencer note retunes the pair through Pitch and an envelope shapes it, with the Diode mixer adding grit. Try the Range setting at ±20 Hz or ±2 kHz and move Beat to change how deep it sits. Beat Oscillator: Overdriven Mixer The Mixer setting on Overdriven adds harmonics and sidebands to the beat tone, and Drift keeps it alive and slightly unstable. Compare Ideal, Diode and Overdriven to hear the same beat with three characters. Presets The preset bar of the Beat Oscillator view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Lab Tone Classic heterodyne sine around 260 Hz, slightly alive. Pure Low A steady, drift-free low sine tone, good for sub and tests. Bright Whistle High beat tone around 1.2 kHz, thin and whistly. Diode Buzz Brighter, buzzy beat from a diode mixer: a reedy lead. Overdriven Triangle Squared-off carriers give a triangle-like beat with a little leak. Slow Tremolo Beat of a few hertz: the tone swells and fades like a tremolo. Slow Pulse Sub-audio beat of about one hertz; use as a smooth LFO. Wandering Zero Near zero beat with strong drift: the pitch lurches unpredictably. Locking Stutter Coupled carriers try to lock: uneven blips between near-silences. Hard Lock Strong coupling: the beat vanishes and returns as drift moves across the lock edge. Open Detector Opening the detector lets the sum tone whistle through above the beat. Cold Valve Starts flat and glides into tune like a cold instrument. Hand Capacity Wide Detune range: patch a slow control to it for theremin-like hand moves. FM Siren Mid-high buzzing beat to patch an LFO into FM for sirens. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Carrier 500 Hz – 18 kHz 10 kHz Beat −100 … +100 % (cubic: ± Range ) +51 % (+261.6 Hz on ±2 kHz) Fine −2 … +2 Hz 0 Hz Pull 0 – 100 % 0 % Detector 0 – 100 % 0 % Drift 0 – 100 % 15 % Detune Range 0 – 200 Hz 20 Hz Range ±20 Hz, ±200 Hz, ±2 kHz ±2 kHz Mixer Ideal, Diode, Overdriven Ideal Coupling AC, DC AC Warm-up Off, 10 s, 30 s, 2 min Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Carrier: the frequency of A. Beat: B's offset from A: Range × x³. Fine: added to the offset, for dialling zero beat. Pull: coupling between the carriers; lock range 200 Hz × Pull³. Detector: the mixer's low-pass, 2.5 kHz at 0 % up to 60 kHz at 100 %. Drift: how far the carriers wander, up to ±25 cents. Detune Range: hertz added to B per 1.0 at the Detune input. Range: the full swing of Beat . Mixer: the mixing circuit (see above). Coupling: AC removes DC from Out; DC keeps it. Warm-up: how long the carriers take to come up to pitch. Seed: picks the drift curves. All knobs are modulation destinations. The Cold button restarts the warm-up while the transport is stopped. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct on both carriers (transposes the beat tone) Detune control adds Detune × Detune Range Hz to B FM audio linear, through-zero FM of B: 1.0 = 1 kHz Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the difference tone A, B audio the raw carriers, after pulling and drift Beat pitch the measured beat frequency as 1 V/oct (0 V = 261.6 Hz) Lock gate high while the carriers are locked

title: Dual Osc
text: Dual Osc Dual Osc in the module view Introduction The Dual Osc is two analog-style oscillators, A and B , wired together for the sounds that need two oscillators talking to each other. B can frequency-modulate A, A can sync to B, and the pair runs into a wavefolder that turns soft waves into bright, moving spectra. It is a complete complex-oscillator voice in one module, and still two ordinary oscillators when that's all you need. How does it work? Two cores. Each core reads sine, triangle, saw and pulse from one phase and morphs between them with its Shape knob (as the Oscillator). Saw, pulse, triangle and every sync jump are band-limited at their exact moment in time, so even hard-synced and frequency-modulated waves stay clean. Pitch. A plays C4 × 2^(Octave A + Tune A/12 + Fine A/1200 + Pitch). B follows the same Pitch input while B Track is on, plus its own Pitch B input; with B Track off only Pitch B moves it. B Range Low divides B by 100 (about 0.03–200 Hz), turning it into a vibrato or growl-rate modulator. FM (B → A). B's sine (whatever Shape B is), plus the FM input, modulates A's frequency by FM Depth : Linear is through-zero: A's frequency is f × (1 + 4 × depth × m). When it goes negative the phase runs backwards, so the note stays in tune at any depth. Integer ratios between A and B give harmonic, bell- and brass-like tones. Exponential is analog-style: f × 2^(4 × depth × m), ±4 octaves at 100 %. The pitch drifts upward with depth: the classic growl and siren. Sync (A → B). Each time B finishes a cycle it acts on A. Up to 50 % this is a reversing soft sync: if A is in the last part of its cycle it changes direction instead of jumping, a gentle, vocal colour. From 50 % to 100 % the reset gets harder until, at 100 %, A restarts with every cycle of B: the classic tearing sync lead when you sweep A's pitch. Folder. The A/B mix ( Balance ) is driven by Fold (gain 1 to 12) plus the Fold CV input, biased by Symmetry , and folded back into ±1 by four stages. At Fold 0 the folder is transparent; the first quarter of the knob moves it from clean to a soft sine fold, and further stages join as you turn it up. Symmetry adds even harmonics and makes the folds move. A DC blocker follows (Symmetry adds DC). Oversampled. Cores, FM, sync and folder run at 2× ( Normal ) or 4× ( High ) and every output is decimated by the same filter, so A, B, Mix, Ring, Sub and Out stay in phase with each other. Stereo. With Width above 0, Out L and Out R fold slightly different mixes (Balance ∓ Width/4) and R's Symmetry is mirrored at full width. The image collapses cleanly to mono. At Width 0 both outputs are identical. Drift. A seeded slow wander of each core's pitch, up to ±8 cents at 100 %. The same Seed gives the same drift on every render; it restarts when the transport starts. How to use it? Complex voice: Pitch from Voice In, Out L/R → VCA. Raise Fold and modulate it with an envelope for plucked, west-coast tones. FM bell: Shape A 0 % (sine), Octave B +1 or Tune B +7, FM Depth 30–60 %, Linear. Put an envelope on FM Depth . Sync lead: Sync 100 %, Octave B −1, sweep Tune A or modulate Pitch of A only (patch into Pitch with B Track off and feed B from Pitch B ). Growl: B Range Low, FM Mode Exponential, FM Depth 20 %. Two oscillators: use A and B outputs separately; Ring gives A × B. Wide pad: Width 60 %, a little Fold and Symmetry , Drift 30 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Dual Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Dual Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Dual Osc: Complex Lead Oscillator B frequency-modulates A while an envelope opens FM Depth and Fold on every note: each note starts bright and metallic and settles to a clearer tone. Change Tune B to pick different FM ratios, or raise Fold for more edge. Dual Osc: Sync Sweep A is hard-synced to B and the Sync amount is swept by a slow ramp, so the tone tears from a clean saw into a growling, harmonic-rich buzz. Turn Sync by hand to stop the sweep where you like it. Dual Osc: Drifting Pad Two softly detuned cores with Drift and Width turned up make a slowly moving stereo pad, with a hint of Fold from a slow LFO. Raise Drift for more instability or pull Tune B further from A for a thicker chord. Dual Osc: Ring Bells The Ring output multiplies A and B, giving clangorous, bell-like sidebands that die away with each note. Tune B moves the bell from soft and hollow to harsh and tuneless; choose a fifth or a tritone to hear the difference. Dual Osc: Folded Bass A low note from both cores is driven into the wavefolder; Fold rides a slow LFO and Symmetry shifts the odd and even folds, so the bass flips between mellow and snarling. Try the Exponential FM Mode or a different Symmetry for other growls. Presets The preset bar of the Dual Osc view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Fat Saw Pair Two slightly detuned saws: the classic fat analog voice. Octave Bass A saw over a square sub octave for a solid bass. Hollow Pulse Duo Two pulses with different widths and slight detune: hollow and wide. Sync Lead Hard sync: sweep Tune A for the classic tearing lead. Soft Sync Voice Gentle reversing sync: a vocal, slightly nasal colour. FM Bell Sine FM with a non-integer ratio: patch an envelope on FM Depth. Electric Piano Soft 1:1 FM: a warm, tine-like electric piano tone. Brass FM Harmonic FM with a touch of fold: a punchy brass-like tone. Growl Exponential FM from a low sine: growling, siren-like bass. West Coast Fold A sine pushed into the wavefolder: bright, harmonic. Modulate Fold. Folded Pad Soft waves with gentle folding and wide drift: a moving pad. Wide Stereo Saw Wide, drifting saw pair for pads and chords. Slow Growl Mod B in Low range as a slow vibrato-rate FM for wobbling tone. Metallic Clang Strong inharmonic FM and fold: metal, gongs and noise-like hits. Drifting Duo Two soft waves with strong analog drift: unstable, vintage. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave A, Octave B −4 … +4 (stepped) 0, −1 Tune A, Tune B −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine A, Fine B −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Shape A, Shape B 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw), 0 % (sine) Width A 5 – 95 % 50 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Sync 0 – 100 % 0 % Balance 0 – 100 % 50 % Fold 0 – 100 % 0 % Symmetry −1 … +1 0 Drift 0 – 100 % 10 % Width 0 – 100 % 0 % FM Mode Linear, Exponential Linear B Track On, Off On B Range Audio, Low (÷ 100) Audio Quality Normal (2×), High (4×) Normal Seed 0 – 999 1 Shape A / Shape B: 0 % sine, 33 % triangle, 67 % saw, 100 % pulse. Width A: pulse width of A's pulse end. FM Depth: smoothed over 5 ms, so it can be swept without clicks. Balance: 0 % only A, 100 % only B into Mix and the folder. Quality: High costs about twice the CPU and lowers aliasing of synced and folded sounds further. All knobs are modulation destinations; the settings are not. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct both cores (B only while B Track is on); 0.0 = C4 Pitch B pitch, 1 V/oct added to B only FM audio added to B's sine as the modulator of A, scaled by FM Depth Sync trigger a rising edge restarts both cores (one per note, for example) Fold CV audio added to the folder's input at audio rate Outputs Output Signal What it does A audio core A with FM and sync, shaped by Shape A B audio core B, shaped by Shape B Mix audio A and B by Balance , before the folder Out L, Out R audio the folded mix; identical at Width 0 Ring audio A's sine × B's sine Sub audio square an octave below A; it flips on every cycle of A, also after a hard sync reset A, B, Mix, Ring and Sub run between about −1 and +1; Out L/R stay within about ±1.2 (band-limited folds overshoot slightly). Unpatched outputs cost no CPU for their decimation.

title: Formant Osc
text: Formant Osc Formant Osc in the module view Introduction The Formant Osc is a pulse-formant oscillator. Every cycle of the note fires one short burst of a second, higher oscillation: the formant . The note sets the pitch; the formant sets a resonant peak in the spectrum, like the mouth shape of a voice or the body of an instrument. Sweeping Formant gives vocal, filter-like sweeps with no filter in the patch, and Narrow makes the sound brighter and buzzier. How does it work? Fundamental. The note is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch). A band-limited square and a sub (one octave down) run on the same cycle. Formant. The formant frequency comes from the Formant knob in octaves: Ratio tracking: relative to the note (+1 = twice the note, +2 = four times). The timbre is the same on every key. Fixed tracking: relative to C4. The peak stays put while the note moves, like a vowel sung on different notes. The knob goes through zero : around 0 the formant slows to 0 Hz and then runs backwards for negative values. With Start on Cosine a 0 Hz formant is the window itself, so a sweep from −1 to +1 goes formant → soft pulse → formant without a gap. Formant CV adds octaves; Formant FM modulates the formant frequency linearly (±4× at FM Depth 100 %, through zero). The burst. Each cycle the formant plays under a smooth window. Narrow shortens the window (from the whole cycle to 5 % of it) and sharpens it: fewer formant cycles per burst, a wider peak and a brighter, buzzier tone. At high notes the window is kept at least 12 samples long, so the bursts never alias; Narrow then has less range. Reset. At 100 % every burst starts identically: the spectrum is purely harmonic and the formant is a clean peak. Lower values let the formant drift against the note for inharmonic, ring-modulated and chorused colours; 0 % is a free-running formant gated by the window. Roll moves the window inside the cycle. It wraps, so turning it never cuts a burst; modulated, it gives a phasing movement against the square, best heard with Body around 50 %. Second formant. Out R plays a second formant Spread octaves away from the first, sharing the cycle and the window. At Spread 0 L and R are identical; small values give width, larger ones two peaks, one per ear. Body mixes the square (at half level) and the formant at Out . Roll and Narrow glide over 2 ms, so fast modulation doesn't click. A Sync edge restarts the cycle with a very short crossfade from the old one. How to use it? Talking bass: Octave −1, an envelope on Formant (up 2–3 octaves), Narrow 40 %. Vowel on a melody: Tracking Fixed, Formant +1.5, play notes on Pitch : the peak stays like a sung vowel. Wah: an LFO on Formant (or Formant CV ), Body 90 %. Wide pad: Spread ±0.1, Reset 80 % for slow beating. Pinging modulation: Octave −4 and below: the bursts become rhythmic pings, useful as an odd modulation source. Put Quality on High for bright patches above C6. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Formant Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Formant Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Formant Osc: Vowel Sweep A flowing melody on the Formant Osc while a slow LFO sweeps the Formant peak, so the tone opens and closes like a voice changing vowels, without a filter anywhere. Move Formant by hand, or raise Narrow for a more nasal peak. Formant Osc: Squelch Bass A decaying envelope sweeps the formant peak up and down on every note, giving a squelchy bass that behaves like a resonant filter although there is none. Change Narrow for a sharper squelch, or lengthen the decay for a longer wow. Formant Osc: Wide Choir Slow chord roots on the Formant Osc with Spread and Body opened up make a breathy, choir-like pad that sits wide in the stereo field. Turn Spread to zero for mono, or Roll up to soften the upper end. Formant Osc: Random Vowels A fast arpeggio while a Random module picks a new smooth Formant position every few beats: each note wears a different vowel. Raise Random's Smooth for glides between vowels, or Spread for bolder jumps. Formant Osc: Fixed Resonance With Tracking on Fixed, the formant peak stays put while the notes move, as in a real vowel across a sung tune, instead of rising with the pitch. Switch Tracking back to Ratio and the whole tone shifts with each note. Presets The preset bar of the Formant Osc view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Vowel Tone A sung vowel: the peak stays fixed while the note moves. Talking Bass Bass with a resonant peak: put an envelope on Formant. Wah Lead Sweep Formant with an LFO for a wah-pedal lead. Filter-less Squelch Acid-like squelch with no filter: envelope the Formant. Hollow Ghost Formant near zero: a hollow, soft pulse; sweep through it. Reverse Formant Negative formant runs backwards: a different, hollow colour. Wide Choir Spread and drifting reset: a wide, breathy choir pad. Two Peaks Left and right ears get different formants for a two-peak sound. Buzzy Saw Narrow, bright bursts: a buzzy, sawlike tone. Soft Sine Voice A wide, smooth burst: mellow and almost sinelike. Phasing Roll Roll moves the window; modulate it for phasing against the square. Inharmonic Ring Low reset lets the formant drift: ring-modulated, bell-like colours. FM Formant Open FM depth: patch an audio source to Formant FM for growling timbre. Pinging Sub Very low note turns into rhythmic pings: odd modulation or percussion. Bright Bell High Clean high register thanks to High quality. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave −4 … +4 (stepped) 0 Coarse −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Formant −6 … +6 oct (through zero) +2 oct Narrow 0 – 100 % 30 % Body 0 – 100 % 70 % Reset 0 – 100 % 100 % Roll 0 – 100 % (wraps) 0 % Spread −1 … +1 oct 0 FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Tracking Ratio, Fixed Ratio Start Sine, Cosine Cosine Quality Normal (1×), High (2×) Normal All knobs are modulation destinations; the settings are not. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the note; 0.0 = C4 Formant CV pitch moves the formant in octaves (1.0 = one octave) Formant FM audio linear, through-zero FM of the formant, scaled by FM Depth Sync trigger restarts the cycle (and a new burst) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio square and formant mixed by Body ; R uses the second formant Formant audio the burst train alone (first formant) Square audio band-limited square at the note, ±1 Sub audio square one octave below The formant peaks at about ±1 (up to ±1.6 with very narrow bursts).

title: Macro Osc
text: Macro Osc Macro Osc in the module view Introduction The Macro Osc is sixteen synthesis models behind one Model knob. Every model is played with the same three macro knobs, Tone , Shape and Blend : they stay where they are on the panel, but change their meaning (and their label) with the model. One patch can move from a detuned analog pair to FM, a sung vowel, a plucked string or a snare by turning one knob or by sending it a cable. Each model also has a second voice on Aux : the other oscillator, the modulator, the root of a chord, the noise of a snare. And a Trigger input with a built-in decay envelope and low-pass gate turns any model into a struck, percussive sound without extra modules. It is a sketching tool and a compact voice for Voice Cells. The dedicated oscillators (Dual Osc, Wavefolder, Formant Osc, Additive Osc, Wavetable Osc, Chord Osc, Resonator, Perc Voice) go deeper into one technique each; several Macro Osc models are smaller versions of their cores. How does it work? Pitch. The frequency is C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), kept between 1 Hz and 0.45 × the sample rate. The FM input is linear and through-zero, as on the Oscillator: f × (1 + 4 × FM Depth × FM), so at 100 % a ±1 signal swings the frequency by ±4×. For the noise models the pitch is the centre of their filter, for the drums the body pitch (C4 is a mid tom, Octave −2 a kick). On the models without a playable pitch (Noise Band, Dust, Kick, Snare, Metal) the FM input moves Tone instead (FM Depth 100 % and a +1 signal = the whole knob). Changing models. Model is a dropdown a cable can drive: the cable snaps to the nearest model, read once per audio block. A change crossfades over 5 ms, both models running, so a Step Sequencer or a Random can play the models like notes without clicks. A change asked for during a fade follows when the fade ends. Every model keeps its state while another one plays, so a ringing string carries on when you come back to it. Only the selected model (and, for 5 ms, the previous one) uses CPU. Trigger, envelope and gate. Trigger unpatched: the pitched and noise models sound continuously, Decay and Gate Colour do nothing and Env is 0. Pluck and Modal are excited by a quiet stream of noise instead of a strike: bowed, blown, singing. Kick , Snare and Metal are silent (the view says so). Trigger patched: each trigger lifts the envelope to Accent (unpatched: 1) in 0.5 ms, then it falls to −60 dB in Decay . Env outputs it. Out and Aux of models 1–11 go through a low-pass gate: a VCA and a 2-pole low-pass in series, both following the envelope (smoothed by 3 ms, so the gate closes with a soft tail). Gate Colour 0 % is a plain VCA (cubic), 100 % a pure filter sweep from 20 kHz down to 20 Hz, 50 % both. The struck models ( Pluck , Modal , Kick , Snare , Metal ) are hit by the trigger with strength Accent and decay with Decay themselves; the gate is not applied to them. A new hit adds energy to what is still ringing instead of restarting it, so fast rolls build up. The drums read Tone at the moment of the hit, so a moving knob doesn't smear a hit. Noise and Seed. All noise is seeded from Seed and, inside a Voice Cell, the voice number: renders repeat exactly, and every voice sounds a little different. It is reseeded when the transport starts. Quality. Eco runs everything at the sample rate and Modal with 8 modes. Normal runs Fold, FM and Phase Warp at 2× and the band-limited oscillators (VA Pair, Chord, the Vowel's glottis) at 4×, with 16 modes. High runs the oversampled models at 4× and Modal with 24 modes. At high notes Fold, FM and Phase Warp also rein in their brightness (drive, index, feedback, resonance) so the sound stays clean instead of aliasing. The models The knob names in brackets are what the panel shows for each model. Pitched 1 VA Pair. Two analog-style oscillators (band-limited saw, square and pulse, also through hard sync). Tone [Detune]: up to 70 % detunes oscillator 2 by up to a semitone on a slow curve (50 % ≈ 19 cents, a fat chorus); above, it jumps to a third, fourth, fifth and octave. Shape [Wave]: saw → square over the first half, then the pulse narrows to 5 %. Blend [Sync]: 0 free; turning up hard-syncs oscillator 2 to oscillator 1 and raises its ratio by up to three octaves: the classic sync sweep. Aux : oscillator 2 alone. 2 Fold. A sine (or triangle) folded back on itself by four stages. Tone [Fold]: drive 1…16×. Shape [Bias]: an offset before folding (50 % = none): even harmonics and movement. Blend [Source]: sine → triangle. Aux : the driven source, hard-clipped. 3 FM. Two-operator FM (phase modulation). Tone [Ratio]: the modulator's ratio: ½, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 (centre), 3.5, 4, 5, 7, 9. Each ratio owns a slice of the knob, with a short crossfade between slices. Shape [Index]: modulation index 0…8 (50 % = 2). Blend [Feedback]: the modulator modulates itself, sine → saw-like. Aux : the modulator. 4 Phase Warp. A cosine read through a bent phase, as on the Casio CZ. Tone [Warp]: from a pure sine to a sharp, saw-like wave. Shape [Resonance]: a sine at 1…16× the pitch under a falling window, restarted every cycle: a resonant filter sweep without a filter. Blend [Mix]: warp → resonance. Aux : a square one octave down. 5 Grain. One windowed sine burst per cycle (the Formant Osc's core). Tone [Formant]: the burst's frequency, ½…16× the pitch: a vocal or filter-like peak that moves without changing the note. Shape [Width]: the burst length (100 % = the whole cycle, smooth; low = short, buzzy). Blend [Pair]: adds a second burst at 1.5× the formant. Aux : a sine at the pitch. 6 Harmonic. 24 sine partials with a movable spectral peak. Tone [Centre]: the peak, from partial 1 to 24. Shape [Width]: narrow (one partial sings) → wide (a full, organ-like spectrum). Blend [Odd/Even]: all partials → odd only at 50 % (hollow, clarinet) → even only at 100 % (with the fundamental). Aux : the odd partials. Partials fade out before the Nyquist frequency, so sweeps never alias or click. 7 Table. Eight of the Wavetable Osc's factory banks. Tone [Bank]: Analog, Harmonic, Pulse, Sync, FM, Organ, Digital, Bell (in eighths of the knob; a change crossfades). Shape [X], Blend [Y]: the position on the bank's 8 × 8 grid. Aux : the same wave one octave down. 8 Chord. Four oscillators playing a chord, a few cents apart. Tone [Chord]: octaves, 5th, sus2, sus4, minor, major, m7 (50 %), maj7, 7, m9, maj9, 6/9. Shape [Voicing]: root position, 1st, 2nd and 3rd inversion, Drop 2 (50 %), Open, Wide, Spread. Blend [Wave]: sine → triangle → saw. Aux : the root alone, a bass voice that follows the chord. 9 Vowel. A glottal pulse and breath through three formant filters. Tone [Vowel]: a → e → i → o → u. Shape [Size]: the vocal tract: small (formants an octave up, a child or a chipmunk) → large (an octave down). Blend [Breath]: voiced → whispered. Aux : the breath (unvoiced) part alone. Noise 10 Noise Band. White noise through a resonant filter at the pitch. Tone [Resonance]: Q 0.5 (a wide band) … 40 (a whistling tone). Shape [Mode]: low-pass → band-pass → high-pass. Blend [Clock]: clean → sample-rate-reduced, crunchy noise. Aux : the other side: high-pass for low-pass, notch for band-pass. 11 Dust. Random clicks. Tone [Density]: 1 to 20 000 clicks per second (50 % ≈ 140): from crackle to rain to noise. Shape [Colour]: their filter, from dark (thumps an octave below the pitch) to bright (ticks). Blend [Bipolar]: all positive → half of them negative. Aux : the raw clicks. Struck 12 Pluck. A plucked string (a tuned delay-line waveguide). Tone [Bright]: the pluck: soft finger → hard pick. Shape [Damping]: bright, ringing string → dull, damped. Blend [Position]: where it is plucked: near the bridge (bright) → the middle (hollow). Decay : how long it rings. Aux : the pluck (the exciter) alone. 13 Modal. A struck object: 8 / 16 / 24 resonant modes by Quality . Tone [Material]: string → bar → plate → bell. Shape [Bright]: soft mallet and dark modes → hard mallet and bright. Blend [Stretch]: stretches the modes up to 15 % (more metallic). Decay : how long it rings. Aux : the odd modes. 14 Kick. A swept sine with a click. Patch Octave −2 for a kick drum, higher for toms. Tone [Sweep]: the pitch drop, 0…4 octaves. Shape [Punch]: how fast it drops (80 ms → 4 ms). Blend [Drive]: soft clipping. Decay : the body. Aux : the click. 15 Snare. Two drum-head resonators and noise. Tone [Snappy]: the noise (snares) level. Shape [Tone]: the balance of the two heads (low → high). Blend [Noise Colour]: the noise band, 1.5 → 12 kHz. Decay : body and snares. Aux : the noise alone. 16 Metal. Six detuned square waves, as in the 808's cymbals and hats. Tone [Colour]: the high-pass cutoff: gong → closed hat. Shape [Spread]: the detune between the six: close (a chord) → wide (clang). Blend [Ring]: a ringing band-pass resonance (a cowbell, a bell). Decay : short = hi-hat, long = cymbal. Aux : the unfiltered metal. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Macro Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Macro Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Macro Osc: Plucked Strings The Pluck model struck by the sequencer's trigger: its built-in decay and low-pass gate shape every note, so no envelope or VCA is needed. Turn Decay for longer strings, Tone for brightness and Shape for how hard the string is hit. Macro Osc: Vowel Choir The Vowel model holds slow notes while a slow LFO walks Tone through the vowels, so the choir seems to sing a different syllable on every phrase. Turn Blend to change the voice or Shape for brightness. Macro Osc: FM Electric Keys The FM model as a tine-and-bell keyboard sound: Tone sets the modulator ratio and an envelope on Shape gives each key a sparkle that fades. Change Tone to hop between ratios, or raise Blend for more of the second voice. Macro Osc: Synth Drum Kit Three Macro Oscs on the Kick, Snare and Metal models are struck by a drum grid: a whole beat from one module type. Change each model's Decay and Tone to tune the kit, or switch a model for other percussion. Macro Osc: Modal Marimba The Modal model struck by a trigger rings like a wooden bar. Tone moves from soft wood to bright metal, Decay lengthens the ring, and Accent from the velocity gives the loud and soft notes. Presets The preset bar of the Macro Osc view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Fat VA Pair Two detuned saws: a fat classic analog voice. Sync Sweep Hard-synced pair: move Blend for the classic sync sweep. Wavefold Sine A sine folded back on itself: bright, harmonic timbre. FM Bell Tone Two-operator FM with a bell-like ratio. Phase Warp Bass A bent cosine: a warm, saw-like bass. Vowel Voice A sung vowel: sweep Tone from a to u. Hollow Harmonics Odd harmonics only: a hollow, clarinet-like tone. Chord Stack A minor-seventh chord from one note: Aux plays the root. Wavetable Walk An analog table: move Shape and Blend across the grid. Grain Formant Windowed sine bursts: a vocal, filter-like peak. Plucked String A plucked string: patch triggers to play it. Struck Bell A struck bell with stretched modes: trigger it. Sub Kick A swept-sine kick: patch triggers. Snare Hit Two heads plus noise: a classic synthetic snare. Closed Hat Six metallic squares, very short: a closed hat. Dust Rain Random clicks like rain or crackle; no trigger needed. Controls and jacks Control What it does Model The synthesis model (stepped, modulatable). Octave, Coarse, Fine Pitch: octaves, semitones, cents. Tone, Shape, Blend The three macros (names per model, above). FM Depth Depth of the FM input (or of the Tone modulation for unpitched models). Decay The envelope and the struck models' decay, 5 ms – 10 s. Gate Colour How the gate closes: VCA (0 %) → low-pass (100 %). Level Output level of Out and Aux. Quality Eco, Normal, High (see above). Seed The noise seed. Inputs: Pitch (1 V/oct, 0 V = C4), FM , Trigger , Accent (strength of each hit, 0–1). Outputs: Out , Aux (named after what it carries), Env . How to use it? Model sequencing. A Step Sequencer into Model (and its pitch into Pitch ): every step a different sound, from one module. Instant voice. In a Voice Cell, Voice In › Pitch to Pitch , Trigger to Trigger , Velocity to Accent : a complete polyphonic voice with its own decay and gate. Try Vowel with Gate Colour 100 % for a plucked choir. Drum kit. Three Macro Osc on Kick (Octave −2), Snare and Metal , each with a trigger from a sequencer and Accent from its velocity. Bass and chord. Chord with Aux (the root) one octave down through a filter, Out to a reverb. Talking FM. An LFO into Tone on Vowel , or into Ratio on FM , slowly; Env to a filter elsewhere. Bowed objects. Modal with Trigger unpatched and a long Decay: a singing bowl. Move Material slowly. Rhythmic noise. Dust at low density into a reverb for vinyl crackle; at high density with Clock for rain on a tin roof. Tips Decay and Gate Colour only matter while Trigger is patched. Modulating Model with audio-rate signals is possible but each change takes 5 ms; for timbre modulation use the macros. Unpatched outputs cost nothing extra: Aux is only computed while something reads it (or the view is open). Lower Quality to Eco for many voices; High for exposed high notes.

title: Oscillator
text: Oscillator Oscillator in the module view Introduction The Oscillator is the sound source of most patches. It makes a steady tone whose pitch follows the Pitch input. One knob sweeps its waveform from a pure sine to a buzzing square. It also has through-zero FM for bell-like and metallic tones, hard sync for tearing leads, and a sub-octave output for weight. How does it work? At its core is a phase that runs from 0 to 1 once per cycle. All waveforms are read from that same phase, so they are always in step: Sine , Triangle , Saw and Square , each on its own output. Saw and square are band-limited (polyBLEP), so they don't alias in the high register. Out morphs through the four with the Shape knob: sine → triangle → saw → square. Between two points you hear a crossfade of the two neighbours. Sub is a square wave one octave below. It flips every time the core completes a cycle. Pitch. The frequency is C4 (261.6 Hz) × 2^pitch, where pitch is the sum of Octave , Coarse (semitones), Fine (cents) and the Pitch input (1 V/oct: +1.0 is one octave up, 0.0 is C4). Through-zero FM. The FM input changes the frequency linearly: frequency × (1 + 4 × FM Depth × FM). With deep modulation the frequency can go negative. The phase then runs backwards instead of stopping, so the tone stays in tune even under heavy FM. Hard sync. Each rising edge at Sync (the signal crossing 0.5 upwards) resets the phase to the start of a cycle. How to use it? Basic voice: Voice In Pitch → Oscillator Pitch ; Out → VCA → Voice Out. Pick the tone with Shape (the default, 67 %, is a saw). Transpose: use Octave for whole octaves and Coarse for intervals, e.g. +7 for a fifth on a second oscillator. Detune: two oscillators with Fine at −7 and +7 cents give a wide, chorused sound. Pulse-width modulation: set Shape to 100 % (square) and patch a slow Function onto Pulse Width . FM: patch a second oscillator's Sine into FM and raise FM Depth . Integer ratios between the two ( Coarse 0, +12, +19) give harmonic tones; other ratios give bells and metal. Hard sync: patch a second oscillator's Square into Sync . Set this oscillator higher and sweep its pitch for the classic sync lead. Pitch bend and vibrato: patch a bend or LFO signal into Pitch . For ±2 semitones set the cable amount to 2/12 ≈ 17 %. Weight: mix Sub in under Out for bass. Presets The preset bar of the Oscillator view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Bright Saw The classic sawtooth: a rich, bright starting point for any filter. Pure Sine A clean sine for sub bass, tones and as an FM carrier. Soft Triangle Mellow triangle with only odd, quiet harmonics. Hollow Square A 50 % square: woody, clarinet-like and hollow. Reedy Pulse A narrower pulse with a nasal, reed-like colour. Thin Pulse Very narrow pulse: thin and buzzy, great for chiptune leads. Sub Sine Two octaves down sine for deep, clean sub bass. Fat Bass Saw A saw an octave down, slightly flat: pair it with a second oscillator. Sine To Saw Half-way between triangle and saw: a soft, round buzz; sweep Shape with an LFO. Octave Lead A bright saw-to-square blend one octave up for cutting leads. Detuned Fifth Saw set a fifth up and slightly sharp: layer it with a root oscillator. Gentle FM A sine with the FM input open: patch a modulator in for bell tones. Strong FM Deep through-zero FM for metallic, clangorous timbres. Sync Sweep Base Saw for hard sync: patch a gate or a faster oscillator into Sync and sweep Coarse. Low Rumble Very low pulse: use as a drone, or slow rhythmic modulation. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Oscillator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Oscillator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Oscillator: Shape Sweep A bass line on one Oscillator while a slow LFO turns Shape from triangle through saw toward square, so the same note keeps changing colour. Set Shape by hand to freeze a waveform, or move Pulse Width for a thinner square. Oscillator: Hard Sync Sweep A lead oscillator is reset by the sequencer's gate on every note, while a slow LFO pushes its Coarse tuning upward: the classic tearing sync sweep. Turn Shape toward the saw for more bite, or lower the LFO amount for a calmer tone. Oscillator: Through-Zero Bells A second Oscillator frequency-modulates the first through its FM input, and a decaying envelope on FM Depth makes each bell strike bright and then mellow. Change the modulator's Coarse for different bell families, or raise FM Depth for glassier tones. Oscillator: Sub Octave Weight The main output and the Sub output (one octave down) are mixed under a drum loop, with Pulse Width moving slowly for a hollow, breathing bass. Mute the Sub channel on the mixer to hear how much weight it adds. Oscillator: Three-Voice Pad Three Oscillators a few cents apart play slow chord roots, one pushed a fifth up, and a reverb spreads them wide. Change Fine on any oscillator for faster beating, or Shape for a brighter or softer pad. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave −3 … +3 0 Coarse −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Shape 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw) Pulse Width 5 – 95 % 50 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Octave: shifts the pitch by whole octaves. At 0 and with nothing at Pitch , the oscillator plays C4. Coarse: shifts the pitch in semitones. As a modulation destination it covers 24 semitones over the knob's full travel. Fine: shifts the pitch in cents (1/100 semitone), for detuning and tuning against other instruments. Shape: the waveform at Out : 0 % sine, 33 % triangle, 67 % saw, 100 % square, with smooth morphs between. Modulating it gives an evolving timbre. Pulse Width: the duty cycle of the square, at Square and at the square end of Out . 50 % is a hollow square; narrow pulses sound thin and nasal. It doesn't affect the other waveforms or Sub . FM Depth: how strongly the FM input moves the frequency. At 100 % an FM signal of ±1 swings the frequency by ±4 times its base value, so it passes through zero. With nothing at FM the knob does nothing. Knobs (all except Octave ) are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct added to Octave, Coarse and Fine; 0.0 = C4 FM audio linear, through-zero frequency modulation, scaled by FM Depth Sync gate each rising edge restarts the cycle (hard sync) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the waveform chosen by Shape Sine audio sine Triangle audio triangle Saw audio rising saw, band-limited Square audio pulse with the set Pulse Width , band-limited Sub audio square one octave below All outputs run between −1 and +1.

title: Strange Osc
text: Strange Osc Strange Osc in the module view Introduction Strange Osc is an oscillator that is not a waveform at all: it is a small system of three equations that never settles and never quite repeats, stepped forward in time fast enough to hear (or slowly enough to use as a modulation source). Four classic chaotic systems are built in. A Tame knob bends the system toward periodic order, so one knob takes you from a pitched, almost ordinary tone, through a wavering, rough one, to full chaos that sounds like a living noise. The three state variables come out as X , Y and Z , which makes it as much a source of unruly modulation as a voice. How does it work? The systems. Attractor picks one of four systems of three coupled differential equations: Lorenz (two lobes, with irregular flips between them), Rossler (one slow spiral with sudden spikes), Thomas (smooth, cyclically symmetric tumbling) and Halvorsen (a three-armed star). They are integrated sample by sample with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta step, in double precision, with extra sub-steps when the pitch is high. Pitch is time. The pitch jack and Pitch knobs do not change a table read-out speed: they change how fast time runs inside the equations ( time-scaling ), so the whole orbit speeds up and the loops come round that many times a second. In the tame, periodic regime this is a true 1 V/oct pitch (within a few cents to a few percent, depending on the system). In the chaotic regime the loops are of uneven length, so the pitch is a centre of gravity, which is part of the sound. Range moves the whole thing down: Audio , Low (÷64) and Slow (÷4096, from about 0.06 Hz at C4) for control. Tame. Each system has one parameter whose value decides whether it is chaotic. Tame slides it from the chaotic setting (0 %) to one where the orbit is a clean periodic loop (100 %): Rossler c from 5.7 to 3, Lorenz rho from 28 to 160, Thomas b from 0.17 to 0.32, Halvorsen a from 1.89 to 3. Between the two ends are period-doubling and intermittent regions that give the interesting "almost a note" sounds. Every axis is centred and scaled by measured values at both ends, so levels stay near ±1 on the whole way. Seed. The start point is a pure function of Seed , so a render from a reset is exactly repeatable; another seed starts on another path and, in the chaotic regime, drifts away from the first within a few loops. A trigger in Reset returns to the seed's start point at any time. Force. Force In is added to the X equation, scaled by Force : an external signal pushes the system around. A sine at a nearby frequency can lock a chaotic orbit; noise makes it jitter. Output. Out is X , Y or Z (or a blend: Mix sweeps X → Y → Z), low-passed by Tone , times Level . X , Y and Z are always available unfiltered. Flip is a gate that goes high when X is positive and low when it is negative (with a small hysteresis): at Low or Slow range it is an irregular clock. How to use it? A strange lead: Tame 70–95 %, Pitch from a sequencer, Out through a filter and VCA. The orbit is almost periodic, with a slowly wandering timbre. Noise with a pitch: Tame 0 %, Attractor Lorenz, play it from a keyboard. A chaotic modulation source: Range Slow, X , Y and Z to three different knobs; Tame sets how predictable they are. Irregular clock: Range Low, Flip into a drum or an envelope trigger. Forced chaos: an LFO or a second oscillator into Force In , Force 30 %. Evolving drone: Tame slowly modulated by an LFO through the whole range. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Strange Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Strange Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Strange Osc: Tamed Lead A lead played by a chaotic orbit that has been tamed almost all the way: a clear pitch whose timbre never quite repeats. Lower Tame to roughen the note, or switch Attractor for a different grain. Strange Osc: Chaos Percussion Fully chaotic Lorenz noise, cut into short hits by an envelope, fills in between a kick and snare. Change the Seed for a different texture, or Tame to make the hits more tonal. Strange Osc: Tame Sweep One long note while a slow LFO sweeps Tame over its whole range: the voice drifts from an almost clean tone, through rough, multiplying orbits, to open chaos and back. Try another Attractor to hear where each one breaks up. Strange Osc: Chaotic Modulator A saw riff through a filter whose cutoff and resonance are moved by the X and Y outputs of a slow Strange Osc: a modulation that wanders and never repeats. Use Tame to make it more regular or switch Attractor for a different gait. Strange Osc: Forced Orbit A saw riff pushes a half-tamed orbit through Force In, so the orbit follows the riff's rhythm but keeps its own colour. Raise Force for tighter lock, or lower Tame to let it run away. Presets The preset bar of the Strange Osc view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Tamed Spiral Almost a clean periodic tone, with a slow grain from the orbit. Wobbling Lead Pitched, with a restless wobble in every cycle. Edge of Order Between a note and noise: period-doubling roughness. Lorenz Grit Gritty, irregular low tone from two flipping lobes. Lorenz Loop The tamed Lorenz orbit: a hollow, steady voice. Thomas Glass Smooth, lazy tumbling that rings like glass. Halvorsen Star A three-armed orbit with a cool, buzzy character. Chaos Noise Full chaos high up: noise with a pitch centre. Dark Chaos Slow, dark rumble for sub layers. Y Voice The Y axis: rounder and less spiky than X. Z Spike The Z axis: sharp spikes that cut through a mix. Forced Orbit Patch an audio signal into Force In to push the orbit. Slow Orbit Control-rate chaos: use X, Y and Z as modulation. Irregular Clock Use the Flip gate as a clock that never quite repeats. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct, 0 = C4; added to Pitch and Fine Reset trigger returns to the seed's start point Force In audio pushes the X equation, scaled by Force Out audio the blend of X, Y, Z after Tone and Level X, Y, Z control the three state variables, about ±1 Flip gate high while X is positive Knobs and settings Control Range Default Pitch −36 … +36 st 0 Fine ±100 ct 0 Tame 0 – 100 % 30 % Mix X … Y … Z X Force 0 – 100 % 0 Tone 20 Hz – 20 kHz 20 kHz (open) Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Attractor Lorenz, Rossler, Thomas, Halvorsen Rossler Range Audio, Low, Slow Audio Seed 0 – 999 1 All knobs are modulation destinations; Attractor , Range and Seed are settings. Origin The four systems are textbook mathematics (their equations are in any book on nonlinear dynamics); the module was written from those equations and no code was taken from elsewhere.

title: Test Oscillator
text: Test Oscillator Introduction Test Oscillator is modelled on the lamp-stabilised sine generators of the old electronics lab: a big calibrated dial, a range switch, and a sine that comes from a real self-oscillating loop instead of a counter. The loop's imperfections are the point. The amplitude bounces when you turn the dial or switch the range, the pitch creeps up as it warms, it hums faintly, and below a Loop Gain of 100 % it stops oscillating and becomes a ringing resonator that pings when kicked. One module is a drone, a sweep source and a drum. How does it work? The loop. A band-pass filter tuned by the dial feeds an amplifier, and the amplifier feeds the filter. When the amplifier's gain ( Loop Gain ) is above 100 %, any tiny noise grows into a sine at exactly the dial's frequency. Something has to stop it growing: The lamp. A small lamp in the loop warms up with the signal and turns the gain down when the sine gets louder than its nominal level (±0.5). It takes time to warm and cool ( Settle ), so the regulation lags behind: every disturbance makes the amplitude overshoot, undershoot and settle again over a few Settle times. That is the bounce. The Lamp output carries the lamp's heat: 0 cold, 0.5 at the nominal level, 1 at twice the power. Loop Gain decides the character: Below 100 %: no oscillation. The loop is a resonator that rings and decays: a Kick pings it, Audio In drives it like a tuned filter that saturates when pushed. The closer to 100 %, the longer the ring (at 95 % and 100 Hz it takes about 2.2 s to die away). 100 – 150 %: a clean, lamp-regulated sine of about ±0.5. Higher values start faster and bounce harder. Above 150 %: the lamp runs out of range and the amplifier clips: louder (up to ±1), harder, rich in odd harmonics; at 300 % close to a rounded square. The lamp still moves, so the bounces remain. Settle is the lamp's speed. Long values give slow, deep swells after a disturbance. Very short values let the lamp follow the waveform itself: the sine distorts, and at high loop gains it squeals and flutters in bursts. Turning the dial costs the loop some gain while it moves (up to 30 % on fast sweeps; jumps on Pitch count too). The lamp cools, and when the dial stops the amplitude surges and rings. Changing the Range breaks the loop for 4 ms, like the contacts of a real switch: a click, a dip, a surge. Drift adds the instrument's age: after power-up the pitch starts up to a semitone flat and warms up over about 30 s ( Warm-up ), it wanders by a few cents, and the mains hum ( Mains ) leaks in faintly. Tuned near 50/60 Hz (or 150/180 Hz) the oscillator gets pulled and locks to the hum. At 0 % the instrument is ideal. Square is a comparator on the sine with finite edges, and stays at 50 % duty through the bounces. Sync fires once per period at the sine's upward zero crossing. Both go quiet when the loop is silent. Power-up. With Power-up on On play the oscillator switches on when the transport starts: silent, cold and flat, then it starts up from its noise floor and warms up, the same way on every playback, so renders repeat exactly. On load switches it on when the board loads (or Seed changes) and lets it run free. How to use it? A drone with life: Loop Gain 120 %, Settle 1 s, Drift 60 %. Turn the dial slowly and let it swell. A sweep source: modulate Frequency or Pitch with a slow LFO; the amplitude dips on the fast parts and surges back. A tuned drum: Loop Gain 90–98 %, a clock into Kick , Range ×10. The Kick knob sets how hard it pings; inside a Voice Cell, Voice In › Trigger into Kick and Voice In › Pitch into Pitch give a tuned percussion voice. A resonant filter: Loop Gain 80–95 %, a drum loop or noise into Audio In ; tune the dial to taste. Wobbly tremolo: Settle 5–20 ms, Loop Gain 200 %: the lamp chases the waveform and the tone squeals and stutters. An envelope of the bounces: Lamp into a filter's cutoff. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Test Oscillator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Test Oscillator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Test Oscillator: Warm Hum A lamp-stabilised sine on its own: it warms up, bounces slightly in level and carries a faint mains hum, a slowly breathing drone in a big room. Raise Drift for more wander, or change Mains to Off for a perfectly clean tone. Test Oscillator: Kicked Bell With Loop Gain below 100 % the oscillator dies away on its own, and a trigger on Kick makes it ring like a struck tuning fork. Change Loop Gain for longer or shorter rings, and Kick for how hard it is hit. Test Oscillator: Pure Sine Tune A plain sine melody from the Test Oscillator's Pitch input with a short envelope, about as clean a tone as exists. Add Fm from the LFO for vibrato or raise Drift to hear a warmer, wobblier note. Test Oscillator: Square Bass The square output at the lowest range plays a rounded bass line through a low-pass filter, over a simple beat. Change Range to jump the whole line by decades or move Freq for a different key. Test Oscillator: Lamp Drives Filter The Lamp output, a slow signal showing the oscillator's amplitude loop breathing, opens a filter on a held chord of Oscillators. Raise Settle for slower swings, or Loop Gain for harder bounces. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Frequency 1.0 – 10.0 (log) 4.4 Fine ±50 cents 0 FM 0 – 100 % 0 % Loop Gain 0 – 300 % 120 % Settle 5 ms – 2 s 250 ms Drift 0 – 100 % 40 % Kick 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Range ×1, ×10, ×100, ×1k ×100 Warm-up Off, On On Mains Off, 50 Hz, 60 Hz 50 Hz Power-up On load, On play On play Seed 0 – 999 1 Frequency: the dial; the frequency is 2 Hz × Range × Frequency (4.4 on ×100 is 880 Hz). Fine: fine tuning. FM: depth of linear frequency modulation from the FM input. Loop Gain: resonator below 100 %, regulated sine up to 150 %, clipping above. Settle: how slowly the lamp reacts; the speed of the bounces. Drift: warm-up, wander and mains hum together. Kick: how hard each Kick pulse hits (50 % pings at the nominal level). Power-up: when the oscillator switches on. Seed: picks the noise and the wander. All knobs are modulation destinations. title: Wavetable Osc
text: Wavetable Osc Wavetable Osc in the module view Introduction The Wavetable Osc plays single-cycle waveforms from a bank : a grid of up to 8 × 8 cycles. X and Y pick a point on the grid and the oscillator blends the four nearest waveforms, so sweeping X and Y with envelopes and LFOs moves the timbre in two directions at once, for example brightness along X and vowel along Y. Warp bends how each cycle is read for even more motion. Eleven factory banks are built in, and you can drop in your own WAV files. Every cycle is stored band-limited at several octaves, so the sound stays clean from sub-bass to the top of the keyboard. How does it work? Pitch. C4 × 2^(Octave + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200 + Pitch), then the FM input: linear and through zero, ±4× at FM Depth 100 %. Banks. Bank chooses the grid (a dropdown a cable can drive; changes crossfade over 10 ms): Bank X Y Analog sine → triangle → saw → square → 10 % pulse rounder → brighter Harmonic odd → all harmonics spectral centre low → high Vowel a → e → i → o → u small → large formant shift Pulse width 50 % → 3 % single → double pulse Sync synced saw ratio 1 → 8 saw → triangle carrier FM modulation index 0 → 6 ratio 1 … 8 Fold fold amount symmetry Organ 8 drawbar registrations third-harmonic percussion Digital bit depth 8 → 2 sample-and-hold steps 64 → 4 Spectra seeded random spectra rough → smooth Bell partials compressed → stretched bright → dark User your imported cycles Position. With Path Off, X and Y place the point directly. With a path ( Rows , Snake , Columns , Diagonal , Spiral ) Scan moves along the cells in that order instead and X and Y are hidden. Smooth blend mixes the four nearest cycles; Step plays the nearest one (a stepped, digital sound; each step is crossfaded over 2 ms). Position changes glide over 1 ms. Warp ( Warp Mode , amount by the Warp knob, which takes the mode's name): Bend: squeezes the first half of the cycle and stretches the second: brighter, resonant tones. Sync: reads the cycle up to 8 times per period, like hard sync inside the table. Mirror: folds the reading back halfway: symmetric shapes, a new even/odd balance. Squash: plays the whole cycle in the first part of the period and holds for the rest: pulse-width modulation for any wave. Steps: quantises the reading into stairs (2048 → 2 steps): lo-fi. At 0 % every warp is off. The read automatically uses fewer harmonics when a warp speeds it up, and the jumps of Sync , Steps and the Sync input are smoothed, so warping stays band-limited. Read. Cubic (smoothest), Linear , or Raw : the full table, nearest sample, no band-limiting: aliasing on purpose. Stereo. Stereo moves Out R's position along X (or along the path) from L's; both share the phase, so the sum never cancels the fundamental. At 0 % L and R are identical. Sub. A sine an octave below, in phase with the main cycle (also after Sync ). Sub Level mixes it into Out ; the Sub output is always full level. Your own tables Drop a WAV file on Import… (or click it to choose one). Choose Cycle first if you know your file's cycle length; Auto uses 2048 samples if the file is a multiple of that, else the whole file is one cycle. Up to 64 cycles are taken (the view says when a file has more); each is resampled to the table size, its DC removed and normalised. Fewer than 64 cycles fill the grid row by row and the grid shrinks to the rows used; one cycle plays everywhere. Dropping a WAV on one cell of the grid replaces just that cell (its first cycle). Silent or unreadable files are rejected and the bank stays as it was. The file is kept in the Beautiful Bleep media folder; the board stores only its id. Importing switches Bank to User . With nothing imported, User plays a sine. How to use it? Evolving pad: Analog or Harmonic , slow LFOs on X and Y, Stereo 20 %. Talking lead: Vowel , an envelope on X, Warp Bend 20 %. Scanning: Path Snake, a slow ramp on Scan . Use Pos X/Pos Y to move a filter in step. Sync sweep: Warp Mode Sync, an envelope on Warp . PWM anything: Warp Mode Squash, an LFO on Warp . Bass: Sub Level 50 %. Demo boards Five whole boards show what Wavetable Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Wavetable Osc under Demos by module ; loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Wavetable Osc: Morphing Pad An LFO on Scan walks the Analog bank along the Snake path, with Stereo spread. Wavetable Osc: Vowel Talker The Vowel bank with X and Y moved by random generators: a tune that seems to speak. Wavetable Osc: Bell Garden The Bell bank with an envelope on Y : each note starts bright and fades to a plain tone. Wavetable Osc: Warp Bass Warp in Sync mode opened by an envelope on each note, plus Sub Level for weight. Wavetable Osc: Spiral Crawl Scan crawls the Spiral path in the Spectra bank while the X position output opens a filter. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Wavetable Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Wavetable Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Wavetable Osc: Analog Scan A slow LFO scans through the Analog bank, so the tone evolves from soft to sharp and back across a pentatonic line. Change Bank for a different family of tables, or set Scan by hand to pick one spot in the grid. Wavetable Osc: Vowel Table The Vowel bank with X and Y wandering under two slow LFOs: the pad seems to murmur through different mouth shapes. Try Frame Blend on Step for abrupt vowel changes instead of smooth morphs. Wavetable Osc: Spiral Path With Path set to Spiral, one Scan knob walks the whole 8 by 8 grid in a spiral, and an envelope on Scan sweeps it for every note: each pluck travels through many tables. Try Rows, Snake or Diagonal for other journeys through the grid. Wavetable Osc: Bell Bank The Bell bank played softly and slowly, with Y raised a little by each note's envelope, gives glassy, inharmonic chimes. Change X to pick other bells from the grid, or Read to Linear for a rougher, more digital edge. Wavetable Osc: Warp Bass A low sequence on the Fold bank with Warp Mode on Sync and a slow LFO on Warp, plus a little Sub Level, for a bass that snarls and calms over a beat. Switch Warp Mode to Mirror, Squash or Steps for other kinds of damage. Presets The preset bar of the Wavetable Osc view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Analog Saw A bright analog saw from the first bank. Soft Sine Tri A round sine-to-triangle blend with a little sub. Analog Sweep Scan the path across the shapes: modulate Scan for a sweeping tone. Warm Organ A drawbar-style registration with light stereo width. Vowel Voice A sung vowel: sweep X to change a-e-i-o-u. Harmonic Glass Odd harmonics around a spectral centre: glassy and pure. Pulse Width A pulse table: move X to change the width. Sync Sweep Synced saw ratios inside the table: sweep X for a classic sync lead. FM Table Stored FM spectra: X is index, Y is ratio. Folded Wave Wavefolded cycles: bright, moving harmonics. Bell Table Stretched partials: a glassy, bell-like tone. Spectra Cloud Random seeded spectra with wide stereo: a textural pad. Bent Analog Warp bends the cycle: a brighter, resonant tone. Squashed PWM Squash gives pulse-width movement to any wave; modulate Warp. Mirror Fold A mirrored read: a new even/odd balance. Digital Crush Bit-reduced stepped cycles: lo-fi and gritty. title: Chord Osc
text: Chord Osc Chord Osc in the module view Introduction The Chord Osc turns one pitch into a whole chord. Up to six oscillators play the tones of a chord built on the Pitch input: pick the quality (major, minor, sevenths, sus, add9, …), the inversion and the voicing, and morph the waveform of all voices at once. In Scale mode it builds the chords of a key instead, so a simple melody becomes a chord progression. The Root output carries the root alone, and Pitch 1–4 send the four lowest chord tones to other oscillators. How does it work? Each voice is the Oscillator's core (sine, triangle, band-limited saw and square, morphed by Shape ). The chord is built in four steps whenever the pitch or a stepped knob changes: Tones. The chord has a number of tones (C major 7 has four). With fewer Voices , tones are left out in the order fifth, extension (9th), seventh, third; the root always stays. With more Voices , tones are doubled an octave up: root first, then fifth, third, … Inversion. Positive steps move the lowest tone up an octave, negative steps move the highest tone down. The bass shows in the name ( Am7/C ). Voicing. Close keeps the chord within an octave. Drop 2 , Drop 3 and Drop 2+4 move the second, third (or second and fourth) tone from the top down an octave, as guitarists and arrangers do. Open moves the bass down an octave; Wide spreads the tones over about three octaves. Voicings that need more tones than are playing stay Close . Range guard. If the chord would reach above 8 kHz or below 16 Hz, it moves by whole octaves back into range. Every oscillator keeps "its" tone: the one playing the third plays the third of the next chord. With Glide the voices slide to their new notes (smooth voice leading); without it they jump, keeping their phase, so changes don't click. Voices that start or stop playing fade in or out over 5 ms. Scale mode. The Pitch input is snapped to the nearest note of Root and Scale (exactly between two notes, it goes down). That note's scale degree is the chord root, and the chord is stacked from scale steps: in C major a Triad on D is D minor, on G it is G major, on B it is B diminished. The view shows the chord found and its degree (ii, V, …). Latch. With a cable in Latch , the module takes the pitch and the four stepped settings ( Chord , Inversion , Voicing , Voices ) only at each pulse and holds the chord until the next one. Tune , Shape , Detune and the others stay live. Until the first pulse it plays as if unlatched. Mixing. Out L/R is the sum of the voices divided by √(number of voices), so a four-voice chord is about as loud as two oscillators. With square waves and six voices the peaks can reach about ±2.4. Root Level sets the root voice inside the mix; the Root output is always at full level (±1). Detune gives each voice a fixed offset within ± Detune cents, drawn from Seed : the same seed always gives the same offsets. Stereo spreads the voices across the field, from the centre outwards and alternating sides, so the root stays nearest the middle. How to use it? Chord pad: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; Out L/R → Filter → VCA. A little Detune (5–10 ct) and Stereo at 60 % make it wide. Chord progression from a melody: set Mode to Scale , pick the key, and play a step sequencer into Pitch . Each note becomes the diatonic chord on it. Patch the sequencer's trigger into Latch so chords change exactly on the step. Moving chords: patch a slow LFO onto Chord (Scale mode: Triad, Seventh, Ninth, …) or Inversion for chords that keep changing colour. Voice leading: raise Glide to 100–300 ms and change chords: every voice slides to the corresponding tone of the next chord. Bass plus chords: lower Root Level and send Root through its own filter as a bass voice, or use Pitch 1 to play a separate bass oscillator. Arpeggios elsewhere: Pitch 1–4 carry the chord tones low to high; switch between them with a sequential switch for an arpeggio that follows the chord. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Chord Osc does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Chord Osc under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Chord Osc: Slow Seventh Pad A slow bass line plays the root and Chord Osc stacks a minor seventh on it in the Open voicing, with a little Detune, wide Stereo and Glide so each chord melts into the next. Try other Chord types, change Voicing, or push Inversion up and down to hear the same chord from a different bass note. Chord Osc: Chords From a Melody In Scale mode every note of a simple melody becomes the diatonic chord on that scale degree: major, minor and diminished triads appear by themselves in C major. The melody's trigger is patched into Latch so chords change exactly on the step. Change Scale or Root to re-colour the tune, or set the stack to Seventh. Chord Osc: Bass and Stabs One Chord Osc is two instruments: its Root output, filtered and sub-heavy, is the bassline, and the chord itself plays short offbeat stabs on top (Root Level lowered so they do not double the bass). Try Dominant 9 or Minor add9 in Chord, or open the stab filter. Chord Osc: Chord Tone Arp The four Pitch outputs carry the chord tones from low to high; a Switch steps through them every sixteenth to play an arpeggio on a separate oscillator that always follows the chord. The pad underneath plays the whole chord. Change the Chord, or the Inversion, and the arpeggio changes with it. Chord Osc: Quartal Glass Five voices stacked in fourths with the Wide voicing, near-sine waves and slow Detune make a cool, open sound with no clear major or minor. A slow LFO sweeps the Inversion, so the bass note of the chord keeps changing. Switch Chord to Sus2 or Add9 for a warmer cloud. Presets The preset bar of the Chord Osc view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Major Triad A plain major triad of saws, gently widened. Minor Seventh Warm four-note minor 7 stack for pads and stabs. Power Fifth Root and fifth with extra edge: rock-style power chord. Suspended Pad Open, unresolved sus4 with wide stereo and a little glide. Dream Nine Airy major 9 in open voicing with soft waves. Hollow Fifths Stacked fourths spread wide: modern, ambiguous. Dominant Stab Buzzy dominant 7 for punchy organ-like stabs. Jazz Voicing Drop 2 minor 9 with near-sine tone: soft electric-piano colour. First Inversion Major triad with the third in the bass. Sine Organ Pure sines on a major 7: a clean drawbar-like chord. Pulse Stack Narrow pulse minor chord: thin, nasal and synthetic. Scale Harmony Diatonic mode: plays the matching seventh chord of A minor on each note. Pentatonic Cloud Wide, forgiving cloud on D minor pentatonic. Diminished Dread Symmetrical, tense diminished 7 with heavy detune. Sub Octaves Detuned unison saws an octave down: thick mono-compatible bass. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Chord Chromatic: 24 qualities; Scale: 10 stacks Major / Triad Inversion −4 … +4 0 Voicing Close, Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2+4, Open, Wide Close Voices 1 – 6 4 Shape 0 – 100 % 67 % (saw) Pulse Width 5 – 95 % 50 % Detune 0 – 50 ct 0 ct Glide 0 – 1 s 0 ms Root Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Stereo 0 – 100 % 0 % FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode Chromatic, Scale Chromatic Octave −3 … +3 0 Root C … B (Scale mode) C Scale Chromatic … Hirajoshi (Scale mode) Major Seed 0 – 999 1 Chord: in Chromatic mode the quality: Unison, Fifth, Major, Minor, Diminished, Augmented, Sus2, Sus4, Major 6, Minor 6, Dominant 7, Major 7, Minor 7, Half-diminished, Diminished 7, Minor-major 7, 7sus4, Add9, Minor add9, 6/9, Major 9, Minor 9, Dominant 9, Quartal. In Scale mode a stack of scale steps: Single, Fifth, Triad, Sus2, Sus4, Sixth, Seventh, Add9, Ninth, Quartal. Each mode has its own dropdown; a cable moves them from entry to entry, read once per audio block. Inversion , Voices: stepped knobs; Voicing: a dropdown a cable can drive, see How does it work? . Shape: sine → triangle → saw → square for every voice, as the Oscillator's Shape . Glide: time for a voice to reach a new note (99 %). Also glides pitch changes at the input. FM Depth: scales the FM input: at 100 % an FM signal of ±1 swings each voice's frequency by ±4× its base, through zero. Octave , Tune: transpose the whole chord. Seed: chooses the detune offsets and the voices' start phases. All knobs are modulation destinations; Mode , Octave , Root , Scale and Seed are settings. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the chord root; 0.0 = C4. Scale mode: snapped to the scale first Latch trigger when patched, the chord changes only at its pulses FM audio linear, through-zero FM for all voices, scaled by FM Depth Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio all voices, panned by Stereo , divided by √voices Root audio the chord root alone at full level, whatever the inversion and voicing Pitch 1 … 4 pitch the four lowest voices, low to high; with fewer voices the last ones repeat the highest

title: Swarm
text: Swarm Swarm in the module view Introduction The Swarm is a cloud of up to 16 oscillators played from one pitch. Their notes are spread over a chord or scale around the root, so a single Pitch signal plays anything from a thick unison to a wide, shimmering chord stack. Spread opens the cloud from unison into the chord, and every oscillator glides to its new note at its own pace, so the swarm moves like a flock instead of switching. It is a drone and pad source on its own, and a fat detuned-saw lead with Spread at 0. For a precise chord with named inversions and pitch outputs per tone, use the Chord Osc; for several independent notes, a Voice Cell. How does it work? The stack. Chord chooses a set of notes: a chord (Minor 7, Quartal, Cluster, …) or a whole scale. The stack lists those notes upward through Range octaves, e.g. Minor 7 over two octaves is C E♭ G B♭ C E♭ G B♭ C. The oscillators are spread evenly over the stack, whatever their Count , so 8 oscillators on a 9-note stack skip one note. With Stack on Centred the stack reaches down half the range and up half; on Down , all of it below the root. Spread. At 0 % every oscillator plays the root. As Spread rises, each oscillator aims at its stack note scaled by Spread and snapped to the nearest chord note, so the oscillators leave the root one after another, the highest first: the cloud blooms open. Oscillator 1 always stays on the root. Glide. Each oscillator slides to a new target with its own time, between half and one and a half times Glide (drawn from Seed ). A change of Chord or Spread therefore unfolds note by note. Changes of the root ( Pitch , Octave , Coarse , Fine ) move the whole swarm at once. Warp morphs every oscillator's waveform: sine → triangle → rounded saw (a saw with soft corners, few upper harmonics, gentle in dense chords) → bright saw. Detune offsets the oscillators by up to ± Detune cents in a Pattern : Fan spreads them evenly from flat to sharp, Alternate goes sharp, flat, less sharp, less flat, …, Random draws seeded values, Outer detunes the lowest and highest the most and the middle not at all. Drift adds a slow random walk to each detune (up to half of Detune ), each oscillator at its own pace. The root oscillator is never detuned. Cross FM connects the oscillators in a ring: each one's phase is pushed by the previous one's sine (by up to half a cycle at 100 %). A little adds grit and beating; a lot turns chords into dense, metallic noise. Level and stereo. The oscillators are summed and divided by √ Count , so Count changes the thickness, not the loudness. Width scatters them across the stereo field, alternating sides and wider the further they are from the root; the root stays centred. Oscillators that would play above 0.45 × the sample rate fade out instead of aliasing. Quality. High runs the whole swarm at twice the sample rate with a half-band decimator: cleaner high notes and deep Cross FM, at about twice the CPU. How to use it? Pad: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; Out L/R → Filter → VCA. Default settings (8 oscillators on Minor 7, Spread 30 %) already sound like a chorus of voices. Blooming chord: patch an envelope or slow LFO onto Spread and set Glide to 1–2 s: the chord opens and closes in waves. Supersaw lead: Spread 0, Warp 100 %, Count 7, Detune 15–25 ct, Pattern Fan. Shimmer: Chord on a scale (Major Pentatonic, Hirajoshi), Range 3–4, Spread 100 %, Drift high, Width 100 %. Separate filtering: Upper carries only the oscillators above the root octave; filter it brighter or darker than the main mix. Root is a clean anchor for a sub or for syncing another oscillator. Follow the opening: patch Spread (output) to a filter's cutoff so it opens with the cloud. New variation: press Reshuffle (or send a trigger) for a new random pattern and new glide times. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Swarm does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Swarm under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Swarm: Blooming Pad A slow LFO moves Spread between 0 and 100 %: the eight oscillators sit on the root, then leave it one after another and slide up into a minor ninth stack, and fold back again. Glide sets how lazily they move. Try Chord, Count and Width, or press Reshuffle for a new set of glide times. Swarm: Supersaw Lead With Spread at 0 every oscillator plays the same note, so the swarm becomes a fat unison lead: seven bright saws, Detune in a Fan pattern, a little Width. A filter envelope closes after each note. Raise Spread a touch to hear the lead turn into a chord, or change Pattern to Alternate or Outer. Swarm: Hirajoshi Shimmer Set to a whole scale instead of a chord: sixteen oscillators across four octaves of Hirajoshi, fully spread, with high Drift and Width so the notes shimmer and wander. Soft sine-like Warp keeps it glassy. Change Chord to another scale, lower Range for a narrower cloud, or sweep Drift by hand. Swarm: Metal Cloud Cross FM pushes each oscillator's phase with its neighbour's, turning a Cluster chord into dense, bell-like metal. A trigger at the start of every bar reshuffles the detune pattern and glide times, so each bar is a new cloud, and an envelope on every beat strikes it. Lower Cross FM for gritty chords, or raise it for noise. Swarm: Root and Upper Swarm's Root output is a clean anchor and Upper carries only the oscillators above the root octave.
