Here the Root goes through a low-pass for the bassline, while Upper is filtered brighter and swept by an LFO for the chord. Use two different filters, or one effect on only one of them. Presets The preset bar of the Swarm view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Minor Cloud The default pad: eight oscillators over a minor 7, gently drifting. Unison Supersaw A pile of detuned voices on one note: classic wide lead or pad. Octave Choir Voices spread over octaves: big, huge, simple. Fifths Shimmer Stacked fifths: open and bright. Major Bloom Slow glide lets the chord bloom out from the root; major 9 colour. Dark Quartal Stacked fourths with a little warp: ambiguous and cold. Pentatonic Rain Notes of the scale scattered randomly: soft, safe, endless. Blues Haze Blues-scale swarm: gritty and a little sad. Whole Tone Dream Floating, directionless whole-tone cloud. Hirajoshi Garden Pentatonic Japanese scale; Outer pattern fills from the edges in. Warped Glass Warp bends the oscillator shapes: glassy, metallic colour. Cross-FM Bells Voices modulate each other for bell-like, inharmonic shimmer. Cluster Wall Tight semitone cluster: dense, tense texture. Chromatic Swarm All sixteen voices running through the chromatic scale: a insect-like storm. Sub Swarm Low detuned swarm for fat, moving sub bass. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Octave −4 … +4 0 Coarse −12 … +12 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct Count 1 – 16 8 Chord 16 chords, then the 17 scales Minor 7 Spread 0 – 100 % 30 % Range 1 – 4 octaves 2 Warp 0 – 100 % 0 % (sine) Detune 0 – 50 ct 8 ct Drift 0 – 100 % 20 % Cross FM 0 – 100 % 0 % Glide 0 – 5 s 300 ms Width 0 – 100 % 50 % Pattern Fan, Alternate, Random, Outer Fan Stack Up, Centred, Down Up Quality Normal (1×), High (2×) Normal Seed 0 – 999 1 Count: oscillators sounding; between whole numbers the last one fades in. Chord: Unison, Octaves, Fifths, Sus2, Sus4, Major, Minor, Major 7, Minor 7, Dominant 7, Minor 9, Major 9, Add 9, Quartal (stacked fourths), Quintal (stacked fifths), Cluster (three semitones), then every scale: Chromatic, Major, Natural Minor, …, Hirajoshi. A dropdown: a cable moves it from entry to entry. Seed: chooses start phases, glide times, the drift walks, pan jitter and the Random pattern. The same seed always sounds the same. All knobs are modulation destinations; Pattern , Stack , Quality and Seed are settings. The Reshuffle button does the same as the input. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the root; 0.0 = C4 Reshuffle trigger new random pattern and glide times (from Seed and a counter that restarts with the transport) Sync trigger restarts all oscillators at their start phases Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio all oscillators, panned by Width , divided by √ Count Root audio oscillator 1 alone: the root, never detuned, ±1 Upper audio the oscillators above the root octave, mono Spread control, 0 … 1 how far the cloud has opened, after glide

title: Modal Voice
text: Modal Voice Modal Voice in the module view Introduction Modal Voice is a complete physical-modelling instrument in one module. An exciter (a bow, breath, a mallet, or any audio) sets a resonant body ringing (a string, a bar, a plate, a bell), and a small room places it in a space. A gate sustains bowed and blown sounds for as long as it is held; a trigger strikes. It is built to sit inside a Voice Cell: one module per voice, with an Active output that tells the cell when the sound has died away. Where the Resonator is an effect that makes other sounds ring, Modal Voice is the instrument that plays itself. How does it work? The body is a bank of 16, 32 or 64 ringing partials. Geometry sets their ratios: string (0 %), stiff string (25 %), bar (50 %), plate (75 %) and a bell-like inharmonic set drawn from Seed (100 %), gliding smoothly in between. Damping sets how long it rings, Brightness how bright it is and how fast the high partials die, and Position where the exciter touches it (50 %, the middle, cancels the even partials). The exciters can all play at once: Bow: a friction model. The bow sticks to the body and slips, again and again, which makes the body sing at its own pitch for as long as the gate is held, even a bar or a bell (bowed metal). Bow Timbre goes from a light, airy bow to a heavy, scratchy one. Blow: breath noise, filtered around the pitch. Up to 60 % Blow Timbre it is a breathy rush that colours the body. Above 60 % the breath starts to couple with the body like the air jet of a flute, and the body sings on its own, with breath noise on top. Strike: a mallet hit on every trigger at Strike (or on every new gate when Strike is unpatched). Strike Timbre goes from soft felt through wood and a hard mallet to a sharp tick, and above 70 % adds a grainy scrape. A strike on a ringing body adds to it. Ext In: any audio, added to the exciters at Ext Level . With the other exciters at 0, the module is a resonator with a room. The bow and the breath follow a gate envelope shaped by Contour : at 0 % a slow swell and a long release, at 100 % a fast attack with a short decay to a lower sustain. Velocity scales every exciter. The space is a small stereo room. Size goes from a booth to a hall, Space is its level. At 0 % it is switched off and costs nothing. How to use it? In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Pitch → Pitch , Gate → Gate , Trigger → Strike , Velocity → Velocity , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . Patch Voice In › Pressure onto Bow or Blow so aftertouch swells the sound. Marimba, vibraphone, bells: Strike only, Geometry 50 – 100 %, Damping 30 – 50 %, Strike Timbre 30 – 60 %. Bowed strings and bowed metal: Strike 0 %, Bow 60 – 90 %, Contour low for a slow swell; Geometry 0 – 25 % for strings, 50 % and up for metal. Flute-like tones: Blow 70 %, Blow Timbre 70 – 90 %, Geometry 0 %. A resonator with a room: any audio → Ext In , all exciters at 0. Many voices: set Space to 0 % inside the cell and put one reverb after it: that saves CPU and gives all voices one shared room. Play button: held, it is a gate (and a strike), for trying sounds without patching. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Modal Voice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Modal Voice under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Modal Voice: Wooden Bars A mallet strikes a bar-shaped body on every step of a looping pentatonic pattern. Geometry sits at 50 % (a bar), Damping and Strike Timbre keep it woody. Try Geometry towards 0 for a string, towards 100 % for a bell, or Position at 50 % to cancel the even partials. Modal Voice: Bowed Bells No mallet at all: a Bow sings a bell-shaped body for as long as each gate is held. Contour at a low value gives a slow swell and long release, so the chords of the sequence bloom into each other. Lower Bow Timbre for a light, airy bow, or raise Damping to hear the bell become wood. Modal Voice: Breath Flute A string-like body (Geometry 0 %) is excited only by Blow with a high Blow Timbre: above 60 % the breath couples with the body like an air jet and it sings on its own, with a little breath noise on top. Move Blow Timbre across 60 % to hear the voice appear, or add Strike for a tongued start. Modal Voice: Plate Resonator Audio from a drum beat goes into Ext In with every built-in exciter at 0, so the module is a resonator in a room: the drums ring a tuned plate. Change Coarse to retune the plate, Geometry to move from string to plate to bell, Damping for how long it keeps ringing. Modal Voice: Plucked Strings A hard, bright strike on a stiff string (Geometry 25 %) is a plucked-string sound, played as a broken chord in an open room. Position sets where the string is plucked and Strike Timbre how hard the pick is. Lengthen Damping for a harp, or shorten it for a muted pluck. Presets The preset bar of the Modal Voice view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Mallet A gentle mallet on a resonant bar: a mellow mallet instrument. Plucked String Bright pluck on a string body; fast, natural decay. Bowed String A sustained bow on a string: patch Gate to hold the note. Flute Breath Breath through a tube-like string body: airy, sustained. Glass Bell Inharmonic bell body with long ring. Wood Block Short, dry knock: heavily damped bar. Vibraphone Long metal bar with a rounded mallet and some room. Plate Gong Large plate struck softly: a slow, crashing bloom. Bowed Plate Drone Bowed metal plate: eerie, evolving drone. Dark Marimba Woody, dark bar with short sustain. Tiny Chimes High, small, bright chimes an octave up. Bowed Bell Singing bowl-like sustained tone: hold the gate. Blown Bottle Breathy, hollow bottle tone with a soft attack. Ext Resonator Patch any audio into Ext: it rings through the modal body. Big Hall Strike A struck body in a very large room. Reference Knobs and settings Group Control Range Default Exciter Bow 0 – 100 % 0 % Bow Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Blow 0 – 100 % 0 % Blow Timbre 0 – 100 % 40 % Strike 0 – 100 % 80 % Strike Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Contour 0 – 100 % 30 % Ext Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Resonator Coarse −24 … +24 semitones 0 Fine −100 … +100 cents 0 Geometry 0 – 100 % 25 % Brightness 0 – 100 % 55 % Damping 0 – 100 % 40 % Position 0 – 100 % 30 % Space Size 0 – 100 % 40 % Space 0 – 100 % 20 % Partials 16, 32, 64 32 Seed 0 – 999 1 Bow / Blow / Strike: the level of each exciter. Exciters at 0 % cost nothing. Bow Timbre: bow pressure and roughness: airy → scratchy. Blow Timbre: breath colour, dark rush → bright hiss; above 60 % the breath couples with the body and makes it sing. Strike Timbre: soft felt → wood → hard mallet → tick → scrape. Contour: the shape of the bow and breath envelope: attack from 400 ms (0 %) to 2 ms (100 %), release from 1.5 s to 30 ms; from 50 % up the attack overshoots and settles to a lower sustain. Ext Level: the level of Ext In . Coarse / Fine: transposition in semitones and cents; Pitch adds to it. Geometry: the partial ratios: string → stiff string → bar → plate → bell. Brightness: spectral tilt and how fast the high partials decay. Damping: how long the body rings: 0 % = 20 s, 50 % ≈ 1 s, 100 % ≈ 40 ms. Position: where the exciter touches the body and where it is heard. Size: the room, from a small booth to a hall. Space: the room's level. The body itself always stays at full level. Partials: the number of partials of the body: more sounds richer and costs more. Seed: the bell partials (Geometry 100 %) and the scrape of the mallet. The scrapes repeat from the start of the transport. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct, 0 V = C4 Gate gate while high, bow and breath play; a new gate also strikes when Strike is unpatched Strike trigger fires the mallet Velocity control, 0 – 1 scales all exciters, read at each gate start and strike; unpatched counts as 1 Ext In audio an external exciter, at Ext Level Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the body and the room, stereo Exciter audio the exciters before the body, to watch or to feed another resonator Active gate high while the gate is high or the sound (with the room's tail) is audible; falls 50 ms after it goes below −80 dB

title: Perc Voice
text: Perc Voice Perc Voice in the module view Introduction Perc Voice is one percussion voice that covers kicks, toms, hand drums, bells, metal and noisy hits from a single model. Pitch sets the fundamental, Tone walks the spectrum from a pure sine through drum-membrane and bar partials to inharmonic clang, and Click , Decay and Sweep shape the hit. Three engines give three families of sound behind the same knobs, so a sequencer or an LFO can morph a kick into a bell. Put it in a Voice Cell for a polyphonic, pitched percussion instrument. How does it work? Every hit is made of up to eight partials . Tone picks their frequency ratios: Tone Partials 0 % a pure sine 0 – 33 % the drum-membrane partials fade in 33 % membrane: 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65, … 67 % free bar: 1, 2.76, 5.40, 8.93, … 100 % metal: an inharmonic set drawn from Seed Between these points the partials glide smoothly. Each partial rings with its own decay: Decay is the time the fundamental takes to fall by 60 dB, and Damp makes the higher partials die faster. The engine decides how the partials sound: FM: the partials are sine modulators driving one sine carrier at the fundamental. Morph is the modulation index (0 – 8). The index decays twice as fast as the body, so the attack is bright and the tail purer: classic FM toms, kicks and bells. Modal: the partials are eight struck resonators. Morph balances them: at 0 % the fundamental dominates (drums), at 100 % the upper partials (glassy bells). A second hit adds to the ringing like a real body, so rolls build up naturally. Noise Bank: noise rings through eight band-pass filters at the partial frequencies. Morph is their width: narrow sounds almost pitched (steel drums, wood), wide sounds noisy (snares, shakers). With Tone at 100 % it makes cymbals and gongs. Every hit starts with a click (a short burst of filtered noise and a quick upward pitch blip) and a pitch sweep that falls from up to three octaves above to the set pitch. Accent is the hit's strength: a strong hit is louder, has more click, a deeper sweep and, in FM, a higher index. Soft hits are duller as well as quieter, like a real drum. Retriggering never clicks: a new hit starts on a second internal voice while the previous one fades out in 3 ms (in Modal the body is struck again instead). Choke fades everything out in 5 ms. How to use it? Kick: Modal or FM , Pitch around 50 Hz, Tone 0 – 15 %, Sweep 40 – 70 %, Decay 300 – 600 ms. Tom or hand drum: Tone around 30 %, Pitch 80 – 300 Hz, a little Sweep. Bell or glass: Modal , Tone 60 – 100 %, Morph high, Damp low, long Decay. Snare, shaker, cymbal: Noise Bank , Morph high; Tone 100 % for metal. In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Trigger → Trig , Pitch → Pitch , Velocity → Accent , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . Each voice is freed when its hit has died away. Open/closed pairs: patch the trigger of a closed hat into the Choke of an open one. Hit button: plays the voice at accent 70 %, for trying sounds without patching. The Pitch input adds octaves to the Pitch knob (1 V/oct). It is read at each hit unless Track is on. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Perc Voice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Perc Voice under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Perc Voice: Modal Kit A whole kit from three Perc Voices in different engines: a Modal kick (Tone 8 %, Sweep high), a Noise Bank snare with a wide Morph and a membrane-toned Modal tom. Velocity from the grid goes into Accent, so soft hits are duller as well as quieter. Try Tone and Decay on each voice, or Drive on the kick. Perc Voice: FM Tom Melody In the FM engine the partials modulate one sine carrier, so Morph is the modulation index: bright on the attack, purer in the tail. A sequencer's Pitch tunes the hits, which makes a melody of toms. Raise Morph for metal, lower Decay for wood blocks, or switch Track on to let the pitch follow during the ring. Perc Voice: Glass Bells The Modal engine with Tone at 85 % and Morph high lets the upper partials of a metallic set ring out like struck glass, with long Decay and low Damp. A slow sequence hits the bell, and a second, lower bell answers on the off-beat. Change Seed to get a different bell, or Tone to walk from bell to bar to drum. Perc Voice: Hats and Gong Noise Bank at Tone 100 % is metal: a short one is a closed hat, a long one an open hat, and the closed hat's trigger is patched into the open hat's Choke so it cuts the ring off. A third voice with a very long Decay is a gong that swells in once per phrase. Try Damp, Morph and Pitch on the hats. Perc Voice: Steel Pan Noise Bank with a narrow Morph rings its band-pass filters almost pitched, the sound of a steel drum or a tuned block. A sequencer plays the pitch and each hit gets a small Spread of stereo width. Raise Morph towards 100 % for a noisier shaker, or change Damp to shorten the shimmer. Presets The preset bar of the Perc Voice view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Deep Kick Round sine kick with a downward pitch sweep. Punchy Kick Short, clicky kick with a touch of drive. Long Sub Boom Sub-heavy long kick: a decaying sine boom. Tight Tom Membrane tom, mid-pitched. Low Floor Tom Deep floor tom with longer ring. Snare Body Bright snare-like hit with noisy body. Rim Click Sharp, very short wooden click. Clap Noise Noisy burst for claps and snaps. Closed Hat Short metallic tick. Open Hat Longer metallic shimmer. Wood Block Dry, pitched wooden knock. Bar Marimba Pitched bar sound that follows the Pitch input. Cowbell Metallic FM clang. Bell Ring Long inharmonic bell: play it from the Pitch input. Zap Tom Extreme pitch sweep for sci-fi zaps. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Pitch 20 Hz – 4 kHz 55 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 20 % Morph 0 – 100 % 50 % Click 0 – 100 % 30 % Decay 10 ms – 8 s 400 ms Damp 0 – 100 % 40 % Sweep 0 – 100 % 40 % Spread 0 – 100 % 20 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Engine FM, Modal, Noise Bank Modal Track Off, On Off Drive Clean, Warm, Hot Clean Seed 0 – 999 1 Pitch: the fundamental. Tone: the partial ratios, from sine to metal (see above). Morph: per engine: FM index, partial balance (Modal) or band width (Noise Bank). Its name changes with the engine. Click: the attack transient: a 1 – 6 ms noise burst at 2 – 8 kHz (higher with Tone) plus a +2 octave pitch blip during the first 2 ms. In Modal and Noise Bank it also excites the body. Decay: the time the fundamental takes to fall by 60 dB. Damp: how much faster the upper partials decay. At 100 % a partial an octave up decays 8× faster. Sweep: the pitch drop at the start: up to +3 octaves, falling back in about Decay / 8. Spread: the stereo image. Modal and Noise Bank : odd partials lean left, even partials right (the fundamental stays centred). FM : the two sides are detuned by up to ±8 cents. Level: the output level. Engine: FM, Modal or Noise Bank. A dropdown a cable can drive, so it can be sequenced; it is read at each hit, and a sounding hit finishes with its own engine. Track: off: the Pitch input is read at each hit; on: it is followed live. Drive: soft saturation of the hit: Warm or Hot . It is applied relative to the hit's accent, so soft hits are as warm as loud ones. Seed: the metal partials and the noise. The same seed plays the same sounds; the noise sequence restarts when the transport starts. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Knob changes apply to a sounding hit at once and smoothly. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger plays a hit Accent control, 0 – 1 hit strength, read at each hit; unpatched counts as 70 % Pitch pitch added to Pitch in octaves (1 V/oct); read at each hit unless Track is on Choke trigger fades the sound out in 5 ms Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the voice Env control, 0 – 1 the amplitude envelope of the fundamental, for ducking Active gate high from a hit until the sound has fallen below −80 dB or was choked

title: Speak
text: Speak Speak in the module view Introduction Speak is a small speech synthesiser in the old, characterful sense: a buzzing voice or a hiss pushed through a few resonant filters that imitate a mouth. You write what it says as a string of sounds, set how fast it goes, and it mumbles, hums or chatters it, in pitch if you play it. It is made for musical use: robotic choirs, vowel melodies, spoken rhythm, and odd consonant percussion. The speech is deliberately rough; the output is the same every time. How does it work? Text. The text is a string of sound symbols, not spelling: Group Symbols vowels a (father) e (bed) i (bit) o u (put) ee (feet) oo (boot) ae (cat) uh (cup) er nasals and glides m n ng · l r w y hisses s sh f th h and voiced z zh v dh stops p t k and voiced b d g · ch j marks ' accent the next sound · : lengthen the last · space or . pause · , or - short pause · separate letters Upper case works; anything else is skipped. ae is one vowel, a e is two. Up to 256 sounds are kept. The text is parsed when you edit it and is saved with the node. The voice. Voiced sounds (vowels, nasals, glides, the voiced hisses and stops) start from a band-limited pulse train at the pitch, tilted so the highs are softer, with a little noise ( Breath ) mixed in. It goes through five resonators in a row: three that slide to each sound's own formant frequencies, and two fixed ones for brightness. Hisses and the bursts of stops are noise through one band that is moved to the right place for each sound (an s high and narrow, sh lower, f and th wide and quiet); h is noise through the mouth filters themselves. A stop is a closure (silent, or a faint hum for b d g ), a short burst and a puff of aspiration. Time. Every sound has its own length in units; a unit lasts 1/ Speed seconds (so at 8 u/s a vowel is about 150 ms). Glide sets how fast the formants slide from one sound to the next: low is clipped and consonantal, high is a smooth, vowel-like blur. Formant shifts all formants up or down in semitones: down for a giant, up for a child, with the pitch left alone. Pitch. Pitch (and Fine and the Pitch jack, 1 V/oct) set the voice's pitch. Intonation adds a gentle fall over the text and a lift on accented sounds: at 0 it is a monotone, which is what you want for singing. Modes. Loop speaks the text over and over. Gate speaks it once each time Go rises and stops when it falls. Step speaks one sound at each rising edge of Go ; steady sounds (vowels, nasals, hisses) are held for as long as the gate stays high, so a short gate gives a clipped sound and a long gate sustains it: a sequencer plays the words one by one. Outputs. Sound gives a trigger at the start of every sound (not for pauses); Voiced is a gate that is high while the voice buzzes, Position is how far through the text it is, 0 – 1. How to use it? A robot singer: Mode Loop, Intonation 0, a sequencer into Pitch and a slow Speed ; text 'a ee oo o . Spoken rhythm: short words of stops and hisses ( t k t ch . sh t k ), Speed 12 – 20, Glide low, as a hat or snare layer. Words on a keyboard: Mode Step, notes into Pitch , the keyboard's gate into Go : every key plays the next sound. A choir: two or three Speak modules on the same vowels at different Pitch and Formant , through a reverb. Voiced clock: Sound clocks a drum or an envelope. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Speak does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Speak under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Speak: Robot Choir Sustained vowels on a slowly moving bass line, with no intonation, so the voice sings like a mechanical choir. Change the text to other vowels, raise Glide for smoother changes, or move Formant for a bigger or smaller singer. Speak: Spoken Beat Hisses and stops spoken fast over a drum loop, a percussive layer made only of consonants. Change the text for another rhythm or lower Speed to hear the individual sounds. Speak: Step Words Mode is Step: every note from the sequencer says the next sound of the text, on the note's pitch, so the tune spells out a phrase. Lengthen the gates to hold the vowels or change the text. Speak: Giant and Child Two voices say the same words at different speeds, one with its formants pulled down and one pushed up, so a giant and a child talk over each other. Change Formant on either voice. Speak: Vowel Sweep One long note while a slow LFO moves Formant up and down and the text walks through all the vowels: a singing, shifting drone. Move Glide for blur or Breath for a husky edge. Presets The preset bar of the Speak view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Hello World A greeting, loosely. Robot Choir Sustained vowels on one note: a mechanical choir. Mumble A blurred, low conversation. Hat Talk Hisses and stops as percussion. Giant Formants down: a huge, slow voice. Child Formants and pitch up: a small voice. Whisper All breath and little voice. Vowel Walk Every vowel in turn: a sweeping formant tune. Nasal Hum Long nasals and open vowels. Stutter Plosive stutters into a rising vowel. Spoken Bass A low, pulsing talk: layer it with a bass. Yes No Two short words with a lift at the end. Step Words Step mode: send gates into Go to play one sound at a time. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct, 0 = C4, added to Pitch and Fine Go gate starts (Gate), steps (Step) or is ignored (Loop) Out audio the voice Sound trigger a new sound started Voiced gate the voice is buzzing Position control 0 – 1 through the text Knobs and settings Control Range Default Speed 1 – 40 u/s 8 Pitch −36 … +24 st −12 Fine ±100 ct 0 Formant ±12 st 0 Breath 0 – 100 % 15 % Intonation 0 – 100 % 50 % Glide 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 70 % Mode Loop, Gate, Step Loop

title: Bit Formula
text: Bit Formula Bit Formula in the module view Introduction Bit Formula makes sound from a one-line sum of whole numbers. A counter ticks at a clock rate; at each tick the formula turns the counter and three knobs into a number, and the low eight bits of that number are the next sample. Shifts, masks and exclusive-ors of a rising counter fall into rhythms, melodies and crunchy textures. Sixteen formulas are built in, a seventeenth is yours to type, and the audio input can be part of the maths. How does it work? The clock. Rate ticks per second (250 Hz – 48 kHz, 8 kHz by default), scaled by 1 V/oct from Pitch , advance a counter t . The output is held between ticks, so a low rate is a lo-fi staircase. Smooth low-passes the staircase (from open to about 200 Hz) and Bits keeps only the top 1 – 8 bits of the result. The formula. Each tick evaluates the formula with t (the counter), a , b , c (the three knobs, 0 – 255, all modulatable) and x (the audio input as 0 – 255; 128 when nothing is patched in). The result modulo 256 becomes the sample: 0 is the bottom, 255 the top. Value shows the byte, MSB is its top bit as a gate. The language. Numbers are decimal or 0x hex; the operators follow C's precedence: / % , then + - , > , >= , == != , & , ^ , , && , , and cond ? yes : no ; unary - , ~ and ! ; parentheses. All arithmetic is 32-bit and wraps. Division and remainder by zero give 0 and shift counts are taken modulo 32, so no formula can fail while it runs. There are no functions, loops, names or assignments: the text is compiled once, when you edit it, into at most 64 small instructions, and the audio thread only runs those. A formula that does not fit the language (or is too long or deep) is marked with the position of the first problem and is silent. Built-in formulas. Ramp , Pulse , Stairs , Sierpinski , Sieve , Crawl , Chirp , Warble , Mask , Counting , Echo Ramp , Grid , Mirror , Parity , Input Crush and Input Mod ; the last two use x . Their text is shown in the view. Formula is a stepped knob: a cable can step through them. How to use it? Tune it: Pitch from a sequencer moves the clock, so every formula plays the notes (and their harmonics). Move the maths: an LFO or envelope into A , B or C changes the shifts and masks: the pattern re-forms at every step of the knob. A drum voice: Rate low (500 – 2000 Hz), Bits 4, Reset from a trigger each beat; Value or MSB can also drive other modules. Mangle a signal: Input Crush or Input Mod with a drum loop in In . Write your own: pick Custom , type for example t (a>>5) & (t>>(b>>4)) . Make it gentle: Smooth at 40 – 70 % and Level down turns harsh staircases into something you can put under a pad. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Bit Formula does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Bit Formula under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Bit Formula: Sieve Tune A tune made from the overlap of two shifted counters, played by a sequencer on the clock rate. Move A and B to change which notes appear, or switch Formula to Crawl for a slower creeping line. Bit Formula: Crush the Beat A drum loop goes into In and the formula mixes it, bit by bit, with the counter: the beat comes back crunchy and gritted. Turn A down for a cleaner crush or switch to Input Mod for a more tonal mangle. Bit Formula: Sliding Knobs Three slow LFOs move A, B and C through a creeping formula, so the shifts and masks keep re-forming: a texture that is never the same twice. Change the LFO rates, or Smooth for a softer surface. Bit Formula: Drum Voice The counter is reset by every step and the formula is cut by a short envelope, so a falling squeal becomes a percussive hit. Change the Formula or Rate for a different drum sound. Bit Formula: Hollow Bass A low note on the clock rate of a shifted-mask formula: a hollow, buzzing bass with a built-in sub pattern. A sweeps the harmonic mask; try Bits at 5 for a rawer edge. Presets The preset bar of the Bit Formula view has 17 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Ramp Saw The counter itself: a rising saw that wraps. Pulse Width A pulse; A sets its width. Stair Climb Stepped ramps that climb in shifting groups. Sierpinski Bass A hollow bass pattern from a shifted mask. Sieve Melody A tune from the overlap of two shifted counters. Crawl A slow, creeping melody with a sparse rhythm. Chirp Drops Falling squeals: the counter squared. Warble Pad Smoothed, wavering steps. Mask Rhythm A rhythm of masked bit patterns. Counting Noise Bit-counting noise with a ragged pitch. Echo Ramp Soft Two ramps averaged: a soft buzz. Grid Buzz An angular, buzzy grid of three masks. Mirror Tone A triangle-like tone folded by the top bit. Parity Pulse Parity of two shifted counters: pulsing and crunchy. Crush Input Patch audio into In: it is cut to a few bits and crossed with the counter. Lo-Fi 4 Bit A coarse four-bit staircase saw. Custom Hat Your own formula slot, filled with a noisy hat-like one. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct on the clock rate Reset trigger sets the counter back to 0 In audio becomes x in the formula Out audio the byte as audio, after Bits, Smooth, Level Value control the byte as 0 – 1 MSB gate bit 7 of the byte Knobs and settings Control Range Default Formula 16 built-in + Custom Ramp A, B, C 0 – 255 96, 128, 200 Rate 250 Hz – 48 kHz 8 kHz Smooth 0 – 100 % 0 Bits 1 – 8 8 Level 0 – 100 % 60 % The custom formula (up to 160 characters) is saved with the node.

title: Endless Tone
text: Endless Tone Endless Tone in the module view Introduction Endless Tone is a sound that rises (or falls) for ever and never gets higher. It is an auditory illusion built from a stack of tones one octave apart: all of them glide upward together, but their loudness is controlled by a fixed window, so the ones that leave the top fade out and new ones fade in at the bottom. The ear follows the glide and never notices the hand-over. Use it for tension risers that never arrive, falling drones, spinning pads and as a stereo wash. How does it work? Partials. Count (6 – 12) sine waves, each one octave above the last. Pitch and the Pitch jack set the centre of the pattern (1 V/oct). The window. Every partial's loudness comes from a window over the log-frequency axis: a bell curve (a Gaussian) times a raised cosine that is exactly zero at both ends. Width sets the bell: narrow shows a few clear partials, wide spreads the energy into a dense cloud, a pad of octaves. The glide. Rate (0 – 2 octaves per second) times Direction (−100 … +100 %) moves the whole pattern in log-frequency. After one octave the pattern is exactly where it started; at that moment each oscillator takes over the next one's place (and its phase), so nothing clicks. Direction at 0 stops the glide, a negative value falls, and Direction is modulatable, so you can reverse the tone in mid-air. Timbre and space. Timbre blends each partial from a sine to a sawtooth (band-limited), which also gives the stack harmonics between the octaves. Spread leans alternate partials to the left and right, so the glide also travels across the stereo field. Phase offsets the pattern by up to one octave, which with Rate at 0 is a hand-played glide. Loop output. Loop is a ramp from 0 to 1 that completes once per octave of travel (falling when the tone falls); Wrap is a trigger each time it completes. They make a perfect clock for envelopes, filters and sequencers that must stay in step with the glide: the tone and its modulation spin together. How to use it? A riser that never ends: Rate 0.15, Direction up, Width 40 %, Count 10, into a low-pass that you open slowly. A falling drone: Direction down at 10 – 20 %, Timbre 60 %, a reverb. Impossible staircase: Loop into a quantiser into another oscillator. Rhythm from the loop: Wrap triggers a drum once per octave. Swell and fall: an LFO into Direction so the tone rises, hangs and falls. Wide pad: Spread 100 %, Width 100 %, Count 12. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Endless Tone does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Endless Tone under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Endless Tone: Rising Pad A pad that rises for ever and never gets higher: octave-spaced partials slide up under a fixed window. Change Rate for a faster climb, Width for fewer or more clear partials, or flip Direction to fall. Endless Tone: Falling Drone A low, saw-edged tone that keeps sinking, with a slow LFO on Width so the cloud thickens and thins as it falls. Try a faster Rate for a descent that feels like an alarm. Endless Tone: Loop Clock Wrap gives a trigger every time the tone has climbed an octave: here it plays a kick, and the Loop ramp opens a filter on a saw so the whole patch spins with the tone. Change Rate to change the tempo of the spin. Endless Tone: Wide Swirl Twelve bright partials spread across the stereo field while a slow LFO swings Direction between rising and falling, so the swirl climbs, hangs and sinks. Narrow Width for a clearer, thinner voice. Endless Tone: Chord Riser Three tones a fifth and an octave apart rise together at slightly different rates, a chord that climbs without end and slowly rotates through its own beating. Change the Pitch of each tone for another chord. Presets The preset bar of the Endless Tone view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Endless Riser A slow glide upward that never arrives. Falling Drone A warm tone that falls for ever. Slow Cloud A wide, dense wash of octaves, barely moving. Fast Spin A quick rising swirl. Saw Staircase Bright saw partials in a steady climb. Few Clear Partials Individual voices passing through the window. Frozen Chord No glide: a fixed stack of octaves; Phase moves it. Low Descent A deep, sinking tone. High Shimmer A glittering, wide rise high up. Gentle Mono Quiet and centred: a calm pad. Alarm Rise Tense, fast and bright. Reverse Slow A slow fall across many octaves. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does Pitch pitch 1 V/oct centre of the pattern (0 = C4) Reset trigger pattern back to its start Out L, Out R audio the tone, with Spread panning Loop control 0 – 1 ramp, one cycle per octave of glide Wrap trigger at the end of each cycle Knobs and settings Control Range Default Pitch −36 … +36 st 0 Fine ±100 ct 0 Rate 0 – 2 oct/s 0.25 Direction −100 … +100 % +100 % Width 0 – 100 % 40 % Count 6 – 12 9 Timbre 0 – 100 % 0 Spread 0 – 100 % 30 % Phase 0 – 100 % 0 Level 0 – 100 % 60 % Count is a stepped knob and can be modulated. Origin The illusion (a glide of octave-spaced partials under a fixed spectral envelope) is textbook psychoacoustics; the module was written from that description.

title: Noise
text: Noise Noise in the module view Introduction Noise is random audio: every frequency at once, with no pitch. It's the raw material for snares, hi-hats, wind, breath, surf and risers, and a handy random source for modulation. Noise gives you four classic colours on their own outputs, plus a Colour knob that sweeps smoothly from dark to bright. How does it work? All colours come from one white noise source and are filtered from it: White: equal energy at every frequency. Bright and hissy. Pink: falls by 3 dB per octave, so every octave has the same energy. Sounds even and natural, like rain or a waterfall. Brown: falls by 6 dB per octave. Deep and rumbling, like distant thunder or surf. Blue: rises by 3 dB per octave. Thin and fizzy. Every output is about equally loud (around −10 dB RMS), so you can switch colours without jumping in level. Out follows the Colour knob: −100 % is brown, −50 % pink, 0 % white, +50 % blue and +100 % violet (rising by 6 dB per octave, the brightest). Between those points it blends the two neighbours, so turning the knob, or modulating it, sweeps the noise from dark to bright. Level sets the volume of Out only. Each Noise node plays its own noise. Two nodes, or two voices of a Voice Cell, never play the same noise. How to use it? Snare wires or hi-hats: Noise Out → Multi Filter (band-pass or high-pass) → VCA, with a short ADSR on the VCA's Gain . For ready-made drums, the Ring and Punch drum nodes already include their own noise. Wind and surf: brown or pink noise → a resonant low-pass filter, with a slow Function or Random on the cutoff. Risers: patch a long rising envelope onto Colour , so the noise gets brighter as it builds. Breathy oscillator: mix a little pink noise into an oscillator before the filter. Random modulation: brown noise wanders slowly; patched with a small amount onto a pitch or cutoff, it adds unsteady, analog-style drift. Presets The preset bar of the Noise view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does White Noise Flat, full-spectrum noise: the all-round source for hats and snares. Pink Noise Equal energy per octave: natural, balanced, like rain. Brown Rumble Dark, deep noise: thunder, wind and engine rumble. Soft Hiss A quiet, slightly bright hiss for tape or room atmosphere. Bright Air Bright, airy noise for breaths, cymbals and shimmer. Violet Fizz Only the top end: fizzy, icy noise for hats and sprays. Wind Darkened noise: run it through a band-pass and sweep for wind. Ocean Deep, rolling noise: modulate Level slowly for waves. Snare Noise Full-level near-white noise: gate it with a fast envelope. Hat Noise Very bright noise for closed and open hats. Vinyl Bed A very quiet noise floor to add some grit under a mix. Half Level White noise at half level: a safe starting point for mixing. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Noise does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Noise under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Noise: Blue Hat Patterns Blue noise, cut short by an envelope and high-passed, is played as hi-hats from a drum grid pattern over a soft kick. Slide Colour toward white for a duller tick, or toward blue for a thinner, brighter sizzle. Noise: Ocean Surf Brown noise swells and recedes as two slow LFOs open a low-pass filter and the level together, like waves washing in. Raise Colour for foam and hiss, or speed up the LFO for a stormier sea. Noise: Wind Whistle Melody White noise through a very resonant band-pass filter that follows the sequencer's pitch: a breathy, whistling tune with no oscillator at all. Lower Resonance for a wind that only hints at pitch. Noise: Colour Riser Every four bars a ramp sweeps Colour from dark brown to bright violet while a filter opens, building tension over a steady beat before it drops back. Change the LFO's Sync to lengthen or shorten the build. Noise: Four Colours The white, pink, brown and blue outputs go to four mixer channels whose pans drift on slow LFOs, then through a gently resonant filter into a hall. Mute channels on the mixer to hear each colour alone. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Colour −100 … +100 % 0 % (white) Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Colour: the colour of Out : −100 % brown, −50 % pink, 0 % white, +50 % blue, +100 % violet. Level: the volume of Out . The fixed colour outputs always play at full level. Both knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs None (apart from the knobs). Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio noise in the colour set by Colour , at Level White audio white noise, flat Pink audio pink noise, −3 dB/oct Brown audio brown noise, −6 dB/oct Blue audio blue noise, +3 dB/oct

title: Pulse Generator
text: Pulse Generator Introduction Pulse Generator is a laboratory pulse generator on your board: one precisely timed rectangular pulse per period, with a delay , a width , slewed edges , bursts and double pulses . As a clock it is exact and can lock to the song position. As a sound source its edges excite a ringing resonance, like a badly terminated cable, so the pulses turn into clicks, pings and small drum tones. Its unit is time: set it with the knobs or drag the timing diagram. How does it work? The pulse. Each period starts with a Sync pulse. Delay later the pulse begins: it rises over Rise , stays up, and after Width falls over Fall (both a share of the width; at 0 % the edge is a clean step). The Gate output is the plain logic version: high from the start of the pulse to the start of its fall. Amplitude and Offset set the level of Out . Polarity Complement turns the pulse upside down (Gate too). With Time Units on % of Period , Width and Delay are shares of the period, so they follow it. In Time , a width that would reach the next period is shortened and the Duty lamp lights. Modes. Free Run: a period every Period . With Sync on a note value and the transport playing, periods lock to the song position (stopped, they run at that note length and the current tempo). Reset restarts the period now. Triggered: each Trigger (or the Single button) starts a burst of Burst pulses, one Period apart. A trigger during a burst restarts it; Reset stops it. Gated: while Gate is high, periods run, the first one at the rising edge. After the falling edge no new pulse starts, but the last one plays to its full width. External Width: a gate delay line. Gate 's edges come out Delay later, the pulse as long as the gate was high ( Rise and Fall are still shares of the Width knob). Up to 256 edges can wait; more are dropped and Duty lights. With Gate unpatched, each Trigger becomes a pulse of Width . Sync fires at the input's rising edges. Double gives two pulses per period, at the period start and Delay later. The shortest period is 4 samples (83 µs at 48 kHz). Jitter moves each pulse by a seeded random amount, up to ±25 % of the period (more often small than large). It never moves the period grid, so a synced clock stays on the beat, and Sync is never jittered. The same Seed gives the same jitter every time. Warm-up (Free Run, Sync Free) makes the period settle like a cold instrument: 5 % long at the start (of the transport, or when the module is added), then drifting in. The Warming lamp stays lit until it is within 0.1 %, after about 47 seconds. Ringing. Every edge excites a resonance at Ring Freq (plus Pitch , in octaves). Damping sets how many cycles it lasts: from 200 down to half a cycle. Rising and falling edges ring with opposite sign, so a short pulse gives a two-edge ping whose colour follows the width (half a ring cycle reinforces it, a whole cycle cancels it). Slow edges ring less. Ring mixes it into Out; the Ring output carries it alone, at full strength. A very resonant ring that a pulse train keeps feeding is softly limited. Clean edges. Edges are placed between samples and band-limited, so fast pulse trains don't alias and the ring is clean. All outputs are one sample late for it. How to use it? An exact clock: Sync 1/16, Width 10 %, Gate into a sequencer's clock. Clicks and pings: Period 250 ms, Width 0.2 ms, Ring 100 %, Ring Freq 3 kHz, Damping 60 %. Turn Width to hear the colour change. A small drum: Triggered, Ring output, Ring Freq 180 Hz, Damping 30 %, Width 3 ms: a pitched thump per trigger. One ping per note: in a Voice Cell, Voice In › Trigger into Trigger and pitch into Pitch , Triggered mode. Each voice has its own jitter. Rolls and flams: Triggered, Burst 4, Period 30 ms; or Double with a short Delay for flams. A humanised clock: Sync 1/8, Jitter 15 %. Delay a gate: External Width, Delay 125 ms: the gate comes out late and as long as it went in. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Pulse Generator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Pulse Generator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Pulse Generator: Wobbly Clock A Pulse Generator synced to 1/8 is the clock of the melody, and its Jitter nudges every pulse a little early or late, so the tune sways like a human player. Turn Jitter to 0 for a rigid machine, or up to 40 % for a drunk one; the same Seed always gives the same wobble. Pulse Generator: Tin Drums A whole kit from triggered pulses: the Ring output of each Pulse Generator is a pitched thump, tick or rattle. The tom fires a Burst of four pulses, a quick roll. Change Ring Freq for the tuning, Damping for how long they ring, Width for the colour. Pulse Generator: Glass Chimes One very short pulse per note makes the Ring resonance ping, and the sequencer's pitch tunes Ring Freq (1 V per octave), so each step is a glassy chime. A second, wider pulse a fifth above adds a darker partner. Try Damping for the length of the ring and Width for the brightness. Pulse Generator: Gate Echo In External Width mode the Pulse Generator is a gate delay: each note's gate comes out 190 ms later, as long as it went in, and plays a second voice a fifth higher. The result is a hand-made echo of the melody. Change Delay for the spacing, or Rise and Fall to soften the echoed notes. Pulse Generator: Pulse Choir At audio rate the Pulse Generator is an oscillator: three of them at 110, 165 and 220 Hz, with slow LFOs on Width for a swaying pulse-width sound and soft Rise and Fall on the edges. Switch Double on for a hollow, comb-like voice, or change the Period to retune a note. Presets The preset bar of the Pulse Generator view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Clock 1/16 Exact 1/16 clock pulse locked to the song position. Slow Gate Gentle one-second gate with softened edges: a rhythmic envelope source. Square Wave A 200 Hz square tone. Narrow Pulse Thin 200 Hz pulse: nasal and bright. Click Train A train of 25 Hz clicks: granular and tick-like. Cable Ping Short pulses ringing like a mistuned cable. Small Drum Low ringing resonance: a tiny tuned drum on every beat. Metal Tick High, tight ring for hat-like ticks. Burst Triggered Each trigger fires eight fast pulses: a flam or roll. Double Pulse Two pulses per period for flams and double clocks. Jittery Clock Human-ish wobble on each pulse while the grid stays put. Gated Pulses Pulses run while the gate is high: a buzzy gated tone. Complement Gate Inverted pulse: high most of the time, dips on the beat. Percent Width Width follows the period, so the timbre stays put as you sweep pitch. Soft Edges Slewed edges round a pulse into a soft, nearly triangle tone. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Period 20 µs – 10 s 100 ms Width 1 µs – 5 s, or 0 – 100 % 10 ms (10 %) Delay 0 – 10 s, or 0 – 100 % 0 Rise 0 – 100 % of Width 0 % Fall 0 – 100 % of Width 0 % Amplitude 0 – 100 % 100 % Offset −1 … +1 0 Jitter 0 – 100 % 0 % Ring 0 – 100 % 0 % Ring Freq 20 Hz – 20 kHz 2 kHz Damping 0 – 100 % 50 % Mode Free Run, Triggered, Gated, External Width Free Run Sync Free, 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 bar, 2 bars, 4 bars, 8 bars Free Time Units Time, % of Period Time Double Off, On Off Burst 1 – 64 1 Polarity Normal, Complement Normal Warm-up Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Period: time from one period start to the next (Free Run with Sync Free, Triggered, Gated). The view's ÷10 / ×10 buttons step it by decades; the knob is the vernier. Width: the pulse length. Time Units picks which of the two Width knobs is shown. Delay: period start to pulse start; with Double , the pair spacing. Rise / Fall: the edge times, as a share of the width. Amplitude / Offset: the pulse height and the baseline of Out. Jitter: random timing, up to ±25 % of the period. Ring / Ring Freq / Damping: how much ringing is mixed into Out, its frequency, and how fast it dies. Burst: pulses per trigger (Triggered). Seed: picks the jitter. Period, Width, Delay, Rise, Fall, Amplitude, Offset, Jitter, Ring, Ring Freq and Damping are modulation destinations. The view The timing diagram shows one period: Sync ticks, the pulse with its ringing, and Period, Delay and Width as dimension lines. Drag an arrow's end to change that value, or drag a slope's dot to change Rise or Fall. When Width or Delay is under 2 % of the period the time axis is compressed, so they stay visible. The Duty lamp lights when a width was shortened or pulses or edges were dropped (at most 32 pulses can wait for their Delay at once); Warming during warm-up. Single starts a burst in Triggered mode (and a pulse in External Width with Gate unpatched). Inputs Input Signal What it does Trigger trigger starts a burst (Triggered), or a pulse (External Width, Gate unpatched) Gate gate runs the generator while high (Gated); the signal delayed (External Width) Reset trigger restarts the period (Free Run unsynced, Gated); stops a burst (Triggered) Pitch pitch added to Ring Freq in octaves Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the pulse plus ringing, band-limited Gate gate a clean logic copy of the pulse Sync trigger one pulse at each period start, before Delay Ring audio only the ringing, at full strength

title: Sweep Generator
text: Sweep Generator Introduction Sweep Generator is a function generator with a built-in frequency sweep, like the bench instruments that measure a circuit across the audio band. It glides from Start to Stop over a set time or a number of bars, and puts out everything other modules need to follow it: the sweep ramp, the frequency as pitch (so a filter can track it), and triggers at markers, at the end of each sweep and on every cycle of the waveform. Musically it is a riser, a siren, a tone-burst source and a tracking test signal for feedback patches. The old benches' character is kept on purpose: a slow Drift , a warm-up that settles after the transport starts, and an audible Retrace as the sweep flies back. How does it work? The sweep. One sweep runs from Start to Stop in Sweep Time , or in the note value set by Sweep Sync . Stop may be below Start for a falling sweep. Direction runs it Up, Down, or Up-Down (up and back within the same length). The Law decides the speed: Log spends the same time on every octave (it sounds even), Lin the same time on every hertz: it rushes through the bass and lingers in the treble. Modes. Continuous: the sweep repeats. Synced to a note value while the transport plays, its position follows the song position, so it stays on the bars after a loop or a jump. Trigger restarts it. Triggered: waits at the beginning until a trigger, runs one sweep, fires End and holds the last frequency. A new trigger starts again from the beginning. Gated: the sweep moves only while Gate is high and pauses while it is low. Trigger restarts it. Burst: the sweep runs as in Continuous, but Out is silent until a trigger. Each trigger plays Burst Count whole cycles of the waveform at the frequency the sweep has reached, with short fades. Bursts step through the band like a stepped response measurement. While Hold is high, the sweep position freezes in every mode; the tone keeps playing. When synced, releasing Hold jumps back onto the grid. The waveform is phase continuous: when the frequency jumps (a new sweep, a trigger, a jump in the song), the wave carries on without a click. Edges and corners are band-limited, so even high sweeps stay clean. Symmetry skews the sine and the triangle, sets the duty of the square and the pulse, and bends the ramps. With Phase Reset on, a trigger also restarts the cycle. FM adds linear (through-zero) frequency modulation from the FM input, with the same depth all along the sweep; AM scales the level. Very low sweeps make Out a sweeping LFO. Retrace. When an Up or Down sweep starts over, Instant jumps back. Glide flies back over 5 % of the sweep (at most a quarter of a second), the way a bench sweeper's flyback can be heard. Sweep follows it, End fires as it starts and the markers stay quiet during it. Markers. Up to three marker frequencies (set by Markers ). Marker fires whenever the sweep crosses one, in either direction, and Marker Gate stays high for Marker Width . Use them to trigger events at points in the band. Drift and warm-up. Drift adds a slow, seeded wander of up to about ±37 cents, plus a warm-up offset of up to ±40 cents that settles over Warm-up after the transport starts (or the module is created), like a cold instrument. With Drift at 0 the frequency is exact. Repeatable. The drift comes from Seed and the song position, and starting the transport restarts the sweep, the waveform and the warm-up, so a render from the same position is always identical. How to use it? Riser: Start 100 Hz, Stop 8 kHz, Sweep Sync 8 bars, Mode Continuous, into a filter or straight into the mix. Patch End to a crash. Filter that follows: Freq into a filter's cutoff pitch input: the filter tracks the tone exactly. Or Sweep into any knob as a ramp. Siren: Direction Up-Down, Sweep Time 1.5 s, Waveform Triangle, Law Lin. Tone bursts: Mode Burst, Burst Count 8, a clock into Trigger : short blips that climb through the band. Events along the sweep: Markers 3, Marker into drum triggers or an envelope: hits at 250 Hz, 1 kHz and 4 kHz. One sweep per note: Mode Triggered, a note's trigger into Trigger , Pitch from the keyboard: each note sweeps from its own key. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Sweep Generator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Sweep Generator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Sweep Generator: Eight-Bar Riser A saw tone climbs from 80 Hz to 6 kHz over eight bars while its Sweep output opens a filter on a bed of noise; at the top, the End trigger fires a crash. Edit Start, Stop and Sweep Sync for a shorter or lower riser, or switch Law to Lin to hear it rush through the bass. Sweep Generator: Harbour Siren A triangle wave glides up and down between 300 Hz and 1.2 kHz, two bars each way, on a linear law like an old air-raid horn, with Drift keeping the pitch slightly alive. Change Direction, Waveform or Retrace to turn the siren into a whooping alarm, and let the delay ring behind it. Sweep Generator: Climbing Blips In Burst mode the tone is silent until a trigger, and each trigger plays three clean cycles at the frequency the sweep has reached, so a steady sixteenth pulse becomes blips that climb through the band and start over every two bars. Raise Burst Count for longer blips, or change Stop to widen the climb. Sweep Generator: Marker Drums A slow sweep from 100 Hz to 8 kHz crosses three Markers, and each crossing, in both directions, fires a kick and a hat, while the End trigger calls the snare once per cycle. Move a Marker to shift the rhythm, change Sweep Sync for a faster or slower pulse, or set Markers to 1 for a sparse beat. Sweep Generator: Laser Zaps In Triggered mode each sequencer note fires one quick downward sweep that begins on its own pitch (the Pitch input), so a bassline of zaps shoots across the speakers. Change Sweep Time for longer or shorter zaps, Waveform for a different edge, or Direction to make them rise. Presets The preset bar of the Sweep Generator view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Up Sweep A repeating four-second sine rise. Riser 4 Bars Tempo-locked rise over four bars. Falling Zap Short falling zap on every trigger. Siren Up-down sweep: an emergency siren. Square Siren Harder, buzzier siren. Laser Very quick falling saw: classic laser shot. Noise Whoosh LFO Sub-audio sweep: use Out as an LFO that accelerates. Linear Rush Linear law rushes through the bass and lingers up high. Tone Bursts Each trigger plays four cycles at the current sweep position. Pulse Riser Narrow pulse rising: thin, urgent sound. Gated Climb Climbs only while the gate is held. Marker Scan Sine sweep that fires a trigger at three frequencies. Glide Retrace Audible flyback after each sweep, like a bench sweeper. Wobbly Bench Strong drift: an unstable old function generator. Deep Fall Long sub drop for impacts. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Start 0.01 Hz – 20 kHz 100 Hz Stop 0.01 Hz – 20 kHz 5 kHz Sweep Time 10 ms – 100 s 4 s Symmetry −100 … +100 % 0 % Marker 1–3 0.01 Hz – 20 kHz 250 Hz, 1 kHz, 4 kHz FM 0 – 100 % 0 % Drift 0 – 100 % 15 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Waveform Sine, Triangle, Square, Ramp Up, Ramp Down, Pulse Sine Mode Continuous, Triggered, Gated, Burst Continuous Sweep Sync Free, 1/4, 1/2, 1 bar, 2, 4, 8, 16 bars Free Law Log, Lin Log Direction Up, Down, Up-Down Up Retrace Instant, Glide Instant Burst Count 1 – 64 4 Markers 0 – 3 0 Marker Width 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 ms 10 ms Phase Reset Off, On Off Warm-up Off, 10 s, 30 s, 2 min 30 s Seed 0 – 999 1 Start / Stop: the frequencies at the beginning and the end of the sweep. Drag the curve's ends in the view to set them. Sweep Time: the length of one sweep when Sweep Sync is Free . Symmetry: skew of sine and triangle, duty of square (5 … 95 %) and pulse (1 … 25 %), curve of the ramps. Marker 1–3: the marker frequencies; drag a marker line in the view to move it. FM: the depth of the FM input (at 100 %, an input of ±1 swings the frequency by ±200 %, through zero). Drift: the slow wander and the warm-up offset. Level: the size of Out . Sweep Sync: a note value for one sweep (4/4); the length follows the tempo. Law: Log (equal time per octave) or Lin (equal time per hertz). Retrace: how an Up or Down sweep returns to its beginning. Burst Count: the cycles in each burst (Mode Burst). Markers: how many markers are active. Marker Width: how long Marker Gate stays high. Phase Reset: a trigger also restarts the waveform's cycle. Warm-up: how long the warm-up offset takes to settle (to 5 %). Seed: picks the drift. Start , Stop , Sweep Time , Symmetry , the markers, FM , Drift and Level are modulation destinations. Waveform is the row of icons in the view. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trigger trigger starts a sweep (Triggered), a burst (Burst), or restarts the sweep (Continuous, Gated) Gate gate in Gated mode, the sweep runs only while high Hold gate while high, the sweep position freezes Pitch pitch shifts Start , Stop and the markers together (1.0 = one octave) FM audio linear frequency modulation, depth set by FM AM audio amplitude modulation: the level × (1 + AM), never below 0 Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the waveform, times Level Sweep control the sweep position: 0 at Start , 1 at Stop Freq pitch the current frequency as pitch (0 = C4), drift included Marker trigger a pulse when the sweep crosses an active marker Marker Gate gate high for Marker Width after each marker End trigger a pulse at the end of each sweep (each half in Up-Down) Sync trigger a pulse at the start of every cycle of the waveform

title: ADSR
text: ADSR ADSR in the module view Introduction The ADSR is the classic envelope generator: attack, decay, sustain, release . A gate starts it and it draws one shape over time. That shape opens a VCA so a note gets loud and fades, or sweeps a filter's cutoff. It also has an Active output that stays high while the envelope is running. Inside a Voice Cell this tells the cell when a voice has gone quiet and can be reused. How does it work? The envelope moves through four stages: Attack: when the Gate goes high, the level rises in a straight line to its peak. The rise starts at the current level, not at zero, so retriggering a note that is still sounding doesn't click. Decay: the level falls to the sustain level along an exponential curve. Sustain: the level holds there for as long as the gate stays high. Release: when the gate goes low, the level falls exponentially to silence. When the release reaches −80 dB, the envelope stops, End fires one trigger and Active goes low. The peak depends on velocity. With Vel Amount at 0 % every note peaks at 1.0. At 100 % the peak equals the Velocity input, so soft notes stay quiet. Sustain is a share of that peak: a soft note sustains lower than a loud one. A trigger at Retrigger while the gate is high restarts the attack from the current level. Use it for repeated accents within one long note. How to use it? Amplitude envelope: patch Gate from a Voice In (or a sequencer's gate), Env onto a VCA's Gain knob. Since Gain starts at 0, the envelope opens it completely. In a Voice Cell: also patch Active into Voice Out › Active . The cell then frees the voice exactly when its sound has faded, and not while the release is still audible. Filter envelope: patch Env onto a filter's Cutoff knob and set the cable's amount. Use a short decay and a low sustain for a plucky sound. Velocity: patch Velocity from Voice In and raise Vel Amount . Chaining: End fires when the release is done. Patch it into another envelope's gate or a Function's Trig to start the next event. Presets The preset bar of the ADSR view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Classic Synth All-round envelope for lead and bass. Pluck Instant attack, decays to nothing. Short Stab Tight stab with a little tail. Slow Pad Gradual fade-in and long release. Soft Swell Smooth swell that stays at full level. Organ Gate On-off gating with tiny declick ramps. Bass Punch Punchy bass with strong velocity response. Strings Bowed-style onset and soft release. Long Bell Ringing decay for bells and mallets. Reverse Pad Very slow rise, quick fall-off. Plucky Filter Good for cutoff: a snappy sweep per note. Velocity Dynamic Full velocity sensitivity for expressive playing. Drone Hold Slow in, very long ghostly release. Staccato Click Ultra-short blip for percussive clicks. Demo patches Five whole patches show what ADSR does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick ADSR under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows ADSR: Plucked Strings Two ADSRs share each note: one shapes the volume, the other sweeps a low-pass filter from open to closed, so every note starts bright and darkens. Shorten Decay for staccato plucks, or raise Sustain to let the notes ring. ADSR: Slow Pad Swell With a long Attack and a long Release, each held note rises out of silence and melts away over the next one, so the chords seem to breathe. Try a shorter Attack to turn the pad into a soft organ. ADSR: Velocity Touch The sequencer sends a different velocity with every note into the ADSR, and Vel Amount decides how much it matters: soft notes are quiet and mellow, accented ones loud and bright. Set Vel Amount to zero and the phrase goes flat. ADSR: Bass Under a Beat A fast Attack with a medium Decay and a high Sustain gives the bass a tight thump that then holds its note until the gate closes. Lower Sustain for a plucked bass, lengthen Release to let notes blur into each other. ADSR: End Trigger Echoes When each note's envelope finishes, its End output fires a rim shot, so the percussion trails after the melody at a distance set by Decay and Release. Lengthen the Release and the echo hits arrive later. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Attack 1 ms – 10 s 5 ms Decay 1 ms – 10 s 300 ms Sustain 0 – 100 % 70 % Release 1 ms – 20 s 400 ms Vel Amount 0 – 100 % 50 % Attack: how long the rise from silence to the peak takes. The rise is linear, so short attacks stay punchy. The knob's centre is 200 ms; the lower half gives fine control over short times. Decay: time to fall from the peak to the sustain level. The curve is exponential and gets close to the target after the set time. The centre is 400 ms. Sustain: the level held while the gate stays high, as a share of the peak. At 0 % the envelope decays to silence even with the gate held: a percussive shape. At 100 % there is no decay. Release: time from the gate going low to silence (−80 dB). The centre is 600 ms. A gate that ends during the attack or decay starts the release from wherever the level is. Vel Amount: how much velocity lowers the peak. Peak = 1 − Vel Amount × (1 − Velocity). At 0 % velocity is ignored; at 100 % a velocity of 0.3 gives a peak of 0.3. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Inputs Input Signal What it does Gate gate high (≥ 0.5) starts the attack; low starts the release Retrigger trigger while the gate is high, restarts the attack from the current level Velocity control, 0 – 1 scales the peak through Vel Amount ; unpatched counts as full velocity Outputs Output Signal What it does Env control, 0 – 1 the envelope End trigger one pulse when the release reaches silence Active gate high from the first attack until the release has finished

title: Contour
text: Contour Contour in the module view Introduction Contour is an envelope and LFO that plays shapes from a library instead of building them from stages. There are 96 ready-made shapes (percussive decays, plucks, swells, sustained envelopes, bounces, stairs, rhythmic gates, classic and unusual LFO waves, organic textures) and 8 slots for shapes you draw yourself. Pick a shape, set how long it takes, and trigger it: a one-shot envelope. Hold a gate and it waits at the shape's sustain point. Loop it and it's an LFO. Shapes that no attack-decay-sustain-release could ever make (echoing bounces, stutters, irregular gates) are one click away. How does it work? Choosing. Shape picks one of 104: 0–95 are the library, 96–103 your own ( User 1 … 8 ). The dropdown shows the shape's name. Browse opens a grid of thumbnails grouped by family; hover one to see it big, click to choose it. With the view focused, ← and → step through the shapes. Morph blends the shape into its neighbour in the list. Neighbours are related (Short exp → Long exp, Bounce 5 → Bounce 8), so Morph moves smoothly between them; across a family boundary it blends unlike shapes, which can be fun too. Time is how long the whole shape takes (1 ms – 60 s), or one cycle in Loop. With Sync it's a note value instead. Skew warps time without changing the length: + plays the start faster and the end slower (at +1 the first half takes a quarter of the time), − the other way. Reverse plays the shape backwards. Level scales the output, and Vel Amount lets the Velocity input scale it: at 0 % every start is full level, at 100 % the level follows the velocity. Velocity is read at each start. Modes One-shot: Trig or a rising Gate plays the whole shape once; End fires at the end and the output stays at the last value (0 for envelopes). A new start while it plays restarts it with a 2 ms crossfade (no click), or, with Retrigger on Ignore , is ignored until it's done. Gated: like One-shot, but while the Gate is high the shape waits at its sustain point (the dashed line in the preview), and plays the rest when the gate falls. A short gate that ends before the sustain point just plays through. Shapes without a sustain point behave as One-shot; Trig starts the shape like a very short gate. Loop: the shape repeats every Time ; End fires at each wrap. Trig or Gate restart it (crossfaded). Envelope shapes loop too: a repeating decay is a classic rhythmic effect. With Sync and the transport playing, the loop is locked to the song position: always at the same place in the bar, after loop jumps too, and every render is the same. In One-shot and Gated a new Shape is picked up at the next start; in Loop it crossfades over 5 ms. Morph works at any time. Phase outputs where the playback is (0 … 1): a ramp for other modules. Active is high while the shape plays (always in Loop). Inv is the upside down shape ( 1 − Out , or −Out for bipolar shapes). Drawing your own Select a user slot ( User 1 … 8 ) and press Draw . Drag to draw freehand, or choose Line to drag straight segments. Smooth softens the drawing, Mirror makes it symmetric, Snap 8 / 16 turns it into steps. Sustain lets you click where Gated mode should wait ( No sustain removes it). Envelope / Cycle decides whether the shape loops seamlessly (a cycle ends where it starts), ± Bipolar whether it spans −1 … +1. On a library shape, Copy to puts the shape as you see it (with Morph, Skew and Reverse) into a user slot, ready to be changed. Every stroke is one undo step. Drawn shapes are saved with the board. How to use it? Percussive accents: Decays or Plucks, Time 200 ms, One-shot, triggered by a sequencer, onto a VCA. Echoing gate: Bounces › Echoes 1/8 , Sync 1/2, triggered on the beat: a VCA that echoes the note. Rhythmic chopper: Gates family, Loop, Sync 1 bar, onto a VCA: a trance gate. Morph between two patterns for variations. Pad envelope in a Voice Cell: Sustains › Pad , Gated, Gate from Voice In , Active into Voice Out › Active . Breathing LFO: Wobbles › Breathing , Loop, Time 4 s, onto a filter. Your own groove: draw a shape in User 1 , Snap 16, Loop, Sync 1 bar: a step-like modulation drawn in seconds. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Contour does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Contour under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Contour: Pluck Library Every note triggers a one-shot shape from the library, a soft 1:8 pluck, that opens both volume and filter. Try the other plucks, Bounce and Echoes shapes, or move Morph to change its curve. Contour: Looping Wobble Bass In Loop mode the Wobble shape repeats once per beat and swings the cutoff of a held bass, locked to the tempo. Switch Sync to another note length for faster or slower wobble, or try Double wobble and Swing wobble. Contour: Breathing Pad A pad is held steady while one looped Contour breathes its volume over two bars and a second one slowly sways its filter over four. Choose Heartbeat or Sway shapes, or change Sync, and the whole pad takes on a new pulse. Contour: Drawn Rhythm Gate The rhythm shapes are patterns drawn as amplitude: one looping shape chops a held chord into syncopated stabs, another carves a bass note into a different pattern. Pick any of the x.xx shapes, or change Sync, to make a new groove. Contour: Reversed Swells With Reverse on, a plucked shape plays backwards: each note swells up and is cut off at its peak, like a tape played in reverse. Switch Reverse off for normal plucks, or lengthen Time for slower swells. Presets The preset bar of the Contour view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Short Pluck Quick plucked decay for synth bass and leads. Snappy Click Tiny transient: for percussive attacks or pitch snaps. Long Exp Decay Slow exponential fade for sustained tails. Organ Gate Held while the key is down: organ-like on and off. ADSR Classic A conventional attack, decay, sustain, release contour. Slow Pad Gentle swell and long release for pads. Reverse Rise Rises slowly toward the end: for risers and swells. Bounce Ball Bouncing, ever-quicker hits: a dropped ball. Echo Taps Decaying repeats from one trigger, like a rhythmic echo. Heartbeat Looping double-thump pulse at about 60 BPM. Breathing Slow organic in and out for pads and filters. Sine LFO Plain looping sine at 4 Hz: vibrato or tremolo. Synced Stutter Rhythmic gate pattern locked to the tempo. Swing Wobble Tempo-synced wobble with a shuffle feel. Morphing Texture Irregular looping texture, shifted by Morph: organic movement. Reversed Roll A drum roll played backwards: builds into the next beat. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Time 1 ms – 60 s 500 ms Shape 104 shapes (96 library, 8 user) Click Morph 0 – 100 % 0 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Vel Amount 0 – 100 % 0 % Skew −1 … +1 0 Every knob is a modulation destination; a cable on the Shape dropdown steps through the library. Settings Setting Values Default Mode One-shot, Gated, Loop One-shot Sync Off, 16 bars … 1/32T (straight, dotted, triplet) Off Reverse Off, On Off Retrigger (One-shot, Gated) Restart, Ignore Restart Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger starts the shape Gate gate starts the shape; in Gated mode holds it at the sustain point while high Velocity control scales the level through Vel Amount (unpatched: full) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control the shape Inv control the shape upside down Phase control the playback position, 0 … 1 End trigger the shape finished (or wrapped, in Loop) Active gate the shape is playing

title: Segments
text: Segments Segments in the module view Introduction Segments draws any envelope you like out of up to eight pieces. Each piece (a segment ) is a ramp, a step or a hold with its own time, level and curve. Chain four of them and you have an ADSR; add a hold and it's an AHDSR; add a second peak and it's a swell that breathes twice. Mark some segments as a loop and the chain keeps cycling through them: an LFO of any shape you can draw, or an envelope whose sustain wobbles. Each segment has a gate output that is high while it runs, and a trigger input that can end it or jump to it, so segments can wait for events and announce when they play. Where ADSR is fixed to four stages and Function is one rise and one fall, Segments is the general case, edited by dragging points on a graph. How does it work? Segment types Every segment starts from wherever the output is when it begins, so jumps and retriggers never click. Ramp moves to its Level over its Time . Shape bends it: 0 is straight, +1 exponential (a slow start rising, a quick drop falling: the snappy feel of an analog envelope), −1 the opposite. Step jumps to its Level and stays there for its Time . With Shape above 0, it glides there over that share of the time instead. A few steps in a loop make a little stepped sequence. Hold keeps the level it starts with. Its Wait decides when it ends: after its Time ; while the Gate is high (a sustain); or at the next pulse on its Seg input (or when the Gate falls). Time runs from 0.5 ms to 30 s; Time Scale multiplies every time at once, so patching velocity or pitch onto it makes the whole envelope faster or slower. Modulating a Time knob bends the segment while it plays. Gates, loops and release Gate rising: the chain starts again at segment 1, from the current level. Active goes high, and Velocity is read: with Vel Amount up, softer notes reach lower levels. The loop: the segments from the first to the last with Loop on. After the last loop segment the chain goes back to the first and Loop fires. A single looped Ramp restarts from the level before it each time: a saw. The sustain point is the last Hold that waits for the Gate, or else the end of the loop. Everything after it is the release . Gate falling , Release = Jump : if the chain hasn't passed the sustain point yet, it jumps straight to the release, from the current level, like any envelope whose key is let go early. Release = Finish : the loop completes its pass and the earlier segments play out, then the release follows. Without a sustain point or a loop the chain is a one-shot: how long the gate stays high doesn't matter. End fires when the last segment finishes; the output stays at its level and Active falls. Seg 1 … 8 inputs. With Seg In on Advance , a pulse ends that segment if it's running (whatever its type). With Jump , a pulse makes the chain jump to that segment from wherever it is. The Seg outputs are high while their segment runs, exactly one at a time. Free running and sync Run = Free starts the chain on its own (and again at every transport start): with a loop it's an LFO, without one a single sweep. A rising Gate still restarts it. Sync turns each segment's time into a note value (8 bars … 1/64T, straight, dotted and triplet), chosen in the segment's row. With Run = Free and the transport playing, the chain is locked to the song: the part before the loop plays from the transport start, and the loop sits on the bar grid, so it is at the same place in every bar, survives loop jumps and renders the same every time. (Holds then last their note value too.) A Gate or Seg pulse unlocks it until the next transport start; when the transport stops it keeps running at the current tempo. The editor The graph shows the chain; each segment's width grows with its time. Drag a point up and down for the segment's Level , left and right for its Time (with Sync, through the note values). Drag a curve up and down for its Shape . Click a segment to select it. Its row below sets Type , Wait (holds), Loop , Seg In and the note value (with Sync), and shows its three knobs, with their modulation rings and cables. Drag across the strip at the top to set the loop region; click a lone looped segment there to clear the loop. − / + change the number of segments; Templates rewrites the chain as an AD, ADSR, AHDSR, two-peak swell, ramp or triangle LFO, a 4- or 8-step loop, or a gated burst (one undo step). A dot follows the output, and the running segment's label lights up. How to use it? Envelope with a hold: Templates › AHDSR, Gate from a sequencer or Voice In , Out onto a VCA, Active into Voice Out › Active . Pluck with a second bloom: Templates › Swell, Run Gated, onto a filter. Custom LFO: Templates › Triangle LFO, then drag the points: a lopsided, curved wave. Turn Sync on for a tempo-locked shape. Stepped sequence: Templates › 8-step loop, Sync on, each step 1/16: Out onto a quantizer, Seg outputs as triggers for drums. Wait for the beat: set a Hold to Wait: Trigger and patch a clock into its Seg input: the envelope pauses there until the next beat. Swell and burst: Templates › Gated burst: a pulsing attack while the key is held, then a smooth release. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Segments does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Segments under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport.
