Synced Bars One new value per bar: slow, tempo-locked changes. Burst Trigger Frequently fires bursts of triggers: fills and rolls. Rapid Burst Roll Long fast trigger rolls from the burst output. Chaotic Stream Chaos adds unpredictable behavior to the stream. Fast Jitter Fast small-depth jitter: adds life to pitch or pan. Unipolar Level Positive-only random values: for levels and mixes. Quiet Shimmer Low-depth random flutter for subtle shimmer. Seeded Pattern Steps from another seed: a different random pattern. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Rate 0.02 – 40 Hz 1 Hz Smooth 0 – 100 % 50 % Wobble 0 – 100 % 60 % Chaos 0 – 100 % 0 % Burst 0 – 100 % 25 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Sync Free, 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 bar, 2 bars, 4 bars, 8 bars Free Burst Size 2 – 8 4 Polarity Bipolar, Unipolar Bipolar Seed 0 – 999 1 Rate: steps per second, when Sync is Free and Clock is unpatched. Smooth: how slowly Smooth and Wobble follow the steps. Wobble: the resonance of the Wobble output. Chaos: feedback from the outputs into the values, the clock and the bursts. Burst: the chance of a burst on each step. Level: the size of Stepped, Smooth and Wobble. Burst Size: the most pulses a burst can have. Polarity: Bipolar −1 … +1, Unipolar 0 … 1. Seed: picks the sequence of values. Rate , Smooth , Wobble , Chaos , Burst and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Clock trigger each pulse is a step; overrides Rate and Sync Sample control when patched, each step samples it instead of a random value Hold gate while high, no new values and no Clock pulses Outputs Output Signal What it does Stepped control the current value Smooth control the values, glided without overshoot Wobble control the values, glided with overshoot and ringing (±1.5 at most) Burst trigger clusters of quick pulses Clock trigger one pulse per step Compare gate high while Stepped is above Smooth

title: Chart Recorder
text: Chart Recorder Introduction Chart Recorder is a pen drawing a signal onto a looping strip of paper; the strip plays back as modulation. The pen is a heavy, sprung mechanism: it lags, overshoots, sticks and bangs into its end stops, so even a plain envelope comes out with character, live at Pen . The strip replays at another speed, backwards, locked to the song or scrubbed by hand, and you can draw on the paper with the mouse. How does it work? Detector. In goes through Gain into the detector, which decides what the pen draws: DC: the signal itself, −1 … +1. For control signals. Rectified, RMS: the average level, smoothed over Response . Peak: jumps up at once and falls back over Response . Log dB: the RMS level in decibels, like a level recorder: 0 dBFS at the top edge, − Log Range at the bottom. Audio into In is fine with the level detectors. With DC, Pen and Replay are bipolar (−1 … +1); with the others they are unipolar (0 … 1). The pen is a weight on a spring with a damper. Writing Speed is how fast it can move and how stiff the spring is: fast, it follows closely; slow, it draws straight ramps between levels. Damping low makes it overshoot and wiggle around each new level; high makes it creep. Friction makes it stick: small changes don't move it until they add up (up to 4 % of the paper width), so smooth movement turns into small steps. At the edges of the paper the pen hits its end stops and bounces back a little: an overdriven input draws flattened tops with a small kick. Pen always carries the pen's position, whether it is writing or not. There is no randomness: the same input draws the same line. Paper. The strip is Length long and loops. With Paper on Transport it moves with the song (1 … 64 bars) and stands still while the transport is stopped; on Free it runs all the time (1 s … 10 min), at Paper Speed . Hold Paper (the input or the button) stops the paper while the pen keeps writing into the same spot; in Transport mode the paper rejoins the song when you let go. The strip keeps 200 points per second (coarser beyond 2 minutes). Changing Length resamples it; a tempo change stretches it with the song. Recording. Record decides when the pen writes: Always: whenever the paper moves. Gate: while the Record input is high. Armed: a rising edge on Record (or the Arm button) arms; writing starts when the paper next comes round to the start, and stops after exactly one pass. The view shows Armed, Writing and Done. Writing replaces what was on the paper. Clear (input or button) wipes the strip and its marks. Mark puts a tick on the paper edge where the pen is. Replay. The replay head reads the strip at Replay Speed : 1× is the paper's own speed, negative runs backwards, 0 parks it. With Replay Sync on Song its position follows the song position (it holds while stopped); on Free it runs on its own and Reset sends it back to the start (to Offset ). Offset is added to the head, so with Replay Speed at 0 it scrubs through the strip. Interpolation reads between points: Step holds each point, Linear draws lines, Smooth draws curves. Unwritten paper reads the last ink before it; an empty strip reads 0. Marker fires whenever the replay head passes a mark, in either direction. Position is the replay head, 0 at the start of the strip and 1 at the end. Drawing. In the view, drag on the paper to draw ink, Shift-drag for one straight line, right-drag to erase and Alt-click to add or remove a mark. Each drag is one undo step. The strip is saved with the board; what the module records is saved too (when recording stops, after each pass and every few seconds while writing). How to use it? A character envelope: an ADSR into In , Writing Speed 30 mm/s, Damping 20 %: Pen is the envelope with momentum, overshoot and ringing. Sticky steps: a slow LFO into In , Friction 70 %: Pen moves in irregular little steps. Record a gesture, play it back: a Dial into In , Record on Armed, press Arm and move the dial for one pass. Replay loops it in time with the song; set Replay Speed to −1 to play it backwards or 0.5 for half speed. A level follower: a drum bus into In , Detector Log dB, Response 100 ms: Replay gives the loop's loudness contour, ready for ducking or filter moves. A scrubbed table: Replay Speed 0 and a modulation source into Offset : the strip becomes a drawn transfer curve. Events from the drawing: Alt-click marks onto the paper and patch Marker into an envelope's trigger. Inside a Voice Cell: every voice has its own pen and replay head; only the first voice records. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Chart Recorder does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Chart Recorder under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Chart Recorder: Backwards Filter A random wander is drawn onto four bars of paper, and the strip is read backwards to sweep a filter over a bass line, so the sweeps are a reversed memory of the pen's line. Set Replay Speed to 1 for the forward path, or draw on the paper yourself. Chart Recorder: Half-Speed Memory Pen and replay run on free paper: the line a random source draws is read back at half speed, so a second voice bends its pitch along a slower, stretched copy of what the first one is doing. Try Replay Speed 2 or Paper Speed to change how the two relate. Chart Recorder: Heavy Pen A square wave goes in, but the sprung pen overshoots and wobbles round every edge, and that ringing line opens and closes a filter on a bass line. Raise Damping to calm the pen, or Friction to make it stick in steps. Chart Recorder: Level Recorder The pen records the loudness of a drum loop, as a level recorder would, and the strip replays at double speed to open a filter on a pad twice as often as the drums hit. Change Detector to Peak or Log dB, or put the Replay Speed back to 1. Chart Recorder: Marked Hits Every half bar the LFO puts a mark on the paper, and the replay head, shifted by Offset, fires a snare each time it passes a mark: a rhythm that runs slightly out of step with the beat. Change Offset to slide the hits, or Replay Speed for another pattern. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Gain −24 … +24 dB 0 dB Response 1 ms – 2 s 50 ms Writing Speed 1 – 1000 mm/s 100 mm/s Damping 0 – 100 % 70 % Friction 0 – 100 % 0 % Paper Speed 0.25 – 4× 1× Replay Speed −4 … +4× +1× Offset 0 – 100 % 0 % Detector DC, Rectified, RMS, Peak, Log dB DC Log Range 10, 25, 50, 75 dB 50 dB Paper Free, Transport Transport Length (Free) 1 s, 2 s, 5 s, 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 5 min, 10 min 10 s Length (Transport) 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 bars 4 bars Record Always, Gate, Armed Gate Replay Sync Free, Song Song Interpolation Step, Linear, Smooth Linear Gain: the input level before the detector. Response: the averaging time of Rectified, RMS and Log dB; the fall time of Peak. Writing Speed: the fastest the pen moves; also its stiffness. Damping: low overshoots and wiggles, high creeps. Friction: how much change it takes to move the pen. Paper Speed: the paper's speed in Free mode (only shown there). Replay Speed: the replay head's speed; negative runs backwards. Offset: shifts the replay head along the strip. Log Range: the span of the paper with the Log dB detector (only shown then). The eight knobs are modulation destinations. The Clear , Arm and Hold Paper buttons act like the inputs (Hold Paper toggles). Inputs Input Signal What it does In control the signal to draw (audio is fine with the level detectors) Record gate writes while high (Gate); a rising edge arms one pass (Armed) Mark trigger puts a mark on the paper at the pen Hold Paper gate stops the paper while high Clear trigger wipes the strip and its marks Reset trigger sends the replay head back to Offset (Replay Sync Free) Outputs Output Signal What it does Pen control the live pen position, writing or not Replay control the strip, read at the replay head Marker trigger a pulse whenever the replay head passes a mark Position control the replay head, 0 … 1 along the strip

title: Envelope Follower
text: Envelope Follower Envelope Follower in the module view Introduction The Envelope Follower turns how loud a signal is into a smooth control signal. Patch a drum loop or a voice in, and the Env output rises with every hit and falls back between them, ready to move a filter, a VCA or anything else. It works on audio and on CV alike: followed CV becomes a slew limiter with separate rise and fall times. For a meter with bars and a clip light use the Level Meter ; the Envelope Follower is the tool when you want the shape of the signal, with your own attack and release. How does it work? The detector looks at the size of each sample. When the signal gets bigger than the current envelope, the envelope rises with the Attack time; when it gets smaller, it falls with the Release time. Times are the time to cover 63 % of the way, as on any one-pole smoother. Short attack and release follow every wave; a short attack with a long release follows the peaks of a drum pattern. Detector picks how the size is measured: Peak follows the absolute value of the signal (or one half of it, see Rectify ): fast and punchy. RMS follows the average power: smoother and closer to how loud the signal sounds. Attack and Release apply to the power, and Rectify has no effect. Gain multiplies the result, so a quiet source can still reach 1. The Gate output opens when Env reaches Threshold and closes again when it falls under 80 % of it, so a hovering level does not chatter. Trigger sends one short pulse every time the gate opens. How to use it? Ducking: a kick into In , Inverted into a VCA's Gain on the pad. A short attack and a release of 150–300 ms gives the pump. Loudness to brightness: Env into a filter's Cutoff . Audio to triggers: a drum loop into In , Trigger into another module's trigger input: it plays on every hit above Threshold . Slew a CV: set Rectify to None (signed) and patch a stepped CV in: Env follows it with Attack going up and Release going down, and Inverted is the same signal upside down. Only the positive part of an LFO: Rectify = Positive . Presets The preset bar of the Envelope Follower view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Smooth Follow General loudness follower for modulation. Fast Peak Snappy peak tracking that catches every hit. Drum Trigger Use the trigger output to fire envelopes from drums. Ducker Use the inverted output to duck a pad under a kick. Slow Swell Slow average level for gentle, musical movement. RMS Level Smooth perceived-loudness meter. Hot Gain Boosts quiet signals to a strong control range. Gate Sense High threshold gate for loud passages only. Low Threshold Gate Gate that opens on almost any signal. Positive Half Follows only positive swings of the input. Signed Follow Passes the signal with smoothing, handy for CV. Long Tail Slowly falling level for lingering effects. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Envelope Follower does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Envelope Follower under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Envelope Follower: Auto Wah A plucked bass line is followed by the Envelope Follower, and the result opens a resonant filter on every note, so the tone speaks with the playing. Try a longer Release for a lazier wah, or more Gain for a wider sweep. Envelope Follower: Kick Ducker The kick drum is followed and its Inverted output closes a VCA on a sustained pad, so the pad ducks on every beat and swells back in between. Lengthen Release for a slower pump, or shorten it for a tight, subtle push. Envelope Follower: Notes Fire Claps The follower listens to a melody and its Trigger output fires a clap every time a note rises above the Threshold, so the drum part is written by the tune. Raise Threshold to skip the softer notes, or change Detector to RMS. Envelope Follower: Drone Swell A slow Attack and long Release turn a sparse drum loop into a gentle level that fades a drone in and out, so the drone breathes with how busy the drums are. Shorten both times to make it follow each hit instead. Envelope Follower: Slewed Pitch With Rectify set to None (signed), the follower becomes a slew limiter: stepped random values glide into one another and bend a voice's pitch. Raise Attack for slow climbs and Release for slow falls, or play with the Gain. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Attack 0 – 2 s 10 ms Release 0 – 5 s 200 ms Gain 0 – 8 × 1 × Threshold 0 – 100 % 30 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Detector Peak, RMS Peak Rectify (Peak only) Full, Positive, Negative, None (signed) Full Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the signal to follow; control signals work as well Outputs Output Signal What it does Env control the followed level times Gain ; with None (signed) it can go negative Inverted control 1 − Env , limited to 0…1; with None (signed) , − Env Gate gate high from Threshold up (closes at 80 % of it) Trigger trigger one sample when the gate opens

title: Pitch Follower
text: Pitch Follower Pitch Follower in the module view Introduction The Pitch Follower listens to one voice or instrument at a time and tells the rest of the board which note it plays. Its Pitch output is a V/oct signal, so it can drive an oscillator, a quantizer or a filter's cutoff; Gate says whether there is a note at all, Confidence how sure the module is, and Env follows how loud the sound is. It is for single notes . Chords and dense mixes have no single pitch, and the output will wander. For loudness alone use the Envelope Follower ; to just look at the pitch and see how far off it is, use the Tuner . How does it work? The module looks for the period of the sound: how long it takes for the wave to repeat. It compares the signal with copies of itself shifted by every period that could be right and takes the first shift for which the two match well. The method is the standard difference-function search from the pitch-detection literature, written for this module (nothing is copied from anywhere). A new result arrives every few milliseconds. How well the shifted copy matches is the confidence . A clean sung vowel scores above 90 %, a breathy sound 60 %, noise 20 %. Only results above the Confidence setting count as a note. Low and High say which pitches to look for. The lower Low is, the longer the stretch of sound the module needs to see, so the slower it answers and the more it costs. Set them around the range of the instrument: raising Low from 60 to 150 Hz halves the delay. Glide slides the output between notes. Short values give steps, long values a portamento. A new note after a pause starts at its own pitch without gliding from the last one. Hold keeps the Gate open for a while after the pitch is lost, so a note survives a gap or a breath. The Pitch output holds its last value for as long as no new note is heard, so a synth that is still sounding does not fall to 0 V. Octave Guard fights the most common mistake of any pitch tracker: jumping an octave (or a twelfth) because of a strong overtone. With the guard on, a jump of more than half an octave is only believed once it has been heard steadily for 30 ms (Light) or 80 ms (Firm). A real octave leap arrives after that short delay; a one-frame mistake never does. Vote takes the median of the last 3, 5, 7 or 9 results: single outliers vanish and the pitch becomes steadier, at the price of a little delay. Env Release is how fast the Env output falls (it rises in 2 ms). How to use it? Voice to synth: Pitch into an oscillator's pitch input and Gate into an envelope. Hum a line and the synth plays it. Use Smooth Glide for a smooth result and Fast and Twitchy to hear every wobble. Harmony: Pitch into a Quantizer so the synth always lands on the scale, or add a fifth with an Attenuverter . Filter that follows the note: Pitch into the cutoff of a filter, so that high notes are brighter. Gate by confidence: Confidence into a VCA's gain: only clear tones pass. No gate, only pitch: if a sound has no pauses leave Hold long, so the gate stays open all the time. Octave trouble? Set Octave Guard to Firm and Vote to 5, or narrow Low and High around the instrument. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Pitch Follower does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Pitch Follower under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Pitch Follower: Voice to Synth Bridge A bright plucked melody is followed note by note, and two soft synth voices play it for you an octave and a fifth lower, each note opened by the follower's Gate. Try Smooth Glide-like values on Glide to slide between the notes, or raise Confidence to hear the bridge hesitate. Pitch Follower: Brightness Follows Note A melody that leaps across two octaves is followed, and its Pitch opens the filter on a held two-note drone: low notes make the drone dark, high notes make it shine. Change the filter's Keytrack to make the effect stronger or gentler. Pitch Follower: Only Clear Tones Pass A source alternates every bar between a clear melody and bursts of noise. The follower's Confidence drops for the noise, so the chime voice it drives plays the tune and falls silent in between. Lower the Confidence knob to let the noise start false notes. Pitch Follower: Guard and Vote A jumpy melody on a sound with a loud second harmonic is the hard case for any pitch tracker. Octave Guard Firm and a Vote of 5 keep the follower on the right note, and a Quantizer tidies it onto the scale for a plucked voice. Set Guard to Off and Vote to Off and listen for octave slips. Pitch Follower: Portamento and Env A slow, legato melody is followed with a long Glide, so the synth slides from note to note like a portamento voice. The Env output opens a filter and the delay mix with each note's loudness. Shorten Glide for steps, or lengthen Env Release for a longer tail. Presets The preset bar of the Pitch Follower view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Voice All-round setting for a singing or speaking voice. Bass Low range for a bass; the firm guard ignores octave mix-ups on heavy low notes. Guitar Plucked strings: a vote of three evens out the first wobbly cycles. Flute and Whistle High and pure sounds with a quick response. Fast and Twitchy No stabilisers and almost no glide: every little movement reaches the output. Smooth Glide Notes slide into each other, a portamento from any voice. Rock Steady A firm guard and a vote of nine: slow to believe, then very stable. Long Hold The gate stays open for a second and a half after the sound stops. Strict Confidence Only clean, clearly pitched sound counts. For dirty input. Loose Tracker Follows rough and breathy sounds, at the price of the odd wrong note. Pad Follower Slow envelope and gate for driving pads and drones from a voice. Deep Range Sub-bass territory; the longest analysis window, so the slowest to answer. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Low 30 – 500 Hz 60 Hz High 200 – 5000 Hz 1500 Hz Glide 0 – 2 s 30 ms Hold 0 – 2 s 250 ms Confidence 30 – 98 % 75 % Vote Off, 3, 5, 7, 9 Off Env Release 5 ms – 2 s 150 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Octave Guard Off, Light, Firm Light Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the sound to follow, one note at a time Outputs Output Signal What it does Pitch pitch the pitch in V/oct, 0 V = middle C; holds while nothing is heard Gate gate high while a note is heard, plus the Hold time Confidence control 0…1, how clear the pitch is Env control the loudness of the input, fast attack, release from Env Release Origin The pitch search is the published difference-function method for monophonic pitch detection (a normalised squared-difference search with an absolute threshold and a parabolic refinement). It was written for this module from the description; no source code was ported.

title: Dual Filter
text: Dual Filter Dual Filter in the module view Introduction The Dual Filter is two multimode filters under one Cutoff . A Spread knob pulls their cutoffs apart, symmetrically around the centre. Routed in series, in parallel or one per stereo channel, the pair becomes a band-pass with two independent edges, a vowel-like two-peak formant filter, a band-reject, or a stereo filter whose left and right sit at different frequencies. One cable on Cutoff moves both filters; one on Spread opens and closes the gap. Use the Multi Filter when you want a particular character (ladders, shelves, phasers). Use the Dual Filter for shapes that need two filters working together. How does it work? Both filters are zero-delay-feedback state-variable filters (12 dB/oct), the same as the Multi Filter's SVF Multimode and SVF Saturating (Rough) . They stay in tune and click-free under fast modulation, even at audio rate. Cutoff is the centre between the two cutoffs. Spread is their distance in octaves: at +2 oct and 1 kHz, filter 1 sits at 500 Hz and filter 2 at 2 kHz. Negative Spread puts filter 2 below filter 1. Both work in octaves, so modulation sounds even across the range. Res 1 , Res 2 set each filter's resonance (Q 0.5 to 25, the Multi Filter's curve). Mode 1 , Mode 2 morph each response: LP → BP → HP → Notch. Routing decides how the two work together: Serial in ─► F1 ─► F2 ─► out (Balance > 0 lets part of F1 bypass F2) Parallel in ─► F1 + F2 ─► out (Balance: level of F1 vs F2) Parallel (inv.) in ─► F1 − F2 ─► out Stereo in L ─► F1 ─► out L, in R ─► F2 ─► out R Changing the routing crossfades over 10 ms, so it's safe while playing. Link ties the modes together. Same : Mode 2 becomes an offset from Mode 1 (at LP, both filters have the same response), so one cable on Mode 1 morphs both. Mirror : filter 2 moves the opposite way (Mode 1 LP → Notch makes filter 2 go Notch → LP), plus the Mode 2 offset. Character : Clean never self-oscillates; Saturating growls when driven and with high resonance. In Serial, the saturation of filter 1 shapes what filter 2 sees, like an overdriven two-stage filter. Drive saturates the input (tanh) before the filters. Key Track moves both cutoffs with the Pitch input. Mix blends the dry input back in. Two resonant peaks at the same frequency in series could get very loud. In Clean Serial, filter 2's input is turned down while the cutoffs are within a semitone of each other (back to full over the next octave of Spread), and every output passes a soft limiter that is linear up to ±2 and never exceeds ±8. The view draws each filter's response (thin) and the result of the routing (bright; in Stereo, left and right). Drag the centre marker for Cutoff , the f1 and f2 markers for Spread (hold Alt to move only that cutoff), and drag a marker up or down for that filter's resonance. How to use it? Wide band-pass with two edges: Serial, Mode 1 HP, Mode 2 LP, Spread +2 oct. Each edge has its own resonance; Cutoff moves the band, Spread sets its width. Steep low-pass: Serial, both LP, Spread 0: 24 dB/oct with two coinciding resonance peaks. Vowels / formants: Parallel, both BP, Spread around +1.5 oct, Res 60–80 %. Modulate Spread (and Cutoff a little) to change the vowel. Band-reject with steep sides: Parallel (F2 inverted), both BP. Band-pass from two low-passes: Parallel (F2 inverted), both LP: what lies between the two cutoffs. Stereo filter: Stereo routing with a mono source on In L . Spread places the left and right cutoffs apart; an LFO on Spread makes the stereo image breathe. One-knob morph: Serial, Link Mirror, sweep Mode 1 : from two low-passes through band-pass to two notches. Separate processing: take F1 Out and F2 Out to different effects. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Dual Filter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Dual Filter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Dual Filter: Vowel Talker A buzzy saw drone goes through two band-pass filters pulled apart by Spread, which an LFO moves back and forth: the pair of peaks sounds like a vowel changing from 'oo' to 'ah' and back. Change Spread for a different mouth shape, or the Cutoff for a different voice. Dual Filter: Serial Squelch In Serial routing the two filters stack into a steep, resonant low-pass that an envelope snaps open on every note. Raise Spread to make the second stage cut lower or higher than the first, or set Character to Saturating for more grit. Dual Filter: Stereo Split Arp Stereo routing sends the left channel through one filter and the right through the other, with Spread putting their cutoffs apart: a busy arpeggio ends up with a dark side and a bright side, which an LFO swaps over time. Try Link set to Mirror or a negative Spread. Dual Filter: Hollow Pad Parallel (F2 inverted) combines a low-pass and an inverted copy, carving a moving hole out of a wide chord. Move Cutoff slowly to sweep the gap, or change Balance to favour one side. Dual Filter: Drum Crush A drum loop runs through a driven Dual Filter in Serial mode with Mode 1 and Mode 2 at opposite ends, so lows and highs are both trimmed into a narrow band that opens with a slow LFO. Turn up Drive or Mix to push it harder. Presets The preset bar of the Dual Filter view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Warm Serial LP Two low-passes in a row: a steep, smooth roll-off. Wide Band-Pass High-pass into low-pass: an adjustable band you widen with Spread. Formant Pair Two resonant band-passes side by side, like vowel formants. Vowel Sweep Sweep Cutoff with an LFO for a talking vowel movement. Stereo Split Left and right get different cutoffs for a wide, shifting image. Phase Notch Inverted parallel sum: moving, hollow notches. Dark Pad Filter Closed, soft low-pass to tuck a pad behind a mix. Thin Radio Lo-fi band-limited voice. Mirror Morph Linked modes move opposite ways: sweep Mode 1 to morph. Resonant Bass Round, resonant low end with a bit of drive. Acid Twin Squelchy two-stage low-pass; envelope on Cutoff. Crossed Filters Negative spread swaps the filters: low-pass above, high-pass below. Ringing Pair Highly resonant pings: pluck or noise input rings like a bell. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 1 kHz Spread −5 … +5 oct +1 oct Res 1, Res 2 0 – 100 % 20 % Mode 1, Mode 2 LP → BP → HP → Notch LP Balance −100 … +100 % 0 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Key Track 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Routing Serial, Parallel, Parallel (F2 inverted), Stereo Serial Link Off, Same, Mirror Off Character Clean, Saturating Clean Cutoff: the centre, exponential over ten octaves; 10 % of modulation ≈ one octave. f1 = Cutoff × 2^(−Spread/2), f2 = Cutoff × 2^(+Spread/2), each kept between 5 Hz and just below half the sample rate. Spread: distance between the cutoffs in octaves. Res 1 / Res 2: resonance of each filter. Mode 1 / Mode 2: each filter's response. With Link on, Mode 2 is an offset (shown as Mode 2 Offset ). Balance: Serial: the share of filter 1 that bypasses filter 2 (0 to 100 %; negative values do nothing extra). Parallel: the level of filter 1 (negative) vs filter 2 (positive). Stereo: a left/right balance. Drive: tanh saturation before the filters. Key Track: how far Pitch moves both cutoffs (100 % = one octave per octave). Mix: dry/wet. Routing, Link, Character: see above. Not modulatable. Changing Character starts the filters from silence. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct moves both cutoffs, scaled by Key Track Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the routed result, after Balance and Mix F1 Out audio filter 1 alone, mono (Stereo: the left channel's filter) F2 Out audio filter 2 alone, mono (Serial: after filter 1; Stereo: the right channel's filter) Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on Out (5 ms attack, 120 ms release)

title: Filter Bank
text: Filter Bank Filter Bank in the module view Introduction The Filter Bank splits a sound into ten bands with fixed band-pass filters. Each band has its own level, its own audio output and its own envelope output. Shape the spectrum by hand or with modulation (a Tilt knob, an odd/even balance, a window that scans across the bands), send single bands to different effects, or let the envelopes make other sounds follow this one's spectrum. With a voice on the Sidechain input and the Vocode knob up, it's a ten-band vocoder. How does it work? Ten band-pass filters (zero-delay-feedback state-variable filters) sit on fixed frequencies. Each has unit gain at its centre: a sine on a band's frequency comes out of that band at the level it went in. Tuning sets the frequencies: Spectral: spread evenly in octaves from 55 Hz to 14 kHz (55, 102, 188, 349, 645, 1194, 2209, 4088, 7565, 14000 Hz): the classic fixed filter bank. Harmonic: the first ten partials of a note, 65.4 Hz (C2) × 1 … 10, transposed by the Pitch input: a resonant bank that plays in tune. Scale: ten consecutive notes of Scale from Root in octave 2, transposed by Pitch (snapped to the scale): a chord-like resonator. Shift moves all bands together (±2 octaves). Spacing stretches or squeezes them around the middle (between bands 5 and 6). Both work in octaves, so an LFO on Shift sweeps the whole bank like a phaser. Bands pushed above the top of the audio band are muted. Q sets how narrow every band is. The default (2.2) gives an almost flat sum: with all levels at 0 dB the bank sounds like the input. Higher values make the bands ring (great in Harmonic and Scale tuning). Slope 24 dB/oct uses two filter sections per band: steeper bands and an even flatter sum (every other band is polarity-inverted, as in a crossover, so the overlaps add up). Edge Bands Low-pass/High-pass lets band 1 also carry everything below it and band 10 everything above it, so the bank covers the whole spectrum. The gain of each band is the product of: Level (−60 dB = silent … +12 dB; 0 dB at 75 % of the knob), Tilt (dB per octave around 1 kHz: positive is brighter), Odd/Even (−100 %: only odd bands, +100 %: only even bands), the Scan window: a window Width bands wide, centred on band 1 + 9 × Scan , with soft edges. At Width 10 the window is off; with Width 1, sweeping Scan plays one band after the other, Vocode (below). Gains glide over 5 ms, so even fast modulation doesn't click. Envelopes. Each band has an envelope follower ( Attack , Release ) fed by the band's signal before its gain, so the envelopes describe the source and don't change when you turn levels. Env From picks the source: the input, or the Sidechain signal through its own ten filters. A full-scale sine in one band reads about 1. Vocode multiplies each band by its envelope: at 100 % a band is as loud as the matching band of the sidechain (×4, up to +12 dB); lower values blend the unvocoded sound back in. With Env From = Input , it works as a per-band expander (loud bands get louder). Stereo. The filters run per channel. With Stereo = Odd/Even split , Sum L carries the odd bands and Sum R the even bands: a spectral widener for mono sources. The Band , Odd and Even outputs are mono. Jacks chooses which of the many outputs the node shows: just the sums, also the ten band outputs, also the ten envelopes, or the envelopes only. Hidden jacks keep their cables. Bands that are silent and whose outputs are not patched cost nothing. The view shows the ten levels as sliders (drag across them to draw a curve, double-click a band for 0 dB), the effective gain of each band as an outline, the live envelopes below, and the band frequencies (or note names). The Presets menu sets all ten levels at once: Flat , Smile , Telephone , Odd only , Comb . How to use it? Spectral EQ: draw a curve on the sliders, or use Tilt for a quick brighter/darker. Vocoder: a voice (audio input port) into Sidechain , a bright synth (saw chords, noise) into In L , Env From = Sidechain, Vocode 100 %. Attack 2–5 ms, Release 50–150 ms. Try Slope 24 dB/oct for clearer words. Scanning filter: Width 2, an LFO or a sequencer on Scan . Phaser-like sweep: an LFO on Shift , some Q . Resonator: Tuning Harmonic or Scale , Q 15–30, noise or drums in, Voice In Pitch into Pitch : the bank rings in tune. Stereo widening: a mono pad in, Stereo = Odd/Even split. Multiband effects: Jacks = Bands, send Band 1–3 to a distortion and the rest elsewhere. Spectral follower: Jacks = Envs, Env 2 onto a kick-related modulation, Env 8 onto hi-hat-related ones. Vocoder with cables: two banks, Env k of the first into Level k of the second (levels at 0, amount 100 %). Swap cables to shift formants. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Filter Bank does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Filter Bank under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Filter Bank: Drum Vocoder A held saw chord goes into the bank while a drum loop drives the Sidechain: with Vocode up, each band opens only when the drums have energy in that range, so the chord chatters in the rhythm of the beat. Change Vocode, Release or Q to tighten or smear it. Filter Bank: Scanning Window A bright, buzzy drone passes through only a few neighbouring bands; an LFO on Scan slides that window up and down the spectrum like a slow wah. Widen Width for a fuller sound, or raise Q for whistling. Filter Bank: Noise Chimes Plain noise goes into ten very narrow bands tuned to a minor pentatonic scale (Tuning set to Scale), so it rings as a soft, wind-like chord. Change Root or Scale, move Shift to transpose the whole set, or lower Q to lose the pitch. Filter Bank: Odd-Even Stereo Odd bands go left and even bands go right, so one saw arpeggio is pulled apart into two interlocking halves. Swing Odd/Even with the LFO and the sound moves between the speakers; set Stereo to Normal to hear it fold back to the middle. Filter Bank: Band Split Mixer Jacks is set to Bands: four of the ten band outputs go to their own mixer channels, panned from left to right, so the low end of a drum-and-bass loop sits in the middle and brighter bands spread out. Change the mixer levels to rebalance the spectrum, or tilt the bank with Tilt. Presets The preset bar of the Filter Bank view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Flat Bank All ten bands at unity: a transparent starting point. Warm Tilt Tilts the spectrum darker. Bright Tilt Tilts the spectrum brighter. Scooped Mids Classic smile curve: mids pulled down. Telephone Bands Only the speech range survives. Odd Harmonics Only odd bands: hollow, clarinet-like colour. Even Harmonics Only even bands: octave-ish, reedy colour. Scanning Window Two-band window: sweep Scan with an LFO or sequencer. Single Band Pinger One band at a time: sequence Scan for a melodic filter. Phaser Sweep Modulate Shift with an LFO to slide the bands like a phaser. Harmonic Comb Bands on harmonics of the pitch input: resonant comb tones. Scale Chimes Bands snapped to a scale: noise and pads ring with chords. Robot Vocoder Patch a voice into the sidechain and a buzzy synth into the input. Soft Vocoder Smoother vocoder for pads and choirs. Stretched Bands Wider band spacing: inharmonic, metallic resonances. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1 … 10 −60 (silent) … +12 dB 0 dB Q 0.5 – 30 2.2 Tilt −6 … +6 dB/oct 0 Odd/Even −100 … +100 % 0 % Scan 0 – 100 % 50 % Width 1 – 10 bands 10 Shift −2 … +2 oct 0 Spacing 50 – 200 % 100 % Attack 0.5 – 100 ms 3 ms Release 5 ms – 2 s 80 ms Vocode 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Tuning Spectral, Harmonic, Scale Spectral Root C … B C Scale the Step Sequencer's scales Minor Pentatonic Slope 12 dB/oct, 24 dB/oct 12 dB/oct Edge Bands Band-pass, Low-pass/High-pass Low-pass/High-pass Env From Input, Sidechain Input Stereo Normal, Odd/Even split Normal Jacks Sums, Bands, Bands + Envs, Envs Sums Level k: the gain of band k. Q: the sharpness of every band. Low values blur the bands into each other; high values ring. Tilt: spectral slope around 1 kHz. Odd/Even: fades out the even (negative) or odd (positive) bands. Scan / Width: the window over the bands. Shift / Spacing: move and stretch the band frequencies, in octaves. Attack / Release: the envelope followers' times. Vocode: how much the envelopes multiply the band gains. Mix: dry ↔ bank for Sum L/R . Root / Scale: only in Scale tuning. The settings are not modulatable; all knobs are modulation destinations, including the ten levels. Gains and frequencies update every 8 samples and glide in between. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Sidechain audio analysis input for the envelopes when Env From = Sidechain (the voice in a vocoder) Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct transposes the bands in Harmonic and Scale tuning (shown only there) Outputs Output Signal What it does Sum L, Sum R audio all bands after their gains, plus the dry signal per Mix Odd audio bands 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, mono Even audio bands 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, mono Band 1 … 10 audio each band alone, mono, after its gain (shown with Jacks = Bands or Bands + Envs) Env 1 … 10 control, 0 – 1 each band's envelope (shown with Jacks = Bands + Envs or Envs) All audio outputs pass a soft limiter (linear up to ±2, never beyond ±8): +12 dB levels, steep tilt and vocoding can stack up.

title: Low Pass Gate
text: Low Pass Gate Low Pass Gate in the module view Introduction A low pass gate is a filter and an amplifier in one, opened by light. Inside sits a model of a vactrol : a lamp shining on a light-sensitive resistor. When the light comes on, the gate opens almost at once. When it goes out, the gate closes slowly and unevenly, getting darker as it gets quieter. That is how struck and plucked things die away, so one trigger at Ping gives a natural, organic pluck without any envelope. It is stereo and cheap, and its Active output makes it a good last stage in every voice of a Voice Cell. How does it work? The light is Level plus the CV input (together clipped to 0 – 100 %), plus a short flash from every Ping . The cell follows the light: Opening is fast: a few milliseconds. Closing is slow, and it gets slower as the cell darkens. The first half of the decay goes quickly, the quiet tail lingers. Memory: after a long, bright gate the cell closes more slowly than after a short ping, as a real photoresistor does. The cell's openness (shown on the Light output) drives a low-pass filter and a gain together. As the gate closes, the sound gets both quieter and darker. The cutoff rises quickly at the start of a pluck and lingers in the low range as it fades. A Ping is a 2 ms flash of light. A full ping with the Classic cell opens the gate to about half and fades to silence (−60 dB) in about 0.6 s. A ping on a gate that is still open adds to it instead of restarting it, so fast rolls swell like a real struck object. How to use it? Pluck: Oscillator → In L ; a trigger (a sequencer, a clock) → Ping . Out L/R to the output. Turn Response to make the plucks shorter or longer. In a Voice Cell: Voice In › Trigger → Ping , Voice In › Velocity → Velocity , Out L/R → Voice Out , and Active → Voice Out › Active . The cell then frees each voice exactly when its pluck has faded. Held notes: also patch Voice In › Gate → CV . The gate opens the cell, and the release is the cell's own slow fall. Envelope for other modules: Light is a ready-made pluck envelope: patch it onto a wavefolder's fold or a filter's cutoff so louder plucks are brighter, too. Ping button: fires a manual ping, for trying out Response and Cell . Demo patches Five whole patches show what Low Pass Gate does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Low Pass Gate under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Low Pass Gate: Wooden Pluck A bright saw is silent until each sequencer trigger pings the gate: it snaps open and then darkens as it closes, like a plucked string. Raise Response for longer notes, Ping for harder hits, or switch Cell to Fast. Low Pass Gate: Skin Drums Low, sine-like tones pinged by the drum grid through the Fast cell sound like tuned skin drums, with a short, sharp attack and a quick roll-off. Try Resonance for a ringing pitch, or change Response to tighten or loosen the hits. Low Pass Gate: Slow Breath With the Slow memory cell and a slow LFO on the CV input, the gate opens and closes like breathing over a held two-voice chord, getting brighter as it swells. Change the LFO rate or the Response to alter the pace. Low Pass Gate: Filter Mode Bass Mode is set to LP, so the gate only acts as a filter on a steady buzzing bass: every ping opens the cutoff and it dulls again, while a Level of about a quarter keeps the note audible between hits. Switch Mode to VCA to hear only the volume change. Low Pass Gate: Leaky Marimba A softly pinged triangle wave with some Bleed lets a little signal through even when the gate is shut, so each note sits on a quiet bed of sound. Raise Bleed to blur the gaps, or lower Brightness for a more muffled wooden tone. Presets The preset bar of the Low Pass Gate view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Classic Pluck Ping it with a trigger for a natural, darkening pluck. Short Blip Tight, percussive blips for rhythmic lines. Bongo Tone Short resonant knock: good on sine and triangle. Soft Mallet Rounded, mellow hit. Long Decay Slow, ringing close with a long dark tail. Dark Pad Gate Slow swells and fades from a CV. Filter Only Just the low-pass: a vactrol-style filter on a steady tone. VCA Only Just the amplitude gate with vactrol smoothing. Resonant Ping Resonance gives the pluck a vocal, ringing pitch. Driven Hit Saturated, punchy attack. Leaky Gate Never fully closes: a muffled signal always leaks through. Open Bright Mostly open and bright, nudged by CV. Slow Memory Pluck The vactrol remembers earlier hits, so fast repeats bloom. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 0 – 100 % 0 % Response 0 – 100 % 50 % Ping 0 – 100 % 80 % Resonance 0 – 100 % 0 % Brightness 0 – 100 % 75 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Bleed 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode LP, VCA, Both Both Cell Fast, Classic, Slow memory Classic Level: constant light, added to CV . At 0 % the gate is closed until something opens it; at 100 % it is fully open. Response: the speed of the cell. Every time constant is scaled from 0.25× (0 %, snappy) through 1× (50 %) to 4× (100 %, slow and ringing). Ping: the strength of the flash on each Ping pulse (times Velocity ). Resonance: emphasis at the cutoff (Q 0.5 – 6), in LP and Both . Both turns the level down a little as the resonance rises. Brightness: the cutoff when fully open, 1 kHz – 20 kHz. Drive: soft saturation of the input before the gate, for warmth on loud plucks. It is anti-aliased, so it stays clean on high notes. Bleed: how much the closed gate leaks. At 100 % the dark state still passes a muffled −24 dB. Mode: LP: only the filter. Closed, it still passes the lowest bass (30 Hz). VCA: only the amplifier, no change in tone. Both: filter and amplifier together: the classic low pass gate. Cell: the character of the vactrol. Fast is short and snappy, Classic is the familiar bright-then-dark pluck, Slow memory has long, lingering tails that grow after long notes. Every knob is a modulation destination: patch a cable onto it to move it. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is unpatched In R audio right input CV control, 0 – 1 the light driving the cell, added to Level Ping trigger a short flash of light: a pluck Velocity control, 0 – 1 scales the next ping; unpatched counts as 1 Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the gated signal Light control, 0 – 1 the cell's openness: a pluck envelope for other modules Active gate high while the cell is open or the output is still audible; falls 50 ms after it goes quiet

title: Multi Filter
text: Multi Filter Multi Filter in the module view Introduction The Multi Filter shapes the tone of a sound by removing or emphasising frequencies. It's stereo and offers 32 filter algorithms, from clean state-variable and ladder filters to shelves, phasers and a flanger, and on to a Sallen-Key filter with a hard wall, a vowel filter, a tuned comb and a staircase of 1-pole sections. Most of them have a low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch response that you can morph between continuously. It comes with drive and key tracking. An envelope output tells the rest of the patch how loud the filtered signal is. How does it work? The algorithms follow Vadim Zavalishin's book The Art of VA Filter Design . They are "zero-delay feedback" models of analog circuits: they stay in tune up to high frequencies and stay click-free under fast modulation, even at audio rate. Type picks the algorithm; the dropdown groups them by family. Cutoff sets where the filter acts. The knob is exponential: 20 Hz at the bottom, 20 kHz at the top, about ten octaves in total. Modulation therefore works in octaves: a cable at 10 % moves the cutoff by about one octave, whatever the cutoff is. Resonance boosts the frequencies around the cutoff. On the ladder and allpass types it's the feedback amount; some types self-oscillate near the top (see the table). Drive saturates the input before the filter (a soft tanh curve) for warmth and grit. The saturating types add their own distortion on top. Mode is a dropdown that picks the response on the multimode types: Low-pass, Band-pass, High-pass or Notch. A cable into it steps through the four. On the phasers and the flanger it does something else (see below). Gain sets the boost or cut of the shelving types, in dB. On the vowel filter it stretches or squeezes the spacing of the formants. Vowel (only shown for the vowel filter) moves through A, E, I, O, U. Damping (only shown for the comb types) dulls the loop, so the upper peaks die away. Slope (only shown for the staircase types) sets the steepness, 6 to 48 dB per octave. Key Track moves the cutoff with the Pitch input, so high notes are as bright as low ones. Mix blends the dry input with the filtered signal. The algorithms State Variable (12 dB/oct) — the all-round filter: smooth, clean, every response at once. Type What it is Mode Gain SVF Multimode LP / BP / HP / notch morph ✓ SVF Bandpass (unit gain) band-pass with 0 dB at the cutoff, whatever the resonance; resonance makes the band narrower SVF Band Shelf boosts or cuts a band around the cutoff; resonance narrows it ✓ SVF Peaking low-pass minus high-pass: a resonant peak with full bass and treble SVF Allpass flat level, phase turns around the cutoff (resonance makes the turn steeper) 1-Pole (6 dB/oct) — gentle tone shaping. Resonance has no effect. Type What it is Gain 1-Pole Low-pass / High-pass the softest possible slopes 1-Pole Allpass flat level, 180° phase turn 1-Pole Low Shelf / High Shelf tilt the lows or highs by Gain ; Cutoff is the middle of the slope ✓ Transistor Ladder (24 dB/oct) — four low-passes in a feedback loop: the classic fat, steep synth filter. Mode morphs LP → BP → HP → notch, all built from the ladder's taps. In low-pass mode the input is boosted with the resonance, so the bass doesn't thin out. Type What it is Self-oscillates Ladder Linear the clean, ideal ladder no (stops just short) Ladder Feedback HP a high-pass at 250 Hz in the feedback: no resonance below it, full bass at any resonance no Ladder Tanh a tanh saturator at the feedback point: warm overdrive, bounded self-oscillation above ~80 % Ladder Hyperbolic the same with a softer x / (1 + abs x) saturator: rounder, quieter oscillation above ~80 % Ladder Nonlinear Stages every stage saturates, like the real circuit: the cutoff sags on loud signals above ~80 % Diode Ladder (24 dB/oct) — the coupled stages of a diode ladder give a squelchier, less predictable resonance than the transistor ladder. Low-pass only ( Mode has no effect). Type What it is Self-oscillates Diode Ladder Linear the clean model no Diode Ladder Tanh with a saturator at the feedback point above ~80 % Allpass Effects — the dry signal plus allpass-filtered copies: notches and peaks that move with Cutoff . Patch a slow Function onto Cutoff for the classic sweep. Resonance is feedback (sharper peaks). Set Mix to 100 %: the dry signal is already part of the effect. Type What it is Mode Phaser 1-Pole ×4 four 1-pole allpasses: two notches, around 0.4× and 2.4× the cutoff below 50 %: normal; from 50 %: inverted (peaks and notches swap) Phaser 2-Pole ×2 two 2-pole allpasses: two notches whose spacing you set notch spacing: wide at 0 %, close at 100 % Flanger a short delay of 1 / Cutoff (20 Hz = 50 ms, 1 kHz = 1 ms): a comb of evenly spaced notches as the 1-pole phaser Classic Digital — the textbook digital filters the book improves on, kept for comparison and for their sound. Type What it is Naive 1-Pole Low-pass the simplest digital low-pass; above a few kHz the cutoff no longer tracks and it opens fully Biquad (Direct Form I) the classic biquad of the SVF multimode ( Mode works); same sound when static, but fast cutoff modulation at high resonance can make it misbehave (a safety limit keeps it bounded) Nonlinear State Variable (12 dB/oct) — the SVF with saturation inside. Mode morphs LP → BP → HP → notch. Type What it is SVF Atanh Damping the damping grows on loud signals: resonance that compresses itself, bounded self-oscillation at the top SVF Hyperbolic Damping the same with a harder-acting curve: gentler, quieter oscillation SVF Saturating (Rough) saturating integrators: growls when driven, gritty and bounded. Drives harder than the others at the same Drive Sallen-Key (12 dB/oct) — a two-pole filter modelled on the Sallen-Key topology: two resistors, two capacitors and an amplifier whose gain sets the resonance. Resonance raises that gain towards the edge of self-oscillation (a peak of Q = 1/(3 − gain)). The twist here: the amplifier clips against a hard-knee wall, so quiet signals ring cleanly but the resonance bites as soon as it hits the wall, and at 100 % the filter holds a bounded, self-sustaining tone. Mode has no effect. Type What it is Sallen-Key Low-pass 12 dB/oct, half level at the cutoff when Resonance is 0 Sallen-Key High-pass the mirrored topology Formant Type What it is Vowel A-E-I-O-U four parallel resonators placed like the first four formants of a voice. Vowel morphs A → E → I → O → U (the positions move smoothly, in pitch and level). Cutoff is the size of the throat: 2 kHz leaves the formants where they are, an octave up makes a smaller mouth, an octave down a larger one. Resonance narrows them (low: breathy, high: ringing). Gain stretches (+) or squeezes (−) the spacing of the formants. Mode has no effect. Feed it a bright, harmonic source: a saw or a pulse Tuned Comb — a delay line fed back on itself, tuned by the Cutoff : the peaks sit at the cutoff frequency and its multiples. Patch Voice In Pitch into Pitch with Key Track at 100 % and it plays in tune, like a string or a pipe. Resonance is the feedback (0 – 98.5 %); the output is scaled so the peaks stay at unity. Damping lowers the cutoff of a low-pass inside the loop, so highs die faster, like a plucked string. Set Mix to 100 %. Type What it is Comb Positive positive feedback: peaks at 1×, 2×, 3× … the cutoff, a full harmonic ring Comb Negative negative feedback: peaks at 1×, 3×, 5× … the cutoff, hollow like a closed pipe. The cutoff is still the pitch you hear Staircase — a cascade of 1-pole sections, 1 to 8 of them ( Slope : 6, 12, … 48 dB/oct). The cutoff is always the −3 dB point, whatever the slope. Resonance is not a feedback here but the spread : at 0 % all sections share the cutoff (the steepest, tightest corner), at higher values their corners fan out up to an octave apart, so the slope builds up step by step from the cutoff and the shoulder softens. No resonant peak. Type What it is Staircase Low-pass the cascade of low-passes Staircase High-pass the cascade of high-passes The Env output follows the level of the filtered signal (fast 5 ms attack, 120 ms release). The view shows the filter's response curve for the selected type. It is drawn from the modulated values, so you can see it move. For the saturating types it shows the quiet-signal (linear) response. How to use it? Subtractive synth: Oscillator Out → Filter In L → VCA. Start with SVF Multimode or Ladder Tanh , Mode at LP, Cutoff around 1 kHz and some Resonance . Self-oscillating sine: pick Ladder Tanh or SVF Atanh Damping , turn Resonance to 100 %, patch Voice In Pitch into Pitch with Key Track at 100 %. The filter rings at the cutoff and plays in tune. Phaser / flanger: pick a type from Allpass Effects , Mix at 100 %, some Resonance , and a slow Function on Cutoff . EQ: a 1-Pole Low Shelf or High Shelf with Gain tilts a track's tone; SVF Band Shelf boosts or cuts a band. Filter envelope: patch an ADSR's Env onto Cutoff . The cable amount sets how many octaves the envelope opens: 30 % ≈ 3 octaves. Key tracking: patch Voice In Pitch into Pitch and set Key Track to 100 %. The cutoff then follows the keyboard one octave per octave. Talking pad: Vowel A-E-I-O-U , a saw chord in, a slow Random or an LFO onto Vowel ; Resonance around 30 %. Plucked string from noise: Comb Positive , Mix 100 %, Resonance 90 %, Damping 50 %, a short noise burst in, Pitch patched with Key Track at 100 %. Squealing resonance: Sallen-Key Low-pass with Resonance at 85 – 100 % and an envelope on Cutoff ; the wall keeps it bounded. Filter sweeps: patch a slow Function or Random onto Cutoff , or onto Mode for a sweep from low-pass to high-pass. Process a track: route a track's audio onto the board with an input port, through the filter, and back out with an output port. Sidechain-style movement: patch Env onto another module, e.g. a pad's cutoff or a VCA's gain with a negative amount, so it reacts to this signal. Presets The preset bar of the Filter view has 20 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Warm Low-Pass Gentle, round low-pass for taking the fizz off a saw. Dark Room A soft 6 dB slope that darkens everything without a peak. Ladder Bass Fat ladder low-pass with some bite from the resonance. Acid Squelch Screaming diode ladder: sweep the cutoff and add an envelope. Self-Oscillating Ladder Resonance at the top makes the ladder ring as a sine; play it with Key Track. Telephone Narrow band-pass: a thin, nasal voice. Thin Air High-pass that leaves just the sparkle. Rumble Cut Clears out the sub-bass below 90 Hz. Notch Sweep A notch you can sweep for a hollow, phasing colour. Vocal Peak A resonant peak with the lows and highs still intact. Presence Boost Lifts the upper mids by 6 dB. Bass Shelf Adds weight under 200 Hz. Air Shelf A little air on top. Slow Phaser Notches that sound best when you modulate the cutoff with an LFO. Jet Flanger Comb filtering: sweep the cutoff slowly for a jet sound. Gritty Drive Overdriven, saturating state-variable filter. Wall Squeal A two-pole low-pass whose resonance rings clean, then bites against the wall when pushed. Vowel Mouth Four formants: sweep Vowel from A to U, or move Cutoff to change the size of the throat. Hollow Tube A tuned comb with negative feedback: only the odd harmonics ring, like a closed pipe. Terraced Lows Six 1-pole sections with staggered corners: a steep, stepped slope without a resonant peak. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Filter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Filter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Multi Filter: Ladder Bass Sweep A raw saw bass runs through a warm ladder-style low-pass whose Cutoff is opened by an envelope on every note, then closes again for a classic squelch. Raise Resonance or Drive for more bite, or switch Type to another ladder. Multi Filter: Phaser Pad The Type is set to a four-stage phaser: a slow LFO sweeps Cutoff through a held, slightly detuned saw chord so the notches drift up and down. Try the 2-Pole phaser, more Resonance, or a faster LFO. Multi Filter: Telephone Drums A whole drum loop goes through the unit-gain band-pass type while an LFO sweeps Cutoff: the beat shrinks to a thin radio sound, then opens up again. Move Mix to blend the original back in, or lower Resonance for a wider band. Multi Filter: Key-Tracked Pluck The sequencer's pitch also goes into the filter, and Key Track at full makes Cutoff follow every note, so high and low notes keep the same brightness. Lower Key Track to hear the low notes go dull, or move Mode to morph from low-pass to high-pass. Multi Filter: Flanger Jet Type is the flanger algorithm: a long single note rings through a sweeping comb of resonances that rise and fall with a slow LFO on Cutoff. Push Resonance for a metallic jet sound, or pull Mix back for a gentle swirl. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 2 kHz Resonance 0 – 100 % 20 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Mode LP · BP · HP · Notch (dropdown) LP Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Key Track 0 – 100 % 0 % Gain −24 – +24 dB 0 dB Vowel A · E · I · O · U (only with the vowel filter) A Damping 0 – 100 % (only with the comb types) 30 % Slope 6 dB – 48 dB, in steps of 6 (only with the staircase types) 24 dB Type 32 algorithms in 11 groups SVF Multimode Cutoff: the corner (LP, HP) or centre (BP, notch) frequency. Exponential over ten octaves; 10 % of modulation ≈ one octave. Resonance: emphasis at the cutoff (Q from 0.5 to 25 on the SVF types, feedback on the ladders, phasers and flanger). Low values are smooth; high values ring and whistle. Self-oscillating types sing on their own near the top. No effect on the 1-pole types. Drive: how hard the input is saturated before filtering. At 0 % the signal is untouched. Turn down the source level if you want drive without much extra loudness. Drive and the filter run at four times the sample rate, so even hard drive and the saturating types stay clean, without the harsh, out-of-tune overtones of aliasing. Mode: the response, morphed continuously: 0 % low-pass (removes highs), 33 % band-pass (keeps a band around the cutoff), 67 % high-pass (removes lows), 100 % notch (removes a band). Applies to SVF Multimode , the transistor ladders, the biquad and the nonlinear SVFs. On Phaser 1-Pole ×4 and Flanger it flips the effect's polarity at 50 %; on Phaser 2-Pole ×2 it sets the notch spacing. Gain: boost or cut of 1-Pole Low Shelf , 1-Pole High Shelf and SVF Band Shelf ; the formant spacing of Vowel A-E-I-O-U (±24 dB = ±50 % spacing). No effect on the other types. Resonance on the new types: the amplifier gain of the Sallen-Key (Q up to ∞), the formant bandwidth of the vowel filter (10× narrower at the top), the feedback of the comb (up to ±98.5 %), the corner spread of the staircase (up to 1 octave per section). Mix: dry/wet. 100 % is only the filter; lower values mix the unfiltered input back in. The response curve shows the result. Key Track: how far the cutoff follows the Pitch input. At 100 % the cutoff moves one octave per octave of pitch; at 50 %, half an octave. No effect when Pitch is unpatched. Type: the filter algorithm (see above). Not modulatable. Switching type starts the new algorithm from silence. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct moves the cutoff, scaled by Key Track Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio filtered left channel Out R audio filtered right channel Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on the filtered output The outputs lag the inputs by 71 samples (about 1.5 ms at 48 kHz), the cost of oversampling. The dry signal of Mix lags by the same amount, so the two stay in phase.

title: Wave Analyzer
text: Wave Analyzer Introduction Wave Analyzer is a very narrow band-pass that you tune like an old lab receiver. Turn the big dial and the single partials of a sound come out one by one. Let it sweep and it draws the spectrum on its plotter while it plays a melody of partials. Let it lock and it hunts for the strongest partial in a window and follows it. The imperfections are part of the sound: the filter rings when it moves, the oscillator drifts, and the lock loop springs and wobbles before it settles. How does it work? Tuning. The analyser listens at one frequency, the tuned frequency: the Frequency dial (or the sweep, or the lock loop) with Pitch added in octaves and a little Drift . Bandwidth sets how wide it listens: 3 Hz picks out a single partial even high up, 100 Hz lets neighbours through, 1/3 octave grows with the frequency like a graphic-EQ band. The skirts are steep (24 dB per octave on each side). Band is the isolated partial at its own pitch. Shifted is the same partial moved to the Listen frequency: every partial you tune to is heard at the same pitch, and a partial slightly off the dial is heard slightly off Listen , so vibrato and drift become small bends. At wide bandwidths neighbouring partials beat against each other, and it whistles and talks. Isolated partials are quiet: Gain (+12 dB by default) lifts both outputs, which are softly limited. Ringing. A narrow band needs time: about 1 / bandwidth seconds (a third of a second at 3 Hz). Move the dial faster and the band smears and rings. Level is the loudness of the band on a dB scale, from Floor (0) to 0 dBFS (1), with the ballistics of a moving-coil meter: the needle swings over in about 300 ms and overshoots a hair. Ballistics: Fast follows within milliseconds. Peak fires when Level rises through Threshold ; while sweeping, each loud partial fires once, a rhythm read from the spectrum. Modes Manual: the band sits where the dial is. Sweep: the band moves from Frequency up by Span octaves (or down, or up and down) in Sweep Time , or in a note length when Sync is set and the transport plays (then the sweep follows the song position). Reset restarts a free sweep, Hold pauses it. When the sweep is faster than the band can follow, Too Fast lights: partials then read low and draw late and wide, as on the bench. Lock: the band scans the window Frequency ± Capture once, remembers the loudest place, jumps there and locks on with a phase-locked loop. Locked goes high and Track follows the partial: a crude pitch tracker. If the partial fades by more than 20 dB, or runs out of the window, it hunts again. Reset starts a new hunt, Hold freezes it. Range is the lab range switch: in a decade range the dial covers only 20–200 Hz, 200 Hz–2 kHz or 2–20 kHz, ten times finer. Drift lets the oscillator wander like a warm valve set, up to ±24 cents, slowly. A partial slides out of a 3 Hz band and back; in Lock the loop chases it. The drift follows Seed and the song position, so renders repeat. The view Needle meter: Level on a dB scale from Floor to 0 dB, Threshold as a red tick. Frequency dial: printed with the Range scale. Drag it (Shift for fine, double-click resets); the pointer shows where the band actually is, with Pitch , the sweep, the lock loop and drift. Lights: Locked (blinking while hunting) and Too Fast . Plotter: level against frequency from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Each sweep draws in ink; the previous sweep stays faded, so a spectrum builds up sweep by sweep. In Manual and Lock the pen leaves a trace wherever the band goes. Click the strip to clear it. How to use it? Harmonic melodies: a rich oscillator into In , Mode: Sweep , Frequency at the oscillator's pitch, Span 4, Bandwidth 10 Hz: Band plays the harmonic series. Peak into a drum: the rhythm of the spectrum. One pitch from everything: Shifted with Listen at a note of your track: whatever you tune to sings at that pitch. Pitch tracker: a voice or a bass into In , Mode: Lock , Capture 12 st around its range; Track into an oscillator's pitch, Locked into a VCA. Spectrum on the bench: Sync 4 bars, Bandwidth 30 Hz, Span 10, Frequency 20 Hz: one full spectrum every four bars on the plotter. Frozen partial: Hold from a gate: the band stays put while you play. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Wave Analyzer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Wave Analyzer under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Wave Analyzer: Partial Picker A low saw drone has many partials; the analyzer is a very narrow band-pass that an LFO moves slowly over them, so you hear single sine-like overtones appear and fade, over the dry drone. Change Bandwidth for a wider or glassier peak, or move Frequency by hand. Wave Analyzer: Spectrum Sweep Mode is Sweep: the narrow band glides from low to high and back across a bed of noise and drums, drawing out a rising and falling whistle. Change Sweep Dir, Span or Sweep Time, or widen Bandwidth for a softer tone. Wave Analyzer: Pitch Shadow In Lock mode the analyzer finds the strongest partial of a melody and its Track output drives a pure sine that shadows every note an octave up. Change Listen to move the range it hears, or Threshold to make it more or less eager to lock. Wave Analyzer: Kick Pump The analyzer is tuned to the kick's low note and its Level output follows how strong that partial is; the level swells a chord pad in time with the beat. Move Frequency to follow a different drum, or Gain to make the pad react more. Wave Analyzer: Shifted Harmony A wide band-pass picks the fundamental of a plucked line and the Shifted output moves it up by the Capture amount, a seventh semitones for a fifth, so a thin sine harmony chases each note. Change Capture for other intervals, or Bandwidth to let more of the original through. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Frequency 20 Hz – 20 kHz (or one decade, see Range ) 440 Hz Span 0 – 10 octaves 4 oct Sweep Time 0.1 – 120 s 8 s Capture 0 – 24 semitones 7 st Drift 0 – 100 % 15 % Listen 50 Hz – 4 kHz 800 Hz Threshold 0 – 100 % 60 % Gain −20 … +40 dB +12 dB Mode Manual, Sweep, Lock Manual Bandwidth 3 Hz, 10 Hz, 30 Hz, 100 Hz, 1/3 octave 10 Hz Range Full, 20–200 Hz, 200 Hz–2 kHz, 2–20 kHz Full Sweep Dir Up, Down, Up-Down Up Sync Free, 1/32 … 8 bars, 16, 32, 64 bars Free Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Ballistics Needle, Fast Needle Seed 0 – 999 1 Frequency: the tuning dial; the sweep's start in Sweep , the window's centre in Lock . The small knob text shows the Full scale; the big dial shows the Range scale. Span, Sweep Time, Sweep Dir, Sync: the sweep (shown in Sweep ). Capture: the lock window, ± semitones around Frequency (shown in Lock ). Drift: how far the oscillator wanders. Listen: the pitch of Shifted . Threshold: where Peak fires on the Level scale. Gain: on Band and Shifted . Floor: the bottom of the Level scale. Ballistics: Needle swings like a meter, Fast follows at once. Seed: picks the drift. Frequency , Span , Sweep Time , Capture , Drift , Listen , Threshold and Gain are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the sound to analyse Pitch pitch added to the tuned frequency in octaves (1 V/oct) Reset trigger restarts a free sweep; in Lock starts a new hunt Hold gate while high, the tuned frequency is frozen Outputs Output Signal What it does Thru audio In , unchanged Band audio the isolated band at its own pitch Shifted audio the band moved to Listen Level control the band's level, 0 at Floor … 1 at 0 dBFS, with needle ballistics Track pitch the tuned frequency (0 = C4) Peak trigger a pulse when Level rises through Threshold Locked gate high while the lock loop holds a partial

title: Audio Console
text: Audio Console Introduction A mixing console for the board. It brings up to 32 sources (oscillators, drums, Voice Cells, the output of whole cells) into one stereo pair, and every channel has what you expect on a console: a high-pass and a low-pass filter, a three-band EQ, up to four aux sends, a pan, a fader with a meter, and solo, mute and record arm. Aux buses come back through returns, the master has its own filters, EQ and a limiter, and every channel can leave on its own through a direct output. The console also records : every armed channel, aux bus and the master is written to a file of its own, so you can record a whole session as separate stems. For a small mixer with four channels, the Audio Mixer is lighter. How does it work? The number of channels, aux buses and direct outputs are settings ( Channels , Aux Buses , Direct Outs ). The strips, jacks and knobs above the number are hidden; a cable patched to a hidden jack stays where it is. Each channel's signal goes through, in this order: Mono or stereo. A mono channel reads In L ; a stereo channel reads In L and In R , and its pan becomes a balance. High-pass (20 Hz to 1 kHz, off at 20 Hz) and low-pass (1 kHz to 20 kHz, off at 20 kHz), 12 dB per octave. EQ: a low shelf at 100 Hz, a mid bell at 1 kHz and a high shelf at 8 kHz, each −15 to +15 dB. A band at 0 dB is skipped. Level (−60 dB, silence, to +6 dB; 0 dB sits at about 80 % of the travel), Mute and Pan . Solo: when any channel is soloed, only soloed channels reach the main output. The sends and the direct outputs are not affected, so a reverb keeps its tail while you solo. Sends. Each channel has a Send knob for each aux bus (−60 dB, silence, to 0 dB). Send Point decides where the send is taken, for each bus: after the fader (post-fader, the default: the send follows the fader) or before it (pre-fader: the send ignores the fader and the solo and only follows the mute). The sum of every channel's send comes out of Send 1…4 L/R . Patch it into an effect, and the effect's output into Return 1…4 L/R . A return has a fader, a balance and a mute and joins the main output. The cable that brings a return back is a feedback cable, so the return arrives about 0.7 ms late: inaudible for a reverb or a delay, wrong for parallel compression. Master. The main bus (the channels and the returns) goes through the master's high-pass, low-pass and EQ, its balance, fader and mute, and then the limiter , a lookahead peak limiter at −0.3 dBFS that keeps the sum from clipping. Mono Main sums the whole console to mono. Direct outputs. Direct Outs gives the first n channels an output pair of their own, taken after the fader or, with Direct Point on Pre-fader , after the filters and EQ but before the fader and mute. Other outputs. Level follows the loudness of the main output (for ducking). Recording is high while a take is written. The view A row of channel strips, then the aux strips, then the master. A channel strip has, from the top: its name (click it to rename; the name is also the name of the recorded file), Mono / Stereo , the filters, the EQ, the sends, the pan, the fader with its meter (a peak meter with a hold line and a clip light; click the light to reset it) and the S M R buttons: solo, mute and record arm. Double-click a knob or a fader to reset it. Below the strips is the Record panel: the Record button, Arm all and Unarm all , the time left, the Setup (channels, aux buses, direct outs, send points, mono main, limiter), the Record settings and the View toggles. The View toggles hide the EQ, the filters, the sends or the S / M / R buttons to make the strips more compact. A hidden section keeps working; only the view changes, and the choice is saved with the board. Recording See Recording for the steps. In short: Arm channels, aux buses (they record their send bus) and the master, then press Record . Each armed track is its own file in the Recordings folder ( ~/Music/Beautiful Bleep/Recordings on a Mac; change the default in Settings → Recordings, or give this console its own folder in the field of the Record panel), in a folder named after the time you started. Start and Stop: Manual is one take from Record to Stop, however often the transport starts and stops; Follow Transport makes one take for every play-to-stop. Channel Tap: Input records the channel as it arrives (the dry stem), Post-fader records it after the filters, EQ, fader and mute. Format: WAV at 16-bit, 24-bit or 32-bit float. The panel shows how long you can still record. If the disk cannot keep up, the take ends and the panel says why. The tracks armed when you press Record are the tracks of that recording; arming during a recording changes the next one. In the browser (Bleep Play) the recording is kept in memory: after Stop it is listed in the Record panel, with Download .zip (a WAV file for every track of every take) and Discard . The time left is what is left of a fixed memory budget. How to use it? A drum kit on separate channels: each drum into its own channel, Out L/R to an audio output port. Arm them all and record a take of the whole kit as stems. A shared reverb: turn up each channel's Send 1 , patch Send 1 L/R into a reverb and the reverb's output into Return 1 L/R . Raise the return fader to taste. Stems with processing in Live: use Direct Outs with Direct Point on Pre-fader and send every channel to its own port. Ducking: patch the Level output with a negative amount onto another VCA's gain.

title: Audio Mixer
text: Audio Mixer Audio Mixer in the module view Introduction A small stereo mixer for the board. It brings up to eight sound sources (oscillators, drums, Voice Cells) together into one stereo pair, with a level, a pan, mute and solo for each, and a send for a shared effect. A limiter on the master keeps the sum from clipping. How does it work? Each channel's signal goes through: Level: a fader in dB, from silence to +6 dB. 0 dB (unchanged) sits at about 80 % of the travel. Mute and Solo: a muted channel is silent; when any channel is soloed, only soloed channels reach the master. Changes fade over 5 ms. Pan: a mono channel (only L patched) is placed in the stereo field at even loudness; a stereo channel is balanced (moving right turns the left side down). Send: a copy of the channel goes to the Send outputs at the Send level, after the fader, or before it with Send Point Pre-Fader . The channels in use and the Return (at Return Level ) are added, scaled by Master , and pass the limiter . It holds the output below −0.3 dBFS by turning the gain down just before a peak (a 1 ms lookahead) and releasing it over 50 ms. Switching it off leaves the signal untouched. Solo doesn't affect the sends, so a reverb keeps its tail while you solo. Mono sums every channel (and the return) to mono: Pan is ignored and Out L and Out R carry the same signal. The view The view is a horizontal row of channel strips. Each has a Pan dial, a Send dial, M ute and S olo buttons and a Level fader with a level meter beside it (peak, with a hold line and a clip light; click the light to reset). The meter shares the fader's scale, so 0 dB lines up on both. The master strip has the Master fader with a stereo meter, the Limiter and Mono buttons, and the limiter's gain reduction. Double-click a control to reset it. How to use it? Mix a drum kit: each drum into its own channel, Out L/R to an audio output port. A shared reverb or delay: turn up each channel's Send , patch Send L/R into the effect and the effect's output into Return L/R . The return arrives about 0.7 ms late (the board treats the loop as feedback), which is inaudible for reverbs and delays. Rhythmic muting: a clock or a gate pattern into Mute 1 : the channel is silent while the gate is high. Ducking: the Level output follows the master's loudness; patch it with a negative amount onto another VCA's gain. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Audio Mixer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Audio Mixer under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Audio Mixer: Four-Piece Band Drums, a bass, a chord line and a lead each sit on their own channel with their own level and pan: bass in the middle, chords left, lead right. Pull a Level down or move a Pan to rebalance the band. Audio Mixer: Send to Reverb Each channel's Send feeds one reverb whose output returns on Return: the lead is awash in it, the bass stays dry. Raise Send 1 for more space, and switch Send Point to Pre-Fader to keep the reverb when a channel's Level is turned down. Audio Mixer: Muting Arrangement Mute inputs are fed from drum-grid tracks, so the hats, the chord stabs and the bass drop in and out of the mix on their own in a repeating pattern. Switch a Solo on to isolate one part, or turn a Mute on by hand. Audio Mixer: Limiter Squash All four channels are driven hot, well above 0 dB, and the built-in Limiter holds the master bus below full scale, giving a loud, dense and slightly pumping sound. Turn the Limiter setting off to hear how far past clipping the inputs are, and lower Master to keep it safe.
