Audio Mixer: Mono Check Two arpeggios are panned hard left and hard right with wide detune, then summed to the middle by the Mono setting: a quick way to hear what happens to a wide mix on a single speaker. Switch Mono off to open them back out, or change the Pan values. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Level 1–8 −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Pan 1–8 −1 (left) … +1 (right) 0 Send 1–8 −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB silence Return Level −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Master −60 dB (silence) … +6 dB 0 dB Mute 1–8 Off, On Off Solo 1–8 Off, On Off Send Point 1–8 Post-Fader, Pre-Fader Post-Fader Channels 1 … 8 4 Limiter Off, On On Mono Off, On Off Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 L audio Left (or mono) input of each channel In 1–4 R audio Right input; unpatched, the channel is mono Return L, R audio The effect return; Return R unpatched copies L Mute 1–8 gate Mutes the channel while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, R audio The master mix Send L, R audio The send bus Level control The master's loudness, 0 … 1 (10 ms attack, 200 ms release)

title: Crossfader
text: Crossfader Crossfader in the module view Introduction The Crossfader blends between two stereo signals with one knob: dry and wet of an effect, two oscillators, two drum loops, or two modulators. Patch an LFO or an envelope onto Fade and one sound turns into the other. How does it work? Fade at 0 plays only A , at 1 only B ; in between, both are mixed. Curve decides how: Equal Power: the loudness stays even across the fade. Use it for two different sounds. Linear: the gains add up to exactly 1. Use it for dry/wet of the same sound (where equal power would be 3 dB louder in the middle) and for modulation and pitch signals, where the output should be the exact average. If only the left input of a pair is patched, it feeds both sides. How to use it? Dry/wet: the dry signal into A , the effect's output into B , Curve Linear . Morph two oscillators: two different oscillators into A L and B L , a slow LFO onto Fade . Blend two modulators: two LFOs into A L and B L , Curve Linear ; Out L is a modulation source that moves between them. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Crossfader does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Crossfader under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Crossfader: Two Voices Morph A soft sine arpeggio on side A and a bright buzzy line on side B share one Crossfader; a slow LFO on Fade moves between them. Drag Fade by hand, or try the Linear curve and listen for the dip at the middle. Crossfader: Beat Swap Two different drum loops run at once, a steady four-on-the-floor and a broken pattern, and a square LFO flips the Crossfader between them every two bars. Change the LFO's Sync for faster swaps, or move Fade by hand to blend both beats. Crossfader: Dry Wet Blend A plucked line is split: side A is the dry signal and side B goes through a long, fully wet reverb. Random values on Fade walk the blend between a close, dry sound and a distant, washed one. Turn Fade by hand to set your own mix. Crossfader: Dark to Bright The same saw line goes through a dark low-pass on A and a bright, resonant high-pass on B, and an envelope on Fade sweeps from one colour to the other on each note. Change either filter's Cutoff to retune the two colours, or the envelope's Decay for a slower change. Crossfader: Linear Curve Curve is set to Linear: two similar sustained chords are cross-faded back and forth by a triangle LFO, and the sum dips slightly in the middle where an equal-power fade would stay full. Switch Curve to Equal Power to hear the dip disappear. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Fade 0 (A) … 1 (B) 0.5 Curve Equal Power, Linear Equal Power Inputs Input Signal What it does A L, A R audio Source A; A R unpatched copies A L B L, B R audio Source B; B R unpatched copies B L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio The blend

title: Spatial Pan
text: Spatial Pan Spatial Pan in the module view Introduction Spatial Pan places a sound in a space around your head, for headphones. Instead of just moving it left and right it uses the cues the ear really uses: sound reaches the near ear earlier and louder, the head shadows the far ear's highs, the shape of the outer ear changes with height, the back is duller than the front, distance makes sounds quieter, softer and more reverberant, and a source that moves toward or away from you bends in pitch. All the cues are synthesised from simple formulas, so there is no data to install. How does it work? Azimuth, distance, elevation. Azimuth is the angle around you: 0° is in front, +90° at your right ear, ±180° behind. Distance runs from 0.25 m (right at the ear) to 25 m. Elevation is −90° (below) to +90° (above). Everything is smoothed so moving them (or modulating them) is clean. Orbit spins the azimuth continuously at up to 2 turns per second in either direction. Time difference. The sound reaches the far ear later by (a/c)(θ + sin θ), with Head radius a (7 – 11 cm), the speed of sound c and the angle θ from the midline: up to 0.65 ms. Delays are read with cubic interpolation. Level difference and head shadow. Each ear has a first-order filter whose gain depends on the angle between the source and that ear: the near ear gets a slight lift of the highs, the far ear a growing roll-off, up to −15 dB at 6 kHz for a source at the side. Height and rear. A notch in the highs moves from about 5 kHz (below) to 10 kHz (above) and deepens away from the horizontal plane. The back is a low-pass that closes from 16 kHz to about 5 kHz. Distance. The level falls with 1/(1 + 1.5·(d − 0.25 m)); Air removes highs with distance. The propagation delay d/c is applied in proportion to Doppler : when the distance changes, the delay changes, and the pitch bends as it would in air (a source receding at 34 m/s is 10 % flat). At 0 % there is no delay, so a moving distance changes only level and brightness. Room. Six early reflections from the same source, panned around its direction, arrive between 6 and 32 ms (spaced by Size ), quieter with distance, low-passed. Room sets their level. Side. A control output with the source's left/right position, −1 … +1. How to use it? Headphone mixes: one Spatial Pan per instrument at different azimuths and distances; keep the Level knobs matched. A source in orbit: Orbit 0.2 turns/s, Distance 40 %, Doppler low. A fly-by: an envelope or LFO into Distance with Doppler up. Movement from a sequencer: noise or random CV into Azimuth . Stereo input: with both inputs patched they are mixed to one source. Speakers: the cues are made for headphones; on speakers keep Head small and Room up for a softer effect. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Spatial Pan does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Spatial Pan under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Spatial Pan: Orbiting Lead A plucked melody circles the listener once every five seconds. Wear headphones: the time and level differences, the duller back and the early reflections make the circle. Change Orbit for a faster or reversed spin or Distance to pull it in. Spatial Pan: Drifting Kit A drum loop swings from side to side over four bars with a little room around it. Reduce the Room knob for a drier, closer kit or make Distance bigger for a kit heard from the back of the hall. Spatial Pan: Fly-By A bright riff passes by: it comes from the far left, sweeps close to the middle and leaves to the far right, and its pitch bends the way a passing source does. Lower Doppler to hear the path without the pitch bend. Spatial Pan: Overhead Rain Bell-like plucks high in the scale move up and down in elevation and wander in azimuth under two slow random LFOs, so notes seem to fall around and above the head. Reduce Elevation depth for a flatter field. Spatial Pan: Two Places The drums sit behind and to the right, the melody in front and to the left, each with its own distance and room. Move Azimuth on either to rearrange the stage. Presets The preset bar of the Spatial Pan view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Front Centre Straight ahead, a little room. Hard Left At the left ear. Hard Right At the right ear. Behind Behind you: duller, with the highs rolled off. Above Overhead: the pinna notch moves up. Below Left Low and to the left. Slow Orbit A source circling the head every seven seconds. Fast Orbit A quick spin, close in. Distant Far away: quiet, soft and reverberant. Close Whisper At the ear, almost dry. Big Room A large space of long reflections. Dry Booth No reflections: pure head cues. Giant Head A large head: longer time differences. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does In L, In R audio the source; two inputs are summed to mono Out L, Out R audio the binaural pair Side control the source's lateral position, −1 … +1 Knobs Control Range Default Azimuth −180 … +180 ° 0 Distance 0.25 m … 25 m (0 – 100 %) 35 % Elevation −90 … +90 ° 0 Orbit −2 … +2 turns/s 0 Doppler 0 – 100 % 100 % Room 0 – 100 % 30 % Size 0 – 100 % 50 % Air 0 – 100 % 50 % Head 7 – 11 cm 8.75 Level 0 – 100 % (50 % = unity gain) 50 % Origin The time-difference and head-shadow formulas are standard published spherical-head models (path-length formula and a first-order pole/zero shadow); the module was written from those descriptions and uses no measured response data.

title: VCA
text: VCA VCA in the module view Introduction A VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets the volume of a signal. On its own it's a stereo volume knob. Patch an envelope or an LFO onto its Gain and the volume follows that signal. This is how a note gets its loudness shape, and how tremolo and ducking work. How does it work? Both channels are multiplied by the same gain: Out = In × gain Gain is a 0 – 400 % knob. With the Linear response, gain is the knob value. With Exponential , it is the value cubed up to 100 %: 50 % on the knob is about −18 dB, and the bottom of the range fades smoothly toward silence. This sounds more natural for fades and envelopes. Above 100 % the curve continues linearly, up to 4× (+12 dB). Gain starts at 0 % (closed). Modulation adds to the knob, so an envelope patched at 100 % amount sweeps the whole knob range, from silence up to 400 %, so use an amount of 25 % to open the VCA exactly to unity. Gain above 100 % lifts a quiet signal; mind the level after it. If only In L is patched, it feeds both channels. A mono oscillator then comes out on both sides. How to use it? Note volume: Oscillator Out → VCA In L ; ADSR Env → VCA Gain knob. VCA Out L/R goes to Voice Out or an output port. Tremolo: turn Gain up to about 50 % and patch a Function (cycling) onto Gain with a small amount. Ducking: set Gain to 100 % and patch an envelope onto Gain with a negative amount of about −25 % (a full envelope sweeps the whole 400 %): each trigger dips the volume. Plain volume or mute: use the knob without any cable. To shape a control signal instead of audio, use Utility . The VCA is built for audio. Demo patches Five whole patches show what VCA does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick VCA under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows VCA: Exponential Pluck A saw note shaped by a short envelope into the VCA's Gain, with Response on Exponential so the decay sounds natural and plucked. Switch Response to Linear to hear a stiffer, more abrupt tail, or change the envelope's Decay. VCA: Tremolo Chords A held chord goes through a VCA whose Gain rests at a middle value while a triangle LFO swings it up and down, a classic tremolo. Raise the LFO Rate for a flutter, change its amount for a deeper chop, or move the VCA's Gain to rebalance. VCA: Linear Swell A very slow attack on the envelope lets a rich pad fade in and out through a VCA with Response set to Linear, so the volume rises evenly instead of rushing in at the end. Compare it with Exponential, or lengthen Attack and Release. VCA: Kick Ducking Every kick fires an envelope that pushes the pad VCA's Gain down by a negative amount, so the chords dip on the beat and swell back between hits. Change the envelope Release for a longer pump, or raise the VCA's Gain for an even bigger pad. VCA: Rhythm Gate A sustained saw chord is chopped into a rhythm by a drum-grid track that fires a tight envelope into the VCA's Gain, the stuttering gate used in trance and electro. Edit the pattern, or lengthen the envelope Release to soften the chops. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Gain 0 – 400 % 0 % Response Linear, Exponential Exponential Gain: the amplification, from silence (0 %) through unity (100 %) up to 4× (400 %, +12 dB). Patch envelopes and LFOs here; the ring around the knob shows the gain really used. Response: how the gain value maps to volume. Linear: volume = gain. Good for amplitude modulation at audio rate and for signals that should stay proportional. Exponential: volume = gain³ up to 100 % (about −60 dB to 0 dB), then linear. Fades and envelopes sound even, the way our ears expect. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio left input × gain Out R audio right input × gain

title: Sampler
text: Sampler Sampler in the module view Introduction Sampler plays a WAV file like an instrument. Load a sample, optionally cut it into slices (by hand, at the transients, or into beats), and play it from notes or triggers with up to 16 independent playheads . A play mode decides how each playhead ends, an ADSR envelope and a filter shape it, and Speed, Transpose and Position move it around. Sampler is the module for "play a sample" and "chop a loop and sequence the pieces"; Splice is the one for recording onto a reel, Grains for a moving cloud. How does it work? Loading. Drop an audio file on the view (or press Import audio ): WAV, or MP3, AIFF, FLAC, OGG or M4A, which are converted to WAV on import. Clear sample removes the sample again (and stops a recording in progress). Loading another sample while one is loaded replaces it. The file is stored in the media folder, so the board keeps working on any computer that has it. 8, 16, 24 and 32-bit files, mono or stereo, any sample rate. Slices. Markers cut the sample into slices. Slicing chooses how they are made, and all three write the same markers, so you can start automatically and finish by hand: Manual: double-click the waveform to add a marker, double-click a marker to remove it, drag a marker to move it. Threshold: Detect finds the transients. Sensitivity sets how many (more to the right), Min gap the shortest slice. Beats: Equal cuts Divisions equal slices. On BPM cuts the sample on a grid: Divisions over Bars bars at BPM . Detect BPM estimates the tempo of a loop. Click a slice to select it; its own settings (mode, transpose, level, pan, reverse, choke group) appear below the waveform. Shift-click or Audition plays it. Starting a playhead. With Trigger By = Note , the Notes input plays the sample: in whole-sample mode the note sets the pitch (the sample sounds as recorded at Root Note ); with Slice Mode on, each key plays one slice, slice 1 on the root note and the following slices on the keys above it (keys beyond the last slice do nothing). With Trigger By = CV , a pulse at Trigger starts a playhead: Slice (0 – 100 % picks slice 1 … n) or the selected slice plays, Pitch sets the pitch, Velocity the level. A Gate holds the playhead open; without one, the sample plays to the end of its region. Patch only Gate , without Trigger , and the gate's rising edge starts it. Step moves the selected slice to the next one (and wraps); the Next and Random buttons do the same by hand. Stop releases every playhead. Play modes. Mode decides how a playhead ends; each slice can override it. Gate: plays while the note is held, then fades out over Release . Reaching the end of the sample or slice stops it. To end of sample: plays on to the sample end, whatever the gate does. To end of slice: plays to the next marker, whatever the gate does. Loop: loops the sample (or the slice) until released. Loop Style can be Ping-pong ; Loop Crossfade hides the seam. One-shot: plays the whole slice, ignoring the gate. End fires whenever a playhead reaches its end or wraps its loop. Region. Start and End trim the sample. In slice mode they trim each slice, as a fraction of it, so End at 50 % plays the first half of every slice. Pitch and speed. Transpose (semitones) and Fine (cents) set the pitch; Pitch adds 1 V per octave to CV-triggered playheads. Speed is the playback ratio and negative plays backwards; Speed (input) adds 1 V per octave. With Warp on Repitch pitch and speed are one thing, like tape: playing twice as fast sounds an octave higher. The other Warp modes stretch time on their own, with overlapping grains, so Speed changes the tempo and only Transpose (and the note) changes the pitch: Beats (short grains, for drums and percussion), Tones (long grains, smooth, for pads and melodies) and Texture (scattered grains, for noise and ambience). Key Tracking sets how much the note number moves the pitch (100 % is normal; 0 % plays every key at the same pitch). Quality is the interpolation: Linear (cheapest), Cubic , or Sinc (cleanest when pitching down). Tempo sync. Turn Tempo Sync on and Speed is scaled so the sample lasts Beats beats at the tempo of the board: Transport follows the transport, Clock measures the pulses on the Clock input (set Clock PPQN to match) and Auto uses the clock while the jack is patched, else the transport. ÷2 and ×2 halve and double Beats (twice as fast, half as fast); Fit guesses it from the detected BPM. Use Beats or Tones in Warp to keep a drum loop's pitch while it follows the tempo. It matches the tempo; it does not line the loop up with the bar, so start it on the beat. Gain. Gain (±24 dB) boosts or cuts the sample before the filter and envelope, and the waveform display follows it, so a quiet file can be seen and heard at a useful level. Recording. Patch audio into In L (and In R for stereo; a lone In L is recorded as mono) and press Record (or raise the Rec gate). Press it again, or drop the gate, to stop: the take becomes the sample and loops at once, and is saved with the project. Recordings can be up to 20 seconds. Rec Mode Overdub adds what comes in on top of the take at the playhead, keeping the old audio at Feedback (100 % layers forever, lower values fade the old layers out like an echo). It needs a take made here; after loading a project, make a new one. Rec Length Beats records exactly Beats beats at the current tempo and stops by itself: a perfect bar for a looper. Together with Tempo Sync the loop follows later tempo changes. Monitor sends the input to the output while recording, or always. With Overdub , Feedback below 100 % and Rec Length in beats, the Sampler is a tempo-synced looper-delay. Overdub assumes the playhead moves at Speed 1. Tabs. The controls are in five tabs under the waveform: Sample (Gain, Start, End, Position, Pitch, Warp and Tempo Sync), Slices (the slicing tools and the selected slice's settings), Envelope & Filter , Output (Output and Voices) and Record . The waveform shows Start and End as lines marked S and E with the part that is not played dimmed (in slice mode, in every slice), and the volume envelope drawn over the played part, at the current Speed. Moving the playhead. With Position Mode Scrub , turning Position (or modulating it) moves every sounding playhead to that point of its region, with a 3 ms crossfade, so an LFO or a sequencer can scan through the sample. With Offset , Position is read when a playhead starts and sets where in the region it begins (random-access starts). Many playheads. Voices sets how many play at once (1 – 16). Poly gives each note its own playhead; when all are in use the oldest (or the quietest one already releasing) fades out in 5 ms. Mono plays one at a time and goes back to the previous held note when you let go; Legato does the same but changes pitch without restarting the sample. Layers starts several playheads with every note: Layers sets how many, Layer Pitch the interval between them and Layer Offset a delay between starts, for unison, octaves or chords. Choke groups. Slices in the same choke group cut each other off: set a closed and an open hi-hat to the same group. Envelope, filter, level. Every playhead has an ADSR envelope (attack linear, decay and release exponential) and a low-pass filter. Filter Env opens (or closes, when negative) the cutoff with the envelope, up to six octaves. Velocity sets how much a note's velocity changes the level and the brightness. Crush lowers the sample rate and bit depth for a gritty sound. Pan balances a stereo sample, or places a mono one. Outputs. Out L and Out R carry the mix. With Voice Outs on, a jack for each of the 16 voices appears; a voice whose jack is patched is taken out of the mix, so each can have its own effects. Playhead is the position of the newest playhead in the file (0 – 100 %); Active is the share of voices in use; Slice pulses when a playhead starts. How to use it? Play a sample from a keyboard: Mode Gate , Voices 8, a Release of 100 ms. Set Root Note to the note the sample was recorded at. Drum rack from a loop: Slicing Threshold and Detect , then Slice Mode on, Mode To end of slice . A drum sequencer's Notes plays the slices from the root note up. Resequence a break: Beats with 16 divisions, Trigger By CV, a trigger source into Trigger and a control signal (0 – 100 %, from a sequencer or a random source) into Slice . Hi-hats: give the closed and open slices choke group 1. Pad from a one-shot: Mode Loop , Loop Crossfade 20 ms, Attack 300 ms, Release 1 s. Scanning: Mode Loop , a very short region ( Start 40 %, End 41 %) and a slow LFO on Start and End together, or Position Mode Scrub with an LFO on Position . Reverse cymbals: Speed −1 with Mode To end of slice . Chord from one note: Voice Mode Layers , Layers 3, Layer Pitch 4. Factory samples. The demo patches and the Samples cells carry short pieces of recordings that are free to use, so they work on any computer. All of them come from the University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios' Musical Instrument Samples (Lawrence Fritts, ; free for any project, without restrictions): piano, crotale, Thai gong, tam-tam, crash cymbal, hi-hat, claves, castanets, granite block, tambourine and a balloon pop. We cut, fade and normalise them and turn them into mono, 16-bit, 48 kHz WAV files; the wood loop is a bar we arranged from the single hits. The rain used with Grains is Rain loopable by Ylmir ( , CC0). Every file, its original and its licence is listed in patch/presets/samples/README.md in the source tree. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Sampler does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Sampler under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Sampler: Wood Bar Shuffle One bar of claves, castanets and granite blocks is cut into sixteen equal slices. With Slice Mode on, each key plays one slice (slice 1 on the Root Note), so a step sequencer re-orders the bar into a new groove; two slices are set to Reverse in the view. Edit the sequence, drag a marker, or select a slice to change its pitch and level. Sampler: Two-Note Piano Two recorded piano notes, C3 and C4, each sit on their own Sampler with the right Root Note, and a step sequencer plays the left hand on one and the right hand on the other. Sampler pitches the single recording across the keyboard, tape-style. Try Quality for cleaner pitch shifting, Release for staccato, or Cutoff for a softer touch. Sampler: Gong Garden A Thai gong played in Layers voice mode: every note starts three playheads a fifth apart (Layer Pitch 7), each a little later than the last, so one gong becomes a bell cluster. Slow notes ring into each other. Change Layers, Layer Pitch or Layer Offset for other stacks, or switch Voice Mode back to Poly for a single gong. Sampler: Tam-Tam Drone A short, steady stretch of a tam-tam recording is looped (Mode Loop with a crossfade that hides the seam) and played slowly from the keys as a shimmering metallic pad. A slow LFO scrubs the Position inside the region and another opens the filter. Move Start and End to choose a different part of the gong, or shorten the region for a more electronic drone. Sampler: Shaker Choke A tambourine shake is cut into four slices, all in choke group 1, so each new hit cuts off the one before it. Trigger By is CV: a trigger starts a playhead and a random control signal on the Slice input picks which part of the shake plays, one of them reversed. Change the sequence, or select a slice in the view and give it another group. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Start 0 – 100 % 0 % End 0 – 100 % 100 % Position 0 – 100 % 0 % Transpose −48 … +48 semitones 0 Fine −100 … +100 cents 0 Speed −4 … +4 +1 Attack 0.5 ms – 10 s 1 ms Decay 1 ms – 10 s 100 ms Sustain 0 – 100 % 100 % Release 1 ms – 10 s 50 ms Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Pan −100 … +100 % 0 Velocity 0 – 100 % 50 % Crush 0 – 100 % 0 % Cutoff 20 Hz – 20 kHz 20 kHz Resonance 0 – 100 % 0 % Filter Env −100 … +100 % 0 % Layer Pitch −24 … +24 semitones 7 Layer Offset 0 – 200 ms 0 Gain −24 … +24 dB 0 Feedback 0 – 100 % 100 % Beats 0.25 – 256 4 Every knob is a modulation destination. Layer Pitch and Layer Offset show in Layers voice mode. Settings Setting Values Default Trigger By Note, CV Note Slice Mode Off, On Off Mode Gate, To end of sample, To end of slice, Loop, One-shot Gate Loop Style Forward, Ping-pong Forward Loop Crossfade 0 – 50 ms 5 ms Voices 1 – 16 8 Voice Mode Poly, Mono, Legato, Layers Poly Layers 1 – 8 2 Root Note 0 – 127 (MIDI) 60 Key Tracking −100 … +200 % 100 % Quality Linear, Cubic, Sinc Cubic Position Mode Scrub, Offset Scrub Warp Repitch, Beats, Tones, Texture Repitch Tempo Sync Off, Auto, Clock, Transport Off Clock PPQN 1, 2, 4, 8, 24, 48 24 Rec Mode Replace, Overdub Replace Rec Length Free, Beats Free Monitor Off, Recording, Always Off Voice Outs Off, On Off Output Stereo, Mono Stereo Per-slice settings Mode (or Inherit ), Transpose (±48 semitones), Level (0 – 200 %), Pan, Reverse and Choke group (none, 1 – 8). They are saved with the markers. Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes plays the sample ( Trigger By Note) Trigger trigger starts a playhead ( Trigger By CV) Gate gate holds CV-triggered playheads open; alone, its rising edge starts one Slice control picks the slice for the next trigger, 0 – 100 % → 1 … n Pitch pitch 1 V/oct for CV-triggered playheads Speed pitch 1 V/oct, added to Speed Velocity control velocity of CV-triggered playheads (full when unpatched) Stop trigger releases every playhead Step trigger moves the selected slice to the next one Clock trigger tempo for Tempo Sync ( Auto and Clock ) In L, In R audio what is recorded Rec gate high records (or overdubs), low stops Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the mix End trigger a pulse when a playhead reaches its end or wraps Slice trigger a pulse when a playhead starts Playhead control the newest playhead's position in the file, 0 – 100 % Active control voices in use ÷ Voices Voice 1 … 16 audio each voice on its own (with Voice Outs on) Not yet Time-stretching (changing the speed without changing the pitch) is planned; for now Speed and pitch go together.

title: Splice
text: Splice Splice in the module view Introduction Splice is a tape-style sampler and looper. You record onto a reel of up to two minutes of stereo, cut it into splices with markers, and play them back at any speed, forwards or backwards. Inside a splice, Window Size , Position and Overlap break playback into small repeating pieces, from micro-loops to a granular cloud. Triggers move between splices, a control signal picks one directly, and WAV files can be dropped onto the reel. Splice is the module for "record something, then play with it"; Grains is the one for a live, moving cloud. How does it work? Recording. Press ● Rec (or send a gate or trigger to Record ) to start and again to stop ( Record Mode Toggle ); with Gate , recording runs while the gate is high. Record Target decides where it goes: New splice (default): the take is appended to the reel as a new splice, which becomes the current one and plays as soon as you stop. Current splice : overdubs into the splice that's playing, at the play head and at its speed (tape style). Overdub sets how much of the old audio stays: 0 % replaces it, 100 % layers on top. Whole reel : clears the reel and records from the start. Reel Length (15 s – 2 min) is how much the reel can hold. Monitor passes the input through: never, while recording, or always. Splices. Mark (button or trigger) cuts: while recording, it splits the take there; while playing, it splits the current splice at the play head. In the view, double-click the reel to add a marker, double-click a marker to remove it (the two splices merge), drag a marker to move it, click a splice to pick it. Playback. Speed is the playback ratio: 1 normal, 2 an octave up, negative backwards, 0 stops the tape. The Speed input adds 1 V per octave, so a sequencer plays the reel melodically. At the end of the splice it loops, or with Loop on One-shot it stops until Play . End fires at the end of each pass. With Sync on 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars, the speed is set so the splice lasts exactly that long at the song's tempo (pitch follows, like tape) and stays locked to the bars, even after a loop jump. Moving between splices. Next steps to the next splice (and wraps). Select (0 … 1, a control input) picks a splice directly; without it, the Pick knob does. Shift decides when the change happens: Immediate (crossfaded over Fade ), End of window , or End of splice . The view shows a pending splice with a dashed outline. Play restarts the current (or pending) splice. Windows. Window Size is the length of a piece of the splice (down to 0.5 ms), Position where in the splice it sits. Overlap decides how the windows play: 0 – 30 %: each window plays once, then a gap: rhythmic stutter (the gap shrinks as Overlap rises). 30 – 50 %: windows repeat back to back with a short crossfade: a clean loop. This is the default; at Window Size 100 % the whole splice loops. 50 – 100 %: 2 to 4 overlapping windows with soft edges: a granular texture. Above 75 % some windows play an octave up or down or a fifth up, spread across the stereo field (from Seed , so it repeats). A slow LFO on Position scrubs through the splice. With End Mode on Window , End fires at every window: a clock taken from the audio. Position and Splice (outputs) report the play head within the splice and which splice is playing. Fade sets the crossfades at window and splice boundaries and the record punch-in and out; at 0 the playback is sample-exact. Level sets the output level. Saving. The reel is stored as a WAV file in the media folder; the view saves it whenever the audio has changed and recording has stopped (the header says "unsaved" until then), and the board keeps its name, markers and current splice. Import audio : drop a file on the reel or the Import audio box; it replaces the reel. Clear reel empties it. How to use it? Live looper: Monitor Always , record a phrase, it loops when you stop. Record Target Current splice and Overdub 100 % to layer more. Chopped break: import a drum loop, add markers on the hits, patch a sequencer's trigger into Next (Shift Immediate ), or a stepped random source into Select . Tape tricks: an envelope onto Speed for tape-stop; Speed −1 for reverse. Melodic sampler: a sequencer's Pitch into the Speed input, Window Size 100 %, Loop One-shot , its trigger into Play . Texture: Window Size 3 %, Overlap 90 %, a slow LFO on Position . Phrase in time: Sync 2 bars : whatever you recorded fits two bars. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Splice does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Splice under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Splice: Two-Bar Loop A plucked phrase is recorded onto the reel for two bars, then the splice loops it back with Sync on 2 bars, so the loop stays on the beat. The live phrase is heard while it is recorded (Monitor). Try Sync, Speed or Window Size to bend the loop, or set Record Target to Current splice and Overdub to layer more on top. Splice: Tape Stop A drum bar is recorded, then plays from the reel while a ramp pulls Speed down towards zero every two bars: the whole loop slows, drops in pitch and winds to a halt before the tape snaps back to full speed. Edit the ramp's Rate or amount, or try a negative Speed to run the tape backwards. Splice: Reel Keyboard One recorded note is replayed as an instrument: a sequencer's Pitch drives the Speed input (1 V per octave) and its trigger restarts the splice, with Loop on One-shot. Change the sequence for a new tune, or Window Size for another timbre; pitch and speed move together, like tape. Splice: Break Chopper A drum bar is recorded and then replayed one eighth at a time: Window Size is 1/8 of the splice and a stepped random source picks Position every eighth note, so the break is re-cut into a stuttering new beat. The random loops after eight steps, so the pattern repeats; raise Loop towards 0 for endless variation. Splice: Micro Cloud A short chord arpeggio is recorded, then replayed in 3 % windows with Overlap at 90 %, which turns it into a granular cloud; a slow LFO scrubs Position across the splice. Raise Window Size to hear the phrase re-emerge, or lower Overlap below 30 % for a rhythmic stutter. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Speed −4 … +4 (×1 in the middle) +1 Window Size 0.001 – 100 % of the splice 100 % Position 0 – 100 % 0 % Overlap 0 – 100 % 40 % Pick 0 – 100 % 0 % Overdub 0 – 100 % 100 % Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Fade 0 – 50 ms 3 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Reel Length 15 s, 30 s, 60 s, 120 s 60 s Record Mode Gate, Toggle Toggle Record Target New splice, Current splice, Whole reel New splice Shift Immediate, End of window, End of splice End of splice End Mode Splice, Window Splice Loop Loop, One-shot Loop Monitor Off, Input while recording, Always Input while recording Sync Free, 1 bar, 2 bars, 4 bars, 8 bars Free Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the recording source; In L alone feeds both sides Record gate starts/stops recording (per Record Mode ) Mark trigger adds a marker at the record or play head Next trigger moves to the next splice Select control 0 … 1 picks splice 1 … n Play trigger restarts the current splice Speed pitch 1 V/oct on top of Speed Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the playback (and the input, per Monitor ) End trigger the end of each splice pass (or window) Position control the play head within the splice, 0 … 1 Splice control which splice plays, 0 … 1 The reel takes 46 MB at 48 kHz (always sized for two minutes); inside a Voice Cell each voice has its own reel.

title: Bender
text: Bender Bender in the module view Introduction Bender is a glitch effect in the spirit of circuit-bent samplers and skipping CDs. It listens to the input, grabs short pieces of it and, by chance, repeats, re-pitches, reverses, slices and corrupts them. Low settings add the odd stutter to a beat; high settings shred it. Every decision comes from Seed and the song position, so a glitch you like comes back every time you play that section, and the render sounds exactly like what you heard. How does it work? Segments. Bender cuts time into segments. With a note value in Sync and the transport playing, segments sit on the song grid (a 1/16 segment starts on every sixteenth, also after a loop jump). With Sync on Free , or while the transport is stopped, segments follow each other at Time (synced note values keep their length at the last tempo). With a cable in Clock , each pulse starts a segment. Segment fires at every segment start. Decisions. At each segment start Bender decides: pass the input, or glitch . Chance is the probability of a glitch. A glitch repeats the segment that just ended, Repeats segments long, then the input passes again; no new decision is made while a glitch plays. The decisions are drawn from Seed and the segment's number, so turning Chance up only adds glitches (the ones you had stay), and changing Seed gives a different pattern. A pulse at Glitch (or the Glitch button) makes the next segment a glitch; with Now on, it starts one immediately. Random puts out the segment's seeded value (−1 … +1) for modulation that matches the glitches; Active is high while a glitch plays. Bend is the playback speed of the repeats: 1 normal, 0.5 an octave down, 2 an octave up, negative values play backwards, and 0 stops the head on a 2 ms buzz. Bend Steps snaps it to octaves, octaves and fifths, or semitones. Bend Var lets each glitch pick a different speed from a set around Bend (half, double, reversed …). The repeat always lasts its full length: faster speeds loop the source within it. Slice makes each repetition shorter than the last: the accelerating stutter. In sync, the lengths are powers of two of the segment (1/16 → 1/32 → 1/64 …), so the ratchets stay on the grid. Corrupt sets the amount of the damage Mode picks: Mode What Corrupt does Crush lower sample rate (down to 1 kHz) and fewer bits (down to 3), no filter Dropout splits each repetition into 16 cells and silences cells by chance Fold up to +24 dB into a wavefolder, then a hard clip Shuffle cuts the source into 8 slices and plays some of them out of order Smear jitters the read position by up to 20 ms: a scratchy copy With Corrupt When on Always , Crush, Dropout and Fold also act between glitches. At 0 % every mode is exactly transparent. Edge is the crossfade at every switch (pass → glitch, repetition → repetition, glitch → pass, and the loop point of a re-pitched repeat): 100 % is 8 ms, 0 % hard cuts. Bender only clicks when you ask it to. Freeze (the button or the gate) loops the current source for as long as it's held and stops recording; Bend , Slice and Corrupt keep working on it. When you let go, the glitch ends at the next segment start, on the grid. Transport. When the transport stops mid-glitch, the glitch finishes its repeats and the input passes again. Bender has no tail. The view shows the decisions of this bar and the next while the transport plays in sync (the upcoming ones dimmed), otherwise the recent segments; the bar below shows the read head inside the source. How to use it? Occasional stutter on a beat: Sync 1/16, Chance 10 %, Repeats 2. Ratchets: Sync 1/8, Chance 30 %, Repeats 2, Slice 40 %. Tape-stop flavour: Bend 0.5, Bend Steps Octaves, Bend Var 50 %. Shredder: Chance 70 %, Mode Shuffle, Corrupt 80 %, Slice 30 %. Glitch on demand: Chance 0 %, Now on, a sequencer's trigger into Glitch . Matching movement: Random onto a filter's cutoff: it jumps with each decision. In a Voice Cell: each voice glitches on its own; with the same Seed they glitch together unless Voice In › Random moves a knob. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Bender does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Bender under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Bender: Beat Crusher Crush mode grabs sixteenth-note pieces of a drum loop and repeats them, with pitch steps by octave and a little corruption. Raise Chance for a busier mess, or lower Repeats for a gentler stutter. Bender: Dropout Tune Dropout mode punches holes into an arpeggio, as if the signal kept losing contact. Move Chance for more or fewer gaps, Time for the length of each hole, and try another Seed. Bender: Fifths and Octaves Fold mode with Bend steps set to Fifths + octaves repeats short pieces of a slow melody a fifth or an octave away, so the glitches stay musical. Switch Bend Steps to Free for wild slides, or raise Bend Var. Bender: Shuffle Slicer Shuffle mode with Slice cuts a swung beat into small pieces and reorders them, so the groove is always almost the same and never quite. Turn Slice down for longer chunks, or Chance up for more reshuffling. Bender: Smear and Freeze Smear mode melts a chord arpeggio together while a square LFO holds Freeze for a bar at a time, looping one grain until the gate lets go. Try the LFO's rate, or latch Freeze on and off by hand. Presets The preset bar of the Bender view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Stutter Repeats Occasional clean repeats of a sixteenth slice. Reverse Slices Shuffled slices that play back reversed. Dropouts Pieces of the signal drop out like a bad connection. Smear Clouds Smeared, blurred repeats for soft textures. Fold Mangle Folded, harsher glitches. Bit Crush Bursts Crushed bursts on random sixteenths. Slicer Chopped, rearranged slices for rhythmic breaks. Constant Corruption Always-on digital damage with occasional glitches. Free Roll Unsynced rolls with wandering pitch. Semitone Chaos Dense, random, chromatic glitch storm. title: Meta Mod
text: Meta Mod Meta Mod in the module view Introduction The Meta Mod combines two audio signals, a Carrier and a Modulator , into one. A single Algorithm knob sweeps through eight ways of combining them, from a plain crossfade over wavefolding and ring modulation to a vocoder, and Timbre changes the character of whichever algorithm is selected. An internal oscillator stands in for an unpatched input, so the module is a sound source on its own, and a ring modulator or vocoder for any track with one cable. How does it work? Inputs and the oscillator. The internal oscillator is the Oscillator's core (sine → triangle → saw → square with Osc Shape ) at C4 × 2^(Osc Octave + Osc Tune/12 + Pitch). It fills in for one input: Carrier patched Modulator patched Carrier is Modulator is no no oscillator silence no yes oscillator Modulator yes no Carrier oscillator yes yes Carrier Modulator So a synth voice needs only the Modulator cable (the oscillator plays the notes), and a track needs only the Carrier cable (the oscillator is a tunable modulator: a classic ring modulator). Patching or unpatching fades over 5 ms. Carrier Level and Mod Level set the gain into the algorithm (up to 200 %, +6 dB, which drives the nonlinear ones harder). Signals within ±1 pass unchanged; hotter ones are softly limited towards ±4. Algorithms. With carrier a , modulator b and Timbre t : # Algorithm What it does Timbre 0 Crossfade equal-power blend of a and b 0 = carrier, 50 % = both, 100 % = modulator 1 Fold sine-folds the sum a + b fold depth, 1× to 8× 2 Analog ring a diode-ring model: about a × b , saturating at high levels 0 = matched diodes, clean; 100 % = mismatched, carrier bleeds through with odd harmonics 3 Digital ring a × ( b + t ) / (1 + t ) 0 = ring modulation (only sum and difference tones), 100 % = amplitude modulation (carrier audible) 4 Bitwise a and b as integers, combined by Bitwise Op (XOR, AND, OR, wrap-around sum) resolution, 16 bits down to 2 5 Comparator 0–50 %: a square that is +1 where a > b , softening as Timbre rises; 50–100 %: towards max( a , b ) hardness, then the diode maximum 6 Vocoder the carrier through 12 bands, each shaped by the modulator's level in that band formant shift, ±1 octave (50 % = none) 7 Chebyshev the n -th Chebyshev polynomial of a : a full-scale sine becomes its n -th harmonic the order n , 1 to 16; the modulator sweeps it at audio rate Between two whole numbers the neighbours crossfade, so Algorithm 2.5 is half analog, half digital ring; modulating it at audio rate is a sound of its own. Every algorithm is levelled so two full-scale sines come out about equally loud at every position. Vocoder. The modulator is split into 12 bands from 100 Hz to 8 kHz; a follower (2 ms attack, 40 ms release) measures each band. The carrier goes through the same bands (moved by the formant shift), each levelled by its own follower, and each takes the modulator's band level. So the carrier's own spectrum hardly matters, only that it has energy in a band: noise and buzzy waves (saw, square) work best. The modulator's hiss above 8 kHz is added at −6 dB, which keeps consonants intelligible. Anti-aliasing. Fold, both rings, Bitwise, Comparator and Chebyshev create frequencies far above their inputs. Standard runs them at 2× the sample rate, High at 4× (Fold also uses antiderivative anti-aliasing); Eco doesn't oversample, for big Voice Cells. Crossfade, the vocoder and the dry signal are delayed to match, so morphing stays in phase. The outputs are delayed by 1 ms ( Standard , 47 samples) or 1.5 ms ( High , 70.5 samples). Output. A 5 Hz high-pass removes the DC that the comparator, bitwise and ring imbalance produce. Outputs stay within ±4. How to use it? Ring modulator for a track: Audio In → Carrier L/R . Algorithm 2 (default), tune the oscillator with Osc Tune and Osc Octave . Patch an LFO into Osc Tune for sweeping bell tones. Vocoder: a voice or drum loop into Modulator , a saw or noise into Carrier L , Algorithm 6. Patch Pitch from a sequencer for a robot choir with the internal oscillator as the carrier (leave Carrier unpatched and set Osc Shape to saw). Synth voice: Voice In Pitch → Pitch , a second Oscillator into Modulator , sweep Algorithm with an envelope. Harmonic sweeps: Algorithm 7 with a sine carrier; patch an LFO onto Timbre for a harmonic arpeggio. Envelope follower: Env follows the modulator (5 ms attack, 120 ms release); patch it to a filter or VCA for ducking and auto-wah. Dry/wet: Mix blends the carrier (after Carrier Level ) with the result. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Meta Mod does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Meta Mod under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Meta Mod: Ring Bells With no modulator patched, the internal oscillator multiplies a simple melody in analog ring mode, giving clangorous bell tones. Change Osc Tune to move between consonant and metallic, or sweep Algorithm to the neighbours. Meta Mod: Talking Drums In vocoder mode a buzzing saw carrier is shaped by the drum beat as modulator, so the pad seems to pump and speak in the rhythm of the kit. Change Timbre for a different band balance, or the saw's pitch for another vowel colour. Meta Mod: Bitwise Grit Bitwise mode combines a bass line with the internal oscillator number by number, producing digital edge and odd harmonics that move with Osc Tune. Switch Bitwise Op between XOR, AND and OR, or sweep Timbre. Meta Mod: Algorithm Sweep A slow triangle LFO walks the Algorithm knob from crossfade through fold and ring modulation and back, so the same two tones keep changing character. Narrow the LFO's amount to stay in one family, or move Timbre by hand. Meta Mod: Chebyshev Glow The last algorithm adds harmonics to a plain sine bass line, with a slow LFO moving Timbre from a pure tone to a bright, organ-like glow. Try Quality for cleaner top end, or Mix to blend the pure sine back in. Presets The preset bar of the Meta Mod view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Analog Ring Diode-style ring modulation with the internal oscillator. Ring Bells Inharmonic, bell-like sidebands from a sine carrier. Tremolo AM Amplitude modulation: slow oscillator wobbles the sound. Crossfade Blend Equal-power mix of carrier and modulator; sweep Timbre. Folded Input Wavefolded carrier with the modulator as fold source. Digital Ring Clean digital ring modulation: only sum and difference tones. Bitwise XOR Gritty digital combination of two sources. Bitwise AND Hollow, buzzy intersection of the two waveforms. Comparator Edge Hard-edged comparator tones that follow the input. Robot Vocoder Voice or drums in Modulator talk through a buzzy Carrier. Harmonic Pick Chebyshev: turns a sine into its Nth harmonic; sweep Timbre. Harmonic Shimmer Added harmonics blended under the dry signal. Algorithm Drift Between two algorithms: modulate Algorithm for morphing. Sub Osc Ring Low internal oscillator ring-modulates for growling bass. Metallic Clang Mismatched diodes and a bright oscillator: clangorous metal. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Algorithm 0 – 7 2 (analog ring) Timbre 0 – 100 % 50 % Carrier Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Mod Level 0 – 200 % 100 % Osc Tune −24 … +24 st 0 st Osc Shape 0 – 100 % 0 % (sine) Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Osc Octave −3 … +3 0 Quality Eco (1×), Standard (2×), High (4×) Standard Bitwise Op XOR, AND, OR, Sum mod XOR All knobs are modulation destinations, evaluated every sample (audio-rate Algorithm and Timbre work). Osc Octave , Quality and Bitwise Op are settings. The view's algorithm strip sets Algorithm with a click. Inputs Input Signal What it does Carrier L audio the carrier; unpatched: the oscillator Carrier R audio right carrier; patched, the module runs in stereo, otherwise Carrier L feeds both sides Modulator audio the modulator (mono, shared); unpatched while the carrier is patched: the oscillator Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the oscillator's pitch, added to Osc Octave and Osc Tune ; 0.0 = C4 Sync trigger restarts the oscillator's cycle (hard sync) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the result after Mix ; Out R equals Out L in mono Osc audio the internal oscillator, whatever it is used for Env control, 0 … 1 envelope of the modulator

title: Spectral Blend
text: Spectral Blend Spectral Blend in the module view Introduction Spectral Blend takes two sounds apart in frequency and puts them together again in a different way. Every sound has a magnitude spectrum (which partials are there and how loud) and a phase spectrum (where each of them is in its cycle). By default the output uses the magnitudes of In A with the phases of In B : A's loudness shape, B's texture and timing. Two knobs let you morph either of them from A to B. Around the blend sit Blur and Smear (soften partials across frequency and time), a spectral gate in three frequency regions, Freeze , and Tilt , which bends the blend across the spectrum: low frequencies can follow A while the highs follow B. How does it work? The module cuts both inputs into overlapping frames, Hann-windowed, and takes the Fourier transform of each. In every frequency bin it picks a magnitude and a phase from A and B, does the blur, gate and smear, turns the bins back into sound and overlaps the frames again. The result is delayed by one frame ( FFT Size : 512 – 4096 samples, 11 – 85 ms at 48 kHz). Magnitude is where the loudness shape comes from: 0 % = A, 100 % = B. Phase is where the phases come from: 0 % = A, 100 % = B. With Magnitude 0 and Phase 100 you get cross-synthesis; the other way round swaps the roles; 0 and 0 is A alone (delayed), 100 and 100 is B alone. Morph Law : Linear mixes magnitudes by amplitude; Geometric mixes them in dB, so a partial present in only one sound stays quiet halfway: a cleaner morph. Tilt bends the Magnitude and Phase knobs across the spectrum around the Pivot : at +1 everything below the pivot is A and everything above is B, with a smooth crossover about two octaves wide; at −1 it is the other way round. Between, the knobs and the tilt share the work. Blur averages the magnitudes of neighbouring bins: partials widen and lose their edges. Smear makes the magnitudes fall slowly (up to about four seconds), so sounds leave a spectral afterglow. Gate Low / Mid / High remove every bin below a threshold in dB. The regions are separated by Split Low and Split High . At −90 dB a region is open. Invert Gate keeps what is below instead. Freeze (knob or Freeze gate input) holds the spectrum: the magnitudes stay and each bin keeps turning at its own rate, so tones go on as a steady drone. Mix blends the result with In A (delayed to match), Level sets the output gain. If nothing is patched into In B it is copied from In A . How to use it? Voice and synth: a spoken or sung line into In A , a rich pad into In B . The pad is articulated like the voice. Swap them to hear the difference. Drums with a texture: a drum loop into In A and sustained noise into In B : the beat in a different material. Two instruments in one: Tilt at +1 with a bass in A and a bright synth in B. Hold a chord: set Freeze while a chord plays. Add Blur for a pad. Clean up or destroy: use the gate to cut quiet bins and keep the skeleton, or Invert Gate to keep only the quiet bins. Single input: with B unpatched, Blur , Smear and the gate act as a spectral processor for A alone. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Spectral Blend does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Spectral Blend under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Spectral Blend: Drums Wear a Pad A drum loop in A and a sustained minor chord in B: it keeps the pad's colour while every hit chops it into the beat's spectral shape. Swap Magnitude and Phase (0/1 against 1/0) to hear which sound lends the rhythm and which the tone. Spectral Blend: Bass Below, Arp Above A bass line in A and a bright arpeggio in B are joined at a pivot frequency: with Tilt up, the lows come from the bass and the highs from the arp, so one sound seems to play both. A slow LFO moves the Pivot up and down; try a Tilt of -1 to turn the roles around. Spectral Blend: Frozen Moments A pluck melody runs through Spectral Blend while a gate from a clock divider freezes the spectrum on every other bar, turning a single note into a long drone under the live line. Change the divider for shorter or longer holds, or add Blur to soften the frozen chord. Spectral Blend: Partials Come and Go A drum loop goes into In A alone, and the spectral gate removes every frequency bin below a threshold while Smear leaves a spectral afterglow; a slow LFO on the mid gate lets partials appear and vanish. Raise Smear for a bigger wash or turn on Invert Gate to keep only what is quiet. Spectral Blend: Geometric Morph Two different melodies, a soft sine line in A and a buzzy saw line in B, are morphed in the geometric law, where a partial only one of them has stays quiet halfway, so the change is smooth. Slow random values move Magnitude and Phase; try Linear for a cruder cross-fade. Presets The preset bar of the Spectral Blend view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Cross Synthesis The loudness shape of In A with the phases of In B: A speaks with B's texture. Phase Swap The reverse: B's shape on A's phases. Half and Half Both magnitudes and phases halfway between the two sounds. Geometric Morph A morph that follows loudness in dB: partials present in only one sound stay quiet. Low A, High B Below 1 kHz it is A, above it is B, with a smooth crossover. High A, Low B The other way round: B's lows under A's highs. Soft Blur A single input made hazy; the blur softens its partials. Wash Blur and a long smear turn anything into a slowly fading wash. Spectral Tail Half dry, half a lingering ghost of the spectrum. Ghost Gate A spectral gate removes everything quiet: what is left is a skeleton of the loudest partials. Inverse Gate Keeps only what is below the threshold: the sound without its loudest partials. Bass Keeper Lows pass untouched, the mids and highs are gated hard. Frozen Moment Holds the spectrum at the moment of switching on, as a steady drone. Crisp Cross Short frames: tighter timing, rougher pitch resolution. Dark Tilt Mostly B's shape and A's phases, with B's highs pushed back. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Magnitude 0 – 100 % 0 % Phase 0 – 100 % 100 % Tilt −1 – +1 0 Pivot 100 Hz – 8 kHz 1 kHz Blur 0 – 100 % 0 % Smear 0 – 100 % 0 % Gate Low / Mid / High −90 – 0 dB −90 dB (open) Split Low 80 Hz – 2 kHz 400 Hz Split High 800 Hz – 12 kHz 3 kHz Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Level −24 – +12 dB 0 dB Settings Setting Values Default Morph Law Linear, Geometric Linear Invert Gate on / off off Freeze on / off off FFT Size 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 2048 Inputs Input Signal What it does In A audio the first sound In B audio the second sound; copied from In A when unpatched Freeze gate holds the spectrum while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the blended sound, delayed by one FFT size Origin Short-time Fourier analysis with overlap-add resynthesis, and the idea of combining one sound's magnitudes with another's phases, are textbook signal processing. The code was written for this module; nothing was ported.

title: Delay
text: Delay Delay in the module view Introduction Delay is a simple stereo echo. Each side has its own time, either free in milliseconds or locked to the song's tempo. The echoes return through a low cut and a high cut, so they can get thinner or darker with every repeat, and Ping-Pong bounces them from side to side. Put it after anything that needs echoes: a lead, a drum bus, a vocal. For long, strange or reversed delays use Zone Delay instead. How does it work? The input goes into one delay line per side. What comes out of the line is mixed with the dry signal ( Mix ), and a part of it ( Feedback ) goes back in, after the filters, so every echo is a little quieter than the one before. Free: Time L and Time R in milliseconds. Tempo: Rate L and Rate R are note values (1/32 … 1/1, straight, dotted . and triplet T ) at the song's tempo. Change the tempo and the echoes follow. Link L/R: with this on, the right side uses the left side's time (or rate), in both Free and Tempo. Turn one knob and both sides follow. Stereo: both sides are independent. A mono source patched into In L only is heard in both ears, and with different times on the two sides you get a wide stereo echo. Ping-Pong: the first echo is on the left, the second on the right, the third on the left again. The input is mixed to mono first. Changing a time while the sound plays, by hand, with a modulator or by changing the tempo, makes the echoes slide in pitch like a tape echo. They never click. Turn Time quickly for a classic dub effect. Feedback at 100 % repeats forever without getting louder; up to 200 % the repeats grow until the soft limiter holds them. Low Cut and High Cut only work on the repeats, so the first sound stays untouched. How to use it? Slapback: Free , both times 80–120 ms, Feedback 0–10 %. Dotted eighth: Tempo , Rate 1/8., Feedback 40 %. The classic rhythm echo that fills the gaps. Wide echo: Tempo with Rate L 1/8 and Rate R 1/8., Mode Stereo . Ping-pong: Mode Ping-Pong , both rates 1/4, High Cut around 4 kHz. Dub: Feedback 70–90 %, Low Cut 200 Hz, High Cut 2 kHz and turn Time . Send effect: Mix 100 % on an effect track or a send; keep the dry signal in the mixer. Presets The preset bar of the Delay view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Eighth Echo A clean tempo-synced eighth-note echo. Dotted Eighth The rhythmic dotted echo that fills gaps. Tape Slap Short slapback with a dull top. Ping-Pong Bounce Repeats bounce left and right. Stereo Offset Different times per side widen the echo. Dub Echo Filtered, long repeats that darken as they fade. Triplet Ping-Pong Rolling triplet bounce. Quarter Note Wash Spacious quarter-note repeats. Chorus Doubler Very short times thicken a sound like a double-track. Comb Resonance Millisecond delays with feedback ring as a metallic comb. Long Haunt Slow, distant repeats for ambience. Half Note Ping-Pong Wide, slow bounces. Thin Radio Echo Band-limited, small-speaker echo. Endless Repeat Near-infinite feedback; the filters keep it from blowing up. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Delay does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Delay under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Delay: Dotted Echo A bright pluck line gets a left echo on a dotted eighth and a right echo on a quarter note, so the repeats weave a rhythm of their own. Change Rate L and Rate R, or raise Feedback for longer trails. Delay: Ping-Pong Bounce Ping-Pong mode bounces each note from one side to the other in sixteenth steps while the arpeggio itself stays sparse. Switch Mode to Stereo to hear the same echoes stay put, or push Feedback up. Delay: Slapback Kit A very short free-time delay of about 80 ms with almost no Feedback thickens the drums into a live-room slap. Try Time L and Time R a few milliseconds apart for width, or lengthen both until it becomes an echo. Delay: Dub Spiral High Feedback keeps the echoes spiralling while High Cut slowly closes and opens under an LFO, so each repeat gets darker and then brighter. Edit the LFO rate, or raise Low Cut to thin out the build-up. Delay: Wide Double Two unrelated short times, 23 ms on the left and 37 ms on the right, fatten a slow pad into a wide stereo cloud with no audible echo. Move the Time knobs a little, or turn on Link L/R and watch the image collapse. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Time L 1 … 2000 ms 300 ms Time R 1 … 2000 ms 300 ms Feedback 0 … 200 % 40 % Low Cut 20 … 2000 Hz 20 Hz (off) High Cut 500 … 20000 Hz 20 kHz (off) Mix 0 … 100 % 50 % Sync Free, Tempo Free Rate L 1/32 … 1/1 1/8 Rate R 1/32 … 1/1 1/8 Mode Stereo, Ping-Pong Stereo Link L/R Off, On Off Time shows with Sync on Free , Rate with Sync on Tempo . The longest time is 4 seconds. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio Left input In R audio Right input; unpatched it follows In L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L audio Dry and echoes, left Out R audio Dry and echoes, right

title: Delay Net
text: Delay Net Delay Net in the module view Introduction Delay Net is a network of up to eight delay lines whose repeats feed each other. One Time knob sets the span of the network, Taps how many lines take part and Scatter how they're spaced, from even rhythmic echoes to clustered bursts. Some lines can play backwards, every pass through the network can be filtered, saturated or worn down, and Routing decides how the lines feed each other. Small settings give multi-tap rhythms; large ones turn a single hit into an evolving texture. How does it work? Taps. Each tap is its own delay line. The last one sits at Time ; the others are spread before it. With Scatter at 0 they're evenly spaced (4 taps over 1 s: 250, 500, 750, 1000 ms); turning it up bunches them towards the end, down towards the start. Jitter moves every tap away from its place by a seeded random amount (up to half the gap to its neighbours), so the groove is loose but the same every time. Taps is continuous: between two whole numbers the next tap fades in and the others slide to their new places, so modulating it is smooth. Time. In Free , Time is 5 ms – 8 s. With a note value in Sync , the network spans that note at the song's tempo and the Time knob scales it by ¼, ½, 1 or 2 (four zones of the knob): 4 taps over 1/2 give straight eighths. With a cable in Clock , the span is the pulse interval × ¼, ½, 1, 2, 3 or 4. Time Change picks how time changes sound: Crossfade (the default; a second head jumps to the new time and the two crossfade over 40 ms, the pitch stays) or Tape (the heads glide, the repeats bend in pitch). Reverse turns a share of the active taps around: they play the last stretch of audio backwards (windows as long as the tap's own time, up to about 5 s). Which taps turn follows a seeded order, so raising Reverse adds them one at a time. Character processes every repeat before it goes back into the network, so later repeats are darker, dirtier or more worn than early ones: Character Each pass 0 % Clean nothing 20 % Warm 6 kHz low-pass, 60 Hz high-pass, soft saturation 40 % Filter a band-pass per tap, spread over ±1 octave around 1.2 kHz: every echo its own colour 60 % Drive asymmetric saturation (+12 dB), 4 kHz low-pass 80 % Crush 8 kHz sample rate, 8 bits 100 % Wear wow and flutter, a little noise, 3 kHz low-pass, a little level loss: an old tape loop Positions in between blend two neighbours. Tone moves every filter up or down by up to two octaves. Routing decides where each repeat goes: Routing Where Sound Parallel each line into itself independent multi-tap echoes Chain line 1 → 2 → 3 …, the last nowhere a cascade that grows longer, then stops Ring 1 → 2 → … → last → 1 repeats walk around the network Mesh all into all (Hadamard) dense, diffuse, reverb-like build-up Feedback at 100 % is the edge of stability for every routing; above it the loop's soft limiter holds the level, up to 200 %. Switching Routing crossfades over 50 ms. Stereo. The taps alternate left and right, spread by Width (0 % is centred). Tap 1 … Tap 4 put out those lines on their own, before panning. Pulse fires at each tap's time after every input onset: a rhythm of the echoes to clock other modules with. Freeze (the button or the gate) fades the input out, sets the feedback to exactly 1 and bypasses the character: the network circulates without loss (Ring and Mesh keep the material moving; Chain loops back to its start while frozen). Clear empties every line with a short fade. Tails and renders. Stopping the transport leaves the network ringing. With Clear on Play the lines are emptied when the transport starts; Jitter, the reverse order and Wear's wow and noise come from Seed , so renders repeat. How to use it? Multi-tap rhythm: Parallel, Sync 1/2, 4 taps, Feedback 30 %, Jitter 20 % for a human feel. Rotating echoes: Ring, Sync 1 bar, 3 taps, Scatter +0.5, Width 100 %. Instant ambience: Mesh, Time 150 ms, 8 taps, Feedback 85 %, Character 20 %. Reverse swells: Reverse 50 %, Time 1.5 s, Feedback 50 %. Lo-fi tape loop: Character 100 %, Feedback 95 %, then Freeze. Echo clock: patch Pulse into a drum's trigger: it plays along with the repeats of whatever you feed in. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Delay Net does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Delay Net under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Delay Net: Ring Cloud Six taps pass the signal round a ring, so a sparse melody dissolves into a drifting cloud of repeats. Try Taps, Scatter and Character, or switch Routing to Parallel to hear the ring unravel. Delay Net: Parallel Rhythm Taps In Parallel routing each tap is a separate echo, locked to a dotted eighth so the taps spread into a rhythm around a bright pluck. Change Sync, Scatter or Taps to re-space the pattern. Delay Net: Reverse Tide Chain routing with a large Reverse amount turns the repeats backwards, so every note swells in before it arrives. Lower Reverse for normal echoes, or raise Jitter to blur the swells. Delay Net: Mesh Swarm Mesh routing lets every line feed every other, and a slow LFO sweeps Scatter so the swarm of repeats keeps rearranging itself. Try more Jitter and Character for a rougher texture, or less Feedback to calm it. Delay Net: Frozen Moment A square LFO closes the Freeze gate every few bars, trapping the network's contents as a sustained wash while the melody carries on over it. Change the LFO's Sync, or latch the gate with your own control. Presets The preset bar of the Delay Net view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Ring A modest four-line ring that blooms into a cloud. Parallel Taps Four separate scattered echoes. Chain Cascade Each line feeds the next: cascading repeats. Mesh Cloud Every line feeds every other: a dense, reverb-like cloud. Tempo Scatter Eighth-note grid with uneven tap spacing. Wobbly Tape Jittered times and a worn character. Reverse Bloom Mostly reversed repeats. Dark Tunnel Long, dark repeats receding into the distance. Bright Glimmer Short bright taps shimmer around the signal. Slow Drift Multi-second delay lines for ambient layering. Dirty Loop Saturated feedback that builds a gritty loop. Granular Smear Tiny jittered lines smear into textures. Mono Pulse A single plain echo line in mono. Swell Cathedral Near-unity feedback: swells for ages; turn the mix down first. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Time 5 ms – 8 s 600 ms Taps 1 – 8 (continuous) 4 Scatter −1 … +1 0 Jitter 0 – 100 % 0 % Reverse 0 – 100 % 0 % Feedback 0 – 200 % 45 % Character 0 – 100 % 20 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Width 0 – 100 % 70 % Mix 0 – 100 % 40 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Routing Parallel, Chain, Ring, Mesh Ring Sync Free, 4 bars … 1/16T Free Time Change Tape, Crossfade Crossfade Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the input (mixed to mono into the lines); In L alone feeds both Clock trigger the span is a multiple of the pulse interval Freeze gate the network circulates without loss while high Clear trigger empties all lines Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry and wet mixed by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the network only Tap 1 … Tap 4 audio lines 1 – 4 on their own Pulse trigger each tap's time after an input onset The lines hold 8 seconds each (about 16 MB at 48 kHz), so put Delay Net after a Voice Cell rather than inside one.

title: Room Print
text: Room Print Room Print in the module view Introduction Room Print is a convolution reverb: it makes any sound ring as if it had been played in the space whose "print" you load. The print is an impulse response, the recording of a clap or a sweep in a room, a spring, a tank or anything else, and you can drop your own WAV file on the module. Ten built-in prints are made in code, so it works without files. Because the print is just audio, you can stretch it, cut it, darken its tail, delay it and move the balance between its first reflections and its late wash. How does it work? Convolution. Every sample of the input is replaced by a copy of the whole print, scaled by that sample, and the copies are added. Done directly that is millions of multiplications per second, so Room Print splits the print into 512-sample parts and does the long ones with fast Fourier transforms ( partitioned convolution ). The first 512 samples are done directly, which makes the reverb latency-free . Impulse. Impulse chooses the print: Room , Hall , Cathedral , Plate , Spring (chirped echoes), Tank (ringing metal modes), Cave (dark, with large echoes), Swell (a tail played backwards), Gate (a dense burst cut off sharply), Echoes (ping-pong repeats), or Sample : the audio file you dropped on the view (WAV, or anything the app can decode), used as a stereo print (a mono file feeds both sides). Prints up to 4 s are used. Shape. These settings re-prepare the print (a moment after you move them): Stretch plays it at 0.5× – 2× speed (2× is half as long and an octave up), Trim Start and Trim End cut the front and the back, Damp Low and Damp High make the low (below about 220 Hz) or high (above about 3 kHz) part of the tail die away faster and leave the first sounds alone. The result is scaled to the same energy whatever the file, so changing prints does not change the level. Early and late. Early/Late is a balance: at the middle both are heard, down only the first reflections (the first 60 ms or so), up only the tail (from about 120 ms), with a smooth hand-over between. It can be modulated freely. Predelay (up to 0.5 s) delays the input before the print. Stereo. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides; with both, each input runs through its own channel of the print. Width narrows or widens the reverb's side signal (0 – 200 %). How to use it? A natural room: Hall or Room , Mix 20 – 30 %. Your own room: drop a recording of a room, set Impulse to Sample. A tail with no wash: Early/Late at 20 % keeps the room sound and drops the long tail: good for drums. A pad bloom: Swell at Mix 50 %, Predelay 80 ms. Metal and springs: Tank or Spring on a drum loop. A bigger or smaller room: Stretch 0.7 for larger and darker, 1.6 for a closet. Dark and distant: Damp High 70 % and Trim End 60 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Room Print does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Room Print under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Room Print: Hall Pluck A plucked melody in the built-in Hall response. The late part is cut a little with Early/Late and the highs of the tail damp early, so the hall sounds warm. Raise Mix for a bigger space or switch Impulse to Cathedral. Room Print: Drum Tank A drum loop through the ringing Tank response: every hit excites metal modes and the kit gets a resonant, clanging halo. Early/Late at the low end keeps only the first reflections for a tighter kit. Room Print: Spring Bounce A bass-heavy riff through the Spring response: chirping, repeating echoes that bounce behind every note. Stretch changes the pitch and length of the boing, and Damp High softens it. Room Print: Swell Bloom Short chords go through the Swell response: its tail is played backwards, so each note blooms into a rising wash after the sound has gone. Predelay moves the bloom; Trim Start makes it arrive sooner. Room Print: Gated Kit A drum loop in the Gate response: a dense burst that stops abruptly, giving every hit a big, short, cut-off space. Stretch lengthens or shortens the burst, Mix sets how much is added. Presets The preset bar of the Room Print view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Small Room A short, close room. Warm Hall A hall with the highs fading early. Cathedral A very long, lofty tail. Bright Plate Dense and bright, without early reflections. Spring Tank Chirped, boingy echoes. Metal Tank Ringing metal modes. Deep Cave Dark, with a few large echoes. Swell Bloom The reverb grows before the sound. Gated Burst A dense burst cut off sharply. Ping Pong Echoes Repeats that bounce left and right. Tight Early Only the first reflections: room without wash. Distant Wash Only the late tail, dark and far. Big and Dark Stretched to a huge, murky space. Closet A tiny, bright box. Wide Plate A plate with exaggerated width. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does In L, In R audio the dry input (one patched: mono) Out L, Out R audio dry/wet mix Knobs and settings Control Range Default Impulse 10 built-in, Sample Hall Mix 0 – 100 % 35 % Predelay 0 – 500 ms 0 Early/Late 0 – 100 % 50 % Width 0 – 200 % 100 % Level 0 – 100 % 50 % Stretch 0.5 × – 2 × 1 × Trim Start 0 – 90 % 0 Trim End 5 – 100 % 100 % Damp Low, Damp High 0 – 100 % 0 Impulse and the Shape settings are plain settings; the others are modulation destinations. Samples are stored in the shared media folder; the board keeps only the file's id. Room Print uses several megabytes of memory per instance: in a Voice Cell it multiplies, and the board will warn you.

title: Verb
text: Verb Verb in the module view Introduction Verb is a stereo reverb built to be played , not just set. Every knob, including Size and Decay , can be modulated, even at audio rate, without zipper noise or clicks. It goes from small rooms through halls to endless, slowly drifting pads, and Freeze holds whatever is in the reverb for as long as you like. Patch an envelope onto Size for swelling spaces, an LFO onto Decay for breathing tails, or a sequencer onto Freeze for rhythmic holds. Switch Type to Spring and the same knobs drive a different tank: a metallic, dispersive, boingy spring-like tail. How does it work? The sound first passes a pre-delay , then four diffusers per channel (allpass filters that smear the onset into a dense wash), then the tank : a feedback delay network of 16 delay lines (8 in Eco quality) whose outputs are mixed and fed back into each other. Every line loses a little level and a little treble on each pass, which sets how long and how dark the tail is. Slow internal modulation of the line lengths keeps the tail from ringing metallically. Size scales every delay in the tank, from a small booth (≈ 3 m) to a huge space (≈ 60 m). Moving it bends the tail in pitch like tape speeding up or slowing down, never a click; very fast modulation turns into a shimmer. Decay is the time the tail takes to fall by 60 dB (T60), 0.1 s to 60 s. Above that the knob enters the infinite zone: between 92 % and 96 % the decay stretches towards endless, and from 96 % up the tail never fades (the view says Infinite ). New sound keeps piling up there, so a soft limiter steps in whenever the tank gets loud. Damping makes the highs die faster than the mids (at 100 % the treble decays ten times faster). Bass stretches (up to 2×) or shortens (down to ½) the lows. Diffusion : low values keep the early echoes audible; high values give a smooth wash. Mod Rate and Mod Depth : speed and amount of the internal movement. 0 % depth is static (and can ring); 100 % is a seasick chorus. Tone tilts the reverb around 800 Hz, ±6 dB: dark ↔ bright. Width sets the stereo width of the reverb: 0 % mono, 100 % as the tank makes it, 150 % wider. Mix blends dry and wet with equal power. Wet L/R always carry the reverb alone. Type: Hall and Spring Hall (the default) is the tank described above. Spring replaces it with a coil: for each channel a delay line the length of the coil, in a feedback loop with 36 chained allpass filters. The allpasses delay the lows more than the highs, so on every round trip a note is smeared into a falling chirp, and the echoes pile up into the metallic "sproing" of a real spring. The two channels are coils of different length, so a mono input still gives a stereo tail. A soft limiter (tanh) sits at the loop's write point, so loud input makes the tail compress, never explode. With Spring the knobs mean: Size is the length of the coil: 22 ms per round trip at 0 % (a tight, fast flutter) to 122 ms at 100 % (slow, separate drips). Moving it bends the pitch of the tail. Diffusion is the dispersion : how strongly the lows lag the highs. At 0 % the coil is only a ringing delay; at 100 % each hit becomes a long, drooping chirp. Decay , Damping and Bass work as in the hall (T60 per round trip, treble loss, low-band T60). Damping at 40 % already gives the dull, wet tone of a coil. The infinite zone holds the coil indefinitely. Mod Depth makes it boing: the level of what enters the coil shortens the loop for a moment, so every hit bends upward and then sags back as the hit dies away. A slow wobble of the length (speed: Mod Rate ) is added. At 0 % the coil is static. Pre-delay , Tone , Width , Mix , Freeze and Clear behave as before. Quality and Seed only belong to the hall and are hidden while Spring is selected. Switching Type goes through the same 10 ms fade as Quality and Seed : the old tail is cut cleanly, the new tank starts empty.
