Room: early reflections Real rooms announce themselves before the tail starts: the first few echoes off the walls, floor and ceiling arrive as separate, panned clicks that tell the ear how big the room is and where you stand in it. Room adds exactly that, ahead of either tank: Booth , Studio , Club , Hall or Chapel ( Off by default). Verb places a source and a listener in a box of that size and works out where the sound bounces: the 24 earliest echoes, each with its own delay, level, stereo position and darkening (walls and air swallow the highs with every bounce). Early sets their level (100 % has the energy of the dry sound), and Size stretches the room from half to double its size. Pre-delay, Tone, Width and Freeze apply to the reflections as to the tail. Freeze (the gate input, or the latching Freeze button in the view): within 20 ms the input to the tank fades out and the tail stops decaying. The modulation keeps running, so the held sound shimmers instead of freezing solid. Size and Mod Depth still act on it; Decay , Damping and Bass return when you release. The dry path is untouched, so you can play over a frozen pad. Clear (trigger input or button) fades the reverb out over 10 ms, empties it and fades back in. Clear on Play empties it when the transport starts, so two renders of the same section are identical. Otherwise a tail from before keeps ringing, as on a hardware reverb. The internal modulation restarts from Seed on every transport start, so it repeats too. Changing Quality or Seed also goes through a short fade. Pre-delay Sync sets the pre-delay to a note value at the song tempo (1/64 to 1/2, straight, dotted or triplet, at most 1 s); the Pre-delay knob is hidden then. The view shows the decay of the lows, mids and highs from the current (modulated) settings on a log time axis, with the pre-delay as a gap, a Freeze button that lights while frozen (from the button or the gate), and a meter of the wet level. How to use it? Send effect: Mix 100 %, feed it from a send or a mixer's aux, take Out (or Wet ) back in. Insert: Mix 20–40 % directly after a voice or a drum bus. Swelling space: an ADSR onto Size (and a little onto Decay ). Breathing tail: a slow LFO onto Decay or Damping . Endless pad: Decay at the top (Infinite), Mix 100 %, play chords in, then lower Decay to let it go. Or Freeze with a gate from a sequencer for rhythmic holds. Ducked reverb: the Env output of a drum bus onto Mix with a negative amount. Tempo pre-delay: Pre-delay Sync 1/16 or 1/8 keeps the reverb off the transient, in time. Shimmer-ish: Mod Depth high, Mod Rate 2–4 Hz, Tone bright. Boing spring: Type Spring, Size about 40 %, Diffusion 70 % or more, Mod Depth 40 %. Feed it short, bright hits (a click, a snare, a plucked tone) and sweep Size for a coil being stretched. Dub throw: Type Spring, Mix 100 % on an aux, a gate or a drum trigger onto the input, Decay about 3 s; ride Decay up for a throw. A place for a dry sound: Room Studio, Early 60 %, Decay about 1 s, Pre-delay 0: a close, believable room around a drum or a voice. Spatial effects: an audio-rate oscillator onto Size turns the tail into a frequency-modulated cloud. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Verb does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Verb under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Verb: Endless Hall Sparse, soft notes sink into a huge hall: Size is almost full, Decay is over twenty seconds and Pre-delay leaves each note clean before the bloom. Try Decay and Size together, or push Mix to 100 %. Verb: Drum Booth A drum beat in a tiny, dry room: low Size, a short Decay and high Damping glue the kit together. Raise Size and Decay to move the same beat into a hall, or widen it with Width. Verb: Frozen Chord A square LFO closes the Freeze gate for a couple of bars at a time, holding whatever is in the tank as an endless chord, then lets go so the next phrase can be caught. Edit the LFO's Sync, or latch Freeze yourself. Verb: Tide Pool Slow LFOs ride Size and Tone while Mod Depth swirls the tail, so the room seems to inhale and exhale around a gentle arpeggio. Every Verb knob modulates click-free: patch your own LFO into Decay. Verb: Dark Cellar A low plucked bass line in a cellar: Bass is boosted, Tone and Damping pull the tail dark, and Eco quality keeps it light. Lower Bass or lift Tone to hear the same room turn into a bright stairwell. Presets The preset bar of the Verb view has 18 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Small Room A tight room for natural ambience. Medium Hall General-purpose hall. Bright Plate Dense, bright and fast building plate. Vocal Space Pre-delay keeps a voice clear in front. Warm Chamber Dark and cozy. Big Cathedral Huge stone space with a long tail. Wide Pad A lush, wide wash for sustained sounds. Shimmer Mod Heavy modulation gives a chorus-like shimmer. Gated Snap Short, punchy burst for snares. Dub Spring Sparse, metallic-sounding tail. Dark Abyss Very long, dark and rumbling. Infinite Freeze Practically endless; gate Freeze to hold a chord. Mono Closet Very small and mono: a hint of space. Eco Wash A cheaper eight-line reverb for busy patches. Boing Spring A bright coil that bends up on every hit and droops back: feed it clicks and snares. Long Drip A long coil with slow, separate drips; the lows trail behind the highs. Tight Flutter A short coil: fast metallic flutter with little chirp. Held Coil An endless, wobbling metal drone; play into it, then lower Decay to let it go. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Size 0 – 100 % 50 % Decay 0.1 s – 60 s, then ∞ (top 8 % of the knob) 2.5 s Pre-delay 0 – 1000 ms 20 ms Diffusion 0 – 100 % 70 % Damping 0 – 100 % 40 % Bass 0.5× – 2× 1× Mod Rate 0.05 – 8 Hz 0.6 Hz Mod Depth 0 – 100 % 25 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Width 0 – 150 % 100 % Mix 0 – 100 % 35 % Pre-delay Sync Free, 1/64 … 1/2 (triplet, straight, dotted) Free Quality Eco (8 lines), Fine (16 lines) Fine Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Freeze (latch) Off, On Off Type Hall, Spring Hall Room Off, Booth, Studio, Club, Hall, Chapel Off Early 0 – 100 % 50 % Decay: the knob reads seconds; past 60 s (92 %) it is the infinite zone, from 96 % fully infinite. Damping: high T60 = Decay × (1 − 0.9 × Damping). Bass: low T60 (below ≈ 250 Hz) = Decay × Bass. Type: the tank. Hall is the 8/16-line FDN, Spring the dispersive coil (see above). Not modulatable. Diffusion is the coil's dispersion, Size its length (22 – 122 ms) and Mod Depth the boing in Spring . Room / Early: the early-reflections box and its level (see above); both types. Quality: Eco costs about half the CPU; Fine is denser. Hall only. Seed: the start phases and rates of the internal modulation. Hall only. Freeze (latch): the view's Freeze button; saved with the board (the reverb itself opens empty). The settings are not modulatable; all knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Freeze gate while high, the reverb holds its contents (ORed with the latch) Clear trigger empties the reverb with a 10 ms fade Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the dry/wet mix set by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the reverb only (after Tone and Width ) Env control, 0 – 1 envelope follower on the wet signal (5 ms attack, 200 ms release) Verb uses about 2.5 MB of memory per instance at 48 kHz (the Spring tank needs less). Inside a Voice Cell every voice gets its own reverb, so it's usually better placed after the cell.

title: Zone Delay
text: Zone Delay Zone Delay in the module view Introduction Zone Delay is one stereo delay for every delay time worth having: tuned combs and flanging, doubling and slapback, rhythmic echoes and loops of up to 20 seconds. Zone picks the time range and Time moves within it. The other knobs shape what happens to the repeats: how they sound, how much they smear into a cloud and how they move across the stereo field. Three switches turn it into a performance instrument: Reverse , Hold and Ping-Pong . How does it work? Zones. Each zone is a time range; Time moves through it exponentially. Zone Name Free range Synced values 1 Comb 0.25 – 12 ms – (follows Pitch ) 2 Short 8 – 120 ms 1/128 … 1/32 3 Echo 80 ms – 1.2 s 1/32 … 1/2 4 Long 0.6 – 5 s 1/4 … 2 bars 5 Vast 3 – 20 s 1 bar … 8 bars The view prints the actual time. With Sync on Transport , Time steps through the zone's note values (straight, dotted and triplet) at the song's tempo. With a cable in Clock , the time is the interval between the last two pulses, and Time picks a ratio of it (¼, ⅓, ½, ⅔, 1, 3/2, 2, 3, 4). In the Comb zone with a cable in Pitch , the delay is tuned to that note ( Time becomes ±12 semitones), so a Voice Cell's pitch plays the comb in tune. Time changes. Time Change decides what happens when the time moves: Tape: the read head glides to the new time ( Glide ), so the repeats bend in pitch like a tape echo. Modulating Time fast gives FM-like wobbles, always without clicks. Crossfade: a second head jumps to the new time and the two crossfade (30 ms in Comb and Short, 60 ms in Echo, 120 ms in Long and Vast). The pitch never changes; fast modulation becomes stepped. The repeats. Feedback sets how much of each repeat comes back; above 100 % the loop grows until the character's saturation holds it, a stable, compressed drone. Character morphs through five loop sounds: Character Sound 0 % Clean flat, only a 20 kHz low-pass 25 % Tape 7 kHz low-pass, 40 Hz high-pass, soft saturation, a little hiss 50 % Dark 2.2 kHz low-pass, 120 Hz high-pass, gentle saturation 75 % Band a band-pass at 1 kHz: telephone repeats 100 % Lo-Fi 12 kHz sample-rate reduction, 10 bits, 5 kHz low-pass Positions in between blend two neighbours. The character colours every pass, so later repeats are darker or dirtier than early ones. Tone moves all its filters up or down by up to two octaves. Diffuse adds allpass diffusion in the feedback path: the first echo stays clear, later ones dissolve into a cloud; at 100 % with high feedback it becomes a reverb with the delay time as its pre-delay. Stereo. Offset makes the right side's time longer (positive) or shorter (negative) than the left's. Wobble adds slow tape wow and a little flutter, chorus-like in the short zones and subtle in the long ones. Ping-Pong crosses the feedback over, and the first repeat starts on the left only, so even a mono source bounces from side to side. Reverse plays the last Time worth of audio backwards in overlapping windows; the reversed sound is fed back, so repeats alternate direction. Hold stops recording and loops what is in the buffer, without any loss; Time then changes the loop's speed (Tape) or its length (Crossfade), and Reverse plays the held loop backwards. Release Hold and the input comes back. The three buttons in the view latch; the gate inputs work while high. Tails and renders. Stopping the transport leaves the echoes ringing. With Clear on Play the buffer is emptied when the transport starts, so renders start from silence and repeat exactly; Wobble restarts from Seed either way. How to use it? Dub echo: Zone 3, Sync on Transport , Time on 1/8., Feedback 70 %, Character 30 %. Ride Tone and Feedback by hand. Karplus pluck in a Voice Cell: Zone 1, Pitch from Voice In › Pitch , a short noise burst into In L , Feedback 95 %, Mix 100 %. Flanger: Zone 1 without Pitch , an LFO on Time , Feedback 60 %. Tape-stop scratches: Tape mode with a short Glide, a stepped random source on Time . Looper: Zone 5, Mix 50 %, press Hold to keep a phrase; Reverse plays it backwards. Ambient wash: Zone 4, Feedback 90 %, Diffuse 80 %, Wobble 40 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Zone Delay does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Zone Delay under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Zone Delay: Tuned Combs Zone 1 turns the delay into a tuned comb: a drum loop is pushed through it while a sequencer plays its Pitch input, so the beat rings out a melody. Change Feedback for a longer ring, or Zone to leave the comb behind. Zone Delay: Tape Echo Zone 3 in Tape mode with a little Wobble: a plucked line is followed by warm, drifting echoes that darken as they repeat. Raise Wobble and Character for a worn tape, or move Time while it plays to hear the pitch slide. Zone Delay: Loop Catcher In the longest zone a square LFO raises Hold every other bar group, so the delay stops listening and loops what it just heard while the live melody plays over it. Change the LFO's Sync, or fire Hold from a Button. Zone Delay: Reverse Bounce Two square LFOs gate Reverse and Ping-Pong on their own cycles, so the echoes of an arpeggio flip backwards and hop between the speakers in changing combinations. Edit either LFO, or turn Diffuse up to blur the reversals. Zone Delay: Smeared Pad Zone 2 with Diffuse and Character turned up blurs a slow chord progression into a soft, slowly shifting wash. Lower Diffuse to bring back distinct echoes, or change Offset to push the left and right times apart. Presets The preset bar of the Zone Delay view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Tape Echo Classic mid-range echo with tape colour. Dub Echo Tempo-synced dub repeats; ride Tone and Feedback. Slapback Short single repeat. Stereo Spread The right side lags the left for a wide echo. Flanger In the comb zone: sweep Time with an LFO. Tuned Comb Resonant ring; patch a pitch in to tune it. Chorus Double Short, modulated times thicken a sound. Diffuse Cloud Repeats melt into an ambient cloud. Ambient Wash Long, washy feedback. Looper Multi-second loop: patch Hold to keep a phrase. Lo-Fi Loop A saturated, degraded loop that gets dirtier with each pass. Crossfade Echo Clean time changes without pitch bending. Tape Dive Slow glide: changing Time bends the echoes. Bright Ping Clear and bright quick repeats. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Zone 1 – 5 (stepped) 3 Time 0 – 100 % of the zone 50 % Feedback 0 – 200 % 40 % Character 0 – 100 % 25 % Tone −1 … +1 0 Diffuse 0 – 100 % 0 % Offset −50 … +50 % 0 % Wobble 0 – 100 % 10 % Mix 0 – 100 % 35 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Sync Free, Transport Free Time Change Tape, Crossfade Tape Glide 5 ms – 2 s (Tape) 150 ms Clear on Play Off, On Off Seed 0 – 999 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio the input; In L alone feeds both sides Clock trigger the time is the pulse interval × the ratio Time picks Pitch pitch Comb zone: tunes the delay to the note Reverse gate repeats play backwards while high Hold gate the buffer loops while high Ping-Pong gate repeats bounce between the sides while high Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry and wet mixed by Mix Wet L, Wet R audio the repeats only Tap trigger a pulse each time the delay time elapses The delay holds 30 seconds per side (about 16 MB at 48 kHz), so put it after a Voice Cell rather than inside one.

title: Chorus
text: Chorus Chorus in the module view Introduction The Chorus makes one sound into several: it mixes the input with copies of itself that are delayed by a few milliseconds, with the delay time swinging up and down. The slightly changing delay detunes the copies against the original, which sounds like several players, or a wide, shimmering instrument. Set to a very short delay with feedback it becomes a flanger , with the sweeping comb-filter whoosh of jet planes and tape machines. How does it work? Each channel has a short delay line. A triangle LFO swings its delay time around the centre Delay , with Depth as the share of the centre time it moves. A bit of the delayed signal is fed back into the delay line ( Feedback ). In Chorus mode every channel has two voices, with the LFO half a cycle apart and slightly different delay times, so the sound is thicker. In Flanger mode there is one voice per channel and the feedback is a little more generous. Rate is the LFO speed, 0.02 to 10 Hz. Slow rates (0.2–0.8 Hz) are lush, fast ones become vibrato. Depth is how far the delay time swings. More depth is a stronger detune. Delay is the centre delay time. Chorus likes 7–20 ms; a flanger 0.5–5 ms. Feedback sends the delayed signal back in. Positive feedback emphasises the comb's peaks (metallic ring); negative feedback emphasises the notches (hollow, "inverted" flanging). Chorus uses little or none. Spread moves the right channel's LFO away from the left, up to half a cycle, which makes a wide stereo movement. At 0 both sides move together. Mode is Chorus or Flanger. Mix blends dry and wet. 50 % is the classic setting; the flanger notches are deepest at 50 %. Mix, rate, depth, delay and feedback can all be modulated. Modulating Delay with another LFO is how tape-style wobble is made. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Lush chorus on a pad: Chorus mode, Rate 0.4 Hz, Depth 50 %, Delay 12 ms, Mix 40 %. Jet flanger: Flanger mode, Rate 0.15 Hz, Depth 80 %, Delay 2 ms, Feedback 70 %, Mix 50 %. Hollow flanger: the same with Feedback −70 %. Vibrato: Rate 5 Hz, Depth 20 %, Mix 100 % (no dry signal means no chorus effect, only pitch wobble). Slap thickener on a guitar: Delay 20 ms, Depth 0 %, Mix 30 %. Origin The modulated-delay voice (swinging delay with feedback, and the flanger's extra sample of delay) is from Chorus and Flanger (DaisySP) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version puts both effects in one stereo module, with an LFO phase spread, cubic interpolation, feedback in both polarities and a rate in hertz. The original licence text is in this module's LICENSE file. Presets The preset bar of the Chorus view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Classic Chorus Lush, general-purpose stereo chorus. Subtle Thicken Barely there doubling for synths and guitars. Wide Ensemble Big, spread string-machine style width. Slow Wash Very slow, deep movement for pads. Shimmer Fast Quick, shallow wobble. Vibrato Fully wet: pure pitch vibrato. Tape Warble Seasick, wobbly detune. Soft Flanger Gentle sweeping comb filter. Jet Flanger Intense jet-plane sweep. Negative Flange Negative feedback: hollow, nasal flanging. Metallic Ring Almost static comb that rings with a pitch. Deep Doubler Long delay times give a slapback-like double. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Chorus does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Chorus under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Chorus: Lush Pad A mono saw pad is turned into a wide, slowly shimmering ensemble by the Chorus: slow Rate, plenty of Depth and full Spread. Raise Rate for a faster wobble or lower Spread to hear the stereo image collapse. Chorus: Jet Flanger In Flanger mode with strong Feedback and a short Delay, a beat and a hat-heavy groove get a slow jet-engine sweep through every sound. Lower Feedback for a mild swirl or raise Depth for a wider sweep. Chorus: Detuned Pluck Ensemble A bright pluck melody gets a gentle Chorus with a short Delay and small Depth: it thickens like a doubled instrument without obvious wobble. Increase Depth to push it toward a seasick vibrato. Chorus: Wobbly Vibrato With Mix at 100 % only the moving delay is heard, which wobbles the pitch like a warped tape: a fast Rate gives vibrato, a slow one a seasick drift. Lower Mix to blend the dry sound back in as a chorus. Chorus: Metallic Comb Sweep A flanger with negative Feedback hollows out a sustained saw, and an LFO slowly moves its Delay, so the tone sweeps through metallic, hollow resonances. Flip Feedback positive for a brighter, ringing comb.

title: Freq Shifter
text: Freq Shifter Freq Shifter in the module view Introduction The Freq Shifter moves every frequency of a sound up or down by the same number of hertz. That's different from a pitch shift: a pitch shift keeps the ratios between the partials, a frequency shift breaks them. A few tenths of a hertz give slow phasing and beating; tens or hundreds of hertz turn harmonic sounds into bells, metal and detuned radio. With feedback the shifted signal spirals up or down endlessly (the barber-pole effect). It's stereo, can shift the two channels in opposite directions, locks to the song's tempo, and its quadrature oscillator is available as a two-phase LFO. How does it work? Each channel goes through a Hilbert transformer : two allpass chains whose outputs are 90° apart at every frequency from 15 Hz up. Multiplied with a sine and cosine oscillator at the shift frequency, they give the two sidebands : Up moves every component up by the shift (1 kHz + 100 Hz = 1.1 kHz). Down moves it down (1 kHz − 100 Hz = 900 Hz). The other sideband is suppressed by about 40 dB. A negative shift swaps the two. Components pushed below 0 Hz come back up as positive frequencies (through-zero shifting), which is part of the sound. Shift sets the amount, as a percentage of Range : at ±200 Hz range, 50 % is +100 Hz. The knob is linear and bipolar (centre = no shift), so an LFO or an audio-rate cable on it is through-zero modulation of the shift. Fine adds −10…+10 Hz, for slow phasing at a wide range. Feedback sends the Up signal back into the input, optionally through a delay ( FB Delay ). At 0 ms (one sample) and a small shift you get the barber-pole phaser: a comb of notches that moves endlessly up or down. With 50–500 ms every echo is shifted a little further: rising or falling spirals. Negative values invert the fed-back signal. A soft limiter keeps ±100 % loud but bounded. Spread moves the right channel's shift from the same as the left (0 %) through stopped (50 %) to the opposite (100 %). With a mono input, Spread at 100 % and a 0.3 Hz shift, the phasing turns in opposite directions in the two ears. Mix blends the dry input with the Up signal for Out . The shifted signal is delayed a little by the allpass chains, so 50 % gives some extra phasing of its own. Sync locks the shift rate to the tempo: one cycle per note value, from 1/32 to 8 bars. The direction follows the sign of Shift ; Fine is not used. With the transport playing, the oscillator phase follows the song position, so a barber-pole phaser lands in the same place after a loop jump. Anti-alias filters the input (6-pole low-pass at 0.42 × the sample rate minus the shift) so content shifted past the top of the audio band doesn't fold back as noise. Down loses the same top end. Reset jumps the oscillator to phase 0 (with a 2 ms fade to hide the jump). The Sin and Cos outputs carry the left oscillator: at sub-audio shifts a two-phase LFO, at audio shifts two sines 90° apart. The view shows the spectrum of the input (grey) and of Out (colour): the shift shows up as a translation. The dial shows both oscillators turning. How to use it? Barber-pole phaser: Shift 0, Fine +0.3 Hz, Feedback 70 %, FB Delay 0, Mix 50 %. Negative Fine for a falling phaser. Bells from a pad: Range ±200 Hz, Shift 20–60 %, Mix 100 %. Harmonic sounds become inharmonic and metallic. Spirals: FB Delay 250 ms (or a dotted eighth by ear), Feedback 60 %, Shift ±10 % at ±200 Hz: each echo climbs or falls by 20 Hz. Stereo rotation: a mono source on In L , Spread 100 %, Fine 0.2 Hz. Through-zero FM: an LFO or an audio oscillator onto Shift with Shift at 0. Two-phase LFO: Range ±10 Hz, Shift a few percent, patch Sin and Cos to two destinations (e.g. the pan of two voices) for circular motion. Rhythmic phaser: Sync 1 bar, Shift slightly positive, Feedback 50 %. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Freq Shifter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Freq Shifter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Freq Shifter: Endless Rising Sweep A saw pad is shifted up by a tiny Fine amount, and strong Feedback sends it round again, so the phasing sweep seems to climb forever. Make Fine negative and it falls forever; raise Mix to hear more of the swirl. Freq Shifter: Pad into Bells With Shift raised on the 200 Hz range and Mix at 100 %, the harmonics of a pad move by a fixed number of Hz instead of staying in tune, so it turns into clanging, inharmonic bells. Reduce Shift toward zero to bring the pad back to a normal pitch. Freq Shifter: Opposite Shifts Widener Spread sends the left channel up and the right channel down by the same few Hz, so a mono riff becomes wide and slowly beating without any delay. Close Spread to hear the plain mono sound again. Freq Shifter: Robot Drum Downshift A broken beat is shifted down a few hundred Hz with some Feedback, so the kick loses its pitch and the snare and hats turn into clanking robot hits. Move Shift through zero and up to hear the effect change character. Freq Shifter: Quadrature Wobble The Shifter's own Sin output, a control signal that runs at the shift rate, opens and closes a filter on the same riff, so the phasing and the filter wobble stay locked together. Change Fine to speed up or slow down both. Presets The preset bar of the Freq Shifter view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Slow Barber Pole Endless, slow phasing against the dry sound. Gentle Detune Beating, chorus-like shimmer. Stereo Widener Opposite small shifts left and right for a wide image. Down Spiral Feedback makes the sound sink in steps. Up Spiral Rising, bell-like spiral. Phase Bells Metallic ringing from resonant feedback. Inharmonic Bell Moves partials off the harmonic series: dissonant, bell-like. Dissonant Shift Fully wet and inharmonic. Negative Shift Pushes downward: reversed-sounding tones. Wide Stereo Spread Different shift per channel for a swirling image. Negative Feedback Cloud Inverted feedback: a darker, diffuse smear. Synced Sweep Tempo-synced shift movement. Extreme Warp Large shift: robotic and alien. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Shift −100 … +100 % of Range 0 % Fine −10 … +10 Hz 0 Hz Feedback −100 … +100 % 0 % FB Delay 0 – 1000 ms 0 ms Spread 0 – 100 % 0 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Range ±10 Hz, ±200 Hz, ±2 kHz, ±10 kHz ±200 Hz Sync Free, 1/32 … 8 bars Free Anti-alias Off, On On Shift: the shift of the left channel, linear. The view shows it in Hz. Fine: added to Shift . Hidden while Sync is on. Feedback: the delayed Up signal mixed back into the input. A DC blocker in the loop stops offsets from building up. FB Delay: the delay in the feedback loop. 0 is one sample; changes glide like tape (the echoes bend in pitch). Spread: right shift = left shift × (1 − 2 × Spread). Mix: dry ↔ Up for Out . Up and Down are always 100 % wet. Range: the span of Shift . Changing it keeps the knob position, so the shift jumps. Not modulatable. Sync: Free, or one cycle per note value. Not modulatable. Anti-alias: the input low-pass against aliasing. Not modulatable. All knobs are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left input; also feeds the right channel when In R is not patched In R audio right input Reset trigger sets both oscillators to phase 0 (ignored while synced to a playing transport) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio dry/wet mix of the Up signal Up L, Up R audio input shifted by +Shift Down L, Down R audio input shifted by −Shift Sin, Cos control, −1 … +1 the left oscillator, 90° apart

title: Phaser
text: Phaser Phaser in the module view Introduction The Phaser makes the slow, swooshing sweep of the 70s: notches that travel up and down through the spectrum. It's best on sustained sounds with a lot of harmonics, like pads, strings, electric piano and guitar, and on drums and noise, where the sweep is easy to hear. How does it work? The sound goes through a chain of allpass filters. An allpass changes only the phase of a signal, not its level, and by a different amount at different frequencies. Mixed with the unprocessed sound, a frequency where the chain has turned the phase by 180° is cancelled: a notch . Every two stages make one notch. An LFO moves the frequency of the allpass filters, so the notches sweep. Rate is the LFO speed, 0.02 to 10 Hz. Depth is how far the notches sweep, up to three octaves up and down from the centre. Centre is the middle of the sweep, 80 Hz to 6 kHz. Low values sound dark and thick, high values thin and airy. Feedback feeds the chain's output back to its input. More feedback makes the notches deeper and the peaks between them sharper and resonant, a more vocal, whistling sweep. Negative feedback gives a hollower sound. It's softly limited, so it can't run away. Stages is how many allpass stages there are: 2 to 12. Two stages give one notch (subtle), four the classic sound, eight or twelve a busy, complex sweep. Spread moves the right channel's LFO away from the left, up to half a cycle, so the sweep rotates across the stereo field. Mix blends dry and wet. At 50 % the notches are deepest. At 100 % you hear only the allpass chain, which has no notches, only changes in phase (and, with feedback, resonant peaks). With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Classic phaser: Rate 0.3 Hz, Depth 60 %, Centre 700 Hz, Feedback 40 %, 4 stages, Mix 50 %. Resonant whistle: Feedback 85 %, 8 stages, Depth 80 %. Slow, wide pad movement: Rate 0.05 Hz, Depth 90 %, Spread 100 %, 6 stages. Envelope phaser: Rate 0, an envelope follower or ADSR onto Centre , for a vocal "wah"-like response. Rhythmic sweep: a clocked LFO onto Centre , with Rate at 0.02 Hz so the internal LFO barely moves. To make the sweep a more sudden swoosh, put a Compressor before it, so the level is constant while notches travel. Presets The preset bar of the Phaser view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Classic Phase Warm four-stage phaser. Gentle Swirl Slow, subtle movement on pads and keys. Deep Sweep Wide, dramatic sweep. Two-Stage Wobble Light, airy phase with one notch. Twelve Stage Glass Dense, glassy notches. Stereo Spin Left and right sweep out of phase. Mono Pulse Faster, centred throb. Resonant Peaks Strong positive feedback: ringing, vocal peaks. Hollow Negative Negative feedback: a hollow, nasal tone. Low Rumble Phase Centred low: moves bass and drums. High Shimmer Bright, airy sweep over the top end. Fast Leslie-ish Quick, shimmering rotary-like movement. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Phaser does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Phaser under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Phaser: Classic Four-Stage Sweep A saw riff passes a four-stage Phaser at a slow Rate with moderate Feedback: two soft notches slide up and down the sound. Change Stages for a busier or gentler sweep. Phaser: Deep Twelve-Stage Swirl Twelve stages and strong negative Feedback on a held pad carve many narrow notches that sweep through the sound with a hollow, vocal quality. Try positive Feedback for a brighter, ringing sweep. Phaser: Wide Stereo Drift With Spread at maximum the left and right LFOs are far apart, so the notches move in opposite places in each ear and a mono pluck melody floats around the stereo field. Lower Spread to centre the movement. Phaser: Fast Rotor A fast Rate with shallow Depth and few Stages gives a quick, rotary-like shimmer on a held organ-style tone. Slow Rate down for a classic sweep or deepen Depth to add warble. Phaser: Jet Noise Sweep Pink noise through a ten-stage Phaser with high Feedback turns into a rolling, whooshing jet over a quiet beat. Change Centre to move the sweep higher or lower, or reduce Feedback for a softer whoosh.

title: Pitch Shifter
text: Pitch Shifter Pitch Shifter in the module view Introduction The Pitch Shifter moves a sound up or down by a musical interval and keeps its rhythm: a vocal an octave up, a pad a fifth down, a guitar doubled at +12 and −12. Unlike the Freq Shifter, which adds a fixed number of hertz and breaks harmony, the Pitch Shifter multiplies every frequency by the same ratio, so chords stay chords. Put it in front of a Verb and feed the reverb back into it, and every echo climbs another octave: a shimmer . The factory cell Shimmer Verb is built that way. How does it work? The signal is written into a short delay line. Two read heads sweep through it. A head that moves against the writing point reads faster than real time, so it plays higher; one that moves with it reads slower, so lower. A head can only sweep so far, so each one fades out as it nears the end of the window and jumps back, while the other, half a window behind, fades in. The two fades are sine-shaped, so one head is always loud. This is the simple, cheap way to shift pitch. It has a character: the jump of the heads leaves a faint flutter at the sweep rate (a few Hz to tens of Hz at big intervals), and the sound is a little "grainy", most on sustained tones. Inside a reverb, that is not heard; on a dry vocal it is a voice. A phase-vocoder shifter is cleaner, but it adds a lot of delay and CPU. Pitch is the interval in semitones, −24 to +24. Modulating it with an envelope or LFO gives dive bombs and vibrato. Fine adds ±100 cents for detuned doubling (+7 and −7 cents on two shifters in parallel is a classic widener). Window is the length of the delay the heads sweep through, 20 to 340 ms. Short windows follow fast notes and give a tight, buzzy character; long windows are smoother and stretch into an echo. Around 60–100 ms suits most material; 150 ms or more for pads. The shifter's latency is about half a window. Drift makes the heads wander randomly, slowly: tape-like flutter and a wide, chorused sound. It also works at 0 semitones. Feedback sends the shifted sound back into the input, softly limited. With +12 semitones every repeat is an octave higher than the one before (a rising spiral), with −12 they fall. Mix blends the dry input with the shifted sound. At 100 % you hear only the shifted signal. The left and right sides are separate shifters (with different drift), so the stereo image stays. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Shimmer: Pitch +12, Window 100 ms, Mix 100 %, into a Verb, and the Verb's output back to the shifter's input through a Utility at 30–40 %. Or use the Shimmer Verb preset. Octave down: Pitch −12, Mix 50 %, for a sub-octave under a bass or a lead. Harmoniser: two Pitch Shifters in parallel, +4 and +7 semitones, Mix 40 %, for a major triad on a single note. Wide doubling: Pitch 0, Fine +12 cents, Drift 30 %, Mix 50 %. Dive bomb: an envelope onto Pitch, down 24 semitones, Mix 100 %. Spiral: Pitch +7, Feedback 60 %, Mix 50 %, into a delay: each repeat is a fifth higher. Origin The pitch-shifting algorithm (two crossfading delay-line heads, and the Fun parameter, here called Drift) is from PitchShifter (DaisySP) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version is rewritten for stereo and our delay line, with a smoothed window size, fine tuning, feedback with a soft clip and a seeded random generator, so offline renders repeat. The original licence text is in this module's LICENSE file. Presets The preset bar of the Pitch Shifter view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Octave Up Straight octave up. Octave Down Straight octave down. Octave Blend Octave up under the dry signal for sparkle. Fifth Up Adds a perfect fifth for power-chord thickness. Sub Octave Dry plus an octave below for weight. Detune Double A slightly sharp copy: classic detune thickening. Wide Detune Flat detune with a little drift. Tape Flutter Wobbling pitch like worn tape. Shimmer Spiral Climbing octaves: put it before a reverb. Dark Descent Falling spiral that sinks into the dark. Minor Third Echo Feedback stacks minor thirds into a diminished haze. Chipmunk An octave and a fifth up: cartoon voice. Monster Dark, slow, huge voice. Granular Window Tiny window: choppy, grainy artefacts. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Pitch Shifter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Pitch Shifter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Pitch Shifter: Octave Shimmer A pluck melody goes up an octave into a Pitch Shifter with Feedback and then a big reverb: each tail climbs in octaves into a glassy shimmer. Lower Feedback for a single octave halo or try +7 for a fifth. Pitch Shifter: Octave Down Weight A bass riff is blended with a copy an octave lower, doubling its depth at half Mix. Try -5 or -7 for a thick parallel line or raise Window for smoother, less grainy low notes. Pitch Shifter: Parallel Fifth The Shifter adds a line a fifth above the melody at half Mix, so every note is paired with a power-chord partner. Change Pitch to +4 for a major third, +3 for a minor third or -5 for a fourth below. Pitch Shifter: Fine Detune Doubler With Pitch at zero and just 12 cents of Fine plus a little Drift, a held pad is doubled by a slightly out-of-tune, wavering copy, which thickens it like an ensemble. Increase Drift for tape-like flutter or Fine for a wider detune. Pitch Shifter: Climbing Spiral Sparse notes enter a Pitch Shifter set a few semitones up with high Feedback: each echo is shifted again and spirals upward until it fades. Make Pitch negative and the spiral falls instead; add Drift for flutter.

title: Pitch Snap
text: Pitch Snap Pitch Snap in the module view Introduction Pitch Snap is a pitch corrector for a voice or any single-note instrument. It finds the pitch of what comes in, picks the nearest note of a scale and moves the sound toward it: all the way and at once for the stepped sound of a hard retune, slowly and partly for an almost invisible nudge. Two things set it apart. Drift corrects the average pitch of a note and lets the fast movement around it, the vibrato, through, so a singer stays a singer. And the Target output tells the rest of the patch which note it is aiming at, so a synth can play along with the corrected voice. It works on one note at a time . Chords and noise are not changed: wherever it cannot hear a pitch the sound passes through, delayed to match. How does it work? A pitch tracker (the one shared by the Pitch Follower and the Tuner ) measures how long one cycle of the sound lasts. The shifting itself cuts the sound into short grains, two cycles long, and lays them down again one new cycle apart. A grain is repeated if the new pitch is higher and skipped if it is lower; the grains are always taken a whole number of cycles apart, so they fit together without a seam. Amount is how much of the error is corrected: at 100 % every note ends on the scale note, at 50 % it ends half-way there, at 0 % nothing changes. Speed is how fast the correction takes hold. At 100 % it is instant (the stepped sound); the lower it is, the slower the pitch slides toward the note. Below about 40 % it takes a few hundred milliseconds, which sounds natural. Drift lets the pitch wander around the note. At 0 % every wobble is flattened. At 100 % only the average pitch over Drift Time is pulled onto the note, so vibrato and scoops survive. Because the average needs time to settle, a note can leave its target for a short while after the attack. Offset (knob and jack: 1 V = 12 semitones) moves the target after the correction: +12 sings an octave above, +7 a fifth. Combined with Target it makes a harmony voice. Formant Preserve keeps the character of the voice: with it on, grains are copied as they are, so a vowel stays a vowel while the pitch moves. Off, the grains are resampled, as in a plain pitch shifter: raise the pitch and the voice becomes smaller. Root and Scale choose the notes. Harmony takes them from a Harmony Master on a bus instead, with Target choosing between the scale, the chord tones or chord tones first. Low and High say which pitches to look for. A lower Low means a longer analysis window: slower and more delay. Tracking decides how stable the detection is: Fast has no stabilisers, Steady has a light octave guard and a vote of three, Rock Solid a firm guard and a vote of five. Latency : Aligned delays the sound by the time the detection needs, so a correction lands on exactly the sound it was measured on and even a quick vibrato is flattened properly (20–30 ms at the default range, about 12 ms with Low at 150 Hz). Quick uses the freshest sound and is about half as late, but a fast vibrato is only partly corrected. Outputs: Out is the corrected sound, Target the note it aims at in V/oct (held while nothing is heard), Pitch the detected input pitch and Shift the applied shift in octaves. How to use it? Hard retune: Hard Snap with Scale Chromatic . Everything is on a semitone. Natural correction: a Scale for the song, Speed near 50 % and some Drift . Keep the vibrato: Drift at 100 % and Drift Time about 350 ms. Harmony voices: two Pitch Snaps in parallel with Offset +4 and +7 (or the two Target chord tones from a Harmony Master bus). Play along: Target into an oscillator: a synth that plays the notes the voice is corrected to. A stepped sound for a synth line: a sawtooth into In , Hard Snap in Minor Pentatonic . Monitoring: Quick Monitor for a short delay while singing. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Pitch Snap does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Pitch Snap under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Pitch Snap: Hard Retune A wobbly saw line with notes that do not belong to the key goes into a Pitch Snap set to hard correction in A minor pentatonic: every note jumps onto the scale with the stepped, robotic sound of a hard retune. Set Amount to 0 to hear the raw out-of-tune line, then bring it back up, or lower Speed for a softer glide. Pitch Snap: Drift Keeps the Vibrato A slow line with a 5.5 Hz vibrato and a drunken detune is pulled onto C major by a Pitch Snap with Drift at 100 %, so the average pitch is corrected while the vibrato stays alive. Set Drift to 0 and the vibrato is flattened into a steady tone; try a lower Drift Time for a quicker grip. Pitch Snap: Three-Voice Harmony One sloppy lead feeds three Pitch Snaps in parallel: the lead itself, one a fifth above (+7 Offset) and one an octave below (-12), each tuned to C major pentatonic and panned apart. Change an Offset to +4 for a major third or +12 for a bright octave double. Pitch Snap: Bass Plays Along A Harmony Master runs an i-VI-III-VII progression on Bus A; a drunken lead is snapped to the chord tones and the Target output drives a bass oscillator, so the bass always plays the exact note the lead is corrected to. Change the Target setting to Chord + Scale to let passing notes through, or the Harmony Master's key to move everything. Pitch Snap: Stepped Offset with Formant A formant oscillator sings a steady line while a slow sequencer feeds the Offset jack, transposing the corrected voice in steps of 0, +5, +7 and +3 semitones with its vowel kept in place by Formant Preserve. Switch Formant off and the vowel slides with the pitch like a plain pitch shifter. Presets The preset bar of the Pitch Snap view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Hard Snap Every note jumps straight to the nearest semitone: the classic stepped sound. Natural Major A gentle pull toward the C major scale that still sounds sung. Gentle Nudge Half the error is corrected, slowly: a tired voice gets a little help. Keep the Vibrato The average pitch lands on the note while the vibrato around it survives. Drifty Slide Slow retune with plenty of drift: notes wander in from the side. Pentatonic Lock Whatever you sing ends up on an A minor pentatonic note. Blues Voice Pulls toward the E blues scale, with the speed of a bent note. Whole Tone Dream Hard retune onto a whole-tone scale: floating, unresolved. Octave Up Snaps, then sings an octave higher with the vowel left where it was. Fifth Above A harmony voice a fifth above the corrected note. Octave Down A second voice an octave below, which keeps the vowel. Chipmunk Formant Preserve off: raising the pitch drags the vowel up too. Follow the Band Takes its notes from a Harmony Master on bus A: chord tones first, then the scale. Chord Tones Only Only the notes of the current chord are allowed. Bass Corrector Low range and a firm tracker for a bass. Quick Monitor As little delay as it can: for monitoring a voice while singing. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Amount 0 – 100 % 100 % Speed 0 – 100 % 85 % Drift 0 – 100 % 0 % Drift Time 50 ms – 1 s 300 ms Offset −24 – +24 st 0 st Low 30 – 400 Hz 70 Hz High 200 – 2000 Hz 900 Hz Settings Setting Values Default Formant Preserve on / off on Root C … B C Scale Chromatic, Major, Natural Minor, Harmonic Minor, Melodic Minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Locrian, Phrygian Dominant, Major Pentatonic, Minor Pentatonic, Blues, Whole Tone, Diminished, Hirajoshi Major Harmony Off, Bus A, Bus B, Bus C, Bus D Off Target (with a bus) Scale, Chord, Chord + Scale Scale Tracking Fast, Steady, Rock Solid Steady Latency Aligned, Quick Aligned Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the voice or instrument to correct Offset pitch added to the target note, 1 V = 12 semitones Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the corrected sound Target pitch the note it is aiming at, in V/oct, held while unvoiced Pitch pitch the detected pitch of the input, V/oct Shift control the applied shift, in octaves (semitones / 12) Origin Pitch tracking is shared with the Pitch Follower. The shifting is pitch-synchronous overlap-add, a classic published technique for changing the pitch of voiced sound without changing its timing. It was written for this module; no source code was ported.

title: 3-Band EQ
text: 3-Band EQ Introduction The 3-Band EQ is the quick, no-fuss tone control: a low shelf , a mid bell and a high shelf . Turn a gain knob up to boost that part of the sound, down to cut it. Use it to add weight to a bass, take the mud out of a mix, or brighten a dull sample. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). Both channels use the same settings. Controls Control What it does Low Gain of the low shelf, -15 to +15 dB. Affects everything below Low Freq . Low Freq Where the low shelf turns over, 40 to 400 Hz. Mid Gain of the mid bell, -15 to +15 dB. Mid Freq Centre of the mid bell, 200 Hz to 5 kHz. Mid Q Width of the mid bell, 0.3 (very broad) to 4 (narrow). High Gain of the high shelf, -15 to +15 dB. Affects everything above High Freq . High Freq Where the high shelf turns over, 1 to 12 kHz. Output Level after the three bands, -12 to +12 dB. With all three gains at 0 dB the module passes the signal through unchanged. How does it work? Each channel runs through three biquad filters in a row: Signal flow: In, low shelf, mid bell, high shelf, Output, Out The filters are the standard RBJ designs (shelves with a slope of 1, a peaking bell with the chosen Q). The knobs are smoothed once per block of 32 samples, so moving them does not click. Frequencies are kept below 45 % of the sample rate.

title: Channel Strip
text: Channel Strip Channel Strip in the module view Introduction On an analogue console the signal of a channel runs through the same few blocks in the same order: a high-pass filter to take the rumble off, an input transformer, an equaliser with a handful of switchable frequencies, and some amplifier that is always working a little. The sound of "a signal that went through a console" is the sum of those, and one detail of the order matters a lot: an EQ boost that runs into a saturating stage pushes it harder , so the colour follows the EQ. The Channel Strip puts the whole channel in one module: a high-pass filter (Off, 30, 50, 80 or 120 Hz; 12 or 18 dB per octave); an input transformer , with core saturation that bites the bass first; a four-band equaliser : low shelf, low-mid bell, high-mid bell, high shelf, +-15 dB, each with four switchable frequencies and a proportional Q : the Q narrows as the gain grows, as on analogue consoles; a drive stage with three characters: Warm (round iron, even harmonics), Punchy (tight op-amp, odd harmonics, a lift on the attack of hits), Clean (tight and subtle); Stage Order : the EQ before or after the drive stage. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It has no latency except the few samples of the Normal quality's oversampling filters, and no Mix control: it is a channel, and the EQ is meant to be heard. How does it work? In -> high-pass -> input transformer -> [ EQ -> Drive ] or [ Drive -> EQ ] -> level compensation -> Output High-pass. The 12 dB per octave filter is a second-order Butterworth section: -3 dB exactly at the corner. The 18 dB per octave filter is a first-order section and a second-order one with Q = 1 (a third-order Butterworth), also -3 dB at the corner. Off is a straight wire. The tests measure the slope and the corner for all eight combinations. Input transformer. The same kind of core as in the Preamp, in a smaller version. The flux integrates the voltage, so low frequencies reach the knee at lower levels. The magnetising current rises steeply past it and is taken from the signal, which squashes the bass and makes odd harmonics, and a lagging sign of the flux rate gives the loop a little hysteresis. Transformer sets how early the core saturates, from 8 Hz (0 %) to 98 Hz (100 %) for a full-scale sine, and the low corner from 4 to 18 Hz. The core sees the signal raised by up to 12 dB when Drive is up (the gain is brought back after it), so more Drive also means more iron. Equaliser. Four second-order sections in series, computed once per block for both channels. The gains glide to their targets in about 10 milliseconds, so switching EQ On or turning a gain does not click. The frequency choices are: Band Type Frequencies LF low shelf 35, 60, 100, 200 Hz LMF bell 250, 500 Hz, 1, 2 kHz HMF bell 1.5, 3, 5, 8 kHz HF high shelf 5, 8, 10, 12 kHz Proportional Q. The bells have Q = 0.55 at no gain, rising to 1.9 at 15 dB (a boost or a cut: both narrow). The shelves have Q = 0.55 to 1.0, so they overshoot slightly more as the gain grows. A small boost is broad and gentle, a big one is focused. The tests check the response of every band at every frequency against the analytic curve of the same filter; the worst error is 0.12 dB. Drive stage. Drive runs from 0 to 24 dB of gain into a curve. The output is level-compensated, so that a -12 dBFS sine at 0 dB EQ comes out at -12 dBFS whatever the Drive or the Character. Warm : a soft clip s / sqrt(1 + s^2) with a bias of 0.3, so the positive and negative halves are shaped differently: strong second harmonic, then the third. A DC blocker (5 Hz) removes what the asymmetry leaves behind. Punchy : a tighter, symmetric knee z / (1 + z^4)^(1/4) : odd harmonics only. A fast envelope (0.4 ms) is compared with a slow one (25 ms), and the ratio lifts the signal by up to about 5 dB right after the knee: the attack of a hit, which the knee would otherwise squash, stands out. Clean : a very gentle soft clip with its knee at three times the level of Warm's: little distortion until you really push it. Anti-aliasing. Warm and Clean use first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing on the non-linear part of the curve (so that the small-signal response stays flat). Punchy relies on oversampling. Normal runs the drive stage at twice the sample rate with all-pass half-band filters; Eco runs it at the base rate. Stage Order. With "EQ, then Drive" a boost raises the level into the saturator, so it distorts more and the colour follows the EQ. A cut eases it. With "Drive, then EQ" the stage is the same whatever you do with the EQ, and the EQ shapes the result, including the harmonics. At low level the two orders have the same frequency response; they only differ in the colour. Input. Auto uses the left input for both channels while nothing is patched into In R (R has been exactly zero for 2048 samples while L is active), and returns to true stereo, smoothly, the moment R carries signal. Stereo and Mono force one or the other. How to use it? Kick drum: HPF 30 Hz (12 dB), Transformer 60 %, Drive 20 %, Warm. LF +4 dB at 60 Hz, LMF -4 dB at 250 Hz, HMF +3 dB at 5 kHz, order "EQ, then Drive": the boosts push the iron. Snare: HPF 80 Hz, Drive 40 %, Punchy. HMF +4 dB at 3 kHz, HF +2 dB at 10 kHz. Punchy lifts the crack. Bass: HPF 30 Hz (18 dB), Transformer 70 %, Drive 25 %, Warm. LF +3 dB at 100 Hz, LMF -3 dB at 500 Hz. Vocal: HPF 80 Hz (12 dB), Transformer 30 %, Drive 15 %, Clean. LMF -3 dB at 250 Hz, HMF +2 dB at 3 kHz, HF +3 dB at 12 kHz. Order "Drive, then EQ" keeps the colour constant while you shape the tone. Mix bus tone: all gains in small steps (below 3 dB, where the Q is broad), Drive 10 %, Clean. Colour that follows the EQ: Warm, Drive 50 %, "EQ, then Drive", LMF +10 dB at 1 kHz: the boosted band drives the stage hard and the sound thickens as you boost. Switch the order and the same boost gets cleaner. Sweeping with frequency switches: the frequency choices are stepped, as on a console. Set the gain first and then step through the frequencies to find the spot. Bypass the tone but keep the colour: EQ On off. The EQ bands are bypassed and the transformer and drive stage remain. CPU: Eco for sessions with many channels. The module's own UI The Channel Strip draws its real frequency response from the knobs, using the same filter formulas as the module (the high-pass, the four bands and the proportional Q), with a handle on each band. Drag a handle up or down for its gain; drag it sideways and it snaps to the band's stepped frequencies. A bar on the right glows with the Saturation probe, with a thin level bar beside it. A test checks that the drawn curve matches the module's measured response to within 1.5 dB. The file is src/channel-strip.view.js . Tricks it demonstrates: recomputing the maths of a module in the UI for a picture (a log frequency axis, an analytic filter response); hit testing handles by distance, then snapping a drag to a list of steps by the nearest value on a log scale; setting stepped (choice) and continuous knobs from the same gesture; the glow of a meter driven by a smoothed probe. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Knobs and switches Control Range Default Meaning HPF Off, 30, 50, 80, 120 Hz Off High-pass corner. HPF Slope 12 dB/oct, 18 dB/oct 12 dB/oct High-pass slope. Transformer 0 to 100 % 35 % How early the input core saturates (8 to 98 Hz knee for a full-scale sine). Drive 0 to 100 % 25 % Gain into the drive stage, 0 to 24 dB (level-compensated). Character Warm, Punchy, Clean Warm The curve of the drive stage. Stage Order EQ then Drive, Drive then EQ EQ then Drive Where the EQ sits relative to the drive stage. EQ On on, off on All four bands. LF Gain / LF Freq -15 to +15 dB / 35, 60, 100, 200 Hz 0 dB / 100 Hz Low shelf. LMF Gain / LMF Freq -15 to +15 dB / 250, 500 Hz, 1, 2 kHz 0 dB / 500 Hz Low-mid bell. HMF Gain / HMF Freq -15 to +15 dB / 1.5, 3, 5, 8 kHz 0 dB / 3 kHz High-mid bell. HF Gain / HF Freq -15 to +15 dB / 5, 8, 10, 12 kHz 0 dB / 8 kHz High shelf. Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level, after the level compensation. Input Auto, Stereo, Mono Auto Where the right channel gets its signal. Quality Eco, Normal Normal Drive stage at the base rate or at 2 times oversampling. Probes Probe Meaning Saturation How far the drive stage bends the signal: 0 is linear, 1 is fully squashed. Level The output level (peak, falling slowly). Numbers worth knowing Cost: about 88,000 operations per 32-sample chunk at the heaviest setting (Normal, both channels); the checker warns above 60,000 and refuses above 400,000. With Drive 0 % and Clean, the strip is transparent: a flat sweep within 0.1 dB from 100 Hz up (the DC blocker and the 4 Hz transformer corner cost 0.4 dB at 20 Hz). A 15 dB boost at 1 kHz keeps 39 % of its gain half an octave away (1.4 kHz); a 5 dB boost keeps 68 %. Transformer 100 %, 40 Hz at -6 dBFS: third harmonic at -15 dBc; the same level at 1 kHz: -49 dBc. At Transformer 0 % both are at -49 dBc. With Warm, Drive 50 %, a +12 dB bell at 1 kHz and a -20 dBFS tone at 1 kHz, the harmonics add up to -16 dB relative to the tone with the EQ first and -34 dB with the drive stage first. A 7 kHz tone at -6 dBFS at Drive 100 %: non-harmonic energy of -33 dBc (Warm, Eco), -43 dBc (Warm, Normal), -37 dBc (Clean, Eco), -60 dBc (Clean, Normal), -20 dBc (Punchy, Eco), -43 dBc (Punchy, Normal; Drive 60 %).

title: Compressor
text: Compressor Compressor in the module view Introduction A compressor turns loud parts of a sound down, so the difference between loud and quiet gets smaller. Used lightly, it makes a bass or a vocal sit evenly in a mix; used hard, it makes drums punch and pumps; with a very high ratio it is a limiter that keeps a signal below a ceiling, for instance inside a feedback loop or on the output of a patch. How does it work? A detector measures how loud the signal is, in decibels. Above the Threshold , the compressor turns the level down so that every Ratio dB over the threshold at the input becomes 1 dB over at the output. At 4:1, a peak 12 dB over comes out 3 dB over. The gain is turned down gradually, over the Attack time, and let go again over the Release time, so the sound doesn't click. Threshold is the level (−60 to 0 dB) where compression starts. Ratio goes from 1:1 (nothing) to 40:1. From 40:1 on the Compressor is a limiter: nothing passes the threshold. Attack (0.1 to 100 ms) is how fast it clamps down. A slow attack lets the start of a note through (punch); a fast one catches every peak. Release (10 ms to 2 s) is how fast it lets go. Short releases pump with the rhythm, long ones are smooth and invisible. Knee (0 to 24 dB) softens the corner at the threshold. A wide knee starts compressing gently before the threshold. Makeup adds gain after compression to bring the level back up. Mix blends the compressed signal with the dry one: parallel compression . 30–50 % keeps the transients and adds weight. Link is how much the two channels follow each other. At 100 % the louder channel controls both, so the stereo image doesn't shift. At 0 they work independently. Detector is Peak (reacts to every peak, fast) or RMS (measures average power over 10 ms, closer to how loud the sound seems and gentler on drums). The Sidechain input lets another signal control the compression: a kick drum pumping the pads (put the kick into Sidechain and a fast attack, release 150–300 ms, ratio 8:1, low threshold). The gain is applied to In L/R . Without a cable there, the detector listens to the input itself. The Reduction output is a control signal from 0 (no compression) to 1 (24 dB of reduction or more). Use it to open a filter when the sound gets squashed or to light a lamp. The display The top of the view shows what the compressor is doing to the last two seconds of sound: The volume envelope graph draws the level going in (grey) and coming out (green) as two lines over each other, on a dB scale, so you can see how far the peaks are pulled down. The dashed line marks the threshold. Gain reduction below it shows, in dB, how far the compressor is turned down at each moment (0 at the top, 24 dB at the bottom), and the current amount in numbers under its label. The number changes four times a second, showing the deepest reduction since the last change, so it can be read. Watch the curve to set Attack and Release by eye. The IN and OUT meters next to each other on the right show the peak (light bar), RMS level (solid bar) and a held peak line for each channel, with the held peak in dB below. The red mark at the top is a clip light (a sample over 0 dBFS). Click a meter to reset it. How to use it? Glue on a mix: threshold −18 dB, ratio 2:1, attack 30 ms, release 200 ms, knee 12 dB. Punchy drums: ratio 6:1, attack 20 ms, release 80 ms, Makeup to taste. Parallel smash: ratio 20:1, threshold −40 dB, attack 1 ms, Mix 30 %. Limiter: ratio 40:1, attack 0.1 ms, release 50 ms, threshold −3 dB. Put one at the end of a feedback loop, like the Shimmer Verb's, to keep it under control. Ducking: a kick on the Sidechain input, ratio 10:1, threshold −35 dB, release 200 ms. Presets The preset bar of the Compressor view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Gentle Glue Light bus compression that holds a mix together. Vocal Leveler Even out a voice or lead with smooth RMS detection. Drum Punch Slow attack lets the transient through, then clamps the body. Bass Control Keeps a bass line steady and solid. Parallel Smash Hard compression blended under the dry signal for density. Soft Limiter Catches peaks at the end of a chain. Brick Wall Near-hard limiting; nothing gets past the ceiling. Slow Opto Slow, smooth levelling with a wide knee. Sustain Boost Pulls up tails: guitars and plucks ring longer. Pump Duck Audible pumping on loud material; patch a kick into Key for ducking. Transient Tamer Fast attack rounds off clicks and spikes. Wide Squash Heavy squash with loosely linked channels for a wider image. Gain Reduction Source Take the Reduction output as a control signal for pumping other modules. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Compressor does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Compressor under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Compressor: Kick-Ducked Pad A sustained saw pad runs through the Compressor while the kick drum feeds its Key input: every kick pushes the pad down and it swells back between beats. Lower Threshold or lengthen Release for a deeper, slower pump. Compressor: Parallel Drum Squash A broken beat is flattened with a high Ratio, fast Attack and a lot of Makeup, then blended back with Mix at about half: the room and tails come up while the hits keep their punch. Sweep Mix from 0 to 100 % to hear what the squash adds. Compressor: Bass Leveller A bass line with wildly different velocities is evened out by an RMS Compressor with a soft Knee, so soft notes sit as firmly as loud ones. Raise Threshold until the quiet notes drop back out again. Compressor: Reduction Opens the Filter The Compressor's Reduction output is a control signal that rises with every kick, and here it also closes a Multi Filter on the pad: the sound ducks and darkens on each hit. Raise the cable amount or lower Threshold for a heavier effect. Compressor: Pluck Sustainer Short plucks pass through a very fast, high-ratio Compressor with high Makeup: the tails are pulled up so every note rings on like a held string. Lengthen Release to hear the sustain breathe, or cut Makeup to hear the plain pluck.

title: EQ
text: EQ EQ in the module view Introduction The EQ turns parts of the spectrum up or down: more bass, less mud around 300 Hz, a cut of harsh 3 kHz, more air above 8 kHz. It has six bands, each of which can be a bell, a shelf, a cut, a notch or a band-pass, in stereo. How does it work? Every band is a biquad filter (the formulas of the well-known "Audio EQ Cookbook"), calculated with the band's settings and applied one after another. The display shows the spectrum going in (grey) and coming out (blue) with the EQ curve on top, and one numbered point per band. Select a band by clicking its point in the display or its tab (1–6) under the display. The controls below show that band. Drag a point sideways to change its Freq , up and down to change its Gain . Hold Cmd (macOS) or Ctrl (Windows) while dragging to change its Q instead (or the Slope of a cut): up is narrower. Hold Shift for fine movement, double-click a point to set its gain back to 0 dB, and turn the mouse wheel over a point to change its Q (or the Slope of a cut). Dragging a point of a band that is off switches it on. A band that is off is drawn hollow, with its response dashed, so you can see what it would do. The display: the frequency under the pointer is shown at the bottom left. The dB scale is at the left, next to two magnifiers that zoom it (±3 to ±24 dB). A cut's response leaves the chart where it falls below the scale. Click in , out or EQ curve in the legend to hide or show that drawing; the zoom and the legend choices are remembered. Type of a band: Bell : boosts or cuts around Freq by Gain (±18 dB). Q sets the width: 0.1 is very broad (a gentle tonal tilt), 1 is a typical bell, 18 is a narrow spike for a single ringing frequency. Low Shelf / High Shelf : raises or lowers everything below / above Freq by Gain . Q sets how steep the shelf is (0.7 is smooth; higher values overshoot a little before the corner). Low Cut / High Cut : removes everything below / above Freq , 3 dB down at Freq . Slope sets how steeply: 6, 12, 18, 24, 36 or 48 dB per octave (Butterworth, so no ringing). Notch : removes a narrow band around Freq ; Q sets how narrow. Band Pass : keeps a band around Freq and removes the rest; Q sets how narrow. Algorithm of a band chooses how its filter is designed. The sound of an existing patch does not change: the default is Clean . Clean : the textbook "Audio EQ Cookbook" filter. Transparent and predictable. Modern : a bell designed so that its width follows the analog bell all the way up the spectrum. With Q 1 at 12 kHz the bell is half its gain 6 kHz either side, where the Clean bell is cramped narrower towards the top of the spectrum; a boost and a cut of the same size and Freq cancel exactly. Shelves, cuts, notch and band-pass are the same as in Clean. Vintage : analog-style. A bell or shelf is proportional-Q : a small boost or cut is broad (half the Q you set) and a large one gets narrower (1.3 times the Q at ±18 dB), as on classic consoles. The band's output is also gently saturated (a soft clip that is unity for small signals and about 0.4 dB down at full scale), adding a little odd-harmonic warmth to loud signals. Cuts get the saturation but keep their Butterworth response. The curve in the display shows the Vintage widths, not the saturation. On switches a band off without losing its settings. Bands 1 and 6 start as switched-off cuts, bands 2 and 5 as shelves and bands 3 and 4 as bells at 400 Hz and 2 kHz; any band can be changed to any type. A bell or shelf at 0 dB is bypassed, so unused bands cost nothing. Level (−18 to +6 dB) is the gain after the equaliser, to make up for boosts. Freq , Gain and Q of every band can be modulated; the filters are updated every 16 samples, which is smooth for sweeps. Modulating the Freq of a bell with an LFO or envelope while boosting 10 dB gives a wah-wah. The band's type, algorithm, slope and on switch, and the band being edited, are settings. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Remove rumble: band 1 on, Low Cut at 40 Hz, 24 dB/oct. Clean up mud: a bell at 300 Hz, −4 dB, Q 1. Add presence: a bell at 3 kHz, +3 dB, Q 0.8. Air: band 5, High Shelf at 10 kHz, +4 dB. Telephone voice: Low Cut at 400 Hz and High Cut at 4 kHz, both 24 dB/oct, and a bell at 1.5 kHz, +6 dB. Find a resonance: boost a bell +12 dB with Q 6 and sweep its frequency (drag the point sideways) until the problem sticks out, then cut it, or turn the band into a Notch. Wah: a bell, +12 dB, Q 3, an envelope or LFO onto its frequency. Presets The preset bar of the EQ view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Smile Curve Boosted lows and highs: instant polish. Bass Boost More weight below 80 Hz. Low Cut Lite Removes rumble below 90 Hz and clears a little mud. Mud Remover Cuts the boxy low-mids. Presence Lift Brings the sound forward. Air Open, airy top end. Warm Darkness Rolls off the top and warms the bottom. Vocal Clarity Cuts the rumble, cleans up and brightens a voice. Telephone Steep cuts below 400 Hz and above 4 kHz, a nasal band in between. Hollow Notch Two deep notches for a phase-like, hollow tone. Resonant Peaks Narrow, ringing boosts: formant-like colour. Kick Shaper Weight and click for kick drums. Lo-Fi Radio Small-speaker colouration. Tilt Down Dark tilt; tames harsh sources. Rumble Remover A steep cut below 35 Hz: clears sub-bass rumble and DC drift. De-Harsh Two narrow dips and a soft top cut tame a piercing source. Demo patches Five whole patches show what EQ does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick EQ under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows EQ: Small Radio A full-range saw riff and a beat are squeezed through a steep Low Cut, a steep High Cut and a Bell boost in the midrange: the sound shrinks to a tiny speaker. Switch bands 1 and 6 off to open the sound again, or move the Bell around. EQ: Sweeping Bell Wah A narrow Bell boosted by 14 dB glides up and down the spectrum under an LFO on its Freq, so the riff sings like a wah pedal. Widen Q for a gentler vowel, or give the LFO a faster rate. EQ: Warm Bus Tilt A mix of bass, riff and drums gets a Low Shelf lift, a small Bell cut in the muddy low mids and a High Shelf cut: a darker, rounder balance. Flip the Shelf gains to the other side for a bright, thin version. EQ: Twin Notch Phaser Two Notch bands moved in opposite directions by one slow LFO carve gaps in a sustained saw line, giving a hollow, phaser-like sweep without any feedback. Raise Q for thinner, sharper gaps. EQ: 48 dB Cutoff Rise A High Cut with the steepest 48 dB/oct slope is pushed open by a slow LFO over a riff and beat, like a filter riser. Choose a gentler Slope for a softer glide, or turn the sweep depth down.

title: Limiter
text: Limiter Introduction A limiter keeps a signal under a ceiling, whatever comes in. Where the Compressor shapes dynamics, the Limiter is a safety: put it at the end of a patch, in a feedback loop or before a loud effect, and nothing gets past the Ceiling . How does it work? The Limiter looks a few milliseconds ahead. When a peak is coming, it turns the gain down gradually so that the gain has reached the right value exactly when the peak arrives, then lets go again over the Release time. The sound is delayed by the lookahead to make this possible. Both channels always get the same gain, so the stereo image doesn't move. Ceiling (−12 to 0 dB) is the level nothing passes. The default of −0.3 dB leaves a little room. Release (10 ms to 1 s) is how fast the gain comes back. Short releases are loud but can pump; long ones are smooth. Input (0 to 24 dB) turns the signal up before it is limited. This is how you make something louder: raise Input until the Reduction output shows the amount you want. Lookahead is Off , 1 ms , 2 ms or 5 ms . Longer lookahead gives gentler, cleaner limiting and adds the same delay to the sound. With Off there is no delay and the gain follows the signal instantly, which can sound harsher on low notes. The Reduction output is a control signal from 0 (no limiting) to 1 (12 dB of reduction or more). Use it to light a lamp or to open a filter when the sound is being squashed. The display The view shows an IN and an OUT level meter, with the controls beside them: Each meter shows the peak (light bar), the RMS level (solid bar) and a held peak line per channel, with the held peak in dB below. The red mark at the top is a clip light (a sample over 0 dBFS). Click a meter to reset it. The orange limit line across the IN meter is the level the input has to reach before the limiter turns it down: the Ceiling minus the Input gain. The part of the input bar above it is what the limiter takes off. It moves when you change either knob. With the ceiling below 0 dB the OUT meter should never reach it. Gain reduction under the meters is the amount the limiter is turning down, in dB. It changes four times a second, showing the deepest reduction since the last change, so it can be read. How to use it? Safety at the end of a patch: Ceiling −1 dB, Release 100 ms, Lookahead 2 ms. Louder, not clipped: raise Input by 3 to 6 dB, Lookahead 5 ms, Release 200 ms. Inside a feedback loop: Lookahead Off , so the loop gets no extra delay. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Limiter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Limiter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Limiter: Drums Turned Up A broken beat is driven 18 dB into a fast, low-ceiling Limiter: the peaks are shaved flat and the whole kit gets denser and louder at the same top level. Lower Input to hear the open dynamics return, or lower Ceiling for more squash. Limiter: Slow Release Pump A bass line and a four-on-the-floor beat are pushed hard into a Limiter with a long Release, so the bass dips on every kick and comes back slowly. Shorten Release for a tight, clean sound or lengthen it for a heavy breathing groove. Limiter: Flattened Swells A pad that swells slowly in and out is driven into a low-ceiling Limiter, which holds it at one constant level: the fade-ins vanish and notes simply appear. Pull Input down to let the swells return. Limiter: Reduction Brightens Lead A kick-heavy beat is limited, and the Limiter's Reduction output opens the cutoff of a filter on a lead, so the lead brightens exactly when the drums hit hardest. Raise Input for more reduction and a wider swing. Limiter: Final Stage The finished mix of lead, bass and drums passes through a transparent Limiter with 5 ms Lookahead and a ceiling just under full scale, as the last module before the output. Raise Input and watch the reduction build while the peaks never pass the ceiling.

title: Mic Colour
text: Mic Colour Mic Colour in the module view Introduction A synth, a DI guitar or a sampled drum has no microphone, no room and no distance in it. That is part of why it can sound flat or too clean. The Mic Colour puts one back: choose a microphone model , move the source closer or farther away , and the module adds what a real capsule and a real space do. Ribbon : a gentle roll-off at the top, a figure-8 style proximity bass bloom, a soft resonance in the bass, and softness on loud bass. Dynamic : a presence peak around 4 kHz, little below 80 Hz and above 15 kHz, a mid-focused sound, and fast softening of transients. Condenser : extended highs with a presence and air lift, a Diaphragm control that moves the peak, clean with a hint of transistor-style saturation. Tube Condenser : the same with warm, soft valve colour. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It can also be used purely as a tone shaper with Room and Self-Noise at 0. How does it work? In -> tone filters -> saturation -> capsule high-pass -> model dynamics -> off-axis comb + early reflections -> Output -> Mix -> Out ^ Self-Noise (hiss) Tone filters. Each model is a chain of analog prototypes (second-order and first-order sections), discretised with the bilinear transform and pre-warped so that every corner lands on its stated frequency. The tests compare the realised response of each model with its intended analog curve; below about a fifth of the sample rate the two agree within a fraction of a decibel, and in the top octave the digital curve is slightly squeezed (closer at 96 kHz). Ribbon Dynamic Condenser Tube Condenser Low cut (2nd order) 35 Hz 90 Hz 18 Hz 22 Hz Proximity lift at full Proximity, 5 cm up to +10 dB +7 dB +4 dB +5 dB Bass character bump at 140 Hz, +3 dB mid focus at 700 Hz, +1.5 dB none warmth at 120 Hz, +1.5 dB Presence / top bell at 3.2 kHz (Presence only) bell at 4.2 kHz, +5 dB bell at the diaphragm peak, +1.5 to +4.5 dB the same, +1 to +3 dB Top low-pass 2nd order, 9.5 kHz low-pass 15 kHz open low-pass 18 kHz Air lift (shelf at 7 kHz) none none up to +6 dB up to +3 dB Saturation soft, low-band symmetrical (odd harmonics) a hint, with asymmetry warm, even harmonics The gains of the Colour-dependent parts are for the Colour knob at 50 %; they scale with the knob (0 % is half the character, 100 % is double it). Distance and proximity. Closer than 40 cm a bass shelf (200 Hz) lifts the low end: the proximity effect. It grows as the source approaches 3 cm and as the Proximity knob goes up, and each model has its own strength (the ribbon the most, the condenser the least). Beyond 100 cm the bass falls away by up to 2 dB. Beyond 50 cm air absorption dulls the highs by up to 4 dB. The direct level drops by up to 3 dB between 40 cm and 3 m, and the early reflections become stronger relative to it. Presence lifts the model's presence region: up to 6 dB at 3.2 kHz for the ribbon, and up to 4 dB added to the model's own peak at 4.2 kHz (dynamic) or at the diaphragm peak (condensers). Diaphragm moves the condenser peak from about 13 kHz (small capsule, 0 %) down to about 7.5 kHz (large capsule, 100 %). Off-Axis turns the capsule away from the source: a high shelf cuts up to 8 dB (smoothly at the top) and a faint comb (a delay of about 0.35 ms mixed in negatively, high-passed above 2 kHz so only the highs are affected) adds the ripple of an off-axis response. The left and right delays differ slightly. Room is a handful of early reflections: six taps between 3 and 29 ms with alternating signs and falling levels, low-passed at 5 kHz. The right channel's delays are 7 % longer than the left one's, so the two sides are decorrelated. The level grows with distance (a source at 5 cm gets about a third of the room that one at 2 m gets at the same setting). There is no feedback, so the reflections stop 30 ms after the sound. Saturation. A smooth sigmoid with unity small-signal gain, so it only adds harmonics as the level rises and does not change the loudness at low levels. A bias in the condenser and tube models gives even harmonics; the ribbon and dynamic models are symmetrical. It is evaluated with first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing: a loud 7 kHz tone at nominal Colour keeps folded harmonics below about -45 dB, and quieter tones are far cleaner. On top of that the ribbon softens large bass excursions (a low-band saturator below about 200 Hz), and the dynamic model turns down a transient that is far above the recent average (a fast follower against a slow one), so the beginning of a loud note is about 2 dB softer. Self-Noise adds a very quiet hiss that falls towards the top, independent in the left and right channel, from -100 dB (off) to -50 dB. It is deterministic: the same noise on every run. Mix blends the dry input with the microphone signal. Mix 0 is exactly the input, in phase. The module has no latency. How to use it?
