A synth lead in a room: Condenser, Distance 80 cm, Room 25 %, Presence 30 %. Vintage-sounding drums: Ribbon, Distance 20 cm, Proximity 70 %, Colour 60 %, Room 20 %. DI guitar to cabinet-and-mic: Dynamic, Distance 10 cm, Presence 40 %, Off-Axis 20 %. Warm vocal: Tube Condenser, Distance 15 cm, Proximity 40 %, Colour 60 %. Air on a pad: Condenser, Diaphragm 20 % (small capsule), Colour 75 %, Distance 100 cm. Far away, mono-ish source: Distance 250 cm, Room 50 %, Off-Axis 30 %. Lo-fi hiss: Self-Noise -60 dB. Parallel colour: Mix 40 %: keeps the dry attack and adds the mic's tone. The module's own UI A top-down room. The microphone shows the polar pattern of the chosen model (a figure-8 for the ribbon, rounder for the others); the source is a dot at a distance that follows the Distance knob. Rings round the capsule thicken with the proximity effect, dots bounce off the walls as early reflections (their number follows Room and distance), ripples leave the source with the signal level, and the response curve of the microphone is drawn underneath. Drag the source left or right to set Distance. Grab the microphone and turn it to set Off-Axis; the pattern rotates away from the source. Click a model pill to switch model. Tricks it demonstrates: mapping a logarithmic knob (Distance) to a horizontal position and back; drawing a polar pattern from a formula; animating particles along piecewise paths with a single phase value; a response curve cached and recomputed only when a knob changed, with the module's own analog formulas; easing a polled probe. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input In R audio Right input (in Auto mode, the left signal is used for both channels while nothing is patched here) Out L audio Left output Out R audio Right output Controls Control Range Default Meaning Model Ribbon, Dynamic, Condenser, Tube Condenser Condenser The microphone (the change fades out and in) Distance 3 to 300 cm 30 cm Source distance: proximity bass, air absorption, direct level, room amount Proximity 0 to 100 % 50 % Strength of the close-mic bass lift Presence 0 to 100 % 30 % Extra lift in the presence region, up to 6 dB Colour 0 to 100 % 50 % The model's own tone and saturation amount; 50 % is nominal Diaphragm 0 to 100 % 50 % Condenser models: the peak moves from 13 kHz (0 %) to 7.5 kHz (100 %) Off-Axis 0 to 100 % 0 % High-frequency dulling (up to 8 dB) and a faint comb Room 0 to 100 % 15 % Level of the early reflections Self-Noise -100 (off) to -50 dB -90 dB Hiss level (rms) Output -12 to +12 dB 0 dB Level of the microphone signal Mix 0 to 100 % 100 % Dry / microphone blend Input Auto, Stereo, Mono Auto Auto: the left input feeds both channels while the right one is unpatched (exactly 0 for 2048 samples); Stereo: both inputs; Mono: left to both Notes The module has no latency. Dry and wet stay in phase. The reflection buffer is cleared on reset for sample rates up to 96 kHz. Cost: about 59,000 operations per 32-sample block by the checker's conservative count, just below the 60,000 warning bound.

title: Opto Compressor
text: Opto Compressor Opto Compressor in the module view Introduction An optical compressor does not have an attack and a release knob. Its gain is controlled by a light and a light-sensitive cell, and the cell has a mind of its own: it clamps down quickly on a new loud passage, keeps creeping a little deeper while the loudness lasts, and lets go in two stages: quickly after a short peak, slowly (seconds) after a long stretch of compression. That is why it levels vocals, bass and mixes so gently: it works on the overall level and leaves the short peaks and the natural decay alone. The Opto Compressor models that gain element. You set how hard it works with Peak Reduction , the make-up with Gain , and the rest happens by itself. The module is stereo, with an extra Sidechain input and a Reduction control output. How does it work? In -> make-up gain stage (valve + transformer colour) -> Mix -> Out ^ +-> detector -> photocell -> gain reduction The detector. A light panel follows the level of the signal (the sidechain input if Sidechain is External): it lights up within about 1 ms and fades in about 30 ms. A high shelf in front of it, HF Emphasis , can make the detector hear the highs louder, so that bright sounds (sibilance, cymbals) compress more than the lows. Only the detector is filtered, not the audio. Peak Reduction turns the detector up by 0 to 40 dB: more gain in front of a fixed threshold, so a higher setting compresses quieter material. The compression curve. The level above the threshold turns into a wanted amount of gain reduction with a soft knee: Compress : ratio about 3:1, a wide knee (14 dB), gentle. Limit : ratio about 10:1, a narrow knee (6 dB) and an attack twice as fast, for firmer control. The photocell. The gain reduction is held by two parts that both chase the wanted amount, and the applied reduction is their mean: The fast part attacks in a few milliseconds (faster for a bigger jump in level: program-dependent attack) and releases in about 60 ms, a little longer when it holds more reduction. The slow part attacks with a time constant of about a second (2 s divided by 1 plus an eighth of the wanted reduction in dB) and releases with a time constant from 1 s up to 5.5 s, depending on how much it has charged. The more it holds, the slower it lets go: this is the photocell's memory. A short burst barely charges it; a long, hard stretch of compression charges it fully. What you get: a short peak is attenuated by about half of what it would be in steady state and recovers within a fraction of a second; sustained loud material is compressed deeper over seconds and, when it ends, leaves a tail of several seconds in which the level recovers gently. The module's tests measure all of this: in the default setting, after 0.3 s of compression only about 13 % of the reduction is left after one second, after 20 s of compression about 39 %, and the slow tail has a time constant of about 3 s. The time constants are in seconds, so the behaviour is the same at 44.1, 48 and 96 kHz. The make-up stage. Gain is applied through a stage with a little valve and transformer colour: a smooth curve with a small bias adds an even (2nd) harmonic that grows with the level, and a low-frequency core saturation (only the bass below about 140 Hz feels it) adds odd harmonics when a large low-frequency swing passes. The more gain, the harder the stage works. The small-signal gain is exactly the Gain setting. The curve is evaluated with anti-aliasing, and it is bounded for any input. Link. At 100 % both channels follow the louder one, so the stereo image does not shift. At 0 % they are independent. The photocell state is per channel. Mix blends the compressed signal with the dry one (parallel compression). There is no latency, so the two stay in phase. How to use it? Vocal leveler: Compress, Peak Reduction 40 to 55, Gain to match the level, HF Emphasis 3 dB if sibilance jumps out. Bass control: Compress, Peak Reduction 50, Link 100 %, Gain +4 dB. The slow release keeps notes even without pumping. Bus glue: Compress, Peak Reduction 25, Mix 100 %. You should see 1 to 3 dB of reduction on the Gain Reduction meter. Parallel density: Limit, Peak Reduction 80, Mix 30 %. Peak catching: Limit, Peak Reduction 60: faster attack, higher ratio. Ducking: put a kick drum into the Sidechain input, set Sidechain to External, Limit mode, Peak Reduction 60. De-essing by ear: HF Emphasis 9 to 12 dB with moderate Peak Reduction: the sibilants trigger the compression and the body does not. Use the Reduction output to open a filter or light something when the signal is squashed: 0 is no reduction, 1 is 24 dB or more. The module's own UI A lamp glows with the gain reduction. Beside it the photocell shows two bars: the fast stage and the slow stage (the charge), so you can see the slow one fill over seconds and linger after the fast one has let go. A needle on a spring shows the reduction in dB, and a strip scrolls the history of the reduction (bright) and the charge (faint). At silence the lamp breathes and the needle trembles, so the picture never looks dead. Drag the lamp up or down to turn Peak Reduction (the ring around it shows the setting). Click the dial to switch between Compress and Limit. Tricks it demonstrates: easing the polled probes with a frame-rate independent exponential; a mass-on-a-spring needle (semi-implicit Euler with damping); ring buffers allocated once for the history; a layout expressed as fractions of the canvas width so it works in a narrow node; vertical drags mapped to a knob's range. Cost: about 29,000 operations per 32-sample block by the checker's conservative count.

title: Tone EQ
text: Tone EQ Tone EQ in the module view Introduction Most equalisers are surgical: a parametric band finds a problem and removes it. The Tone EQ is the opposite. It is a passive, interactive, musical tone control, the kind of EQ you reach for to make a bass bigger, a vocal brighter or a bus warmer, and where moving one knob changes what the others do. It has three modes: Passive Shelf is a network of shelves with stepped frequencies. The low boost and low attenuation are two separate knobs at the same frequency, and they overlap: used together they give a big, smooth, tight bottom with a gentle dip above it, instead of a boomy bass. The high section has a broad boost with a bandwidth control and a separate high attenuation shelf. Tilt is a two-knob seesaw: bass down and treble up, or the reverse, with broad gentle slopes around a pivot. Tone Stack is a guitar-amp style bass / mid / treble network with its characteristic mid scoop and insertion loss. After the EQ a valve make-up stage adds a little level-dependent warmth, Output sets the level, and Age lets the component values wander slowly, a little differently in the left and right channel. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). How does it work? The signal passes through one of three filter networks, then the make-up stage: In -> [ Passive Shelf Tilt Tone Stack ] -> valve make-up stage -> Output -> Out The filters are analog prototypes. Every filter starts as the transfer function of an analog circuit and is turned into a digital filter with the bilinear transform, pre-warped so that the filter's own frequency lands exactly where the knob says. The module's tests compare the realised response with the analog curve at several settings. Below about a fifth of the sample rate the two agree within a fraction of a decibel; in the top octave the bilinear transform squeezes the curve a little (a bell at 12 kHz is narrower on its upper side than the analog one at 48 kHz) and the match is better at 96 kHz. Passive Shelf. Four sections in a row: Low boost : a second-order low shelf at the chosen frequency (20, 30, 60 or 100 Hz) with a small resonance, up to about +15 dB. Low attenuation : a first-order (6 dB per octave) low shelf that turns over about 2.4 times higher than the boost, up to about -12 dB. Because it works higher up than the boost, the two overlap: boost and attenuation at the same setting leave a net lift at the very bottom and a dip in the octave above it, which is what keeps the low end smooth instead of boomy. High boost : a bell at 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 12 or 16 kHz, up to about +16 dB, with a Bandwidth control from narrow (Q 2) to very broad (Q 0.35). High attenuation : a first-order high shelf cut at 5, 10 or 20 kHz, up to about -14 dB. All the frequencies are stepped choices, so every position is a known, repeatable sound. Changing a step glides the filter rather than jumping. Tilt. Two broad first-order shelves, a low shelf 2.5 times below the pivot and a high shelf 2.5 times above it, with opposite gains. The pivot frequency itself stays where it is; one side goes down as the other goes up, with a slope of a couple of dB per octave. Tone Stack. The module solves the real circuit: a treble capacitor and pot, a bass pot with an audio taper, a mid pot, a slope resistor and two more capacitors (textbook values: 250 k, 1 M and 25 k pots, 56 k slope resistor, 250 pF and 2 x 20 nF capacitors). At block rate it builds the nodal admittance equations of the network at four values of the Laplace variable, takes the determinant (the denominator) and the output voltage times it (the numerator), and interpolates the two cubics. The result is a third-order transfer function that is then discretised. Because it is a passive network it has the real behaviour: a mid scoop whose depth and position depend on all three pots, a large insertion loss (everything is turned down), and interaction between the controls. A fixed make-up gain of 9 dB brings the level back up. Valve make-up stage. A smooth asymmetric curve with a small bias, so it adds mainly even harmonics (a 2nd harmonic that grows with the input level and is much smaller than the 3rd at low levels), unity gain for small signals (so changing Drive does not change the loudness), and a bounded output for any input. The part of the curve beyond a straight line is evaluated with first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing, so the straight part keeps its flat response up to the top and loud high tones do not fold back audibly. The small DC offset an asymmetric curve makes is removed by a high-pass. Age. Three slow random walkers per channel, with a time constant of a few seconds. They scale the gains of the shelves and bells by a few percent, their frequencies by a couple of percent, and in the Tone Stack the pot positions and capacitor values. The left and right generators are different, so a slightly different stereo image appears over time. With Age at 0 nothing moves and both channels are identical. The drift is deterministic: the same input gives the same output on every run. How to use it? Big, tight bass: Passive Shelf, Low Freq 60 Hz, Low Boost 6, Low Atten 5. The bottom gets heavier and the low mids above it get cleaner. Kick weight without boom: Low Freq 100 Hz, Low Boost 4, Low Atten 4. Silky top on a vocal or a mix bus: High Freq 10 kHz, High Boost 3, Bandwidth 7. Add High Atten 2 at 20 kHz to take the edge off the very top. Presence on a guitar: High Freq 5 kHz, High Boost 4, Bandwidth 3. Darker, warmer master: Tilt mode, Tilt -2 dB, Pivot 650 Hz. Brighter without EQ harshness: Tilt +3 dB, Pivot 1 kHz. Guitar amp tone: Tone Stack, Bass 6, Mid 4, Treble 6, Drive 50 %. Turn Mid down for the classic scoop; Mid at 10 fills it in. Warmth on a bus: any mode, Drive 25 %, Output set so the level matches the bypassed signal. Wider, living stereo: Age 50 %, from a mono source with Input set to Mono. Because a passive EQ interacts, move the controls against each other: boost a little, listen, then add attenuation at the same frequency and listen to the bottom tighten. The module's own UI The Tone EQ draws the network you are hearing. In Passive Shelf mode the boost (amber) and the attenuation (red) are two ghost curves, and the white curve is their sum, so you can watch them interact. A dot sweeps along the curve and glows with the output level. Drag a round handle: up and down set its amount, left and right snap its stepped frequency. Click a mode pill (Passive Shelf, Tilt, Tone Stack) to switch mode. In Tilt mode drag the diamond: vertical is Tilt, horizontal snaps Pivot. In Tone Stack mode drag a dial up or down. Tricks it demonstrates: the curve is computed in the UI with the same analog formulas the module designs from (and checked against the module's measured response in its test); curves are cached and recomputed only when a knob moved; the polled level probe is eased with 1 - Math.exp(-dt k) so the glow is smooth at any frame rate; hit testing picks the nearest handle; a pointer is captured while dragging, and a continuous drag is snapped to a list of steps. Cost: about 44,000 operations per 32-sample block by the Bleep Script checker's conservative count, below the 60,000 warning bound.

title: Cheap Speaker
text: Cheap Speaker Cheap Speaker in the module view Introduction A bit crusher makes a sound digital. The Cheap Speaker does something different: it makes a sound small . It puts the signal through the narrow, resonant, overloaded playback of a poor device: a phone line, a car radio on a long drive, a laptop speaker, a megaphone. The character comes from the band-limiting, the peaks in the response and the way each device distorts, not from sample-rate or bit-depth tricks (use a crusher for those). Six devices are built in. Each is a designed curve, and the controls scale it: Telephone : 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz, a nasal peak in the mids, the asymmetric harmonic distortion of a carbon microphone, line hiss and a faint mains hum. AM Radio : 120 Hz to 4.5 kHz, the uneven distortion of an envelope detector, crackling static, hiss and a heterodyne whistle between stations that drifts. Car Speaker : small cone, bass rolled off from 80 Hz, a boxy cavity resonance, cone breakup in the top, a short cabin reflection, road rumble. Cassette Player : high-frequency loss, a mild head bump, slow wow, bright tape hiss and a trace of motor hum. Tiny Speaker (laptop or phone): steep bass cut at 300 Hz, a sharp resonance near 2.2 kHz, an excursion limit that loses bass at high level, and rattle when the cone is overdriven. Megaphone : 500 Hz to 4 kHz, a horn resonance and hard clipping. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It adds a fixed delay of about 3.7 milliseconds (the dry signal in the Mix is delayed by the same amount). How does it work? In -> wobble delay -> excursion limit -> non-linearity (2x oversampled) -> + noise -> low cut (4th order) -> two resonances -> high cut (4th order) -> cabin reflection (car) -> + hum and rumble -> Output Corners. The low and high corners of each device are fourth-order Butterworth sections, so the number in the table is exactly the -3 dB point and the slope is 24 dB per octave. The tests check the realised corner of every device (within a fraction of a dB of -3 dB), at 44.1, 48 and 96 kHz. Bandwidth multiplies both corners at once: 200 % lowers the low corner to half and raises the high corner to double, 50 % does the reverse. Resonances. Two peaking filters per device give its character: the nasal peak of the telephone, the 2.2 kHz squeal of the tiny speaker, the horn of the megaphone. Resonance scales their height in decibels: 50 % is as designed, 0 % is perfectly flat, 100 % is twice as high. At 0 % the response is a plain band-pass, which is how the corners are measured. In the car the same knob scales the cabin reflection (two delayed copies at 2.9 and 5.1 milliseconds, which comb the response). Distortion. Each device has its own non-linearity, driven by the Distortion knob, and all of them depend on level, so quiet material stays clean: Telephone and AM radio use an asymmetric curve (a bias before a soft limit). This gives strong even harmonics, the carbon-microphone and detector sound. Megaphone uses hard symmetric clipping: odd harmonics only and heavy compression. Car and Tiny Speaker first run the bass through an excursion limit (the cone can only move so far): the part of the signal below about 450 Hz is soft-limited, so a loud bass note loses bass relative to the treble. On the tiny speaker, whatever the cone could not follow excites a short band-limited rattle . All curves are gently shaped polynomials, evaluated with first-order anti-derivative anti-aliasing at twice the sample rate. A hard-driven 5 kHz tone keeps its non-harmonic components about 58 dB below the tone or lower. The make-up gain compensates part of the drive, so more distortion does not simply mean more volume. The default loudness of all six devices is within 8 dB of the input, measured on a broadband test signal. Noise. The noise knob sets the level of each device's own noise: line hiss and hum (telephone), static, hiss and a whistle (AM), road rumble (car), tape hiss (cassette), amplifier hiss and hum (tiny speaker), hiss and static (megaphone). Hiss, static and the whistle are added before the filters, so they take on the sound of the device (telephone hiss lives in 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz); hum and rumble are added after them. Left and right have independent hiss; hum and the whistle are common to both. Wobble. A seeded slow random drift moves the level a little and the high corner a few percent; on the cassette player it also bends the pitch (up to about 7 cents of slow wow at 100 %), on the radio only slightly (the station is drifting) and moves the whistle. How to use it? Phone call: Telephone, Bandwidth 100 %, Resonance 50 %, Distortion 25 %, Noise 20 %, Wobble 0 %. Use it on a vocal for an intro or a breakdown. Distant radio: AM Radio, Noise 50 %, Wobble 40 %, Distortion 40 %. The static and the whistle give it a station-between-stations feel. Car stereo: Car Speaker, Resonance 60 %, Distortion 40 %, Noise 15 %. Bass is thin and boxy, the room is small. Old tape deck: Cassette Player, Noise 40 %, Wobble 50 %. Dull, wobbly and hissy. Laptop playback: Tiny Speaker, Distortion 50 %, Resonance 50 %. Turn the signal up and the bass pumps away as the cone runs out of travel. Bullhorn: Megaphone, Distortion 70 %, Resonance 70 %. Wider or narrower: Bandwidth 140 % opens any device up (a "better" telephone); 60 % squeezes it. Parallel lo-fi: Mix 30 % keeps the original body and adds the device's mids and grit. The dry signal is time-aligned. The module's own UI The node shows a cartoon speaker. Its cone pumps with the sound, stops at its travel limit on the devices that have one (car and tiny speaker) and jitters when overdriven, and static speckles around it follow Noise. Next to it is the frequency response of the chosen device, drawn with the same formulas the module designs it from, so the corners and the peaks move as you turn Bandwidth and Resonance. Click a device tile to change the device. Drag one of the two vertical corner lines sideways to set Bandwidth. What the UI demonstrates: Drawing a response from analytic formulas. The curve is the sum, in decibels, of two fourth-order Butterworth sections and two peaking bells; the tests compare it with the measured module within 1.5 dB. A logarithmic frequency axis , both ways: frequency to x for drawing and x to frequency for dragging. Dragging an edge. Dragging the low corner to a frequency f sets Bandwidth to the device's corner divided by f . Hit testing small targets with a distance tolerance, and tiles laid out from the canvas width. Probe added for the picture: excursion (how far the cone is pushed towards its limit, 0 to 1). Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Devices Device Low corner High corner Peaks Distortion Telephone 300 Hz 3.4 kHz 1.2 kHz (+6 dB), 2.4 kHz (+2.5 dB) asymmetric, strong even harmonics AM Radio 120 Hz 4.5 kHz 1.8 kHz (+2.5 dB), 300 Hz (+2.5 dB) asymmetric (detector) Car Speaker 80 Hz 7.5 kHz 300 Hz (+4 dB), 5.5 kHz (+4 dB) mild, bass excursion limit Cassette Player 50 Hz 9 kHz 100 Hz (+2.5 dB), 6.5 kHz (-3 dB) light tape saturation Tiny Speaker 300 Hz 9.5 kHz 2.2 kHz (+9 dB, Q 5), 900 Hz (+3 dB) medium, excursion limit, rattle Megaphone 500 Hz 4 kHz 1.5 kHz (+8 dB), 2.7 kHz (+4 dB) hard clipping The peak heights are at Resonance 50 %. Bandwidth 50 to 200 % 100 % Scales both corners. Resonance 0 to 100 % 50 % Height of the characteristic peaks (and the cabin reflection of the car). Distortion 0 to 100 % 40 % How hard the device is driven. Noise 0 to 100 % 30 % Level of the device's noise. The level follows the square of the knob. Wobble 0 to 100 % 20 % Slow level and top-end drift; pitch wobble on the cassette and the radio. Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level, after the device's make-up gain.
