The cost estimate is about 130,000 per 32-sample chunk, below the 150,000 this project allows for the heaviest modules. The output is limited to plus and minus 16 so that extreme settings cannot produce huge values.

title: Crunch
text: Crunch Crunch in the module view Introduction Crunch dirties up a sound in two ways. Drive is analogue-style overdrive: from a slight warmth through crunchy guitar-amp distortion to a square-wave fuzz. Bits and Rate Red. are digital: they throw away resolution and sample rate until the sound turns into the grit of a 90s sampler, an old game console or a broken phone. Use them separately or together. How does it work? The signal passes through, in this order: Overdrive. A gain stage followed by a soft clipper: the louder the input, the more it is rounded off. Soft clipping creates odd harmonics, which is why overdrive sounds "warm". Drive sets the gain before the clipper. The Drive knob is level-compensated, so more drive changes the colour without getting louder. Sample-rate reduction. Rate Red. holds every sample for several sample periods. This turns the sound into a stair-step wave and folds high frequencies back down as inharmonic, metallic aliasing. At 100 % the signal is held for 96 samples. Bit crushing. Bits rounds the level to a coarse grid of 2^(bits−1) steps per unit. At 16 bits nothing happens; at 8 bits you hear a faint hiss on quiet parts; at 4 bits the sound is rough; at 1 bit it's a square wave. The knob is continuous, so you can sweep it. Tone. A low-pass filter at the end, from 500 Hz to 20 kHz (20 kHz is off) takes the harshest top off the digital sound. Level sets the processed signal's volume, Mix blends it with the dry input (parallel distortion keeps the transients). With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Warm saturation on a bus: Drive 20 %, Mix 50 %. Crunchy bass: Drive 60 %, Tone 4 kHz, Mix 70 %. Fuzz lead: Drive 100 %, Tone 3 kHz. Lo-fi drums: Bits 8, Rate Red. 25 %, Tone 8 kHz. Broken radio: Bits 4, Rate Red. 60 %, Tone 2 kHz. Sweep: an LFO or envelope onto Bits or Rate Red. for sounds that dissolve and rebuild. Origin The overdrive curve and its gain structure are Émilie Gillet's (Mutable Instruments, Plaits , 2014), the sample-rate reduction is from DaisySP's Decimator , both through Overdrive and Decimator (DaisySP, from Plaits) by Electrosmith, github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP, MIT licence. Bleep's version has both in one stereo module; the Drive knob covers the useful part of Plaits' curve with level compensation, the bit crusher rounds (and takes fractional bit depths) instead of truncating, and a tone filter and output level were added. The original licence texts are in this module's LICENSE file. Presets The preset bar of the Crunch view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Warm Saturation Gentle tube-like warmth on anything. Overdrive Classic mid-gain overdrive. Fuzz Wall Thick, compressed fuzz with the top rolled off. Lo-Fi Bits 8-bit quantisation noise, old sampler style. Telephone Crush Narrow, crushed and aliased. Rate Grinder Sample-rate reduction aliasing without much bit loss. Broken Machine Harsh digital breakdown. Parallel Grit Crunch blended under a clean signal for grit with body. Drum Crunch Adds bite and crackle to drum loops. Dark Dirt Heavy drive filtered dark for bass. Bit Dust Subtle degradation, like a worn digital converter. Square Wave Mangler Two bits turn everything into buzzing pulses. Total Destruction Everything at once; keep the level low. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Crunch does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Crunch under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Crunch: Overdriven Bass A plain bass line is pushed into Drive with Tone rolled down to 3 kHz: warm, thick overdrive with the harshest top cut away. Raise Drive for fuzz, or open Tone for a more biting edge. Crunch: Bit-Crushed Breaks A broken beat loses bits and sample rate, so the kick turns gritty and the hats turn into digital hiss; Mix keeps some of the clean drum underneath. Push Bits toward 1 for noise, or pull Rate Red. down to restore the highs. Crunch: Aliased Lead Rate Red. at about 55 % with full 16-bit depth leaves the lead's pitch intact but folds new, glassy partials around it, like an old video-game chip. Sweep Rate Red. slowly while the riff plays. Crunch: Dissolving Pad A slow LFO sweeps Bits from clean to coarse and back on a held pad, so the sound breaks into steps and re-forms in long waves. Change the cable amount for a shallower sweep or move Rate Red. for another kind of breakup. Crunch: Parallel Grit A four-on-the-floor beat gets near-maximum Drive and 8 bits but only 35 % Mix, so the clean punch stays and the crunch adds weight and fizz around it. Move Mix to find where the grit starts to take over.

title: Folder
text: Folder Folder in the module view Introduction The Folder is a stereo wavefolder: six folding stages in a row turn a simple waveform into a rich, bright, vocal tone. Its Fold knob sweeps through the harmonics the way a filter sweeps through a spectrum, only upwards. Symmetry adds even harmonics, Tap chooses how many stages you hear. It is anti-aliased, so deep folds on high notes stay clean. With a cable in Pitch it plays its own sine/triangle oscillator, which makes it a complete "west coast" voice on its own. How does it work? Folding. When a signal goes past ±1, a folder reflects it back instead of clipping it: a sine driven twice as hard comes back with a dip at each peak, driven harder it folds again and again. Every fold adds harmonics. Shape chooses the fold curve: at 0 % a soft fold (a sine curve, which already rounds a full-scale signal a little), at 100 % a hard, mirror-like fold that leaves signals within ±1 untouched. Stages. The signal runs through six folders in a row. Each multiplies it by the Fold gain (1× at 0 %, 4× at 100 %) before folding, so the folds multiply from stage to stage. Symmetry adds an offset before the first stage (and half of it before the second): the folds become lopsided and even harmonics appear. Tap picks the stage you hear, 1 to 6; between two whole numbers it crossfades the neighbouring stages, so modulating Tap opens the sound from a gentle fold to a dense one without changing the level. Stages after the tapped one are not computed. Anti-aliasing. Folding creates harmonics far above the audible range; without care they fold back down as inharmonic noise. The Folder runs the stages at 4× the sample rate ( Normal ) or 2× ( Eco ), and each stage uses antiderivative anti-aliasing, which smooths the corners. At Normal a C5 sine folded with Fold 100 % at Tap 2 keeps aliases about 84 dB below the fundamental; very deep settings (high Fold at Tap 4–6) are meant to sound like dense noise and do. Dry and DC. Mix blends the dry signal back in; the dry signal is delayed by the same 1.5 ms as the folded one, so the two stay in phase. A 5 Hz high-pass on the outputs removes the offset that Symmetry creates. Symmetry and Level changes are smoothed over 2 ms; Fold and Tap follow audio-rate modulation. Internal oscillator. With Source on Auto , a cable in Pitch and none in In L turns on the oscillator: a sine (or, with Wave , a triangle) at C4 × 2^(Octave + Pitch + Coarse/12 + Fine/1200), at ±1 into both channels. Internal always uses the oscillator; In L then becomes its FM input. Input always folds the inputs. Switching fades over 5 ms. Stereo. In R unpatched: In L feeds both channels. Spread offsets Symmetry (by ±Spread/2) and Fold (±10 %) between left and right, which makes a mono source wide. A mono source with Spread at 0 is computed once. How to use it? Complex oscillator voice: Voice In Pitch → Pitch ; an envelope onto Fold ; Out L → VCA. Wave 0 % (sine) gives the classic sound. Moving timbre: a slow LFO onto Symmetry and another onto Tap . FM plus folding: set Source to Internal , patch another Oscillator into In L and raise FM Depth . Brighten anything: put it after an oscillator or a filter and use low Fold with Mix at 50 %. Stereo width: Spread 30–60 % on a mono source. Tame hot sources: lower Level rather than Fold : it changes how far the signal reaches into the folds. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Folder does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Folder under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Folder: Folded Saw Riff An external saw riff enters the Folder's input and an LFO moves Fold up and down, so each note folds back on itself into a growl that opens and closes. Change Symmetry for a hollower tone or lower Tap for a gentler fold. Folder: Evolving Sine Drone With Source on Internal the Folder is its own voice: a slow sequencer sets the pitch, Wave and Fold drift under two LFOs, and a plain sine turns into a shifting, metallic drone. Try Coarse and Fine for beating pairs of partials. Folder: Lopsided Bass A low note from the internal sine is pushed off-centre with Symmetry and folded at Tap 3, giving a bass with strong even harmonics and a nasal, vocal edge. Change Symmetry to the other side or raise Fold for a buzzier note. Folder: Spread Pad A slow pad goes through the Folder with Spread turned up, so the left and right channels fold by different amounts and the pad opens into a wide, shimmering stereo image. Pull Spread down to bring it back to the centre. Folder: Folded Drum Kit A drum beat passes through the Folder at half Mix: the kick gains a hard, clicky harmonic edge and the hats shimmer, while the dry hits keep their weight. Raise Fold or Mix for a more broken, industrial kit. Presets The preset bar of the Folder view has 13 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Fold Mild folding that adds a few bright harmonics. Classic Fold The classic folded-sine timbre. Hollow Fold Asymmetry adds even harmonics for a reedy sound. Vocal Folds Formant-like tone when the fold is swept. Metal Bright Deep folding: bright, metallic and inharmonic. Low Tap Tame Heavy fold but only the early stages, so it stays smooth. Wide Folder Spread decorrelates left and right: a mono source becomes wide. Internal Sine Lead Use the built-in oscillator; play it from Pitch. Triangle Fold Folded triangle from the internal oscillator: softer and rounder. FM Fold FM adds sidebands before the folder for glassy tones. Detuned Growl An octave down with asymmetric folding: a growling bass. Parallel Fold Folded signal mixed under the dry one. Eco Chaos Extreme settings with cheaper oversampling; aliasing is part of it. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Fold 0 – 100 % 0 % Symmetry −100 … +100 % 0 % Tap 1 – 6 6 Shape 0 – 100 % 50 % Spread 0 – 100 % 0 % Level 0 – 100 % 100 % Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Wave 0 – 100 % 0 % (sine) Coarse −24 … +24 st 0 st Fine −100 … +100 ct 0 ct FM Depth 0 – 100 % 0 % Source Auto, Input, Internal Auto Octave −3 … +3 0 Quality Eco (2×), Normal (4×) Normal Fold: the gain into each stage, 4^Fold (1× … 4×). Symmetry: offset before the folds: even harmonics, a reedy sound. Tap: which stage is heard; fractions crossfade two stages. Halfway between stages whose outputs are opposite, the sound can thin briefly. Shape: soft (0 %) to hard (100 %) fold curve. Level: input gain before folding (cubic curve, silent at 0 %). Wave, Coarse, Fine, FM Depth: the internal oscillator: sine → triangle, transposition, and through-zero FM from In L (±4× the frequency at 100 %). Quality: Normal (4×) is clean for almost any setting; Eco (2×) costs half and suits moderate folds or many voices. All knobs are modulation destinations; Source , Octave and Quality are settings. Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio the signal to fold; also feeds the right channel when In R is unpatched. FM input while the oscillator runs on Internal In R audio right input Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the internal oscillator's pitch; 0.0 = C4. On Auto , patching it (without In L ) switches the oscillator on Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the folded signal after Tap , Mix and DC blocking. Within ±1, up to about ±2 with strong Symmetry Osc audio the internal oscillator before folding; silent while it is off The folded path (and the dry path with it) is delayed by about 1.5 ms (70.5 samples plus a fraction at 48 kHz in Normal , 47 in Eco ); patch parallel paths around the Folder with that in mind.

title: Preamp
text: Preamp Preamp in the module view Introduction A transformer-coupled preamp does not sound the way it does because of its gain stage alone. Most of the character is in the two transformers , one at the input and one at the output. A transformer has an iron core, and the core can only carry so much magnetic flux. Low frequencies carry the most flux for a given level, so a hard-pushed transformer squashes and thickens the bass long before it touches the treble. It also has a little memory (hysteresis), it rolls off the top end through its leakage inductance and winding capacitance, and it interacts with the source that feeds it. The Preamp models exactly that chain: input transformer, gain stage, output transformer . The part that makes it different from a clipper is that the distortion depends on frequency and level together . Play a bass note at a low level and nothing happens. Play it louder and it fattens, with odd harmonics that sit above the note. Play a hi-hat at the same level and it stays clean. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It oversamples its gain stage and delays the dry signal by the same amount, so the Mix knob is phase-correct. How does it work? In -> Trim -> bass weight bell -> input core -> gain stage (Class A / AB, oversampled) -> coupling capacitor -> output core -> leakage roll-off (Air) -> level compensation -> Mix -> Out The cores. Each transformer is a small simulation of its magnetising branch. The state is the flux , which is the integral of the voltage across the branch, so for a sine of a given level it is proportional to the level divided by the frequency: a note an octave lower carries twice the flux. The magnetising current is proportional to the flux until the core approaches saturation, and then it rises steeply (with the fifth power of the flux). That current flows through the source impedance and is subtracted from the signal. At low level the result is a plain high-pass filter (the corner is set by Impedance , between 10 and 32 Hz). When the flux gets near the knee, the current climbs and the output flattens out: a soft, level-dependent compressor for the bass with odd harmonics. The simulation is stable however hard it is driven. Iron sets how early the cores saturate. It is the frequency below which a full-scale sine reaches the knee: from 6 Hz at 0 % to about 126 Hz at 100 %. At Iron 100 % a 50 Hz tone at -6 dBFS is past the knee, a 1 kHz tone at the same level is at one twentieth of it. Hysteresis. A lagging, smoothed sign of the flux rate shifts the saturation curve a little to the right while the flux rises and to the left while it falls. The loop pinches closed at small flux, so a quiet signal does not see it. Its width grows with Iron. The result is that the output is not a function of the input alone: the core remembers where it has been. Impedance sets the source: a higher impedance moves the high-pass corner up, adds a bump of up to 8 dB around 62 Hz (the bass weight, in front of the core, so that the core sees it and saturates earlier), and adds a gentle resonance (Q from 0.6 to 1.05) to the roll-off at the top. The gain stage. It runs at 2 times (Eco) or 4 times (Normal) the sample rate, between polyphase all-pass half-band filters. It is anti-aliased in two ways: the oversampling, and first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing on the non-linear part of the curve. Class A is a soft clip that is biased off-centre (a bias of 0.3 in units of the curve's knee): the positive and negative halves are shaped differently, so it makes even harmonics in the first place (H2 and H4), then odd. Class AB is a pair of devices that each conduct only past a small threshold (a smooth dead zone of 0.06 around zero), so the harmonics are odd only and the crossing makes a little grit at low level. A coupling capacitor (8 Hz) removes the DC the asymmetry leaves behind. Air sets the roll-off of the leakage inductance and winding capacitance: a second-order low-pass from 4 kHz (0 %) to 24 kHz (100 %, clamped below 0.45 of the sample rate). Level compensation. The gain stage is compensated so that a -12 dBFS sine at the input comes out at -12 dBFS whatever the Drive and Trim. Louder passages are squeezed, quieter ones lifted, so you can compare settings at the same loudness. Output adds to that. Age. A seeded, very slow random drift (a few tens of seconds per cycle), different for left and right. It moves the gain by up to 0.5 dB, the bias by 9 %, the core threshold by 8 % and the roll-off by 4 %. Nothing about it depends on the clock: two renders are identical. Latency. The oversampling filters delay the signal by about 3.2 samples (Eco) or 3.9 samples (Normal) at 48 kHz at low frequencies. The dry path of Mix is delayed by the same amount with a fractional delay. Input. Auto uses the left input for both channels while nothing is patched into In R (R has been exactly zero for 2048 samples while L is active), and returns to true stereo, smoothly, the moment R carries signal. Stereo and Mono force one or the other. How to use it? Bass guitar, weight and glue: Iron 70 %, Impedance 60 %, Drive 20 %, Class A, Air 50 %, Age 25 %. Play a low note hard and listen to it grow harmonics that lift it out on small speakers. Kick that needs body: Iron 85 %, Impedance 50 %, Drive 15 %, Class AB, Trim +3 dB. The click on top stays clean; the thump is rounded and denser. Warmth on a bus: Drive 25 %, Iron 50 %, Class A, Air 60 %, Mix 100 %. Level compensation means you can switch it in and out without a jump. Vocal presence: Drive 35 %, Iron 25 %, Class A, Air 85 %, Impedance 30 %. Mostly the gain stage; the transformers contribute a small amount of low-end weight. Gritty drums: Class AB, Drive 70 %, Iron 60 %, Mix 40 %. The dry signal keeps the transients, the wet one adds the crossover edge. Stereo width without drift: Age 0 % makes left and right identical for a mono source. A little Age (20 to 30 %) makes the sides differ by the slight amount that two real channels would. CPU: Eco halves the oversampling of the gain stage. The aliasing stays below -55 dBc even at Drive 100 %. The module's own UI The Preamp draws its own picture instead of the standard panel (the knobs stay below it). It shows the transformer core's B-H loop : flux against magnetising force. A dot rides round the loop with the signal level, the loop tints from amber to red as the core saturates (the Core probe), and it breathes gently when nothing is playing. Drag inside the picture: left and right sets Iron (the loop widens and its knees drop), up and down sets Drive (the dot swings further out). The file is src/preamp.view.js . Tricks it demonstrates: smoothing polled probes with 1 - Math.exp(-dt rate) , so a value that arrives 10 times a second moves smoothly at 60 frames a second; idle animation (a slow sine on the swing) so the picture never looks dead in silence; drawing one closed path for the two branches of a loop, and tinting it by stacking two translucent fills; mapping a pointer position to a knob with setNormalised , which works whatever the knob's units are. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Knobs Knob Range Default Meaning Trim -12 to +12 dB 0 dB Level into the first transformer. Drive 0 to 100 % 20 % Gain of the gain stage, 0 to 36 dB. The output is level-compensated. Iron 0 to 100 % 60 % How early the cores saturate (6 to 126 Hz knee for a full-scale sine). Also the width of the hysteresis loop. Impedance 0 to 100 % 40 % Source impedance: the low corner (10 to 32 Hz), the bass bump (up to +8 dB at 62 Hz) and the resonance of the top. Class A, AB A The gain stage: asymmetric, even harmonics (A) or dead zone, odd harmonics (AB). Air 0 to 100 % 60 % High roll-off, 4 kHz to 24 kHz. Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level, after the level compensation. Mix 0 to 100 % 100 % Dry against processed. The dry signal is delayed to stay in phase. Age 0 to 100 % 25 % Slow drift, different for left and right. Input Auto, Stereo, Mono Auto Where the right channel gets its signal. Quality Eco, Normal Normal 2 times or 4 times oversampling of the gain stage. Probes Probe Meaning Core How close the transformer cores are to saturation (1 is the knee). Level The output level (peak, falling slowly). Numbers worth knowing Cost: about 122,000 operations per 32-sample chunk at the heaviest setting (4 times oversampling, both channels). The checker reports a warning above 60,000; the limit is 400,000. Class AB, Drive 0 %, Iron 100 %: a 40 Hz tone at -6 dBFS has a third harmonic at -5.7 dBc (the core is deep in saturation), at -12 dBFS -17 dBc, at -26 dBFS -43 dBc. The same tone at 1 kHz and -6 dBFS has its third harmonic at -37 dBc, and that is the gain stage's own crossover, not the iron. A 7 kHz tone at -6 dBFS driven hard leaves about -68 dBc of non-harmonic energy at Normal and -61 dBc at Eco (Drive 50 %); -64 and -56 dBc at Drive 100 %.

title: Saturator
text: Saturator Saturator in the module view Introduction Saturator adds warmth and harmonics without the brittle, fizzy edge that digital distortion usually has. It is a small model of an analogue gain stage: a smooth curve, a frequency-dependent drive, a power supply that gives way under load and parts that slowly drift. Use it from a hint of warmth on a bus to a thick amp-like crunch. For deliberately digital grit (bit crushing, sample-rate reduction) use Crunch . For metallic, folded harmonics use Folder . How does it work? The signal passes through, in this order: Colour (pre-emphasis). Before the curve, the highs (or lows) are boosted by up to 12 dB. The stage then distorts those frequencies harder. After the curve the boost is undone exactly, so Colour changes what gets distorted , not the overall tone. Bias and Drive. Drive is gain into the curve (0 to 36 dB). Bias moves the signal off the curve's centre, so the top and bottom of the wave are rounded differently. That makes even harmonics (the octave, warm and full) next to the odd ones a symmetrical curve makes. The curve (Character). Tube : a smooth tanh curve. Reacts most to Bias and Sag. Warm, round. Tape : a softer knee and a little memory: the stage hears a lagged copy of its own output, like the magnetic lag of tape. Gentle and glued. Diode : soft on top, harder at the bottom. Asymmetric by itself, even without Bias. Edgier and more vocal. Sag. A model of a power supply: loud signals lower the stage's gain and push its bias, then it recovers over about 150 ms. The result is compression and a "bloom" after hard hits. Quiet signals are left alone. Age. Slow random drift of bias and gain (a few seconds per cycle), different on the left and the right. Nothing ever sounds exactly the same twice, as with real hardware. Clean-up. DC from the bias is removed, then Tone (a 12 dB/oct low-pass, 500 Hz to 20 kHz; 20 kHz is off) rolls off the top, the way analogue stages do. Why it does not sound digital. The curve runs at 2× or 4× the sample rate with first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing, so the harmonics it creates do not fold back down as inharmonic noise. Quality chooses 2× (Eco) or 4× (Normal). Level sets the output. Drive is level-compensated: a signal at 0.5 comes out near 0.5 at any drive, so more drive changes the colour without getting much louder. Mix blends with the dry input; the dry path is delayed to match the oversampling, so parallel use stays in phase. With only In L patched, the signal feeds both sides. How to use it? Warmth on a bus: Tube, Drive 25 %, Bias 20 %, Sag 30 %, Mix 100 %. Tape glue on drums: Tape, Drive 45 %, Sag 50 %, Colour −20 %. Amp-like crunch: Tube, Drive 70 %, Colour +40 %, Tone 5 kHz. Fat bass without fizz: Tube, Drive 55 %, Colour −60 %, Tone 3 kHz, Mix 70 %. Edgy vocal: Diode, Drive 40 %, Colour +30 %. Alive pads: Age 80 % and a little Drive: the harmonics breathe slowly. Dynamic saturation: an envelope or LFO on Drive or Bias . Presets The preset bar of the Saturator view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Subtle Warmth A hint of even harmonics on anything. Bus Glue Soft, compressed tape-like cohesion for a mix bus. Tape Drums Rounded transients and a fatter body for drum loops. Tube Crunch Amp-like crunch with edge in the upper mids. Fat Bass Thick low end that stays smooth on top. Sub Weight Even-harmonic weight under a sub. Diode Bite Edgy, vocal asymmetry. Vocal Heat Gentle presence and density for a voice. Breathing Pad Slow drift makes a held chord shimmer and breathe. Loose Gear Everything wanders a little, like old hardware. Sagging Supply Hard hits squash and bloom. Fuzz Wall Thick, compressed, anti-aliased fuzz. Parallel Grit Hard-driven copy blended under the clean signal. Eco Warmth Light on CPU for many instances. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Saturator does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Saturator under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Saturator: Tube Warmth A thin sine-and-triangle melody gains harmonics from the Tube curve at moderate Drive: rounder, fuller and gently compressed. Raise Drive to move from warmth to overdrive, or compare with the Tape and Diode characters. Saturator: Tape Drum Bus A shuffled beat runs through the Tape curve with some Sag and Age: the peaks soften, the highs round off and the kit glues together. Raise Age for a worn, uneven machine or Drive for heavier compression. Saturator: Diode Bite A saw lead hits the Diode curve hard, with Color tilted toward the highs: a bright, snarling edge that stays musical. Pull Color negative for a darker growl, or lower Drive for a cleaner sound. Saturator: Wandering Bias A slow LFO moves Bias on a soft sine pad, so the curve becomes lopsided and even harmonics come and go: the tone drifts between hollow, nasal and full. Change the cable amount to wander more, or switch Character. Saturator: Worn Machine Bass and a sparse beat go through heavy Sag and Age on the Tape curve: the level sags on loud hits and the sound slowly drifts like a tired old machine. Turn Sag and Age to zero to hear the clean, steady version.

title: Shape Table
text: Shape Table Shape Table in the module view Introduction Shape Table is a waveshaper where you draw the shape. A waveshaper maps every input level to an output level through a curve; a straight line leaves the sound alone, a bend adds warmth, a zig-zag adds buzz and bite. Here the curve is a picture you paint with the mouse, or start from one of eight presets, and the module tells you which harmonics it will make. It is anti-aliased, so extreme curves stay clean, and the same curve is also a function generator for control signals. How does it work? The curve. The curve has 65 points between −1 and +1 on both axes, joined by a smooth spline. Input goes along the bottom, output up the side. Soft , Hard , Fold , Stairs , Asym , Rectify , Sine and Linear are the presets; click on the curve and drag to draw. The dot on the curve shows where the signal is right now. Drive and bias. Drive (−12 … +36 dB) multiplies the input before the curve: the more you drive, the more of the curve you use, and the further the sound moves from the input. Bias adds an offset, which makes the curve act asymmetrically and creates even harmonics (and a DC offset, which the DC Block switch removes with a very low high-pass). Edge. What happens when the input goes beyond ±1: Clip holds the ends of the curve, Fold mirrors the curve (a bent triangle of the input), Wrap repeats it. With Wrap and a smooth curve, the module turns a ramp into any waveform you drew: an oscillator-like table. Anti-aliasing. A curve with corners makes harmonics far above the audible range; unless they are handled they fold back down as harsh, inharmonic noise. Shape Table uses two defences together: oversampling ( Quality Off, 2× or 4×) and first-order antiderivative anti-aliasing, which is exact here because the curve is a table made of straight pieces whose integral is another table. At 4× a hard fold at high drive stays tens of decibels cleaner than without. The dry path is delayed by the same latency, so Mix keeps both in phase. Harmonics. The bar chart shows the first 16 harmonics that a full-scale sine would get through the current curve, Drive , Bias and Edge , in dB: a quick way to see why a curve sounds the way it does. A symmetric curve has bars only at 1, 3, 5, … Function out. Func In (a control signal, −1 … +1) goes through the same curve, without oversampling, to Func Out : a custom response curve for sequencers, a velocity map or a waveshaped LFO. How to use it? Warm it up: Soft , Drive 6 – 12 dB, Mix 50 %. Fold a sine into a voice: Fold , Drive 12 dB, an envelope on Drive . Bit-like steps: Stairs with Drive 0 – 6 dB. Even harmonics: Asym or Bias 20 %, DC Block on. A custom oscillator: Edge Wrap, a saw or triangle in, draw a waveform. Parallel distortion: Mix 30 % on drums. Draw a response: draw a curve and patch an LFO into Func In . Demo patches Five whole patches show what Shape Table does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Shape Table under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Shape Table: Soft Bass A pure sine bass is driven into the soft curve: the peaks round off and odd harmonics grow with Drive, so it gets warm and then gritty. Draw on the curve to change the harmonics, or raise Drive for more edge. Shape Table: Fold Lead A saw lead goes through a folding curve while an envelope pushes Drive up on every note: the first moment of each note is rich and bright and settles to a simpler tone. Change Drive or draw a new curve. Shape Table: Wrap Table Edge is Wrap: a slow triangle sweeps its way through the repeating sine curve, so the shaper becomes an oscillator-like table whose spectrum moves with Drive. Move Bias to shift where the curve is read. Shape Table: Crushed Drums A drum loop through the Stairs curve mixed back under the dry kit: eight steps give a crunchy, digital grain on every hit without losing the punch. Turn Mix up for more grit, down for a subtle bite. Shape Table: Function Curve A slow triangle LFO goes through the drawn curve (Func In to Func Out) and the result opens the cutoff of a filter on a saw riff: a custom-shaped sweep. Redraw the curve to reshape the sweep. Presets The preset bar of the Shape Table view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Warmth Gentle saturation blended under the dry sound. Hard Clip A hard limit with bright, odd harmonics. Fold Over A sine folded into a rich, vocal tone. Staircase Eight steps: a digital, quantised edge. Lopsided Soft on one side, harder on the other: even harmonics. Rectifier Full-wave rectification: the octave jumps up. Sine Table Wrap The curve repeats beyond the edges: a wavetable of one sine. Mirror Fold The curve mirrors at the edges: folding with a smooth bend. Gentle Saturator Subtle warmth for a full mix. Octave Up Rectifier blended with the dry signal. Bias Growl A biased soft curve: growly and asymmetric. Wrap Chaos Extreme drive with wrapping: dense and metallic. Crunch Eco No oversampling: raw, aliased crunch. Linear Pass A straight line: the sound passes unchanged. Draw on it. Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Signal What it does In L, In R audio the signal (R unpatched: L feeds both) Func In control through the curve without oversampling Out L, Out R audio the shaped signal, mixed with the dry one Func Out control the curve's output for Func In Knobs and settings Control Range Default Drive −12 … +36 dB +6 dB Bias −100 … +100 % 0 Mix 0 – 100 % 100 % Out −24 … +12 dB 0 Edge Clip, Fold, Wrap Clip Quality Off, 2×, 4× 2× DC Block on / off on The curve (65 values) is saved with the node.

title: Tape Machine
text: Tape Machine Tape Machine in the module view Introduction Tape does not just add a little distortion. It is a whole chain of small, level-dependent effects that together make a recording sound glued, rounded and slightly alive : the treble squashes before the bass does, the low end gets a soft bump, the top end rolls off more at slow speeds, the pitch wanders a few cents, and a faint hiss sits under everything. The Tape Machine models that chain, so it is much more than a saturator with a tape-coloured curve. Typical uses: warmth and glue on a drum bus or a mix, a vintage lo-fi sound on a loop or a synth (slow speed, Rough tape, some wow and dropouts), or a subtle "this was recorded on a machine" finish on a single instrument (fast speed, Modern tape, a touch of drive). The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It adds a fixed delay of about 6.7 milliseconds (the dry signal in the Mix is delayed by the same amount, so dry and wet stay in phase). How does it work? Each channel runs this chain: In -> wow / flutter delay -> compression -> Input Level -> record pre-emphasis -> magnetic hysteresis (oversampled) -> hiss, modulation noise, dropouts -> playback de-emphasis -> head bump -> gap and spacing loss -> Output Wow and flutter. The signal first goes through a delay line whose length moves, which bends the pitch like an uneven tape transport. Wow is the slow part (0.5 to 2 Hz): a sine whose frequency itself wanders, plus a random walk. Flutter is the fast part (6 to 15 Hz): two tones that jitter in frequency, plus a little noise. The delay is read with cubic interpolation. A real transport moves both channels together, so most of the modulation is shared; the Stereo Drift knob mixes in an independent part for each channel. Slower speeds wobble more than faster ones. Compression. A slow, soft gain reduction that follows the level (it reacts in a couple of milliseconds and lets go over about a tenth of a second). It is the "tape squashes the peaks" part, before the magnetic saturation. Pre-emphasis. The signal is multiplied by the Input Level and then boosted in the treble by about 9 dB above a corner that depends on the speed (2.3 kHz at 7.5 ips, 4.6 kHz at 15 ips, 9.1 kHz at 30 ips). Treble therefore hits the tape harder than bass and saturates earlier: at slow speeds the corner is lower, so more of the spectrum is affected. After the tape the playback de-emphasis is the exact inverse of the pre-emphasis, so for a small signal the pair cancels and the response is flat. Magnetic hysteresis. This is the heart of the module, a compact reduced form of the Jiles-Atherton model of magnetisation. The field H (the signal divided by the saturation field of the tape) magnetises the tape. Two things happen: the reversible part follows the smooth saturation curve tanh(H) ; the irreversible part moves towards that curve only while the field is travelling in the direction that pulls it there, and only a fraction x / (1 + x) of the way, where x is the field travel divided by the loop width. When the field reverses, the irreversible part stays where it was until the curve comes back to it. That is the hysteresis loop. The output is a mix of the two parts. The model is stable by construction: the irreversible part never overshoots the curve, and nothing can exceed full magnetisation, so the output is bounded and finite for any input and any knob setting. For small signals the loop is nearly closed and the sound is the smooth saturation, mostly odd harmonics with a little even harmonic from a slight asymmetry of the tape. With a wide loop (under-bias) small signals do not move the irreversible part at all, so the gain rises with level and low-level distortion appears. The stage runs at twice (Eco) or four times (Normal) the sample rate so that the sharp corners of the loop do not alias. Noise and dropouts. Hiss is added at the tape, before the playback de-emphasis, so it is shaped like real tape noise. On Vintage and Rough tape a small modulation noise wobbles the level of the signal itself. Dropouts are short, smooth dips of 4 to 22 dB lasting 5 to 60 milliseconds at random (seeded) times, different in each channel. Playback. After the de-emphasis come the head bump (a broad low-frequency peak, near 150 Hz at 7.5 ips, 90 Hz at 15 ips and 50 Hz at 30 ips, with a gentle low cut below it) and the gap and spacing loss , a smooth high-frequency roll-off that gets higher with speed (the -3 dB point is about 11 kHz at 7.5 ips, 17 kHz at 15 ips and 24 kHz, that is, beyond the audio band, at 30 ips, scaled by the tape type). Level compensation. The output gain is set so that a signal at about -18 dBFS comes out at about the same level for any Input Level. Turning up the drive therefore adds colour and compresses the peaks, instead of just making the signal louder, so you can compare settings at equal loudness. How to use it? Warmth on a drum bus: Speed 15 ips, Tape Vintage, Input Level +6 dB, Bias 0, Compress 30 %, Wow 0 %, Flutter 0 %, Hiss 0 %. Raise Input Level until the snare's transient softens and the cymbals lose their edge. Subtle tape finish on a mix: Speed 30 ips, Tape Modern, Input Level +3 dB, Compress 15 %, Wow and Flutter 5 %, Hiss 5 %. Almost transparent, with a faint low-end bump and glue. Lo-fi loop: Speed 7.5 ips, Tape Rough, Input Level +9 dB, Wow 60 %, Flutter 35 %, Hiss 40 %, Dropouts 25 %, Stereo Drift 30 %. Dull, wobbly and noisy. Gritty guitar or synth: Speed 15 ips, Tape Vintage, Input Level +14 dB, Bias -50 %, Compress 50 %. Under-bias adds the crackly low-level distortion of a machine that is not aligned. Dark, polished sound: Speed 7.5 ips, Tape Modern, Bias +60 %, Input Level 0 dB. Over-bias is clean and a little dull. Only the wobble: Input Level -12 dB (almost linear), Compress 0 %, Hiss 0 %, then set Wow and Flutter. The tape then acts mostly as a slightly dulling, wavering delay. Parallel tape: Mix 40 % with Input Level +12 dB for heavy saturation underneath the clean signal. Dry and wet are time-aligned. Eco halves the processing of the magnetic stage. Use Normal for bright, hard-driven material; Eco is fine for bass, drums or anything dull. The module's own UI The node shows two reels instead of a plain row of knobs. They turn at the tape speed, the tape pack moves from the left reel to the right one, and the tape sags and the reels speed up and slow down with the wow and flutter the module is producing right now. A VU needle follows the output, the head glows warm as the tape saturates, sparkles show the hiss and the whole machine flashes at a dropout. Click a reel to change the speed; drag up or down anywhere else to set Input Level. The normal knobs stay below the picture. What the UI demonstrates: Smoothing polled probes. The module reports its probes a few times a second; the UI eases each value towards its probe with 1 - Math.exp(-dt k) (fast attack, slow release for the needle), so the picture moves smoothly at 60 frames a second. Idle animation. The reels always turn, so the picture is alive even when no sound plays. Hit testing. A click inside a reel's circle (a distance test) changes the speed; anything else is a drag. Reading and writing knobs. bleep.param(id) gives the value in its own units and set or setNormalised changes it. Probes added for the picture: dropout (depth of the current dropout) and wobble (pitch deviation in cents). Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Knobs and settings Control Range Default Meaning Speed 7.5 / 15 / 30 ips 15 ips Head bump frequency and size, high-frequency loss, pre-emphasis corner, hiss and wobble. Tape Modern / Vintage / Rough Vintage Saturation level, loop width, asymmetry, hiss, modulation noise, top end and dropout rate. Stereo Drift 0 to 100 % 20 % How independent the wobble of the two channels is (0 is identical, 100 % is independent). Wow 0 to 100 % 20 % Slow pitch wander (0.5 to 2 Hz). 100 % is up to about plus and minus 10 cents at 15 ips. Flutter 0 to 100 % 15 % Fast pitch flutter (6 to 15 Hz). 100 % is up to about plus and minus 4 cents at 15 ips. Input Level -12 to +24 dB +6 dB The level driven into the tape. The output is level-compensated. Bias -100 to +100 % 0 % 0 is the optimum. Negative widens the loop (more low-level distortion, brighter). Positive is cleaner but duller and a little quieter. Compress 0 to 100 % 30 % Soft, slow compression of the level before the saturation. Hiss 0 to 100 % 20 % Tape hiss. At 100 % it is about -56 dBFS at 15 ips on Vintage tape, about 5 dB louder at 7.5 ips and about 4 dB quieter at 30 ips. Dropouts 0 to 100 % 0 % Rate of dropouts. 100 % is about 1.3 per second on Vintage tape, somewhat fewer on Modern and about twice as many on Rough. Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level, after the level compensation. Mix 0 to 100 % 100 % Dry against processed. Input (setup) Auto / Stereo / Mono Auto Auto uses the left input for both channels when the right input has been silent (exactly zero) for 2048 samples. Mono always uses the left input. Quality (setup) Eco / Normal Normal Oversampling of the magnetic stage: 2 times or 4 times. Probes Probe Meaning Saturation How far into saturation the tape is driven (0 to 1; 1 is full magnetisation). Level The output level. Things to know The module needs about 145,000 cost units per 32-sample chunk by the checker's conservative estimate (it counts the Normal setting), which is below the 150,000 this project allows for the heaviest modules and well below the refusal limit of 400,000. Eco costs less at run time. Extreme settings can alias: a very bright tone (above 10 kHz) driven by +12 dB or more is squared by the saturation, and harmonics that fold back into the band are heard as a faint non-harmonic hash, especially on Eco. Normal keeps them at least 10 dB lower. Tape type Vintage and Rough add modulation noise, so a steady tone does not have a perfectly steady level. Modern does not.

title: Valve Stage
text: Valve Stage Valve Stage in the module view Introduction A tube amplifier stage is not a waveshaper in a box. It is a small circuit whose parts argue with each other: the tube's plate current, the load on its plate, the capacitor between it and the next stage, the cathode resistor, the power supply that feeds all of it. Each of those has a time constant and a limit, so what comes out depends on how loud you play, how long you have played it and how fast the signal moves. The Valve Stage models a cascade of one to three such stages, one after the other, with the things that make tubes sound like tubes: an asymmetric transfer curve : the plate current starts abruptly at cutoff and rises softly, the plate voltage bottoms out on the load line; grid-current clipping : when the signal drives the grid positive it conducts, which clips the positive peaks hard; blocking : that grid current charges the coupling capacitor, so for a moment after a loud peak the stage is biased colder, and quiet notes after a hit are weaker until the charge has leaked away; Miller roll-off whose corner falls with the gain of the stage; cathode bypass : a frequency-dependent gain, from flat to a bright, bass-light stage; a sagging supply : the louder you play, the lower the plate voltage, so the gain and the headroom shrink and recover over a fraction of a second; a starved plate that gives the stage the gated, sputtering, crackly sound of a tube run with too little voltage. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). The two channels share one power supply (a loud left channel sags the right as well). How does it work? In -> Gain -> [ Miller low-pass -> coupling capacitor and grid -> cathode -> tube -> plate load ] x 1..3 -> DC block -> level compensation -> Mix -> Out Each bracketed stage runs at twice the sample rate (Normal) or at the base rate (Eco). Between the stages, the signal is scaled so that each stage drives the next one a little harder than it was driven itself (by 2.5 times for the 12AX7, 3 times for the 12AU7). The tube. The grid-to-cathode voltage is measured in units of the bias voltage, so that the quiescent point is 0 and cutoff is at -1. The voltage is soft-rectified (a smooth knee about 0.12 wide for the 12AX7, 0.22 for the 12AU7, 0.08 for the EL34) and the plate current is that value to the power 1.5, the Child-Langmuir law of a triode. A load line turns the current into a plate voltage: the voltage across the load is z / (1 + z) of the supply for a current-scaled value z , a soft knee, or for the pentode z / (1 + z^4)^(1/4) , a hard one. The stage's small-signal gain is set to 28 (12AX7), 9 (12AU7) or 14 (EL34). The polarity is corrected, so the module does not invert. The EL34 is a push-pull pentode power stage. Two halves see opposite grid voltages and their plate voltages are subtracted, so the transfer is odd (even harmonics cancel) and the knee is hard. When the EL34 is chosen, the stages before the last are 12AX7 drivers, and the last is the power stage. On its own (Stages = 1) its input is scaled down, so you will want more Gain. Grid and coupling capacitor. Each stage has a coupling capacitor that leaks to the signal's mean: a high-pass filter (about 2.5 Hz for the first stage, 6 to 10 Hz for the others). When the grid voltage passes the conduction point, the excess is turned into grid current. That current clamps the grid (a hard-ish positive clip with a smooth start) and charges the capacitor. The charge decays through the same high-pass, so the stage takes tens of milliseconds to recover. This is the blocking. Miller capacitance. The input of every stage is a low-pass whose corner falls as the stage gain rises: about 90 kHz divided by 1 + 4 miller gain for the first stage (60 kHz for the others), with a Miller factor of 0.12 (12AX7), 0.05 (12AU7) and 0.04 (EL34). A cascade of 12AX7 stages therefore loses its top end quickly; a 12AU7 hardly does. When the supply sags, the gain falls and the corner moves up. Cathode bypass. The cathode voltage follows the plate current through a capacitor. What the capacitor cannot hold is negative feedback. Bright sets the capacitor: at 0 % it is large (corner 12 Hz) and the gain is flat; at 100 % it is small (corner 1.2 kHz) and the bass loses gain to the feedback while the top does not (an 8 kHz tone against an 80 Hz tone tilts by about 8 dB between 0 and 100 %), which also linearises the bass. Plate and Sag. The Plate knob sets the supply voltage (35 % of nominal at 0 %, 100 % at 100 %) and, as it goes down, moves the bias towards cutoff and sharpens the knee. A low supply makes the load line steeper, so the stage compresses earlier; near cutoff low-level signals only cross the threshold on one side, which gates them. A random bias flicker (a new value about every 0.7 ms, bounded and seeded so that two renders are identical, different on the two channels) is added when the plate is starved: that is the crackle. Sag follows the output level (fast up, slow down) and lowers the supply by up to half of the nominal at Sag 100 % and a loud signal. The level compensation is done without the sag, so you can hear it. Level compensation. At each block the module evaluates the static curve of the whole cascade for a -12 dBFS sine and sets the gain that brings it back to -12 dBFS. More Gain means more colour, not more volume. The weak and very loud ends are free to differ: that is what compression is. Turning knobs. Gain, Bias, Plate, Bright and Sag are followed, not jumped to: the circuit takes about 40 ms to arrive at a new setting, so turning a knob (or sweeping it with a cable) makes no zipper noise or clicks. Tube, Stages and Quality cannot be followed: when one changes, the input fades out over about 3 ms, the new circuit starts from rest and the input fades back in over 5 ms. How to use it? Warm a DI bass: 12AX7, 1 stage, Gain 30 %, Plate 90 %, Sag 20 %, Bright 10 %. The even harmonics come in as you play harder; the bass stays full. Classic crunch: 12AX7, 2 stages, Gain 55 %, Bias 0 %, Plate 85 %, Sag 35 %, Bright 30 %. The grid current clips the peaks and the second stage squares them off. Clean-ish lead channel: 12AU7, 2 stages, Gain 60 %, Bright 40 %. Less gain per stage, a bright top, odd and even harmonics in balance. Power amp in the red: EL34, 2 stages, Gain 70 %, Sag 60 %, Plate 90 %. The driver pushes the push-pull pair: odd harmonics, a hard knee and a supply that gives way on hard hits. Sputtery lo-fi synth: 12AX7, 3 stages, Gain 60 %, Plate 15 %, Bias -30 %. At low levels it gates and crackles, louder notes open the stage up and clean it a little. Blocking on a drum hit: 12AX7, 1 stage, Gain 80 %, Sag 0 %. After a loud hit, listen to the quiet notes that follow: they come back over about a tenth of a second. Parallel warmth: Mix 35 %. The dry signal is delayed to match the oversampling. CPU: Eco runs the stages at the base rate: it is the cheapest, but a hard-driven cascade will alias. Normal runs them at twice the rate. The module's own UI The Valve Stage shows glowing tubes , as many as the Stages knob says. The plate glows with the supply and dims in a brownout when the supply sags (Supply probe), blue-white sparks jump at the grid when it conducts (Grid probe), and a starved plate sputters orange sparks. Click a tube to cycle the tube type; drag a tube up or down to set Gain. The file is src/valve-stage.view.js . Tricks it demonstrates: a fixed pool of particles, allocated once and reused, so a busy picture creates no garbage per frame; telling a click from a drag by how far the pointer moved before it was released; setting a choice knob by its index ( tube.set(i) ) and reading its names from choices ; hit testing by dividing the canvas into one slot per tube; driving effects from several probes at once (supply, grid, level) and from knob values (Plate, Stages). Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Knobs Knob Range Default Meaning Tube 12AX7, 12AU7, EL34 12AX7 The tube. High gain and soft knee; low gain and clean; push-pull pentode power stage. Stages 1 to 3 2 How many stages are cascaded. Gain 0 to 100 % 40 % The level into the first grid, -12 dB to +20 dB (the 12AU7 and a single EL34 are scaled down). Bias -100 to +100 % 0 % Bias point. Cold (negative) sits near cutoff; hot (positive) sits near grid current. Plate 0 to 100 % 85 % Plate voltage. Low is starved: less gain, more compression, gating and crackle. Sag 0 to 100 % 30 % How far the supply gives way under a loud signal. Bright 0 to 100 % 25 % Cathode bypass: flat (0 %) to bass-light and bright (100 %). Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level after the level compensation. Mix 0 to 100 % 100 % Dry against processed. Input Auto, Stereo, Mono Auto Where the right channel gets its signal. Quality Eco, Normal Normal Base rate or 2 times oversampling. Probes Probe Meaning Supply How much of the supply voltage is left (1 is full). Grid How far the first coupling capacitors have been charged by grid current (0 to 1). Level The output level (average, scaled so that a loud signal reads near 1). Numbers worth knowing Cost: about 149,000 operations per 32-sample chunk at the heaviest setting (3 stages, 2 times oversampling); the checker warns above 60,000 and refuses above 400,000. A 4 times mode did not fit under 150,000. With the 12AX7, 2 stages, Gain 40 %, a 1 kHz tone has its second harmonic at -41 dBc at -40 dBFS and at -13 dBc at -12 dBFS (the third stays 30 to 40 dB lower until the peaks start to clip); the fundamental's gain falls from -1.9 dB at -12 dBFS to -8.0 dB at -1 dBFS (the output is compensated at -12 dBFS). Top roll-off at 12 kHz against 500 Hz, Bright 0 %, small signal: 12AX7 two stages -14 dB, 12AU7 two stages -1 dB; one 12AX7 stage -6 dB, three -23 dB. Aliasing, Normal, a 7 kHz tone at -6 dBFS: -63 dBc of non-harmonic energy at Gain 30 % (two stages), -61 dBc for one stage at Gain 60 %, -50 dBc for two cascaded stages at Gain 60 % (two hard clippers in a row). Eco has no oversampling and is about -19 dBc in that last case.

title: Vinyl
text: Vinyl Vinyl in the module view Introduction A record is not just crackle on top of a clean signal. Everything that is wrong with it follows from how it is made and played: the bass is made mono and thinned out to keep the stylus in the groove, the treble is boosted and then taken down again, the stylus cannot follow loud bright sounds towards the centre of the disc, the platter rumbles, the disc is never quite round, and the dust and scratches sit at fixed places that come round every revolution. The Vinyl module models that chain. Use it to make a sample, a loop or a whole mix sound as if it came from a record: warm bass, a darker and slightly distorted top end that gets worse with level, a gentle wobble and a believable surface. The module is stereo (In L / In R, Out L / Out R). It adds a fixed delay of about 4.5 milliseconds (the dry signal in the Mix is delayed by the same amount). How does it work? In -> bass mono -> eccentricity delay -> RIAA record curve -> stylus tracking limit -> crosstalk -> hiss + rumble -> inner-groove roll-off -> RIAA playback curve -> cartridge response -> + dust, pops and scratches -> Output Bass mono. A cutting lathe cannot cut strong out-of-phase bass (the stylus would jump out of the groove), so the stereo difference signal is high-passed (second order) at the Bass Mono corner and only the shared bass remains. Centred bass is untouched. Eccentricity. The disc is never perfectly centred or flat, so the pitch drifts a little, once per revolution (and half as much twice per revolution). The module delays the signal by an amount that follows the revolution of the platter; the Speed (33 1/3, 45 or 78 rpm) sets the frequency of the wobble (0.56, 0.75 or 1.3 Hz), and Warp its depth (100 % is about plus and minus 14 cents). RIAA curves. The record curve is the RIAA standard, built from its three time constants of 3180, 318 and 75 microseconds: the bass is cut (about -17 dB at 50 Hz relative to 1 kHz) and the treble boosted (about +14 dB at 10 kHz). The playback curve is its exact inverse, so cut followed by playback is flat. The module's tests check the curve in the groove against the standard (within 1 dB up to 10 kHz) and the round trip (flat within 0.3 dB). Each of the three corners is placed exactly by pre-warping the digital filter; the cut stage also has one more corner far above the audio band, which the playback matches, because a filter that boosts forever cannot be inverted. The groove limit. Between the two curves is where the stylus can fail. The signal in the groove is bright and boosted, and the stylus can only follow so much: a soft limit (a hyperbolic tangent, at twice the sample rate to avoid aliasing) squashes loud, high-frequency passages. Since the cut curve boosts 10 kHz about five times (and 3 kHz about 1.7 times) relative to 1 kHz, this is level- and frequency-dependent : bass at the same level passes cleanly, a loud 3 kHz tone gets a third harmonic that is easy to measure. Inner Groove tightens the limit and adds an asymmetry (even harmonics) as the stylus approaches the label, and also rolls off the top end (a one-pole low-pass that moves from about 30 kHz at 0 % down to 4.8 kHz at 100 %). Noise. Surface hiss and rumble are picked up after the cut, so the playback curve shapes them: the hiss comes out dark (more at 1 to 2 kHz than at 10 kHz) and the rumble, between about 5 and 40 Hz, is boosted by the bass lift. The part of the rumble that is the same in both channels is the horizontal motion, the part that is opposite is the vertical one. Crosstalk. A real pick-up leaks a little of each channel into the other. The leak here goes through an all-pass filter at 1.8 kHz, so it arrives with a phase shift (about 58 degrees at 1 kHz) and widens or smears the image instead of just narrowing it. At 100 % the leak is 12 dB down. The cartridge. After de-emphasis a small residual response models the pick-up: Hi-Fi is flat, Standard has a small rise near 11 kHz and a little bass loss, Cheap has a pronounced rise near 9 kHz and loses more bass. At the defaults the whole chain is within plus or minus 0.3 dB from 100 Hz to 10 kHz. The cartridge also sets how soon the stylus loses track: Hi-Fi tracks 40 % further, Cheap gives up at roughly half the Standard level. Dust, pops and scratches. They are added after the pick-up (they are damage on the playing surface, not part of the signal). All random events are seeded, so a render is repeatable. a bed of tiny crackle, about 1400 x Dust events a second at 33 1/3 rpm; ticks , small sharp clicks, 50 x Dust^2 a second; pops , rare loud clicks with a low thump, 12 x Dust^2 a second (so about one a second at 30 %, about four at 60 %); scratches : from 40 % Dust there is one, from 65 % two, from 85 % three. Each sits at a fixed place on the revolution and has the same waveform every time round, so you hear it come round once per turn (every 1.8 s at 33 1/3 rpm, 1.33 s at 45, 0.77 s at 78). Faster records are busier: the rates are multiplied by (rpm / 33.3) to the power 0.7. How to use it? A used record, subtle: Speed 33 1/3, Cartridge Standard, Inner Groove 20 %, Dust 30 %, Noise 40 %, Rumble 25 %, Warp 25 %, Crosstalk 30 %, Bass Mono 120 Hz (the defaults). Warm bass, a hint of crackle, a gentle wobble. Pristine pressing: Dust 0 %, Noise 15 %, Rumble 10 %, Warp 10 %, Cartridge Hi-Fi. Only the groove and the curve are left. Beaten-up charity-shop record: Dust 85 %, Noise 70 %, Rumble 50 %, Warp 55 %, Cartridge Cheap, Inner Groove 60 %. Three scratches come round every turn. Old 78: Speed 78 rpm, Inner Groove 80 %, Cartridge Cheap, Dust 60 %, Bass Mono 300 Hz. The wobble is fast (1.3 Hz) and the highs are gone. Tighten the bass of a loop: Bass Mono 200 Hz with everything else at 0 % and Mix 100 %. Wobble only: Dust, Noise and Rumble at 0, Warp 70 %, Inner Groove 0 %, Bass Mono 0. Keep the punch: Mix 50 %. The dry signal is delayed to line up. The module's own UI The node shows a turning record with a tonearm. The disc turns at the chosen speed and wobbles with Warp, specks of dust appear as Dust goes up, and from 40 % Dust the scratches the module plays are drawn on the disc. The module reports where it is on the turn, so a scratch reaches the needle at the moment it is heard, and the needle flashes on every click and glows with the level in the groove. The label shows the cartridge. Drag on the disc or the arm to move the needle in and out, which sets Inner Groove; click the label to change the cartridge. What the UI demonstrates: Syncing a free-running animation to a probe. The disc turns by itself, and whenever a new turn value arrives the UI nudges its phase towards it along the shortest way round, so there is no jump at the end of a turn. Pointer geometry to a knob. The distance from the centre of the disc becomes the needle position, which maps straight onto Inner Groove. Things fixed on a rotating body. Dust and scratches are drawn at fixed positions on the disc and rotated with it. Deterministic pseudo-random numbers (a small hash) keep the specks in the same places from frame to frame. Probes added for the picture: turn (position on the current turn, 0 to 1) and click (loudness of the dust, pops and scratches, decaying). Reference Inputs and outputs Jack Type Meaning In L audio Left input. In R audio Right input. With Input set to Auto, nothing patched here means the left input feeds both channels. Out L audio Left output. Out R audio Right output. Knobs and settings Control Range Default Meaning Speed 33 1/3 / 45 / 78 rpm 33 1/3 rpm Wobble frequency, scratch period, how busy the surface is. Cartridge Hi-Fi / Standard / Cheap Standard Response residual and tracking ability. Inner Groove 0 to 100 % 20 % Tracking distortion (with asymmetry) and high-frequency roll-off. Dust 0 to 100 % 30 % Condition of the record: bed, ticks, pops, scratches. 0 is silent. Noise 0 to 100 % 40 % Level of the surface hiss and of the crackle bed. Hiss at 100 % is about -34 dBFS, at 40 % about -46 dBFS. Rumble 0 to 100 % 25 % Turntable rumble, 5 to 40 Hz. At 100 % it is about -28 dBFS. Warp 0 to 100 % 25 % Eccentricity wobble, once per revolution. 100 % is about plus and minus 14 cents. Crosstalk 0 to 100 % 30 % Channel leak: 0 is perfect separation, 100 % a leak at -12 dB. Bass Mono 0 to 400 Hz 120 Hz Corner below which the stereo difference is removed. Below 10 Hz it is off. Output -24 to +12 dB 0 dB Output level. Mix 0 to 100 % 100 % Dry against processed. Input (setup) Auto / Stereo / Mono Auto Auto uses the left input for both channels when the right input has been silent (exactly zero) for 2048 samples. Probes Probe Meaning Groove The peak signal in the groove after the cut curve: 1.0 is a full-scale 1 kHz tone. Bright, loud passages push it up. Level The output level. Things to know The cost estimate is about 140,000 per 32-sample chunk, below the 150,000 this project allows for the heaviest modules. The record curve in the groove sits up to 1 dB above the strict standard near 10 kHz at 48 kHz, because of the way the digital filter is mapped; cut and playback still cancel exactly. The warp wobble is real pitch modulation: a bright tone sounds slightly blurred if you look at its spectrum, which is why measuring its level takes in the sidebands.

title: Grains
text: Grains Grains in the module view Introduction Grains records its input into a buffer of a few seconds and plays it back as many short, overlapping grains . Where the grains read, how long they are, how high they play and how many there are turn any sound into shimmering textures, stretched pads or stuttering rhythms. Freeze holds the buffer, so the cloud plays on after the input has stopped. Every grain's random choices come from Seed , so a texture renders the same way every time. How does it work? The buffer. The input is recorded continuously into a stereo buffer of Buffer seconds. Position says where grains read: 0 % is the newest audio, 100 % the oldest. Freeze (the setting or the gate) stops recording; Position then counts from the moment of the freeze, so the frozen sound stays put. The seam where recording stopped is crossfaded, so a frozen buffer loops cleanly. A grain is a short piece of the buffer under a window. Size is its length (5 ms – 2 s), Texture its window shape: 0 % nearly square, 25 % trapezoid, 50 % smooth bell, 75 % narrow bell, 100 % percussive (a fast attack and a decay). Pitch transposes every grain (−24 … +24 semitones); the Pitch input adds 1 V per octave, so a sequencer plays the cloud melodically. Pitch Quant snaps the result to semitones, octaves, or octaves and fifths. Reverse is the chance that a grain plays backwards. How many. In Continuous mode, Density sets the number of grains per second, from one every two seconds to 200. Below 50 % they also come irregularly; the middle of the knob is a smooth cloud. With a note value in Sync , grains start on the song's grid instead: above 50 % Density adds subdivisions, below it skips grid points. In Triggered mode each pulse at Trigger starts a grain (above 50 % Density, a burst of up to 8); in Continuous mode a pulse adds an extra grain. When the grains run into Max Grains , the oldest one fades out quickly to make room. The level is normalised to the overlap, so turning up Density or Size doesn't get louder. Scatter. Spread gives every grain a random offset from Position (up to ±25 % of the buffer) and a random place in the stereo field. Pitch Jitter detunes each grain randomly by up to that many semitones (before quantizing). Space. Feedback writes the output back into the buffer with the input (soft-clipped), building dense, evolving textures. Blur smears the grains into a reverb-like wash; it sets both its level and its length (0.3 – 8 s). With Feedback, the blur's tail goes back into the buffer, so frozen pads never end. Mix blends the dry input with the result. Grain fires at each grain start; Grain Env follows the window of the latest grain, to move something else along with the cloud. The view shows the buffer (oldest on the left, the write head on the right), the area grains read from, and each grain as a dot. Drag on it: left/right sets Position, up/down sets Size. While frozen, Keep frozen buffer saves the buffer to the media folder, so it comes back with the board (the module then starts frozen on it); unfreezing lets it go. How to use it? Pad from anything: Size 400 ms, Density 60 %, Texture 50 %, Spread 40 %, Blur 40 %. Freeze when you hear something you like. Shimmer: Pitch +12, Pitch Jitter 7 with Octaves + fifths , Feedback 30 %, Blur 50 %. Rhythmic stutter: Sync 1/16, Size 60 ms, Texture 100 %, Density 50 %. Melodic cloud: a Step Sequencer's Pitch into Pitch , Pitch Quant Semitones. Granular delay: Position 30 %, Spread 5 %, Mix 40 %. Scrubbing: a slow LFO on Position while frozen. Factory samples. The demo patches and the Samples cells play a granular cloud over short recordings that are free to use: Rain loopable by Ylmir ( , CC0) and pieces of the University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios' Musical Instrument Samples (Lawrence Fritts, ; free for any project, without restrictions). The files are cut, faded and normalised, and each preset carries the ones it uses. The full list with originals and licences is in patch/presets/samples/README.md in the source tree. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Grains does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Grains under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Grains: Rain Curtain A recording of steady rain is played as a cloud of 300 ms grains, scattered wide by Spread and slowly scanned by an LFO on Position, with Blur smoothing the grains into a soft, deep curtain of sound. Lower Size and raise Density for a crisp downpour, or raise Pitch for a lighter, more distant shower. Grains: Raindrop Melody In Triggered mode each sequencer step fires one short, percussive grain of rain, and the sequencer's Pitch is patched into Grains' Pitch input, so the raindrops play a tune. Texture at 100 % gives a plucked attack. Change Size for longer notes, Pitch Quant to Off for glides, or Pitch Jitter for a more scattered melody. Grains: Frozen Piano A single recorded piano note is turned into a slow, endless pad: grains of 600 ms drawn from around Position, detuned by Pitch Jitter and snapped by Pitch Quant to octaves and fifths, so the cloud sings in stacked octaves and fifths. A slow LFO moves Position from the attack to the tail. Try Size, Density and Feedback. Grains: Gong Shimmer A struck gong is stretched into grains an octave higher, with Feedback and Blur feeding the cloud back into itself so each hit blooms into a glassy halo. A sequencer plays the gong's pitch (Pitch input) and fires a grain burst on each note. Raise Feedback for a longer afterglow, or lower Pitch to hear the gong's own size. Grains: Crotale Stutter Triggered mode with Sync on 1/16: a grid of tiny, percussive grains cut from a crotale recording makes a glittering rhythmic stutter, with some grains reversed. A stepped random source jumps Position on every beat so each bar pulls a different piece of the bell. Raise Density for bursts, or Size for a ringing tail. Presets The preset bar of the Grains view has 14 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Soft Cloud A gentle grain cloud over the recent input. Shimmer Up Octave-up grains with feedback for a shimmering halo. Deep Down An octave below, smoothed into a pad. Fifth Harmonies Random octaves and fifths stacked on the source. Frozen Pad Holds what was playing and sustains it as a pad.
