Harmony Master: Stepping by Trigger With Advance set to Trigger, the progression moves one chord every time a trigger arrives; here an off-beat sequencer rhythm does the stepping and each change plucks the chord. Edit the trigger rhythm and the chords change when you decide. Harmony Master: Key Change Up A slow two-step sequence feeds the Transpose input, so after four bars the whole progression, bass and follower lead move up two semitones together. Change the transposing sequence to climb through more keys. Harmony Master: Modern Colours Four chosen chords written as fixed roots and rich qualities: minor 11, dominant 13, major 7 sharp 11 and dominant 7 sharp 9. The Tone outputs get the whole stack. Click a slot in the view to try another quality. Harmony Master: Phrygian Dominant Drone Manual source: one held fifth in E Phrygian Dominant, with a follower line that wanders by Variation but never leaves the scale. Change Degree or the scale to colour the drone, or Quality to a richer chord. Presets The preset bar of the Harmony Master view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does C Major Home The board in C major on the tonic triad. A Minor Home A natural minor, tonic triad: a sad, simple centre. Seventh Colours Diatonic sevenths on the second degree: soft and jazzy. Dorian Groove D Dorian with a minor seventh chord. Lydian Lift A bright, floating Lydian centre. Phrygian Tension E Phrygian with a minor chord: dark and tense. Harmonic Minor Drama The dominant of A harmonic minor: ready to resolve. Blues Dominant Dominant seventh in an A blues scale. Pentatonic Open Open pentatonic sus2: nothing to resolve. Progression Stepper Plays its stored progression, moving with the song. Triggered Changes Steps the progression on each pulse into Next. Chord Detector Follows chords you play into Notes. Low Bass Root Fourth degree power chord, an octave down: a strong bass centre. Quartal Mood Stacked fourths over D Dorian for modern pads. Bus B Whole Tone Floating whole-tone harmony on bus B. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Degree 1 – 7 1 Slot 1 – 16 1 Velocity 1 – 100 % 70 % Degree: the scale degree of the chord in Manual (and in Detect with Latch off and nothing held). Slot: the slot that plays in Progression with Advance = Select ; wraps round the number of slots. Velocity: the velocity of the Notes output. Settings Setting Values Default Source Manual, Progression, Detect Manual Key C … B C Scale the 17 scales Major Quality Diatonic Triad, Diatonic Seventh, Unison … Major 7♯11 Diatonic Triad Advance Transport, Trigger, Select Transport Scale Policy Keep, Adapt Keep Latch on / off on Octave −3 … +3 0 Bus A, B, C, D A Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes held notes for Detect Next trigger Trigger advance: the next slot Reset trigger slot 1 ( Trigger ), or the progression restarts on the next beat ( Transport ) Transpose pitch shifts key and chord by whole semitones Outputs Output Signal What it does Key pitch the key's root (C … B = 0 … 11/12 V at Octave 0) Root pitch the chord's root Bass pitch the chord's lowest note, an octave below Root Tone 1 … Tone 4 pitch the chord tones upwards from the root; triads repeat the root an octave up as Tone 4 Notes notes the chord as notes; common tones held across changes Change trigger a pulse at every chord change Degree control, 0 – 1 (degree − 1) / 6; 0 when the root is not in the scale

title: Quantizer
text: Quantizer Quantizer in the module view Introduction The Quantizer snaps a pitch to the nearest note of a scale. Feed it an LFO, a random voltage or an envelope, and an oscillator plays a melody that always fits the key. A trigger on every note change lets the melody play envelopes too. How does it work? The signal goes through these steps: Range: In is scaled, so a full-scale LFO (−1 … +1) spans ± Range octaves. Transpose is added. Because this happens before quantizing, the result stays in the scale. Clock (optional): when patched, the value is only taken on each clock pulse and held until the next. Quantize to the scale chosen by Root and Scale . Rounding picks the nearest note, the one below, or the one above. Shift is added after quantizing: a chromatic transposition that may leave the scale. Glide smooths the jumps between notes. Hysteresis stops flicker: the input has to move a bit past the halfway point between two notes before the output changes. Notes In is a second way in. Patch notes (a keyboard, a sequencer, an arpeggiator) and each note is snapped to the scale and sent out of Notes : Transpose is added before quantizing, Shift after, and Root , Scale and Rounding apply. Range , Clock , Hysteresis and Glide belong to the pitch path and are ignored for notes. The note-off ends the note that was sent, so a scale change while a key is held cannot leave a note hanging. Velocity, controllers, bend and the other messages pass through unchanged. Trigger fires and Gate drops for one millisecond each time the note changes, so an envelope or CV to Notes can start a new note. Other tunings. Tuning leaves the twelve-note world. Equal Divisions splits the octave into 5 to 72 equal steps (19 and 31 are popular, 24 gives quarter tones); Divisions sets how many. Scale File loads a scale from a text file (a file with a description line, the number of notes, then one pitch per line as cents like 701.955 or as a ratio like 3/2 ; the last line is the period, usually 2/1 ): press Load scale file… in the view. Many tuning archives use this format. In these modes Out carries the exact pitch, the keyboard is not used, Root still moves the whole grid by semitones, Hysteresis counts in steps, and notes arriving at Notes In keep their exact tuned pitch (their note number is the nearest key). To build your own scale, click keys on the keyboard. Clicking a key while another scale is selected copies that scale and switches Scale to Custom , so any scale is a starting point. How to use it? Melodies from an LFO: a slow LFO into In , Out into an oscillator's Pitch . Try Minor Pentatonic : no wrong notes. Random melodies: Random into In , a clock into Clock , Trigger into an ADSR's gate. Key changes: a sequencer or another quantizer into Root In sets the key; everything stays in the new scale. Arpeggios: a sawtooth LFO into In plays the scale upwards. Portamento: raise Glide for slides between notes. Presets The preset bar of the Quantizer view has 15 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does C Major Snaps any pitch to C major: the safe, bright default. Natural Minor A natural minor: melancholic and familiar. Minor Pentatonic Five notes that can't clash: great for random melodies. Major Pentatonic Open and folky: nothing sounds wrong. Dorian Walk Minor with a lifted sixth: cool, jazzy lines. Lydian Float A major scale with a raised fourth: dreamy and airy. Phrygian Dark Flat second gives a tense, Spanish-tinged colour. Harmonic Minor Dramatic minor with a leading tone. Blues Blue notes for gritty, soulful lines. Whole Tone Dream Six equal steps: ambiguous, floating melodies. Hirajoshi A five-note scale with an east-Asian flavour. Gliding Major A little slide between notes for a singing feel. Wide Range Stretches the input over three octaves with a steadier hold. Round Down Always rounds down to the scale note below. Round Up Chromatic Chromatic, rounding up: plain semitone steps with no hold. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Quantizer does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Quantizer under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Quantizer: Triangle Climb A slow triangle LFO is a smooth, continuous voltage; the Quantizer turns it into stairs of pentatonic notes and fires a trigger on every new one, so the voice climbs and falls by itself. Widen Range for more octaves, or pick another Scale. Quantizer: Dorian Wanderer A stepped Random sends any value it likes; the Quantizer is clocked by a sequencer and, on each tick, snaps it into D Dorian, so the wandering always sounds like a tune. Try a different Scale (Whole Tone, Blues) or a smaller Range. Quantizer: Chromatic Run to Hirajoshi The sequencer plays an ordinary chromatic run, every semitone, and the Quantizer squeezes it into the five-note Hirajoshi scale, so repeated notes appear where the notes were pushed together. Switch Scale to Chromatic for the original run, or Rounding to Up. Quantizer: Glide Between Notes A sine LFO sweeps a legato voice; the Quantizer picks scale notes but Glide turns each jump into a slide, like a fretless line stepping through a scale. Set Glide to zero for hard steps, or Rounding to Down to favour the lower note. Quantizer: Shift Echo One sequencer line is quantized to the blues scale; a square LFO adds a step to the Transpose input every other bar, lifting the whole line to a new key area that is still in the scale. Change the LFO Sync or the amount of the Transpose cable. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Range 0 … 4 octaves 1 octave Hysteresis 0 … 50 % of a semitone 10 % Glide 0 … 2 s 0 s Root C … B C Scale the Step Sequencer's 17 scales, plus Custom Major Rounding Nearest, Down, Up Nearest Tuning 12 Notes, Equal Divisions, Scale File 12 Notes Divisions 5 … 72 19 Range: how many octaves a full-scale input covers in each direction. It applies to In only. Hysteresis: how far past the midpoint between two notes the input must move before the note changes. 0 is plain quantizing. Glide: a smoothing time on Out . Trigger still fires at the change. Tuning , Divisions: the grid. 12 Notes uses Scale ; Equal Divisions splits the octave into Divisions steps; Scale File uses the loaded file. Root , Scale: the key. Custom uses the keys set in the keyboard. Rounding: Nearest rounds to the closest scale note (an exact tie goes down), Down to the one at or below, Up to the one at or above. Inputs Input Signal What it does In pitch The signal to quantize, 1 V/oct (0 = C4) Clock trigger Optional: the output changes only on a clock Transpose pitch Added before quantizing (stays in the scale) Shift pitch Added after quantizing (chromatic) Root In pitch Optional: overrides Root with this note's pitch class Notes In notes Optional: notes to quantize, sent out of Notes Outputs Output Signal What it does Out pitch The quantized pitch, plus Shift , after Glide Trigger trigger A pulse at each note change Gate gate Low for 1 ms at each note change, high otherwise Notes notes The notes from Notes In , snapped to the scale

title: Quantizer Suite
text: Quantizer Suite Quantizer Suite in the module view Introduction Four quantizers in one module. Each channel snaps a pitch to a scale, and can also transpose it in scale steps, arpeggiate a chord on it, or follow the board's Harmony Master. Unpatched inputs take the previous channel's signal, so one melody into In A gives a four-voice diatonic harmony on Out A … D without another cable. How does it work? Allowed notes. Each channel quantizes to its Root and Scale , minus the notes you switch off on its keyboard in the view (the mask). With Link on, channels B – D use channel A's Root, Scale and Harmony. Halfway between two notes the lower wins; Hysteresis keeps a note until the input is clearly in the next one's range. Modes (per channel): Quantize: the nearest allowed note. Transpose: the nearest allowed note, moved by Steps allowed notes. +2 in C major turns C into E and A into the C above. The defaults (A 0, B +2, C +4, D +6) turn one melody into seventh chords moving with it. Arp: at each Trig a chord is built on the input's note from scale steps ( Chord : Triad, Seventh, …) over Span octaves, and the channel plays its next tone in Order (Up, Down, Up-Down, Converge, Random). Steps shifts the starting tone. With no trigger patched on this or an earlier channel, it steps in 1/16 notes with the song. Follow: needs Harmony on a bus with a Harmony Master (otherwise it quantizes and says "no harmony"). Target chooses what it lands on: Scale (the Harmony Master's scale), Chord (the nearest chord tone, then Steps chord tones up or down), Chord + Scale (scale notes, but a chord tone within a semitone wins), or Root (the chord's root in the nearest octave: a bass line from any contour). A continuous channel changes on the chord change itself. Sample. Continuous follows the input. Trigger reads it on each pulse at Trig and holds it (a pulse on the same note plays it again). Track & Hold follows while Trig is high and holds while it is low. Unpatched Trigs take the previous channel's, so one clock on Trig A samples all four. Octave shifts the result, Slew glides to each new note in the same time however far it jumps. Notes. Each channel with Notes on plays its note on note channel 1 – 4 (A – D) at Velocity ; a new note starts before the old one ends (legato). How to use it? Instant harmony: a sequence into In A , Notes into a Voice Cell. Pentatonic only: click notes off on the keyboard. An arpeggiator: channel A Mode Arp , a clock into Trig A . A bass that follows the chords: Mode Follow , Target Root , any melody or LFO into the input. Harmoniser: Mode Follow , Target Chord , Steps 1 and 2 on B and C. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Quantizer Suite does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Quantizer Suite under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Quantizer Suite: Chord-Tone Mask A random line goes into channel A, where the note mask keeps only the notes of a C major seventh chord (C, E, G, B): any value lands on a chord tone, so the melody always outlines the harmony. Click other keys in the view's keyboard to change which notes are allowed. Quantizer Suite: Fifths and Octaves One melody goes in on A; channels B, C and D transpose it in the scale by 4, 7 and minus 7 steps, which is a fifth up, an octave up and an octave down. Four voices play the thickened line. Change a Steps knob for other intervals. Quantizer Suite: Rising Ninths Channel A turns each slow root into a ninth chord and plays it converging towards the middle over two octaves; B plays a sus2 chord downwards on the same clock. Change an Order or Chord and the run reshapes at once. Quantizer Suite: Follow the Changes In Follow mode every channel listens to a Harmony Master on the bus: A snaps a random line to the current chord, B to chord and scale, C holds the chord root. When the progression moves, all three move with it. Change a Target, or the Harmony Master's key. Quantizer Suite: Track and Hold Slides Channel A follows a slow LFO but only changes pitch when its clock ticks, and Slew slides the voice between the held notes; channel B tracks continuously, so it keeps wobbling into new notes. Try Sample Trigger for hard steps, or Slew A at zero. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Steps A … D −14 … +14 0, +2, +4, +6 Slew A … D 0 – 2 s 0 Hysteresis 0 – 50 % of a semitone 10 % Velocity 1 – 100 % 80 % Every knob is a modulation destination. Steps means scale steps (Transpose, Follow · Scale), chord tones (Follow · Chord) or the arpeggio's start (Arp). Settings (per channel) Setting Values Default Mode Quantize, Transpose, Arp, Follow A Quantize, B – D Transpose Root C … B C Scale the 17 scales Major Harmony Off, Bus A – D Off Sample Continuous, Trigger, Track & Hold Continuous Octave −3 … +3 0 Chord Triad, Seventh, Sus2, Sus4, Fifth, Ninth, Octave Triad Order Up, Down, Up-Down, Converge, Random Up Span 1 – 4 octaves 1 Target Scale, Chord, Chord + Scale, Root Chord Notes on / off on Shared: Link (on), Seed (0 – 999, for the Random order). Inputs Input Signal What it does In A … In D pitch the pitch to quantize; unpatched B – D take the previous channel's Trig A … Trig D trigger sampling and arpeggio clock; unpatched B – D take the previous channel's Reset trigger every arpeggio starts again at its first tone Outputs Output Signal What it does Out A … Out D pitch the channel's note, after Slew Change A … Change D trigger a pulse when the note changes (and at each Trigger sample) Notes notes all four channels on note channels 1 – 4

title: CV to MIDI
text: CV to MIDI CV to MIDI in the module view Introduction CV to MIDI turns control signals into MIDI control changes (CC). Patch an LFO, an envelope or an Envelope Follower into one of its four lanes, and the value goes out as a CC message that other modules, plugins in Live or outside hardware can use to move a parameter. Its Notes output carries the messages, as any notes cable does: patch it into a MIDI output, a Voice Cell's neighbour or the Monitor to see what is sent. How does it work? Each lane has an input and its own CC number (0–127) and Channel (1–16). Only patched lanes send anything. The signal is read as 0 … +1 (or −1 … +1, see Input Range ) and mapped onto the lane's Min … Max data range, which you can use to limit a parameter's travel or, with Min above Max, to invert it. A message is sent only when the 7-bit value changes , so a still input is silent and a slow LFO sends a handful of messages per second, not thousands. Max Rate caps how often one lane may send. When the signal moves faster than that, in-between values are skipped, but the latest one always arrives. When a lane is patched, or when you press Resend , its current value is sent at once, so the receiver starts in sync. With Resolution set to 14 bit , lanes on CC 0–31 send the high part on the CC number and the low part on CC + 32, the MIDI standard for fine control. Lanes on higher CCs stay 7 bit. How to use it? Filter sweep in Live: an LFO into In 1 , CC 74 on the channel your instrument listens to, then map CC 74 to the cutoff. Loudness to a parameter: Envelope Follower 's Env into a lane: the audio moves a MIDI-mapped control. Bipolar sources: set Input Range to −1 … +1 so an LFO's centre sends Smooth controls: use 14 bit on CC 0–31 for receivers that support it. Demo patches Five whole patches show what CV to MIDI does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick CV to MIDI under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows CV to MIDI: Filter Sweep Out A slow LFO opens and closes the filter of a plucked line, and the same cable also feeds lane 1 of CV to MIDI, which sends the sweep out as CC 74 (open the Monitor to watch the messages). Change CC 1 to send it as another controller, or narrow Min 1 and Max 1. CV to MIDI: Envelope as Expression Each note's envelope shapes the filter and is also sent as CC 11 through lane 1, so a hardware synth could breathe with the same contour. Lower Max Rate to thin out the messages, or stretch the envelope's Decay and watch the table fill. CV to MIDI: Vibrato in 14 Bit A bipolar LFO bends the pitch a few cents and goes out as CC 1 at 14-bit resolution, so slow movement stays smooth instead of stepping. Switch Resolution back to 7 bit, or Input Range to 0 to +1, and compare the table. CV to MIDI: Four Moving Controls Four LFOs at different speeds move cutoff, resonance, tone and the reverb, and each is sent on its own lane as CC 74, 71, 91 and 93 on separate channels with their own Min and Max. Drag a lane's Max down to squeeze its range. CV to MIDI: Random Steps A stepped Random changes the filter on every eighth note and CV to MIDI sends each new level as CC 74: only values that moved are sent, so the table shows one message per step. Turn Smooth up on the Random and the messages arrive in streams. Reference Settings Setting Values Default CC 1–4 0 – 127 1, 74, 71, 91 Channel 1–4 1 – 16 1 Min 1–4, Max 1–4 0 – 127 0, 127 Input Range 0 … +1, −1 … +1 0 … +1 Resolution 7 bit, 14 bit (CC 0–31) 7 bit Max Rate 10 – 1000 per second per lane 200 Buttons Button What it does Resend sends every patched lane's value again Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1–4 control the value for each lane Outputs Output Signal What it carries Notes notes the control change messages

title: CV to Notes
text: CV to Notes CV to Notes in the module view Introduction CV to Notes turns a pitch and a gate into notes . Voice Cells and note outputs take notes, while sequencers, Random and other mono sources make pitch and gate signals. Put CV to Notes in between, and any mono source can play a polyphonic synth or a MIDI instrument. How does it work? The module watches the Gate and the Pitch inputs: Gate goes high: a note-on is sent. The note number is the pitch rounded to the nearest semitone (0.0 = C4 = MIDI note 60). The exact pitch, including any fraction of a semitone, travels with the note. Velocity comes from the Velocity knob. Gate goes low: a note-off for that note. Pitch moves to another semitone while the gate is high: a legato change. The new note starts first and the old one is released right after. A mono or legato Voice Cell glides without restarting its envelopes; a poly cell plays the new note on another voice. No pitch cable? When nothing is patched into Pitch , the Note knob sets the note instead. Patch only a gate (a clock, a button, a drum pattern) and CV to Notes plays that one note on every gate. Pitch changes smaller than a semitone don't start a new note. Only one note sounds at a time. How to use it? Sequencer into a synth: patch the sequencer's Pitch and Gate here, and Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes input. Generative melodies: Random Out (with Semitones on) → Pitch , and a Function's A (or Random Trig through a short envelope) → Gate . Accent and dynamics: patch a control signal onto the Velocity knob to vary the velocity of each note. Legato lines: keep the gate high and move the pitch. Set the Voice Cell's Mode to Legato and add some Glide for slides. Need a gate from a trigger? A short ADSR or a Function in envelope mode turns a trigger into a gate. Demo patches Five whole patches show what CV to Notes does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick CV to Notes under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows CV to Notes: Octave Runs A slow sequencer line becomes notes through CV to Notes, and the Arpeggiator turns each one into a three-octave run. Change the Arpeggiator's pattern, or raise Velocity on CV to Notes to hit the voice harder. CV to Notes: Gates Become Drums Plain gates from a Drum Grid carry no pitch, so CV to Notes sends its fixed Note: 36 is the kick and 38 the snare to a Drum Notes module that turns General MIDI notes back into hits. Change a Note setting to 42 and the snare becomes a hat. CV to Notes: Self-Playing Triangle A slow LFO sweeps a Quantizer, whose pitch and gate pass through CV to Notes and out as notes to a Notes to CV voice: nothing sequenced, yet a melody. Change the LFO rate for faster runs, or the Quantizer's scale for another colour. CV to Notes: Harmony Listens A bass line from a sequencer is sent as notes by CV to Notes into a Harmony Master, which follows the line and holds a chord around it; four oscillators play its chord tones above. Change the Harmony Master's Quality to dress the same line differently. CV to Notes: Soft and Hard Touch The notes leave CV to Notes with a fixed Velocity, and Notes to CV passes it on to open the filter: a low Velocity gives a mellow pluck, a high one a bright bite. Move the Velocity knob while the line plays. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Note 0 – 127 (MIDI note) 60 (C4) Velocity 0 – 100 % 80 % Note: the note to play while Pitch has no cable. It is ignored as soon as a cable is patched into Pitch . It is a modulation destination. Velocity: the velocity of each new note, read at the moment the note starts. It's a modulation destination: patch a Random or an LFO onto it for changing dynamics. Inputs Input Signal What it does Pitch pitch, 1 V/oct the note's pitch (when unpatched, the Note knob is used); 0.0 = C4, +1.0 = one octave up; notes are limited to MIDI 0 – 127 Gate gate high (≥ 0.5) plays a note, low releases it Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes note-on and note-off events; connects to any notes input

title: Drum Notes
text: Drum Notes Introduction Drum Notes turns the General MIDI drum notes of a MIDI track into triggers: one output per drum. Patch Kick into a kick drum's trigger, Closed Hat into a hat voice, and the keys of a drum pad or a MIDI clip play your kit. It is how the drum machines in Bleep Instrument take MIDI from Live while their own pattern keeps playing. How does it work? Notes in, triggers out. Each note-on whose note belongs to a drum sends a one-sample pulse to that drum's output. Note-offs are ignored: a drum is a hit, not a held note. Notes that are not on the table below do nothing. Velocity. Velocity carries the velocity of the last hit (0 … 1) for a moment (about a millisecond) around the trigger, and is 0 the rest of the time. Patch it into the Velocity (or Accent ) input of a drum voice that also gets a velocity from a sequencer: the voice then plays a key's hit at the key's velocity and the sequencer's hits unchanged. Several drums on one voice. An output can go to any number of inputs, and an input takes any number of cables, so two drums can share one voice, for example Closed Hat and Open Hat into one hat. How to use it? Play a kit from the keys: a Notes source (a MIDI input, or a drum machine cell's Notes input) into Notes ; each drum output into one voice's trigger. Add MIDI to a pattern: keep the sequencer's cables and add Drum Notes next to them. Triggers merge, so the pattern and the keys both play. Fewer voices than drums: send Closed Hat and Open Hat , or the three toms, to the same voice. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Drum Notes does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Drum Notes under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Drum Notes: Backbeat Kit One sequencer plays kick and snare as General MIDI note numbers, another plays closed and open hats; Drum Notes turns each note into a trigger for the right drum. Edit a step's pitch in the sequencer to move a hit to another drum. Drum Notes: Ring Kit Shuffle The same note-to-drum routing drives a softer, rounder kit of resonant drums on a swung sixteenth grid, with claps on the backbeat. Change the Swing on the sequencers, or swap a kit voice's Tune, and the pattern keeps its feel. Drum Notes: Percussion Circle Toms, a woody rim click, a cowbell and a clap are all played from note numbers: Drum Notes has an output for each. Mute one of the sequencers' steps, or tune the toms down, to open up the groove. Drum Notes: Ride and Crash A lazy jazz feel: the ride pattern, a pedal hi-hat, a feathered kick and one crash at the top of the bar, all as note numbers. Try the Cymbal's Voice or Decay, or lengthen the ride's pattern. Drum Notes: Ghost Notes Drum Notes also passes each hit's velocity, so the quiet ghost snares between the backbeats really are quiet while the accents bite. Raise or lower a step's velocity in the sequencer and hear the dynamics change. Reference Notes Output Drum General MIDI notes Kick Bass drum 35, 36 Snare Snare 38, 40 Rim Side stick 37 Clap Hand clap 39 Closed Hat Closed and pedal hi-hat 42, 44 Open Hat Open hi-hat 46 Tom Low to high toms 41, 43, 45, 47, 48, 50 Cowbell Cowbell 56 Ride Ride cymbals 51, 53, 59 Crash Crash cymbals 49, 52, 55, 57 Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes the MIDI notes to listen to, all channels Outputs Output Signal What it does Kick, Snare, Rim, Clap, Closed Hat, Open Hat, Tom, Cowbell, Ride, Crash trigger a one-sample pulse for each note-on of that drum Velocity control, 0 … 1 the hit's velocity for about a millisecond, then 0 The module has no knobs.

title: Notes to CV
text: Notes to CV Notes to CV in the module view Introduction Notes to CV turns notes into pitch , gate and friends. Notes come from a MIDI port, a MIDI Device or the Step Sequencer's Notes output; this module lets them play an oscillator, open an envelope or move a filter outside a Voice Cell. It is the opposite of CV to Notes . How does it work? The module remembers which notes are held. One of them is the active note , chosen by Priority : Last: the most recent note. Releasing it goes back to the note held before, like a classic mono synth. Lowest / Highest: the lowest or highest held note. First: the oldest held note; others take over only when it is released. Pitch and Velocity follow the active note and hold their values after release. Gate is high while any note is held. Trigger fires each time the active note changes. With Retrigger On , the gate drops for one sample when the active note changes while another is held, so envelopes restart. With Off (Legato) , the gate stays high and only Trigger marks the change. Glide smooths Pitch . With Glide Mode Legato Only , it only glides between overlapping notes; detached notes jump. All held notes are released when the transport stops or the Notes cable is removed, so the gate never hangs. How to use it? A mono synth from MIDI: MIDI port Notes → Notes to CV; Pitch → Oscillator Pitch ; Gate → ADSR gate; ADSR → VCA. Acid lines: Retrigger off, Glide Mode Legato Only , some Glide : overlapping notes slide, others don't. Velocity to the filter: Velocity onto the filter's cutoff knob. Key tracking for modulation: Pitch onto an LFO's rate, so higher notes move faster. Bass from chords: Priority Lowest always plays the lowest held note. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Notes to CV does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Notes to CV under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Notes to CV: Accent Lead A sequencer's notes come in, and Notes to CV hands out pitch, gate, trigger and velocity: the velocity opens the envelope harder on the accented steps. Try Retrigger Off to hear the tied notes run together. Notes to CV: Gliding Bass Tied notes slide into each other because Glide is up and Glide Mode is Legato Only; separate notes still jump. Turn Glide to 0 for a plain bass, or set Glide Mode to Always to slide into every note. Notes to CV: Lowest and Highest A Chord Quantizer sends four-note chords as notes; one Notes to CV follows the lowest note for a bass, another the highest for a bright lead. Change either Priority to Last or First to follow a different note of the chord. Notes to CV: Drifting Pad Overlapping long notes with Retrigger Off and a slow Glide make the pad drift from chord root to chord root without restarting its envelope. Switch Retrigger to On and every note swells again. Notes to CV: Trigger Out Kick Every note that arrives also leaves Notes to CV as a trigger, here firing a kick drum in step with a bass line, while Pitch plays the bass. Change the sequencer's pattern and the kick follows it. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Glide 0 … 2 s 0 s Priority Last, Lowest, Highest, First Last Retrigger Off (Legato), On On Glide Mode Always, Legato Only Always Channel All, 1 … 16 All Channel: only notes on this MIDI channel are used. Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes The note stream Outputs Output Signal What it does Pitch pitch The active note, 1 V/oct (0 = C4); holds after release Gate gate High while any note is held Trigger trigger A pulse at each new active note Velocity control The active note's velocity, 0 … 1; holds after release Release control The last note-off's release velocity, 0 … 1 Pressure control The active note's pressure, 0 … 1; 0 after release Count control Held notes ÷ 16

title: Level Meter
text: Level Meter Level Meter in the module view Introduction The Level Meter shows how loud a signal is : a bar per channel for the peak and the average (RMS) level, a peak-hold line and a clip light. Put it anywhere in an audio path: the audio passes through unchanged, so it can sit between a mixer and an output, or hang off a cable on the side. Its Level output turns the loudness into a control signal, so a sound can move other things: an envelope follower. How does it work? Open the meter's view to see the bars. The bright part of each bar is the RMS level (roughly how loud it sounds), the pale part above it the peak level (the highest sample). The thin line is the peak hold ; the numbers below show the held peak and the RMS level in dB. The clip light turns red when a sample goes over 0 dBFS, the point where the signal would distort on its way out of the computer, and stays red until you click it (or the meter). With only In L patched, the meter shows one mono bar. Response sets how quickly the RMS level and the Level output follow the signal: short for punchy drums, long for a smooth average. Floor is the bottom of the scale: everything quieter shows as empty and gives 0 on Level . Level Follows picks what Level tracks: RMS (smooth) or Peak (fast attack, falling over Response ). Peak Hold is how long the hold line stays up. How to use it? Check the mix: put it before an Audio Out and keep the RMS around −18 dB to −12 dB with the peaks below 0. Ducking: a kick's Out into the meter, Level into a VCA's Gain with a negative cable amount: the pad ducks under the kick. Loudness to brightness: Level into a Multi Filter's Cutoff , so louder playing opens the filter. Watch the output: leave one before the last Audio Out with Peak Hold at Until Reset : the hold line and the clip light tell you afterwards if anything overloaded while you weren't looking. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Level Meter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Level Meter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Level Meter: Master Check A small band passes through a Level Meter on its way to the output: watch the RMS bars dance and the peak marks stop at the top of each hit, with the clip lights staying dark. Turn the band's mixer up until a clip light shows, then back off. Level Meter: Level Ducks the Pad The drums run through a Level Meter whose Level output, inverted, pulls the pad's volume down on every kick: a sidechain pump made from a meter. Raise Response for slower, wider pumping, or turn the cable amount down for a gentler duck. Level Meter: Loudness Opens the Filter The loudness of a drum loop, read by the Level Meter's Level output, opens the filter of a saw bass: loud passages sound bright, quiet ones muffled, like an envelope follower. Change Response for smoother or twitchier brightness. Level Meter: Before and After Two Level Meters sit either side of a Compressor: the first shows the raw band, the second what is left after the squeeze, so you can see the dynamics shrink. Drop the Compressor's Threshold and watch the second meter's peaks come down. Level Meter: Watching a Tail Fade Sparse bell notes ring into a long reverb, and a Level Meter with its Floor at minus 96 dB lets you watch the tail die away to nothing, long after the notes are gone. Change Floor to minus 24 dB to see how much of the tail the meter hides. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Response 10 ms – 2 s 300 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Level Follows RMS, Peak RMS Peak Hold Off, 1 s, 3 s, Until Reset 3 s Inputs Input Signal What it does In L audio left channel, or mono In R audio right channel; unpatched, it follows In L Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the inputs, unchanged Level control 0 at Floor and below, 1 at 0 dBFS, on a dB scale; the louder channel Clip gate high while a sample goes over 0 dBFS, and 50 ms after

title: Monitor
text: Monitor Monitor in the module view Introduction The Monitor shows what is on a cable . Patch a Notes cable into it to see every note, controller, program change and bend in a table; patch audio for a level meter, a control signal for a readout and a gate or trigger for a pulse meter. Everything passes through: each input comes out of the output with the same name, so the Monitor can sit in the middle of a patch or hang off a cable on the side. Use as many of the inputs as you need; the others stay dim. How does it work? Open the Monitor's view. MIDI. Every event that arrives on Notes becomes a row, newest on top: the time since you opened the window, the MIDI channel (1–16), the kind of event, its number and its value. A note shows its name and number (60 is C4), a controller its number and, where it has a standard name, the name (74 is Cutoff ). The small bar under a value shows it from 0 to 127; for a bend it shows the position of the wheel. Under the table, a keyboard lights the notes that are on right now. A note that stays lit after you let go is a stuck note : its note-off never arrived. All Notes Off (controller 123) clears them. The chips above the table choose what you see: Notes , CC , Program , Bend , Pressure and Clock . Clock is off at first, since it sends 24 events per quarter note and would bury everything else. Pause stops adding rows (the events still pass through); Clear empties the table. If more events arrive than the window can follow between two updates (a knob sweeping a controller), the count says how many were missed . The cables are not affected. Audio. A bar per channel: the solid part is the RMS level (about how loud it sounds), the pale part the peak, and the thin line the held peak. The numbers show both in dB, and the lamp turns red when a sample goes over 0 dB. With only Audio L patched you get one mono bar. Click the bars to reset the hold and the lamps. Response is how quickly the RMS level follows, Floor the bottom of the scale. CV. The value as a number, the note name it would play if you read it as 1 V per octave with 0 as C4 (0.25 reads D♯4 ), a history graph with a band for the lowest and highest value of each update, and the lowest and highest value since you last clicked the graph. A short spike is never missed. The graph's scale follows the signal. Gate. A lamp and HIGH or LOW , a strip of the recent gate history, and numbers: Pulses counted since you last clicked the strip, the Rate of the pulses in Hz and in BPM (taken from the last two; it shows a dash when the pulses stop), the Length of the last gate and the Duty , the share of the last second the gate was high. A one-sample trigger lights the lamp for a moment, so even the shortest pulse shows. How to use it? What does my controller send? MIDI In or MIDI Device into Notes ; turn the knob you are interested in and read its controller number. Give one of the MIDI In 's CC settings that number to get it as a control signal. Find a stuck note: keep an eye on the keyboard under the table; a lit key with no note-off row means the sender missed one. Check a clock: a clock or sequencer Gate into Gate ; the BPM is the pulse rate × 60, so a clock with four pulses per beat shows four times the tempo. Check an envelope or LFO: into CV . The graph shows its shape, the numbers its range. Set a level: a source into Audio L and R , with the RMS around −18 dB and the peaks below 0. Chain it: the outputs follow the inputs, so a Monitor can sit between a MIDI In and a Voice Cell without changing anything. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Monitor does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Monitor under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Monitor: Note Table The sequencer's notes pass through a Monitor on their way to a synth voice: its table lists each note on and off with pitch and velocity as it happens. Change a step's note or velocity in the sequencer and read the difference in the table. Monitor: Watch a Control Signal A slow LFO runs through the Monitor's CV input before it sweeps the filter of a gentle line: the readout shows the value moving between its extremes while you hear the same thing. Change the LFO's rate or wave and watch the shape change. Monitor: Gate Meter on the Kick The kick's gate from the Drum Grid goes through the Monitor's gate meter, which lights on every hit and shows how long the gate lasts, before it triggers the drum. Lengthen the Drum Grid's Gate Length and watch the meter stay lit. Monitor: Stereo Meter A ping-pong delay bounces a pluck line left and right through the Monitor's audio meters, so you see the two channels take turns. Raise the Floor to see only the loud part, or lower Response to make the bars fall slowly. Monitor: Everything at Once One Monitor watches four kinds of signal on a single synth voice: the notes going in, a vibrato CV, the envelope's gate and the stereo audio coming out. Change the vibrato LFO or the sequence and see which panel reacts. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Response 10 ms – 2 s 300 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Floor −24, −36, −48, −60, −72, −96 dB −60 dB Inputs Input Signal What it does Notes notes the MIDI events for the table and the keyboard Audio L audio left channel, or mono Audio R audio right channel; unpatched, it follows Audio L CV control the signal for the CV readout Gate gate the gate or trigger for the gate meter (high at 0.5 and above) Outputs Output Signal What it does Notes notes the input's events, unchanged Audio L, Audio R audio the inputs, unchanged CV control the input, unchanged Gate gate the input, unchanged

title: Rate Counter
text: Rate Counter Introduction Rate Counter measures how often something happens. Give it a tone and it tells you the frequency; give it a clock, a drum pattern or your own taps and it tells you the tempo. The result comes out as signals: the rate as a pitch, the tempo as a control signal, an average that ignores a shaky beat, and a Steady gate that goes high when the rhythm is even. How does it work? Finding the beats. Set Input Is to Wave for tones and any continuous signal: the counter learns the signal's own range and counts every time it rises through its middle. Set it to Pulse Train for gates and triggers: it counts every rising edge. Each edge is timed more finely than a sample, so a 4 kHz tone is measured to a fraction of a per cent. Intervals and the average. The time between two edges is an interval. The counter keeps the last sixteen. Rate and BPM follow the latest interval, a little smoothed. Average BPM is taken from the mean of the last Average Of intervals: with 8, one late hit only moves it a little; with 2 it follows quickly. Per Beat says how many edges make one beat: 1 for a quarter-note clock, 4 for sixteenth notes, 24 for a MIDI-style clock. Steady. The gate is high while the last four intervals are within Steady Within of each other. A drummer that drifts or a modulated clock makes it flicker; a sequencer's clock keeps it high. Tap. Press Tap in time with the music. The taps count like edges, so after a few of them Average BPM is the tempo you tapped. Clear starts over. If nothing arrives for Start Over After seconds the counter forgets the old rhythm, and the next edge starts a new count. The BPM outputs are the tempo divided by 240, so 120 BPM is 0.5 and 240 BPM is 1. Rate is a pitch signal: it can drive an oscillator at the frequency it measured, one octave per volt. How to use it? Tempo follower: a drum track's kick (as a trigger) into the counter, Pulse Train ; Average BPM shows the tempo and Steady says when it holds. A tuner for any tone: Wave , Rate into a Quantizer or an oscillator's pitch. Tap tempo: press Tap with your music; read the Average BPM. Gate by stability: Steady into a VCA, or into a switch that only lets a sequence run once the clock is stable. Echo of a source: Rate into an oscillator two octaves lower (with a Math module for the offset) makes a sub that follows the tone. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Rate Counter does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Rate Counter under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Rate Counter: Wave Tuner A slow drone changes pitch and the Rate Counter, in Wave mode, counts its cycles; its Rate output, a pitch signal, plays a sine a fifth and an octave above the drone. Change Input Is to Pulse Train to see it lose the wave, or lower Average Of. Rate Counter: Tempo Brightens the Lead The lead's own gate is a clock that the Rate Counter measures in Pulse Train mode, two edges to a beat; its Average BPM output, about 0.5 at 120 BPM, lifts the lead's filter cutoff. Change the song tempo and the brightness follows. Rate Counter: Sixteenths Per Beat 4 A run of sixteenth notes is counted four edges to the beat, so the Rate Counter reads the true tempo, and its Average BPM bends the pitch of a low drone a little. Change Per Beat to 2 to see the reading double and the drone jump. Rate Counter: Steady Opens the Pad Four bars of even eighth notes are followed by four bars of uneven ones; the Steady gate of the Rate Counter is high only while the beat is even, and it swells a pad in and out. Make Steady Within wider and the pad stays open longer. Rate Counter: Edge Echo A sparse melody is read by the Rate Counter, and its Edge trigger, one pulse per counted note, plays a rim click and a high bell a moment after each note. The long gaps clear the count, so the count starts fresh with each phrase. Shorten Start Over After to clear it sooner. Reference Knobs and settings Control Values Default Input Is Wave, Pulse Train Wave Per Beat 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 1 Average Of 2 – 16 4 Steady Within 0.5 – 25 % 5 % Start Over After 1 – 20 s 4 s Buttons: Tap , Clear . Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the wave or pulse train to count Outputs Output Signal What it does Rate pitch the latest rate, 1 V/oct, 0 = middle C BPM control the latest tempo ÷ 240 Average BPM control the tempo of the average interval ÷ 240 Steady gate high while the last four intervals agree Edge trigger a pulse on every edge found

title: Scope
text: Scope Introduction Scope draws up to four signals over time and holds them still. Patch an oscillator in, set the trigger, and its wave stands on the screen. Two pairs of cursors measure how long and how tall. It also measures for you: the amplitude and the frequency of one trace come out as signals, so a patch can react to what the scope sees. The audio passes through unchanged. How does it work? Time. Time / Div sets how much time one of the ten divisions across the screen stands for, from 50 µs to a second. A fast setting shows single cycles of a tone; a slow one shows an envelope or a slow modulation. From 10 ms/div on, the picture is drawn while it is being captured, from left to right. Trigger. A sweep starts when the Source trace crosses the Trigger Level in the direction of Edge . Because the crossing is timed to a fraction of a sample, a steady wave starts each sweep in the same place and appears to stand still. The marker at the left edge of the screen shows the level. Auto starts a sweep anyway when nothing triggers, so the screen never goes dark; Normal waits and keeps the last picture; Free Run sweeps without a trigger at all. Hold freezes the picture (the measurements go on). Traces. Traces chooses two, three or four inputs. Each has a Scale (how tall it is drawn, 1 × fills four divisions with a signal of ±1), a Position (shift up and down in divisions) and a Colour . These only change the drawing, not the signal. Cursors. With Cursors on, drag the two vertical lines to measure a time: the readout shows Δt, the frequency 1/Δt and, from the two horizontal lines, the level difference ΔV in the units of the measured trace. Their positions are saved with the patch. Measuring. Measure picks the trace that Amplitude , Frequency and Valid follow. Amplitude is half the peak-to-peak swing. Frequency is a pitch signal (1 V/oct, 0 is middle C), so it can drive an oscillator or a quantizer directly; it holds its last value when Valid goes low, which happens on silence or when the signal stops repeating. How to use it? See a wave: any oscillator into In 1, Time / Div 1 ms, Mode Auto. Compare two: a signal and the same signal after a filter or a delay into In 1 and 2; the shift between them reads off with the cursors. Watch an envelope: an envelope into In 1, Time / Div 200 ms, Mode Normal, Trigger Level at 0.1, with the gate wired to In 2 so you see the gate and the envelope together. A tuner for a patch: put a tone into In 1 and take Frequency to a Quantizer to follow its pitch, or compare it with a keyboard's pitch in a Math module. Level follower: Amplitude is a slow, smooth loudness signal, less quick than a peak meter. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Scope does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Scope under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Scope: A Wave Standing Still A saw lead passes through the Scope, which holds each wave still on the screen; the Frequency and Amplitude readouts follow the notes. Turn Time / Div up to see more cycles or down to see one, and change the Edge to Falling to flip the picture. Scope: Filter In and Out A saw riff is drawn twice: raw on the first trace, after a swept resonant low-pass on the second. Watch the corners round off as the cutoff sinks. Change Measure to Trace 1 to read the raw pitch, or raise the filter's Resonance. Scope: Envelope in Normal Mode The first trace shows the envelope of each note, caught by a trigger set just above zero in Normal mode, so every sweep starts exactly when a note starts and the picture waits between notes. Raise Trigger Level to start later on the rise, or change Mode to Auto. Scope: Frequency Plays Along The Scope measures the pitch of a bass line and its Frequency output, snapped to a scale by a Quantizer, plays a bell an octave and a fifth above, gated by Valid: a harmony made by measuring. Change the Quantizer's Scale or Root, or turn the follower up to hear its small delay. Scope: Amplitude Opens the Bass A drum loop is drawn on the Scope and its Amplitude output, the size of the wave, opens the filter of a saw bass: each hit brightens the bass for a moment. Change the cable amount into Cutoff, or move the bass filter's base Cutoff. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Time / Div 0.05 – 1000 ms 1 ms Hold off, on off Traces 2 – 4 2 Cursors off, on on Trigger Level −2 … +2 0 Edge Rising, Falling, Either Rising Source Trace 1 – 4 Trace 1 Mode Auto, Normal, Free Run Auto Scale 1 – 4 0.05 – 20 × 1 × Position 1 – 4 −4 … +4 div 0 Colour 1 – 4 Mint, Amber, Sky, Rose, Lime, Violet, White, Orange Mint, Amber, Sky, Rose Measure Trace 1 – 4 Trace 1 Inputs Input Signal What it does In 1 – In 4 audio the traces (In 3 and In 4 with that many traces) Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1 – Out 4 audio the inputs, unchanged Amplitude control half the swing of the Measure trace Frequency pitch frequency of the Measure trace, 1 V/oct, 0 = middle C Valid gate high while the Measure trace is a clear repeating signal

title: Spectrum
text: Spectrum Introduction Spectrum shows which frequencies are in a sound, low on the left and high on the right, with the frequency axis spaced the way you hear it. It also listens for you: the strongest partial , the centroid (how bright the sound is) and a flux trigger (a new sound has arrived) come out as signals. The audio passes through unchanged. How does it work? The picture. The sound is cut into short windows and analysed several times per window length; each analysis updates the curve. Resolution chooses the window: a long one separates close partials and low notes but reacts slowly, a short one is quick but blurry. Average smooths the curve over time so it stops flickering. The Peak Line keeps the highest levels: Falling lets them sink slowly, Hold keeps them until you press Reset Peaks . Tilt leans the curve by a number of decibels per octave, which only changes how it looks: +4.5 dB per octave makes a pink noise look flat. Floor is the bottom of the picture. Strongest. The loudest partial between 20 Hz and the top of the axis, found precisely between the bins. It comes out of Dominant as a pitch signal (1 V/oct, 0 is middle C) and is shown in Hz and as a note name. When the input falls below −60 dBFS, Dominant holds its last value. Centroid. The centre of gravity of the spectrum, from the same average. A sine has its centroid at its pitch; adding harmonics pulls it up. Patch it into a filter cutoff to make a brightness follower. Flux. Each analysis is compared with the one before. When much more energy than usual has arrived (a new note, a drum hit) Flux sends a short pulse and Flux Amount shows how much changed. Flux Sensitivity sets how little is enough; a steady tone triggers nothing. How to use it? Look at a patch: put a Spectrum anywhere in an audio path; at Average 0.15 s it follows the sound smoothly. A tuner: an instrument into In L, Dominant into a Quantizer: it snaps to the note the instrument plays. Brightness follower: Centroid into a Math module (to scale it) and on to a filter or a reverb mix. Onset trigger: Flux as a clock for a sequencer or an envelope: it follows what is played, even when the notes are soft. Find a resonance: switch Peak Line to Hold, sweep a filter's cutoff and read where the curve rose. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Spectrum does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Spectrum under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Spectrum: The Band at a Glance A small band plays through the Spectrum: the kick and bass fill the left, the lead and hats the right, and the dashed line follows the strongest partial. Change Tilt to +4.5 dB/oct to flatten the slope, or Peak Line to Hold to keep the highest marks. Spectrum: Siren to Bells A quiet siren glides up and down; the Spectrum's Dominant output hears its strongest partial and a Quantizer turns that into bell notes of a minor scale, struck whenever the note changes. Change the Quantizer's Scale, or slow the siren down. Spectrum: Brightness Drives the Pad A drum loop is analysed and its Centroid, the spectrum's centre of gravity, sets the filter cutoff of a saw pad: when hats and snares crowd in the pad opens, when only the kick is left it dulls. Turn the pad filter's Key Track down to lessen the effect. Spectrum: Flux Plays the Hats Plucked notes go through the Spectrum, whose Flux trigger fires whenever new energy appears: it plays a closed hat and a rim click on every note, so the percussion follows the melody. Raise Flux Sensitivity to catch the quiet notes too. Spectrum: Sweeping Pad, Tilted A saw pad with a slowly sweeping filter, seen on a long 8192 point average with the Tilt at +4.5 dB/oct so the slope looks level and the peak line stays up in Hold. Press Reset Peaks to clear the line, or lower Average for a jumpier picture. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Resolution 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192 4096 Average 0 – 3 s 0.15 s Tilt −6 … +9 dB/oct 0 Peak Line Off, Falling, Hold Falling Flux Sensitivity 0 – 100 % 50 % Floor −120 … −30 dB −90 dB Button: Reset Peaks . Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio analysed as their average; R unpatched: L alone Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the inputs, unchanged Dominant pitch the strongest partial Centroid pitch the spectrum's centre of gravity Flux trigger new energy arrived Flux Amount control how much is new, 0 – 1

title: Tuner
text: Tuner Tuner in the module view Introduction The Tuner shows which note a sound is and how far from it, in cents (one hundredth of a semitone). Patch an instrument, a voice or an oscillator into In : a large note name, a needle, the heard frequency and the frequency it should be appear in the view. A green needle means in tune. It also works as a module in a patch : Cents is the error as a CV, In Tune a gate that is high while the note is within the window, and Pitch the V/oct of what it hears. How does it work? The module uses the same pitch tracker as the Pitch Follower and the Pitch Snap , with a vote of three and a firm confidence, so only a clear, steady tone is shown. The heard frequency is turned into the nearest note of equal temperament around the Reference A and the error in cents. Reference A sets the pitch of A4: 440 Hz is concert pitch; 415 is a semitone lower for period instruments; 442 is common for orchestras. In Tune is the window in cents around the note that counts as in tune. The gate opens when the sound has stayed inside it for 60 ms and closes when it leaves a window 1.4 times as wide, so a note on the edge does not flicker. Damping smooths the reading. A long time gives a calm needle; a short one shows every vibrato. A new note, more than 60 cents away from the old one, shows at once. Low and High limit the range (as in the Pitch Follower: a lower Low makes the answer slower). Octave Guard keeps one stray octave estimate from showing up on the needle. Names chooses sharps or flats for the display. When the sound stops the last note stays on the screen, dimmed. How to use it? Tune an instrument: patch it into In , pluck a string and turn the peg until the needle is green. Use Guitar , Bass Tuner or Violin and Voice for a range that fits. Tune a synth by ear: put an oscillator into In and adjust its fine tune until In Tune lights. Patch the result: Cents into a VCA or a light: it moves with the error. In Tune can fire a trigger once a note is right. Watch a vibrato: Fast Needle and the history strip below the needle. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Tuner does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Tuner under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Tuner: Tuning Game A pure tone drifts slowly sharp and flat of a note; each time it slides through the In Tune window the Tuner's gate strikes a soft bell, so you can hear the moment it is right. Widen In Tune for more bells per sweep, or narrow it to catch only the exact centre. Tuner: Detune Pan Two saw voices a fifth apart share a pad; the upper one wanders in pitch and the Tuner's Cents output pans it and opens a filter, so how sharp or flat it is becomes the movement. Try a wider Damping for lazier motion, or invert the cable amounts. Tuner: Drift Chime A drone pair floats in pitch, and whenever one voice passes through tune the Tuner strikes a mallet voice that plays the note it is hearing, a fifth up, into a long reverb. Change Reference A to shift where the chime lands, or raise In Tune for a busier shimmer. Tuner: Gated Octave A pluck line slowly slips out of tune and back; the Tuner follows its pitch and re-pitches a second voice an octave up, which only sounds while the line is in tune. Make In Tune smaller for shorter, rarer answers, or shorten Damping for a quicker tracker. Tuner: Baroque Pitch A melody is played a semitone low, and the Tuner's Reference A is set to 415 so it reads each note as exactly in tune, ticking a hi-hat on every sure note. Move Reference A away from 415 and the ticks stop; at 440 the whole line reads flat. Presets The preset bar of the Tuner view has 11 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Standard Concert pitch, A = 440 Hz. Baroque 415 A = 415 Hz, a semitone lower, for period instruments. Bright 442 A = 442 Hz, as many orchestras tune. Warm 432 A = 432 Hz. Bass Tuner Low range for bass strings; slower and steadier. Guitar Six strings and a tight in-tune window. Violin and Voice High range for strings and singers, with a forgiving window. Strict Only within two cents counts as in tune. Loose A wide window for a quick check of a rough sound. Slow Needle The needle takes its time and hardly twitches. Fast Needle Shows every movement at once, e.g. to watch a vibrato. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Reference A 400 – 480 Hz 440 Hz In Tune 1 – 25 ct 5 ct Damping 10 – 600 ms 80 ms Low 25 – 400 Hz 40 Hz High 200 – 4000 Hz 1400 Hz Settings Setting Values Default Names Sharps, Flats Sharps Octave Guard Off, Light, Firm Light Inputs Input Signal What it does In audio the sound to tune Outputs Output Signal What it does Cents control the error, −1…+1 for −50…+50 cents In Tune gate high while the note is within the In Tune window Pitch pitch the smoothed pitch in V/oct, held while nothing is heard Origin Pitch detection is shared with the Pitch Follower (the published difference-function method, written for this project); the note arithmetic is plain equal temperament. No source code was ported.

title: XY Scope
text: XY Scope XY Scope in the module view Introduction XY Scope is an oscilloscope with a green phosphor screen, made for the old bench trick of comparing two oscillators by eye. Patch one into X and one into Y : the beam draws a Lissajous figure. It stands still when the two are in a simple ratio and turns slowly when they are slightly off. A Y-T mode shows ordinary waveforms. It also turns what you see into signals: Phase , Correlation , Ratio and a Still gate. Patch Still into a sequencer's clock and the music moves on whenever two drifting oscillators happen to lock. How does it work? The screen. X moves the beam left and right, Y up and down; at 1 × gain ±1 reaches the edge of the graticule. The beam glows where it moves slowly and is faint where it moves fast, as on a real tube, and the trace fades over Persistence . Focus sets how sharp the line is, Intensity how bright, and the Z input modulates the brightness (−1 blanks the beam, +1 doubles it). Character Vintage adds the tube's flaws: a slightly bulging picture, softer corners, a trace of mains hum and a short warm-up when the view opens. None of this reaches the outputs. Frequencies. Both inputs are measured by timing their rising zero crossings, from about 0.2 Hz to 10 kHz. A channel counts as valid while it is patched, louder than −60 dBFS and crossing zero at least every 5 s. The readout shows both frequencies, or a dash while a channel is not valid. Ratio is fy / fx as an interval: 1.0 is an octave, 0.585 a fifth, −1 an octave down. From it the scope picks the figure ratio p:q, the simplest fraction (up to 8:8) within 3 % of it; it shows in the readout and decides what Phase compares. A new figure ratio takes over after 200 ms, so it doesn't flicker between neighbours. Phase is the phase of the figure, −1 … +1 for −180° … +180°. At 1:1 it is the plain phase difference: 0 for a diagonal line, +0.5 for a circle with Y leading, ±1 for the other diagonal. At other ratios it is constant as long as Y is exactly p/q times X. When the oscillators drift apart, Phase becomes a sawtooth at the rate the figure turns: two detuned oscillators make a slow LFO from their own beating. Correlation is +1 when X and Y move together, −1 when they move opposite, and near 0 when they are unrelated or a quarter cycle apart. Still goes high once the figure has stood still for 100 ms: both channels valid, the ratio within 0.25 % of p/q and the figure turning slower than the Still Tolerance (Tight 0.05, Normal 0.2, Loose 1 turn per second). It goes low 50 ms after that stops being true. While a channel isn't valid, Ratio and Phase hold their last value and Still is low. Y-T mode draws Y over time, one sweep per Timebase . Trigger Y Rising starts each sweep at a rising zero crossing of Y, so a steady wave stands still; Auto does the same but sweeps anyway when no crossing comes; Beat starts a sweep on every beat while the transport plays. X, when patched, is drawn as a second, dimmer trace. Out X and Out Y pass the inputs on unchanged, so the scope can sit in a signal path. The scope has no random parts: the same input always gives the same outputs. How to use it? Tune by eye: two oscillators into X and Y, tune one until the figure stands still. A circle or line is unison, a figure-eight an octave. Beating as an LFO: two oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, Phase into a filter's cutoff: a slow sweep that speeds up as they drift apart. Music that waits for a lock: two free-running oscillators slightly detuned (or slowly modulated), Still into a sequencer's clock. Stereo width: a stereo signal's left and right into X and Y. A line at 45° is mono, a round cloud is wide; Correlation below 0 warns of phase problems. Interval follower: Ratio into an oscillator's pitch makes it follow the interval between two others. Classic scope: Mode Y-T, any signal into Y. Demo patches Five whole patches show what XY Scope does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick XY Scope under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows XY Scope: Locked Fifth Knot Two sines a fifth apart draw a slow-turning knot on the scope; each time the pattern stands still enough, the Still gate fires a bell. Change Still Tolerance to Loose and the bells come more often, or tune the Y oscillator by ear to lock them. XY Scope: Stereo Width Pad A pad's left and right channels go into X and Y, so the scope shows the stereo image: a diagonal line means near-mono, a round cloud means wide. The Correlation output opens the reverb when the image narrows. Turn the Chorus's Spread down and watch the cloud pinch. XY Scope: Bass Waveform In Y-T mode the scope is an ordinary oscilloscope: a bass line's waveform stands still on screen, triggered on every rising edge. Shorten Timebase to see single cycles, or turn the Oscillator's Shape and watch the wave change under the sound. XY Scope: FM Knots A bell-like FM pair plays a pentatonic line; the carrier goes to X and the modulated tone to Y, so each note draws a tangled knot that unwinds as it decays. Raise the Oscillator's FM Depth for a busier knot, or X Gain to stretch the figure. XY Scope: Ratio Plays a Voice A fixed sine on X and a sweeping sine on Y: the scope measures their ratio and its Ratio output, as a pitch, plays a third voice that follows the interval between them. Change the sweep rate and the follower glides along; try Timebase for a clearer picture. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default X Gain 0.1 – 10 × 1 × Y Gain 0.1 – 10 × 1 × Timebase 1 ms – 2 s 20 ms Persistence 10 ms – 5 s 150 ms Focus 0 – 100 % 80 % Intensity 0 – 100 % 60 % Mode X-Y, Y-T X-Y Trigger Y Rising, Auto, Beat Y Rising Phosphor Green, Amber, Blue-White Green Character Clean, Vintage Vintage Still Tolerance Tight, Normal, Loose Normal X Gain, Y Gain: the size of the picture across and up. Timebase: the length of one sweep (Y-T mode only). Persistence: how long the trace glows: the time it takes to fade by 40 dB. Focus: 100 % is a fine line, 0 % a soft, wide glow. Intensity: the beam's brightness. Trigger: what starts a sweep (Y-T mode only). Phosphor: the screen colour. Character: Vintage adds the tube's flaws, Clean draws none. Still Tolerance: how slowly the figure must turn for Still . The six knobs are modulation destinations. Only Timebase (in Y-T mode) changes anything but the picture; the others never touch the outputs. Inputs Input Signal What it does X audio horizontal deflection; the reference for Phase and Ratio Y audio vertical deflection; the signal compared with X Z control beam brightness: 0 normal, −1 off, +1 double Outputs Output Signal What it does Out X audio X, unchanged Out Y audio Y, unchanged Phase control the figure's phase, −1 … +1 = −180° … +180° Correlation control how alike X and Y are, −1 … +1 Ratio pitch fy / fx as an interval (1.0 = an octave) Still gate high while the figure stands still

title: Button
text: Button Button in the module view Introduction The Button is a pad to press while the patch plays. Click it, tap it or press Space: it opens a gate, fires triggers, or switches something on and off. Use it to start an envelope by hand, reset a sequencer, fire a drum or mute a part. How does it work? In Momentary mode, Gate is high for as long as you hold the pad. In Toggle mode, each press switches Gate on or off, and it stays there. Whatever the mode: Trigger fires a short pulse each time you press, Release fires one each time you let go, Toggle switches on or off with every press. Once you've clicked the pad, Space and Enter press it too. The toggle's state is saved with the set, so a part you switched off stays off when you open it again. How to use it? Play an envelope by hand: Gate into an ADSR's Gate , the ADSR into a VCA. Restart the music: Trigger into a Step Sequencer's or an LFO's Reset . Fire a drum: Trigger into a drum's Trig . Mute a part: Toggle mode, Gate onto a VCA's Gain (or into a Switch to choose between two sources). Demo patches Five whole patches show what Button does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Button under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Button: Hold To Brighten A dark, muffled saw riff plays on its own; hold the Button and its Gate output opens an envelope that sweeps the filter wide open, then lets it fall back when you let go. Try the Toggle mode to latch the bright sound. Button: Toggle Bell Layer A warm pad-like line carries the patch; click the Button in Toggle mode and a second, bell-like line fades in on top and stays until you click again. Switch Mode to Momentary to bring the bells in only while you hold it. Button: Clap On Press A bass line and a half-time beat play by themselves; every press of the Button sends a Trigger to a clap, so you add hand claps by tapping it in time. The Trigger fires on the press, not on the release, and its Gate output would stay high while you hold. Button: Cymbal On Release Press and hold the Button, then let go: its Release output fires a long crash cymbal at the moment you lift your finger, like a drum-fill finish. Use the Trigger output on the same Button to hit the cymbal on the way down instead. Button: Freeze Hold In Toggle mode the Button's Toggle output latches the reverb's Freeze input: click it while a note is ringing and the tail is held as an endless chord under the following notes. Click again to let the room empty. Reference Settings Setting Values Default Mode Momentary, Toggle Momentary Outputs Output Signal What it does Gate gate high while held (Momentary) or while toggled on (Toggle) Trigger trigger a pulse on every press Release trigger a pulse on every release Toggle gate switches on or off with every press

title: Dial
text: Dial Dial in the module view Introduction The Dial is one big knob whose position comes out of a jack as a control signal. Patch Out onto several knobs at once, at different cable amounts, and one turn moves them all together: a macro for the filter, the mix and the decay of a sound. How does it work? Turn the dial (drag up and down, Shift for fine, or use the wheel; double-click resets it). Out goes from Min with the dial fully left to Max fully right. Set Max below Min to turn the dial around, or Min to −1 for a bipolar dial that moves its destinations both ways. Steps gives the dial detents: with 4, it only stops at four positions, evenly spaced, and each wheel notch moves one step. Handy for choosing between a few settings, or for octave jumps on a pitch. Smooth glides Out to a new position instead of jumping, so fast turns don't click. At 0 it follows the dial exactly. A cable into Value moves the dial like a hand would: the big dial shows the modulation as a ring. How to use it? Macro: Out onto a Multi Filter's Cutoff , a VCA's Gain and an LFO's Rate ; set each cable's amount for how far each one moves. Morph between two sounds: Out onto a Crossfader's Mix . Octave switch: Min −1, Max +1 and Steps 3 into an Oscillator's Pitch input: an octave down, unchanged, an octave up. Slow manual sweep: Smooth at 1 s turns any quick move into a sweep. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Dial does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Dial under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Dial: Filter Sweep One Dial, set to the middle of its range, opens the cutoff of a dark saw riff. Drag the big knob up and down while it plays to sweep the filter, or raise Smooth to make the knob glide between positions. Dial: Stepped Transpose With Steps set to 12 the Dial jumps between fixed positions instead of sliding, and it feeds the sequencer's Transpose input so the whole tune moves up and down in whole notes. Set Steps to 0 to get a smooth slide, or change Steps to 5 for coarser jumps. Dial: Reverb Blend The Dial rides the Mix knob of a very long reverb behind a slow bell tune: at the bottom you hear the dry notes, at the top only their wash. Move it slowly and listen to the tune sink into the room. Dial: Flipped Range Min is higher than Max, so turning the Dial up closes the filter and eases off the drive while the bass sits on a beat. Swap Min and Max to turn the action around, or narrow them to limit how far the knob can go. Dial: Morph Macro One Dial fans out to three destinations at different strengths: the oscillator shape, the filter cutoff and the delay mix, so a single gesture takes a soft sine pluck to a bright, echoing saw. Change the cable amounts to rebalance the macro. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Value 0 – 100 % 50 % Min −1 – +1 0 Max −1 – +1 +1 Smooth 0 – 2 s 20 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Settings Setting Values Default Steps 0 (continuous), 2 – 24 0 Outputs Output Signal What it does Out control the dial's position, scaled from Min to Max

title: XY Pad
text: XY Pad XY Pad in the module view Introduction The XY Pad gives you two control signals from one touch . Drag a point over the pad: its horizontal position comes out of X , its vertical position out of Y . Patch the two onto a filter's cutoff and resonance, or a pair of mix knobs, and one finger plays both. How does it work? X and Y go from Min at the left and bottom edges to Max at the right and top edges; both axes share the range. The default is 0 to 1; set Min to −1 for a pad that moves its destinations both ways from the centre. Smooth glides both outputs to a new position instead of jumping. A cable into the X or Y knob moves the point like a hand would. In a panel, an XY pad control drives this module. How to use it? Filter sweep: X onto a Multi Filter's Cutoff , Y onto its Resonance . Morph: X and Y onto two Crossfader mixes for a four-way blend. Demo patches Five whole patches show what XY Pad does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick XY Pad under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows XY Pad: Filter Plane The pad's X axis drives the cutoff and its Y axis the resonance of a saw bass, so dragging across the pad goes from dull to bright and up from smooth to squelchy. Drag the dot around while the groove runs. XY Pad: Echo Room X sets how much echo you hear and Y how many repeats it feeds back on a bell melody, so the bottom left is dry and the top right is a cloud of repeating notes. Try dragging along the edges to change only one thing at a time. XY Pad: Timbre Map X morphs the oscillator through its waveforms and Y changes its pulse width, so each corner of the pad is a different voice for the same slow tune. Park the dot in a corner or move it while the notes sound. XY Pad: Variation Field X controls the sequencer's Variation, the chance that notes are shifted away from the programmed ones, and Y its Gate Length, so you can shake up the tune and make it shorter or smoother at the same time. Park the pad low-left for the plain tune. XY Pad: Bipolar Range Min and Max are set to -1 and +1, so the pad's centre is zero: X bends the pitch a little either way and Y pushes the filter above or below its starting point. Narrow Min and Max for gentler moves. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default X 0 – 100 % 50 % Y 0 – 100 % 50 % Min −1 – +1 0 Max −1 – +1 +1 Smooth 0 – 2 s 20 ms Every knob is a modulation destination. Outputs Output Signal What it does X control horizontal position, scaled from Min to Max Y control vertical position, scaled from Min to Max

title: Keyboard
text: Keyboard Keyboard in the module view Introduction The Keyboard is a piano keyboard on the board . Play it with the mouse, a finger or your computer keyboard to try a sound without reaching for a MIDI controller. Its Notes output plays a Voice Cell directly; Pitch and Gate play a single oscillator and envelope. How does it work? Mouse and touch. Press a key to play it; drag across the keys for a glissando. Computer keyboard. Click the keys once, then play: the row A S D F G H J K L holds the white keys from C, the row above ( W E T Y U O P ) the black ones, like a piano. Z and X move down and up an octave. It goes by the keys' positions, so any keyboard layout works. Octave (or the ‹ › buttons) chooses which three octaves the keys show. Velocity sets how hard every key is played. Hold latches keys: a click starts a note and it keeps playing until you click it again. Switch Hold off, or press All off , to end them. Notes sends every key you play, so a Voice Cell plays chords. Pitch , Gate , Velocity and Trigger follow one note at a time, chosen by Priority (the last key pressed, the lowest, the highest or the first), and fall back to a key still held when you let go. Glide slides Pitch from note to note. How to use it? Try a synth: Notes into a Voice Cell's Notes ; the cell's output to Audio Out. Hold a few keys for a chord. A mono synth without a cell: Pitch into an Oscillator's Pitch , Gate into an ADSR, the ADSR onto a VCA. Raise Glide for slides. A drone: switch on Hold and click a few keys. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Keyboard does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Keyboard under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Keyboard: Transposing Keys A pentatonic riff loops by itself; the Keyboard's Pitch output goes to the sequencer's Transpose input, so playing a key moves the whole riff to that note. Change Octave to shift the range of the keys, or Priority to choose which key wins when you hold several. Keyboard: Glide Lead A soft bell arpeggio plays underneath; the Keyboard's Pitch and Gate drive a separate saw lead, and Glide is set to 0.25 s so notes slide into each other as you play. Raise Glide for slower portamento or bring it to 0 for clean steps. Keyboard: Mallet Layer A bass loop plays alone until you press keys: the Keyboard's Pitch, Trigger and Velocity strike a marimba-like Modal Voice, so harder Velocity makes brighter hits. Try the Velocity knob, or play a run down the keys.
