title: Clock Mult
text: Clock Mult Introduction One clock in, six faster (or slower) clocks out. Every output has its own ratio: 2, 3 or 4 ticks per input clock, but also fractions such as 3/2, 5/4 or 2/3 that drift against the beat and meet it again every few clocks. Each output can skip ticks by chance, and one Swing and one Humanize knob move only the in-between ticks, so the beat itself stays exactly where the clock puts it. Patch a trigger into Clock , or leave it empty and the module follows the song: it reads the song position, so it stays on the grid after loop jumps and in renders. For the opposite job (slower outputs from a clock) see Clock Div. How does it work? Ratios. Ratio 1 … Ratio 6 are chosen from 1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 1, 5/4, 4/3, 3/2, 5/3, 7/4, 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 16, 24 and A ratio of p/q ticks p times in q input clocks. Output k ticks at 0, then every q/p clocks. Ticks that land exactly on an input clock are the anchors ; the others are the in-between ticks . Swing and Humanize. Swing delays every second in-between tick by up to half an interval. Humanize delays every in-between tick by its own random amount, up to 40 % of an interval. Anchors never move, and a tick is never moved earlier, so nothing can arrive before the clock that causes it. The random amounts come from Seed : the same seed always plays the same feel. Skips. Skip 1 … Skip 6 is the chance that an output drops a tick. With Keep Beat on (the default) the anchors are never dropped, so a heavily thinned output still marks the beat; turn it off and the pulse itself can go. Phase Lock. With a patched clock the module measures the time between pulses and runs its ticks inside it. Phase Lock at 100 % pulls the phase onto the incoming pulse every time: the outputs follow a drifting or jittery clock, and wait for it when it stops. At 0 % the phase is never pulled: the outputs run on as a flywheel at the learned tempo, even if the clock stops. In between the clock is followed more loosely. Reset starts a new count: the next pulse is the first beat. On the song position (no clock patched) the phase is exact, so Phase Lock has no effect there; Reset makes the next base step the start. Base. Unpatched, one input clock is Base (a quarter note by default) at the song's tempo. Gates. Gate output holds each tick for Width of its interval; Trigger output sends a one-sample pulse. Any is high whenever any output is. How to use it? Layered percussion from one pulse: ratios 4, 3/2 and 5/4 into three drums; the 3/2 and 5/4 drift against the beat and line up again every few bars. A swung hat that keeps the kick honest: a ratio-4 output into the hats with Swing at 60 %, a ratio-1 output into the kick. Ghost notes: a fast output with Skip at 50 % and a little Humanize . A clock for a sequencer: an output into a Step Sequencer's Clock makes it run at a fraction of a step, with a swing it does not have by itself. Slow gates: ratios 1/2, 1/4 or 2/3 for chord changes and slow modulation. Tempo that stays: Phase Lock at 0 keeps a patch moving through a gap in the incoming clock. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Clock Mult does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Clock Mult under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Clock Mult: Drifting Percussion One quarter-note clock becomes a kick on the beat, hats at four per beat, a rim at 3/2 and a cowbell at 5/4: the last two drift against the kick and meet it again every few beats. Change a Ratio knob and the layer re-tunes. Clock Mult: Swung Hats Swing on a Clock Mult output moves only the in-between ticks: the kick and the snare sit on the beat while the sixteenth hats lean late. Turn Swing up for a harder shuffle, Humanize for a looser hand, or raise Skip 3 for fewer ghost hats. Clock Mult: Clock for a Line A Step Sequencer has no clock of its own: it takes Out 1 of Clock Mult at four ticks per beat with a late swing, and the bass takes Out 2 at one per beat. Change Ratio 1 to 3 or 3/2 for a different gait; the line follows the multiplier. Clock Mult: Fractional Bells Four bell tones ring at 2/3, 3/4, 5/4 and 7/4 of the clock with Skip on the busy ones, so a calm pentatonic cloud never quite repeats. Move one Ratio by a step and the whole constellation shifts. Clock Mult: Chained from a Divider Clock Div turns the 16th grid into a slow beat-rate pulse, and Clock Mult's Clock jack counts those pulses and multiplies them back up: tight at full Phase Lock, and a flywheel that keeps going at zero. Try 3 and 5/4 against the divider's own outputs. Presets The preset bar of the Clock Mult view has 16 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Ratio Ladder Whole and fractional ratios side by side: 2, 3, 4, 3/2, 5/4 and 8 per clock. Straight Doubles Powers of two up from the clock, plus a half-speed output: everything lines up. Triplet Roll Threes in every size, from a lazy 3/4 to a rolling 12 per clock. Five Against Four Fifths over a four-beat feel: the odd outputs slide against the plain ones. Seven Over Septuplets against halves and quarters; the anchors meet on every clock. Shuffled Sixteenths Swing on the in-between ticks only: the beat stays put, the offbeats lean late. Loose Hands Every in-between tick lands a little late, differently each time round; anchors stay tight. Thinning Out The same fast clock, each output losing more ticks than the one before. Ghost Hats Half the eighths and most of the sixteenths drop out; what is left feels played. Free Skips Keep Beat off: even the ticks on the clock can drop, so the pulse itself gets loose. Half-Time Pulses Slower than the clock: gates for pads, chord changes and slow modulation. Dotted Feel Ratios of three over two give dotted spacing; a little swing leans the in-betweens. Flywheel Phase Lock at zero: the outputs keep running on the learned tempo when the clock stops. Soft Lock A partial lock: a wobbly input clock is smoothed instead of followed tick for tick. Long Gates Gate output at 80 % of each interval: legato gates for envelopes and holds. Swung Everything Heavy swing, a hint of humanize and an occasional dropped tick on the busy output. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Ratio 1 … Ratio 6 1/8 … 32 (see above) 2, 3, 4, 3/2, 5/4, 8 Skip 1 … Skip 6 0 – 100 % 0 % Swing 0 – 100 % 0 % Humanize 0 – 100 % 0 % Phase Lock 0 – 100 % 100 % Width 1 – 99 % (Gate output) 50 % Settings Setting Values Default Base 1/1 … 1/32, dotted and triplet 1/4 Output Gate, Trigger Gate Keep Beat Off, On On Seed 0 – 999 1 Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Inputs Input Signal What it does Clock trigger patched: each pulse is one input clock Reset trigger the next input clock is the first of a new count Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1 … Out 6 gate ticks at its ratio of the input clock Any gate high while any output is high

title: Rotating Div
text: Rotating Div Rotating Div in the module view Introduction Eight clock dividers on one clock. Out 1 fires every step, Out 2 every second step, Out 3 every third, and so on, and the Rotate knob shifts the whole set across the outputs: one turn (or an LFO on Rotate ) turns a steady hi-hat into half time, odd meters or sparse accents. Everything is worked out from the song position, so it stays on the bars, after loop jumps and in renders. How does it work? The base step. Unpatched, one step is Base (1/16 by default) at the song's tempo. Patch a trigger into Clock and every pulse is a step instead. Sets. Set chooses the eight divisions: Integers (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8), Odds (1 3 5 …), Evens (2 4 6 …), Primes (1 2 3 5 7 11 13 17), Powers of 2 (1 2 4 … 128), Fibonacci (1 2 3 5 8 13 21 34), or Custom (your eight values, typed in the view). Rotate. Wrap cycles the eight values round the outputs: Rotate 1 on Integers gives 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 1. Extend keeps going along the series, so the outputs get slower: Rotate 4 gives 5 … 12. Custom always wraps. Rotate Sync. A new Rotate (or Set) waits for the next base step ( Next Step ), the next bar ( Next Bar ; with a clock: the next step where all outputs line up), or applies at once ( Immediate ). A gate that is already high always finishes its length. Realign. Odd divisions drift against the bar: /3 of 1/16 notes repeats only every 3 bars. Realign restarts every output every 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars; the last cycle before the restart is shortened, and its gate ends at least 1 ms before the next one starts. Gates. In Gate output, an output is high for Width of its own period ( Gate Length = Division ) or of one base step ( Base Step ). Trigger output sends a one-sample pulse instead. Stair reads the eight outputs as a binary number (Out 1 the highest bit), so it is a stepped shape that repeats with the pattern; into a quantizer it makes a melody. Align fires when all eight outputs start together. Reset makes the next base step the start of every output's cycle. When the transport stops, every output goes low; on play, nothing fires until the next due step. How to use it? Drum variations: Out 1 … 8 into drum triggers; an LFO or a Random on Rotate . Odd meters that still land on the one: Set Odds , Realign 1 bar. A melody from rhythm: Stair into a Quantizer Suite. Phrase starts: Align resets a sequencer or advances a Harmony Master. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Rotating Div does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Rotating Div under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Rotating Div: Shifting Drum Roles A slow stepped LFO turns Rotate, so the same set of divisions moves from output to output: the part that was the kick becomes the hats, then the clap, and the groove reshapes every few bars. Turn Rotate by hand to hear one fixed arrangement, or set Rotate Sync to Next Bar to move on the downbeat. Rotating Div: Prime Bells The Primes set (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and on) rings eight soft bell tones, each on its own division, so they only coincide rarely and the texture keeps shifting. Change Rotate to give each bell a different, slower or faster clock without touching the tuning. Rotating Div: Powers of Two Groove With the Powers of 2 set (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...) every output lands on a regular beat, giving a tidy four-to-the-floor skeleton of kick, claps and hats. Raise Rotate by one and each part jumps to the next division for an instant half-time or double-time feel. Rotating Div: Fibonacci Staircase The Stair output reads all eight gates as one binary number, a jumpy staircase that repeats with the pattern, and a Quantizer snaps it to a scale so the Fibonacci set (1, 2, 3, 5, 8...) writes a melody. Change the Quantizer's Scale, or Rotate, for a different tune from the same clocks. Rotating Div: Extending Evens In Extend mode, Rotate does not wrap around the set but continues it, so with the Evens set each turn of the knob brings in longer divisions (2, 4, 6... then 18, 20 and beyond). A slow sawtooth LFO turns Rotate up through the bars, thinning the hats and claps out as it climbs. Presets The preset bar of the Rotating Div view has 12 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Integer Set Divisions 1 to 8 across the outputs: the plain starting point. Integers Rotated The same set shifted three outputs along, wrapping round. Odd Divisions Divisions 1, 3, 5, 7 and so on: off-kilter, interlocking pulses. Even Divisions Divisions 2, 4, 6 and so on: steady, related pulses. Prime Rotation Prime divisions shifted by two: very slow to repeat. Binary Ladder Powers of two: classic halving for kick, snare and hats. Fibonacci Spiral Fibonacci divisions for organic cross-rhythms. Extending Rotate Rotate extends the set upward instead of wrapping. Triggers Instant Triggers for drums; rotation changes take effect at once. Bar-Locked Rotation Rotation moves only at the bar line, resyncing each bar. Eighth Base Pulses A slower base clock with long gates. Triplet Fibonacci Triplet base with base-step gates for skittering hits. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Rotate 0 – 16 0 Width 1 – 99 % 50 % Settings Setting Values Default Set Integers, Odds, Evens, Primes, Powers of 2, Fibonacci, Custom Integers Rotate Mode Wrap, Extend Wrap Rotate Sync Immediate, Next Step, Next Bar Next Step Base 1/1 … 1/32, dotted (.) and triplet (T) 1/16 Realign Never, 1, 2, 4, 8 bars Never Output Gate, Trigger Gate Gate Length Division, Base Step Division Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Sync To: what steps the module. Auto : the clock pulses while Clock is patched, otherwise the transport. Clock : only the pulses step it. Transport : the song position steps it, and a patched Clock is ignored. Inputs Input Signal What it does Clock trigger patched: each pulse is one base step Reset trigger every output starts a new cycle on the next base step Outputs Output Signal What it does Out 1 … Out 8 gate fires every d base steps, d the output's division Stair control, 0 – 1 the eight gates as a binary number / 255 Align trigger a pulse when all eight outputs start together

title: Scene Arranger
text: Scene Arranger Introduction A song-form machine for the things that choose patterns. It holds up to sixteen scenes and a play order of up to sixteen slots; each slot says which scene plays and how many times. When a scene has played out, its follow action decides what comes next: carry on down the list, go to the next or previous scene, jump to a given one, pick one at random, hold, or flip a weighted coin. The current scene leaves as a Scene CV that a pattern selector reads directly (the Drum Grid's Pattern input, for one), as a Change trigger on every new scene, and as eight Lane gates that light up for the scenes you give each lane. You can launch scenes by hand with the Launch knob, the Launch jack, Next , Previous , and have the switch wait for the next beat or bar. How does it work? Time. Unpatched, the module follows the song: one beat is a quarter note. With a trigger in Clock , each pulse is one beat. Beats per Bar (4) tells it where the bar lines are. Scene Length is how long one play of a scene lasts: 1 or 2 beats, or 1 … 16 bars. Play order. Order Steps is how many slots are used. Slot n holds a scene ( Slot n ) and how many lengths it plays ( Repeat n ). After the last slot the list starts again and Cycle sends a trigger. Scenes that are not in the list can still be reached by launching or by a follow action; a scene that is on the list plays the repeat count of its first slot, any other plays once. Follow actions. When a scene's repeats are over, its Follow decides: Order : the next slot of the play order. Next / Previous : the scene above or below (wrapping at Scenes ). Random : any other scene, chosen from Seed so renders repeat. Hold : stay on the scene until something launches another one. Jump : go to the scene in Jump . Chance : go to Jump with the probability in Chance , otherwise carry on down the list. Launching. Launch (a stepped knob, 0 = none), the Launch jack (scene = ⌊value × 16⌋ + 1, acting when it changes), Next and Previous (trigger jacks and buttons) all ask for a scene. Launch Quantize decides when it happens: Immediate , at the next Beat , or at the next Bar . While a launch waits, the Queued gate is high. A newer request replaces an older one. A launch starts a new visit: the scene plays its repeat count from that moment, counting the part of the length that is already running as the first. Restart (button) and Reset (jack) go back to slot 1. A launch made while the song is stopped decides which scene play starts on. Outputs. Scene is the number of the scene: Slot of 16 puts scene n in the middle of slot n of 16, which is exactly what a 16-pattern selector reads; Linear gives n / 15. Change is a short pulse every time a scene starts (also when the list plays the same scene twice in a row). Lane 1 … 8 : lane k is high while the scene is between Lane k From and Lane k To (From 0 turns a lane off); with Lane Output on Trigger it pulses when a scene inside its range starts. Lanes are low while the song is stopped. How to use it? Song form for a drum machine: Scene into the Drum Grid's Pattern , scenes 1 to 4 for intro, groove, fill and break. A fill every fourth round: give a scene Chance with Jump to the fill scene. Sections by lane: lane 1 on scenes 1 … 8 for the kick, lane 2 on 3 … 8 for the hats, lane 3 on 5 … 8 for the lead, each into a VCA's gain or a mixer mute. Live launching: Launch Quantize on Bar, Order Steps 1 and Follow Hold: nothing moves until you ask, and then it lands on the bar. Generative sections: every scene on Random , with Lane gates doing the arrangement. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Scene Arranger does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Scene Arranger under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Scene Arranger: Song Form The Scene output drives the Drum Grid's Pattern input: intro, groove, fill and break are four patterns, played in the order intro, groove x2, fill, groove x2, break by the arranger's play order. Change Repeat or Slot knobs to rewrite the song; the Cycle trigger marks each time round. Scene Arranger: Chance Fills Scene 2 is the groove and holds on a Chance follow action: each time round there is a one in three chance of jumping to the fill scene, otherwise it plays on. The fill always returns to the groove. Raise Chance 2 for busier fills, or change the Seed for another sequence. Scene Arranger: Lane Arrangement Four scenes of four bars bring layers in and out through the lane gates: the pad from the start, the bass from scene 2, the lead from scene 3 and the bells only in scene 4. Edit a lane's From and To to rearrange who plays when. Scene Arranger: Random Bells Six scenes that all follow Random: the arranger wanders between them and each scene's lane fires a trigger into its own bell tone, so the tune is a random walk that repeats exactly while the Seed stays put. Change the Seed for a new walk or the Scene Length for a faster one. Scene Arranger: Filter Staircase Eight scenes of one bar each, and the linear Scene output climbs a staircase that opens a low-pass filter on the arp; the Cycle trigger plays a clap when the staircase starts again. Change Scenes to shorten the climb or Follow on a scene to Previous to make it zigzag. Presets The preset bar of the Scene Arranger view has 17 factory presets. Pick one to set the knobs, then change them to taste; your own presets sit next to them. Preset What it does Four Scene Loop Scenes 1 to 4, one bar each, round and round; manual launches wait for the bar line. Verse and Chorus A song shape: two verse rounds, two chorus rounds, then a bridge and an outro. Long Form Eight scenes of four bars, every odd one twice: a 48-bar arrangement. Ping Pong Up through the scenes and back down without repeating the end scenes. Random Walk Every scene hands over to a random other one; the seed makes the walk repeatable. Drift Forward Follow action Next on every scene: the order list is ignored and the scenes simply step on. Hold the Last Plays 1, 2, 3 and settles on scene 4 until you launch something else. Chance Breakdown After scene 3 there is a one in three chance of dropping back to scene 1 instead of moving on. Stutter Back Scene 2 always falls back to 1; scene 4 flips a coin between 3 and the start. Beat Launcher Nothing moves on its own: launches from the knob, buttons or jack land on the next beat. Bar Launcher Sixteen scenes for a pattern selector, launched on the bar; the Queued gate shows what is waiting. Immediate Switch Scenes change every beat and a launch cuts in at once: for fast, hands-on switching. Phrase Lengths Eight-bar phrases, the second and fourth played twice. Lane Groups Each lane covers a range of scenes: pairs, the whole run, the middle and the centre two. Lane Triggers Lane outputs give a short trigger when their scene starts instead of holding a gate. Linear Scene CV The Scene output climbs from 0 to 1 over scenes 1 to 16: a staircase for filters and pitch. Odd Meter Bars Seven beats to the bar: scene length and launches follow the odd bar. Reference Knobs Knob Range Default Scenes 1 – 16 8 Order Steps 1 – 16 8 Launch 0 (none) – 16 0 Slot 1 … 16 scene 1 – 16 1 … 16 Repeat 1 … 16 1 – 16 1 Follow 1 … 16 Order, Next, Previous, Random, Hold, Jump, Chance Order Jump 1 … 16 scene 1 – 16 (Jump and Chance) 1 Chance 1 … 16 0 – 100 % (Chance) 50 % Lane 1 … 8 From 0 (off) – 16 1 … 8 Lane 1 … 8 To 1 – 16 1 … 8 Settings Setting Values Default Scene Length 1 beat, 2 beats, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 bars 2 bars Launch Quantize Immediate, Beat, Bar Bar Beats per Bar 1 – 16 4 Scene CV Slot of 16, Linear 0-1 Slot of 16 Lane Output Gate, Trigger Gate Seed 0 – 999 1 Sync To Auto, Clock, Transport Auto Inputs Input Signal What it does Clock trigger patched: each pulse is one beat Reset trigger back to slot 1; the next beat is beat 0 Next trigger launch the scene after the current (or queued) one Previous trigger launch the scene before it Launch control scene = ⌊value × 16⌋ + 1, launched when it changes Outputs Output Signal What it does Scene control the scene number, for pattern selectors Change trigger a scene (visit) starts Cycle trigger the play order wraps to slot 1 Queued gate a launch is waiting for its beat or bar Lane 1 … 8 gate / trigger the scene is in the lane's range

title: Transport
text: Transport Transport in the module view Introduction Transport is the control panel for the song's clock. Set the tempo, switch Ableton Link on or off, send MIDI clock to a drum machine, follow the MIDI clock of another device, and start and stop the song from the module's buttons, from cables or from incoming MIDI. Everything on the board that keeps time (sequencers, delays, LFOs) follows what Transport sets. Transport changes the clock in the standalone app . In Live the host's own transport leads, and in the browser there is none: there it still sends MIDI clock and shows the tempo, but cannot change it. How does it work? Tempo. Move Tempo to set it. With Tap , tap a few times in the beat you want. The tempo stays what you set; loading a board does not change it, so a project keeps its own tempo. With Link on, the tempo is shared with the other Link apps and devices, and they can change it too. Link. Link turns Ableton Link on or off. Playing and stopping is always shared with the other Link apps. Link needs an app built with it; without, the switch has no effect and the app runs on its own clock. MIDI clock out. With MIDI Clock Out on, Transport sends 24 pulses per beat while the song plays, plus Start when it begins at the beginning, Continue when it resumes anywhere else, and Stop. Patch MIDI Out into a MIDI Out module. MIDI clock in. With MIDI Clock In on, patch a MIDI In or MIDI Device module's Notes into MIDI In . Transport measures the incoming clock and sets the tempo from it; it settles after about a beat and follows changes within a bar. Start, Continue and Stop from the device start and stop your song. This sets the tempo, but does not line up the beats exactly: for that, use Link. Play and Stop. The Play button starts a stopped song and lights up while it plays; the Stop button stops it. A trigger in Play starts a stopped song from the beginning, a trigger in Stop stops it. Patch a Button or a pad to either. How to use it? Tempo on a knob: put a Dial on the Tempo knob's input (or play with the knob itself). Drum machine follows you: MIDI Clock Out on, MIDI Out → MIDI Out (the drum machine's port). Start your song and the machine starts with it. You follow the drum machine: MIDI Clock In on, its MIDI Device's Notes → MIDI In . Press play on the machine. Tap tempo: press Tap to the beat, four times or more. Footswitch: a MIDI Device's gate or a Button into Play and Stop . A lamp that shows the song runs: Playing into a Level Meter or a light. Tempo-linked effects: Tempo into a control input (BPM / 100: 120 BPM is 1.2). Do not connect the module's MIDI Out back into its own MIDI In with both clock settings on: that makes a loop. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Transport does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Transport under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Transport: Playing Gate Pad The Transport's Playing output is high whenever the song runs, and here it opens an envelope that slowly fades in a warm pad under a beat, then lets it ring out when you press Stop. Move the Tempo knob to change the speed of everything, or press Stop and Play to hear the pad breathe in and out. Transport: Tempo Brightness The Tempo output carries the speed as a control value (BPM divided by 100) and here it also sets the cutoff of a filter on an arpeggio, so a faster song is automatically a brighter one. Drag the Tempo knob up and down and listen to the tone follow the speed. Transport: Tempo Ride A very slow LFO is patched into the Tempo knob, so the whole song speeds up and slows down by a few BPM over about a minute like a band pushing and pulling. Lower the cable amount on the LFO, or unpatch it to hold the tempo steady. Transport: MIDI Clock Out Groove MIDI Clock Out is switched on, so while this groove plays the Transport also sends clock, start and stop to a connected MIDI Out, keeping outboard gear in time with it. You will hear a driving bass line over a four-on-the-floor kick; use Tap to set the tempo. Transport: Link Session Arp Link is switched on, so this song shares its tempo and start with any other Link-enabled app on the network, while a dreamy arpeggio and a soft beat play. Turn Link off to go solo, or use MIDI Clock In to follow a drum machine instead. Reference Knobs, settings and buttons Control Range Default Tempo 20 … 400 BPM 120 Link Off, On On MIDI Clock In Off, On Off MIDI Clock Out Off, On Off Play button Stop button Tap button If the board also has a Link node, its Start/Stop Sync setting decides. Inputs Input Signal What it does Play trigger Starts the song from the beginning Stop trigger Stops the song MIDI In notes The MIDI clock to follow (MIDI Clock In) Outputs Output Signal What it does MIDI Out notes MIDI clock, Start, Continue and Stop (MIDI Clock Out) Playing gate High while the song runs Tempo control The tempo in BPM divided by 100 (120 BPM is 1.2)

title: Ring Clap
text: Ring Clap Ring Clap in the module view Introduction A hand clap: band-passed noise opened by a few quick bursts, as if several people clapped a few milliseconds apart, then a short diffuse tail like a small room. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Each hit fires Bursts short bursts of noise, Spread apart. Every burst snaps open and fades before the next one. The last burst also starts the tail, which fades over Decay . The noise passes through a band-pass filter centred on Tone , which gives the clap its pitch. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds starts the bursts again. How to use it? Clap on the backbeat: with or instead of a snare, on beats 2 and 4. Tighter clap: fewer Bursts , smaller Spread . Big, loose clap: 5 or 6 Bursts , Spread around 20 ms, longer Decay . Snap: 1 burst, Tone around 2.5 kHz, short Decay . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tone 500 Hz – 4 kHz 1.1 kHz Decay 50 ms – 1.5 s 300 ms Spread 3 – 30 ms 11 ms Bursts 1 – 6 4 Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tone: the centre of the band-pass: the clap's pitch. Decay: how long the tail lasts. Spread: the time between bursts. Bursts: how many bursts play before the tail. A setting, not a knob. Level: the output volume. Tone , Decay , Spread and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Cowbell
text: Ring Cowbell Ring Cowbell in the module view Introduction A cowbell: two square waves, a fifth-ish apart, through a band-pass filter, with a sharp initial hit and a softer tail. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Two square-wave oscillators run at an inharmonic interval. A band-pass filter, set by Tone , picks out the clang. The envelope has two parts: a loud hit that fades in a few tens of milliseconds, and a quieter tail that lasts Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts both parts of the envelope. How to use it? Accent pattern: a few syncopated hits per bar. Darker bell: Tone low, Tune down a few semitones. Melodic cowbell: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune at 50 % amount. Tune spans 24 semitones, so the bell follows the notes in tune. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 50 ms – 2 s 400 ms Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: how long the tail lasts. Tone: the band-pass centre: dark … bright. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Cymbal
text: Ring Cymbal Ring Cymbal in the module view Introduction A cymbal from the same six square waves as Ring Hats, split into two bands: a low clang that fades first and a long, high sizzle. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? The metallic source is split by a band-pass (the low clang) and a high-pass (the sizzle). The sizzle lasts Decay ; the clang lasts less than half of that. Tone balances the two bands. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts both bands. How to use it? Crash on the one: the first beat of a new section, Decay 2 – 4 s. Ride-like pattern: quarter notes, Decay around 1 s, Tone high. Gong-ish: Tune down 12 semitones, Tone low, Decay at maximum. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 300 ms – 8 s 2 s Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: how long the sizzle lasts; the clang dies sooner. Tone: the balance of the two bands: clang … sizzle. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Drums
text: Ring Drums Introduction The Ring drums are a drum kit, one node per instrument. They are built the way the classic analog drum machines of the early eighties built their sounds: resonators that are struck and ring away, band-passed noise, and six detuned square waves for everything metallic. The result is deep, round and a little soft: long booming kicks, ringing toms, gentle hats. For a tighter, harder kit, see the Punch drums. The voices Node What it is Main controls Ring Kick a struck resonator, from tight to booming Tune, Decay, Sweep, Tone, Drive Ring Snare two ringing heads and a burst of noise Tune, Tone, Snappy, Decay Ring Clap quick bursts of noise and a short tail Tone, Decay, Spread, Bursts Ring Tom a ringing tone that falls in pitch; also hand drums Tune, Decay, Bend, Noise Ring Rim rim shot or clave Voice, Tune, Decay Ring Cowbell two squares through a band-pass Tune, Decay, Tone Ring Hats closed and open hats; closed cuts open Tune, Closed Decay, Open Decay, Tone Ring Cymbal a low clang and a long sizzle Tune, Decay, Tone Each node has its own manual behind the ? button in its window. How does it work? Every Ring drum works the same from the outside: A rising edge at Trig plays it (Ring Hats has two inputs, Closed and Open ). Triggers and gates both work. Velocity , when patched, sets the loudness of each hit, read at the moment of the trigger. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes the loudness only, not the sound. Level sets the output volume. It starts at 80 %, so a few drums mixed together leave some headroom. Out is mono audio. Every knob is a modulation destination, as everywhere on the board. How to use it? A basic beat: a Step Sequencer per drum, each one's Trigger into a drum's Trig and its Velocity into the drum's Velocity . Patch every drum's Out into the same Audio Out port: cables into one jack add up. Hats with a choke: two sequencer patterns into Ring Hats' Closed and Open ; the closed hits cut the open ones. A drum kit as one node: select the drums and their sequencers and group them into a cell, with a single audio output. Bass kick: a long Ring Kick, with a sequencer's Pitch on Tune at 50 % amount. Effects: run a drum through a Multi Filter, or patch a Random onto a knob, for drums that change on every hit. Reference Inputs (every Ring drum) Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the drum (Ring Hats: Closed and Open ) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs (every Ring drum) Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum, mono

title: Ring Hats
text: Ring Hats Ring Hats in the module view Introduction Closed and open hi-hats in one node. The sound comes from six square waves at inharmonic frequencies, a dense metallic clang, filtered down to its top. A closed hit cuts a ringing open hat short, like a real hi-hat pedal. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Six square-wave oscillators sum to a metallic tone. A band-pass and a high-pass keep only its bright top; Tone moves the high-pass up for a thinner, crisper hat. Closed and Open share one envelope: each hit starts it with its own decay ( Closed Decay or Open Decay ), so a closed hit chokes an open one. Playing it. A rising edge at Closed or Open plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts the envelope with the decay of the input that was hit. How to use it? Eighth-note hats: a sequencer's Trigger into Closed . Open hat on the offbeat: a second pattern into Open ; the next closed hit cuts it. Shaker: short Closed Decay (around 20 ms), Tone high, sixteenth notes with varied velocity. Trashy hats: Tune down 5 – 12 semitones. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Closed Decay 10 – 300 ms 60 ms Open Decay 50 ms – 3 s 500 ms Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Closed Decay: how long a closed hit lasts. Open Decay: how long an open hit lasts. Tone: the high-pass: full … thin. Level: the output volume. Tune , Closed Decay , Open Decay , Tone and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Closed trigger plays the closed hat Open trigger plays the open hat; a closed hit cuts it short Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Kick
text: Ring Kick Ring Kick in the module view Introduction A deep, round bass drum. A resonator is struck and rings at Tune , dying away over Decay : short and tight, or a long booming tone you can play bass lines with. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? The body is a resonator, a circuit that rings like a bell when struck. Each hit starts the ring with a soft, rounded attack. Sweep starts the pitch higher and lets it settle onto Tune within the first few tens of milliseconds, for more punch. Tone adds the click of the strike itself, a short thump on top of the body; higher values make it louder and brighter. Drive saturates the whole sound, from warm to distorted. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing, like hitting a real drum twice. How to use it? Classic kick: the defaults on every beat (a Step Sequencer's Trigger into Trig ). Long bass kick: Decay at 1.5 s or more, Drive around 30 %. To play bass lines, patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune at 50 % amount: Tune spans two octaves, so the kick then follows the notes in tune. Tight kick: Decay around 200 ms, Tone up for more click. Accents: patch the sequencer's Velocity into Velocity . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 30 – 120 Hz 50 Hz Decay 50 ms – 3 s 800 ms Sweep 0 – 100 % 30 % Tone 0 – 100 % 30 % Drive 0 – 100 % 0 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the body rings at. Decay: how long the body rings (until it has fallen by 60 dB). Sweep: how far above Tune the pitch starts. At 100 % it starts 2.5 times higher. Tone: the click of the strike: louder and brighter as you turn it up. Drive: saturation, from clean to heavily distorted. The peak level stays the same. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Sweep , Tone , Drive and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Rim
text: Ring Rim Ring Rim in the module view Introduction Short, high, woody clicks: a rim shot (the stick hitting the rim of a snare) or a clave (two hardwood sticks). It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Rim strikes two high resonators at once and passes them through a high-pass and a little saturation, for a sharp crack. Clave is one resonator, higher and purer, that rings a little longer. Decay multiplies each voice's own ringing time, from a quarter to four times as long. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Rim on the offbeats: a light, ticking pulse that leaves room for a snare. Clave pattern: Voice Clave, on a syncopated pattern. Wood block: Clave tuned down 7 – 12 semitones, Decay around 2×. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Voice Rim, Clave Rim Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 0.25 – 4 × 1 × Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Voice: which sound plays. A setting, not a knob. Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: multiplies how long the voice rings. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Snare
text: Ring Snare Ring Snare in the module view Introduction A snare drum: two ringing drum heads for the body, and a burst of bright noise for the snare wires. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? Two resonators ring at Tune and a little below twice Tune , like the low and high modes of a drum head. Tone blends between them: low and full, or high and ringing. White noise, high-passed so it doesn't muddy the body, plays at the same time; Snappy sets its level and Decay how long it lasts. The body rings for about half of Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts the noise and adds to the ringing heads. How to use it? Backbeat: the defaults on beats 2 and 4. Tight, dry snare: Decay around 120 ms, Snappy 40 %. Rattly, bright snare: Snappy at 100 %, Tone high. Ghost notes: low velocities between the main hits. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 100 – 400 Hz 180 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Snappy 0 – 100 % 60 % Decay 50 ms – 1 s 250 ms Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch of the lower head; the higher one follows. Tone: the balance of the two heads, low … high. Snappy: the level of the noise (the snare wires). Decay: how long the noise lasts; the body rings for about half as long. Level: the output volume. Tune , Tone , Snappy , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Ring Tom
text: Ring Tom Ring Tom in the module view Introduction A tom or hand drum: a ringing tone that falls slightly in pitch as it dies away, with a little noise for the skin. With Noise at 0 it becomes a pure, conga-like tone. It belongs to the Ring drums: deep, round voices built from struck resonators, noise and detuned square waves. How does it work? A resonator rings at Tune . Bend starts the pitch above Tune and lets it fall back over the whole note, the way a drum head's pitch falls as it loses tension. Low-passed noise adds the sound of the stick on the skin; it fades in less than half the time of the tone. Use several Ring Tom nodes, tuned apart, for a set of toms. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Tom fills: three Ring Toms at about 100, 140 and 200 Hz, played by the last steps of a sequence. Hand drums: Noise at 0, Decay around 200 ms, Tune 200 – 400 Hz. Melodic toms: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune and adjust the cable's amount until the intervals sound right. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 50 – 600 Hz 140 Hz Decay 50 ms – 2 s 400 ms Bend 0 – 100 % 30 % Noise 0 – 100 % 30 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the tom settles on. Decay: how long the tom rings. Bend: how far above Tune the pitch starts; at 100 % it starts 50 % higher. Noise: the level of the skin noise. 0 % is a pure tone. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Bend , Noise and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Clap
text: Punch Clap Punch Clap in the module view Introduction A bright, roomy hand clap: tight bursts of noise and a louder tail than Ring Clap. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit fires Bursts short bursts of noise, Spread apart; the last one starts the tail, which fades over Decay . The noise passes through a wide band-pass centred on Tone and a high-pass, for a bright, open clap. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds starts the bursts again. How to use it? Clap on the backbeat: layered with Punch Snare, or on its own. Big room clap: Decay 600 ms or more. Tight clap: 2 – 3 Bursts , Spread around 5 ms. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tone 500 Hz – 4 kHz 1.5 kHz Decay 50 ms – 1.5 s 350 ms Spread 3 – 30 ms 8 ms Bursts 1 – 6 4 Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tone: the centre of the band-pass. Decay: how long the tail lasts. Spread: the time between bursts. Bursts: how many bursts play before the tail. A setting, not a knob. Level: the output volume. Tone , Decay , Spread and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Cymbal
text: Punch Cymbal Punch Cymbal in the module view Introduction A crash or a ride cymbal: bright, slightly crunchy metal with a long decay. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Crash mixes six square waves with plenty of noise, high-passed, with an extra burst of energy at the start that settles into a wash lasting Decay . Ride uses a different set of square waves, less noise, and a band-passed bell tone on top, for a ping you can play in patterns; it rings 1.5 × Decay . Tone moves the high-pass, Crunch adds grit as in Punch Hats. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Crash on the one: Voice Crash on the first beat of a section. Ride pattern: Voice Ride, quarter or eighth notes, varied velocity. Reverse-style swell: patch a rising envelope onto Level . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Voice Crash, Ride Crash Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 300 ms – 8 s 2 s Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Crunch 0 – 100 % 30 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Voice: which cymbal plays. A setting, not a knob. Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: how long the cymbal lasts (the ride rings 1.5 × as long). Tone: the high-pass: full … thin. Crunch: bit and sample-rate reduction: clean … gritty. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Tone , Crunch and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Drums
text: Punch Drums Introduction The Punch drums are a drum kit, one node per instrument. They are built the way the drum machines of the mid eighties built their sounds: sine waves that restart on every hit and sweep down fast, with a click of noise on top, and bright metal for the hats and cymbals, with an optional crunch like the early samplers those machines used. The result is tight, hard and forward: a kick that punches through, a snappy snare, crisp hats. For a deeper, rounder kit, see the Ring drums. The voices Node What it is Main controls Punch Kick a sine that sweeps down fast, with a click Tune, Decay, Sweep, Attack, Drive Punch Snare two swept sines and filtered noise Tune, Tone, Snappy, Decay Punch Clap tight bursts of noise and a roomy tail Tone, Decay, Spread, Bursts Punch Tom a sine that drops in pitch, with a touch of noise Tune, Decay, Bend, Noise Punch Rim a hard, bright crack Tune, Decay Punch Hats closed and open hats; closed cuts open Tune, Closed Decay, Open Decay, Tone, Crunch Punch Cymbal crash or ride Voice, Tune, Decay, Tone, Crunch Each node has its own manual behind the ? button in its window. How does it work? Every Punch drum works the same from the outside: A rising edge at Trig plays it (Punch Hats has two inputs, Closed and Open ). Triggers and gates both work. Velocity , when patched, sets the loudness of each hit, read at the moment of the trigger. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes the loudness only, not the sound. Level sets the output volume. It starts at 80 %, so a few drums mixed together leave some headroom. Out is mono audio. Crunch (hats and cymbals) lowers the bit depth and sample rate of the metal, for the gritty sheen of an early sampler. At 0 % it's clean. Every knob is a modulation destination, as everywhere on the board. How to use it? A basic beat: a Step Sequencer per drum, each one's Trigger into a drum's Trig and its Velocity into the drum's Velocity . Patch every drum's Out into the same Audio Out port: cables into one jack add up. Four on the floor: Punch Kick on every beat, Punch Clap on 2 and 4, Punch Hats Open on the offbeats and Closed on the sixteenths. A drum kit as one node: select the drums and their sequencers and group them into a cell, with a single audio output. Mix the kits: Ring and Punch drums share the same jacks; a Punch Kick with Ring Hats is just as easy. Reference Inputs (every Punch drum) Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the drum (Punch Hats: Closed and Open ) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs (every Punch drum) Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum, mono

title: Punch Hats
text: Punch Hats Punch Hats in the module view Introduction Bright, crunchy closed and open hi-hats in one node, with the slightly gritty sheen of the early samplers that drum machines of the eighties used for their cymbals. A closed hit cuts a ringing open hat short. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Six square waves at inharmonic frequencies are mixed with white noise and high-passed; Tone moves the high-pass up for a thinner hat. Crunch lowers the bit depth and sample rate of the sound before the envelope, for grit; at 0 % it's clean. Closed and Open share one envelope, each with its own decay, so a closed hit chokes an open one. Playing it. A rising edge at Closed or Open plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts the envelope with the decay of the input that was hit. How to use it? Sixteenth hats: a sequencer's Trigger into Closed , with velocity on Velocity for groove. Offbeat open hat: a second pattern into Open . Clean, modern hats: Crunch 0, Tone high. Dirty hats: Crunch 100 %. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Closed Decay 10 – 300 ms 50 ms Open Decay 50 ms – 3 s 400 ms Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Crunch 0 – 100 % 40 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Closed Decay: how long a closed hit lasts. Open Decay: how long an open hit lasts. Tone: the high-pass: full … thin. Crunch: bit and sample-rate reduction: clean … gritty. Level: the output volume. Tune , Closed Decay , Open Decay , Tone , Crunch and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Closed trigger plays the closed hat Open trigger plays the open hat; a closed hit cuts it short Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Kick
text: Punch Kick Punch Kick in the module view Introduction A hard, tight bass drum: a sine wave that starts high and sweeps down fast onto Tune , with a click of noise on top. It cuts through a busy mix. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit restarts a sine oscillator at the top of its cycle and drops its pitch from far above Tune : a very fast fall in the first few milliseconds, then a slower settle. Sweep sets how far it falls. Attack adds a short burst of noise and a thump, the beater hitting the skin. The body fades over Decay . Drive saturates the sound, rounding the sine toward a square for a harder, louder kick. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it; the previous hit is cut off. How to use it? Four on the floor: the defaults on every beat. Long, booming kick: Decay 1 s or more, Drive up. Soft, round kick: Sweep and Attack low, Drive 0. Accents: patch the sequencer's Velocity into Velocity . Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 30 – 120 Hz 50 Hz Decay 50 ms – 2.5 s 600 ms Sweep 0 – 100 % 50 % Attack 0 – 100 % 50 % Drive 0 – 100 % 30 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the kick settles on. Decay: how long the body lasts. Sweep: how far the pitch falls at the start. At 100 % it starts more than six times higher. Attack: the level of the click. Drive: saturation. The peak level stays the same. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Sweep , Attack , Drive and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Rim
text: Punch Rim Punch Rim in the module view Introduction A rim shot: a hard, bright crack, shorter and more metallic than Ring Rim. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Three high resonators are struck at once, together with a tiny burst of noise. A high-pass and saturation turn them into a sharp crack. Decay multiplies how long they ring. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds adds to the ringing. How to use it? Rim accents: sparse hits between snare and hats. Stick click: Decay at 0.25 ×, Tune up. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune −12 … +12 st 0 st Decay 0.25 – 4 × 1 × Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: shifts the whole voice up or down, in semitones. Decay: multiplies how long the voice rings. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Snare
text: Punch Snare Punch Snare in the module view Introduction A snare with a hard, forward body: two sine waves that drop slightly in pitch, and filtered noise for the snare wires. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Two sine oscillators, at Tune and about 1.6 × Tune , restart on each hit and fall a little in pitch, then fade quickly. White noise passes through a low-pass, set by Tone , and a high-pass that keeps it out of the body; Snappy sets its level and Decay its length. Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Backbeat: the defaults on beats 2 and 4. Crisp snare: Tone high, Snappy 80 %, Decay around 200 ms. Fat snare: Tune low, Decay 500 ms. Rolls: fast hits with rising velocity. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 120 – 400 Hz 200 Hz Tone 0 – 100 % 50 % Snappy 0 – 100 % 60 % Decay 50 ms – 1 s 300 ms Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch of the body. Tone: the brightness of the noise (its low-pass). Snappy: the level of the noise. Decay: how long the noise lasts. Level: the output volume. Tune , Tone , Snappy , Decay and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Punch Tom
text: Punch Tom Punch Tom in the module view Introduction A tom: a sine wave that starts above its pitch and drops onto it, with a touch of noise. Punchier than Ring Tom, with a clear pitch drop. It belongs to the Punch drums: tight, hard voices built from swept sine waves, noise and crunchy metal. How does it work? Each hit restarts a sine oscillator. Its pitch starts above Tune and falls: quickly at first, then slowly over the whole note. Bend sets how far. A short burst of low-passed noise adds the stick; Noise sets its level. The tone fades over Decay . Playing it. A rising edge at Trig plays the voice. Velocity , when patched, is read at that moment: 100 % is full volume, 50 % half volume. Unpatched, every hit is at full velocity. Velocity changes only the loudness, never the sound, so soft hits keep their character. Hitting again while the voice still sounds restarts it. How to use it? Tom fills: three Punch Toms at about 90, 120 and 170 Hz. Electronic toms: Bend at 100 %, Decay long, Noise 0. Melodic toms: patch a sequencer's Pitch onto Tune and adjust the cable's amount until the intervals sound right. Reference Knobs and settings Control Range Default Tune 50 – 500 Hz 110 Hz Decay 50 ms – 2 s 450 ms Bend 0 – 100 % 50 % Noise 0 – 100 % 20 % Level 0 – 100 % 80 % Tune: the pitch the tom settles on. Decay: how long the tom lasts. Bend: how far the pitch drops; at 100 % it starts about twice as high. Noise: the level of the stick noise. Level: the output volume. Tune , Decay , Bend , Noise and Level are modulation destinations. Inputs Input Signal What it does Trig trigger a rising edge plays the voice (gates work too) Velocity control, 0 … 1 the loudness of each hit, read at the trigger; unpatched = 100 % Outputs Output Signal What it does Out audio the drum

title: Recorder
text: Recorder Introduction Recorder bounces what you play to a file. Arm it, play, and the take starts by itself when the sound begins; a short pre-roll catches the attack that crossed the threshold. When the take ends it is saved as a stereo WAV file in the media folder, and a button shows you the file. The audio passes through, so the Recorder can sit at the end of a patch, or in the middle of it to catch one voice. How does it work? Starting. Press Arm : the Recorder listens. With Armed Start on On Signal the take begins when the input passes Signal Level , and Pre-roll seconds from before that moment are included. With By Hand press Record . A Gate cable can start and stop takes too (set Gate Input to Starts and Ends ): the take lasts as long as the gate is high. Record works from any state and starts at once. Stopping. Stop , the end of the gate, or the Length Limit ; whichever comes first. The Recording output is high during a take and Done pulses at its end; Progress shows how much of the limit is used, which is handy for a patch that should do something at the end of a take. Saving. The take lives in memory until you save it. With Save When Done on, the view saves it as soon as the take ends; for that the Recorder's view has to be open. Otherwise press Save Take . The file is a 32-bit float WAV in the media folder (on a Mac under Music / Beautiful Bleep / Media); Show File opens that folder with the file selected. Saving the same sound twice makes one file. A new take replaces the old one in memory (the saved files stay). Memory. The Recorder reserves room for two minutes of stereo audio when it is created. A Voice Cell should not contain one. How to use it? Catch an idea: Arm, play; the take starts with your first note. Press Stop, then Show File and drag the file into your session. Bounce a pattern: a pattern's gate into Gate with Starts and Ends ; every run of the pattern is a take. Take and loop: Done into a Sampler's trigger, with the saved file loaded into it. A fixed length: Length Limit 10 s and Armed Start By Hand: Record takes exactly ten seconds. Demo patches Five whole patches show what Recorder does. In the standalone app open File → Presets… (⌘P) and pick Recorder under Demos by module ; on the website, Run in Play opens one in your browser. Loading one replaces the project and starts the transport. Patch What it shows Recorder: A Take per Phrase A gate pattern starts a take at the start of each phrase and ends it when the phrase ends (Gate Input is Starts and Ends); a rim click answers each finished take. Each new take replaces the last one in the Recorder's view. Change Pre-roll to catch the notes before the gate. Recorder: Recording Lamp and Whistle While a take runs, the Recording gate sounds a steady tone and Progress raises the pitch of a whistle as the take fills toward its 10 s limit. The takes are started by a gate pattern every few bars. Change Length Limit to 30 s and the whistle rises more slowly. Recorder: Armed, Waiting for Sound After a bar of nothing a melody begins and the band joins later. Press Arm and the take starts by itself on the first note, with a half second of pre-roll, and a soft bell marks Done when you press Stop. Raise Signal Level to wait for a louder moment. Recorder: Bounce a Four Bar Loop A gate that stays high for four bars records exactly one loop of the band into a take, then a crash rings out when the Done trigger fires. The loop repeats every eight bars with the take replaced each time. Press Show File after the first take to see the WAV. Recorder: Ten Second Sweep A pad's filter opens as Progress climbs to the 10 s limit of a gate-started take; at the limit Done fires a kick and the take ends even though the gate is still high. Choose a longer Length Limit and the sweep slows down. Reference Settings Setting Values Default Length Limit 10 s, 30 s, 60 s, 90 s, 2 min 30 s Armed Start By Hand, On Signal On Signal Signal Level −60 … −6 dB −36 dB Pre-roll 0 – 2 s 0.25 s Gate Input Ignored, Starts and Ends Ignored Save When Done off, on on Buttons: Arm , Record , Stop , Clear . Inputs Input Signal What it does In L, In R audio what is recorded (R unpatched: L to both) Gate gate starts and ends takes with Gate Input on Outputs Output Signal What it does Out L, Out R audio the inputs, unchanged Recording gate high during a take Done trigger a pulse when a take ends Progress control how much of the limit the take fills
